ILAIOS minimizes standing privilege and uses task-specific authority for governed execution. Role, group, or organizational membership establishes potential eligibility; it does not by itself grant permission to perform a material operation.

Execution authority is represented through constrained capabilities or an equivalent explicit authorization construct. The authority binds the tenant, task, subject or workload, approved action, resource and target, Tool Gateway operation, parameter boundaries, environment, validity window, usage limits, policy decision, risk treatment, approval where required, and revocation state.

Capabilities are attenuable, non-transferable unless controlled delegation is explicitly permitted, time-bound, observable, and revocable. They do not contain reusable enterprise secrets. A capability for one tool, repository, environment, destination, or operation cannot be reused for another. A capability issued for a plan digest or Immutable Context version becomes invalid when the bound material state changes.

The consumer of a capability validates it at the point of use. Possession alone is insufficient when the capability is expired, revoked, already consumed, replayed, presented by the wrong workload, used from the wrong tenant or environment, or inconsistent with the requested parameters. Denial and attempted misuse are material audit events.

Administrative privileges follow the same principle. Routine operations use ordinary bounded roles. Elevated privileges are issued just in time for an approved purpose and terminated immediately after the approved period or task.

### Continuous Verification and Adaptive Enforcement

Security evaluation continues after authentication and initial authorization. ILAIOS re-evaluates trust when a material event occurs, including context change, privilege change, device posture degradation, workload replacement, policy publication, risk escalation, capability use, approval expiry, anomalous behavior, target change, data reclassification, integration state change, evidence failure, or incident declaration.

Continuous verification does not require every component to repeat every check continuously. It requires authoritative security state to have defined freshness and revocation semantics, material changes to propagate to enforcement points, and sensitive operations to revalidate current authority before use.

The possible enforcement outcomes include continue, reduce scope, require renewed authentication, require additional approval, issue a new capability, suspend, quarantine, revoke, deny, terminate execution, or initiate incident handling. Adaptive treatment is policy-governed and evidence-bearing. A risk signal may increase controls, but it cannot silently relax a mandatory control.

Long-lived sessions, connections, workers, approvals, and capabilities require explicit renewal and maximum lifetime. Heartbeat or activity alone does not extend authority. Reconnection, process restart, deployment failover, or device resumption does not automatically restore prior privilege without required revalidation.

### Network and Service-to-Service Zero Trust

Network segmentation, private routing, ingress protection, egress control, service isolation, and encrypted channels are defense-in-depth controls. They reduce exposure but do not create trust. A request arriving from an internal address, trusted subnet, private connection, cluster, host, or administrative network remains subject to authenticated identity, request integrity, tenant, service policy, and resource authorization.

Every service-to-service interaction uses an authenticated workload identity and an explicitly permitted caller-to-operation relationship. Services reject requests with an invalid audience, tenant mismatch, unsupported protocol or schema, expired authorization, missing correlation, or unexpected caller. General network reachability does not imply application permission.

East-west communication is minimized. Components expose narrow interfaces and do not provide unrestricted database, filesystem, queue, administrative, or debugging access to adjacent services. Direct data-store access is limited to the component or controlled data service that owns the authoritative state.

Egress is governed by destination, purpose, data classification, tenant, integration, tool, and capability. Restricted workers and analyzers cannot access arbitrary external destinations merely because the hosting environment has network connectivity. Domain, address, or route allowlisting may support enforcement but does not replace destination identity and policy.

### Intelligence and Model Boundary

The AI & Intelligence Layer is an untrusted analytical capability from the perspective of authorization and execution. Its output may be useful, structured, high-confidence, or generated by an approved provider, but it remains a proposal or recommendation. It has no direct path to policy publication, capability issuance, human-approval mutation, Tool Gateway dispatch, execution credentials, validation acceptance, delivery, or Trust Core history rewriting.

The Model Gateway applies the Zero Trust boundary to every intelligence invocation. It verifies the task and tenant, selects a permitted processing path, minimizes data, enforces classification and residency, binds request and response provenance, applies schemas, and returns the output to the Control Plane for deterministic evaluation.

Model and provider replaceability is preserved. No provider receives implicit trust because of commercial relationship, deployment location, model quality, or prior success. Provider eligibility is evaluated for the applicable data, tenant, purpose, region, retention rule, and contract. Fallback routing cannot use a less protective path.

Prompts, retrieved context, repository comments, uploaded documents, tool results, and model output are untrusted content. Embedded instructions cannot override policy, change tenant, request secrets, broaden tool authority, suppress validation, or redefine the acceptance criteria. Content-origin and instruction-authority boundaries shall remain explicit.

### Tool Gateway and Restricted Execution

The Tool Gateway is the exclusive governed boundary for supported tool invocation. It revalidates the active capability, tenant, task, tool, operation, target, parameters, path or resource boundary, time, usage limits, data classification, and required control state before dispatch.

Tool registration does not make every operation permissible. Each adapter exposes a narrow contract describing operations, input and output schemas, side effects, credential needs, idempotency, cancellation, compensation, evidence, and error semantics. Unknown tools, unregistered operations, path escape, target drift, parameter expansion, expired authority, and direct invocation attempts are denied.

Execution occurs in a restricted environment with only the approved filesystem, network, process, tool, credential, duration, and resource access. Workers cannot inherit unrestricted ambient credentials or host privileges. They cannot authorize themselves, alter policy, modify approval, broaden capability, accept their own result, or write trusted audit history directly.

Execution completion is not evidence of correctness. Outputs are treated as untrusted until the independent Validation Pipeline evaluates the integrity-bound result. High-risk or irreversible operations may require preconditions, dry-run or preview where appropriate, explicit human approval, stronger isolation, additional validation, staged execution, or compensation capability.

### Device-Bound and Endpoint Access

Where ILAIOS uses a device-bound companion or local execution component, the endpoint is treated as a separate trust boundary. Device ownership or enterprise enrollment does not make local files, processes, credentials, network access, or user input universally trusted.

Device-bound access verifies the user, device registration, local component identity, session binding, requested resource, tenant, and capability. The local component receives only the approved task scope and cannot browse unrelated files, use standing credentials, access other users' data, or continue after capability expiry.

Device posture may inform policy and risk where the deployment supports reliable posture evidence. Posture signals have defined source, freshness, and assurance. Missing or stale posture does not become a passing result. A compromised or non-conformant device may be restricted to low-risk operations, require remediation or step-up approval, or be denied.

Local execution produces the same material audit and evidence obligations as hosted execution. Offline operation, where supported, requires bounded pre-issued authority, protected local state, expiry, replay protection, deferred evidence delivery, and fail-closed behavior when required evidence cannot be preserved.

### Data-Centric Zero Trust

Data access is governed independently from network and application access. Every material data object is associated with tenant, classification, purpose, authoritative source, integrity or version where material, retention, residency, and permitted processing paths.

Components receive the minimum data needed for their responsibility. The intelligence layer receives a minimized reasoning projection. Approvers receive the review projection necessary for an informed decision. Workers receive task-specific inputs. Validators receive read-only integrity-bound subjects. Audit events contain references and classifications rather than unnecessary sensitive payloads.

Data transformation does not erase security obligations. Derived artifacts, embeddings, indexes, summaries, exports, caches, temporary files, validation results, and backups inherit applicable tenant, classification, purpose, residency, retention, and disclosure controls. Aggregation or pseudonymization does not automatically remove sensitivity.

Data movement between regions, providers, execution environments, tenants, or external destinations requires explicit eligibility. If the required secure path is unavailable, the operation is denied or suspended; convenience does not authorize alternate processing.

### Repository, Software Supply Chain, and Build Trust

Repositories, packages, build inputs, generated code, dependencies, manifests, and toolchains are untrusted until verified according to their role. A repository hosted by the enterprise or previously analyzed by ILAIOS may still contain malicious or altered content.

Repository-scoped work is bound to the verified root, origin or source identity, branch or source reference, immutable baseline, and working-state treatment defined by the Immutable Context. Path escape, unexpected origin, baseline drift, unapproved submodule, symbolic-link escape, or unverified overlay prevents the repository from being treated as the intended subject.

Code Intelligence uses constrained static analysis by default and does not execute repository-supplied content. Build scripts, package lifecycle hooks, macros, tests, binaries, and generated commands require a separately authorized Tool Gateway execution in an isolated environment.

Software changes and produced artifacts remain untrusted until validation. Provenance, dependency state, source digest, build context, test results, security checks, and artifact digest support assurance. A trusted contributor, signed commit, approved repository, or passing build is valuable evidence but does not eliminate independent policy and validation obligations.

### Human Approval and Accountability

Human approval is a controlled security decision, not a ceremonial confirmation. Where policy or risk requires approval, the approver receives sufficient context to understand the exact request, proposed action, target, capabilities, data, risk, side effects, reversibility, validation plan, and expiry.

Approval is bound to the reviewed Immutable Context, plan or action digest, target, capability scope, risk class, and validity period. A materially changed proposal or context invalidates the approval. Silence, inactivity, a prior similar approval, requester seniority, or user-interface convenience is not approval.

Separation of duties may prevent the requester, proposer, executor, validator, or administrator from approving the same high-risk action. Approvers receive only the authority assigned to their role and tenant. They cannot approve a capability prohibited by policy or broaden the scope beyond the reviewed request.

Emergency approval remains governed. It requires a defined emergency condition, named authority, narrower scope, shorter validity, stronger audit, mandatory follow-up review, and immediate termination when the emergency ends.

### Administrative and Break-Glass Access

Administrative access is a high-risk Zero Trust path. It uses named identities, stronger authentication, just-in-time and purpose-bound privilege, explicit scope, short duration, separation of duties, session protection, complete audit, and review. Administrative access must not be hidden in ordinary service credentials or shared accounts.

Break-glass access is permitted only for documented conditions where normal controls cannot satisfy urgent safety, security, or continuity requirements. It is not a general bypass mechanism. Activation requires the strongest available identity verification, an explicit reason, bounded scope, limited time, notification, evidence preservation, and post-event review.

Break-glass authority cannot erase audit history, disable Evidence Chain integrity, create unrestricted cross-tenant access, or permanently weaken policy. Where immediate dual approval is impossible, the policy must define compensating controls and mandatory retrospective review.

Support access follows the same model. Customer-support purpose does not imply unrestricted tenant-data access. Access is tenant-bound, time-bound, minimized, approved where contract or policy requires, and auditable.

### Third-Party and Integration Trust

External integrations are independent trust domains. Contractual approval, marketplace listing, vendor reputation, or prior successful operation does not establish continuing technical trust. Each integration has a registered identity, tenant relationship, permitted operations, data classifications, destinations, credential method, rate and resource limits, failure behavior, retention obligations, and termination process.

Inbound integration requests pass through the Secure Access Gateway or an equivalent governed boundary. Outbound interactions pass through the Tool Gateway or another explicitly controlled interface. Integrations do not receive direct access to internal policy state, unrestricted tenant data, Trust Core storage, or execution credentials.

Webhook endpoints, asynchronous callbacks, external transaction results, and delivery receipts are verified for origin, integrity, freshness, replay, tenant, correlation, and expected state. External success responses do not replace independent validation or evidence.

Integration credentials are scoped and rotated according to Sections 3.4 and 3.5. Revocation, vendor compromise, contractual termination, or configuration drift can suspend the integration without redesigning the task system.

### Audit, Evidence, Detection, and Response

Zero Trust decisions are continuously auditable. Material events include authentication outcomes, tenant resolution, context establishment, policy decisions, risk classification, approval, capability issuance and use, Tool Gateway decisions, execution boundary changes, validation, administrative access, cross-tenant attempts, evidence failures, revocation, and security response.

The Audit Engine provides the attributable event history described in Section 2.10. The Evidence Chain provides tamper-evident continuity described in Section 2.9. Neither replaces preventative controls. A valid evidence chain does not prove that every recorded decision was correct, and a blocked action still requires an audit event when material.

Security monitoring correlates identity, capability, policy, execution, data, integration, and administrative signals. Detection may trigger renewed verification, reduced authority, suspension, containment, or incident response. Absence of an alert is not proof of trust.

Zero Trust controls support investigation by preserving who requested access, what was evaluated, which authority was issued, what was attempted, which resource was affected, and how the system responded. Incident response may impose broader restrictions, revoke capabilities, isolate workers, preserve evidence, or suspend integrations without modifying historical decisions.

### Failure, Degraded Operation, and Recovery

Security-control failure produces an explicit state. Examples include unavailable identity authority, stale policy, tenant-resolution conflict, revocation-service failure, invalid capability, posture uncertainty, Tool Gateway unavailability, execution-isolation failure, audit-ingestion backpressure, Evidence Chain failure, and inconsistent recovery state.

The default outcome for a missing or unverifiable mandatory control is deny or suspend. Policy may define carefully bounded continuity modes for low-risk, reversible, or safety-critical operations, but such modes require preapproved scope, limited duration, stronger local constraints, explicit degraded-assurance status, complete evidence, and review. A continuity mode cannot silently weaken high-risk controls.

Recovery does not automatically restore prior trust. Restored services validate identity, tenant boundaries, policy versions, capability revocation state, key and secret state, audit continuity, evidence checkpoints, execution isolation, and authoritative data consistency before resuming governed operations.

Queued or retried requests are re-evaluated against current policy and authority. A request that was eligible before an outage may be denied after recovery if its approval, capability, session, context, target, or risk state is no longer valid.

### Governance, Assurance, and Measurement

Zero Trust governance defines protected resources, identity classes, trust boundaries, policy owners, privileged roles, risk tiers, approval requirements, capability templates, enforcement points, evidence obligations, exceptions, and review cadence. Ownership is explicit across product, security, engineering, operations, compliance, and tenant administration.

Exceptions are narrow, time-bound, attributable, risk-assessed, approved by the designated authority, monitored, and automatically expired where possible. An exception does not alter the canonical architecture. A recurring exception is treated as a control defect or architecture decision requiring formal review.

Conformance is tested through architecture review, policy tests, identity and authorization tests, tenant-isolation tests, capability misuse tests, replay tests, session revocation tests, service impersonation tests, egress tests, execution escape tests, administrative-access review, recovery exercises, and evidence-completeness checks.

Security indicators include standing-privilege count, privileged-access duration, capability scope and lifetime, denied cross-tenant attempts, stale authorization decisions, revocation propagation time, unverified service calls, direct Tool Gateway bypass attempts, administrative-access exceptions, incomplete evidence, isolation failures, and time to containment. Metrics support assurance but do not convert an architectural violation into acceptable risk.

### Zero Trust Limitations

Zero Trust reduces implicit trust and limits blast radius; it does not eliminate compromise, software defects, insider risk, social engineering, incorrect policy, malicious approved actions, or failures in external systems. Strong enforcement can still produce an unsafe outcome if the authoritative policy or reviewed context is wrong.

The architecture therefore combines Zero Trust with human accountability, secure engineering, threat modeling, independent validation, monitoring, incident response, recovery, and evidence. No single identity mechanism, network product, policy engine, encryption layer, or audit system can provide the complete security model independently.

### Zero Trust Invariants

The following invariants are canonical:

- no subject, component, device, integration, model, repository, or network location receives implicit trust;
- every material interaction is bound to authenticated identity, tenant, purpose, resource, and current decision context;
- authentication establishes identity assurance but never grants unrestricted authorization;
- tenant isolation is enforced at every control, data, execution, query, evidence, backup, recovery, and disposal boundary;
- authority is least-privilege, task-specific, time-bound, scope-limited, observable, and revocable;
- role membership establishes eligibility and never substitutes for an active capability where execution authority is required;
- material changes to context, proposal, target, risk, approval, or security state require renewed evaluation;
- service-to-service communication is explicitly authenticated and authorized regardless of network location;
- the AI & Intelligence Layer produces proposals and recommendations but cannot grant permission or initiate execution;
- all supported tool invocation passes through the Tool Gateway and all execution occurs within the approved restricted boundary;
- execution output remains untrusted until independent validation and acceptance;
- repositories and software-supply-chain content remain untrusted until baseline verification and applicable validation;
- human approval is explicit, attributable, scope-bound, time-bound, and invalidated by material change;
- administrative and break-glass access is named, temporary, minimized, evidenced, and reviewed;
- missing, stale, conflicting, or unverifiable mandatory security information fails closed or enters an explicitly governed degraded state;
- Audit Engine and Evidence Chain coverage remains continuous across successful and unsuccessful paths; and
- recovery verifies current trust state and never assumes that pre-failure authorization remains valid.

An implementation is non-conformant if it treats an internal network, registered device, authenticated user, administrator role, approved provider, repository ownership, or prior successful interaction as sufficient trust; if it issues broad standing execution credentials; if it permits service calls without explicit workload identity and authorization; if it allows cross-tenant access through shared identifiers or caches; if a model or tool output can bypass policy; if repository content executes during ordinary analysis; if Tool Gateway mediation or independent validation can be skipped; if approval survives a material context change; if emergency access is unbounded or unaudited; if unavailable security controls become implicit permission; or if successful recovery automatically reinstates expired, revoked, or unverifiable authority.

## 3.2 Authentication

### Purpose and Security Boundary

Authentication establishes and verifies the identity of a subject interacting with ILAIOS at a defined assurance level, for a defined audience, tenant context, session, purpose, and validity period. Subjects include human users, tenant administrators, platform personnel, workload identities, services, execution workers, device-bound components, integrations, validators, recovery processes, and approved external systems.

Authentication answers who or what is presenting itself and how strongly that identity has been verified. It does not answer which resources the subject may access or which actions it may perform. Authorization remains a separate decision governed by Section 3.3, the deterministic Policy Engine, current Immutable Context, risk treatment, approval state, capability constraints, and the applicable enforcement point.

An authenticated subject receives no implicit execution authority. A successful sign-in, valid service identity, registered device, trusted enterprise identity provider, or valid authentication artifact establishes eligibility for subsequent evaluation only. It does not permit Tool Gateway invocation, protected-data access, policy change, tenant administration, approval, artifact delivery, or audit export by itself.

Authentication is applied at every relevant trust boundary rather than only at external login. Human access, service-to-service calls, device connections, integration requests, administrative sessions, validation runners, recovery processes, and sensitive reauthentication events each require an identity mechanism appropriate to their threat model.

The architecture remains implementation-independent. ILAIOS may support multiple standards-based authentication methods and enterprise identity systems, provided that all methods preserve identity uniqueness, tenant binding, assurance, replay resistance, lifecycle control, revocation, auditability, and the separation of authentication from authorization.

### Authentication and Authorization Separation

Authentication and authorization are intentionally distinct control functions.

| Control question | Authentication responsibility | Authorization responsibility |
|---|---|---|
| Subject identity | Verifies the human, workload, device, service, or integration identity | Determines whether the verified subject is eligible for a requested resource or action |
| Tenant relationship | Establishes or verifies the asserted tenant association from an authoritative source | Determines what the subject may do within that tenant |
| Assurance | Records authentication method, strength, freshness, and relevant factors | Requires an assurance level appropriate to resource, action, risk, or policy |
| Session | Establishes a protected, bounded continuity context | Limits the resources and actions available within that context |
| Step-up | Re-verifies identity at a stronger or fresher level | Triggers step-up when a requested action requires it |
| Device or workload posture | Verifies origin and available posture evidence | Uses posture as one policy input without treating it as identity |
| Execution authority | Provides no execution authority | Issues constrained, task-specific authority only after policy, risk, and approval requirements are satisfied |

Authentication information is an input to authorization, not a substitute for it. Role, group, entitlement, or directory attributes carried with an identity assertion remain claims that must be validated, normalized, and evaluated by the authorization architecture. Authentication components must not embed hidden business permission that bypasses the Policy Engine.

### Canonical Identity Classes

ILAIOS distinguishes identity classes because their proof, lifecycle, and misuse risks differ.

- **Human workforce identity:** an employee, contractor, administrator, approver, reviewer, auditor, operator, or support user acting under an accountable personal identity.
- **Human external identity:** a customer user, partner, guest, external auditor, or other approved external person associated with a tenant and purpose.
- **Workload identity:** a non-human identity assigned to a deployed service, scheduled process, worker, validation runner, adapter, or controlled automation component.
- **Device identity:** the identity of an approved endpoint, companion component, managed device, or execution host, used in combination with user or workload identity where applicable.
- **Integration identity:** an identity representing a registered external application, connector, webhook source, or enterprise system.
- **Recovery and continuity identity:** a narrowly governed identity used for restore, failover, reconciliation, or emergency continuity operations.
- **Resource identity:** an identity or integrity-bound reference used to verify the intended service, endpoint, repository, tool, destination, or protected resource.

An identity belongs to one primary identity class at the authentication boundary. A workload may act on behalf of a human through explicit delegation, but it does not become a human identity. A human approval cannot be attributed solely to a shared service account. A registered device cannot stand in for the person operating it.

Each identity has an authoritative issuer, unique subject identifier, lifecycle owner, tenant or platform relationship, allowed audiences, assurance characteristics, status, and termination process. Display names, mutable email addresses, usernames, network addresses, repository names, device labels, and service names are not sufficient unique identity keys.

### Authentication Assurance

Authentication assurance expresses the confidence that the subject is correctly identified and remains in control of the authenticated interaction. The required assurance level is determined by the requested access path, tenant policy, data classification, administrative sensitivity, action risk, device context, location or residency constraint, and current security signals.

Assurance considers at least:

- identity proofing appropriate to the subject and account type;
- strength and independence of authentication factors;
- resistance to phishing, replay, credential theft, and verifier impersonation;
- protection and binding of authentication artifacts;
- freshness of authentication and time since the last strong verification;
- subject, device, workload, session, and audience binding;
- issuer trust and federation configuration;
- revocation and termination effectiveness;
- account-recovery strength;
- observed anomaly, compromise, or policy condition; and
- availability and integrity of the authoritative identity source.

ILAIOS shall define assurance profiles rather than rely on an undocumented strong-or-weak label. A profile specifies acceptable methods, factor combinations, maximum authentication age, session lifetime, step-up conditions, device requirements where applicable, recovery restrictions, and evidence obligations.

Low-risk read access may accept a different assurance profile from tenant security administration, privileged support, policy publication, key management, high-risk approval, destructive execution, or evidence export. Higher-risk operations require stronger and more recent authentication but remain subject to independent authorization.

An assurance level cannot be inferred solely from the number of factors. Two factors that depend on the same compromised channel may not provide meaningful independence. A stronger factor followed by an insecure recovery process does not create strong end-to-end assurance.

### Human Authentication

Every human user shall authenticate through a unique, attributable identity. Shared human accounts, generic administrator identities, and unauthenticated approval identities are prohibited. A person may hold several tenant or organizational relationships, but each active session must preserve the exact subject and current tenant context.

Enterprise deployments should support federation with the customer's authoritative identity service using standards-based protocols and current security profiles. Federation reduces duplicate credential management and allows enterprise joiner, mover, leaver, risk, and authentication policies to remain under accountable organizational control.

Where direct ILAIOS-managed human authentication is supported, the method shall provide equivalent lifecycle, compromise, recovery, factor, and audit controls appropriate to the deployment. Local authentication must not become an undocumented fallback that bypasses a tenant's federation or multifactor requirements.

Authentication interfaces shall protect users against account enumeration, credential phishing, session fixation, factor fatigue, malicious redirection, open redirect, cross-tenant confusion, and ambiguous approval prompts. Error responses should provide the legitimate user with useful recovery direction without disclosing whether a targeted account exists or which factor failed to an unauthenticated party.

Human authentication results record the stable subject, tenant relationship, issuer, method class, assurance profile, authentication time, session identifier, device or application context where relevant, and applicable risk state. Raw credentials and reusable factor secrets are never included in ordinary logs, audit events, model context, or support records.

### Enterprise Federation and Tenant Binding

Federation is a controlled trust relationship between ILAIOS and an approved identity issuer. Each tenant federation configuration defines the issuer, tenant mapping, expected audience, permitted authentication methods or assurance information, subject-identifier rules, required claims, signature and key validation policy, session behavior, provisioning relationship, logout and revocation behavior, and operational owner.

ILAIOS shall not infer tenant membership solely from an email domain, display name, redirect parameter, user-provided tenant identifier, or issuer similarity. Tenant association is resolved from an approved federation configuration, authoritative membership record, invitation, or other governed binding.

Federation assertions are validated for issuer, audience, signature or equivalent integrity, validity period, freshness, subject, tenant, intended use, replay protection where applicable, and required assurance. Unsupported, unsigned, expired, future-dated beyond permitted clock tolerance, incorrectly addressed, or ambiguously tenant-bound assertions are rejected.

Claim normalization must preserve meaning and provenance. A role or group name from one issuer cannot be assumed equivalent to a similarly named ILAIOS entitlement or another tenant's claim. Claims used by authorization are mapped through an explicit tenant configuration and remain subject to policy.

Federation configuration changes are high-impact administrative events. Adding an issuer, changing tenant mapping, altering subject identifiers, weakening assurance requirements, changing signing trust, or enabling a fallback authentication path requires appropriate authorization, validation, audit, and controlled activation.

Account linking between federated identities is never based solely on matching email address or display name. Linking requires an authoritative, conflict-resistant process that prevents takeover through duplicate, reassigned, guest, or attacker-controlled identifiers. The original and linked identities remain traceable.

### Multifactor and Phishing-Resistant Authentication

Multifactor authentication is required according to assurance profile, tenant policy, role, action sensitivity, and risk. Privileged administration, security configuration, high-risk approval, support access, break-glass activation, credential or key operations, and other material security actions require strong authentication appropriate to the threat.

Phishing-resistant authentication shall be required for ordinary privileged administration, security configuration, high-risk approval, release signing, production promotion, and secret or key administration where the approved deployment profile supports it. Where temporarily infeasible, a documented, time-bound exception shall define the alternate assurance, compensating controls, monitoring, and migration plan. Break-glass authentication may use a separately governed emergency method only where the primary phishing-resistant path is unavailable; it remains strongly authenticated, short-lived, attributable, monitored, and reviewed.

Factor enrollment is itself a sensitive authenticated operation. It verifies the subject at an assurance level at least appropriate to the resulting factor, records the factor class and lifecycle metadata, prevents unauthorized replacement, and notifies the subject or tenant where required. Adding a weaker factor must not silently reduce the assurance of an account.

Factor reset, removal, replacement, and recovery require equivalent protection. A support operator cannot bypass factor requirements merely because the user reports loss of access. Recovery evidence, waiting periods, administrative approval, user notification, and restricted post-recovery sessions may be required according to risk.

Repeated or unsolicited authentication prompts shall not be treated as positive user intent. Approval-style factors must present sufficient context and apply anti-fatigue controls. A user denial or report of an unexpected prompt is a material security signal.

### Password and Reusable Credential Controls

Where passwords or other reusable human credentials are supported, they are treated as sensitive authentication secrets. ILAIOS shall never store recoverable plaintext passwords. Verification data is protected using an approved adaptive one-way derivation method with unique per-credential randomness and parameters governed through security policy.

Password policy shall prioritize resistance to compromise rather than arbitrary complexity rituals. Controls include minimum strength appropriate to the assurance profile, screening against known compromised or prohibited values where permitted, rate limiting, secure reset, prevention of credential disclosure, and detection of automated guessing or credential stuffing.

Periodic forced change without evidence of compromise is not relied upon as the primary security control. A credential is changed or revoked when compromise is suspected or confirmed, when required by tenant policy or applicable obligation, when administrative ownership changes, or when the authentication architecture requires migration.

Passwords are not exposed to application components that do not perform credential verification. They are excluded from telemetry, audit payloads, error messages, analytics, exports, model inputs, support tickets, and diagnostic captures. Authentication interfaces shall not return secrets after enrollment.

Reusable credentials alone are not sufficient for privileged or high-risk access where the applicable assurance profile requires stronger protection.

### Workload and Service Authentication

Every service, worker, validator, adapter, and controlled process that crosses a trust boundary uses an explicit workload identity. Network location, host membership, executable name, process identifier, deployment namespace, or possession of a shared environment secret is not sufficient authentication.

Workload identity is bound to the expected deployment, service role, tenant or platform scope, environment, and audience. Authentication artifacts have short validity appropriate to automated rotation and are issued through an approved trust path. Long-lived shared service credentials are minimized and, where unavoidable for an external dependency, are managed under Section 3.4 rather than treated as the canonical internal identity mechanism.

Receiving services validate the caller identity, issuer, audience, environment, validity, request integrity, and applicable channel binding before accepting the request. A service authenticated for one audience cannot replay the same artifact to another. A development or test workload identity cannot authenticate to production unless a formally governed cross-environment function explicitly permits it.

Worker identities are task-bound or otherwise constrained where practical. Ephemeral execution workers do not inherit the full identity of the orchestration service. Validation runners use identities distinct from execution workers to preserve separation of duties.

Workload identity lifecycle is connected to deployment and service lifecycle. Replacement, scaling, restart, migration, failover, decommissioning, or compromise invalidates or rotates the applicable authentication state according to policy. Restored infrastructure does not automatically inherit trusted identity from an unverified snapshot.

### Device Authentication and Session Binding

Device authentication establishes the identity of an approved device or device-bound component. It is supplemental to human or workload authentication and does not independently authorize access. A device may be registered, managed, or cryptographically enrolled while still being non-compliant, compromised, or used by the wrong person.

Device registration verifies ownership or administrative authority, associates the device with the appropriate tenant or platform domain, records the device identity and security capabilities, and establishes revocation. Duplicate, cloned, reset, transferred, or retired devices receive explicit lifecycle treatment.

Where device posture is used, the authentication result records the source, freshness, and integrity of the posture evidence. Posture is not silently inferred from registration. Stale or unavailable posture cannot be represented as compliant.

Sessions may be bound to a device, application instance, protected key, or channel where supported. Binding reduces replay but does not eliminate the need for expiry, revocation, step-up, and authorization. A device change, application reinstall, secure-state loss, or suspicious clone condition may invalidate the session and require renewed authentication.

Device-bound components operating offline follow preapproved bounded-authentication rules. Offline state has strict expiry, local protection, replay prevention, limited scope, and reconciliation requirements. Offline operation must not create indefinite or unauditable identity continuity.

### Integration and API Client Authentication

Every external application, connector, webhook source, enterprise system, and API client authenticates using a registered integration identity appropriate to its communication pattern. A generic tenant credential shared across unrelated integrations is prohibited.

Integration registration defines the accountable owner, tenant, client or source identity, permitted authentication methods, expected audience, redirect or callback endpoints where applicable, credential lifecycle, contact, data classification, rate policy, and termination conditions. Registration does not grant resource authorization.

Interactive integrations acting on behalf of a user preserve both the integration identity and the human identity. The platform distinguishes the application that initiated the request from the person represented. Delegation is explicit, audience-bound, purpose-bound, and revocable.

Non-interactive integrations use workload-style identity and cannot simulate a human approval. Webhook and callback authentication verifies source integrity, freshness, expected event relationship, tenant, correlation, and replay state. Static network allowlists may supplement but never replace cryptographic or equivalent source authentication.

Client credentials, assertions, and endpoint trust are rotated and revoked according to risk. Integration compromise or vendor termination can disable the specific identity without affecting unrelated tenants or integrations.

### Secure Access Gateway Authentication Flow

The Secure Access Gateway is the canonical external authentication enforcement boundary for supported interactive and integration requests. The authentication flow performs the following logical steps:

1. Identify the supported authentication route without trusting user-controlled tenant or redirect data.
2. Validate the identity issuer or credential authority and the intended ILAIOS audience.
3. Verify artifact integrity, validity, freshness, method, assurance, replay state, and channel requirements.
4. Resolve the stable subject and identity class.
5. Establish the authoritative tenant relationship or reject ambiguity.
6. Evaluate authentication risk signals and any required step-up.
7. Establish a protected session or authenticated request context with explicit expiry and revocation semantics.
8. Produce a normalized identity envelope for downstream context creation.
9. Emit material authentication events through the protected Audit Engine path.

The normalized identity envelope contains verified claims and references only. Raw credentials, private keys, factor secrets, and unnecessary identity-provider payloads are not propagated. Downstream components receive the minimum identity attributes required for their role.

Authentication failure does not create a partially trusted session. The gateway rejects unsupported methods, invalid issuer or audience, tenant ambiguity, replay, expired proof, unresolved subject, failed step-up, revoked identity, or unavailable mandatory verification.

### Authentication Artifacts

Authentication artifacts include session identifiers, assertions, proof objects, workload credentials, device proofs, integration credentials, and other representations used to demonstrate authenticated identity. Each artifact has a defined issuer, subject, audience, tenant relationship, method or assurance reference, issue time, expiry, unique identity where required, integrity protection, and revocation behavior.

Artifacts are purpose-specific and minimally disclosed. An artifact intended for the Secure Access Gateway is not accepted by an execution worker. A user session artifact is not an execution capability. A workload identity proof is not a tenant administrator credential. Authentication artifacts do not contain standing authority to enterprise resources.

The architecture prevents replay through a combination of short validity, unique identifiers, one-time state where applicable, audience restriction, channel or key binding where supported, nonce or request correlation, and server-side detection. Clock tolerance is explicit and bounded.

Artifacts are protected in transit and at rest according to Sections 3.5 and 3.6. Browser, application, device, and service storage minimizes exposure to scripts, logs, memory scraping, backup leakage, and cross-application access as applicable to the deployment.

Authentication artifacts must not appear in URLs, general application logs, analytics, crash reports, support exports, model context, or Audit Engine payloads. Audit records use non-reusable identifiers, hashes, or protected references sufficient for correlation without enabling authentication.

### Session Establishment and Continuity

A session is a bounded continuity context for an authenticated subject. It records the subject, identity class, active tenant, issuer, authentication method and assurance, authentication time, session creation time, maximum lifetime, inactivity policy, device or application binding where relevant, risk state, and revocation state.

A session does not preserve authorization indefinitely. Resource access is evaluated at use time, and sensitive actions may require fresher or stronger authentication. Tenant switching, role change, privilege elevation, device change, federation change, identity disablement, factor reset, security incident, or material risk change may require session termination or renewed authentication.

Session identifiers are unpredictable and protected. Session fixation is prevented by issuing new session state after successful authentication and privilege transition. Concurrent session behavior is governed by tenant policy and risk; users and administrators can identify and terminate active sessions where appropriate.

Maximum lifetime and inactivity limits are explicit. Activity does not extend a session beyond its maximum lifetime. Background clients and long-lived connections periodically re-establish current identity assurance and revocation state rather than treating connection persistence as trust.

Logout terminates the relevant local session and invalidates associated continuation where supported. Enterprise logout and identity-provider termination are handled according to the configured federation capabilities, but ILAIOS maintains its own revocation and maximum-lifetime controls rather than relying entirely on external notification.

### Step-Up and Reauthentication

Step-up authentication obtains a stronger or fresher identity proof when the current session does not meet the assurance required for a requested operation. It is triggered by policy, action sensitivity, data classification, privilege elevation, administrative access, high-risk approval, unusual context, stale authentication, device change, recovery status, or security detection.

Step-up does not broaden authorization automatically. After successful reauthentication, the requested action still passes through policy, risk, approval, and capability evaluation. The step-up result is bound to the subject, tenant, session, purpose, requested operation, time, and assurance achieved.

Reauthentication must present the user with sufficient context to understand why verification is required. Authentication prompts generated by one tenant, action, or destination cannot be reused silently for another. Failed, cancelled, expired, or denied step-up leaves the original session at its prior assurance and does not grant the requested higher-risk access.

Sensitive actions may require transaction-specific user intent in addition to session authentication. Where applied, the proof is bound to the material action details and cannot authorize a changed target, amount, recipient, policy, capability, or artifact.

### Identity Lifecycle and Provisioning Relationship

Authentication depends on authoritative identity lifecycle management. Creation, invitation, federation, activation, suspension, disablement, deletion, tenant transfer, employment change, contract expiry, and service decommissioning must propagate to the authentication boundary within defined service objectives.

Provisioning systems may create or update identity records and tenant relationships, but provisioning is not authentication. A provisioned user or workload must still prove identity through an approved method. Conversely, an authenticated external subject is not automatically provisioned with application entitlements.

Joiner, mover, and leaver processes preserve stable identity while updating current relationships. Reassigned email addresses, recycled usernames, renamed services, and transferred devices must not inherit the prior subject's sessions, history, approvals, or authentication factors.

Identity disablement revokes or terminates active sessions and prevents new authentication according to the defined urgency. High-risk termination and confirmed compromise require expedited revocation. Historical audit attribution remains linked to the original immutable subject identity even after account deletion or pseudonymization.

Tenant administrators may manage tenant-scoped identities according to authorization policy but cannot create platform identities, alter immutable audit attribution, or weaken global authentication requirements without governed authority.

### Revocation and Termination

Authentication state is revocable. Revocation may apply to an identity, session, factor, device, workload, integration, credential, federation relationship, or authentication method. Triggers include user action, tenant administration, lifecycle change, compromise, risk detection, policy change, device loss, integration termination, incident response, and recovery.

Revocation propagates to enforcement points within a defined maximum interval based on risk. High-risk identities and privileged sessions require faster propagation than ordinary low-risk sessions. Short-lived artifacts reduce exposure but do not replace revocation where immediate termination is required.

Receiving components validate revocation or current session state at boundaries appropriate to the operation. Cached authentication state has explicit maximum age and fail behavior. A stale cache cannot be used indefinitely during identity-service unavailability.

Revocation is attributable and audited. The record identifies the object revoked, actor or automated authority, reason, time, scope, and propagation outcome. A failed revocation attempt triggers escalation and may require broader containment.

Revocation of authentication does not by itself reverse actions already completed. It prevents future use and initiates the applicable incident, compensation, validation, or recovery process.

### Account and Factor Recovery

Account recovery is an authentication process with security consequences equal to or greater than initial enrollment. Recovery shall not become a weaker alternate route that allows an attacker to bypass multifactor, federation, device binding, or tenant controls.

Recovery requirements are based on identity class, assurance profile, tenant policy, privilege, and current risk. Methods may include verified enterprise identity administration, pre-established recovery factors, supervised identity proofing, dual control, waiting periods, restricted post-recovery access, and notification through previously registered channels.

Knowledge that is public, easily researched, or controlled by the same compromised channel is not sufficient for high-assurance recovery. Support personnel cannot view or retrieve existing passwords, factor secrets, private keys, or reusable authentication artifacts.

Recovery creates new authentication state and revokes superseded or suspected state. It records the recovery method, responsible authority, assurance achieved, affected factors and sessions, restrictions, notification, and review requirement. A recovered account may require step-up and a cooling period before privileged actions.

Failed or suspicious recovery attempts are material security events and may trigger identity protection, tenant notification, or incident response.

### Privileged, Support, and Break-Glass Authentication

Privileged authentication uses named personal identities, high-assurance methods, fresh verification, controlled devices or environments where required, and separate administrative sessions. Routine user authentication is not silently elevated into platform administration.

Administrative session establishment records the requested duty, tenant or platform scope, approval or just-in-time privilege reference where applicable, assurance, start time, maximum duration, and review obligations. Authentication establishes the administrator; authorization separately limits the administrative action.

Support access follows tenant, contract, and purpose controls. A support identity does not authenticate as the customer and must not impersonate a user without an explicit, visible, attributable, and policy-governed mechanism. Any assisted access preserves the identities of both support personnel and the represented tenant context.

Break-glass authentication uses a separately governed process protected against routine use. It requires the strongest available identity verification, explicit emergency reason, restricted environment where feasible, immediate notification, short lifetime, complete audit, and mandatory post-event review. Break-glass credentials are not shared through ordinary operational channels and cannot disable Audit Engine or Evidence Chain protections.

### Abuse Resistance and Authentication Threat Controls

Authentication services shall resist automated guessing, credential stuffing, replay, enumeration, factor fatigue, malicious federation, session fixation, token theft, redirect manipulation, callback substitution, account linking abuse, workload impersonation, device cloning, and denial of service.

Controls include risk-sensitive rate enforcement, bounded retries, progressive friction, replay detection, proof freshness, audience restriction, request correlation, secure enrollment, device or channel binding where appropriate, anomaly detection, and containment. Protective responses shall avoid creating a predictable denial-of-service mechanism against legitimate users.

Rate controls distinguish identities, tenants, sources, methods, devices, integrations, and global service health as appropriate. A distributed attack cannot bypass controls simply by rotating one visible attribute. Legitimate enterprise federation traffic and continuity scenarios receive controlled capacity without disabling abuse protection.

Authentication error handling is deterministic and does not leak sensitive account, tenant, factor, federation, or policy information to unauthenticated callers. Detailed diagnostics are available only through authorized operational channels and protected audit records.

### Privacy and Data Minimization

Authentication collects and retains only the identity information necessary to establish security, tenant association, accountability, lifecycle, fraud prevention, and applicable legal obligations. Identity-provider payloads are minimized before propagation. Downstream services receive verified attributes required for their responsibility rather than unrestricted directory profiles.

Sensitive identity attributes, factor metadata, device data, network signals, risk signals, and recovery evidence are classified and access-controlled. They are not repurposed for unrelated analytics, model training, profiling, or cross-tenant comparison without a separately governed purpose and lawful basis.

Authentication logs and audit events exclude raw credentials, private keys, recovery secrets, authentication artifacts, and unnecessary personal data. Retention is defined by security purpose, tenant contract, investigation need, and applicable obligations. Deletion or pseudonymization preserves the minimum immutable attribution required for historical audit where permitted.

User-facing interfaces disclose material authentication activity, active sessions, factor enrollment, recovery, and security notifications appropriate to the product and tenant policy. Transparency does not disclose information that would weaken security.

### Audit and Evidence

Material authentication events are recorded continuously through the Audit Engine. Events include sign-in initiation where material, success, failure, federation outcome, tenant resolution, factor challenge, step-up, session creation, session renewal, logout, revocation, device enrollment, factor enrollment or reset, recovery, workload identity issuance, integration authentication, privileged authentication, break-glass use, and detected abuse.

Audit events record stable non-secret subject and session references, identity class, tenant, issuer, method class, assurance profile, outcome, reason code, time, relevant device or workload context, risk disposition, and correlation. They never include passwords, private keys, one-time codes, complete assertions, reusable session artifacts, or recovery secrets.

Designated authentication policy versions, issuer configurations, revocation events, assurance decisions, and high-risk session records may be bound into the Evidence Chain. Evidence demonstrates what authentication controls and results were recorded; it does not prove that an identity provider, device, or human was impossible to compromise.

Authentication query and export access is itself controlled and audited. Tenant administrators can review tenant-scoped events without receiving unrestricted platform or other-tenant identity information.

### Availability and Degraded Authentication

Authentication is a critical security dependency. The architecture defines availability, latency, recovery, revocation-propagation, and failover objectives appropriate to each identity class and deployment model.

Failure of an authoritative identity source, federation dependency, factor service, revocation service, time source, or key-verification path produces an explicit state. Mandatory verification failure does not become implicit authentication. High-risk and privileged access fails closed.

Policy may permit a bounded continuity mode for specifically approved low-risk scenarios. Such a mode relies only on recently verified, non-revoked, locally protected state; has short expiry and limited tenant, resource, and action scope; forbids privilege elevation and high-risk approval; records degraded assurance; and requires reconciliation when normal service returns.

Recovery verifies issuer configuration, keys, identity state, tenant mapping, factor state, revocation, session consistency, time integrity, Audit Engine continuity, and evidence before normal authentication claims resume. Sessions or artifacts that cannot be verified after recovery are invalidated.

### Testing, Governance, and Metrics

Authentication governance defines supported identity classes, methods, assurance profiles, federation requirements, lifecycle owners, privileged access rules, recovery methods, session limits, revocation objectives, continuity modes, evidence obligations, and deprecation policy.

Each authentication method and federation profile undergoes threat analysis, protocol and implementation testing, replay testing, audience and issuer testing, tenant-confusion testing, account-linking tests, session fixation tests, revocation tests, factor reset tests, recovery abuse tests, workload impersonation tests, device clone tests, failover tests, and audit-completeness tests.

Changes to accepted methods, assurance mappings, issuer trust, tenant binding, factor policy, session lifetime, recovery paths, or privileged authentication require security review and controlled rollout. A material weakening of the canonical model requires an ADR and applicable risk acceptance.

Quality and security indicators include authentication success and failure by reason, step-up completion, phishing-resistant method adoption, privileged-session assurance, replay attempts, credential-stuffing detection, factor-reset activity, suspicious recovery, issuer-validation failures, tenant-binding conflicts, session-revocation propagation, stale-session use, workload-authentication failures, shared-credential findings, break-glass use, and incomplete audit events.

Metrics are interpreted with context. A lower failure rate is not inherently safer if controls were weakened, and a higher denial rate may reflect successful protection. Known authentication defects remain defects regardless of aggregate success percentages.

### Authentication Limitations

Authentication cannot prove benevolent intent, correct authorization, safe device state, accurate external claims, absence of coercion, or correctness of a requested action. A legitimate user may approve a harmful action; a valid workload may be compromised after authentication; an enterprise identity issuer may be misconfigured; and a strong factor may be used from an unsafe environment.

ILAIOS therefore combines authentication with authorization, Immutable Context, least privilege, risk classification, human approval, Tool Gateway mediation, restricted execution, independent validation, monitoring, incident response, Audit Engine, and Evidence Chain controls.

### Authentication Invariants

The following invariants are canonical:

- every human, workload, service, device, and integration crossing a trust boundary has an explicit identity class and authoritative issuer;
- human users and privileged operators use unique attributable identities; shared human accounts are prohibited;
- authentication establishes identity assurance and never grants unrestricted resource or execution authority;
- tenant membership is resolved through an authoritative binding and never inferred solely from an email domain, display name, network location, or user-controlled parameter;
- every authentication artifact is integrity-protected, audience-bound, tenant-aware where applicable, time-bounded, minimally disclosed, and revocable according to risk;
- raw credentials, private keys, factor secrets, recovery secrets, and reusable authentication artifacts are excluded from ordinary logs, audit events, model context, analytics, and support exports;
- federation assertions are validated for issuer, audience, integrity, validity, subject, tenant, assurance, and replay conditions;
- multifactor and phishing-resistant authentication are required according to assurance profile, with stronger controls for privileged and high-risk use;
- factor enrollment, reset, recovery, account linking, and federation changes receive protection equivalent to their security impact;
- workload identities are distinct from human identities and are bound to the expected service, deployment, environment, and audience;
- device identity supplements but never replaces human or workload authentication and authorization;
- sessions have explicit creation, maximum lifetime, inactivity, renewal, binding, tenant, assurance, and revocation semantics;
- step-up authentication strengthens or refreshes identity proof but does not independently broaden authorization;
- identity disablement, compromise, device loss, or integration termination propagates to applicable sessions and artifacts within defined risk-based objectives;
- privileged, support, and break-glass authentication is named, strong, time-bound, purpose-bound, auditable, and reviewed;
- unavailable or unverifiable mandatory authentication controls fail closed or enter an explicitly governed limited continuity mode; and
- authentication events are continuously recorded without exposing reusable secrets.

An implementation is non-conformant if it treats authentication as authorization; uses shared human administrator accounts; infers tenant membership from an unverified domain or parameter; accepts assertions without issuer, audience, tenant, integrity, validity, and replay validation; permits privileged access with an assurance profile intended for ordinary low-risk use; provides a weaker recovery route than enrollment; stores plaintext passwords or reusable authentication artifacts in logs; uses one shared service credential across unrelated workloads or tenants; allows a user session artifact to function as an execution capability; preserves sessions indefinitely through activity; restores unverifiable sessions after failure; permits unaudited impersonation; or allows identity-service unavailability to become implicit authentication.

## 3.3 Authorization

### Purpose and Authority Boundary

Authorization determines whether an authenticated subject may perform a specific action on a specific resource, within a specific tenant, purpose, task, environment, time, and control context. It converts verified identity and authoritative context into an explicit decision without granting broader or longer-lived authority than the governed operation requires.

Authentication establishes who or what the subject is and at what assurance level. Authorization establishes what that subject may do under current conditions. A successful authentication, role assignment, group membership, internal network location, registered device, approved integration, or prior authorization does not create unrestricted access.

ILAIOS uses a layered authorization architecture. Eligibility is established through governed identity and enterprise attributes. The deterministic Policy Engine evaluates the exact request and Immutable Context. The Risk Classification Engine determines required treatment. The Human Approval Engine supplies accountable approval where required. The Identity and Capability Manager issues narrowly constrained execution authority. Enforcement points validate the current decision or capability immediately before protected use.

Authorization does not execute actions. The Policy Engine cannot call tools, the approval mechanism cannot broaden policy, the capability issuer cannot grant prohibited authority, and enforcement points cannot manufacture permission when required context is missing. The AI & Intelligence Layer has no authorization authority.

The architecture remains implementation-independent. Different policy languages, decision services, entitlement stores, and capability representations may be used provided that they preserve determinism, default denial, least privilege, tenant isolation, explicit decision context, separation of duties, revocation, evidence, and the invariants defined in this section.

### Canonical Authorization Model

Every material authorization request is evaluated against a canonical decision tuple:

| Decision dimension | Required meaning |
|---|---|
| Subject | Authenticated human, workload, service, device-bound component, integration, or delegated identity requesting access |
| Tenant | Authoritative tenant security domain in which the request is evaluated |
| Action | Normalized operation requested, including material sub-operation where applicable |
| Resource | Exact protected object, class, path, repository, tool, artifact, policy, data set, destination, or administrative function |
| Purpose | Approved business or operational purpose associated with the task |
| Task and context | Task identity, Immutable Context version, request identity, proposal or plan reference, and applicable state |
| Environment | Deployment, execution boundary, data residency, device or workload context, and target environment |
| Data classification | Sensitivity, regulated status, residency, retention, and disclosure constraints |
| Risk | Deterministic risk class and required control treatment |
| Approval | Required human decision, reviewed scope, approver authority, conditions, validity, and revocation state |
| Time and usage | Decision time, validity interval, permitted count, rate, sequence, expiry, and replay state |
| Policy | Applicable policy set, policy version, rule outcomes, obligations, conflicts, and decision identifier |
| Evidence state | Required audit, Evidence Chain, validation, or prior-stage evidence necessary for the operation |

A decision is valid only for the tuple evaluated. Changing the subject, tenant, purpose, resource, action, target, parameters, proposal digest, data classification, environment, risk, approval, policy version, or validity condition may require a new decision.

Authorization inputs are normalized and integrity-protected. Free-form text, model output, user-supplied labels, tool output, or unverified metadata cannot redefine the subject, tenant, action, resource, or policy facts.

### Default Deny and Explicit Permission

ILAIOS applies default deny. An action is permitted only when an applicable, valid, and current policy explicitly allows it and every required obligation is satisfied. Absence of a rule, missing attribute, unsupported resource type, unresolved tenant, stale policy, ambiguous action, conflicting decision, unavailable mandatory dependency, or unverifiable approval produces denial, suspension, or a defined clarification state rather than permission.

Permissions are enumerated through normalized actions and resources. Broad constructs such as all access, unrestricted administrator, any tool, any repository, or any tenant are prohibited except where an explicitly governed platform function requires a bounded equivalent and applies compensating separation, time, purpose, and audit controls.

Negative and restrictive policy takes precedence according to a documented deterministic conflict model. Tenant policy may strengthen platform baselines but cannot weaken non-overridable global security requirements. Product edition, commercial status, or support urgency never silently supersedes security policy.

Error and indeterminate are distinct from deny but are non-permitting outcomes. A policy-engine error must not be converted to permit by a caller. Clarification requests and additional-control requirements remain non-authorizing until the missing condition has been resolved and the request has been re-evaluated.

### Policy Authority and Deterministic Evaluation

The Policy Engine is the canonical deterministic authorization decision component in the Control Plane. It evaluates versioned policy against the normalized authorization tuple and produces a structured decision. For the same canonical inputs, policy version, and explicit environmental facts, it shall produce the same result.

Time, risk, environment, posture, residency, ownership, data classification, and external attributes that affect a decision are passed as verified inputs with source and freshness. The Policy Engine does not obtain hidden nondeterministic facts, call a reasoning model, or interpret natural-language recommendations as authority.

Canonical policy outcomes include:

- permit subject to stated constraints and obligations;
- deny with stable reason and applicable policy reference;
- require human approval of a defined class;
- require stronger or fresher authentication;
- require additional validation, isolation, evidence, or monitoring;
- require clarification or corrected context; or
- return an explicit non-permitting error or indeterminate result.

The decision includes the policy set and version, evaluated subject, tenant, action, resource, context reference, result, rule outcomes, obligations, constraints, approval class, capability limits, evidence requirements, validity conditions, and stable reason codes.

Policy evaluation may consume bounded advisory signals from Code Intelligence, confidence scoring, security analytics, or the AI & Intelligence Layer only where policy defines their semantics. Advisory signals may increase scrutiny, expand validation, require approval, or cause denial. They cannot independently create permission or waive a deterministic requirement.

### Policy Precedence and Tenant Policy

Authorization policy is layered to support platform security, deployment obligations, tenant governance, resource ownership, and task-specific controls. Precedence is explicit and deterministic.

Global non-overridable policy defines minimum ILAIOS security requirements, prohibited actions, tenant isolation, Trust Core protection, mandatory Tool Gateway use, separation of duties, and other architectural invariants. Deployment or jurisdictional policy may add residency, operational, or regulatory constraints. Tenant policy defines organizational roles, approvals, resources, environments, risk tolerance, and permitted integrations within the global boundary.

Resource-level or workflow-specific policy may further restrict access. A task-specific approval or capability cannot override a higher-level denial. When policy layers conflict, the result follows the documented restrictive precedence model and records the conflict.

Tenant policy is isolated. One tenant cannot publish rules that apply to another tenant or change platform-wide policy. Shared templates may be distributed as controlled artifacts, but each activation retains tenant ownership, version, and review.

Policy inheritance and composition shall remain explainable. An authorization decision must identify which layers and rules contributed to the outcome. Hidden precedence, undocumented defaults, and order-dependent evaluation that changes with storage or deployment topology are prohibited.

### Role, Attribute, Relationship, and Capability Controls

ILAIOS may combine role-based, attribute-based, relationship-based, and capability-based controls. These mechanisms have distinct purposes.

Roles group eligibility and duties such as tenant administrator, approver, auditor, operator, developer, security reviewer, or support user. Role membership is not standing execution authority. It establishes which requests or approvals a subject may be eligible to make under current policy.

Attributes describe verified subject, resource, environment, task, classification, risk, or organizational facts. Authorization uses only attributes from approved authoritative sources with defined freshness and integrity. User-provided attributes and model-generated labels are not authoritative.

Relationships express governed associations such as resource ownership, team membership, approver assignment, repository responsibility, delegated administration, or review duty. Relationship existence is tenant-bound, versioned where material, and revocable.

Capabilities represent operational authority issued after policy, risk, and approval requirements are satisfied. They are narrow, time-bound, task-bound, observable, and validated at use time. Capability-based execution prevents broad user or service roles from being passed directly into restricted workers.

Combining these mechanisms allows enterprise flexibility without conflating eligibility, context, and operational authority. No single mechanism may bypass mandatory policy or tenant isolation.

### Resource and Action Model

Authorization requires a canonical resource and action taxonomy. Each protected resource type has an owner, tenant behavior, identifier semantics, supported actions, classification rules, parent or containment relationships, and enforcement point.

Resource classes include task state, Immutable Context, proposals, policies, approvals, capabilities, repositories, source indexes, tools, execution environments, credentials, artifacts, validation results, audit records, evidence records, exports, integrations, administrative settings, backups, and delivery destinations.

Actions are normalized to express material intent rather than generic interface verbs. Examples include read metadata, read protected content, create, propose, approve, reject, execute, modify, publish policy, issue capability, revoke, validate, accept, deliver, export, restore, and dispose. An interface-level operation may require several separately authorized material actions.

Resource identifiers are exact and tenant-bound. Path prefixes, wildcard patterns, labels, aliases, and parent access require governed semantics. Authorization shall prevent path traversal, identifier substitution, confused-deputy behavior, ambiguous case handling, and target redirection.

Bulk, recursive, transitive, or wildcard actions receive explicit scope and blast-radius controls. Permission to modify one object does not imply permission to modify its parent, children, related resources, backups, evidence, or another environment.

### Immutable Context and Authorization Binding

The Immutable Context provides the authoritative subject, tenant, purpose, target, classification, repository or resource reference, environment, constraints, and correlation used by the authorization path. A policy decision binds to the exact context version and relevant proposal or action digest.

Material change does not mutate an accepted decision. A new target, expanded parameter range, different tool, changed repository baseline, altered artifact, new destination, elevated classification, changed approver condition, or modified proposal requires renewed context and authorization.

Non-material changes may be treated under a policy-defined equivalence rule, but the rule itself is explicit, versioned, testable, and evidence-bearing. Callers cannot decide unilaterally that a change is non-material.

Authorization components receive protected references to large or sensitive context data rather than uncontrolled copies. The referenced content is integrity-bound, and the exact version used for decision remains reconstructable.

### Risk Classification and Control Treatment

The Risk Classification Engine assigns deterministic control treatment based on governed factors such as action type, target environment, data sensitivity, requested privilege, blast radius, reversibility, external side effects, execution isolation, validation coverage, and security signals.
