Highest-impact production key material shall remain under an approved managed cryptographic boundary, external qualified custody, or another independently controlled mechanism, or the affected capability shall remain in a constrained prerelease state. The bootstrap profile cannot waive dual control where compromise would create unacceptable platform, tenant, evidence, signing, or recovery risk, and it shall have dated exit criteria before Stable release.

Custodian identities are named, strongly authenticated, currently authorized, trained, and subject to lifecycle controls. Personnel transfer or departure triggers timely replacement of custody, review of access, and rotation where exposure risk requires.

Key ceremonies are documented and attributable. They define participants, roles, purpose, environment, approved equipment, generation or recovery steps, verification, inventory updates, evidence, exception handling, and secure cleanup. Ceremony evidence proves that governed steps were recorded; it does not disclose key material.

Emergency custody follows the break-glass model and cannot eliminate independent review, tenant isolation, or evidence integrity.

### Key Generation

Keys are generated within an approved cryptographic boundary using an approved random-bit generation or key-establishment process suitable for the algorithm and security-strength profile. Human-chosen cryptographic keys are prohibited.

Generation binds the key to its inventory identity, purpose, tenant, environment, algorithm profile, permitted operations, cryptoperiod, export policy, owner, and governing authorization. The system verifies successful generation and boundary ownership before activation.

Derived keys use an approved key-derivation method and explicit context that prevents collision across tenant, purpose, environment, resource, or protocol domains. Source key material, salt or nonce requirements, labels, output length, and derivation purpose are governed and reproducible where necessary.

Repeated generation, partial failure, entropy-source degradation, duplicated output, unsupported parameters, or boundary self-test failure produces a non-active state. A caller cannot retry until a convenient key appears or bypass health checks.

Test keys are generated separately and cannot be promoted to production by metadata change. Imported legacy keys undergo origin, strength, purpose, custody, exposure, and lifecycle assessment before acceptance.

### Key Import and Migration

Key import is permitted only when business, interoperability, customer custody, migration, or recovery requires it. Imported keys receive the same inventory, classification, policy, cryptoperiod, access, audit, and destruction controls as generated keys.

The import path verifies source authority, key type, algorithm profile, key integrity, tenant, environment, intended use, prior exposure, exportability, and target cryptographic boundary. Import does not silently extend the original cryptoperiod.

Transfer uses wrapped or otherwise strongly protected key material, authenticated endpoints, restricted operators, one-time transaction identity, replay resistance, and complete reconciliation. Temporary transfer material is destroyed after successful import.

Migration confirms that the target boundary can perform required operations, consumers use the new key, protected data or subordinate keys remain accessible, verification audiences receive updated trust material, and the source copy is revoked, archived, or destroyed according to the plan.

Failed migration does not leave two undocumented active authorities. Overlap is explicit, bounded, and monitored.

### Activation, Use, and Cryptoperiod

A generated or imported key is not usable until formally activated. Activation confirms inventory, purpose, authorized consumers, cryptographic profile, key relationships, policy, target systems, recovery posture, audit readiness, and required approval.

Every key has a cryptoperiod appropriate to algorithm strength, key type, data sensitivity, usage volume, exposure, environment, threat, rotation capability, contractual requirements, and the period during which protected information must remain secure.

Operational requests identify the authenticated workload or custodian, tenant, task or service purpose, key reference, requested operation, target data or artifact reference, environment, validity, and applicable authorization. The boundary rejects unregistered operations, wrong purpose, wrong tenant, expired state, revoked state, unsupported parameters, and excessive usage.

Keys are not exposed to the AI & Intelligence Layer, repository content, logs, telemetry, Audit Engine payloads, Evidence Chain payloads, support systems, or ordinary configuration. Model output cannot select an unapproved cryptographic key or authorize a key operation.

Use counters, rate, data volume, signature volume, peer identity, or other operational limits may be enforced where relevant. Unexpected use patterns are security signals.

### Key Access and Authorization

Key access follows Zero Trust, default deny, least privilege, and explicit authorization. Permissions distinguish create, register, read metadata, activate, request cryptographic operation, wrap, unwrap, derive, rotate, suspend, revoke, recover, export, archive, and destroy.

Possession of a key identifier, certificate, ciphertext, wrapped key, secret reference, capability, or administrative role does not authorize key use. The authorization tuple includes subject or workload, tenant, purpose, environment, key class and version, operation, target, data classification, policy, risk, approval, validity, and lifecycle state.

Applications receive permission to perform a defined operation, not blanket key administration. A service that may encrypt tenant data cannot automatically decrypt all historical data, export keys, sign artifacts, or rotate root trust.

Key administrators manage lifecycle and policy but do not receive unrestricted application-data access. Data administrators do not receive key custody. Auditors can inspect metadata and evidence without private-key use.

Administrative key operations require high-assurance authentication, just-in-time authorization, separation of duties, short sessions, enhanced monitoring, and review.

### Key Distribution and Availability for Use

Secret and private key material is not distributed in plaintext to ordinary consumers. Where possible, the consumer sends an operation to the protected cryptographic service or receives a wrapped, derived, task-bound, or ephemeral key suitable only for the approved context.

Public verification keys and trust material may be distributed broadly but are integrity-protected, versioned, attributable, and revocable. Consumers validate the authoritative source rather than accepting embedded or downloaded keys solely by location.

Distribution prevents substitution, rollback, replay, cross-tenant reference, wrong-environment use, and downgrade to a deprecated cryptographic profile. Key identifiers and trust bundles are pinned or resolved through an approved trust mechanism appropriate to the service.

Caches of key material are minimized. High-level keys are never cached outside their boundary. Derived or data keys may be cached only when encrypted, tenant-bound, process- or workload-bound, short-lived, revocable where feasible, and justified by performance requirements.

Availability designs replicate protected cryptographic capability without exposing plaintext keys or creating conflicting authority. Failover preserves key identity, version, usage policy, revocation, audit, and tenant isolation.

### Data Encryption Key Management

Data-encryption keys are scoped to limit blast radius. Scoping may use tenant, data classification, object class, storage domain, region, environment, time period, service, or data set. A single platform-wide data key is prohibited where it would create unacceptable cross-tenant or systemic exposure.

Every encrypted object or protected data set can be associated with the key identifier and version required for authorized decryption without embedding secret key material. Metadata supports rotation, re-protection, re-encryption, recovery, and destruction.

Key-encryption keys protect data-encryption keys. Rotation of a key-encryption key re-wraps or otherwise re-protects subordinate keys under controlled reconciliation. Rotation of a data-encryption key applies to new data and, when required, re-encrypts existing data through an attributable migration.

Deletion or cryptographic destruction of a data key may render associated ciphertext irrecoverable. Such action is treated as destructive disposal, requires explicit authorization, dependency analysis, legal-hold verification, backup treatment, and evidence.

### Signing and Verification Key Management

Signing keys are separated by signer identity, purpose, environment, artifact class, and assurance. Code signing, release signing, identity assertions, audit or evidence checkpoint signing, administrative policy publication, and transport authentication do not share one private key.

Signing occurs within the approved boundary after verifying the subject, artifact or message digest, purpose, policy, and required approval. The private key is not delivered to build workers, release pipelines, administrators, or model processes.

The signed object identifies or references the signing key version, algorithm profile, signer, time, purpose, and relevant provenance. Verification confirms signature validity, trust path, key status at signing time where supported, object integrity, signer authority, and intended purpose.

Revocation of a signing key affects future trust and may affect historical verification. The architecture preserves status, timestamps, transparency, evidence, or archival trust information sufficient to evaluate historical signatures according to policy.

Compromise response distinguishes between signatures created before, during, and after the suspected compromise window. A replacement key does not automatically make prior malicious signatures harmless.

### Trust Anchors, Certificates, and Machine Identity

Trust anchors and certificates establish service, workload, device, integration, or signing identity under a defined trust domain. Their issuance, renewal, revocation, distribution, and validation are governed as key-management operations.

Certificate or assertion validity is bounded and does not replace authorization. Consumers validate the expected identity, audience or endpoint, trust chain, purpose, environment, validity, revocation state, and applicable naming constraints.

Automated renewal is preferred for short-lived machine identity where the deployment supports it. Automation uses authenticated workloads and cannot issue arbitrary identities or broaden authorization.

Private identity keys are non-exportable where supported and bound to the workload, device, cryptographic module, or deployment. Cloning, image restoration, device transfer, or workload migration receives explicit re-enrollment and revocation treatment.

Trust-store changes are high-impact administrative actions. Adding a root, removing a trust anchor, changing validation rules, or accepting an external authority requires controlled review, testing, activation, audit, and rollback.

### Device and Endpoint Key Management

Device-bound keys support device identity, protected local storage, user authentication, and secure communication. They are generated within the strongest protected device boundary available and are non-exportable where supported.

Device keys are bound to device registration, user or workload relationship, tenant, application, purpose, and lifecycle. A registered device key does not grant unrestricted access and remains subject to authentication and authorization.

Device loss, secure-state reset, reinstallation, ownership transfer, clone detection, compromise, or retirement revokes associated trust and requires fresh enrollment. Backup or synchronization of device private keys is prohibited unless an explicitly designed protected recovery process exists.

Local data-encryption keys may be wrapped to device and user context. Offline access uses narrow scope, expiry, protected counters or replay controls where supported, and reconciliation. Endpoint keys do not become a route for exporting tenant master keys.

### Customer-Managed and Externally Controlled Keys

ILAIOS may support platform-managed keys, customer-managed keys, customer-supplied keys, or customer-held keys according to deployment and product policy. The selected model defines custody, generation, location, availability, rotation, revocation, recovery, audit, support, and service-termination responsibilities.

In a customer-managed model, ILAIOS uses an authorized key reference or cryptographic operation without silently copying the key into an unmanaged platform store. Customer custody does not weaken ILAIOS tenant binding, workload authentication, authorization, purpose limitation, audit, or failure controls.

Customer key revocation or unavailability may make tenant data or operations inaccessible. This behavior is explicit in the service contract and operational design. ILAIOS does not bypass customer control by retaining an undisclosed recoverable copy.

Customer-supplied import follows the controlled migration process. Key origin, strength, exposure, purpose, and cryptoperiod are assessed. Importing a key does not prove that its prior custody was secure.

Support and recovery procedures respect customer custody. Secret key material is never requested through ordinary support communication.

### Rotation, Re-Wrapping, and Re-Encryption

Rotation is driven by cryptoperiod, usage, data volume, algorithm transition, personnel or workload change, tenant policy, provider requirement, compromise, vulnerability, or operational risk.

Rotation creates a new key version. Activation, consumer migration, trust distribution, data re-protection, overlap, retirement, and destruction are controlled stages. Historical key state remains attributable.

Re-wrapping changes the key-encryption protection applied to subordinate keys without necessarily decrypting the protected application data. Re-encryption decrypts and encrypts data under a new data key within a protected migration path. The architecture identifies which operation is required and validates completion.

Overlap between old and new keys is minimized and purpose-specific. Old encryption keys may remain decrypt-only for a bounded migration period. Old signing keys stop producing signatures at cutover but may remain available for historical verification under controlled policy.

Rotation must not create data loss, unverifiable evidence, invalid artifacts, or indefinite dual authority. Reconciliation counts affected objects, subordinate keys, services, signatures, trust stores, and failures.

### Revocation, Suspension, and Compromise

Suspension temporarily prevents key use while preserving the option of controlled restoration. Revocation permanently withdraws authority for defined operations. Destruction removes or renders key material irrecoverable according to policy.

Triggers include suspected compromise, confirmed exposure, unauthorized use, cryptographic weakness, expired cryptoperiod, owner termination, device loss, workload compromise, provider incident, algorithm deprecation, tenant termination, or trust-domain change.

Compromise response identifies the key class, version, parent and child relationships, protected data, signatures, identities, tenants, regions, consumers, backups, devices, and time window affected. The response may suspend operations, revoke trust, rotate dependent keys, re-encrypt data, re-sign artifacts, invalidate sessions, or initiate incident response.

Compromise of a parent key requires analysis of all subordinate keys and protected material. Replacing only the exposed leaf key is insufficient when wrapping or trust hierarchy may also be affected.

Revocation status propagates to enforcement and verification points within risk-based objectives. Cached or offline verifiers receive explicit freshness and fail behavior.

### Key Backup, Escrow, and Recovery

Key backup is permitted only when recoverability is required and does not undermine the intended non-exportability or destruction model. Ephemeral, session, or replaceable keys may be intentionally non-recoverable.

Backup copies are encrypted or wrapped under separate recovery protection, stored in a distinct security domain, tenant-bound, integrity-protected, inventoried, access-controlled, and subject to dual control. Backup operators do not receive plaintext keys.

Key escrow is not assumed. Where legal, contractual, product, or customer requirements mandate escrow, the scope, custodian, release conditions, jurisdiction, audit, notification, dual control, and destruction are explicit.

Recovery requires named authority, strong authentication, purpose, incident or continuity reference, dual control where required, source integrity verification, target cryptographic boundary verification, inventory reconciliation, and post-recovery rotation when exposure risk warrants.

Recovery testing verifies that protected data and services can be restored without exposing production key material in test evidence. Test results record process and outcome, not key values.

Restored keys retain their original identity and lifecycle state. Expired, revoked, compromised, or destroyed keys are not reactivated merely because a backup exists.

### Key Destruction and Cryptographic Erasure

Key destruction is an irreversible high-impact operation. It requires confirmation of owner, tenant, key version, dependencies, protected data, signatures, backups, replicas, recovery copies, legal hold, retention, active consumers, and approval.

Destruction removes key material from the primary cryptographic boundary and addresses replicas, caches, devices, migration copies, backup copies, recovery shares, and external providers according to the declared assurance.

Cryptographic erasure uses destruction of the controlling key to make ciphertext inaccessible. It is valid only when the key is not recoverable elsewhere and all protected data dependencies are understood. It does not delete plaintext copies or data encrypted under another key.

Lifecycle metadata, public verification material where needed, destruction evidence, and non-secret audit records may remain. They clearly state that private or secret material is no longer available.

Failed or partial destruction remains an unresolved security state. The system does not report cryptographic erasure complete while recoverable copies remain.

### Algorithm Policy and Crypto-Agility

ILAIOS maintains a versioned cryptographic policy defining approved algorithms, modes, key sizes or security-strength profiles, random generation, derivation methods, protocols, module requirements, permitted legacy verification, transition dates, prohibited uses, and exceptions.

Application code and persisted data formats identify algorithms and key versions through controlled metadata rather than hidden assumptions. Cryptographic implementations are replaceable behind governed interfaces. Keys are not hardcoded to one provider, hardware product, algorithm family, or deployment topology.

Crypto-agility includes inventory, dependency mapping, dual-read or dual-verification capability where required, controlled migration, rollback safety, performance assessment, interoperability testing, and evidence. Agility does not mean arbitrary runtime selection by callers.

Deprecated algorithms or insufficient security profiles are disabled for new protection by policy. Legacy decryption or verification may remain temporarily where required for migration or historical validation, under narrow controls and explicit deadlines.

The architecture maintains readiness for post-quantum migration. Long-lived confidentiality, signatures, identity, evidence retention, and external interoperability are assessed for future transition. Adoption occurs through approved cryptographic policy and validated implementation rather than ad hoc algorithm substitution.

### Evidence Chain and Long-Term Verification

Evidence Chain records are protected through cryptographic hashes and, where the deployment requires, signed checkpoints, manifests, attestations, or verification packages. Keys used for evidence signing are distinct from application, transport, tenant data, and code-signing keys.

Evidence key rotation preserves the ability to verify records produced under prior authorized versions. Verification packages identify the key version, trust chain, algorithm profile, validity, revocation information, and historical verification limitations.

Private evidence keys are protected from event producers and ordinary audit administrators. A producer cannot sign, reorder, or rewrite canonical evidence merely because it emits an event.

Key compromise does not permit silent repair of historical evidence. The incident records the suspected interval, affected checkpoints, verification consequences, replacement trust, and any independent corroboration.

The Evidence Chain does not require blockchain infrastructure. Key management supports controlled cryptographic trust without introducing a distributed ledger requirement.

### Logging, Audit, and Evidence

Private and secret key material never appears in logs, traces, metrics, crash dumps, diagnostic exports, source repositories, task state, model context, Audit Engine payloads, or Evidence Chain payloads.

Material key events include request, generation, import, activation, use where required, denial, derivation, wrapping, unwrapping, distribution, certificate issuance, renewal, rotation, re-wrapping, re-encryption, suspension, revocation, compromise, recovery, export, archive, destruction, policy change, trust-store change, and break-glass access.

Audit records identify key reference and version, key class, tenant, environment, requested operation, authenticated subject or workload, policy decision, approval, cryptographic boundary, target, outcome, reason, time, and correlation without exposing key bytes.

Designated inventory records, key ceremonies, trust changes, signed checkpoints, rotation confirmations, recovery outcomes, and destruction evidence are bound to the Evidence Chain.

Access to key metadata and audit records is separately authorized. Metadata may reveal high-value systems, tenant relationships, cryptographic topology, or compromise response.

### Availability, Failure, and Degraded Operation

Key management is a critical dependency. Boundary unavailability, failed authentication, denied authorization, tenant mismatch, invalid key state, expired cryptoperiod, revocation uncertainty, trust-path failure, random-source failure, self-test failure, replication inconsistency, time failure, backup corruption, or algorithm-policy conflict produces an explicit non-success state.

Consumers fail closed when a mandatory key operation cannot be performed or verified. They do not use hardcoded fallback keys, development keys, unrelated tenant keys, expired cached keys, weaker algorithms, disabled trust anchors, or unapproved local cryptography.

Policy may define bounded continuity for specific low-risk verification or encryption scenarios using recently validated local material. Such continuity has narrow scope, short lifetime, no key administration, declared degraded assurance, protected local state, audit, and reconciliation.

High-risk signing, key issuance, root trust, key export, recovery, destructive cryptographic erasure, and privileged identity operations fail closed when current authority or boundary assurance is unavailable.

Recovery verifies inventory, hierarchy, active versions, cryptographic policy, module health, tenant isolation, revocation, trust stores, protected data accessibility, audit continuity, Evidence Chain checkpoints, and consumer readiness.

### Governance, Testing, and Metrics

Key-management governance defines cryptographic policy, key classes, hierarchy, assurance boundaries, ownership, custody, tenant models, cryptoperiods, rotation, recovery, escrow, destruction, algorithm transitions, customer-managed patterns, exceptions, and review cadence.

Conformance testing includes generation quality, wrong-purpose use, cross-tenant access, wrong-environment access, unauthorized export, boundary enforcement, hierarchy isolation, derivation context, wrapping, rotation, re-wrapping, re-encryption, revocation, certificate renewal, trust-store change, backup restore, dual control, break-glass, algorithm transition, destruction, failover, and audit-completeness tests.

Cryptographic module and implementation assurance is selected according to deployment risk and applicable obligations. Validation of a module is evidence about that module's controls; it does not by itself establish correct application integration, key policy, supply-chain trust, or operational governance.

Metrics include unregistered keys, keys past cryptoperiod, ownerless keys, excessive-purpose keys, exportable high-impact keys, failed rotations, rotation duration, re-encryption backlog, trust-store drift, certificate expiry risk, revoked-key use attempts, cross-tenant attempts, unauthorized export attempts, recovery-test outcomes, partial destruction, algorithm-policy exceptions, deprecated-algorithm use, compromise-response time, and incomplete key evidence.

Metrics do not justify extending unsafe cryptoperiods or retaining deprecated algorithms. A key with no observed misuse may still require immediate replacement when custody or cryptographic strength is inadequate.

### Key Management Limitations

Strong key management cannot compensate for incorrect cryptographic design, vulnerable application use, compromised authorized workloads, plaintext data exposure before encryption or after decryption, malicious endpoints, incorrect policy, or weak external systems.

Key protection reduces risk but cannot make a compromised root of trust harmless. ILAIOS combines key management with Zero Trust, authentication, authorization, Secrets Management, encryption, restricted execution, secure engineering, validation, monitoring, incident response, Audit Engine, and Evidence Chain controls.

### Key Management Invariants

The following invariants are canonical:

- every production key and trust anchor has an accountable owner, tenant or platform domain, purpose, environment, algorithm profile, permitted operations, cryptoperiod, lifecycle state, and authoritative inventory record;
- keys are generated or imported only through approved cryptographic boundaries and governed lifecycle processes;
- human-chosen production keys and unregistered production keys are prohibited;
- private and secret key material never appears in source code, ordinary configuration, model context, task state, logs, telemetry, audit payloads, evidence payloads, reports, or support systems;
- key purpose is explicit, and encryption, signing, authentication, key wrapping, message authentication, tokenization, evidence, and recovery keys are not reused across unrelated purposes;
- tenant, environment, region, and purpose isolation apply to key namespace, policy, generation, storage, use, backup, recovery, and destruction;
- production and non-production key domains are separate and cryptographically non-interchangeable;
- root and key-encryption keys receive stronger protection, minimal use, and separation of duties appropriate to their blast radius;
- high-level private and secret keys remain inside the approved boundary in plaintext and applications request operations rather than key bytes;
- key access is authenticated, default-deny, least-privilege, purpose-bound, tenant-bound, time-bound, and auditable;
- possession of a key identifier, certificate, ciphertext, wrapped key, role, or capability does not independently authorize key use;
- key hierarchy and parent-child relationships are inventoried and compromise analysis includes dependent keys and protected data;
- rotation creates a new version and controls activation, overlap, re-wrapping, re-encryption, retirement, and historical verification;
- revocation propagates to use and verification points according to risk and cannot be bypassed by stale caches;
- customer-managed custody changes the key boundary but never weakens ILAIOS identity, authorization, tenant, audit, or failure controls;
- backup and recovery preserve key identity, lifecycle, tenant isolation, dual control, and revocation state;
- destroyed or revoked key material is never reactivated from backup;
- cryptographic erasure is claimed only when all recoverable controlling key copies are addressed and dependencies are understood;
- algorithm and security-strength policy is versioned, replaceable, transition-ready, and independent of caller preference;
- long-term evidence verification remains possible across governed key rotation and cryptographic transition; and
- all material key lifecycle events are recorded without exposing key material.

An implementation is non-conformant if it uses one key for unrelated purposes or tenants; stores private keys in source, configuration, logs, model context, audit, or evidence payloads; allows applications or administrators to export high-level keys routinely; accepts human-chosen or unregistered production keys; mixes production and test trust; permits a key identifier or role to authorize use; bypasses the protected cryptographic boundary; rotates metadata without migrating or revoking actual key use; restores revoked keys from backup; destroys a key without dependency and legal-hold analysis; claims cryptographic erasure while recoverable copies remain; allows caller-selected deprecated algorithms; lacks transition capability; or permits key-management failure to trigger hardcoded fallback keys or weaker cryptography.

## 3.6 Encryption

### Purpose and Security Boundary

Encryption protects the confidentiality of ILAIOS data against unauthorized disclosure while data is stored, transmitted, replicated, backed up, exported, processed through approved external services, or retained on supported endpoints. Where integrity and authenticity are required, encryption is combined with approved authenticated-encryption, message-authentication, signature, or protocol controls appropriate to the data and threat model.

Encryption is one security control within the ILAIOS Zero Trust architecture. It does not grant authorization, prove identity, validate business correctness, establish tenant ownership, prevent an authorized application from misusing plaintext, or replace the Audit Engine and Evidence Chain. A subject that can decrypt data must still be authenticated, authorized, purpose-bound, tenant-bound, and audited.

The Policy Engine determines the required protection profile from verified data classification, tenant, purpose, environment, residency, lifecycle, destination, and risk. The Key Management architecture in Section 3.5 supplies governed cryptographic keys and trust material. Secrets Management in Section 3.4 protects credentials and confidential configuration. This section defines how cryptographic protection is applied to data and communication.

The architecture remains technology-agnostic. Algorithms, modes, protocols, modules, and providers are selected through a versioned cryptographic policy rather than embedded permanently in product architecture. Implementations may differ while preserving approved security strength, authenticated protection, key separation, tenant isolation, nonce discipline, protocol validation, crypto-agility, auditability, and failure behavior.

### Security Services and Terminology

ILAIOS distinguishes cryptographic security services to prevent inaccurate assurance claims.

| Security service | Purpose | What it does not prove |
|---|---|---|
| Encryption | Conceals plaintext from parties without authorized decryption capability | Does not prove the sender, integrity, permission, or correctness by itself |
| Authenticated encryption | Protects confidentiality and detects unauthorized modification within the defined construction and associated context | Does not establish business authorization or semantic truth |
| Message authentication | Detects modification and authenticates possession of approved shared key material | Does not provide confidentiality |
| Digital signature | Binds integrity and signer authority to a signed object under the applicable trust model | Does not conceal content or prove the signer made a correct decision |
| Cryptographic hash | Produces a fixed-length integrity representation for controlled uses | Does not encrypt content and does not prove origin without additional controls |
| Tokenization or pseudonymization | Replaces sensitive values with controlled representations | Does not necessarily anonymize data or remove regulatory obligations |

The term encrypted shall be used only where an approved cryptographic mechanism protects confidentiality. Encoding, compression, serialization, masking, redaction, hashing, obfuscation, access control, proprietary file format, or private network placement is not encryption.

Plaintext means data in a form accessible without the intended cryptographic protection, regardless of whether the representation is human-readable. Decrypted data, data in application memory, transformed sensitive data, and keys accessible to a process may all be plaintext from the threat model's perspective.

### Data-State Protection Model

Encryption requirements apply according to data state:

- **Data at rest:** persistent data in databases, object stores, filesystems, volumes, repositories, indexes, artifacts, logs, backups, archives, snapshots, endpoint storage, and removable or migration media.
- **Data in transit:** data crossing process, service, host, device, network, region, provider, tenant, integration, administrative, replication, backup, or delivery boundaries.
- **Data in use:** plaintext present in application memory, execution workers, validation environments, cryptographic modules, processors, or device-bound components during authorized processing.
- **Transient data:** queues, caches, buffers, temporary files, intermediary artifacts, working directories, crash state, and short-lived replicas.
- **Exported or delivered data:** customer downloads, evidence packages, reports, external-system payloads, recovery media, and controlled inter-organizational transfers.

Protection is selected per state and threat. Storage-layer encryption may protect lost media but not an attacker using authorized database credentials. Application-layer encryption may protect selected fields from storage operators but adds key, search, migration, and availability complexity. Transport encryption protects the communication path but not compromised endpoints. The architecture selects layered controls according to the risk rather than claiming that one encrypted layer protects every state.

### Data Classification and Encryption Policy

Every governed data object has a tenant, classification, authoritative source, purpose, residency, retention, and permitted processing path. Encryption policy maps those attributes to a protection profile.

A protection profile defines:

- whether encryption is mandatory at rest, in transit, in transient storage, on endpoints, and in exports;
- the approved algorithm and mode profile;
- key class, tenant domain, environment, cryptoperiod, and customer-managed requirements;
- authenticated associated context;
- protocol, peer-authentication, and downgrade requirements;
- allowed processing regions, providers, devices, and execution boundaries;
- plaintext exposure limits;
- backup, replication, recovery, and destruction behavior;
- legacy read or verification rules;
- migration and re-encryption requirements; and
- audit and evidence obligations.

Classification may increase after aggregation, transformation, indexing, or enrichment. Derived content does not become less sensitive merely because identifiers were removed or the output was generated by an intelligence capability.

Unknown, conflicting, or missing classification prevents use of a weaker protection profile. A caller cannot request no encryption or select an algorithm directly to improve performance or compatibility. Exceptions require formal risk review, defined scope, expiry, compensating controls, and approval.

### Encryption at Rest

Sensitive and tenant data at rest shall be encrypted according to the applicable protection profile. Coverage includes primary stores, replicas, indexes, caches, search projections, task state, artifact stores, audit payload stores, evidence payload stores, temporary persistence, endpoint storage, backups, snapshots, exports under platform custody, and disaster-recovery copies.

Storage or volume encryption provides a baseline against media theft, decommissioning failure, and certain infrastructure exposures. It does not replace object-, field-, application-, or tenant-level encryption where administrators, database processes, backup systems, or shared infrastructure must be excluded from plaintext access.

Application or object-level encryption is used where data classification, tenant isolation, operator access, external provider risk, legal requirement, or cryptographic deletion requires stronger separation. The encryption boundary and plaintext processing component are documented.

Encrypted objects include metadata sufficient to identify the cryptographic profile, key reference and version, format version, nonce or initialization data, integrity tag or equivalent, associated-data version, and migration state without exposing secret material.

Plaintext temporary files, unencrypted indexes, materialized views, search caches, debug copies, and export staging areas are prohibited unless an approved bounded process explicitly requires them and applies equivalent access, isolation, duration, cleanup, and audit controls.

### Database and Structured Data Encryption

Database encryption uses layered controls selected by data classification. Storage encryption protects underlying media. Connection encryption protects communication. Column, field, record, or application-layer encryption may protect sensitive values from broader database access.

Schema design identifies which fields remain queryable metadata and which require stronger encryption. Sensitive values shall not be duplicated into unencrypted derived columns, search terms, analytics stores, audit text, or cache keys.

Deterministic or searchable encryption, format-preserving encryption, and similar specialized mechanisms reveal patterns or structural information and receive explicit threat assessment. They are not used by default. The leakage profile, key scope, collision behavior, query purpose, and migration path are documented.

Database identifiers and tenant keys remain tenant-bound. A record from one tenant cannot be decrypted under another tenant's context. Backup, replica, read-only, analytics, and disaster-recovery access apply the same cryptographic domain.

Application code handles decryption only in the component and operation authorized for plaintext use. General database administrators, analytics users, and support personnel do not receive decryption authority by virtue of data-store access.

### Object, File, and Artifact Encryption

Files, objects, generated artifacts, evidence packages, repository snapshots, validation subjects, and delivery packages are encrypted when required by classification, tenant policy, destination, or retention.

Object encryption binds ciphertext to the object identity, tenant, version, classification, and intended context through authenticated associated data or equivalent integrity-bound metadata. Moving ciphertext to another identifier or tenant does not make it valid in the new context.

Large artifacts use streaming or segmented protection that preserves per-segment and whole-object integrity. Partial reads, resumable transfer, and range access cannot omit authentication or permit segment substitution.

The exact artifact validated for acceptance and delivery is integrity-identical to the protected artifact referenced by the task. Encryption or packaging performed after validation is itself governed and verified so that the underlying accepted bytes remain traceable.

Encrypted archives and containers do not excuse unsafe internal files. Extraction occurs in a restricted, tenant-bound workspace with path, size, recursion, and cleanup controls. Archive passwords are not an approved enterprise encryption architecture.

### Encryption in Transit

All material data crossing a trust boundary uses an approved secure transport profile that provides confidentiality, integrity, peer authentication appropriate to the connection, replay protection where applicable, and resistance to protocol downgrade.

Encryption in transit applies to:

- user and administrator connections;
- service-to-service communication;
- control-plane and execution-plane communication;
- Tool Gateway and adapter traffic;
- device-bound and companion communication;
- model and provider requests;
- database, messaging, storage, cache, and search connections;
- audit and evidence ingestion;
- replication, backup, recovery, and migration traffic;
- integration callbacks and webhooks;
- artifact upload, download, export, and delivery; and
- management, monitoring, and support interfaces.

Internal networks, private links, local host communication, cluster placement, or shared infrastructure do not remove the requirement. Encryption may be omitted only for a specifically assessed communication boundary where equivalent physical or cryptographic isolation exists and policy explicitly permits it.

Clients and services validate the intended peer identity, trust path, endpoint, validity, purpose, and revocation state. Encryption to an unverified endpoint protects confidentiality from passive observers but may deliver plaintext to an attacker.

Plaintext fallback, silent protocol downgrade, acceptance of invalid trust, disabled verification, and opportunistic encryption for mandatory protected traffic are prohibited. Connection failure produces denial or explicitly governed degraded behavior, not insecure retry.

### Service-to-Service and Workload Communication

Service-to-service channels bind transport protection to authenticated workload identity and authorized audience. A secure channel from an unknown or unauthorized service is not sufficient access.

Mutual peer authentication is required where the risk and deployment model demand verification of both endpoints. Short-lived machine identity and automated trust renewal are preferred where supported, but rotation does not interrupt tenant isolation or authorization.

Service meshes, proxies, gateways, or platform transport layers may provide encryption, but application owners remain accountable for verifying coverage, peer identity, termination points, plaintext hops, policy, certificate lifecycle, and failure mode.

Where encryption terminates at an intermediary, the downstream plaintext boundary is explicit, isolated, authorized, and protected. An external secure connection does not justify an unencrypted internal hop containing sensitive data.

Diagnostic packet capture, proxy logging, tracing, and performance tooling shall not record decrypted payloads by default. Exceptional capture requires narrow scope, authorization, secure handling, short retention, and review.

### Authenticated Encryption and Integrity

Confidential data shall use an approved authenticated-encryption construction where applicable. Encryption without integrity protection may permit undetected modification, reordering, truncation, substitution, or manipulation.

Authenticated associated data binds relevant non-secret context such as tenant, object identity, version, content type, schema, sequence, purpose, and key reference to the ciphertext. Associated data is canonicalized and verified consistently. It is not a location for secrets.

Authentication tags or equivalent integrity results are validated before plaintext is released to downstream processing. Failure produces rejection and a material security event. Applications must not expose partially decrypted unauthenticated content.

Where separate encryption and integrity mechanisms are required for an approved design, their key separation, ordering, canonicalization, and verification behavior are explicit and tested. Custom cryptographic constructions are prohibited unless formally approved through specialist review and an ADR.

Signatures may provide origin and public verifiability for artifacts, releases, or evidence. They do not replace confidentiality when content must remain secret.

### Nonce, Initialization Value, and Randomness Discipline

Encryption modes and protocols that require a nonce or initialization value shall generate and manage it according to the approved cryptographic profile. Uniqueness, unpredictability, or both are enforced according to the selected mechanism.

Reuse under the same key is prohibited where it compromises confidentiality or integrity. Distributed workers, retries, failover, backup restoration, clock rollback, counter reset, and parallel processing must not cause unsafe reuse.

Nonce construction is controlled by the cryptographic implementation rather than arbitrary caller input. If callers provide context, the implementation validates format, domain, uniqueness, and relationship to the key.

Randomness used for keys, nonces, salts, padding, and protocol challenges comes from an approved source. Degraded random-source health fails the cryptographic operation rather than falling back to timestamps, predictable counters, process identifiers, or general-purpose pseudorandom generation.

Nonce and initialization data may be stored with ciphertext when the cryptographic profile permits. It is not treated as a secret unless the selected construction requires secrecy.

### Envelope Encryption and Key Binding

Envelope encryption separates data-encryption keys from higher-level key-encryption keys. Data is protected with a scoped data key, while the data key is wrapped or otherwise protected under a managed parent key.

The encrypted object records the data-key reference or wrapped key, parent-key version, cryptographic profile, and authenticated context required for authorized decryption. It does not contain plaintext key material.

The wrapping context includes tenant, environment, purpose, resource class, and other domain-separation attributes where supported. A wrapped key copied to another tenant or context cannot be unwrapped successfully.

Key rotation and re-wrapping follow Section 3.5. Re-wrapping a data key changes its parent protection; it does not claim that application data was re-encrypted. Re-encryption creates a new ciphertext under a new data key or profile and requires integrity verification and reconciliation.

Failure to unwrap, key-version mismatch, wrong tenant, invalid associated data, or revoked key produces denial. The application cannot try arbitrary keys until plaintext appears plausible.

### Tenant Cryptographic Isolation

Tenant separation applies to keys, encryption context, ciphertext metadata, caches, backups, exports, recovery, re-encryption, and destruction. A tenant identifier is cryptographically or policy-bound to protected data where appropriate, not merely stored as an unverified label.

Per-tenant or more granular data-encryption keys are used where the sensitivity and blast-radius model require them. Shared keys are permitted only for explicitly defined platform data whose cross-tenant risk is acceptable and whose access remains tenant-governed.

Ciphertext from one tenant cannot be moved, replayed, restored, or decrypted in another tenant context. Cross-tenant analytics or aggregate processing uses a separately approved data treatment and cryptographic domain.

Customer-managed key models preserve tenant control without allowing silent platform fallback to an undisclosed key. If the customer key is unavailable or revoked, affected operations fail according to the declared service model.

Tenant termination or cryptographic deletion verifies key dependencies, legal holds, backups, shared data, derived data, exports, and recovery copies before destruction.

### Data in Use and Plaintext Exposure

Encryption cannot protect data while an authorized process is actively using plaintext unless an additional protected-computation architecture is employed. ILAIOS therefore minimizes plaintext exposure through isolation, least privilege, process boundaries, memory hygiene, short-lived workers, data minimization, and controlled interfaces.

Only the component responsible for an authorized operation receives plaintext. Orchestrators, model gateways, audit services, monitoring systems, and support tools do not receive plaintext merely because they coordinate or observe the task.

Restricted workers decrypt only task-specific inputs in an isolated workspace and remove plaintext after use. Validation runners receive read-only protected subjects and decrypt only the material required for approved checks.

Memory dumps, swap, hibernation, crash reports, debugging, process inspection, shared memory, inter-process communication, and temporary storage are evaluated as plaintext-exposure paths. High-risk workloads may require stronger memory, host, or hardware isolation according to deployment policy.

Protected-computation technologies may be used where justified, but their availability does not eliminate authentication, authorization, key management, side-channel analysis, output control, or validation.

### Transient Data, Queues, and Caches

Queues, caches, buffers, temporary objects, intermediate transformations, staging files, and retry stores inherit the classification of the source data and are encrypted when the protection profile requires it.

Message encryption binds tenant, producer, consumer, topic or queue, task, sequence, schema, and expiry where appropriate. Broker-level encryption does not replace message-level protection when broker administrators or shared infrastructure must not access plaintext.

Cache keys and indexes shall not reveal sensitive content. Cached plaintext is minimized, tenant-bound, process- or service-scoped, time-limited, access-controlled, and invalidated with the source. Caches are not exempt from residency or deletion.

Retry and dead-letter storage must not become long-lived unencrypted archives. Failed messages retain protected content, reason, tenant, and lifecycle controls.

Temporary plaintext is deleted promptly after success, failure, cancellation, or timeout. Cleanup failure creates a material event and may quarantine the affected worker or storage boundary.

### Secrets, Credentials, and Key-Material Encryption

Secrets and confidential credentials are encrypted at rest and in transit, but encryption alone is insufficient. They remain subject to the specialized access, delivery, rotation, revocation, runtime, and logging controls in Section 3.4.

Private and secret keys are protected within the cryptographic boundaries defined in Section 3.5. Encrypting a private key file in general storage is not equivalent to non-exportable key custody or a governed cryptographic service.

Passwords, authentication factors, session artifacts, capabilities, and recovery material follow their own approved protection models. Values that require one-way verification are not stored through reversible encryption merely for convenience.

Encryption keys and the ciphertext they control shall not be stored under the same unprotected access boundary. Separation of key and data administration reduces the risk that one infrastructure compromise reveals both.

### Tool Gateway, Execution, and External Actions

The Tool Gateway enforces the approved encryption profile for data passed to and returned from tool adapters. It validates the target, tenant, data classification, transport profile, destination identity, execution environment, and required key domain before release.

Execution workers do not disable transport verification, accept untrusted certificates, select deprecated algorithms, or downgrade protection to accommodate a tool. If a target cannot meet the required profile, the operation is denied or uses an explicitly approved compensating design.

Credentials are resolved only after capability validation and are transmitted through protected channels. Tool outputs are treated as untrusted and may require encryption before persistence, validation, or return to the Control Plane.

External side effects and delivery destinations receive only the approved data projection. Encryption to a destination does not authorize the disclosure; destination authorization remains separate.

Retry, compensation, and callback flows revalidate destination identity, protocol, key status, and current authorization. Previously successful secure connection state is not assumed indefinitely.

### AI, Model, and Provider Encryption Boundary

Data sent through the Model Gateway uses an approved secure transport profile and a processing path eligible for the tenant, classification, purpose, residency, retention, and provider policy.

Transport encryption to a provider does not authorize sending the data, prevent provider-side plaintext processing, or prove compliant retention. ILAIOS minimizes input, removes secrets, applies policy, and records provenance before transmission.

Where tenant or deployment policy requires data to remain under a particular key or processing boundary, the Model Gateway selects a conformant local or approved protected path or denies the request. Provider availability does not justify decrypting or routing data through a weaker location.

Model responses are protected in transit and classified according to their source and derived content. They remain untrusted until structural validation, policy evaluation, and the downstream control path.

Encrypted prompts or payloads that the provider cannot process do not create meaningful end-to-end confidentiality. Claims of end-to-end encryption must identify every point at which plaintext is available and which party controls the keys.

### Endpoint, Mobile, Desktop, and Offline Encryption

Supported endpoints protect local tenant data, cached context, artifacts, credentials, device identity material, and offline state using the strongest approved platform protection available for the deployment.

Application-level protection is bound to the user, device, tenant, application, and purpose where supported. General full-disk encryption is a baseline control but does not prevent another authorized local process or user from reading application plaintext.

Backups, cloud synchronization, device transfer, screenshots, clipboard, notifications, accessibility services, removable media, file sharing, and crash reporting are evaluated as disclosure paths. Protected data is excluded or receives equivalent encryption and access controls.

Offline content has explicit scope, expiry, revocation behavior, key availability, replay protection, and deletion. A lost or retired device triggers revocation and, where risk requires, rotation of affected keys.

Device compromise may expose plaintext while the application is active. Endpoint posture, session security, restricted local execution, data minimization, and remote revocation reduce but do not eliminate this risk.

### Backup, Snapshot, Archive, and Disaster-Recovery Encryption

Backups, snapshots, archives, replicas, and disaster-recovery copies receive encryption at least equivalent to the source classification. Backup operators and storage administrators do not gain decryption authority automatically.

Backup keys are separated from ordinary storage credentials and governed under Section 3.5. Recovery copies preserve tenant, environment, region, key version, retention, legal hold, and revocation state.

Restore verifies backup provenance, ciphertext integrity, key availability, tenant destination, environment, data classification, retention eligibility, and current authorization before plaintext becomes available.

A restored historical snapshot does not reintroduce revoked secrets, expired keys, deleted tenant data, superseded policy, or vulnerable cryptographic configuration silently. Reconciliation applies current lifecycle and security state.

Long-term archives preserve the cryptographic information necessary for authorized decryption and integrity verification over the retention period, including migration plans when algorithms or key services change.

### Export, Delivery, and Customer-Controlled Encryption

Exports and deliveries are separately authorized and use a protection profile appropriate to destination, recipient, classification, retention, and transfer mechanism. Encryption protects the package but does not prove that the recipient is authorized.

Encrypted packages include a manifest identifying scope, tenant, source references, artifact digests, cryptographic profile, key or recipient trust reference, creation time, expiry where applicable, and verification instructions without exposing key material.

Password-protected archives are not the default enterprise transfer mechanism. Where legacy interoperability requires them, password delivery uses a separate protected channel, strong generated values, short validity, and formal exception.

Customer-controlled encryption may allow the recipient or tenant to hold decryption authority. Responsibilities for key custody, loss, rotation, revocation, recovery, and support are explicit. ILAIOS does not retain an undisclosed universal decryption key.

Export staging and temporary delivery copies follow the same classification, tenant, encryption, retention, and cleanup requirements as the final package.

### Tokenization, Pseudonymization, and Data Minimization

Tokenization and pseudonymization may reduce exposure by replacing sensitive identifiers with controlled representations. They are governed transformations with their own key, mapping, tenant, purpose, reversibility, access, retention, and deletion controls.

Reversible tokenization protects the mapping or cryptographic key as a high-value resource. Deterministic representations may enable correlation and pattern disclosure and require explicit risk assessment.

Pseudonymized data remains personal or sensitive where re-identification is reasonably possible. It is not described as anonymous solely because direct identifiers were removed.

Data minimization precedes encryption. ILAIOS does not collect or retain unnecessary data on the assumption that encryption makes all storage acceptable.

### Audit, Evidence, and Cryptographic Integrity

Audit records and Evidence Chain records are encrypted at rest and in transit according to classification, tenant, retention, and access requirements. Their append-only and hash-chain integrity remains distinct from encryption.

Evidence Chain hashes detect unauthorized modification of canonical records under the defined construction. Hashing does not conceal event content. Where evidence payloads contain sensitive information, confidentiality is provided by separate encryption and access controls.

Audit events record encryption policy version, cryptographic profile identifier, key reference and version, tenant, resource, operation, component, outcome, failure reason, migration state, and integrity status without storing plaintext, keys, nonces where sensitive, or reusable credentials.

Material events include encryption, decryption where required by policy, failed authentication, wrong-tenant attempts, protocol downgrade, invalid peer trust, key mismatch, migration, re-wrapping, re-encryption, export protection, restore, exception, and cryptographic deletion.

Evidence packages preserve verification across key and algorithm rotation. A successful decryption or valid tag does not prove business correctness, policy permission, or evidence completeness.

### Re-Encryption and Cryptographic Migration

Re-encryption is required when data changes key domain, tenant custody model, algorithm profile, provider, environment, residency, classification, or cryptoperiod according to policy.

Migration creates an attributable plan containing source profile, target profile, affected data, key relationships, batching, availability, rollback, validation, failure handling, evidence, and completion criteria.

The migration process decrypts and re-encrypts only within an approved protected boundary. Plaintext is not written to general staging storage. Each migrated object is verified for source integrity, target integrity, tenant, version, metadata, and accessibility.

Mixed-profile operation may be supported temporarily through explicit format and version metadata. New writes use the target profile after cutover. Legacy reads are bounded to migration and do not allow new data to use deprecated protection.

Completion reconciles all primary, replica, index, cache, backup, archive, export, and recovery dependencies. The former key or algorithm is not retired until required data and verification paths are accounted for.

### Crypto-Agility and Post-Quantum Transition

Encryption implementations use versioned profiles and replaceable cryptographic interfaces. Data formats identify the algorithm family, mode, parameters, key version, and format version required for controlled migration without allowing untrusted callers to select them.

Crypto-agility includes discovery of cryptographic use, dependency mapping, inventory, policy, interoperability testing, dual-profile transition where justified, performance and capacity planning, rollback, evidence, and deprecation.

The platform assesses long-lived confidentiality against future cryptographic threats. Data whose confidentiality must survive for extended periods receives a transition plan appropriate to current approved guidance, provider capability, interoperability, and risk.

Post-quantum migration affects key establishment, identity, transport, signatures, stored encrypted data, evidence retention, device support, external integrations, and customer-managed boundaries. Adoption occurs through validated profiles and controlled rollout, not by combining algorithms ad hoc.

Algorithm deprecation prevents new encryption under the deprecated profile. Time-limited legacy decryption may remain for migration under explicit authorization and monitoring.

### Error Handling and Failure Semantics

Cryptographic errors are explicit and fail closed. Invalid authentication tag, wrong key, wrong tenant, unsupported format, malformed ciphertext, truncated content, nonce violation, trust failure, expired certificate, deprecated profile, random-source failure, module self-test failure, and unavailable key service do not produce partial plaintext or fallback protection.

Error messages do not reveal whether guessed plaintext, key identity, padding, tag, or internal validation step was correct. Detailed diagnostics are restricted to authorized security channels.

Applications do not distinguish attacker-controlled cryptographic failures in a way that creates a practical oracle. Retry is bounded and does not attempt arbitrary keys, formats, or weaker profiles.

When encryption is mandatory and the service is unavailable, data is not stored or transmitted in plaintext. The task is denied, suspended, quarantined, or enters an explicitly governed bounded continuity mode.

Corrupted ciphertext is preserved as evidence where required and is never silently replaced with an empty, default, or reconstructed value.

### Availability and Degraded Operation

Encryption depends on cryptographic modules, keys, trust anchors, time, random generation, protocol endpoints, metadata, and policy. Each dependency has availability and recovery objectives appropriate to the data class.

High-risk decryption, signing, export, administrative access, cross-boundary transmission, and destructive key operations fail closed when current assurance is unavailable.

Policy may allow bounded continuity for specific low-risk local operations using recently validated protected key state and an approved current profile. Such continuity has strict expiry, tenant and resource scope, no algorithm downgrade, no new high-risk external transmission, declared degraded assurance, audit, and reconciliation.

Recovery verifies cryptographic policy, key state, trust stores, module health, tenant mapping, encrypted-object metadata, nonce or counter state where applicable, audit continuity, and access to protected data.

Restored services do not accept obsolete protocols, revoked trust, or deprecated algorithms solely because they existed in a backup configuration.

### Governance, Testing, and Metrics

Encryption governance defines data-state coverage, classification mappings, approved profiles, key relationships, module requirements, tenant models, endpoint controls, external-provider treatment, exception authority, migration, post-quantum readiness, and review cadence.

Conformance testing includes plaintext discovery, wrong-key and wrong-tenant decryption, authentication-tag failure, ciphertext modification, truncation, replay, nonce collision and reset, protocol downgrade, invalid peer trust, expired trust, service-to-service coverage, storage-layer bypass, index and cache leakage, temporary-file leakage, backup restore, endpoint loss, export protection, re-encryption, mixed-profile migration, cryptographic deletion, failure mode, and audit completeness.

Known-answer, interoperability, negative, fuzz, boundary, performance, recovery, and migration tests are applied according to the cryptographic profile. Custom cryptographic code receives specialist review and is avoided where approved implementations exist.

Metrics include unencrypted sensitive stores, plaintext network flows, deprecated-profile use, invalid-tag events, protocol-downgrade attempts, peer-validation failures, nonce-reuse detections, wrong-tenant attempts, encryption-policy exceptions, key-service failures, unencrypted temporary data, backup coverage, endpoint protection gaps, re-encryption backlog, migration failures, crypto inventory completeness, and long-lived data without a transition plan.

Metrics do not justify weaker protection. High encryption coverage does not excuse one known plaintext path for high-impact data.

### Encryption Limitations

Encryption protects data only while the attacker lacks authorized access to plaintext or controlling keys. It cannot prevent disclosure by a compromised authorized process, malicious recipient, unsafe endpoint, incorrect destination, overprivileged administrator, vulnerable application, or provider that legitimately receives plaintext for processing.

Encryption also does not prove data correctness, business authorization, lawful processing, complete deletion, or absence of metadata leakage. ILAIOS combines encryption with data minimization, Zero Trust, authentication, authorization, Secrets Management, Key Management, isolation, validation, monitoring, incident response, Audit Engine, and Evidence Chain controls.

### Encryption Invariants

The following invariants are canonical:

- encryption requirements derive from tenant, data classification, purpose, state, environment, residency, retention, destination, and risk;
- sensitive data is protected at rest, in transit, in transient storage, backups, exports, and supported endpoints according to its approved profile;
- encryption never substitutes for authentication, authorization, tenant isolation, validation, signing, hashing, audit, or evidence integrity;
- encoding, compression, masking, redaction, obfuscation, hashing, and access control are never represented as encryption;
- approved authenticated encryption is used where confidentiality and integrity are required;
- authentication or integrity verification completes before plaintext is released to downstream processing;
- keys are purpose-separated, tenant-bound, environment-bound, managed under Section 3.5, and never embedded with ciphertext in plaintext form;
- nonce and initialization-value requirements are enforced per approved profile, and unsafe reuse under the same key is prohibited;
- random generation failure produces cryptographic failure rather than predictable fallback;
- encrypted objects bind relevant tenant, object, version, schema, purpose, and key context through authenticated metadata or equivalent controls;
- internal networks, private links, local hosts, clusters, and service placement do not remove in-transit protection requirements;
- secure transport validates the intended peer and prohibits plaintext fallback, invalid trust, and silent downgrade;
- tenant ciphertext, keys, wrapping context, caches, backups, exports, recovery, and deletion remain isolated across tenants;
- only the authorized processing component receives plaintext, and exposure in memory, temporary storage, logs, diagnostics, and workers is minimized;
- secrets, credentials, and private keys retain their specialized controls and are not considered safe merely because stored in encrypted files;
- Tool Gateway and Model Gateway enforce classification, destination, tenant, transport, and provider eligibility before protected data crosses a boundary;
- backup, restore, archive, and disaster-recovery protection is at least equivalent to the source and never restores revoked trust silently;
- re-wrapping is distinguished from re-encryption, and migration verifies every affected data and key dependency;
- cryptographic profiles are versioned, replaceable, transition-ready, and not selected arbitrarily by callers;
- long-lived confidentiality receives crypto-agility and post-quantum transition planning;
- cryptographic errors fail closed without partial plaintext, oracle behavior, arbitrary-key retry, or weaker fallback; and
- material encryption, decryption, failure, migration, exception, and deletion events are auditable without exposing plaintext or keys.

An implementation is non-conformant if it labels encoding, masking, hashing, private networking, or storage permissions as encryption; encrypts without required integrity protection; releases unauthenticated plaintext; permits nonce reuse; accepts caller-selected or deprecated algorithms; stores the key beside ciphertext under the same unprotected boundary; leaves sensitive indexes, caches, backups, temporary files, or internal traffic unencrypted; disables peer verification; falls back to plaintext after failure; routes classified data to an ineligible provider because the channel is encrypted; treats volume encryption as protection from an authorized database process; restores revoked trust or obsolete profiles from backup; claims cryptographic deletion while keys or plaintext copies remain; or allows cryptographic failure to return partial, default, or reconstructed plaintext.

## 3.7 Secure Software Development Lifecycle

The ILAIOS Secure Software Development Lifecycle, or SSDLC, establishes the mandatory security system through which software, infrastructure, configuration, policy, schemas, integrations, documentation, and release artifacts are conceived, designed, implemented, verified, delivered, operated, changed, and retired. Security is a continuous engineering responsibility and an acceptance condition for every material change. It is not a final-stage assessment, a specialist-only activity, or a release-hardening exercise performed after functional completion.

The SSDLC protects both the software supply chain that produces ILAIOS and the product behavior delivered by that chain. It ensures that security requirements are explicit, architectural risks are understood before implementation, changes are attributable, dependencies are governed, builds are trustworthy, verification is independent where required, releases are immutable and traceable, deployed environments remain within approved state, and operational findings are returned to engineering through a controlled remediation process.

This section defines the security obligations and decision boundaries of the lifecycle. Section 4 defines the detailed engineering standards, repository rules, testing strategy, quality gates, integration and delivery controls, branching and review model, versioning, and release standards. Section 5 defines the broader product development workflow, feature and defect lifecycles, Definition of Done, change management, and continuous improvement. Those sections shall implement this security model without weakening it or duplicating its canonical requirements.

### Purpose and Security Objectives

The SSDLC has the following objectives:

- prevent known and reasonably foreseeable security defects from entering accepted designs, source repositories, release artifacts, or operating environments;
- convert security, privacy, tenant-isolation, resilience, evidence, and compliance obligations into traceable and testable engineering requirements;
- ensure that each material change has an identified owner, justified purpose, verified origin, approved scope, controlled implementation path, and retained evidence;
- preserve the canonical architecture and require a formal Architecture Decision Record when an accepted architectural decision must be superseded;
- separate development, validation, release authorization, deployment, and production operation according to risk and segregation-of-duties requirements;
- protect source, dependencies, build systems, credentials, signing identities, artifacts, deployment paths, and update channels against unauthorized modification;
- detect defects, malicious changes, vulnerable components, configuration drift, and supply-chain compromise before or as close as possible to introduction;
- ensure that security failures block or constrain progression rather than being silently converted into warnings;
- support timely, risk-based remediation and controlled emergency response without abandoning minimum security controls; and
- produce durable evidence sufficient to reconstruct what was required, changed, reviewed, tested, approved, built, released, deployed, and retired.

The SSDLC applies to all product and platform components, including Control Plane services, Trust Core modules, Tool Gateway, Model Gateway, Policy Engine, Approval Engine, Validation Pipeline, Audit Engine, Evidence Chain, Code Intelligence, user interfaces, APIs, clients, adapters, deployment definitions, infrastructure as code, policy packages, database changes, cryptographic profiles, telemetry configurations, build pipelines, operational automation, and security documentation. It also applies to prototypes or experiments that can access enterprise data, credentials, internal services, production-like environments, or reusable product repositories.

### Canonical SSDLC Principles

Secure by design requires security objectives, trust boundaries, failure behavior, abuse cases, and control ownership to be established before implementation becomes the default constraint on the design. Secure by default requires the delivered configuration to deny unapproved access, minimize exposure, enable required evidence, and avoid dependence on customers discovering and correcting unsafe initial settings.

Least privilege applies to people, services, build workers, repositories, deployment identities, test environments, automation, integrations, and released software. Privilege is specific to purpose, environment, tenant, resource, operation, and time. Development convenience does not justify standing production access, broad credentials, or bypass of review and release controls.

Defense in depth requires independent preventive, detective, and responsive controls. No scanner, review, test type, network boundary, cryptographic mechanism, or approval is treated as sufficient by itself. Controls shall fail independently where practical and shall not share a hidden single point of compromise that invalidates the stated protection.

Evidence first requires every lifecycle decision of material security significance to be supported by machine-verifiable or independently reviewable evidence. Assertions of review, testing, approval, artifact identity, or deployment state are not accepted when the underlying record cannot be related to the exact change and exact artifact.

Reproducibility and provenance require the released artifact to be derivable from identified source, approved dependencies, defined build instructions, controlled configuration, and an attributable build execution. Where byte-for-byte reproducibility is not feasible, the build shall still be repeatable in behavior and fully explainable through retained provenance.

Automation increases consistency but does not remove accountability. Automated recommendations, generated changes, test generation, dependency updates, remediation proposals, or risk classifications are treated as untrusted inputs until they pass the same ownership, review, verification, and authorization controls as human-authored changes. Automation may expand detection and verification; it may not reduce a mandatory baseline or authorize its own exception.

Security gates are decision controls, not reporting conventions. A failed mandatory gate prevents progression unless an authorized, documented, time-bound exception is granted through a separate process. Changing a threshold, suppressing a finding, excluding a file, or relabeling severity is itself a security-relevant change and is subject to review.

### Lifecycle Control Model

Every material change progresses through defined lifecycle states. A state may be combined operationally with another state for low-risk work, but its security outcome and evidence shall remain distinguishable.

| Lifecycle stage | Required security outcome | Representative evidence | Progression condition |
|---|---|---|---|
| Governance and planning | Ownership, classification, applicable obligations, and risk method are defined | accountable owner, component classification, control baseline | governed work item exists |
| Requirements | Security and privacy obligations are testable and traceable | security acceptance criteria, abuse cases, data classification | requirements are approved |
| Architecture and design | Trust boundaries, privileges, threats, and failure behavior are acceptable | design record, data flow, threat model, ADR where required | design risk is accepted |
| Implementation | Change follows approved design and secure implementation constraints | attributable change set, local verification, dependency record | implementation is review-ready |
| Review | Independent reviewers verify correctness, security, and scope | review comments, resolutions, approvals, verified diff | required approvals are complete |
| Build | Artifact is produced in a controlled and attributable process | build record, source identity, dependency manifest, artifact digest | build integrity is established |
| Verification | Required functional, security, resilience, and negative tests pass | test results, scan results, validation attestations | quality and security gates pass |
| Release | Exact candidate is approved, identified, signed where required, and immutable | release manifest, provenance, approvals, signatures | release authority accepts candidate |
