| Deployment | Approved artifact enters an eligible environment through a controlled path | deployment record, environment policy, rollout and rollback status | deployment validation succeeds |
| Operation | Vulnerabilities, drift, abuse, and failures are detected and remediated | telemetry, findings, incidents, remediation records | operating risk remains acceptable |
| Retirement | Access, data, secrets, support obligations, and artifacts are safely concluded | decommission record, revocation and disposition evidence | retirement acceptance is complete |

Skipping a lifecycle state does not remove its obligations. For example, an emergency correction may compress planning, review, verification, and approval, but it may not eliminate attribution, risk assessment, minimum testing, artifact identity, release authorization, deployment evidence, or post-change review.

### Governance, Accountability, and Segregation of Duties

Every governed component has an accountable engineering owner and an identified security classification. Ownership includes responsibility for design currency, dependency health, threat-model maintenance, vulnerability remediation, test adequacy, operational risk, and retirement. Shared ownership may support delivery, but ambiguity about final accountability is prohibited.

Product ownership defines the intended capability, customer impact, acceptance criteria, and business priority. Security architecture defines applicable control objectives and resolves material security design questions. Engineering authors and maintains implementation. Independent reviewers evaluate the exact proposed change and its consequences. Release authority accepts a specific verified candidate for a defined maturity level. Platform and operations functions deploy and operate only authorized artifacts. Incident response coordinates containment and recovery when a security event affects the lifecycle or product.

No single person, service, or automated mechanism shall unilaterally author, approve, build, and release a high-impact change. Required independence increases with privilege, data sensitivity, tenant reach, external exposure, cryptographic significance, policy authority, recovery impact, and reversibility. Changes to authentication, authorization, tenant boundaries, Policy Engine semantics, Approval Engine behavior, Tool Gateway enforcement, Model Gateway data handling, validation criteria, audit generation, evidence integrity, secrets, keys, encryption, build trust, release signing, or production access receive specialized review appropriate to their impact.

During a registered Single-Maintainer Bootstrap Profile, one person may temporarily perform multiple lifecycle roles only with exact change attribution, mandatory automated Quality Gates, immutable evidence, explicit self-review, recorded absence of independence, constrained release maturity, and dated exit criteria. High-impact changes shall obtain qualified external review before Stable release or remain blocked or limited through formal risk treatment. The bootstrap profile shall not be represented as independent review or Enterprise segregation of duties.

Conflicts of interest and emergency access are visible and auditable. A reviewer shall not approve a change that the reviewer cannot independently evaluate. Approval is invalid when it refers only to a work item while the reviewed source, dependency set, configuration, or artifact has changed afterward.

### Security Requirements Engineering

Security requirements are derived from product purpose, canonical architecture, tenant and data classification, threat model, deployment model, legal and contractual obligations, operational risk, recovery objectives, and accepted enterprise control baselines. Requirements shall be specific enough to verify. Statements such as “use industry best practice,” “secure the endpoint,” or “apply encryption” are insufficient without defined subject, condition, assurance, and expected failure behavior.

Each material feature or change evaluates at least:

- identity, authentication, authorization, tenant, environment, resource, and purpose boundaries;
- data categories, source, destination, residency, retention, deletion, export, and recovery behavior;
- confidentiality, integrity, availability, non-repudiation, evidence, and audit obligations;
- external interfaces, tool capabilities, model providers, third-party services, and transitive trust;
- expected, erroneous, adversarial, replayed, duplicated, delayed, reordered, and partially completed requests;
- safe default, fail-closed behavior, timeout, cancellation, rollback, compensation, and recovery;
- human approval conditions and the information necessary for meaningful approval;
- privilege creation, delegation, use, expiration, revocation, and observation;
- secrets, keys, cryptographic profiles, signing, and secure transport requirements;
- observability needed to detect misuse without exposing sensitive content; and
- migration, backward compatibility, end-of-support, and retirement consequences.

Security acceptance criteria are linked to the work item and to one or more verification methods. Requirements remain traceable through implementation, tests, findings, risk decisions, release evidence, and operational controls. A requirement may be refined as understanding improves, but it may not be silently removed to obtain a passing result.

### Architecture and Security Design Review

Architecture review confirms that the proposed design remains consistent with this canonical document, preserves the Development System and Runtime System separation, locates deterministic authority in the correct Control Plane components, and does not grant decision or execution authority to the AI Reasoning and Recommendation Engine or Model Orchestration and Provider Abstraction.

Design review identifies system context, trust boundaries, data flows, execution flows, privilege transitions, storage locations, external dependencies, tenant boundaries, administrative paths, security-sensitive states, failure modes, and recovery paths. Review shall determine which component owns each control and whether the control remains effective when an adjacent component is compromised or unavailable.

A formal ADR is required when a change establishes, reverses, or supersedes a material architectural decision. The ADR records context, decision, alternatives, security consequences, operational consequences, migration, rollback or irreversibility, and relationships to existing decisions. Implementation approval does not implicitly amend the canonical architecture.

Designs shall minimize exposed interfaces, mutable security state, trusted computing base, standing privilege, sensitive data movement, and irreversible actions. They shall prefer explicit capability boundaries, narrowly scoped interfaces, independent validation, idempotent or compensable operations, bounded resource use, and recoverable failure. Compatibility behavior shall not silently preserve an unsafe prior default.

### Threat Modeling Integration

Threat modeling is continuous and risk-based. It begins when requirements and system boundaries are known, is refined before implementation, is checked during review and verification, and is updated when operational evidence changes the understood threat. Section 3.8 defines the canonical Threat Model in detail; the SSDLC makes that model an active lifecycle control.

A threat-model review is required when a change introduces or materially changes an external interface, authentication method, authorization rule, tenant boundary, privileged action, approval path, tool capability, provider, data category, data destination, cryptographic mechanism, parser, code-execution path, administrative function, build dependency, update channel, recovery mechanism, or trust relationship.

Threat analysis considers malicious users, compromised identities, insiders, compromised services, tenants attempting cross-boundary access, manipulated dependencies, untrusted inputs, poisoned context, forged approvals, replay, race conditions, resource exhaustion, data exfiltration, evidence tampering, rollback abuse, insecure recovery, provider compromise, and control-plane degradation. It also considers misuse by an otherwise authorized actor and unsafe behavior produced without malicious intent.

Threats are related to preventative controls, detection, response, verification, residual risk, and ownership. A threat is not considered addressed merely because it appears in a document. Open threats that exceed the accepted risk threshold block progression or require an authorized exception with compensating controls and expiry.

### Secure Implementation

Implementation shall use approved languages, frameworks, libraries, interfaces, and patterns appropriate to the component’s assurance level. Technology selection does not replace secure engineering judgment. Implementation-independent requirements remain controlling even where a framework supplies a partial default.

Code and configuration shall treat all external, cross-tenant, cross-process, persisted, restored, model-produced, tool-produced, and previously validated data as untrusted at the receiving boundary. Inputs are parsed using defined schemas, bounded in size and complexity, canonicalized where necessary, validated for type and semantics, and rejected safely. Output handling is appropriate to the destination context. Parsing failure, malformed data, unexpected enumeration values, unknown fields, and incompatible versions do not create permissive behavior.

Authorization checks occur at the authoritative service and at the point of action. Client-side controls, hidden interface elements, route naming, network location, or possession of an identifier do not establish authorization. Tenant and Immutable Context information is propagated through trusted mechanisms and is not reconstructed from untrusted payload fields.

Implementation minimizes memory, storage, log, trace, diagnostic, and error exposure. Secrets are never embedded in source, examples, tests, build output, images, or generated artifacts. Sensitive values are redacted structurally rather than by best-effort string replacement. Errors provide operators with actionable correlation while withholding internal detail from unauthorized callers.

Resource use is bounded. Concurrency, retries, queues, recursion, decompression, parsing, upload, batch, and fan-out behavior have explicit limits. Race conditions, time-of-check to time-of-use gaps, duplicate delivery, partial failure, and retry after uncertain completion are addressed in design and tests. Security-sensitive comparisons and cryptographic operations use approved implementations and failure behavior.

Generated or transformed code, automatically proposed patches, low-code definitions, copied examples, migration scripts, and vendor-supplied snippets receive the same ownership, review, testing, provenance, and licensing checks as manually authored code. The apparent confidence or origin of a proposal does not constitute assurance.

### Repository and Change Integrity

The repository is a controlled security boundary. A change is evaluated against a verified repository root, origin, baseline, branch, commit, and worktree state. Security decisions shall not rely on ambiguous paths, untracked substitutions, unverified mirrors, or a diff generated against an unknown baseline.

Protected branches, access control, attributable identities, required review, mandatory checks, and controlled merge mechanisms preserve change integrity. Direct, unreviewed modification of a release branch or released artifact is prohibited. History rewriting, force updates, tag movement, and branch-protection changes are restricted and audited according to repository criticality.

Each material change is traceable to an authorized work item, security requirements, relevant design or ADR, review, verification result, and release. Changes should remain cohesive enough that their security effect can be understood and reversed. Unrelated changes bundled into a security-sensitive modification increase review uncertainty and may be rejected.

Repository configuration, ownership rules, review requirements, pipeline definitions, policy checks, dependency update rules, and security suppressions are code and receive commensurate protection. A change to the mechanism that evaluates other changes cannot approve itself without independent control.

Detailed naming, commit, branching, review, merge, and repository structure standards are defined in Section 4. These mechanics shall preserve the attribution, integrity, independence, and evidence requirements established here.

### Secure Code Review

Review verifies the exact change, not merely the stated intent. Reviewers examine the verified diff, relevant surrounding code, generated changes, dependency modifications, configuration effects, tests, threat-model impact, data and tenant boundaries, failure behavior, observability, and rollback. Review depth is proportional to risk rather than line count.

Security-sensitive changes require a reviewer competent in the affected control domain. Reviewers challenge assumptions, identify bypass paths, evaluate negative behavior, confirm that enforcement occurs at the authoritative boundary, and verify that tests would fail if the control were removed or inverted. Approval shall not be granted while material comments remain unresolved.

A previous approval becomes stale when the reviewed change set, dependency graph, build instructions, security configuration, generated output, or relevant baseline changes materially. Re-approval scope may be limited to the new delta only when the system can prove that the previously reviewed content is unchanged and the delta has no broader effect.

Review tooling may prioritize findings and provide context, but it may not suppress the mandatory human or independent review required by risk. Self-review may supplement but does not satisfy independent approval for high-impact work.

### Dependency and Software Supply-Chain Security

Dependencies include source packages, libraries, frameworks, container bases, operating-system components, build tools, compiler and interpreter toolchains, actions, plugins, code generators, schemas, models used in the build process, externally hosted assets, and services required to produce or operate the product. Transitive dependencies are included even when not declared directly.

Dependencies originate from approved sources and are resolved through controlled registries or verified distribution channels. Version constraints, lock data, integrity digests, signatures or provenance where available, and acquisition records make resolution repeatable. Names, publishers, ownership changes, package age, update practices, malicious-package history, license terms, maintenance health, and known vulnerabilities are evaluated according to risk.

ILAIOS minimizes dependency count and privilege. A component is not adopted merely because it accelerates development. The expected value is weighed against added attack surface, supply-chain trust, maintenance obligation, data exposure, operational dependency, and exit cost. Unmaintained, unverified, unexpectedly renamed, or typosquatted components are prohibited.

Install-time and build-time scripts execute with restricted privilege in isolated environments. Dependency acquisition does not receive production credentials, tenant data, release signing authority, or unnecessary network access. Caches are integrity-protected and cannot silently substitute unverified content for an approved dependency.

A software bill of materials or equivalent component inventory is produced for release artifacts at the granularity necessary to identify affected versions and transitive components. Inventory is associated with the immutable artifact rather than only the source branch. Vulnerability intelligence is evaluated both before release and throughout supported operation. A newly disclosed vulnerability can reopen the risk decision for an already released artifact.

Dependency updates follow the normal lifecycle. Automated update proposals are not self-authorizing. Security patches may receive expedited handling, but compatibility, provenance, tests, and release identity remain controlled. Removal or replacement plans exist for critical dependencies whose trust, support, license, availability, or security posture becomes unacceptable.

### Build and Pipeline Security

The build system is part of the product security boundary. Build workers use isolated, preferably ephemeral execution contexts; least-privilege identities; controlled network paths; verified tools; protected inputs; and explicit outputs. Workers do not retain tenant data, reusable secrets, untracked state, or mutable artifacts between unrelated builds.

Pipelines obtain short-lived credentials through approved identity mechanisms. Standing deployment, registry, signing, or production credentials are not stored in source or exposed to untrusted build steps. Secret material is scoped to the exact job and is prevented from entering logs, caches, test reports, artifacts, or forked execution contexts.

Build instructions are version-controlled and reviewed. The pipeline records source identity, dependency resolution, toolchain and builder identity, relevant configuration, executed checks, timestamps, artifact digests, and outcome. The released artifact shall be the same artifact that passed required verification. Rebuilding after approval creates a new candidate and requires identity and verification to be re-established.

Untrusted contributions do not execute in a privileged pipeline context before approval. Build steps from external contributions, dependency hooks, generated scripts, and test fixtures are treated as code execution. Network access and credential availability are restricted so compromise of one step cannot silently modify the repository, release channel, evidence store, or production environment.

Development build systems and Runtime System services remain separated. Product runtime credentials, tenant data, production keys, and runtime control authority are unavailable to ordinary development and validation workers. Conversely, production runtime components do not modify source, approve changes, or manufacture release evidence.

### Security Verification and Testing

Verification combines complementary techniques selected according to component risk. The mandatory baseline may include compiler and type checks, linting, unit and integration tests, static analysis, secrets detection, dependency analysis, license checks, configuration analysis, infrastructure-as-code scanning, container and image analysis, API and schema testing, authorization and tenant-isolation tests, cryptographic tests, dynamic analysis, fuzzing, resilience tests, and manual security assessment.

High-impact components receive explicit negative, misuse, boundary, and failure-path testing. Verification covers denied authorization, expired and revoked identity, wrong tenant, malformed and oversized input, replay, duplication, race conditions, partial completion, unavailable dependency, timeout, retry, rollback, corrupted evidence, invalid signature, wrong key, unsafe provider destination, audit failure, and recovery from known state.

Tests verify enforcement at the authoritative boundary and demonstrate that a security control can fail the operation. A test that only confirms a user interface hides an action is not an authorization test. A test that observes a successful request without checking retained evidence does not verify audit completeness. A test that mocks away the security boundary does not establish the behavior of that boundary.

Test data is synthetic, minimized, or irreversibly transformed by default. Production data, production secrets, private keys, tenant exports, and live credentials are prohibited in development and ordinary test environments. Any exceptional use requires explicit purpose, legal and security approval, access restriction, monitoring, retention, and verified deletion.

Code Intelligence may expand analysis, identify relationships, prioritize review, and recommend additional tests. It does not replace the mandatory security baseline and cannot authorize a change, lower severity, suppress evidence, or attest its own correctness. Independent tools and reviewers remain available for validating Code Intelligence output.

Penetration testing and adversarial assessment are scheduled according to exposure and risk and are additionally required after material changes to externally reachable or high-trust boundaries. Findings enter the governed vulnerability process and are traceable to resolution, exception, or documented non-applicability.

### Security and Quality Gates

Security gates evaluate objective evidence before progression. Gate policy defines required checks, applicability, severity thresholds, acceptable evidence age, independence, and failure behavior. Gate configuration is versioned, reviewed, and attributable. A missing, timed-out, stale, incomplete, or unverifiable required result is a failed gate unless the policy explicitly defines a safer state.

Blocking findings are resolved before progression unless an authorized exception exists. Resolution means the defect is remediated and verified, demonstrated to be a false positive with reproducible evidence, or accepted temporarily under the exception process. Merely changing labels, excluding files, weakening patterns, disabling checks, or moving detection to a later phase is not remediation.

Security gate results contribute to, but do not solely constitute, the Definition of Done. Functional success cannot offset a failed security invariant. Similarly, a clean automated scan does not establish that architecture, authorization, tenant isolation, or business misuse is safe.

### Release Integrity and Authorization

A release candidate is an immutable set of artifacts, manifests, dependency inventory, configuration expectations, migration instructions, known limitations, security findings, verification results, and provenance. The candidate has a unique version and cryptographic digest or equivalent immutable identity.

Release authorization applies only to that candidate and a defined maturity class, deployment scope, and support posture. Alpha, Beta, Release Candidate, Stable, and Long-Term Support stages may have different eligibility criteria, but no stage may misrepresent its assurance or bypass the minimum protections required for its data and environment. Detailed release policy is defined in Section 4.10.

Required signatures and attestations are created only after the artifact identity is known. Signing keys and release identities follow Sections 3.2 through 3.6. A valid signature proves association with an authorized identity; it does not replace vulnerability assessment, testing, approval, or safe operation.

Release notes disclose security-relevant configuration, migration, compatibility, known limitations, required operator action, and support consequences without providing unnecessary exploit detail. Security fixes are not obscured in a way that prevents customers from assessing urgency. Embargoed information is handled under controlled disclosure rules.

### Secure Deployment and Environment Promotion

Deployment uses approved artifacts from controlled repositories and a traceable promotion path. Production systems do not compile or alter release source. Environment-specific configuration, tenant routing, secrets, keys, trust stores, provider eligibility, policy versions, network controls, data stores, and observability settings are supplied through governed mechanisms and validated before serving traffic.

Development, test, staging, and production environments have distinct identities, credentials, keys, data, access paths, and authorization policies. Environment separation prevents a compromise or broad permission in a lower environment from becoming a production capability. Production data does not flow backward into lower environments by default.

Deployment begins with precondition validation and completes only after post-deployment checks confirm artifact identity, configuration state, dependency health, required telemetry, security controls, tenant isolation, and service behavior. Progressive rollout, canary, blue-green, or equivalent techniques may reduce blast radius where appropriate, but do not weaken evidence or authorization.

Rollback is designed and tested where feasible. A rollback target is itself an approved artifact and must remain compatible with security state, schemas, keys, policy, and vulnerability requirements. Rollback shall not silently restore revoked credentials, deprecated cryptographic profiles, vulnerable dependencies, unsafe defaults, or obsolete authorization semantics.

Configuration drift and unauthorized mutation are detected. Material drift causes investigation, restoration to approved state, or a governed change; it is not normalized by modifying the declared baseline after the fact.

### Operational Security Feedback

The SSDLC continues after deployment. Runtime monitoring, Audit Engine records, Evidence Chain verification, customer reports, vulnerability disclosures, provider advisories, dependency intelligence, incident investigations, penetration tests, support cases, performance anomalies, and resilience exercises provide security feedback.

Findings are normalized, deduplicated without loss of provenance, classified, assigned, prioritized, and traced to affected components and releases. Operational evidence may trigger containment, capability restriction, provider suspension, configuration change, tenant communication, patch development, re-verification, release, or retirement.

Security controls are assessed for effectiveness, not merely presence. Repeated near misses, false-negative patterns, high exception volume, drift, weak ownership, or unreliable tests result in lifecycle improvement. Metrics shall not create incentives to suppress findings, delay intake, reclassify severity, or ship before detection.

### Vulnerability Management and Coordinated Disclosure

ILAIOS maintains controlled channels for internal and external vulnerability intake. Reports receive acknowledgement, unique identity, confidentiality appropriate to risk, triage, affected-version analysis, exploitability assessment, severity, ownership, and remediation target. Duplicate reports are related without discarding evidence or reporter context.

Triage considers attack preconditions, privilege, user interaction, tenant reach, data classification, execution impact, detectability, exploit maturity, exposure, compensating controls, and availability of containment. Severity is not determined solely by a generic score. A defect that undermines a canonical trust invariant may receive higher priority because it invalidates evidence or multiple downstream controls.

Remediation targets are risk-based, measurable, and governed. When immediate correction is not possible, containment may disable a capability, restrict an integration, rotate credentials, change policy, isolate affected versions, or provide customer mitigation. Temporary containment does not close the underlying defect.

Disclosure balances customer protection, legal obligations, reporter coordination, patch availability, exploit risk, and transparency. Affected customers receive actionable information through approved communication paths. Security advisories identify affected and corrected versions, severity, mitigation, and upgrade requirements. Reporter identity and confidential detail are protected according to policy.

### Emergency Security Changes

An emergency process exists for actively exploited vulnerabilities, material exposure, compromised credentials, unsafe provider behavior, evidence-integrity failures, or other urgent security conditions. Emergency status permits expedited decision-making; it does not permit unattributed source, unknown artifact identity, unreviewed privilege, missing minimum tests, self-authorized release, or undocumented production mutation.

Emergency changes define the incident or threat, affected scope, containment objective, risk of action and inaction, responsible authority, minimum verification, rollback or compensation, communication, and monitoring. Independent review occurs before deployment whenever time and risk permit. When prior independent review is impossible, a separate authorized reviewer conducts retrospective review within the mandated period, and any deficiency becomes tracked remediation.

Temporary controls introduced during an emergency have explicit owners and expiry. Emergency credentials, elevated access, disabled checks, network exceptions, feature restrictions, and diagnostic collection are revoked or normalized through the standard lifecycle after stabilization. The emergency path is periodically tested and its use is audited for misuse.

### Third-Party and Service Provider Security

Third parties that contribute code, components, build capability, hosted services, model access, operational support, or security controls are evaluated according to the trust they receive. Assessment considers security governance, data handling, tenant isolation, personnel access, identity, encryption, vulnerability response, incident notification, availability, change control, auditability, geographic and legal constraints, dependency concentration, and termination support.

Contracts and technical controls define permitted data, purposes, locations, subprocessors, retention, deletion, breach notification, assurance evidence, support, patch expectations, and exit. Provider claims are not treated as technical proof when ILAIOS can independently enforce or verify a boundary.

Provider change is monitored. Material changes to ownership, terms, data use, service architecture, assurance, security posture, support, or region may trigger reassessment. Exit and replacement plans exist for critical providers so that security or continuity concerns do not create permanent lock-in.

### Developer and Engineering Environment Security

Engineering access uses unique identities, phishing-resistant or appropriately strong multi-factor authentication, least privilege, managed endpoints, secure credential storage, and monitored administrative paths according to role and risk. Shared accounts and reusable personal tokens for sensitive automation are prohibited.

Workstations and development environments maintain supported software, endpoint protection, encrypted storage, screen and session controls, secure update mechanisms, and separation from untrusted personal workloads appropriate to enterprise policy. Local administrative privilege is restricted. Loss, compromise, or suspected credential exposure initiates prompt revocation and incident handling.

Developers do not require routine production access to build or test software. Exceptional access is approved, time-bound, purpose-limited, monitored, and removed after use. Diagnostic access does not permit uncontrolled download of tenant data or secrets. Production changes remain governed even when performed to investigate an incident.

### Configuration, Policy, Schema, and Infrastructure Changes

Security treatment is based on effect rather than file type. Infrastructure definitions, policy rules, approval matrices, schemas, migrations, feature flags, workflow definitions, dashboards, alert thresholds, access-control lists, deployment templates, and documentation that instructs operators can change the security posture as materially as application source.

These artifacts are versioned, reviewed, tested, promoted, and rolled back through controlled processes. Policy changes are checked for conflicts, unintended grants, tenant impact, capability expansion, approval bypass, and fail-open behavior. Infrastructure changes are checked for exposure, identity, encryption, logging, resilience, deletion protection, and drift. Schema and migration changes are checked for data loss, tenant mixing, downgraded classification, backward compatibility, partial execution, and safe recovery.

Manual console changes are prohibited as a normal delivery mechanism. Where an authorized manual action is unavoidable, its preconditions, actor, exact action, observed result, validation, and reconciliation into the declared configuration are recorded.

### Security Evidence and Auditability

Security evidence is generated throughout the lifecycle. Relevant records include requirement approval, design review, threat-model decisions, ADRs, repository identity, change authorship, review, dependency resolution, build execution, test and scan results, exceptions, artifact digests, provenance, signatures, release authorization, deployment state, rollback, operational findings, vulnerability remediation, and retirement.

Evidence identifies the subject, actor or workload, tenant or organizational scope where applicable, timestamp, action, decision, basis, result, version, and relationship to other records. Sensitive source, credentials, vulnerability detail, tenant data, and private keys are not copied into evidence merely to demonstrate completeness.

The Audit Engine and Evidence Chain continuously cover material lifecycle decisions according to their respective architecture. Development evidence and runtime evidence may reside in distinct security domains, but their authorized relationships enable reconstruction from a released or deployed artifact to its governing requirements and source without granting the Development System authority over Runtime execution.

Evidence retention reflects product support, legal, contractual, incident, forensic, and release obligations. Records are integrity-protected, access-controlled, searchable by authorized roles, exportable for legitimate assurance purposes, and subject to verified retention and deletion policy. Absence of mandatory evidence is a control failure, not an indication that the event did not require evidence.

### Security Exceptions and Technical Debt

An exception is a temporary, explicit acceptance of residual risk; it is not a permanent alternative standard. The request identifies the unmet requirement, affected components and versions, business justification, threat and impact, likelihood, data and tenant scope, compensating controls, detection, owner, remediation plan, approval authority, creation date, review date, and expiry.

The actor requesting an exception may not be its sole approver. Approval authority is proportional to risk. Exceptions affecting canonical invariants, multiple tenants, high-impact data, signing, key custody, authorization, Policy Engine enforcement, approval, audit, evidence integrity, or release trust require senior security and architecture review and may be prohibited outright.

Expired exceptions automatically fail the associated gate or trigger escalation. Renewal requires new evidence and reassessment; it is not automatic. Exceptions are linked to affected release and deployment state, are visible to authorized operational roles, and are closed only when remediation has been independently verified or the affected capability has been retired.

Security technical debt is recorded even when it does not currently block release. Debt has ownership, priority, risk rationale, target state, and review cadence. Repeated deferral, accumulating exception exposure, or dependency on a temporary compensating control raises the risk classification and may block further feature development in the affected area.

### Retirement and End-of-Support Security

Retirement is planned before support ends. The plan identifies affected customers, versions, tenants, data, dependencies, identities, certificates, secrets, keys, network paths, provider contracts, artifacts, evidence, backups, operational procedures, and legal retention obligations.

Decommissioning disables entry points and capabilities, revokes identities and credentials, removes trust relationships, terminates unnecessary network access, disposes of data according to classification, preserves required evidence, and verifies that scheduled jobs, integrations, mirrors, caches, backups, and disaster-recovery environments do not silently reactivate the retired component.

End-of-support communication defines final supported versions, security patch policy, migration path, relevant dates, customer responsibilities, and consequences of continued use. Unsupported software is not represented as secure or silently permitted to remain in an approved production baseline without a governed risk decision.

### SSDLC Metrics and Assurance

Metrics support risk management and improvement while preserving context. Applicable measures include:

- percentage of material changes with traceable security requirements and acceptance criteria;
- threat-model coverage and age for high-impact components;
- security review coverage, review latency, reopened approvals, and unresolved material comments;
- mandatory gate success, failure, timeout, suppression, exception, and false-positive rates;
- vulnerability discovery phase, escaped-defect rate, time to triage, time to contain, and time to verified remediation by severity;
- dependency inventory and provenance coverage, vulnerable dependency age, unsupported component count, and update latency;
- build reproducibility or repeatability, provenance coverage, signing coverage, and artifact-verification failures;
- authorization, tenant-isolation, negative-path, resilience, and security regression coverage;
- production drift, emergency change frequency, post-emergency deficiencies, and rollback success;
- open exceptions, expired exceptions, exception age, compensating-control failures, and recurring causes;
- security incident contribution from implementation, dependency, configuration, deployment, or process defects; and
- retirement completion, residual identity, residual data, and unsupported deployment exposure.

Metrics are segmented by component criticality and risk. Averages shall not conceal a severe outlier, unsupported high-impact component, or repeated failure in a trust-critical control. Targets may increase assurance but may not redefine a canonical violation as acceptable.

Periodic assurance reviews assess whether the SSDLC is operating effectively, whether evidence is trustworthy, whether control ownership remains clear, and whether observed incidents or near misses require changes to requirements, tools, gates, training, architecture, or governance. Improvement follows the formal change and ADR processes where canonical decisions are affected.

### SSDLC Limitations

An SSDLC reduces the probability, impact, and persistence of software and supply-chain risk; it cannot prove the absence of all defects, malicious behavior, unknown vulnerabilities, provider compromise, operator error, or unsafe customer configuration. Automated analysis has coverage limits. Review quality depends on competence and accurate context. Test environments cannot reproduce every production interaction. Provenance confirms origin and process claims only to the strength of the identities, builders, and evidence system that produce it.

The SSDLC therefore operates with Runtime Zero Trust, continuous audit and evidence, defense in depth, incident response, vulnerability management, recovery, customer security guidance, and ongoing reassessment. Release acceptance is a bounded risk decision for a specific artifact and context, not a permanent declaration that the software is universally secure.

### SSDLC Invariants

The following invariants are canonical:

- security is integrated from governance and requirements through retirement and is not deferred to final testing;
- every material change has accountable ownership, authorized purpose, verified origin, traceable requirements, review, verification, and retained evidence;
- accepted architectural decisions remain controlling unless a formal ADR explicitly supersedes them;
- Development System and Runtime System responsibilities, identities, data, credentials, and authority remain separated;
- security requirements are testable, risk-based, and traceable to design, implementation, verification, release, and operation;
- threat models are updated when trust, data, privilege, interface, provider, execution, build, recovery, or tenant boundaries materially change;
- automatically generated or proposed code, tests, configuration, and remediation receive the same controls as human-authored work;
- no automated mechanism may authorize its own change, exception, release, or evidence of correctness;
- repository, pipeline, gate, policy, suppression, and ownership configuration are security-relevant code;
- high-impact changes require independent, competent review and cannot be unilaterally authored, approved, built, and released by one actor;
- dependencies and build tools have approved origin, controlled resolution, known inventory, and ongoing vulnerability governance;
- untrusted changes do not execute with release, signing, deployment, production, or evidence-administration authority;
- build and release evidence identifies the exact source, dependencies, process, artifact, checks, approvals, and immutable artifact identity;
- the artifact released and deployed is the artifact that passed mandatory verification; any rebuild creates a new candidate;
- security gates fail closed on blocking, missing, stale, incomplete, timed-out, or unverifiable mandatory results;
- security findings are not resolved by silent suppression, threshold reduction, exclusion, reclassification, or transfer to a later phase;
- exceptions are separately approved, risk-bounded, compensating-control-backed, attributable, reviewable, and time-limited;
- emergency delivery may compress timing but may not eliminate attribution, minimum verification, artifact identity, authorization, evidence, or retrospective review;
- production data, secrets, keys, and credentials are excluded from ordinary development and test activity;
- environment promotion preserves identity, configuration, tenant, key, policy, telemetry, rollback, and drift controls;
- operational vulnerabilities, incidents, and near misses feed governed remediation and lifecycle improvement;
- retirement revokes capabilities and trust, disposes of data safely, preserves required evidence, and prevents unintended reactivation; and
- Audit Engine and Evidence Chain continuously record material lifecycle decisions without granting the Development System Runtime authority.

An implementation is non-conformant if it treats security as a final release scan; permits a high-impact change to be authored, self-approved, built, and released by one actor; allows generated code or automated dependency updates to bypass review; builds from unknown source or unverified dependencies; exposes production credentials or tenant data to development workers; executes untrusted contributions with signing or deployment authority; releases an artifact different from the verified candidate; converts missing or failed mandatory checks into success; suppresses findings without governed evidence; grants permanent or silently renewed exceptions; uses emergency status to eliminate attribution, testing, approval, or audit; deploys through manual unrecorded mutation; permits lower environments to share production identities, keys, or data without explicit protected exception; fails to relate a deployed artifact to source, dependencies, review, verification, and release authorization; or retires a component while leaving active credentials, entry points, data copies, provider access, unsupported deployments, or recovery paths capable of restoring it.

## 3.8 Threat Model

The ILAIOS Threat Model defines the canonical security view of the Enterprise AI Operating System, the assets it must protect, the adversaries and failure conditions it must withstand, the trust boundaries it must enforce, the threat scenarios it must address, and the evidence required to demonstrate that risk is controlled. It applies across product architecture, software supply chain, deployment, operation, integration, recovery, and retirement.

The Threat Model is not a claim that every possible attack can be predicted or prevented. It is a governed method for making material threats explicit, assigning controls and ownership, validating control effectiveness, identifying residual risk, and updating the security posture as the product, operating environment, adversary behavior, and enterprise obligations evolve.

This model preserves the canonical ILAIOS architecture. It does not redesign the system, transfer deterministic authority to probabilistic components, or convert an architectural control into an implementation suggestion. The Policy Engine remains a deterministic Control Plane authority. The AI Reasoning and Recommendation Engine may propose plans or actions but may not authorize or execute them. The Model Orchestration and Provider Abstraction component may select and mediate eligible model services but has no policy authority. Tool execution remains constrained by the Tool Gateway. Validation remains independent of the proposing and executing components. Audit Engine and Evidence Chain coverage remains continuous across all material stages.

### Threat Modeling Objectives

The Threat Model has the following objectives:

- identify assets whose compromise would undermine enterprise trust, tenant safety, execution integrity, evidence, compliance, availability, or product viability;
- describe credible adversaries, their access paths, capabilities, motivations, constraints, and potential objectives;
- expose trust assumptions and prevent network location, service identity, model output, prior validation, or administrative status from becoming implicit trust;
- analyze the complete request, planning, authorization, execution, validation, delivery, and evidence lifecycle rather than isolated endpoints;
- address malicious activity, accidental misuse, design error, implementation defect, configuration drift, provider failure, supply-chain compromise, and unsafe emergent interaction;
- ensure that every material threat has preventive, detective, responsive, and evidentiary treatment proportional to risk;
- establish which threats are prohibited by canonical invariants and which may be accepted only as explicit residual risk;
- support secure design, security testing, red-team activity, incident preparation, customer assurance, and risk governance; and
- keep the model current through versioned review, operational feedback, vulnerability intelligence, and formal architectural change control.

### Scope and System Boundaries

The Threat Model covers the ILAIOS Development System and Runtime System, including their controlled interfaces and the external systems on which they depend. It applies to Control Plane components, Trust Core modules, AI and Intelligence Layer components, Tool Gateway, Model Gateway, user and administrative interfaces, enterprise integrations, data stores, caches, queues, cryptographic services, build and release infrastructure, observability systems, backup and recovery paths, deployment infrastructure, and supported client software.

The model includes threats originating outside the enterprise boundary, within a customer organization, within the ILAIOS operating organization, within a service provider, within the software supply chain, and from compromised workloads or identities. It includes cross-tenant threats and threats in which a legitimate tenant attempts to exceed its authority. It also includes non-malicious failure where the outcome is equivalent to an attack, such as misrouting classified data, approving the wrong action, validating the wrong artifact, losing audit coverage, or restoring revoked trust.

Customer business systems, external tools, model services, identity providers, key services, repositories, registries, communications channels, and cloud or on-premises infrastructure are external trust dependencies even when contractually controlled. Their security claims are inputs to risk assessment, not substitutes for ILAIOS enforcement.

Physical security, personnel security, legal enforcement, and customer governance remain relevant dependencies. This section defines how their failure can affect ILAIOS but does not replace the detailed organizational, contractual, or facility controls owned by the corresponding authority.

### Threat Modeling Method

Threat modeling is continuous, structured, risk-based, and evidence-producing. Each material model shall answer four questions: what is being protected and how it operates; what can go wrong; what controls and responses address the risk; and whether the resulting assurance is sufficient for the intended deployment and data.

The method consists of the following activities:

1. establish the system scope, deployment context, tenant model, data classifications, supported capabilities, dependencies, and governing assumptions;
2. identify assets, security objectives, entry points, exit points, trust boundaries, privilege transitions, data flows, control decisions, and recovery paths;
3. identify threat actors and failure sources, including their plausible access and capability;
4. enumerate threat scenarios using architectural analysis, abuse cases, historical incident patterns, adversary behavior, vulnerability intelligence, and domain-specific risk;
5. rate inherent risk before credit is given for controls;
6. assign preventive, detective, responsive, recovery, and evidentiary controls to an accountable owner;
7. assess whether each control is present, independent where required, correctly placed, testable, observable, and resistant to bypass;
8. determine residual risk, affected scope, treatment, exception requirements, and acceptance authority;
9. validate the model through review, negative testing, adversarial assessment, operational exercises, and evidence inspection; and
10. update the model when architecture, interfaces, data, providers, threats, incidents, or control effectiveness materially change.

Threat categories such as spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service, elevation of privilege, abuse of business logic, supply-chain compromise, and unsafe AI interaction may be used to improve completeness. They are analytical aids rather than limitations. A threat shall not be excluded because it does not fit a selected taxonomy.

Every threat record identifies at least the protected asset, source, preconditions, entry path, affected trust boundary, attacker objective or failure outcome, plausible sequence, inherent impact, likelihood factors, controls, detection, response, evidence, owner, validation method, residual risk, status, and review trigger. Compound threats shall preserve their sequence because individually acceptable events can form an unacceptable attack chain.

### Protected Assets and Security Objectives

ILAIOS protects both information assets and decision-making integrity. The following asset classes are canonical:

| Asset class | Representative assets | Primary security objectives |
|---|---|---|
| Identity and authority | user, workload, tenant, administrator, approver, service and deployment identities; sessions; capability grants | authenticity, least privilege, bounded delegation, revocation |
| Context and intent | original request, tenant context, purpose, scope, constraints, risk inputs, Immutable Context | integrity, provenance, completeness, tenant binding |
| Policy and approval | policy definitions, policy versions, evaluation inputs and results, approval requests and decisions | determinism, integrity, non-bypass, accountability |
| Execution authority | capability tokens, time-bound grants, Tool Gateway routes, tool parameters, execution state | constrained use, non-replay, purpose binding, revocation |
| Enterprise data | tenant content, metadata, credentials, regulated data, prompts, outputs, attachments, exports | confidentiality, integrity, residency, minimization, isolation |
| Validation state | expected outcomes, validation rules, test evidence, acceptance or rejection decisions | independence, subject binding, completeness, non-tampering |
| Audit and evidence | audit events, chain links, signatures, digests, timestamps, provenance, export packages | append-only integrity, ordering, verifiability, availability |
| Cryptographic material | secrets, keys, certificates, trust anchors, signing and wrapping material | confidentiality, integrity, purpose separation, lifecycle control |
| Source and releases | source, dependencies, build definitions, artifacts, manifests, versions, release channels | provenance, integrity, reproducibility, authorization |
| Service availability | Control Plane, Trust Core, gateways, queues, stores, validation and recovery services | resilience, bounded degradation, recoverability |
| Intelligence assets | repository index, code entities, knowledge relationships, model configurations, evaluation data | integrity, confidentiality, version accuracy, provenance |
| Governance assets | architecture decisions, risk acceptances, exceptions, customer configuration, control baselines | authority, traceability, expiration, change control |

Compromise of one asset class may invalidate others. For example, theft of a signing key can undermine release provenance; manipulation of Immutable Context can cause a correct policy to authorize the wrong scope; corruption of validation rules can cause an unsafe result to be accepted; deletion of audit events can conceal an otherwise detectable breach. Risk assessment therefore evaluates dependencies and blast radius rather than treating assets independently.

### Security Properties

The Threat Model evaluates confidentiality, integrity, availability, authenticity, authorization, accountability, privacy, tenant isolation, provenance, freshness, non-replay, non-repudiation, resilience, recoverability, and explainability appropriate to the asset.

Deterministic control integrity is a distinct ILAIOS security property. The same approved policy, authoritative inputs, and versioned evaluation context shall produce the same authorization outcome. Model variability may influence a proposal but may not alter the deterministic authority required to permit action.

Evidence completeness is also distinct. An action is not enterprise-trustworthy merely because the resulting business state appears correct. The request, identity, context, plan, policy decision, risk classification, approval, execution authorization, tool action, validation, acceptance or rejection, delivery, and closure shall be reconstructable at the material level required by policy.

### Threat Actors and Failure Sources

The model assumes adversaries can be patient, adaptive, coordinated, and capable of combining weaknesses across components and organizations. Representative sources include:

- unauthenticated external attackers probing public interfaces, credentials, dependencies, and availability limits;
- authenticated low-privilege users attempting to exceed role, tenant, resource, purpose, or data boundaries;
- malicious or compromised tenant administrators using legitimate configuration authority to obtain unintended platform or cross-tenant capability;
- compromised user endpoints, browsers, clients, access tokens, sessions, or enterprise identity systems;
- insiders with engineering, support, operations, security, release, billing, or administrative access;
- compromised workloads, service identities, containers, hosts, clusters, queues, caches, databases, or automation;
- malicious or compromised tool providers, model providers, identity providers, software vendors, package publishers, registries, and infrastructure operators;
- supply-chain attackers modifying source, dependencies, build tools, pipeline definitions, artifacts, update channels, or developer environments;
- attackers controlling documents, web content, repositories, messages, retrieved context, tool output, or other indirect inputs consumed by reasoning systems;
- customers or integrators who unintentionally deploy unsafe configuration, excessive privilege, invalid trust, exposed credentials, or incompatible policy;
- accidental actors making incorrect approvals, misclassifying data, changing the wrong tenant, restoring obsolete state, or disabling required telemetry;
- non-human failure sources such as software defects, race conditions, clock failure, entropy failure, partial transactions, provider outage, corruption, capacity exhaustion, or incompatible versions; and
- environmental and organizational failures affecting facilities, networks, identity, key custody, personnel availability, or disaster recovery.

No actor is trusted solely because it is internal, administrative, contractually approved, authenticated, or operating on a private network. Trust derives from verified identity, current authorization, purpose, context, risk, control state, and evidence.

### Attacker Objectives

Attacker objectives include unauthorized data access, cross-tenant disclosure, credential theft, privilege escalation, execution of unauthorized tools, policy bypass, approval forgery, evidence destruction, manipulation of business outcomes, persistence, lateral movement, provider exploitation, supply-chain compromise, service disruption, extortion, fraud, intellectual-property theft, evasion of accountability, and reputational damage.

An attacker may also seek to degrade assurance without visibly changing the immediate outcome. Examples include causing audit gaps, making actions non-reproducible, substituting an unapproved model, weakening validation, increasing false approvals, forcing unsafe fallback, poisoning a repository index, creating ambiguous evidence, or ensuring that a future investigation cannot determine what occurred.

### Canonical Trust Boundaries

Trust boundaries exist wherever identity, tenant, privilege, purpose, data classification, execution authority, provider control, validation responsibility, evidence custody, environment, or organizational accountability changes.

| Trust boundary | Primary threat concern | Required boundary property |
|---|---|---|
| User or enterprise system to ILAIOS | spoofed identity, malicious input, replay, excessive request scope | authenticated origin, schema validation, rate and purpose controls |
| Tenant to tenant | data disclosure, identifier substitution, shared-state confusion | explicit tenant binding and isolation at every authoritative layer |
| User plane to Control Plane | unauthorized configuration or policy influence | least privilege, protected administrative interfaces, evidence |
| Proposal to authorization | model output treated as permission | deterministic Policy Engine evaluation and risk classification |
| Authorization to execution | altered parameters, replayed grant, capability expansion | exact subject binding, expiry, nonce or replay control, Tool Gateway enforcement |
| Tool Gateway to external tool | data exfiltration, result forgery, excessive side effects | destination eligibility, scoped credentials, isolation, output validation |
| Model Gateway to model provider | sensitive-data leakage, provider substitution, untrusted output | provider eligibility, minimization, routing integrity, output distrust |
| Execution to Validation Pipeline | executor self-attestation, result substitution | independent validation of exact subject and evidence |
| Runtime to Audit Engine and Evidence Chain | event omission, reordering, tampering, disclosure | authenticated append, sequencing, integrity protection, monitoring |
| Development System to Runtime System | source or pipeline authority becoming runtime authority | distinct identities, credentials, data, approvals, and promotion path |
| Build system to release channel | artifact substitution, signing abuse, provenance loss | immutable identity, protected signing, release authorization |
| Primary environment to backup or recovery | restoration of revoked or vulnerable state | equivalent protection, restore validation, trust-state reconciliation |
| ILAIOS to customer-managed infrastructure | configuration ambiguity, shared responsibility failure | explicit contract, eligibility validation, observable control state |

Crossing a trust boundary invalidates implicit trust acquired on the previous side. Data is revalidated according to the receiving component’s authority. A prior component may supply evidence but cannot force the next component to accept its claim.

### Attack Surface

The attack surface includes every interface through which data, code, authority, state, or evidence enters, leaves, or changes the system. It includes public and private APIs, user interfaces, administrative consoles, webhooks, file and repository ingestion, message and event channels, tool and model integrations, identity federation, secret and key services, policy administration, build and deployment pipelines, update channels, observability endpoints, support tooling, exports, backups, recovery controls, and client applications.

An interface is security-relevant even when intended only for internal use, testing, diagnostics, migration, support, or health checking. Undocumented, deprecated, compatibility, debug, and emergency paths remain in scope until removed and verified unavailable.

Attack-surface management requires inventory, ownership, authentication expectations, authorization model, data classification, rate and resource limits, accepted schemas, failure behavior, telemetry, supported versions, dependency mapping, and retirement status. An interface with unknown ownership or unknown exposure is treated as ungoverned risk.

### Canonical Runtime Threat Sequence

The canonical operational flow is evaluated at every stage for direct and chained threats:

| Stage | Representative threats | Required defensive outcome |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Request intake | malicious payload, replay, smuggling, exhaustion, deceptive intent | bounded intake, request identity, schema and integrity controls |
| 2. Identity, tenant, and request verification | account takeover, tenant substitution, stale session, federation compromise | verified identity and explicit tenant/request binding |
| 3. Immutable Context creation | omitted constraint, altered purpose, confused deputy, stale policy input | complete, versioned, integrity-protected authoritative context |
| 4. Plan or action proposal | direct or indirect prompt manipulation, fabricated capability, unsafe decomposition | proposal treated as untrusted and non-authoritative |
| 5. Policy and capability evaluation | policy bypass, rule tampering, evaluation inconsistency, fail-open | deterministic evaluation of exact proposal and context |
| 6. Risk classification | severity manipulation, missing factor, downgrade, stale intelligence | explainable classification with conservative failure behavior |
| 7. Human approval when required | approval phishing, context concealment, wrong approver, approval fatigue | informed, scoped, attributable, independent approval |
| 8. Constrained execution authority | grant theft, replay, parameter substitution, scope or lifetime expansion | purpose-bound, subject-bound, time-bound, revocable capability |
| 9. Isolated Tool Gateway execution | command injection, credential leakage, sandbox escape, excessive side effect | allowlisted, isolated, least-privilege execution of approved parameters |
| 10. Independent validation | forged result, validation bypass, shared failure, wrong subject | independent validation of the exact action, result, and evidence |
| 11. Acceptance or rejection | result substitution, partial-success confusion, override abuse | deterministic disposition with explicit unresolved state |
| 12. Delivery, closure, and review | wrong recipient, data overexposure, premature closure, missing retention | controlled release, complete evidence, safe closure and follow-up |

Audit Engine and Evidence Chain operate continuously across all material stages. They do not begin after execution and are not optional when an operation is rejected, cancelled, times out, or fails before a side effect.

### Identity, Session, and Authentication Threats

Identity threats include credential theft, phishing, token replay, session fixation, weak recovery, federation misconfiguration, service-identity impersonation, certificate misuse, stale role claims, shared accounts, and theft of long-lived automation credentials. A valid authentication event can still be unsafe when the authenticating system, endpoint, session, or recovery process is compromised.

Controls include phishing-resistant or risk-appropriate multi-factor authentication, short-lived sessions, audience and issuer validation, device or workload assurance where required, secure recovery, token binding where supported, revocation, anomaly detection, and reauthentication for high-impact operations. Service identity is workload-specific and environment-specific. Identity proof is separated from authorization and does not carry implicit tenant or administrative power.

Detection includes impossible or anomalous access, unusual token use, repeated recovery, dormant identity activation, cross-region or cross-environment behavior, privilege changes, failed federation validation, and use after revocation. Evidence associates the authentication chain with subsequent policy, approval, and execution decisions without recording reusable secrets.

### Authorization, Tenant Isolation, and Confused-Deputy Threats

Authorization threats include insecure direct object reference, missing server-side enforcement, role inflation, tenant identifier substitution, authorization based on client-controlled claims, policy conflict, stale grants, permission aggregation, and use of a privileged service as a confused deputy.

Every authoritative access decision binds principal, tenant, role or capability, resource, action, purpose, environment, policy version, risk, and time. Tenant scope is established from trusted context rather than request-selected identifiers. Queries, caches, queues, indexes, logs, backups, exports, and observability systems preserve tenant separation. Shared infrastructure does not imply shared authorization.

Cross-tenant negative tests are mandatory for identifiers, search, batch operations, asynchronous workflows, retry, export, restore, support tools, and administrative functions. Any ambiguous tenant context fails closed. A system component may not use its own broad service privilege to perform an action that the initiating principal was not authorized to request.

### Context and Planning Manipulation

Attackers may alter, omit, reorder, or overload context so that a valid control evaluates the wrong facts. Threats include poisoned retrieved content, hidden instructions in documents, forged metadata, stale repository state, conflicting policy context, truncation, prompt injection, indirect instruction injection, and manipulation of tool descriptions or system constraints.

The Immutable Context separates authoritative facts from untrusted content, records source and version, establishes purpose and scope, and prevents downstream components from silently rewriting the basis of authorization. Untrusted instructions embedded in enterprise data, websites, files, messages, repositories, or tool output do not acquire policy authority merely because a reasoning component reads them.

Plans and recommendations are untrusted proposals. They are structurally constrained, checked against available capabilities, subjected to deterministic policy and risk evaluation, and independently reviewed when required. A proposal cannot create a tool, credential, scope, policy exception, approval, or execution authority that was not granted through the Control Plane.

### Policy Engine and Capability Threats

Policy threats include unauthorized rule modification, ambiguous precedence, inconsistent evaluation, stale policy, tenant-policy crossover, fail-open behavior, unvalidated input, policy rollback, shadow policy, and attempts to move policy decisions into a model prompt or application client.

Policy definitions, versions, activation, tests, conflicts, exceptions, and rollback are governed and auditable. Policy evaluation uses normalized, authoritative inputs and returns an explainable decision with the controlling rule set. Missing policy, failed evaluation, unknown capability, or contradictory outcome denies or safely constrains action.

Capability grants are minimal, explicit, purpose-bound, parameter-bound, tenant-bound, environment-bound, time-bound, and revocable. They cannot be widened by the Tool Gateway, tool adapter, caller, or model output. Replay, duplication, partial use, delegation, renewal, and cancellation behavior are defined. A grant for one action or resource is not reusable for a related action without explicit authority.

### Human Approval Threats

Human approval is exposed to phishing, fatigue, habituation, misleading summaries, hidden material parameters, wrong-tenant context, social pressure, collusion, compromised approver identity, stale approval, and approval of a mutable action.

Approval interfaces present the material action, tenant, target, data, side effects, risk, requested capability, expiry, validation expectations, and relevant differences from prior approval. Summaries do not conceal security-relevant details. High-impact approvals require stronger identity, appropriate role, independence, and reauthentication.

Approval binds to the exact immutable proposal and context. Any material change invalidates the approval. Batch and recurring approvals are prohibited unless policy explicitly defines bounded scope, item visibility, duration, revocation, and audit. Silence, timeout, notification delivery, prior approval, or lack of response never constitutes approval.

### Tool Gateway and Execution Threats

Execution threats include command, query, template, path, and argument injection; insecure deserialization; arbitrary file access; credential disclosure; sandbox escape; network pivoting; excessive side effects; tool substitution; unsafe retries; race conditions; output forgery; and execution outside the approved tenant, resource, or environment.

The Tool Gateway verifies the execution grant, tool identity, adapter version, parameter schema, destination, tenant, time, requested side effect, and policy eligibility. Tools operate with dedicated, least-privilege credentials and constrained network, filesystem, process, and resource access appropriate to risk. The gateway does not execute free-form model text as a command.

Execution is isolated from the proposing component. High-impact actions use idempotency, transaction, checkpoint, compensation, or explicit uncertain-state handling where appropriate. Timeout does not prove non-execution. Retry after uncertain completion requires reconciliation to avoid duplicated side effects.

Tool output is untrusted. It is bounded, classified, associated with the exact invocation, and passed to independent validation. A tool cannot authorize its own result, rewrite its audit trail, or cause the system to accept additional instructions embedded in output.

### Model and Provider Threats

Model-related threats include unreliable reasoning, fabricated facts, fabricated evidence, prompt injection, indirect instruction injection, context leakage, memorization, unsafe content generation, inconsistent outputs, model drift, model substitution, provider compromise, routing manipulation, service unavailability, and unauthorized provider data use.

ILAIOS assumes model output may be incorrect, incomplete, adversarially influenced, or inconsistent even when the provider and request are authentic. Models are replaceable reasoning resources, not trusted authorities. Output is constrained to a defined proposal schema where possible and is never treated as policy, approval, evidence, validation, or direct execution authority.

The Model Gateway enforces provider eligibility according to tenant, data classification, region, purpose, contract, retention, and risk. Requests are minimized and sensitive data is redacted or excluded when not necessary. Provider identity, model identity or class, routing decision, material configuration, and response association are recorded at the level required for audit without exposing protected content.

Fallback does not route classified data to an ineligible provider or silently change the assurance profile. Model upgrade, downgrade, fine-tune, configuration change, or provider substitution is a governed change and may require re-evaluation. Provider encryption does not authorize data disclosure, and provider contractual claims do not replace destination policy.

### Validation Pipeline Threats

Validation threats include validating a different artifact than the one executed, executor self-attestation, forged test evidence, incomplete rules, shared dependency failure, stale expected results, permissive defaults, selective validation, suppressed failures, and acceptance based only on model confidence.

The Validation Pipeline is independent of the proposer and executor to the degree required by risk. It binds validation rules and evidence to the exact request, context, grant, tool action, artifact, result, and version. Required rules run in deterministic order or under documented equivalent semantics. Missing, failed, timed-out, corrupted, or inapplicable mandatory validation produces rejection or explicit unresolved state rather than acceptance.

Validation combines syntax, semantic, policy, security, business, evidence, and side-effect checks as applicable. A successful result is not accepted when the execution exceeded authority, evidence is incomplete, or required negative conditions were not evaluated. Overrides are separate, attributable, narrowly scoped, and risk-authorized.

### Audit Engine and Evidence Chain Threats

Evidence threats include event omission, delayed insertion, reordering, deletion, modification, forged actor identity, fabricated timestamps, chain truncation, forked histories, digest substitution, replayed evidence, signing-key misuse, selective export, and disclosure of sensitive payloads through logs.

Material events are generated at the authoritative component and transmitted through authenticated, integrity-protected channels. Audit failures are observable. Buffered or asynchronous operation may support resilience, but it preserves ordering, durability expectations, backpressure, failure detection, and recovery without converting missing evidence into silent success.

Evidence records bind event identity, actor or workload, tenant where applicable, operation, subject, policy and approval references, result, time, version, and preceding chain state. Hash linkage protects sequence integrity but is not represented as blockchain and does not by itself prove that every required event was generated. Completeness controls, independent reconciliation, checkpoints, retention, access control, and protected exports are also required.

Audit and evidence systems do not expose secrets, keys, full sensitive payloads, or unnecessary model content. Redaction is structural and preserves the attributes needed for investigation and proof. Evidence administrators cannot silently rewrite source events, and operational administrators cannot suppress evidence of their own privileged actions.

### Data, Privacy, Secrets, Keys, and Encryption Threats

Data threats include unauthorized collection, excessive retention, cross-tenant access, insecure export, metadata leakage, unsafe logging, secondary use, residency violation, incomplete deletion, backup exposure, inference, and routing to an unauthorized provider or tool.

Data minimization, classification, purpose limitation, tenant isolation, destination eligibility, retention, deletion, access control, monitoring, and privacy governance apply throughout the lifecycle. Encryption protects approved states and channels but does not authorize access or prevent an authorized process from misusing plaintext.

Secrets and keys are threatened by source inclusion, log exposure, broad access, co-location with ciphertext, weak generation, reuse across purpose or tenant, ungoverned export, unsafe rotation, orphaned copies, compromised recovery, and signing abuse. Sections 3.4 through 3.6 define their canonical controls. Threat analysis evaluates the entire lifecycle, including generation, distribution, memory use, cache, backup, rotation, revocation, destruction, and incident response.

### Code Intelligence Threats

Code Intelligence is threatened by malicious source, parser exploitation, oversized or adversarial repositories, path traversal, symlink or archive escape, repository substitution, stale analysis, incorrect symbol resolution, dependency poisoning, index tampering, cross-repository confusion, sensitive-code exposure, and over-trust in inferred relationships.

The canonical dependency sequence remains Code Entity Model, Source File Analyzer, Symbol Extraction, Dependency Extraction, and Repository Code Index. Each stage consumes verified, bounded input and emits versioned output with provenance. Later stages do not silently repair or reinterpret invalid earlier evidence.

Repository identity, root, origin, branch, commit, and file boundaries are verified. Analysis operates without executing untrusted repository code unless a separate, isolated, policy-authorized capability explicitly requires execution. Results are associated with the exact repository state and become stale when that state changes.

Code Intelligence provides analysis and recommendation. It does not authorize repository mutation, merge, release, deployment, policy change, or Runtime action. Incorrect or incomplete analysis is detected through independent tests, source inspection, comparison, and conservative uncertainty handling.

### Administrative and Control Plane Threats

Administrative interfaces can change users, tenants, policy, provider eligibility, approvals, capabilities, evidence access, retention, keys, integrations, and operating state. They therefore represent high-impact attack surfaces.

Controls include dedicated administrative identity, strong authentication, least privilege, just-in-time elevation where appropriate, separation of duties, protected management networks or channels, explicit tenant scope, change preview, dual authorization for critical actions, complete audit, session controls, and rapid revocation.

Support access is purpose-limited and does not create invisible superuser capability. Impersonation, tenant switching, data export, policy override, evidence access, and emergency elevation are prominently indicated, time-bound, and recorded. Break-glass access is tested, monitored, and retrospectively reviewed.

### Availability, Resource Exhaustion, and Economic Abuse

Availability threats include request floods, expensive prompts, recursive planning, unbounded tool fan-out, oversized context, decompression bombs, parser complexity, queue starvation, retry storms, dependency outage, provider quota exhaustion, storage growth, evidence backpressure, and targeted consumption of tenant or platform budgets.
