Actions may update code, configuration, policy, architecture, ADRs, Threat Model, tests, detections, playbooks, access, key management, provider controls, contracts, training, documentation, recovery, or customer guidance.

Emergency containment is not closed merely because it remains enabled. Temporary restrictions, credentials, monitoring, communication channels, and manual processes are either removed or converted into governed permanent controls.

The Incident Commander recommends closure when active threat is contained, eradication and recovery criteria are met, affected stakeholders have received required communication, evidence and retention are secured, residual risks are accepted by proper authority, and corrective actions are owned. Closure authority is proportional to severity.

Incident closure does not erase uncertainty. Known unknowns, unavailable evidence, unverified provider claims, and remaining customer action are documented. An incident can be reopened when new evidence materially changes scope, impact, cause, or recovery confidence.

### Exercises and Capability Validation

ILAIOS validates Incident Response through scheduled and event-driven exercises. Formats include contact checks, walkthroughs, tabletop exercises, technical simulations, evidence drills, cross-tenant scenarios, key-compromise exercises, provider-loss exercises, build and release compromise, ransomware recovery, communication rehearsal, and full operational exercises appropriate to risk.

Exercises test decision authority, alternate communications, role handover, access, detection, containment, evidence, provider coordination, customer communication, legal notification analysis, backup restoration, safe-mode operation, and recovery validation. Success is measured against objectives and evidence, not participant attendance.

Unannounced or adversarial exercises are authorized and safety-controlled. Exercise data is clearly separated from production incident data while preserving realism. Exercise mechanisms cannot accidentally trigger customer notification, destructive action, or unauthorized data access.

Exercise findings become corrective actions and update plans, playbooks, controls, training, and Threat Model. Repeated failure of the same capability raises governance attention and may restrict dependent product operation.

### Incident Response Metrics

Metrics assess readiness, detection, decision quality, containment, recovery, communication, evidence, and improvement. Applicable measures include:

- coverage and currency of plans, playbooks, contact rosters, provider paths, tenant contacts, and exercised scenarios;
- time from first observable evidence to detection, intake, declaration, severity assignment, containment, eradication, recovery, and required communication;
- attacker dwell time, time to revoke compromised authority, and time to stop data or execution propagation;
- incidents detected internally versus by customers or providers;
- scope changes, severity changes, reopened incidents, and false closure;
- evidence completeness, chain-of-custody exceptions, clock or correlation gaps, and unavailable critical telemetry;
- containment verification, recurrence during recovery, rollback, and failed restore rate;
- notification timeliness against the applicable obligation and material communication corrections;
- affected tenants, data categories, versions, providers, capabilities, and service duration;
- corrective-action age, overdue high-risk actions, repeat causes, and verified effectiveness;
- exercise frequency, objective success, role availability, alternate-channel success, and repeated findings; and
- incident cost and business impact where measurable without incentivizing under-reporting.

Metrics are segmented by severity, tenant impact, component, incident class, detection source, and control domain. Fast closure is not rewarded when scope, evidence, notification, or corrective action is incomplete. Low incident count is not presumed to indicate strong security when detection coverage is weak.

### Incident Response Assurance and Continuous Improvement

Periodic assurance reviews verify that authorities, access, plans, contacts, playbooks, tooling, evidence storage, retention, providers, backups, recovery environments, communication templates, and exercises remain operational. Reviews use actual incidents, near misses, exercises, threat intelligence, customer findings, audits, and control testing.

Lessons are incorporated continuously into Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover capabilities. Material lessons update risk registers, Section 3.8 Threat Model, Section 3.7 SSDLC, architecture decisions, quality gates, release controls, monitoring, response playbooks, recovery, and customer security documentation.

Improvement preserves architectural intent. A response failure caused by an implementation defect does not justify removing the deterministic policy, approval, Tool Gateway, Validation Pipeline, Audit Engine, or Evidence Chain boundaries. Architectural change follows formal ADR governance.

### Incident Response Limitations

Incident Response cannot guarantee prevention, immediate detection, complete evidence, full attribution, recovery without loss, provider cooperation, or elimination of every attacker path. Sophisticated attackers can delete evidence, remain dormant, compromise telemetry, manipulate trusted providers, or exploit unknown vulnerabilities. Cloud, customer-managed, and cross-border environments can limit direct access and control.

Containment can disrupt customers or destroy volatile evidence. Credential and key rotation can affect availability and data access. Recovery can reintroduce compromise if clean state is misunderstood. Public, customer, legal, and technical priorities can conflict. These limitations require explicit decision authority, documented uncertainty, independent evidence, conservative recovery, and defense in depth.

The inability to prove complete scope is not treated as proof of limited impact. ILAIOS states confidence and uncertainty, maintains heightened monitoring, preserves reopening criteria, and uses risk-based customer and governance decisions.

### Incident Response Invariants

The following invariants are canonical:

- Incident Response is integrated across governance, identification, protection, detection, response, recovery, and continuous improvement;
- any authorized reporter may raise suspected adverse activity without first proving compromise;
- credible risk to a canonical trust boundary may trigger declaration and containment before complete technical certainty;
- every declared incident has a unique identifier, accountable Incident Commander, severity, authoritative record, decision log, evidence inventory, and communication control;
- severity reflects impact, scope, tenant reach, uncertainty, evidence, attacker capability, and legal or operational consequence and may not be lowered without evidence;
- credible cross-tenant compromise, release-signing compromise, systemic key compromise, arbitrary high-impact execution, Policy Engine manipulation, or systemic Evidence Chain invalidation receives presumptive critical treatment;
- incident urgency does not grant unrestricted, shared, anonymous, standing, or unaudited access;
- emergency authority is purpose-bound, scope-bound, time-bound, attributable, monitored, and retrospectively reviewed;
- AI Reasoning and Recommendation Engine output may assist analysis but never declares scope, authorizes containment, validates recovery, or closes an incident;
- Policy Engine, human-approval, Tool Gateway, Validation Pipeline, Audit Engine, and Evidence Chain boundaries remain controlling during response;
- automated containment is pre-authorized, bounded, auditable, verifiable, and reversible where practical;
- evidence preservation begins at intake and is balanced explicitly against safety, containment, tenant protection, and service impact;
- chain of custody identifies source, collector, integrity, access, transfer, analysis copies, and disposition;
- hash linkage does not by itself prove evidence source, completeness, lawful collection, or event generation;
- missing, disabled, divergent, or unverifiable mandatory telemetry and evidence is an incident condition, not silent absence of compromise;
- analysis distinguishes facts, hypotheses, unknowns, and rejected hypotheses and preserves the basis for each material conclusion;
- scope follows shared identities, credentials, keys, dependencies, builds, providers, backups, releases, tenants, and recovery paths rather than stopping at the first observed asset;
- containment actions define authority, tenant, subject, purpose, expected effect, duration, verification, and rollback;
- timeout, disconnection, crash, or missing response never proves that an external side effect did not occur;
- eradication removes malicious persistence, compromised authority, vulnerable conditions, unsafe configuration, and alternate attacker paths rather than only visible symptoms;
- emergency remediation follows minimum SSDLC, artifact-integrity, review, validation, release, deployment, and evidence requirements;
- recovery restores verified trusted state and reconciles identities, keys, policy, artifacts, data, evidence, providers, monitoring, and uncertain side effects;
- backups do not restore revoked trust, vulnerable artifacts, compromised credentials, deprecated cryptography, unsafe routes, or cross-tenant state silently;
- customer and stakeholder communication is authorized, factual, timely, uncertainty-aware, tenant-appropriate, versioned, and retained;
- notification obligations are determined by applicable law, regulation, contract, role, and jurisdiction and are not reduced by operational severity labels;
- provider incidents are independently assessed through ILAIOS evidence and may trigger protective action before provider investigation concludes;
- incident closure requires contained threat, verified recovery, secured evidence, completed required communication, accepted residual risk, and owned corrective actions;
- closure does not prevent reopening when new evidence changes scope, impact, cause, or recovery confidence;
- near misses, incidents, exercises, and control failures update the Threat Model and dependent controls; and
- corrective actions are not complete until their intended security outcome is independently verified.

An implementation is non-conformant if it requires proof of breach before accepting or declaring a credible incident; suppresses reporting to protect metrics or reputation; leaves a declared incident without accountable command, severity, timeline, evidence, or decision record; treats model or provider output as authoritative scope or recovery evidence; grants responders unrestricted or unaudited access; uses incident status to bypass Policy Engine, approval, Tool Gateway, validation, artifact integrity, audit, or Evidence Chain controls; records only successful response actions; destroys evidence without an explicit safety or containment decision; assumes missing logs prove no compromise; treats hash continuity as proof that no events are missing; resets one credential while derived sessions, grants, keys, or alternate access remain; retries an uncertain external action without reconciliation; restores service from unverified backup or vulnerable artifact; reactivates revoked identities, compromised keys, unsafe policy, or ineligible provider routes during recovery; lowers severity or closes scope without evidence; delays required customer or regulatory analysis until complete attribution; communicates speculation as fact or conceals material uncertainty; accepts a provider conclusion without assessing ILAIOS evidence; closes an incident while required notification, recovery validation, residual-risk acceptance, evidence custody, or corrective-action ownership is incomplete; or treats completion of a post-incident report as verification that corrective actions are effective.

## 3.10 Backup and Recovery

ILAIOS Backup and Recovery establishes the canonical controls through which enterprise data, configuration, policy, evidence, software state, and operational dependencies are protected against accidental deletion, corruption, malicious destruction, ransomware, provider failure, implementation defect, operator error, and other loss events. Its purpose is not merely to create copies. Its purpose is to preserve verifiable, tenant-correct, security-reconciled, and operationally usable recovery capability.

A successful backup operation is not proof of recoverability. Recoverability exists only when the protected scope is known, the copy is complete for its declared recovery point, integrity and authenticity are verified, necessary keys and dependencies remain available, access is controlled, restoration procedures are current, and representative recovery tests demonstrate that the restored service or data meets approved acceptance criteria.

This section defines the backup and recovery foundation used by incident response and disaster recovery. Section 3.9 governs response to security incidents, including recovery from compromise. Section 3.11 governs broader Disaster Recovery, including large-scale service disruption, alternate operating environments, regional or facility failure, failover, and coordinated restoration of critical business capabilities. Backup and Recovery provides the trustworthy copies, recovery metadata, restoration procedures, and validation evidence on which Disaster Recovery depends; it does not duplicate the wider Disaster Recovery command model.

### Purpose and Objectives

The Backup and Recovery capability has the following objectives:

- prevent a single failure, administrative identity, credential, storage boundary, provider, malicious action, or configuration error from destroying both production state and all usable recovery copies;
- establish explicit Recovery Point Objectives and Recovery Time Objectives based on business impact, tenant commitments, data classification, system criticality, and dependency order;
- preserve tenant isolation, authorization, confidentiality, integrity, residency, retention, deletion, evidence, and legal obligations throughout backup, storage, transfer, restore, validation, and disposal;
- protect backup copies from modification, premature deletion, ransomware, destructive administrators, compromised workloads, and unauthorized restoration;
- ensure that application data, policy, configuration, identities, keys, evidence, schemas, dependencies, and versions required for a coherent restore are identified and recoverable;
- prevent restoration from silently reactivating revoked identity, expired capability, compromised key, vulnerable artifact, obsolete policy, unsafe provider route, deleted tenant, or invalid trust;
- support granular item, tenant, service, environment, point-in-time, and full-system recovery according to approved service requirements;
- validate recovery through realistic exercises and exact acceptance criteria rather than backup completion reports alone;
- provide evidence sufficient to demonstrate what was protected, when, from which source, under which policy, with which integrity state, and whether restoration succeeded; and
- integrate recovery lessons, failures, capacity trends, and threat intelligence into architecture, operations, incident response, Disaster Recovery, and customer commitments.

### Scope

Backup and Recovery applies to all ILAIOS-managed production and non-production assets whose loss, corruption, unavailability, or unverifiable state could affect product operation, tenant data, security, evidence, legal obligations, development continuity, or customer assurance. This includes structured and unstructured data, databases, object stores, policy, configuration, schemas, indexes, queues where durable state is required, Audit Engine records, Evidence Chain state, cryptographic metadata, secrets and keys where recoverability is permitted, source repositories, release artifacts, build provenance, infrastructure definitions, observability data, administrative records, and recovery documentation.

The scope includes managed services, customer-managed deployments, hybrid dependencies, third-party providers, backups created by providers, exports retained for recovery, and local or endpoint data when ILAIOS has contractual or architectural responsibility for recoverability.

Assets that are intentionally ephemeral, reconstructible, or excluded from backup remain documented. Exclusion identifies the reconstruction source, procedure, time, dependency, integrity validation, and business impact. “Can be recreated” is not sufficient when the authoritative source, exact version, configuration, model route, provider, or required time is uncertain.

### Canonical Definitions

A backup is a controlled copy of data or system state created for recovery. A snapshot is a point-in-time representation of storage or service state. Replication is the maintenance of one or more additional copies, often with low delay. Continuous data protection captures changes frequently enough to support fine-grained recovery points. An archive preserves information for long-term retention or reference. These mechanisms can complement one another but are not interchangeable.

A restore is the technical act of retrieving backup content and placing it into a target. Recovery is the larger process of selecting a trustworthy recovery point, restoring required components, reconciling security and business state, validating the result, authorizing use, communicating status, and returning the service or data to controlled operation.

The Recovery Point Objective, or RPO, is the maximum tolerable period of data change that may be lost, expressed relative to the disruption or corruption point. The Recovery Time Objective, or RTO, is the target maximum time to restore an agreed service capability after recovery is initiated under defined conditions. Neither is a guarantee unless contractually stated and supported by verified capacity and exercises.

Maximum Tolerable Downtime or Maximum Acceptable Outage represents the business limit beyond which disruption creates unacceptable impact. It constrains the RTO but does not replace it. Recovery Time Actual and Recovery Point Actual record observed performance during a real or exercised recovery.

A recovery point is a uniquely identifiable set of backup state and dependencies from which recovery may be attempted. A known-good recovery point is one whose integrity, provenance, application consistency, security context, dependency compatibility, and relevant threat exposure have been evaluated for the intended recovery.

An immutable copy resists modification and deletion for a defined retention period through controls independent of ordinary production write authority. An isolated copy is inaccessible through the normal production control path or credentials. Offline, air-gapped, logically isolated, and separately administered copies are possible implementation patterns; the canonical requirement is effective independence from the failure and attacker paths being addressed.

### Backup and Recovery Principles

Recovery requirements derive from business and security impact. Storage convenience, provider default, or product tier does not determine protection for high-impact tenant or trust data.

Independent failure domains are mandatory. Critical assets use multiple protected copies or equivalent resilience such that compromise of production credentials, ordinary administrators, one provider service, one region, or one storage implementation does not destroy every recovery option.

At least one recovery path for critical assets is isolated from ordinary production identities and destructive operations. Isolation is verified from the attacker’s perspective, including inherited administration, automation, recovery APIs, key access, and support channels.

Backups preserve security classification. A copy is never less sensitive because it is old, compressed, encrypted, deduplicated, or outside production. Protection is equal to or stronger than the source according to exposure and retention.

Backup data is untrusted until verified. Copies can contain corruption, malware, malicious persistence, invalid policy, compromised credentials, vulnerable artifacts, cross-tenant data, or incomplete transactions. Restore does not imply acceptance.

Recovery is application-aware. Storage blocks or files can be intact while business relationships, tenant ownership, schemas, audit sequence, keys, or execution state are inconsistent. Acceptance occurs at the product and security level.

Deletion and retention are deliberate. Backup is not a permanent exemption from tenant termination, privacy deletion, contractual disposition, legal hold, or evidence-retention policy.

### Governance and Accountability

The Backup and Recovery program has an accountable owner, approved policy, system-specific plans, asset inventory, service objectives, provider responsibilities, access model, retention schedules, test program, exception process, capacity plan, and evidence requirements.

Data and service owners define business criticality, acceptable loss, recovery priority, authoritative sources, customer obligations, and acceptance criteria. Security Architecture defines isolation, encryption, key, identity, evidence, ransomware, and clean-recovery requirements. Platform and Operations implement and operate backup and restore capabilities. Application Engineering defines consistency, schema, dependency, migration, and functional validation. Privacy, Legal, and Compliance define retention, legal hold, deletion, jurisdiction, and regulated-data obligations.

Backup administrators, production administrators, key custodians, recovery authorizers, and evidence custodians are separated according to risk. No single compromised identity shall be able to alter production, delete all protected copies, change retention, replace recovery policy, obtain every decryption key, and authorize its own restore.

Smaller organizations may combine operational roles, but control objectives remain explicit. Compensating measures include dual authorization, just-in-time access, immutable policy, independent alerting, protected evidence, external custody, and retrospective review. Role combination never justifies shared accounts or unlogged destructive authority.

### Business Impact and Recovery Requirements

Recovery requirements are established through a Business Impact Analysis and technical dependency analysis. The assessment identifies critical business capabilities, tenant obligations, data flows, upstream and downstream services, tolerable loss, maximum outage, legal consequences, manual alternatives, recovery sequence, minimum viable operation, staffing, providers, and evidence needs.

Each protected service or asset has, as applicable:

- accountable owner and technical custodian;
- tenant and data classification;
- business criticality and dependency position;
- approved RPO, RTO, retention, and recovery priority;
- backup method, schedule or change-capture strategy, locations, and failure domains;
- encryption and key dependencies;
- consistency grouping and transaction boundary;
- restoration procedure and required clean environment;
- validation and acceptance criteria;
- customer-specific or jurisdictional constraints;
- escalation and incident-response integration; and
- last successful backup, integrity verification, restore test, and observed recovery performance.

RPO and RTO are measurable outcomes. “Near real time,” “highly available,” “daily,” or “rapid recovery” is insufficient without defined measurement boundaries. The RPO specifies which authoritative data state is covered. The RTO identifies the triggering event, start and end conditions, service level restored, dependencies assumed available, and whether security validation time is included. Security validation is always included in actual recovery completion.

### Recovery Tiering

ILAIOS may assign recovery tiers to align controls and investment with impact. The tier labels are implementation-independent; their obligations are explicit.

| Recovery tier | Representative impact | Required capability characteristics |
|---|---|---|
| Tier 0 — Trust-Critical | compromise or loss invalidates authorization, tenant isolation, evidence, key trust, or release integrity | strongest isolation, minimal tolerable loss, independent copies, frequent verification, exercised clean recovery |
| Tier 1 — Mission-Critical | outage or loss materially disrupts core customer operations or high-impact data | defined low RPO/RTO, resilient copy strategy, staged recovery, frequent full tests |
| Tier 2 — Business-Critical | material but bounded operational or customer impact | scheduled protected backup, dependency-aware restore, periodic tests |
| Tier 3 — Standard | tolerable temporary loss or reconstructible operation | documented backup or verified reconstruction, proportionate testing |
| Excluded or Ephemeral | no authoritative or required recoverable state | documented rationale, reconstruction evidence, monitored exclusion |

Tier assignment considers the highest material impact and dependency role. A small dataset that contains tenant routing, policy authority, key metadata, or Evidence Chain checkpoints can be more critical than a large content store.

### Protected Asset Coverage

| Asset category | Backup and recovery requirement |
|---|---|
| Tenant business data | tenant-bound copies, classification-preserving protection, point-in-time recovery where required, item and tenant validation |
| Immutable Context and workflow state | exact request, scope, policy, approval, execution and closure relationships preserved or safely reconciled |
| Policy and configuration | versioned authoritative copies, activation history, tests, tenant scope, rollback safety |
| Audit Engine and Evidence Chain | append-only history, chain state, checkpoints, completeness reconciliation, protected retention |
| Identities and authorization configuration | recoverable configuration without reactivating revoked sessions, grants, credentials, or obsolete roles |
| Secrets, keys, certificates, and trust metadata | recoverable only through approved custody and contingency processes; compromise and revocation state preserved |
| Schemas and migrations | exact version, dependency order, backward and forward recovery behavior, partial-migration handling |
| Source, dependencies, builds, and releases | verified repository history, manifests, provenance, artifact digests, approved released artifacts |
| Code Intelligence and knowledge state | authoritative source binding, versioned index state, reproducible reconstruction where chosen |
| Observability and incident evidence | retention consistent with detection, investigation, legal, customer, and recovery requirements |
| Infrastructure and deployment definitions | versioned desired state, environment variables by reference, recovery prerequisites, validation |
| Backup catalogs and recovery documentation | protected independently so recovery remains possible when production control systems fail |

Asset coverage is reconciled against the architecture, storage inventory, providers, data-flow diagrams, tenant lifecycle, release inventory, and retention obligations. Shadow data stores, temporary exports, migration stores, caches that become authoritative, local operator copies, and provider-created replicas are included or eliminated.

### Backup Architecture and Copy Strategy

The backup architecture separates production data access from backup administration, retention control, and recovery authorization. Backup creation uses narrowly scoped read and write paths. Production workloads do not receive destructive authority over protected copies.

Critical data is protected across failure domains appropriate to its threat model. Diversity may include separate accounts, administrative domains, storage systems, regions, providers, media, or offline custody. Merely labeling two logical locations as separate is insufficient when the same compromised identity, key, control plane, deletion policy, or provider administrator can destroy both.

Copy strategy balances RPO, RTO, integrity, cost, retention, change rate, data size, and recovery complexity. Full, incremental, differential, snapshot, journal, log-shipping, continuous-protection, export, or reconstructed-state approaches may be used. Technology choice is not canonical; verified recovery outcome is.

Backup chains avoid unbounded dependency on a long sequence of incremental copies. The loss or corruption of one link shall not silently invalidate the protected period. Full baselines, synthetic consolidation, independent checkpoints, or equivalent controls limit chain fragility.

Deduplication and compression do not merge tenant security boundaries or expose cross-tenant data through indexes, side channels, or shared encryption context. Shared physical storage retains logical access separation and cryptographic treatment appropriate to classification.

### Isolation, Immutability, and Ransomware Resilience

Ransomware and destructive administrators target backups, catalogs, recovery orchestration, identity, and keys. ILAIOS therefore protects at least one critical recovery path from ordinary online production compromise.

Immutability has a defined enforcement authority, retention period, clock source, administrative override model, and deletion behavior. A production administrator cannot shorten retention or remove every immutable copy unilaterally. Emergency override, where technically possible and legally necessary, requires separate authority and evidence.

Isolation covers data and the dependencies required to use it. An isolated encrypted backup is not recoverable if every decryption key is available only through the compromised production environment. Conversely, storing unprotected recovery keys beside isolated backups defeats isolation.

Offline or logically disconnected copies are updated through controlled, authenticated processes that do not leave a persistent bidirectional path. Reconnection for backup, verification, or restore is time-bound, monitored, and followed by renewed isolation.

Ransomware resilience tests assume compromised production credentials, deleted catalogs, unavailable primary key service, corrupted recent copies, and attacker persistence. The recovery team shall be able to identify an earlier trustworthy point, access instructions and contacts, obtain authorized keys, restore in a clean environment, and validate before reconnecting.

### Tenant Isolation and Data Segregation

Every backup object, catalog entry, recovery request, restore target, key context, retention policy, legal hold, deletion record, and validation result preserves authoritative tenant identity. Tenant scope is not inferred solely from a path, filename, user-supplied identifier, or restored application field.

Backup operations prevent one tenant from affecting another tenant’s schedule, retention, key, copy, restoration, export, or deletion. Shared jobs and media maintain explicit tenant boundaries in metadata, authorization, encryption context, and restore selection.

A tenant-scoped restore verifies that only the intended tenant’s data and dependencies are selected. Cross-tenant relationships, shared indexes, global reference data, and deduplicated storage receive special validation. A correct item count does not prove tenant purity.

Tenant deletion and termination propagate to backup lifecycle according to contract, privacy, legal hold, evidence, and technical retention requirements. Deleted tenant state cannot become active through a later environment or full-system restore. Tombstones, deletion manifests, or equivalent authoritative disposition records survive long enough to prevent resurrection.

### Data Consistency and Recovery Sets

Backups are consistent at the level required by the application. Crash-consistent storage may be insufficient where multiple databases, object stores, queues, indexes, policy stores, evidence systems, or external side effects form one business transaction.

A recovery set identifies components that must be restored to compatible points. It records consistency boundary, ordering, transaction or checkpoint references, schema and application version, key state, policy version, external dependencies, and known reconciliation steps.

Backup procedures coordinate quiescence, transaction logs, snapshots, application checkpoints, export protocols, or equivalent mechanisms as appropriate. The procedure records whether in-flight operations are included, excluded, retried, cancelled, or left uncertain.

Asynchronous and external side effects cannot always be rolled back with data. Recovery reconciles Tool Gateway actions, customer-system state, provider operations, notifications, payments or other external effects, Validation Pipeline decisions, and Evidence Chain history. The system never repeats an uncertain side effect solely because restored local state does not show completion.

### Backup Integrity, Authenticity, and Provenance

Each backup has a unique identity and metadata sufficient to determine source tenant, source system, source version, recovery point, creation time, method, scope, consistency state, classification, encryption profile, key reference, retention, storage location, dependency set, software version, and producing workload.

Integrity controls detect accidental and malicious modification. Cryptographic digests, authenticated encryption, signatures, protected manifests, storage integrity, and independent catalog reconciliation may contribute. A digest generated and stored under the same compromised authority as the backup provides limited assurance and is not the sole protection for trust-critical copies.

Backup creation is authenticated and attributable. An attacker cannot insert a malicious recovery point into the trusted catalog merely by writing data to backup storage. Trusted status requires provenance, policy compliance, completed integrity checks, and where required independent verification.

Integrity is checked after creation, during storage according to risk, before restoration, after transfer, after restoration, and during test exercises. Detection of corruption quarantines the copy, identifies dependent chains and recovery points, assesses affected retention coverage, and triggers incident handling when malicious action or material loss is plausible.

### Encryption and Key Dependencies

Backups are encrypted at rest and in transit according to Section 3.6 and retain equivalent or stronger protection than the source. Keys are managed under Section 3.5 with purpose, tenant, environment, and usage separation.

Backup encryption uses recoverable key arrangements that do not depend exclusively on the failed environment. Key recovery, escrow where approved, split custody, hardware protection, alternate key service, or other mechanisms may support continuity. The method is risk-based, access-controlled, exercised, and does not create a plaintext master-key repository.

Key metadata records which backup generations depend on which keys, wrapping keys, certificates, algorithms, and cryptographic profiles. Rotation evaluates old copies. Re-wrapping and re-encryption are distinguished, and neither is assumed complete until every dependent copy and recovery workflow is verified.

Revocation and compromise state survives restore. An older backup does not authorize use of a key, certificate, secret, or trust anchor that is currently revoked, expired, compromised, deprecated, or outside the intended tenant and purpose. Recovery reconciles historical data decryption needs with current trust policy.

Cryptographic deletion is claimed only when all relevant key copies, wrappers, escrow material, backups, exports, caches, and plaintext copies are addressed and the data cannot be recovered through alternate paths. Retention or legal hold may prohibit immediate cryptographic deletion.

### Identity, Access, and Separation of Duties

Backup creation, policy administration, storage administration, restore initiation, restore approval, key access, legal hold, deletion, and evidence administration use distinct least-privilege capabilities according to risk.

Backup services use dedicated workload identities and short-lived credentials where practical. Credentials are not embedded in scripts, images, logs, recovery documentation, or backup payloads. Production identities cannot browse or restore arbitrary backups merely because they can access source data.

Restore is a high-impact operation. Authorization binds actor, tenant, source copy, recovery point, target, purpose, data classification, requested scope, expected overwrite or merge behavior, time, policy, and approval. High-impact, cross-environment, cross-region, full-tenant, or trust-critical restores require independent authorization.

Emergency access is time-bound, attributable, monitored, and removed after use. Break-glass access does not bypass tenant binding, evidence, key custody, validation, or post-action review. Shared recovery accounts are prohibited.

Entitlements are reviewed periodically and after role change, provider change, incident, or material architecture change. Backup access is included in insider-risk detection and privileged-session monitoring.

### Backup Creation and Pipeline Security

Backup jobs run from versioned, reviewed, and controlled definitions. Scheduling, source selection, exclusions, retention, destinations, encryption, credentials, verification, and alerts are policy-governed. A change to a backup exclusion, retention duration, isolation, key, deletion rule, or failure threshold is security-relevant.

The pipeline validates source identity, tenant, scope, classification, destination eligibility, available capacity, key state, and expected recovery metadata before writing. It does not silently redirect to a less protected destination after failure.

Backup workers are isolated from untrusted workloads and use minimum network and data permissions. Provider or storage hooks, lifecycle scripts, and catalog processors are treated as executable supply-chain dependencies.

Job completion requires more than bytes transferred. It includes manifest creation, integrity verification, catalog update, retention enforcement, failure-domain confirmation, monitoring, and evidence. Partial success is reported explicitly by asset and tenant.

Retries are idempotent or safely reconciled. A retry does not create unmanaged duplicates, weaken retention, omit data, reuse unsafe cryptographic parameters, or overwrite the last known-good copy. Persistent failure escalates before RPO coverage is breached.

### Backup Catalog and Inventory

The backup catalog is a trust-critical recovery asset. It records copies, recovery points, tenants, sources, scopes, dependencies, integrity state, key references, retention, legal holds, storage locations, test results, quarantine, deletion, and recovery eligibility.

The catalog is protected separately from production and from the copies it describes. Recovery remains possible when the primary catalog is corrupted, encrypted, or unavailable. Independent inventory or manifests enable reconstruction and reconciliation.

Catalog records distinguish available, verified, quarantined, expired, deletion-pending, legally held, compromised, restored, and destroyed states. A copy is not selected for recovery merely because storage exists.

Inventory reconciliation detects orphaned backups, untracked snapshots, missing expected copies, storage objects without trusted provenance, expired copies that remain, legal-hold conflicts, tenant mismatch, key mismatch, and copies outside approved jurisdiction or provider.

### Retention, Archival, Legal Hold, and Disposal

Retention is defined by asset type, tenant contract, data classification, business need, recovery coverage, product support, evidence, privacy, legal, tax, regulatory, and litigation requirements. Longer retention is not automatically safer because it increases exposure, key dependency, storage cost, and deletion complexity.

Retention policy defines minimum and maximum duration, number or spacing of recovery points, immutable period, archive transition, review, legal hold, and destruction method. Changes apply predictably to existing and future copies and do not silently shorten protected coverage.

Legal hold suspends ordinary deletion only for the defined information, parties, matter, jurisdiction, and period. Hold issuance, scope, access, review, release, and resulting deletion are attributable and auditable. Legal hold does not grant broad operational access to content.

Expired backups are securely disposed of, including replicas, temporary transfer copies, provider caches, removable media, test restores, catalog entries, and associated keys where appropriate. Deletion is verified and exceptions are tracked. Storage lifecycle settings alone are not sufficient evidence when provider behavior or replication is uncertain.

### Privacy and Data Subject Obligations

Backup design supports data minimization, purpose limitation, retention, tenant termination, and legally required deletion. It avoids using recovery copies as secondary analytics, model-training, test, or development datasets unless separately authorized and governed.

Where immediate deletion from immutable or sequential backups is technically infeasible or conflicts with legal retention, access remains restricted, the data is not restored into active processing without applying current deletion state, and the copy expires under the approved retention schedule. The organization documents the legal and technical basis.

Recovery applies current deletion and suppression records before normal service resumes. A restored historical database cannot reintroduce a deleted account, withdrawn consent state, expired retention, or terminated tenant into active use.

Privacy impact includes backup location, subprocessor, key custody, cross-border transfer, operator access, test restores, incident investigation, and disposal. Customer representations accurately describe backup retention and deletion limitations.

### Replication, Snapshots, and High Availability

Replication, clustering, redundant storage, and snapshots improve availability and may reduce RPO, but they do not automatically constitute independent backup. They can copy corruption, ransomware encryption, malicious deletion, unsafe policy, and tenant crossover rapidly.

A snapshot controlled by the same production administrator, account, credentials, retention policy, and storage service as the source is not the sole recovery protection for critical assets. A replica continuously writable from the compromised source is not isolated.

High availability and Backup and Recovery have distinct objectives. High availability maintains service through localized failure; Backup and Recovery restores trusted historical or replacement state. Both are required where business impact demands them, and neither is represented as the other.

### Restore Request and Authorization

A restore begins with a controlled request specifying incident or business reason, affected tenant, asset, data scope, proposed recovery point, target environment, urgency, overwrite or merge behavior, expected data loss, security context, dependencies, approval, and validation plan.

The request identifies whether the restore is item-level, tenant-level, service-level, environment-level, point-in-time, full-system, forensic, test, or migration-related. The category determines authority and isolation.

Before execution, the recovery team confirms that the source copy is eligible, within retention, not quarantined, integrity-verified, decryptable, tenant-correct, compatible, and appropriate to the threat. The target is verified to prevent restoration into the wrong tenant, region, environment, account, or production service.

Material uncertainty is visible. If the exact corruption or compromise point is unknown, recovery-point selection includes threat analysis and may prefer an earlier point with greater data loss but higher confidence. The decision records tradeoffs.

### Canonical Recovery Workflow

The canonical recovery workflow is:

1. declare the recovery objective, scope, owner, tenant, service level, RPO, RTO, and acceptance authority;
2. identify the loss, corruption, compromise, or availability condition and determine whether Incident Response or Disaster Recovery command is active;
3. preserve required evidence and prevent further destructive synchronization, replication, retention, or overwrite;
4. inventory affected assets, dependencies, external side effects, identities, keys, policy, schemas, versions, and evidence state;
5. select and authorize a candidate recovery point using provenance, integrity, threat exposure, compatibility, and business impact;
6. prepare an eligible target or clean recovery environment with verified identity, network, keys, monitoring, capacity, and isolation;
7. restore the exact authorized scope using controlled tools and attributable identities;
8. reconcile current security state, including revoked identities, expired grants, compromised keys, deleted tenants, retention, provider eligibility, and policy;
9. validate data, application behavior, tenant isolation, evidence continuity, security controls, external side effects, and performance;
10. obtain independent acceptance appropriate to risk and authorize staged return to service;
11. monitor heightened indicators, data reconciliation, customer impact, capacity, and recurrence; and
12. close the recovery record only after evidence, communication, residual risk, temporary access, and corrective actions are complete.

Audit Engine and Evidence Chain record material recovery decisions and actions throughout the workflow. They are not initiated only after service restoration.

### Clean Recovery Environment

A clean recovery environment is used when the integrity of the original environment, administrative plane, identity system, key service, build path, network, or backup catalog is uncertain. It has independently verified infrastructure, identities, tools, network controls, monitoring, and time sources.

The environment receives only the permissions and data required for the recovery. It does not inherit production trust automatically. Connections to production, providers, customers, or backup vaults are explicitly authorized, minimized, monitored, and removed after use.

Recovery tools and images originate from verified sources and are protected from the incident path. The environment does not execute restored application code, automation, scheduled jobs, webhooks, tool actions, model requests, or customer notifications until explicitly enabled after validation.

Forensic analysis, malware scanning, schema inspection, data integrity, tenant validation, and security-state reconciliation occur before restored systems join trusted operation. Clean-room status is an evidence-based condition, not a location label.

### Security-State Reconciliation

Historical backups contain historical trust. Recovery must apply current authoritative security state before normal use. Reconciliation covers:

- disabled and deleted users, terminated tenants, revoked sessions, credentials, tokens, secrets, certificates, and keys;
- expired or cancelled approvals, capabilities, exceptions, legal holds, and temporary elevation;
- current Policy Engine versions, deny rules, provider eligibility, data classification, residency, and retention;
- security patches, supported artifacts, dependency status, cryptographic profiles, trust stores, and configuration baselines;
- known indicators of compromise, containment blocks, incident restrictions, and safe-mode settings;
- deletion, consent, suppression, and tenant-offboarding records;
- release-signing, Evidence Chain, audit, validation, and key-compromise decisions; and
- unresolved external side effects and customer-system state.

Reconciliation is deterministic and evidence-producing. A restored component cannot overwrite newer revocation or incident state merely because the backup is otherwise internally consistent.

### Schema, Version, and Dependency Compatibility

Recovery maps data to the exact schema, application, policy, adapter, cryptographic profile, and dependency versions required to interpret it. Restore procedures define supported forward, backward, and point-in-time compatibility.

Schema migration and rollback are controlled changes. Partial migration, duplicate execution, incompatible indexes, changed identifiers, removed fields, and altered authorization semantics receive explicit handling. A database that opens successfully may still be semantically unsafe.

Historical data may require an older application version for interpretation, but vulnerable or unsupported software is not exposed to production traffic. It may be used in an isolated environment to transform data into a current, validated form.

Provider-managed formats and APIs are included in compatibility planning. Export capability, version availability, rate limits, tooling, and provider support are validated before an incident.

### Restore Validation and Acceptance

Recovery validation is independent from the restore mechanism according to risk. It verifies the exact restored subject and includes:

- backup identity, source, tenant, recovery point, manifest, integrity, authenticity, and decryption;
- record counts, checksums, referential integrity, transaction consistency, object completeness, and expected data loss;
- schema, application, policy, configuration, artifact, dependency, and migration compatibility;
- tenant isolation, authorization, authentication, secrets, keys, encryption, network, and provider routing;
- Audit Engine continuity, Evidence Chain linkage and completeness reconciliation, logging, monitoring, and alerting;
- Tool Gateway and Model Gateway restrictions, Validation Pipeline operation, human approval, and execution safety;
- deleted and revoked state, legal holds, retention, privacy, residency, and customer configuration;
- external side-effect reconciliation, queues, scheduled jobs, webhooks, retries, notifications, and integrations;
- availability, performance, capacity, error rates, and recovery objective achievement; and
- rollback, heightened monitoring, communication, and residual-risk conditions.

Validation failure leaves the recovery in rejected or unresolved state. It does not convert to acceptance because the RTO is approaching. Any override is explicit, separately authorized, risk-bounded, time-limited, and communicated to affected stakeholders.

The acceptance authority is independent of the restore executor for high-impact recoveries. Acceptance identifies the service level restored, remaining limitations, observed RPO and RTO, unresolved data, monitoring period, and rollback criteria.

### Audit Engine and Evidence Chain Recovery

Audit and evidence state receive trust-critical protection. Backups preserve append-only event records, chain links, sequence, checkpoints, signatures, tenant scope, retention, and verification metadata without allowing restoration to rewrite accepted history.

Evidence recovery distinguishes restoration of unavailable evidence from insertion of reconstructed events. Original recovered records retain original identity and chain position. Reconstructed records are explicitly labeled, linked to supporting sources, and do not masquerade as events generated at the original time.

Chain recovery verifies continuity before and after the selected recovery point, identifies missing intervals, reconciles authoritative component records, and creates a documented bridge or incident record where mathematical continuity cannot be restored. A new chain segment may begin under governed recovery only when the discontinuity and prior trusted checkpoint remain explicit.

Backup and restore administrators cannot alter audit history to conceal their own actions. Recovery operations, validation, key access, catalog changes, exceptions, and deletion remain independently auditable.

### Identity, Policy, Approval, and Capability Recovery

Identity stores, roles, policy, approvals, and capabilities are not restored as ordinary business data. Historical state can grant authority that is no longer valid.

Recovery separates durable configuration from transient authority. User and workload identities are reconciled with current employment, tenant, federation, device, credential, and revocation state. Sessions and short-lived tokens are not reactivated. Privileged roles and emergency access are re-approved where required.

Policy restore preserves version and tenant scope but evaluates current activation, exceptions, deny rules, provider eligibility, legal restrictions, and incident controls. A historical policy does not supersede a newer security restriction automatically.

Approvals and capabilities are bound to original immutable context, exact action, time, and purpose. Expired, consumed, cancelled, or uncertain grants remain invalid after restore. An external side effect is reconciled before any replacement capability is issued.

### Secrets, Keys, and Certificate Recovery

Secret and key recovery follows dedicated, tested contingency procedures. Recovery material is not copied into general backups in plaintext or under the same unprotected credentials as application data.

The procedure verifies key identity, purpose, tenant, environment, version, status, custody, quorum where required, and relationship to ciphertext. Use is limited to the recovery purpose and recorded without exposing key material.

Compromised, revoked, or expired keys are not restored to active trust. They may be used in a controlled isolated process solely to recover data when authorized, after which data is protected under current keys and the old material returns to revoked or destroyed status.

Loss of a necessary key is a recovery failure even when backup bytes are intact. Test exercises therefore include alternate key-service availability, custodian availability, recovery authorization, and decryption of representative old generations.

### Source, Build, Release, and Infrastructure Recovery

The Development System protects verified repository history, canonical architecture, ADRs, build definitions, dependency locks, release manifests, software bills of materials, provenance, artifact digests, approved artifacts, signing records, and infrastructure definitions.

Source recovery establishes repository origin, branch, commit, signature or attribution, object integrity, and relationship to released artifacts. A source mirror is not trusted solely because it contains plausible history.

Build and release recovery does not recreate an artifact and assign the old digest or approval. A rebuild is a new candidate unless reproducibility proves exact identity. Compromised signing keys and release channels are reconciled before distribution resumes.

Infrastructure recovery uses versioned desired state and current security baseline. It does not restore hardcoded secrets, vulnerable images, deprecated network exposure, obsolete trust, or incident-containment changes from historical configuration.

### Code Intelligence and Reconstructible Data

Code Intelligence state may be backed up or deterministically reconstructed according to business impact and recovery objectives. The authoritative repository identity and canonical dependency sequence remain controlling.

If indexes, entity models, symbol data, dependency data, or repository relationships are restored, they remain bound to the exact repository root, origin, branch, commit, analyzer version, schema, and configuration. Stale analysis is not represented as current.

Reconstruction may be preferable when the source is authoritative and processing time meets the RTO. Reconstruction jobs run in controlled environments without executing untrusted repository code and produce new provenance and validation evidence.

Model-generated recommendations, transient context, and caches are not assumed authoritative recovery assets. Where retained for evidence or workflow continuity, their original provider, model class, configuration, input relationship, tenant, and non-authoritative status remain explicit.

### Managed Service and Provider Backup

Provider-managed backup does not remove ILAIOS accountability. Contracts and technical assurance define protected assets, schedule, retention, locations, isolation, immutability, encryption, key custody, administrator access, deletion, export, restore support, RPO, RTO, evidence, incident notification, and termination.

ILAIOS verifies provider capabilities through configuration evidence, independent copies where required, restore tests, contractual review, and observed recovery. Marketing claims or a service-level statement do not prove tenant-correct restore.

Critical services have an exit or contingency path for provider outage, account suspension, contract termination, data-format change, region loss, control-plane compromise, or provider business failure. Export duration, volume limits, egress dependencies, and decryption are included in recovery testing.

Provider snapshots that remain under the same compromised account or control plane are not the sole critical backup. Provider support access and deletion authority are included in the Threat Model.

### Customer-Managed and Hybrid Deployments

For customer-managed or hybrid deployments, the shared-responsibility model identifies who owns backup creation, storage, isolation, encryption, keys, monitoring, restore, testing, retention, legal hold, deletion, and evidence. Responsibility is explicit per asset and control.

ILAIOS supplies product requirements, supported procedures, compatibility information, validation criteria, and telemetry necessary for safe recovery. The customer supplies environment controls and evidence within its responsibility. Unsupported or unsafe customer backup configuration is surfaced where technically observable.

Customer-controlled copies do not receive automatic authority to restore into ILAIOS-managed environments. Import and recovery validate tenant, provenance, format, schema, encryption, malware, policy, and authorization.

Customer-facing recovery commitments accurately reflect which layer ILAIOS controls, which assumptions depend on the customer, and which objectives have been exercised end to end.

### Backup Monitoring and Failure Management

Monitoring covers job start and completion, protected scope, bytes and objects, change volume, duration, throughput, integrity, catalog update, encryption, key access, retention, immutability, isolation, replication, capacity, age of last valid copy, RPO coverage, restore tests, and deletion.

Alerts distinguish full failure, partial failure, missed schedule, stale copy, corrupt chain, missing asset, unexpected scope decrease, unusual data growth, retention change, immutability change, deletion attempt, isolation loss, key failure, wrong region, wrong tenant, unauthorized restore, and provider degradation.

Backup alerts route to accountable responders and cannot be suppressed indefinitely by the job owner. Acknowledgement is not resolution. Failures are tracked until protected coverage is restored and the gap’s risk is assessed.

When RPO coverage is breached or a critical copy is lost, the condition receives incident or risk escalation according to impact. The organization identifies the earliest remaining recovery point, affected tenants, data-loss exposure, compensating controls, and customer or contractual consequence.

Capacity forecasting includes source growth, retention, copy strategy, immutable periods, legal holds, test environments, encryption overhead, catalog size, network, provider limits, and recovery throughput. A backup that cannot complete within its schedule or be restored within RTO is not adequate.

### Recovery Testing Program

Recovery testing is scheduled according to criticality, change rate, threat, provider dependency, control maturity, and customer obligation. Trust-critical and mission-critical assets receive more frequent and more complete exercises.

Testing includes:

- automated integrity and readability checks for every backup generation as appropriate;
- representative file, object, database, tenant, and point-in-time restores;
- full application and service recovery with dependency order and business validation;
- clean-environment recovery from isolated copies under assumed ransomware compromise;
- recovery when the primary catalog, identity provider, key service, region, provider, or administrator is unavailable;
- wrong-tenant, wrong-environment, unauthorized, expired, revoked, quarantined, corrupt, and incompatible-copy rejection;
- schema migration, application-version compatibility, key rotation, old-generation decryption, and current-policy reconciliation;
- Evidence Chain continuity, missing-event handling, Audit Engine recovery, and independent reconciliation;
- external side-effect, queue, retry, webhook, notification, and scheduled-job reconciliation;
- retention, legal hold, tenant deletion, privacy suppression, and secure disposal behavior;
- degraded capacity, large dataset, concurrency, rate limit, network constraint, and provider-support scenarios; and
- rollback from a failed recovery without destroying the last known-good state.

Tests use production-representative scale and complexity while protecting customer data. Synthetic or protected datasets are preferred. When production backup content must be used, access, purpose, isolation, retention, privacy, and deletion are explicitly controlled.

Test success requires meeting defined acceptance criteria, preserving evidence, and recording observed RPO, RTO, limitations, manual steps, errors, capacity, and corrective actions. A restore that completes but exceeds business limits or fails security reconciliation is not successful.

### Recovery Exercises and Operational Readiness

Recovery plans, contact paths, access, key custody, provider escalation, clean environments, network routes, monitoring, and customer communication are exercised together. Technical restore competence alone is insufficient when approvals, keys, evidence, or decision authority are unavailable.

Exercises include unexpected role absence, compromised production credentials, isolated copy access, catalog reconstruction, corrupted latest backup, provider outage, and discovery of malicious persistence after an initial restore.

Personnel maintain role-specific training for backup operation, restore, forensic preservation, key recovery, application validation, tenant isolation, communication, and incident coordination. Procedures are sufficiently precise for authorized alternates without embedding secrets.

Exercise findings update documentation, automation, capacity, access, provider agreements, test coverage, Threat Model, Incident Response, and Disaster Recovery. Repeated failure can cause a dependent service to be reclassified or restricted.

### Recovery Communication

Recovery communication identifies the affected service and tenant, cause where known, selected recovery point, expected and actual data loss, restored capability, limitations, required customer action, validation status, heightened monitoring, next update, and support path.

Internal technical status distinguishes restore completion from recovery acceptance. External communication does not state “fully recovered” while data reconciliation, security validation, tenant verification, or evidence gaps remain.

Customer communication preserves tenant confidentiality. Shared infrastructure recovery may affect multiple tenants differently; messages reflect actual impact rather than a generic platform statement.

Material RPO or RTO breach, data loss, failed deletion, integrity uncertainty, or unsupported restore is escalated through Incident Response, contractual, legal, privacy, and executive channels as applicable.

### Integration with Incident Response

Backup corruption, deletion, isolation loss, unauthorized restore, ransomware access, key unavailability, tenant crossover, untracked copy, evidence damage, or repeated RPO breach may constitute a security incident under Section 3.9.

Incident Response determines containment and evidence priorities. Backup and Recovery supplies protected copies, catalogs, clean restoration, and validation. Restoration during an incident uses the incident identifier, command authority, evidence process, communication plan, and heightened monitoring.

Responders preserve affected backups and catalogs as evidence. They do not delete a malicious or corrupt copy merely because it is unsuitable for recovery. Quarantine separates it from eligible recovery points while retaining controlled investigation access.

Recovery from compromise selects a point before the earliest credible intrusion or applies a verified remediation process when no such point is available. The team evaluates whether backups contain persistence, stolen credentials, unsafe policy, poisoned indexes, vulnerable artifacts, or evidence manipulation.

### Relationship to Disaster Recovery

Backup and Recovery provides asset-level and service-level recoverability. Disaster Recovery in Section 3.11 coordinates wider loss of site, region, infrastructure, provider, workforce access, or multiple dependent services and governs alternate-environment activation, failover, enterprise priorities, and return to normal operation.

The distinction does not create separate evidence or security standards. Disaster Recovery consumes only recovery points and procedures that satisfy this section. Replication or failover used by Disaster Recovery remains subject to historical recovery, ransomware isolation, current trust reconciliation, tenant protection, and restore validation.

A backup restore can occur without declaring a disaster. A disaster can require failover without restoring from backup. Both paths converge on the same requirement: controlled service resumes only from known, authorized, validated, and security-reconciled state.

### Backup and Recovery Metrics

Metrics evaluate coverage, reliability, security, performance, and tested recoverability. Applicable measures include:

- percentage of in-scope assets with current owner, classification, recovery tier, RPO, RTO, retention, key dependency, and tested procedure;
- successful, partial, failed, missed, stale, corrupt, quarantined, and untracked backups by tenant and criticality;
- age of last verified recovery point and duration of RPO coverage gaps;
- percentage of critical assets with isolated and immutable recovery paths;
- backup integrity, catalog reconciliation, encryption, isolation, retention, and deletion verification rates;
- restore-test coverage, frequency, success, failure cause, observed Recovery Point Actual, and Recovery Time Actual;
- percentage of tests that include current security-state reconciliation, tenant validation, Evidence Chain, key recovery, and clean environment;
- data-loss volume, unreconciled side effects, failed recovery attempts, rollback, and recurrence during heightened monitoring;
- unauthorized restore attempts, destructive deletion attempts, immutability changes, privileged access, and key-recovery anomalies;
- orphaned copies, copies outside approved region or provider, expired copies retained, and legal-hold conflicts;
- recovery capacity margin, backup-window utilization, restore throughput, catalog reconstruction time, and provider support delay;
- overdue corrective actions, repeated test findings, untested material changes, and open exceptions; and
- customer and contractual RPO or RTO attainment based on exercised and actual outcomes.

Metrics do not reward high backup-job success while restore testing, isolated-copy coverage, tenant validation, or RPO attainment is weak. Averages shall not conceal one critical asset without a usable recovery path.

### Exceptions and Residual Risk

Any exception to backup coverage, RPO, RTO, isolation, immutability, encryption, retention, testing, tenant separation, key recoverability, or validation identifies affected assets and tenants, impact, threat, rationale, compensating controls, owner, acceptance authority, remediation, review, and expiry.

The owner requesting an exception may not be its sole approver for high-impact assets. Exceptions do not silently amend customer commitments or legal requirements. Where a contractual objective cannot be met, the issue follows authorized customer and governance processes.

An asset without a tested recovery path is explicitly reported as unrecoverable or conditionally recoverable. It is not represented as protected because copies exist. Canonical tenant isolation, evidence integrity, current trust reconciliation, and controlled authorization cannot be waived through ordinary operational exception.

### Backup and Recovery Assurance

Periodic assurance verifies asset inventory, policy, architecture, copy independence, identity separation, encryption, keys, retention, catalog, provider controls, monitoring, restore results, privacy, legal hold, deletion, capacity, documentation, and exercises.

Assurance samples actual backups and observed restores rather than reviewing policy alone. It traces a selected service and tenant from authoritative source through backup creation, catalog, isolated storage, key dependency, recovery request, restore, validation, acceptance, and disposal.

Findings enter owned corrective action with risk, due date, validation, and evidence. Material weaknesses update the Threat Model, Incident Response, Disaster Recovery, customer assurance, and investment priorities.

### Backup and Recovery Limitations

Backup and Recovery cannot guarantee zero data loss, instantaneous restoration, absence of corruption, availability of every provider, or preservation of all external side effects. A valid copy may contain unknown compromise. A technically successful restore can exceed business tolerances. Encryption can make data unrecoverable if key continuity fails. Isolation can slow restoration. Immutable retention can conflict with immediate deletion.

RPO and RTO are scenario-dependent. Performance during an exercise may differ under widespread outage, ransomware, provider congestion, staffing loss, legal restriction, or simultaneous tenant recovery. Customer-managed environments can limit ILAIOS control and evidence.

These limitations are managed through business impact analysis, diverse copies, isolation, integrity verification, tested key continuity, clean recovery, security reconciliation, staged restoration, capacity planning, incident command, Disaster Recovery, transparent commitments, and explicit residual risk.

### Backup and Recovery Invariants

The following invariants are canonical:

- backup exists to provide verified recovery capability and is not considered successful merely because copy creation completed;
- every in-scope asset has accountable ownership, classification, recovery tier, authoritative source, dependency mapping, RPO, RTO, retention, and validation criteria appropriate to risk;
- critical recovery design prevents one production identity, administrator, credential, provider, region, control plane, deletion action, or storage failure from destroying all usable copies;
- at least one recovery path for critical assets is effectively isolated from ordinary production compromise and destructive authority;
- backup copies preserve or strengthen source classification, tenant isolation, encryption, residency, retention, privacy, and evidence controls;
- snapshots, replication, clustering, and high availability do not replace independent backup when they share the source failure or attacker path;
- backup and catalog entries retain source, tenant, recovery point, scope, consistency, version, key, retention, location, integrity, provenance, and dependency metadata;
- backup integrity and authenticity are verified after creation, during retention according to risk, before restore, after transfer, after restore, and through exercises;
- backup administration, production administration, key custody, destructive deletion, restore authorization, and acceptance are separated according to risk;
- restore authority binds actor, tenant, source copy, recovery point, target, purpose, scope, time, overwrite or merge behavior, policy, approval, and validation;
- no backup, snapshot, export, replica, cache, test restore, or provider copy is omitted from inventory solely because another party operates it;
- tenant scope remains authoritative through backup, catalog, encryption, retention, restore, validation, deletion, and evidence;
- full-system or historical restoration never silently resurrects a deleted tenant, deleted data, revoked identity, expired session, consumed approval, cancelled capability, compromised key, vulnerable artifact, unsafe policy, ineligible provider, or obsolete trust;
- recovery reconciles current security state before restored data or services return to normal operation;
- timeout, crash, replication lag, or missing local state never proves an external side effect did not occur;
- backup restoration does not repeat an uncertain tool action, notification, integration, or business transaction without authoritative reconciliation;
- encryption keys and recovery material remain recoverable through approved independent custody without being stored unprotected beside the backup;
- key rotation, revocation, compromise, re-wrapping, re-encryption, and cryptographic deletion account for all dependent recovery generations;
- historical keys may be used only under controlled authority necessary to recover data and do not regain active trust automatically;
- Audit Engine and Evidence Chain recovery preserves append-only history, chain state, checkpoints, original identity, and explicit discontinuities;
- reconstructed evidence is labeled and never represented as an event generated at the original time;
- restore validation is independent according to risk and covers data, application, tenant, security, policy, keys, evidence, external effects, privacy, performance, and monitoring;
- approaching or exceeding RTO never converts failed, missing, corrupt, stale, incompatible, or incomplete validation into acceptance;
- clean recovery is used when the integrity of production, identity, keys, network, build, catalog, or administration is uncertain;
- critical recovery tests include isolated-copy access, key continuity, tenant correctness, security-state reconciliation, dependency order, evidence continuity, and realistic scale;
- expired and legally disposable backups are destroyed across replicas, caches, test restores, provider copies, media, and keys with retained deletion evidence;
- legal hold is scoped, attributable, reviewed, and released and does not create general operational access;
- provider-managed and customer-managed backup responsibilities are explicit, testable, and included in end-to-end recovery assurance;
- backup failures, isolation loss, unauthorized restore, corruption, tenant crossover, evidence damage, and material RPO gaps trigger risk or incident escalation;
- Disaster Recovery consumes only recovery points and processes conformant with this section; and
- recovery closure requires validated service, secured evidence, current trust, communication, removed temporary access, accepted residual risk, and owned corrective actions.

An implementation is non-conformant if it represents backup-job completion, snapshot presence, replication, high availability, or provider assurance as proof of recoverability; allows production credentials or one administrator to delete every usable copy; stores all critical copies and keys inside the same failure and attacker domain; backs up multiple tenants without authoritative tenant metadata and restore isolation; permits unencrypted or weakly protected backups because they are outside production; accepts a backup whose source, integrity, scope, version, key, retention, or provenance is unknown; restores into a caller-selected tenant, environment, region, or account without authoritative verification; restores historical identity, approval, capability, policy, key, provider, deletion, or trust state without current reconciliation; retries an uncertain external action because restored local state appears incomplete; treats a database opening successfully as full recovery validation; records Audit Engine or Evidence Chain reconstruction as original evidence; marks a restore successful while security controls, monitoring, evidence, tenant isolation, or business integrity remain unverified; relies on a decryption key that exists only in the failed environment; uses immutable retention to avoid lawful deletion planning; deletes corrupt or malicious backups without preserving required incident evidence; leaves provider, replica, export, cache, or test copies outside inventory and disposal; grants backup administrators unrestricted production or key authority; accepts untested recovery plans as enterprise readiness; or claims an RPO or RTO that has neither defined measurement boundaries nor credible exercised evidence.

## 3.11 Disaster Recovery

ILAIOS Disaster Recovery establishes the canonical governance, architecture, decision authority, operational process, security controls, and evidence required to restore critical ILAIOS services after a disaster or major disruption that exceeds ordinary service restoration. It addresses loss or prolonged unavailability of a site, region, infrastructure control plane, provider, network, facility, workforce access, critical dependency, or multiple interdependent services.

Disaster Recovery is not synonymous with backup restoration, high availability, incident response, business continuity, or ordinary failover. It coordinates these capabilities when the scale, duration, dependency impact, or operating-environment loss requires controlled activation of alternate capacity and prioritized recovery of enterprise services. Section 3.10 defines trusted backup and recovery points. Section 3.9 governs cybersecurity incident command and containment. Business Continuity sustains business outcomes and organizational operations. Disaster Recovery restores the technology capabilities and security state on which those outcomes depend.

The canonical ILAIOS security architecture remains fully applicable during a disaster. Availability pressure does not authorize fail-open identity, cross-tenant ambiguity, non-deterministic policy authority, execution outside the Tool Gateway, ineligible model routing, self-validation, loss of Audit Engine or Evidence Chain coverage, unsigned or unverified artifacts, unprotected secrets, or restoration of revoked trust. An alternate environment is not production-eligible until its security controls and recovered state are independently validated.

### Purpose and Objectives

The Disaster Recovery capability has the following objectives:

- preserve human safety, tenant isolation, data integrity, execution control, evidence, customer trust, and legally required protections during major disruption;
