Every deployment model has a shared-responsibility matrix identifying controls operated by ILAIOS, the customer, the infrastructure provider, model provider, tool provider, integrator, and other material parties.

The matrix distinguishes responsibility for control design, implementation, operation, configuration, monitoring, evidence, incident response, notification, recovery, and assessment. “Customer responsibility” is not one undifferentiated category.

ILAIOS provides safe defaults, configuration constraints, evidence, documentation, and detection of critical misconfiguration where practical. Customers receive clear requirements for identity federation, user administration, data classification, key custody, provider eligibility, retention, approval roles, integrations, endpoints, incident contacts, and customer-managed infrastructure.

Responsibility transfer is contractually and technically coherent. ILAIOS cannot disclaim a control while retaining exclusive ability to perform it. Customers cannot assume ILAIOS operates a control that resides entirely within their environment.

Shared-responsibility evidence is versioned by product, deployment, service, and contract. Material changes require customer communication and may require contract amendment or renewed assessment.

### Information Security Compliance

Information-security obligations are implemented through the canonical security architecture in Sections 3.1 through 3.11. The control environment includes risk management, Zero Trust, authentication, authorization, secrets, keys, encryption, SSDLC, Threat Model, Incident Response, Backup and Recovery, and Disaster Recovery.

Compliance mapping does not substitute for control effectiveness. For example, an encryption control is conformant only when the correct data, state, tenant, purpose, key, destination, and failure behavior are covered. An access-review control is conformant only when actual privileges, service identities, emergency access, providers, and revocations are included.

Security policies define scope, objectives, ownership, review, enforcement, exceptions, evidence, and related procedures. Policies are approved, communicated, versioned, accessible, and reviewed when risk or obligation changes.

Risk assessments relate assets, threats, vulnerabilities, impacts, controls, residual risk, owner, and treatment. A checklist result or external framework mapping is not a complete risk assessment.

### Privacy and Data Protection Governance

ILAIOS applies privacy by design and by default. Personal-data processing is identified before use, limited to authorized purpose, minimized, accurate where required, retained only as justified, protected according to risk, and evidenced through accountable governance.

The privacy program determines legal role and lawful basis or other authorized ground, provides required transparency, manages consent where applicable, protects rights, controls processors and subprocessors, governs transfers, conducts impact assessments, handles incidents, and maintains records.

Product design separates personal data from tenant operational metadata where feasible, limits collection, avoids unnecessary exposure to models and tools, and prevents logs, evidence, diagnostics, backups, test environments, or support workflows from becoming uncontrolled copies.

Privacy requirements apply to metadata and inferred information, not only obvious content fields. Identifiers, usage patterns, prompts, model outputs, approvals, audit events, network data, device data, and support records can be personal data depending on context.

Encryption, pseudonymization, masking, and access restriction reduce risk but do not by themselves eliminate personal-data status or legal obligations. Anonymous-data claims require a documented assessment of re-identification risk and available means.

### Data Inventory and Processing Records

ILAIOS maintains an authoritative data inventory related to system components, tenants, purposes, persons, sources, destinations, providers, regions, classifications, legal grounds, retention, deletion, security, and responsible owners.

Processing records identify, as applicable, processing purpose, categories of persons and data, recipients, transfers, retention, security measures, processors, systems, and accountable roles. They are updated when product behavior or provider routes change.

The Data Flow architecture in Section 2.7, system inventory, provider inventory, Model Gateway routes, Tool Gateway actions, backup catalog, and evidence sources support but do not individually replace the processing record.

Shadow data stores, exports, caches, temporary files, support copies, test data, logs, telemetry, archived evidence, model-provider retention, and customer-managed copies are included or explicitly excluded with basis.

Data inventory is reconciled through technical discovery and ownership review. A documented flow that differs from observed processing creates a compliance finding.

### Purpose Limitation and Data Minimization

Every material data flow has an authorized purpose, minimum necessary data, permitted recipients, retention, tenant, provider eligibility, and evidence. A model or tool receives only data required for the approved task.

Product analytics, support, security, improvement, research, model evaluation, training, and marketing are separate purposes unless approved legal analysis establishes otherwise. Data collected for customer operation is not repurposed silently.

Model providers, tool providers, and subprocessors are configured and contracted according to authorized use, retention, secondary use, training use, human access, region, and deletion. A provider default does not determine ILAIOS’s lawful purpose.

Data minimization includes prompts, context, retrieved documents, code, tool results, outputs, evidence, diagnostics, and error payloads. Redaction and field exclusion occur before crossing a provider or support boundary where feasible.

### Data Subject and Individual Rights

ILAIOS supports the rights and safeguards applicable under the governing law and processing role, including, where relevant, access, information, rectification, erasure, restriction, objection, portability, consent withdrawal, and protections relating to qualifying automated decision-making. Where required, those protections include meaningful human intervention, the opportunity to express a viewpoint, contest the decision, and obtain an appropriate explanation or review.

The rights process authenticates the requester, identifies tenant and legal role, determines scope, searches authoritative and derived data, protects other persons and tenants, applies lawful exemptions, records decisions, meets applicable timing, and communicates securely.

Where the customer acts as controller and ILAIOS acts as processor, their respective responsibilities shall be defined contractually and operationally. Where ILAIOS acts as controller, joint controller, processor, or another legally recognized role for a specific processing purpose, the applicable responsibilities shall be determined through the documented role and applicability assessment. ILAIOS shall provide technical and organizational assistance within its assigned role and shall not make decisions reserved to the competent controller or other responsible authority.

Deletion applies to active data, derived state, caches, indexes, exports, providers, scheduled jobs, and backup reactivation according to Section 3.10. Retention, evidence, legal hold, security, and legal defenses are handled through documented lawful exceptions rather than silent refusal.

Rights handling does not expose another tenant, reveal protected security information unnecessarily, or allow an attacker to use a privacy request for account takeover or data enumeration.

### Privacy and AI Impact Assessments

Impact assessment is performed before processing likely to create elevated privacy, fundamental-rights, safety, discrimination, surveillance, employment, financial, health, public-service, or other material risk, as determined by applicable law and policy.

An assessment identifies intended purpose, affected persons and groups, necessity, proportionality, data, model, providers, decisions, human oversight, transparency, risks, mitigations, evidence, residual risk, consultation, approval, monitoring, and review triggers.

Privacy and AI impact assessments may be coordinated but remain distinct where obligations differ. Threat Modeling focuses on adversarial and failure conditions; an impact assessment also considers lawful but harmful or disproportionate outcomes.

Material changes to purpose, model, data, provider, automation, affected population, deployment, integration, or risk require reassessment. Approval of one use case does not authorize another.

Where law requires consultation, registration, conformity assessment, fundamental-rights assessment, or regulator involvement, product activation waits for the authorized outcome.

### Cross-Border Transfers, Residency, and Localization

ILAIOS identifies where data is collected, processed, viewed, transmitted, stored, backed up, supported, and deleted. Location includes subprocessors, logs, telemetry, model providers, tools, support access, disaster recovery, and customer exports.

Cross-border transfer relies on an approved legal mechanism and supplementary technical, contractual, and organizational safeguards where required. Transfer assessment considers destination law, provider access, government access, encryption, key custody, purpose, onward transfer, data sensitivity, and practical enforceability.

Residency and localization requirements are enforced through provider eligibility, tenant policy, Model Gateway, Tool Gateway, storage, keys, backup, support, and Disaster Recovery. A nominal region setting is insufficient if telemetry, support, subprocessors, or fallback routes cross the boundary.

Fallback during outage or disaster does not override residency or transfer restrictions. A service may remain unavailable or restricted when no eligible destination exists.

Transfer mechanisms, adequacy decisions, contractual clauses, certifications, and provider terms are versioned and monitored. Loss of a valid mechanism triggers containment, migration, contract action, customer communication, or service restriction according to risk and law.

### AI Governance and Management System

ILAIOS maintains governance for AI-assisted capabilities across planning, acquisition, development, integration, evaluation, deployment, operation, monitoring, incident handling, change, and retirement. Governance applies whether the model is developed internally or supplied by a provider.

The AI-system inventory records intended purpose, prohibited use, owner, customer role, model or model class, provider, version or change mechanism, data, context sources, affected persons, capabilities, risk classification, human oversight, evaluation, limitations, monitoring, incidents, and retirement.

AI governance uses the canonical authority separation: the AI Reasoning and Recommendation Engine proposes; the deterministic Policy Engine authorizes or denies; human approval applies according to risk; the Tool Gateway constrains execution; the Validation Pipeline independently evaluates; Audit Engine and Evidence Chain preserve accountability.

Model Orchestration and Provider Abstraction has no policy authority. Provider or model substitution remains governed by tenant, classification, region, purpose, contract, risk, evaluation, and change control.

AI management requirements may be implemented through an integrated management system aligned with recognized AI governance standards. Alignment does not constitute certification unless independently assessed within a defined scope.

### Intended Purpose, Risk Classification, and Prohibited Use

Each AI-assisted capability has a documented intended purpose, supported users, inputs, outputs, operating conditions, limitations, human role, prohibited use, and expected performance. Customer configuration cannot silently convert a general capability into a regulated high-impact use without renewed assessment.

Risk classification is based on actual function and context rather than marketing name. The same technical component can have different obligations when used for employment, finance, health, education, critical infrastructure, public authority, safety, or other consequential decisions.

Prohibited or unsupported uses are enforced through contract, product controls, policy, monitoring, customer guidance, and incident response according to feasibility and legal role. A documentation-only prohibition is insufficient where ILAIOS retains the ability and obligation to prevent the use technically.

Classification and obligations are reviewed when features, autonomy, data, affected persons, provider, model behavior, jurisdiction, or customer purpose changes.

### Human Oversight and Accountability

Human oversight is meaningful when the responsible person has authority, competence, time, context, explanation, alternatives, and ability to stop, reject, reverse, or escalate the relevant outcome.

The Approval Engine presents material action, tenant, data, target, side effects, risk, policy, evidence, and uncertainty. Approval is bound to exact Immutable Context and does not transfer responsibility to the model.

Human-in-the-loop design does not become a compliance fiction through approval fatigue, hidden parameters, excessive volume, automation bias, or rubber stamping. High-impact workflows measure override, rejection, escalation, review quality, and workload.

ILAIOS records accountable organizational and customer roles. “The AI decided” is never accepted as an explanation of authority or responsibility.

### Transparency, Notices, and Explainability

Transparency obligations are identified for customers, users, affected persons, regulators, auditors, and internal oversight. Information is audience-appropriate, accurate, accessible, versioned, and consistent with actual behavior.

Applicable documentation may include AI involvement, intended purpose, data categories, provider role, human oversight, limitations, material risks, output interpretation, logging, security, contact, contest or review mechanisms, and customer responsibilities.

Explainability is proportional to impact. It distinguishes model-generated rationale from the deterministic basis of policy, approval, capability, validation, and acceptance. A fluent model explanation is not evidence of the true causal basis or legal justification.

Notices do not overstate model accuracy, autonomy, safety, compliance, confidentiality, or absence of bias. Material model, purpose, provider, data, or limitation changes trigger notice review.

### Model Evaluation, Monitoring, and Change

AI-assisted capabilities are evaluated before release and monitored in operation according to risk. Evaluation covers task fitness, reliability, robustness, security, privacy, harmful output, discriminatory impact where relevant, instruction manipulation, data leakage, uncertainty, human oversight, provider behavior, and failure under expected conditions.

Evaluation data, method, environment, version, thresholds, limitations, and results are retained. Tests are representative of intended populations and conditions to the extent required and lawful. Passing an evaluation does not establish universal safety.

Model drift, provider update, routing change, context change, evaluation degradation, incident, complaint, or expanded use can trigger reclassification, additional controls, suspension, customer communication, or retirement.

Model changes do not bypass release and change management because a provider applies them remotely. ILAIOS defines monitoring and contractual notice appropriate to provider control and selects provider strategies consistent with required predictability.

### Information Accuracy, Quality, and Bias Governance

Data and output quality requirements derive from intended use and impact. Source provenance, representativeness, completeness, timeliness, labeling, error, bias, and known limitations are assessed at the level necessary for the use case.

ILAIOS does not represent probabilistic recommendations as guaranteed facts. Output requiring independent verification remains labeled and routed through the Validation Pipeline or human review.

Bias and fairness assessment identifies affected groups, legally relevant attributes, proxies, performance differences, data imbalance, feedback loops, and harm. Metrics are selected with domain expertise and legal review; one aggregate fairness metric does not prove absence of discrimination.

Customer-supplied data and configuration responsibilities are explicit. ILAIOS still validates product behavior within its role and does not attribute every harmful output to the customer when a platform control could prevent it.

### Records, Traceability, and Evidence

Compliance evidence is generated throughout normal operation. Relevant records include applicability decisions, obligation versions, policies, risk and impact assessments, architecture reviews, ADRs, training, access, provider diligence, contracts, code changes, tests, releases, configurations, model routes, policy decisions, approvals, executions, validations, incidents, backups, recoveries, audits, findings, exceptions, and corrective actions.

Evidence identifies subject, tenant where applicable, owner, actor or workload, time, source, version, control, decision, result, retention, and integrity. It is protected according to sensitivity and is not expanded with unnecessary personal data, source code, secrets, keys, or privileged legal material.

Audit Engine and Evidence Chain support continuous, tamper-evident operational evidence. Hash linkage does not prove that every required event was generated. Completeness reconciliation, control monitoring, access, retention, source authenticity, and independent assessment remain necessary.

Evidence retention shall follow an approved, record-class-specific schedule that reconciles applicable legal, contractual, certification, product-support, incident, defense, privacy, and data-minimization requirements. Personal data and other protected information shall not be retained longer than necessary or lawfully required for the defined purpose. Conflicting requirements, legal holds, and justified extensions shall be documented, narrowly scoped, authorized, and periodically reviewed. Retention is not indefinite by default.

### Records Management and Legal Hold

Records are classified by business and legal purpose, owner, system of record, format, integrity, access, retention, disposition, and hold eligibility. Draft, duplicate, working, authoritative, and evidentiary records are distinguished.

Legal hold suspends normal deletion for the defined matter and scope. Issuance, collection, preservation, access, transfer, review, release, and subsequent deletion are governed and evidenced.

Records remain retrievable and interpretable throughout retention. Format, encryption key, schema, signature, provider, and software dependencies are managed so long-term retention does not produce unreadable evidence.

Backup is not the system of record unless explicitly designed and governed as such. Section 3.10 controls retention and prevents historical restore from reactivating disposed data.

### Identity, Access, and Segregation of Duties

Compliance-sensitive roles include policy authors, administrators, approvers, key custodians, backup operators, incident responders, evidence custodians, assessors, certification coordinators, legal reviewers, and claim approvers.

Access follows least privilege, purpose, tenant, environment, time, and current role. Joiner, mover, leaver, contractor, temporary, emergency, and service-identity processes are evidenced.

Segregation of duties prevents one actor from defining a high-impact control, approving its exception, operating it, modifying its evidence, and independently assessing it. Where organizational scale prevents full separation, compensating oversight is explicit.

Periodic access review evaluates actual entitlements and use, including nested groups, service accounts, provider support, API tokens, emergency identities, key permissions, evidence access, and customer impersonation. Review of role names alone is insufficient.

### Cryptography, Secrets, and Key Compliance

Cryptographic obligations are met through Sections 3.4 through 3.6. Compliance profiles identify required protection, approved profiles, key custody, customer-managed key commitments, export or localization limits, retention, rotation, incident response, and evidence.

No standard, regulation, or contract is represented as satisfied by “encryption enabled” without verifying data scope, state, algorithm profile, key, tenant, endpoint, destination, backup, temporary storage, error behavior, and access to plaintext.

Customer-managed keys create shared responsibilities for availability, rotation, revocation, backup, disaster recovery, authorization, and deletion. ILAIOS documents which outcomes depend on customer action.

Cryptographic certification or validated-module requirements, where applicable, are separately assessed by deployment and component. Use of a cryptographic library with a certificate does not automatically certify the product or operating environment.

### Secure Development and Product Compliance

Section 3.7 governs the SSDLC. Compliance requirements are traceable to work items, designs, code, configuration, tests, review, build, release, deployment, operation, and retirement.

Product compliance includes supported versions, security updates, vulnerability handling, provenance, dependency inventory, release notes, customer configuration, documentation, compatibility, and end-of-support communication.

Automatically generated code, configuration, documentation, tests, and remediation receive the same controls as other changes. Automated production does not remove intellectual-property, license, privacy, security, accessibility, or review obligations.

Regulated features cannot be released based solely on a general product test suite. Their compliance profile includes scenario-specific acceptance criteria and evidence.

### Open-Source and Intellectual-Property Compliance

Software, models, data, documentation, media, standards content, and third-party materials are used under verified rights and licenses. Provenance and applicable terms are identified before incorporation or distribution.

Open-source dependencies are governed for license obligations, notices, attribution, source-availability requirements, modification, patents, trademarks, export, security, maintenance, and transitive components.

A permissive security posture does not imply permissive licensing, and public availability does not imply unrestricted use. Automatically generated output is reviewed for unauthorized copying, incompatible licensing, confidential content, and provenance risk appropriate to context.

Required notices and source offers are accurate, version-specific, included in the correct distribution, and retained. License exceptions are reviewed by qualified authority and cannot be created by engineering convenience.

### Supplier and Subprocessor Compliance

Third-party due diligence is proportional to access, data, criticality, tenant reach, execution capability, substitutability, and regulatory role. Assessment covers security, privacy, AI governance, resilience, personnel, location, subprocessors, incidents, audit, certifications, financial viability, and termination.

Contracts define permitted purpose, data, confidentiality, security measures, subprocessor control, transfer, retention, deletion, access, incident notification, cooperation, audit or assurance, recovery, support, change notification, and exit.

Provider certifications and reports are evaluated for entity, service, system, location, controls, criteria, period, exceptions, complementary user-entity controls, subservice organizations, and bridge period. A certificate logo or summary is not sufficient.

Subprocessor inventory is current and related to tenant eligibility and notice obligations. A provider cannot introduce an ineligible subprocessor through silent product fallback.

Provider findings and expired evidence produce risk treatment. Critical provider nonconformity may require restriction, replacement, customer communication, or contract enforcement.

### Sector and Customer Compliance Profiles

ILAIOS maintains profiles for supported sectors and customer commitments without forking the canonical architecture. Profiles may strengthen controls for financial services, health, public sector, critical infrastructure, employment, education, or other regulated environments.

A profile defines applicability, customer and ILAIOS roles, data, deployment, required controls, evidence, provider eligibility, incident and recovery obligations, retention, audit, documentation, and unsupported uses.

The financial-sector profile may address digital operational resilience, outsourcing, audit access, provider concentration, resilience testing, incident reporting, and exit where applicable. A healthcare profile may address protected health information, access, audit, business-associate or processor terms, retention, and availability. A public-sector profile may require sovereign deployment, accessibility, procurement, records, security authorization, or specific supply-chain evidence.

Profiles are activated only when operationally supported and contractually accurate. Sales or customer configuration cannot create an unsupported compliance profile.

### Contractual Compliance and Service Commitments

Material customer obligations are extracted from contracts and mapped to services, tenants, controls, evidence, owners, and reporting. Security schedules, data-processing agreements, service levels, support, recovery, incident notice, audit rights, subprocessor notice, residency, deletion, and exit receive operational implementation.

Conflicting customer commitments are identified before signature. Bespoke terms do not silently create an architecture that violates canonical tenant consistency or cannot be operated reliably.

Service-level measurement defines source, start and stop, exclusions, maintenance, tenant scope, calculation, reporting, and dispute evidence. Marketing availability claims do not replace contractual definitions.

Contract changes trigger control and customer-profile change management. Termination triggers data return, deletion, key action, access revocation, provider cleanup, retention, evidence, and claim withdrawal.

### Accessibility and Inclusive Product Compliance

Applicable accessibility requirements are treated as product requirements and validated across user interfaces, documentation, approval workflows, incident communications, authentication, reporting, and support.

Accessibility includes perceivable information, operable controls, understandable interaction, robust compatibility, keyboard use, focus, contrast, alternatives, error identification, timing, and assistive-technology support according to applicable criteria.

Security and accessibility are designed together. Strong authentication, human approval, time limits, visual evidence, and emergency communication shall not exclude authorized users unnecessarily. Any security-related constraint is assessed for an accessible equivalent that preserves assurance.

Accessibility claims identify product, platform, version, criteria, limitations, and assessment method. Automated testing supplements but does not replace qualified manual and assistive-technology evaluation.

### Regulatory Incident and Breach Obligations

Section 3.9 governs Incident Response. The Compliance function maintains applicable regulatory, contractual, customer, insurer, and authority reporting obligations, including triggers, timing, content, recipient, role, jurisdiction, update, and final-report requirements.

Notification clocks are determined by the applicable source and facts. ILAIOS does not impose one universal deadline or wait for complete technical certainty when an obligation is triggered.

Incident severity, privacy breach assessment, AI-system incident classification, critical-service impact, contract notice, and public communication can follow different definitions. Each is recorded and coordinated.

Regulatory reports are accurate, authorized, versioned, retained, and updated when material facts change. Technical teams do not avoid a reporting obligation by labeling the event as a defect or low internal severity.

### Resilience and Operational Compliance

Sections 3.10 and 3.11 govern Backup and Recovery and Disaster Recovery. Compliance profiles map required RPO, RTO, testing, business continuity, provider resilience, data integrity, crisis communication, and evidence to the exact service and customer.

Resilience claims are based on exercised end-to-end outcomes under stated assumptions. High availability, backup presence, second region, or provider service level is not represented as tested recovery.

Operational controls include monitoring, vulnerability management, capacity, change, incident, backup, disaster recovery, provider performance, support, and customer communication. Compliance requires sustained operation across the assessment period where applicable.

### Government, Regulator, and Law-Enforcement Requests

Requests for data, access, preservation, restriction, information, or technical assistance are authenticated, logged, reviewed by qualified legal authority, scoped, and fulfilled only where lawful and binding.

ILAIOS verifies issuing authority, jurisdiction, legal basis, subject, tenant, data, period, confidentiality, notice restriction, challenge rights, and transfer implications. Informal or technically plausible requests do not create authority.

Responses are minimized to the lawful scope, use controlled collection and transfer, protect other tenants, preserve chain of custody, and retain the decision. Direct provider disclosure is addressed contractually and through transparency where permitted.

Emergency requests receive expedited review but not unverified access. Product backdoors, universal decryption capability, or hidden cross-tenant access are not created as ordinary compliance mechanisms.

### Policy Management and Training

Policies have owner, purpose, scope, authority, requirements, roles, enforcement, evidence, exception, approval, effective date, version, review, and retirement. Procedures and standards remain consistent with controlling policy and this canonical architecture.

Personnel receive baseline and role-specific training for security, privacy, AI governance, incident reporting, acceptable use, records, customer commitments, provider management, development, privileged access, and regulatory responsibilities.

Training is completed before relevant access or responsibility where required and refreshed based on risk, change, incident, and regulation. Attendance alone does not prove competence for high-impact roles; exercises, assessment, review quality, and observed behavior contribute.

Policy acknowledgement does not transfer organizational accountability to personnel. Repeated error triggers review of design, workload, access, procedure, interface, supervision, and training.

### Control Operation and Continuous Monitoring

Controls have defined operating frequency and evidence. Continuous controls may evaluate configuration, identity, tenant, encryption, backup, vulnerability, policy, provider, model route, logging, or artifact state. Periodic controls address governance decisions that cannot be meaningfully automated.

Monitoring verifies control outcome rather than only configuration existence. A policy file present in a repository does not prove active enforcement. A backup schedule does not prove successful restore. A provider certificate does not prove current eligible routing.

Control failure, missing evidence, stale assessment, expired certificate, drift, unapproved provider, overdue access review, or breached objective generates a finding or incident according to risk.

Automation may collect evidence, map controls, identify anomalies, and prioritize review. It may not declare its own compliance, approve its own exception, alter source requirements, or suppress conflicting evidence.

### Compliance Evidence Architecture

Compliance evidence is related through authoritative identifiers: obligation, control, policy, owner, product, version, tenant profile, provider, system, artifact, change, test, decision, incident, exception, and assessment.

Evidence packages identify scope, period, source, completeness, integrity, confidentiality, limitations, and reviewer. A package generated for one customer or audit does not become a universal evidence set.

Evidence access follows least privilege and need. Customer assurance receives sufficient proof without exposing another tenant, proprietary source, vulnerability detail, employee data, secrets, keys, or legally privileged material.

Evidence quality criteria include relevance, reliability, completeness, timeliness, authenticity, reproducibility where appropriate, and relationship to the exact control. Screenshots and self-attestation receive less assurance than authoritative logs, configuration state, independent test, and externally verified evidence.

Evidence gaps are findings. They are not automatically treated as control failure, but the claimed control cannot receive assurance beyond available evidence.

### Internal Assessment and Audit

Internal assessments are risk-based, planned, scoped, independent, evidence-driven, and reported to accountable governance. They evaluate design and operating effectiveness, not only policy existence.

The assessor confirms obligation version, control mapping, population, sample method, evidence period, exceptions, complementary controls, system changes, incidents, and prior findings. Sampling limitations remain explicit.

Audit independence prevents an operator from issuing the sole assurance over the operator’s own control. Specialists are used for cryptography, privacy, AI, resilience, accessibility, legal, or sector matters where competence is required.

Management receives findings, root causes, risk, owners, deadlines, and accepted residual risk. Internal audit does not close a finding solely because management created a remediation plan.

### External Audit, Certification, and Attestation

External assurance has a defined objective, criteria, entity, product and service scope, system boundary, locations, providers, period, exclusions, complementary controls, report audience, and claim rules.

Certification demonstrates conformity only within its certificate and assessment scope. Attestation reports describe the assessed controls and period. Regulatory authorization applies only to the authorized activity and conditions. None automatically certifies customer configurations or unassessed future versions.

ILAIOS verifies assessor or certification-body competence, independence, accreditation where relevant, confidentiality, evidence access, and use of marks. Expiration, suspension, withdrawal, qualification, exception, or scope change triggers claim and customer review.

Bridge letters, management assertions, remediation statements, or self-assessments are labeled accurately and do not substitute for an expired or absent independent report.

Audit preparation does not introduce temporary controls that disappear after assessment. Material audit-specific access and evidence copies are removed or retained through governed processes.

### Customer Assurance and Due Diligence

ILAIOS provides standardized, accurate assurance material appropriate to customer risk. It may include architecture, control descriptions, shared responsibility, provider information, policies, independent reports, penetration-test summaries, recovery evidence, data-flow information, incident process, vulnerability management, and product documentation.

Responses distinguish implemented, planned, not applicable, customer-controlled, provider-controlled, and unsupported controls. Sales commitments do not override technical evidence or create unapproved roadmap obligations.

Sensitive reports are shared under appropriate confidentiality and access controls. Customer-specific responses do not disclose other tenant data, provider-confidential material, exploit detail, employee personal data, secrets, keys, or legally privileged advice.

Questionnaire answers are versioned and linked to evidence. Reusable answers have review and expiry. Conflicting answers are corrected across affected customers and materials.

### Compliance Claims and Public Representations

Every claim identifies, as applicable, the entity, product, service, version, deployment, region, control scope, standard or law, certification body or assessor, report type, period, status, exclusions, customer responsibility, and evidence.

Terms such as compliant, certified, audited, validated, secure, privacy-preserving, sovereign, explainable, zero trust, encrypted, anonymous, human-supervised, or regulatory-ready are not used without approved definitions and support.

“Designed to support,” “aligned with,” “mapped to,” “assessed against,” “certified to,” and “compliant with” are materially different claims. Marketing, sales, documentation, proposals, grant applications, investor materials, and customer responses use the correct form.

Expired, withdrawn, superseded, qualified, limited, or future status is not presented as current unrestricted assurance. Planned certification is labeled as a plan and does not support a present compliance claim.

### Nonconformity and Corrective Action

A nonconformity is a failure to satisfy an applicable requirement or adopted control. Findings are recorded regardless of whether discovered by monitoring, customer, audit, incident, regulator, provider, employee, or self-assessment.

The record identifies source requirement, affected scope, evidence, severity, owner, containment, root cause, corrective action, due date, customer or reporting consequence, residual risk, validation, and closure authority.

Immediate correction addresses the observed problem. Corrective action removes systemic cause. Preventive improvement addresses plausible recurrence elsewhere. These states are not conflated.

Root cause does not stop at “human error,” “provider issue,” or “missing documentation” when governance, workload, design, access, testing, monitoring, contract, or architecture contributed.

Closure requires evidence that the required outcome operates effectively. A revised policy, ticket resolution, code merge, or provider promise is not sufficient by itself.

### Exceptions and Risk Acceptance

Compliance exceptions identify the source requirement, legal or contractual permissibility, affected entity, product, tenant, data, jurisdiction, period, risk, compensating controls, customer impact, owner, approval, remediation, monitoring, and expiry.

ILAIOS cannot waive law, regulation, regulator order, or another party’s contractual right through internal acceptance. Legal or contractual relief requires the competent authority, lawful exemption, amendment, waiver, or customer agreement.

Exceptions to voluntary or internal controls remain governed and may not violate a canonical security invariant. Repeated or renewed exceptions trigger systemic review and can prevent certification, release, market entry, or customer onboarding.

Expired exceptions create nonconformity automatically. Renewal requires current facts and evidence and does not occur silently.

### Regulatory Change Management

ILAIOS monitors authoritative legal publications, regulators, standards bodies, certification schemes, contractual developments, provider changes, enforcement guidance, and sector requirements relevant to supported markets.

A regulatory-change record identifies source, publication, current legal status, affected jurisdictions, entities, roles, products, tenants, data, providers, contracts, dates, uncertainty, legal interpretation, gap, owner, plan, evidence, and communication.

Proposals, drafts, enacted requirements, implementing acts, standards, guidance, and enforcement positions are distinguished. Product planning may prepare for a draft, but public compliance claims use only the correct legal status.

Change implementation follows architecture and engineering governance. It updates the Obligations Register, control framework, policies, assessments, contracts, providers, product, tests, documentation, customer profiles, training, and evidence.

Where a new requirement conflicts with accepted architecture, a formal ADR documents the authorized change. Regulatory pressure is not used to make undocumented redesign.

### Compliance Metrics

Metrics assess applicability, control coverage, evidence, findings, remediation, provider assurance, customer commitments, and change readiness. Applicable measures include:

- percentage of supported products, markets, deployment models, data categories, and customer profiles with current applicability assessment;
- obligations with owner, mapped control, evidence, assessment, status, and review date;
- control design and operating-effectiveness results by domain, criticality, product, tenant profile, and evidence period;
- missing, stale, incomplete, conflicting, or unverifiable evidence;
- open findings by severity, age, source, root cause, owner, affected customers, and overdue status;
- exceptions by obligation class, risk, age, expiry, renewal, concentration, and recurring cause;
- privacy requests, impact assessments, processing-record currency, transfer reviews, deletion, retention, and response performance;
- AI inventory, intended-purpose review, risk classification, evaluation, model or provider change, human oversight, complaints, and incidents;
- provider due diligence, expired reports, unsupported subprocessors, contract gaps, concentration, and remediation;
- audit, certification, attestation, regulatory report, customer assurance, and contractual-delivery timeliness;
- policy, training, access review, resilience exercise, vulnerability, incident, backup, and recovery control performance;
- regulatory changes assessed, implementation lead time, missed milestones, and affected customer communications; and
- inaccurate or expired claims detected, corrected, and prevented from recurrence.

Metrics do not reward low finding counts, fast closure without validation, narrow audit scope, delayed issue recording, or excessive classification as non-applicable. One unresolved binding obligation can outweigh broad voluntary-framework coverage.

### Compliance Assurance and Management Review

Management review evaluates changes in obligations, business context, customers, providers, risks, incidents, audit results, findings, objectives, resources, competence, evidence, certification, complaints, and improvement.

The review determines whether the compliance management system remains suitable, adequate, effective, and aligned with product strategy and canonical architecture. Decisions have owners, dates, resources, validation, and retained evidence.

Assurance traces selected obligations end to end: authoritative source, applicability, interpretation, control, implementation, evidence, assessment, finding, corrective action, customer claim, and current status.

Material compliance risk is visible to executive governance and does not remain confined to a questionnaire, legal memo, or engineering backlog.

### Compliance Limitations

No compliance system can guarantee that every law, interpretation, customer use, provider action, future regulation, or jurisdictional conflict has been anticipated. Legal requirements change, guidance can be non-binding or contested, and enforcement can differ. Customer configuration can create obligations outside the supported profile.

Certifications and audits use defined scope, time, criteria, sampling, and evidence. They do not prove absence of every defect, incident, privacy harm, AI risk, or legal violation. Framework alignment does not equal legal compliance.

Technical controls cannot independently establish lawful basis, fair contractual terms, legitimate purpose, employment compliance, sector authorization, or ethical acceptability. Those outcomes require organizational and qualified human judgment.

ILAIOS manages these limits through applicability review, qualified advice, authoritative source monitoring, conservative claims, transparent shared responsibility, continuous evidence, independent assurance, customer profiling, incident response, corrective action, and periodic management review.

### Compliance Invariants

The following invariants are canonical:

- compliance is a continuous governance and engineering capability and is never inferred from product architecture alone;
- no ILAIOS product, deployment, tenant, use case, legal entity, or organization is declared compliant without verified scope, applicability, controls, operation, evidence, and authority;
- no certification, attestation, authorization, registration, or approval is claimed before completion or outside its current entity, product, system, location, criteria, period, and issuer-defined scope;
- qualified authority determines legal, regulatory, privacy, sector, and contractual applicability; engineering does not replace legal interpretation;
- authoritative source, interpretation, implementation, evidence, and assessment remain distinguishable and versioned;
- binding law, regulatory order, contract, certification criteria, voluntary framework, internal policy, and customer configuration are classified correctly and are not represented as equivalent;
- every applicable obligation has accountable ownership, affected scope, mapped controls, evidence, assessment, status, remediation, and review trigger;
- non-applicability is evidence-based, approved, time-aware, and reviewed when facts or law change;
- one common control framework is used where controls are genuinely equivalent, without weakening stronger canonical architecture;
- an external framework mapping does not prove control design or operating effectiveness;
- compliance requirements enter product planning, architecture, SSDLC, release, deployment, operation, monitoring, incident response, recovery, and retirement;
- Development System and Runtime System responsibilities and authority remain separated throughout compliance evidence and assessment;
- shared responsibility identifies design, implementation, operation, monitoring, evidence, incident, recovery, and assessment responsibilities per party and control;
- customer responsibility does not excuse an ILAIOS-controlled obligation, and ILAIOS responsibility is not claimed for a customer-only control;
- privacy by design and default applies to content, metadata, prompts, outputs, audit, evidence, logs, backups, support, models, tools, and providers;
- personal-data processing has authorized purpose, role, scope, minimization, transparency, retention, security, rights, transfer, provider, and evidence appropriate to governing law;
- encryption, pseudonymization, masking, or access control does not by itself eliminate privacy or compliance obligations;
- AI-assisted capabilities have intended purpose, prohibited use, owner, risk classification, provider, data, human oversight, evaluation, limitations, monitoring, incident, and change governance;
- AI Reasoning and Recommendation Engine remains non-authoritative, Policy Engine remains deterministic, and model output never becomes compliance evidence of its own correctness;
- model or provider change cannot silently alter compliance classification, data destination, customer commitment, evaluation, or human-oversight requirement;
- human oversight is meaningful and provides informed authority to stop, reject, reverse, or escalate rather than ceremonial approval;
- transparency and explainability distinguish probabilistic model rationale from deterministic policy, approval, validation, and accountability;
- cross-border transfer, residency, localization, support, backup, provider, tool, model, and disaster routing are governed consistently;
- fallback never sends regulated or classified data to an ineligible destination to preserve availability;
- compliance evidence is relevant, reliable, complete, timely, attributable, protected, retained, and related to the exact obligation and control scope;
- Audit Engine and Evidence Chain support evidence integrity but hash linkage alone never proves event or control completeness;
- evidence gaps are visible and cannot be filled by unsupported attestation, screenshots, reconstructed history, or model-generated claims;
- provider certifications and reports are evaluated for scope, period, exceptions, subservice organizations, complementary controls, and current validity;
- automatically generated code, tests, documentation, assessments, mappings, and evidence receive normal ownership, review, provenance, and validation;
- legal, regulatory, contractual, certification, licensing, accessibility, and customer obligations cannot be waived by technical convenience;
- internal exceptions cannot waive law, regulator authority, customer rights, or contract without lawful and competent authorization;
- findings remain open until the required outcome is independently verified, not merely documented or scheduled;
- regulatory proposals, drafts, enacted rules, effective obligations, guidance, and amendments are distinguished and monitored through authoritative sources;
- compliance claims are precise, approved, current, scope-bound, evidence-backed, and withdrawn or corrected when status changes;
- accepted architecture is not redesigned for compliance without a formal ADR that preserves authoritative rationale and cross-references; and
- material incidents, findings, provider failures, customer complaints, audit results, regulatory change, and expired evidence update the compliance system.

An implementation is non-conformant if it labels the product or a customer compliant solely because security features exist; represents alignment, mapping, readiness, self-assessment, or provider certification as ILAIOS certification; claims a law or standard applies or does not apply without documented authority and scope; uses an expired, withdrawn, qualified, or out-of-scope certificate as current assurance; maintains obligations without owners, controls, evidence, assessment, or review; copies legal text into policy without implementable control and validation; treats a completed audit as proof of future operation; lets a provider certificate replace ILAIOS due diligence and shared responsibility; routes personal, regulated, or classified data across an unauthorized region or provider during fallback; repurposes customer data for analytics, model training, testing, or marketing without approved purpose and authority; restores deleted or revoked personal-data state from backup without current reconciliation; treats model output as legal interpretation, compliance decision, independent validation, or evidence of its own correctness; uses nominal human approval without meaningful information and authority; conceals a finding by changing scope, mapping, severity, sample, evidence period, or terminology; closes corrective action when only a policy, ticket, code change, or provider promise exists; allows internal exception to waive law, regulation, customer right, or contract; lets sales or marketing create unsupported compliance commitments; provides contradictory or stale customer-assurance answers without correction; or modifies accepted architecture for a perceived compliance need without qualified interpretation, formal governance, and an ADR.

# 4. Engineering Standards

## 4.1 Coding Standards

### Purpose and Engineering Intent

The ILAIOS Coding Standards establish the minimum conditions under which source code may be considered understandable, secure, deterministic, testable, reviewable, supportable, and suitable for inclusion in an enterprise product. They apply the Product Constitution to implementation work by converting architectural intent into enforceable source-level expectations. Their purpose is not to impose aesthetic uniformity. Their purpose is to reduce ambiguity, prevent unsafe behavior, preserve trust boundaries, make failure visible, and ensure that material product behavior can be reconstructed from authoritative code, configuration, tests, and evidence.

Code is an operational control surface. A small implementation decision can alter authorization, tenant isolation, evidence completeness, data retention, failure handling, or customer-facing behavior. Source code therefore receives the same disciplined treatment as other controlled engineering assets. Convenience, delivery pressure, generated output, framework convention, or historical practice does not justify weakening an accepted architectural invariant.

These standards remain implementation-independent wherever possible. They define required outcomes and engineering properties rather than prescribing a single programming language, framework, operating system, cloud platform, database, model provider, editor, formatter, linter, type checker, or build service. Technology-specific rules shall be maintained in approved Coding Standard Profiles subordinate to this section. A profile may strengthen these requirements but may not weaken or contradict them.

### Scope

These standards apply to all source-controlled software and software-adjacent executable material produced, maintained, distributed, or operated as part of ILAIOS, including:

- product services, libraries, command-line interfaces, operator interfaces, companion applications, mobile applications, and supported integration components;
- Policy Engine, Approval Engine, capability issuance, Tool Gateway, execution, Validation Pipeline, Audit Engine, Evidence Chain, Code Intelligence, model orchestration, identity, tenancy, and administration components;
- infrastructure definitions, deployment logic, migration code, build logic, release automation, policy-as-code, configuration schemas, and operational utilities;
- test harnesses, fixtures, simulators, data generators, security checks, recovery utilities, and diagnostic tools that can affect assurance conclusions;
- generated source code, generated schemas, generated clients, vendored code, patches, examples, reference implementations, and reusable templates; and
- prototypes or experiments when they access non-public data, connect to shared environments, influence product decisions, or may be promoted into a supported codebase.

Disposable local exploration that has no access to protected resources and cannot affect a shared product or decision may use a proportionate subset of these controls. It becomes governed as soon as it is shared, retained as an engineering asset, used to support an architecture or product claim, incorporated into a deliverable, connected to a customer or production-like environment, or used as the basis for a material decision.

Third-party source and generated artifacts remain subject to provenance, licensing, security, compatibility, validation, and acceptance requirements. Their origin does not transfer accountability away from ILAIOS.

### Normative Language and Rule Precedence

The terms shall, shall not, must, and must not identify mandatory requirements. Should and should not identify strong expectations that may be departed from only with documented rationale. May identifies a permitted option that remains subject to all applicable controls.

When requirements appear to conflict, implementation shall follow this single authority and conflict-resolution model:

1. Applicable law, court orders, binding regulatory direction, and requirements issued by a competent authority are mandatory within their established jurisdiction and scope.
2. The ILAIOS Product Constitution, accepted canonical architecture, and non-waivable trust controls are the highest internal product and architecture authorities. Protected controls include the deterministic Policy Engine, Approval Engine, tenant isolation, capability restrictions, Tool Gateway, Validation Pipeline, Audit Engine, Evidence Chain, and the applicable security, privacy, safety, authorization, validation, evidence, and human-accountability requirements.
3. Customer and contractual commitments apply only within their lawful, applicable, and formally approved scope. Contractual commitments are binding only within their lawful and formally approved scope and shall not silently weaken the Product Constitution, canonical architecture, or non-waivable security, privacy, safety, tenant-isolation, authorization, validation, audit, evidence, and human-accountability controls.
4. Formally authorized company decisions and accepted Architecture Decision Records apply within the authority and scope granted to their deciders and may not silently weaken a higher authority or protected control.
5. This canonical engineering handbook, approved Coding Standard Profiles, and repository-local engineering rules apply within their authorized scope and may strengthen, but may not weaken, the authorities and controls above them.
6. Authoritative language and framework specifications, established team conventions, and individual preferences remain subordinate implementation guidance and create no authority to alter an approved product, architecture, security, privacy, or contractual decision.

If a contractual requirement conflicts with those controls, implementation shall pause until the conflict is resolved through qualified legal interpretation, scope restriction, contract amendment or waiver by the competent parties, and, where architecture changes, an authorized ADR. Engineering, sales, customers, providers, tools, frameworks, and model-generated recommendations cannot resolve or reinterpret such a conflict unilaterally.

### Coding Standard Profiles

Each supported language and execution domain shall have an approved Coding Standard Profile. A profile defines the concrete rules required to apply this section to a specific implementation context without converting a tool choice into a universal architecture decision. At minimum, a profile identifies:

- covered languages, language versions, runtimes, frameworks, platforms, and repository areas;
- accountable owner and reviewing authorities;
- authoritative language and framework specifications;
- required formatter, linter, type analysis, security analysis, dependency analysis, and build controls;
- permitted and prohibited language features, unsafe operations, reflection mechanisms, native interfaces, dynamic loading, and metaprogramming constructs;
- error, logging, concurrency, resource, serialization, dependency, testability, documentation, and compatibility conventions;
- generated-code boundaries and regeneration requirements;
- severity classification, baseline, suppression, exception, and migration rules; and
- effective date, review date, version, superseded profile, and affected product versions.

Profiles shall be version-controlled and machine-enforced where technically feasible. A profile change that alters a public contract, security boundary, authority decision, persistence model, evidence property, or accepted architecture requires the corresponding design and ADR governance. A tool upgrade or formatting change that has no architectural effect follows controlled engineering change rather than automatically requiring an ADR.

### External Reference Standards

ILAIOS maintains an Engineering Standards Register containing approved external references and their current status. Relevant sources may include the NIST Secure Software Development Framework, OWASP application and mobile verification standards, CISA Secure by Design guidance, SEI CERT language-specific secure coding standards, authoritative language specifications, and sector-specific requirements. These sources inform the controls and profiles used by ILAIOS.

Inclusion in the register does not create an unsupported claim of certification, conformity, or complete adoption. Each entry shall identify the exact source, version, publication status, applicable product scope, adopted requirements, exclusions, mapping, owner, and review date. Drafts and proposals may inform planning but shall not be represented as binding final standards. Where an external source is superseded, ILAIOS shall assess the change rather than silently inheriting new semantics.

### Core Coding Principles

All governed code shall satisfy the following principles:

1. **Correctness before convenience.** Behavior must implement the approved requirement and defined contract, not merely pass a typical demonstration.
2. **Security and privacy by default.** Safe behavior shall be the default state; sensitive capability, data exposure, and permissive behavior require explicit authorization.
3. **Determinism where authority is involved.** Policy, approval, capability, validation, evidence, and acceptance decisions shall not depend on uncontrolled probabilistic or environmental behavior.
4. **Explicitness over hidden convention.** Authority, side effects, failure, retries, mutation, data classification, and external interaction must be discoverable from contracts and code.
5. **Least privilege and least functionality.** Code shall request only the resources and capabilities necessary for its defined responsibility.
6. **Separation of responsibilities.** Planning, authorization, execution, validation, acceptance, audit, and evidence shall remain distinct in implementation as required by the architecture.
7. **Fail closed for trust decisions.** Missing, stale, ambiguous, conflicting, or unverifiable information shall not become permission or successful validation.
8. **Observable failure.** A failure shall produce an attributable state and appropriate diagnostic or evidence; it shall not disappear behind a default, catch-all, retry loop, or fabricated success.
9. **Small, coherent change.** A code change shall have a clear purpose and avoid unrelated refactoring, generated churn, or behavior changes that obscure review.
10. **Reversibility and recoverability.** Material changes shall consider rollback, migration, compatibility, compensation, and evidence preservation.
11. **No trust in origin.** User input, repository content, model output, tool output, provider response, serialized data, event payloads, and generated code remain untrusted until validated at the appropriate boundary.
12. **Accountability for every line.** Human owners remain responsible for accepted code regardless of whether it was written manually, generated, translated, imported, or adapted.

### Ownership and Change Accountability

Every production component shall have an identifiable owning function and a maintained review path. Ownership includes responsibility for correctness, security, privacy, testability, operational behavior, documentation, dependency health, deprecation, and remediation. Shared ownership may be used, but anonymous ownership is not acceptable for a supported component.

Authors shall understand the behavior and consequences of the code they submit. Acceptance of a generated patch, copied example, vendor recommendation, automated refactor, or migration output constitutes acceptance of responsibility for that code. A reviewer shall be able to determine the requirement, affected boundary, expected behavior, validation method, failure behavior, and rollback or recovery implications from the change and its associated records.

Changes shall be limited to the smallest coherent unit that satisfies the approved objective. Unrelated cleanup, formatting, dependency changes, broad renaming, architecture changes, and speculative abstraction shall be separated unless they are inseparable from correctness or safety. Scope control improves review quality, evidence clarity, incident diagnosis, and safe reversal.

### Source Structure and Modularity

Code shall be organized around cohesive responsibilities and explicit contracts. A module, class, function, service, or package should have one primary reason to change. Public boundaries shall expose the minimum surface required by their consumers. Internal implementation details shall not become public contracts through convenience.

High-cohesion, low-coupling designs are required for security-sensitive and frequently changing areas. Shared utilities shall represent stable, genuinely shared concepts rather than becoming unowned collections of unrelated behavior. A common module that bypasses domain ownership, tenant checks, validation, or audit is non-conformant even if it reduces duplicate lines.

Circular dependencies shall be prevented or removed through explicit boundary design. Dependency direction shall follow the accepted architecture. Lower-level deterministic controls shall not depend on higher-level presentation or probabilistic reasoning components. Policy and approval decisions shall not depend on interfaces that can initiate execution. Validation shall be independently invocable and shall not rely on the component whose result it validates to declare its own success.

Cross-component calls shall use defined interfaces rather than internal state access. A consumer shall not reach into another component's private storage, cache, database tables, or implementation-specific object graph unless the relationship is an explicitly governed data contract. Temporary shortcuts must not become permanent implicit integration paths.

### Abstraction and Complexity

Abstraction shall be introduced when it creates a stable contract, removes material duplication, isolates volatility, protects a trust boundary, or enables independent verification. It shall not be introduced solely to anticipate hypothetical future requirements. Premature generic frameworks, excessive inheritance, opaque metaprogramming, and unnecessary indirection increase the cost of assurance and shall be avoided.

Functions and methods shall remain small enough for their behavior, inputs, outputs, side effects, and failure paths to be understood and reviewed. Size is not governed by a universal line limit; complexity, branching, state interaction, and authority are the relevant factors. A short function with hidden global mutation may be less acceptable than a longer function with an explicit deterministic decision table.

Complex control logic should be expressed through explicit state models, decision tables, typed rules, or clearly separated phases where those forms improve verifiability. Security and policy behavior shall not depend on scattered boolean combinations whose effective meaning cannot be reconstructed reliably.

### Naming and Semantic Clarity

Source identifiers shall use clear professional English and accurately represent domain meaning. Names shall distinguish requests from approvals, proposals from permissions, capabilities from roles, execution results from accepted outcomes, audit events from evidence records, and confidence indicators from validation decisions. Terminology defined in the canonical architecture shall be used consistently.

Names shall not overstate assurance. An unchecked value shall not be named validated, trusted, authorized, accepted, immutable, encrypted, complete, or compliant. A function named verify, authorize, validate, persist, or delete must satisfy the documented semantics of that action or be renamed to state its narrower behavior.

Abbreviations are permitted only when established, unambiguous, and documented within the relevant domain. Single-character names are limited to conventional narrow scopes where meaning remains evident. Boolean names shall express a positive, testable proposition. Units and time bases shall appear in names or types when ambiguity is possible.

Repository names, paths, package taxonomy, branch names, and file naming are governed by Section 4.2. Source-level naming remains governed by this section. A language profile may define casing and reserved-word conventions without changing domain terminology.

### Type Safety and Data Models

Typed interfaces and explicit data models shall be used wherever the supported language permits them. Trust-sensitive data shall not be represented as unstructured dictionaries, loosely typed maps, positional arrays, or generic strings when a constrained type can express the valid states. Identity, tenant, capability, policy decision, approval, risk, data classification, resource reference, execution status, validation result, evidence reference, timestamp, duration, and version require explicit semantics.

Null, absent, unknown, not applicable, redacted, unavailable, and empty are distinct states and shall not be conflated. Default values shall not convert missing authorization, configuration, evidence, or validation into success. Sentinel values must be documented and type-safe. Exhaustive state handling is required for closed decision sets where supported.

Data models shall define invariants at creation and preserve them through transformation and serialization. Immutability shall be preferred for identity, authority, decision, evidence, configuration snapshot, and other records whose later mutation would compromise reasoning or traceability. Where mutation is necessary, ownership, allowed transitions, concurrency behavior, audit requirements, and invalid states shall be explicit.

Type-analysis suppressions shall be narrow, justified, attributable, and located as close as possible to the unavoidable condition. Blanket disablement, broad untyped boundaries, and suppression used to conceal design defects are prohibited. A suppression must not substitute for input validation or runtime security control.

### Interface and Contract Design

Every public interface shall define inputs, outputs, preconditions, postconditions, error states, side effects, idempotency, authorization expectations, tenant behavior, data classification, compatibility, timeout, and observability appropriate to its risk. Contracts include in-process APIs, network APIs, events, queues, command formats, database schemas, files, plugins, tool definitions, policy inputs, validation rules, and provider adapters.

Inputs shall be accepted through the narrowest practical schema. Authority-bearing interfaces shall reject unknown or conflicting fields unless forward compatibility explicitly requires a controlled alternative. Default values shall not broaden scope. Parameters that affect target, capability, data access, environment, duration, retry, destination, or validation must be bound into the request and evidence context.

Outputs shall distinguish successful execution from accepted outcome. Partial success, warning, denial, cancellation, timeout, retry exhaustion, compensation, validation failure, and evidence failure require explicit states. A transport-level success code or completed function call shall not be interpreted automatically as business acceptance.

Contracts shall be versioned when consumers can observe their semantics. Compatibility behavior shall be deliberate and tested. Silent reinterpretation of an existing field, state, or default is prohibited where it can change authority, security, persistence, validation, evidence, or customer behavior.

### Boundary Validation and Canonicalization

Validation shall occur at every material trust boundary, not only at the first entry point. Each component validates the assumptions necessary for its own safe behavior. Prior validation may be relied upon only through an authenticated, integrity-protected contract that clearly transfers the assurance.

Validation shall cover structure, type, size, range, encoding, syntax, semantic consistency, tenant, identity, resource ownership, capability, state transition, version, freshness, replay, classification, and contextual authorization as applicable. Validation shall reject or quarantine malformed, ambiguous, duplicate, contradictory, stale, oversized, recursive, or unsupported data.

Canonicalization shall precede security comparison when multiple representations could identify the same resource. Paths, URLs, hostnames, identifiers, encodings, Unicode, timestamps, numeric units, archive entries, and serialized forms require a single documented comparison representation. Canonicalization must not transform an invalid input into a valid but unintended target.

Validation code shall not execute the content being validated. Source repositories, templates, documents, archives, configuration, serialized objects, and model or tool output shall be treated as data. Dynamic evaluation, unsafe deserialization, implicit command interpretation, and executable parsing are prohibited unless the capability is explicitly required, isolated, authorized, and validated under the execution architecture.

### Determinism and Repeatability

Deterministic behavior is mandatory for Policy Engine decisions, capability construction, approval-state evaluation, validation rules, evidence hashing, audit ordering semantics, compatibility checks, migrations, and other trust-critical operations. Given the same versioned inputs, configuration, policy, and authoritative state, a deterministic component shall produce the same material decision or an explicit environmental failure.

Nondeterministic inputs such as current time, randomness, network state, provider response, filesystem order, locale, platform behavior, and concurrency scheduling shall be isolated behind explicit interfaces. They shall be injected, recorded, bounded, or normalized where repeatability matters. Collections used in hashing, signatures, decisions, or serialized evidence shall have defined ordering and canonical encoding.

Probabilistic reasoning may prepare analysis or proposals but shall not be embedded inside deterministic authorization, policy, validation-waiver, acceptance, or evidence-integrity code. A model response cannot be used as proof that its own output is correct, safe, authorized, or compliant.

Reproducibility does not require every operational timestamp or generated identifier to be identical. It requires those values to be created under controlled rules, recorded as inputs or outputs, and excluded from decision semantics unless their role is explicit.

### State Management and Side Effects

State shall have an authoritative owner, defined lifecycle, permitted transitions, concurrency model, persistence expectation, retention class, and recovery behavior. Hidden global state, process-wide mutable singletons, implicit environment mutation, and action at import or module-load time are prohibited in governed product code unless an approved platform constraint requires and documents them.

Functions should separate calculation from side effects. Pure decision logic is preferred where practical because it improves review, testability, and repeatability. Code that changes a repository, external system, policy, approval, credential, configuration, deployment, record, or evidence state must make that effect explicit in its contract.

A component shall not update another component's authoritative state through an undocumented side channel. Cache state is derived and shall not become authority. Cache absence, expiry, or inconsistency must not grant access, validate an outcome, or suppress a required event.

Material state transitions shall use compare-and-set, version checks, transaction boundaries, leases, locks, idempotency keys, or equivalent controls appropriate to the implementation. A stale writer shall not overwrite a newer policy, approval, task, evidence, or configuration state silently.

### Error Model and Failure Semantics

Errors shall be classified and represented deliberately. At minimum, implementations shall distinguish validation failure, authentication failure, authorization denial, policy denial, approval absence, conflict, unsupported operation, dependency failure, timeout, cancellation, retry exhaustion, resource exhaustion, integrity failure, evidence failure, security event, and internal defect where those states are relevant.

Expected denials and invalid requests shall not be disguised as internal failures. Internal failures shall not be converted into expected denial or empty success in a way that conceals defects. Error contracts shall separate stable machine-readable codes from human-readable diagnostics and sensitive internal detail.

Exceptions shall be caught only where the code can add context, translate to a defined boundary error, compensate, retry safely, release resources, record required evidence, or restore a valid state. Broad catch-and-ignore behavior is prohibited. A top-level containment boundary may catch unexpected failures to protect process availability, but it must preserve causal information, emit an attributable failure, and prevent unsafe continuation.

Error messages shall identify the failed operation and relevant correlation information without exposing secrets, keys, tokens, personal data, customer content, exploit details, or cross-tenant information. Original causes shall be preserved through supported exception chaining or structured causal records.

Failures shall not fabricate default data, successful validation, empty evidence, current state, or authorization. Where degraded operation is permitted, its scope, customer effect, security conditions, missing assurance, expiry, and recovery path shall be explicit.

### Resource Lifecycle Management

Files, streams, network connections, database sessions, locks, temporary storage, execution environments, subprocesses, provider requests, credentials, and other resources shall have bounded lifecycles. Acquisition and release shall be paired through constructs that remain safe during success, failure, cancellation, and timeout.

Timeouts shall be explicit for external calls and potentially unbounded operations. Resource limits shall cover input size, output size, memory, CPU, storage, recursion, archive expansion, concurrency, queue depth, and execution duration according to risk. Unlimited defaults are prohibited at untrusted boundaries.

Temporary artifacts shall use controlled locations, restrictive access, collision-resistant naming, tenant separation, and deterministic cleanup. Cleanup failure shall be observable where sensitive data, credentials, untrusted content, or resource exhaustion is involved. Sensitive temporary data shall not persist beyond its approved purpose merely because normal completion failed.

Subprocess and operating-system invocation shall use structured argument passing rather than command-string construction. Working directory, environment, executable identity, allowed arguments, input, output, timeout, resource limits, and exit semantics shall be controlled. Shell interpretation is prohibited unless explicitly required and safely constrained.

### Time, Randomness, Identifiers, and Units

Time values shall identify timezone, precision, clock source, and semantics. Persisted and cross-system timestamps shall use an unambiguous standard representation. Wall-clock time shall not be used for elapsed-duration measurement where a monotonic source is required.
