Source acquisition shall verify canonical repository identity, exact revision, branch or tag relationship, submodule or external-source references, large-file objects, generated inputs, and expected tree state. The working directory shall not contain residual or untracked material that can influence the build.

Checkout credentials shall be read-only unless a specifically authorized workflow performs a controlled write. Build jobs shall not rewrite canonical source, force-push branches, create release tags, or approve their own changes.

Symlinks, path traversal, nested repositories, case collisions, archive extraction, and untrusted filenames shall be handled safely. The workspace shall be bounded to the job and disposed of or cleaned according to the runner profile.

Source provenance shall remain traceable through generated artifacts. A copied source archive without authoritative repository and revision metadata is insufficient for official release.

### Dependency Resolution and Acquisition

Dependencies shall be resolved from approved registries, repositories, or mirrors through authenticated and integrity-verified channels. Version constraints and lock information shall support repeatability and shall not silently resolve to new content during a release build.

Internal namespaces shall be protected against dependency confusion. Registry priority, package identity, publisher, version, digest, signature, provenance, and license shall be evaluated according to the dependency profile.

Build, test, documentation, infrastructure, model, and runtime dependencies are in scope. A dependency used only during build can still compromise the artifact and shall not be treated as harmless.

Caching shall not bypass integrity or freshness rules. A cached object shall be revalidated against expected identity and shall not be shared across incompatible trust or tenant boundaries.

### Deterministic and Reproducible Builds

Builds shall be deterministic to the degree defined by the applicable Quality Profile. The same declared source, build instructions, dependencies, configuration, and controlled environment should produce the defined equivalent artifact.

The pipeline shall control or record timestamps, locale, timezone, ordering, randomness, environment variables, host tools, network inputs, generated metadata, and other sources of variability. Required nondeterminism shall be explicit and excluded only when it cannot alter executable or security-relevant semantics.

Independent reproducibility verification may be required for high-assurance artifacts. A mismatch blocks or triggers investigation; the pipeline shall not sign whichever output was produced without reconciliation.

Reproducibility does not prove correctness, but it makes unauthorized or unexplained change easier to detect and supports reliable incident analysis.

### Hermetic Build Controls

A hermetic build consumes only declared inputs within a defined controlled boundary. Where required, the build shall have no undeclared network, filesystem, toolchain, credential, service, or host dependency.

The pipeline shall verify that dependency acquisition occurs in an approved preparatory stage or through a controlled content-addressed mechanism and that the build cannot fetch mutable code during execution.

A container or virtual machine alone does not establish hermeticity. Host mounts, shared caches, metadata services, mutable base images, external clocks, and dynamic downloads can still influence output.

When full hermeticity is not practical, undeclared inputs and residual risk shall be documented and controlled. The artifact claim shall match the actual boundary.

### Build Toolchain and Environment Governance

Compilers, interpreters, package managers, code generators, signing clients, test tools, workflow components, base images, and worker images are part of the trusted toolchain. They shall have approved source, version, integrity, provenance, license, update process, and owner.

Toolchain versions shall be pinned or otherwise controlled. Automatic background update during a release build is prohibited unless the resulting version is captured, verified, and governed.

Toolchain changes shall trigger appropriate regression, reproducibility, security, compatibility, and artifact review. A new compiler or base image can change behavior even when product source is unchanged.

Obsolete or unsupported toolchain components shall be remediated, isolated, or retired. Long-Term Support obligations shall include the ability to rebuild and verify supported versions securely.

### Generated Code and Generated Artifacts

Generated code, schemas, documentation, clients, policy bundles, indexes, and assets shall identify generator, version, inputs, configuration, expected outputs, and modification policy. Generation shall be reproducible where practical.

The pipeline shall detect drift between controlled inputs and committed or published generated outputs. Hand modification of generated content is prohibited unless the workflow explicitly supports and reconciles it.

Generated content shall undergo the same applicable security, license, test, and review controls as manually written content. Generation does not confer trust.

Non-deterministic or model-assisted generation shall be reviewed for factual, semantic, security, and licensing risk and shall not be the sole producer of an authoritative contract or gate rule.

### Continuous Integration Stage Model

The canonical CI stage model is logically ordered as follows:

1. event and source identity verification;
2. repository and baseline integrity validation;
3. change classification and Quality Profile selection;
4. dependency and toolchain resolution under approved policy;
5. fast static, format, type, schema, secret, and policy checks;
6. deterministic build or compilation of the controlled source;
7. unit, component, contract, integration, and applicable system testing;
8. security, privacy, architecture, license, and supply-chain verification;
9. artifact creation, composition inventory, provenance, signing, and admission;
10. composite Quality Gate evaluation; and
11. publication of immutable CI evidence and feedback.

Implementations may parallelize independent work, but logical dependencies and evidence completeness shall remain intact. Later success shall not conceal an earlier failed or skipped mandatory stage.

### Fast Feedback and Progressive Verification

CI should provide rapid local and proposed-change feedback using reliable checks with high defect-detection value. Deeper integration, security, performance, resilience, recovery, and compatibility tests may run at later stages or on defined schedules when they require specialized environments.

Progressive verification shall not defer a control beyond the point at which an unsafe artifact could be consumed. Secret detection and untrusted workflow checks occur before privileged execution. Artifact provenance exists before registry admission. Deployment readiness is established before promotion.

Change-based test selection may reduce execution time when dependency and risk analysis are trustworthy. Mandatory shared-control, historical-regression, and release-profile tests shall not be omitted solely because direct file impact was not detected.

The full applicable release evidence set shall be complete before release authorization, regardless of which pipeline invocation produced each still-valid result.

### Test Orchestration

CI/CD shall execute tests according to Section 4.5 and interpret them through Section 4.6. Test selection, order, parallelism, retries, timeout, data, environments, sharding, and result aggregation shall be controlled and visible.

Parallel execution shall preserve isolation and deterministic aggregation. A worker failure shall not be interpreted as a product pass. Lost result shards, cancelled jobs, and unreported tests produce Blocked or Inconclusive status according to the Gate Definition.

Retries shall retain the original failure. Automatic retry is appropriate only for classified infrastructure transients or statistically governed evaluations; it shall not create green status by discarding failures.

Test reports shall bind exact source, artifact, suite, configuration, environment, and data. A test performed against an intermediate artifact shall not authorize the final artifact unless equivalence is proven.

### Static, Security, and Policy Analysis

Pipelines shall apply approved static analysis, configuration validation, secret detection, dependency analysis, license checks, policy checks, infrastructure analysis, and other machine-verifiable controls appropriate to the Quality Profile.

Rule sets, severities, suppressions, baselines, and exclusions shall be versioned and reviewed. A proposed change that modifies a rule or exclusion shall expose the effect on its own evaluation and receive independent approval.

Untrusted source shall not be able to upload a fabricated scan result into the authoritative channel. The pipeline control plane shall bind evidence to the actual execution and input.

Passing analysis does not prove absence of defect or vulnerability. The result shall retain tool and rule limitations and be combined with the required human and dynamic evidence.

### Architecture Conformance in CI/CD

CI/CD shall automate architecture conformance where structural rules are machine-testable and shall route semantic issues to the Architecture Gate. It may verify allowed dependencies, component boundaries, interface contracts, prohibited imports, data-flow constraints, deployment separation, and ADR references.

The pipeline shall preserve the deterministic Policy Engine as Control Plane authority; the advisory role of the AI Reasoning and Recommendation Engine; provider abstraction without policy authority; controlled execution through Tool Gateway; independent Validation Pipeline; and continuous Audit Engine and Evidence Chain coverage.

Development System and Runtime System boundaries shall be checked in source, configuration, credentials, network, artifacts, and deployment topology. Code Intelligence build order and compatibility shall respect Code Entity Model, Source File Analyzer, Symbol Extraction, Dependency Extraction, and Repository Code Index.

Automation cannot determine every semantic architecture violation. A green structural check shall not override competent architecture review.

### Policy and Configuration Validation

Policy, feature, deployment, security, observability, retention, and application configuration shall be schema-validated, semantically reviewed, versioned, and tested before promotion. Defaults, precedence, unknown fields, missing values, environment substitution, and secret references shall be explicit.

Policy Engine bundles shall be verified for syntax, deterministic behavior, conflict, default denial, risk classification, capability obligations, approval requirements, and version compatibility. A configuration template shall not be treated as the resolved target configuration.

The pipeline shall detect environment-specific values that violate tenant, region, data, provider, or security restrictions. Sensitive values shall be resolved through approved secret references rather than committed configuration.

Configuration change alone can require full release or migration controls even when executable code is unchanged.

### Infrastructure-as-Code Integration

Infrastructure definitions shall be treated as governed product source. CI/CD shall validate syntax, plan, policy, security, identity, network, encryption, storage, logging, backup, resource, region, and cost implications before application.

A rendered plan or equivalent change preview shall be bound to the exact approved source, current target state, provider context, and intended environment. Material drift between plan and apply invalidates approval.

State files, locks, credentials, and provider metadata shall be protected. Concurrent application to the same scope shall be serialized or otherwise controlled. Unapproved manual infrastructure changes shall be detected and reconciled.

Destructive changes require explicit target verification, backup or recovery readiness, competent approval, and an abort condition. The absence of a tool warning does not establish safety.

### Data and Schema Delivery

Database, index, evidence, queue, and schema changes shall have versioned migration logic, compatibility analysis, test evidence, capacity assessment, reconciliation, and rollback or forward-recovery strategy.

The pipeline shall separate migration preparation, execution, validation, and acceptance. Application deployment shall not assume a migration completed merely because the command exited successfully.

Expand-and-contract or equivalent compatibility strategies should be used where they reduce risk, but the chosen sequence shall be explicit. Mixed-version operation, retries, interruption, duplicate records, tenant boundaries, and long-running transactions shall be considered.

Production data shall not be copied into delivery environments without approved purpose and controls. Migration evidence shall minimize protected content while remaining independently verifiable.

### Documentation Integration

Documentation changes required by product, interface, configuration, security, migration, operation, support, or release shall be included in the same controlled delivery scope or an explicitly sequenced dependency.

The pipeline shall validate metadata, terminology, numbering, links, examples, diagrams, classification, secrets, accessibility, and source-to-publication traceability according to Section 4.4.

Generated Word, PDF, HTML, portal, and package outputs shall be produced from the controlled source through a recorded publication profile. Directly edited derivatives shall not become unreconciled authoritative sources.

Public documentation shall not be published before the corresponding capability and support state are authorized. Internal authoring controls shall be excluded from public artifacts through verified removal.

### Artifact Creation and Immutability

Artifacts shall be created from the verified source and build context and identified by immutable digest. The artifact set may include executables, packages, images, manifests, schemas, migration bundles, policy bundles, documentation, software bills of materials, provenance, signatures, and release metadata.

Once admitted to an authoritative registry or attached to an approved release, artifact bytes shall not be overwritten. Corrections require a new artifact identity and appropriate version or build metadata.

Mutable tags and channels may point to immutable artifacts but shall not be the sole identity in evidence or deployment. Movement of a tag does not change the underlying artifact history.

The pipeline shall detect incomplete, unexpected, duplicate, unsigned where required, or extraneous artifacts before publication. Packaging shall exclude source secrets, temporary files, debug credentials, internal notes, and unrelated customer data.

### Software Bill of Materials

The delivery process shall generate or verify an accurate software bill of materials for artifact profiles that require it. The inventory shall identify component, version, supplier or source, dependency relationship, relevant identifiers, and integrity information as supported.

The bill of materials shall be generated from actual resolved build content rather than solely from declared manifests. Differences between declaration and artifact shall be reconciled.

The inventory shall be bound to the artifact digest, protected from unauthorized modification, retained, and made available to authorized vulnerability, customer, and incident processes.

An inventory does not establish vulnerability absence, license compliance, or provenance by itself. It enables analysis and shall not be marketed beyond its defined claim.

### Build Provenance and Attestations

CI/CD shall produce provenance appropriate to the artifact Quality Profile, identifying what was built, from which source and inputs, by which trusted builder, under which build definition, and with which output digest.

Provenance shall be generated within the trusted build control plane and shall not rely solely on claims supplied by the untrusted source requester. It shall be signed or otherwise integrity-protected where required and distributed with a durable relationship to the artifact.

Consumers and promotion gates shall verify provenance identity, integrity, subject digest, trusted builder, build definition, source, dependencies, and policy before use. Presence of an attestation file is not sufficient.

Provenance claims shall remain scoped. They do not prove that source is correct, tests are complete, vulnerabilities are absent, or release approval exists.

### Artifact Signing and Verification

Signing shall occur only after the artifact passes the required pre-signing gates and within an isolated trusted context. Signing identities and keys shall be environment-, product-, channel-, and purpose-bound according to policy.

Untrusted jobs shall not access signing keys or request arbitrary subjects to be signed. The signing service shall verify artifact digest, authorized pipeline identity, gate state, release scope, and policy before issuing a signature.

Verification shall evaluate signature, trust root, signer identity, purpose, subject digest, timestamp where applicable, certificate or key validity, revocation, transparency or audit evidence, and policy.

A valid signature means that the trusted signer made a defined assertion about exact bytes. It does not independently prove quality, security, or release authority.

### Artifact Registry and Repository Controls

Artifact registries shall be enterprise-controlled, access-controlled, monitored, backed up, and configured for immutable release objects. Namespaces shall separate product, maturity, environment, tenant where applicable, and trust state.

Only approved pipeline identities may publish. Human direct upload shall be prohibited or restricted to a controlled recovery path with equivalent provenance and approval. Pull, replication, export, deletion, and retention shall be governed.

Registries shall distinguish candidate, quarantined, approved, released, deprecated, and revoked artifacts. Search results and default tags shall not make an unapproved candidate appear current.

Mirror and replication integrity shall be verified. A cache, mirror, or copied archive does not become canonical merely because the primary registry is unavailable.

### Quality Gate Integration

Pipelines shall invoke and enforce the Quality Gates defined in Section 4.6 at the correct lifecycle point. Gate definitions, not pipeline convenience, determine which evidence and outcomes are mandatory.

The orchestration layer shall collect the complete required-result set and shall fail closed for Failed, Blocked, Inconclusive, Expired, Cancelled, or missing mandatory outcomes. Waived and Conditional Pass outcomes shall carry their conditions into later stages.

Gate results shall bind exact source, artifact, configuration, environment, policy, schema, data, and transition. Result caching or reuse requires equivalence and freshness evidence.

A green workflow summary without subordinate gate visibility is insufficient. Failed and waived history shall remain accessible after a later pass.

### Manual Approval and Separation of Duties

Manual approvals shall occur where product, architecture, security, privacy, customer, legal, operational, or release judgment is required. Approval shall bind the exact evidence set and proposed transition.

The approver shall see artifact identity, source, target, risk, tests, security findings, waivers, migration, rollback or forward recovery, and deployment conditions. An approval interface shall not reduce the decision to an unexplained button.

The source author shall not be the sole production promoter for high-impact scope. Pipeline administrators shall not approve their own control changes. Signing, release, and deployment authority shall be separated where required.

Approvals expire or are invalidated on material change. An approval attached to an earlier candidate shall not transfer automatically to rebuilt or reconfigured bytes.

### Continuous Delivery Stage Model

The canonical Continuous Delivery sequence is logically ordered as follows:

1. select an immutable candidate artifact that passed CI and artifact admission;
2. verify provenance, composition, signatures, policy, Quality Gate results, and freshness;
3. assemble the release manifest and controlled documentation;
4. validate target environment, configuration, identity, secrets, keys, dependencies, capacity, and drift;
5. validate migration, backup, rollback or forward-recovery, observability, support, and communication readiness;
6. obtain required release and environment-promotion approvals;
7. promote the same immutable artifact through the approved deployment controller;
8. execute deployment and migration under bounded authority;
9. perform post-deployment verification and staged rollout checks;
10. decide continue, expand, hold, rollback, forward recover, contain, or declare incident; and
11. close the transition with reconciled audit, evidence, documentation, and release status.

Parallel preparation is permitted, but no environment transition may occur before its mandatory evidence and authority are complete.

### Environment Model and Separation

Environments shall have stable identity, owner, purpose, data classification, tenant scope, region, network boundary, access model, configuration authority, secret set, Quality Profile, and lifecycle state.

Development, test, integration, staging, performance, security, recovery, and production environments shall be separated according to risk. Production credentials, customer data, trust relationships, and signing authority shall not be copied into lower environments by default.

Environment names alone do not create separation. Effective identity, access, network, storage, keys, data, control planes, and administrative paths shall be evaluated.

Temporary and preview environments shall be bounded, automatically expired, cleaned, and prevented from acquiring production authority. Their public exposure and data use shall be controlled.

### Environment Configuration and Drift

The intended environment configuration shall be versioned, reviewable, validated, and associated with the promoted artifact. Environment-specific values shall be resolved through controlled configuration and secret systems.

CI/CD shall detect material drift between declared and actual state. Drift includes manual changes, provider defaults, external controllers, emergency actions, expired certificates, policy updates, network changes, and unmanaged resources.

Detected drift shall be classified, contained, reconciled, and evidenced. The pipeline shall not overwrite unknown production change blindly merely to restore a template.

Persistent environment differences that are intended shall be represented as approved profiles rather than undocumented exceptions.

### Promotion Model

Promotion is the controlled movement of an exact artifact and configuration into a defined environment, release channel, region, tenant cohort, or customer scope. Promotion is an authorization decision, not a file copy.

The same artifact digest shall progress through environments. Environment-specific configuration may differ under controlled profiles, but executable content shall not be rebuilt after verification.

Promotion shall be monotonic in assurance. Movement toward broader exposure or higher sensitivity requires equal or stronger evidence, not a reduced gate set. Results from one target shall not be generalized to another without equivalence assessment.

Promotion records shall include source state, target, artifact, configuration, approvals, conditions, executor identity, time, outcome, and evidence.

### Deployment Strategies

The deployment strategy shall be selected according to statefulness, compatibility, risk, availability objectives, recovery options, capacity, and customer commitments. Applicable strategies may include all-at-once, rolling, canary, ring, cohort, blue-green, parallel, shadow, feature-controlled, or customer-scheduled delivery.

No strategy is universally safest. Canary limits initial exposure but can still corrupt shared data. Blue-green reduces application switch time but may not reverse an irreversible migration. Feature controls can separate deployment from activation but introduce configuration and stale-code risk.

The strategy shall define batch size, observation period, metrics, abort condition, tenant fairness, dependency behavior, data compatibility, and completion criteria.

Deployment mechanisms remain implementation choices unless an ADR fixes them. The canonical requirement is controlled, evidenced, reversible or forward-recoverable transition.

### Feature Controls and Progressive Exposure

Feature controls may decouple artifact deployment from capability exposure. They shall be owned, versioned, access-controlled, typed, scoped, observable, tested, and retired when no longer needed.

Controls shall identify default, eligible tenant or cohort, environment, expiry, dependency, rollback behavior, and approval. A feature control shall not bypass policy, authorization, approval, Tool Gateway, validation, tenant, or evidence requirements.

Progressive exposure shall use defined success, failure, and safety metrics. Expansion is a promotion decision and shall not occur merely because no alert fired.

Stale or permanent temporary controls create complexity and shall be removed through governed change after rollout stabilizes.

### Database and State Migration Execution

Migration execution shall use the tested versioned migration artifact and target the verified system of record. The pipeline shall verify backup or recovery prerequisites, capacity, locks, tenant scope, compatibility, and authorized window before execution.

Long-running and interruptible migrations shall have checkpoints, idempotency, resume, monitoring, and reconciliation. The pipeline shall not rerun blindly after timeout when partial effects may exist.

Application and schema versions shall remain compatible throughout staged deployment. The transition shall identify when source and target authority changes and when old behavior is no longer safe.

Completion requires semantic reconciliation and acceptance, not only process exit status or record count.

### Rollback and Forward Recovery

Every production change shall identify whether rollback is safe, whether forward recovery is required, or whether both options exist. The term rollback shall not be used as a generic assurance when data, external effects, policy, evidence, or protocol changes are irreversible.

Rollback plans shall specify artifact, configuration, schema, data, keys, feature controls, external integrations, evidence, and customer communication. They shall be tested at the depth required by risk.

Forward recovery shall use an authorized corrective artifact or configuration with equivalent provenance and gate treatment, except under the emergency profile. It shall not become an unreviewed manual patch.

Rollback or recovery decisions shall be attributable, time-bounded, and based on defined triggers. Post-recovery validation and reconciliation are mandatory.

### Post-Deployment Verification

After deployment, the pipeline shall verify actual artifact digest, configuration, health, identity, policy, capability, Tool Gateway path, Validation Pipeline, Audit Engine, Evidence Chain, migrations, telemetry, and critical user journeys as applicable.

Synthetic transactions shall use controlled identities and data and shall not create unapproved customer or external side effects. Verification shall distinguish policy denial, provider degradation, execution failure, validation rejection, and infrastructure failure.

Post-deployment checks shall compare observed behavior with the release and environment profile. Missing telemetry, evidence, or gate correlation is itself a finding.

The rollout shall remain held until the defined observation period and acceptance criteria are satisfied. Absence of reported incidents alone is not success evidence.

### Deployment Cancellation and Concurrency

Pipelines shall define cancellation behavior for queued, running, partially applied, and post-deployment stages. Cancellation shall not leave ambiguous locks, active capabilities, partially migrated state, temporary credentials, or unknown rollout status.

Concurrent changes to the same artifact, environment, tenant cohort, policy bundle, schema, or infrastructure scope shall be serialized or coordinated through a proven concurrency model.

Newer deployment requests shall not silently overtake an active incompatible migration. Obsolete queued changes shall be cancelled before they can deploy after a later version.

Idempotency keys, locks, leases, sequence, and state machines shall be designed to recover from orchestrator restart and duplicate events.

### Release Candidate Assembly

A Release Candidate shall be assembled from immutable artifacts that passed the applicable CI and artifact gates. The release manifest shall identify every artifact digest, version, source revision, provenance, signature, composition inventory, policy, schema, migration, documentation, compatibility, and known limitation.

Candidate assembly shall not rebuild or modify approved artifacts. Packaging transformations shall themselves be controlled builds with new provenance and digest.

The candidate shall be evaluated as a complete set because individually valid components may be incompatible. Cross-component versions, installation order, configuration, data migration, and rollback or forward recovery shall be tested.

Release Candidate status and promotion to Stable or another maturity remain governed by Section 4.10.

### Release Publication and Distribution

Publication shall occur only after release authorization and shall distribute the exact approved artifact set, metadata, documentation, signatures, provenance, and support statement to approved channels.

Channels shall be registered, access-controlled, monitored, and separated by maturity where required. A pre-release artifact shall not appear under a stable default channel.

Replication, marketplace, customer portal, package repository, download site, and offline media distribution shall preserve integrity and version. Propagation state and partial publication shall be observable.

Revocation, withdrawal, correction, and customer notification procedures shall exist for compromised or defective releases. Removing a file without communicating affected versions is insufficient.

### Customer-Controlled Delivery

Customer-controlled delivery shall preserve artifact identity, provenance, signature, documentation, compatibility, and release status while recognizing the customer's environment authority. The delivery package shall include verification instructions and shared-responsibility requirements.

Customer-specific configuration or extension shall not create an untracked private build. If a customer-specific artifact is necessary, it requires its own source, provenance, version, support, security, and lifecycle decisions.

The process shall define who deploys, who approves, who holds keys and secrets, who validates, how evidence is exchanged, and how incidents, updates, rollback, and end-of-support are coordinated.

Customer delay or modification after delivery shall not be represented as an ILAIOS-controlled deployment. Evidence and responsibility shall reflect the actual boundary.

### Offline and Isolated Delivery

Offline and isolated deployments require a signed, integrity-protected, self-contained delivery package with declared artifacts, dependencies, provenance, composition inventory, documentation, migration, verification, and support information.

The package shall be created through the same approved source and build process as connected delivery. Air gap or network isolation does not justify unverified media, manual artifact substitution, or missing evidence.

Import shall verify media custody, package integrity, signer, artifact digest, version, compatibility, and authorization before installation. Exported operational evidence shall be minimized, protected, and reconciled when transferred.

Update and revocation processes shall address delayed vulnerability information, expired keys, disconnected clocks, dependency availability, and customer change windows.

### Mobile, Desktop, and Client Distribution

Client delivery profiles shall account for platform signing, store or enterprise-distribution review, staged rollout, compatibility, update policy, rollback limitations, offline use, local data, secret storage, and customer control.

The pipeline shall produce platform artifacts from the same controlled source and bind platform-specific transformations, signing, entitlements, permissions, and metadata to provenance.

Store approval is a distribution decision by an external channel and does not replace ILAIOS release, security, privacy, or quality approval. Store acceptance shall not be interpreted as certification of product architecture.

Client update mechanisms shall verify authenticity and integrity and shall not permit downgrade to a vulnerable or unsupported version contrary to policy.

### Infrastructure and Platform Delivery

Platform releases shall include infrastructure definitions, runtime configuration, policy bundles, observability, backup, recovery, secrets references, and dependency versions required to reproduce the approved deployment.

Platform changes shall be staged and verified without creating a second ungoverned architecture. Provider-specific implementation may vary across hosted, hybrid, customer-controlled, and isolated profiles, but canonical authority and trust invariants remain constant.

Base images, cluster or orchestration configuration, networking, storage, identity, and managed-service settings shall be treated as release inputs and included in drift and vulnerability management.

Manual provider-console change shall be restricted, attributable, reconciled to source, and reviewed. It shall not become the permanent deployment method.

### Model and Provider Configuration Delivery

Model-provider configuration, routing policy, approved model set, prompt or instruction assets, context policy, safety configuration, response schema, evaluation thresholds, and fallback behavior shall be versioned and promoted through controlled delivery.

Provider updates that occur outside ILAIOS's release process shall be detected and assessed. Mutable provider labels shall not silently change production behavior without evaluation and evidence.

Promotion shall verify data destination, region, tenant eligibility, credential, rate, cost, timeout, retry, fallback, observability, and provider contractual state. Fallback shall not route to an ineligible provider.

Reasoning assets and provider configuration do not gain policy authority through deployment. The Policy Engine remains deterministic and separate.

### CI/CD Observability

CI/CD shall emit structured logs, metrics, traces, events, gate results, and evidence sufficient to understand trigger, source, actor, runner, stages, dependencies, artifacts, approvals, promotions, failures, cancellations, and recovery.

Correlation shall connect repository event to source revision, build, artifact digest, provenance, release, environment, deployment, and post-deployment result. Correlation identifiers shall not expose secrets or customer data.

Alerts shall cover unauthorized trigger, permission escalation, secret access anomaly, runner compromise, disabled gate, signing misuse, artifact substitution, unexpected publication, drift, deployment failure, and evidence loss.

Telemetry shall be minimized, access-controlled, retained by record class, and tested. A successful pipeline status without trustworthy telemetry is not sufficient for high-impact release assurance.

### Audit and Evidence

Material CI/CD events shall be attributable and append-only or otherwise protected against unauthorized alteration. Events include workflow change, trigger, source acquisition, identity issuance, secret access, build, test, gate outcome, waiver, signing, publication, approval, promotion, deployment, rollback, recovery, cancellation, and closure.

Evidence shall bind exact source, toolchain, build definition, runner identity, dependencies, artifact, policy, environment, approver, and result as applicable. Failed and superseded attempts remain part of history.

Audit Engine and Evidence Chain may bind delivery events while respecting Development System and Runtime System separation. They do not make an unauthorized pipeline, incomplete gate set, compromised builder, or unsafe deployment valid.

Buffered or asynchronous evidence admission shall address backpressure, loss before durable admission, ordering, reconciliation, and fail behavior. Evidence shall span the delivery lifecycle rather than appear only as a final release receipt.

### Evidence Retention and Data Minimization

CI/CD evidence retention shall follow an approved record-class-specific schedule that reconciles legal, contractual, certification, product-support, incident, defense, privacy, and data-minimization requirements.

Source fragments, test data, logs, crash dumps, dependency metadata, vulnerability details, approval context, and deployment telemetry may contain protected information and shall be minimized and classified.

Legal holds and justified extensions shall be narrowly scoped, authorized, documented, and periodically reviewed. Retention is not indefinite by default.

Caches and temporary workspaces are not evidence archives. Their deletion schedule may be shorter, but deletion shall not remove records required to support a release or incident.

### Pipeline Failure Semantics

Each stage shall define success, failure, blocked, timeout, cancellation, retry, partial completion, and cleanup behavior. Unknown status shall not map to success.

Failure shall stop dependent stages and revoke or expire unnecessary credentials and leases. Cleanup shall not delete evidence needed for diagnosis or incident response.

Partial artifact publication, signature issuance, migration, or deployment shall trigger reconciliation before retry. Blind restart can duplicate effects or attach authority to the wrong state.

User-facing failure information shall be actionable without exposing secrets, protected topology, or exploit detail. Root cause and recovery state shall remain observable to authorized operators.

### Retry, Idempotency, and Backoff

Retries shall be limited to operations designed for repeat execution or protected by idempotency and reconciliation. The retry policy shall distinguish transient infrastructure failure from deterministic product or gate failure.

A failed test, security finding, approval denial, policy denial, signature mismatch, or invalid artifact shall not be retried automatically to obtain success. Re-execution after correction creates a new attributable attempt.

External side effects, deployments, migrations, notifications, tag updates, and artifact publication require stable operation identity and duplicate handling.

Backoff, rate limits, deadlines, and maximum attempts shall prevent cascading failure and cost amplification. All attempts and final disposition shall remain visible.

### Caching

Caching may improve speed but shall not weaken source, dependency, test, artifact, or evidence integrity. Cache keys shall include all inputs that materially affect output, including toolchain, dependency, configuration, architecture, and environment where applicable.

Untrusted jobs shall not poison caches consumed by privileged builds. Cache namespaces shall separate trust domains, repositories, branches, tenants, and security profiles as necessary.

Cached dependencies and artifacts shall be integrity-verified and subject to freshness and vulnerability policy. A cached gate result shall be reused only when input equivalence and validity are proven.

Cache miss shall reduce performance, not correctness. Cache corruption shall trigger eviction, investigation, and rebuild from authoritative inputs.

### Pipeline Concurrency and Resource Governance

Pipeline concurrency shall be bounded by platform capacity, target-environment safety, tenant fairness, external rate limits, and cost controls. Unbounded fan-out or recursive workflow triggering is prohibited.

Resource requests and limits shall prevent one job from exhausting shared runners, networks, registries, or external services. High-cost model evaluations, security scans, performance tests, and environment creation shall use quotas and accountable budgets.

Priority rules shall favor incident containment and critical remediation without starving mandatory maintenance. Queue state and wait time shall be observable.

Concurrency controls shall not serialize unrelated work unnecessarily, but shared deployment, migration, signing, and release scopes require safe coordination.

### Pipeline Performance and Developer Experience

Pipeline performance shall be optimized for reliable feedback, not superficial speed. Metrics shall distinguish queue, startup, dependency, build, test, scan, approval, deployment, and verification time.

Slow or unstable pipelines encourage bypass and shall be treated as engineering debt. Optimization may use parallelism, caching, test selection, reusable environments, and incremental analysis when risk coverage remains intact.

Developers shall receive clear local-equivalent checks, actionable failures, ownership, and remediation guidance. Hidden enterprise checks that fail only after long delay should be exposed earlier where practical.

No optimization may suppress mandatory evidence, use stale results beyond validity, weaken isolation, or rebuild after approval.

### Pipeline Availability and Continuity

CI/CD shall have availability and recovery objectives proportionate to business and security dependence. The continuity scope includes workflow source, configuration, identities, secrets references, runner images, registries, artifacts, provenance, signing, gate definitions, approvals, and audit records.

Backup shall be tested through restoration. A copy of repository source alone is insufficient if provider settings, registry state, signing policy, or environment mappings are lost.

An alternate delivery path may exist for continuity but shall provide equivalent source verification, gate enforcement, artifact integrity, approval, evidence, and environment control. It shall not be an undocumented manual shortcut.

Recovery exercises shall verify that previously released artifacts remain verifiable and that new releases cannot be forged during degraded operation.

### CI/CD Incident Response

Suspected pipeline compromise, credential exposure, malicious workflow change, runner escape, artifact substitution, signing misuse, registry tampering, unauthorized deployment, or evidence loss shall trigger the incident process.

Containment may include disabling triggers, revoking credentials, isolating runners, freezing registries, suspending signing, blocking promotions, and identifying affected source, artifacts, releases, environments, and customers.

Investigation shall preserve logs, workflow revisions, identities, runner state where feasible, artifacts, provenance, approvals, network records, and gate results. Evidence shall be handled according to classification and legal requirements.

Recovery requires trusted rebuild, re-signing or revocation as appropriate, deployment assessment, customer communication, and restoration of gate integrity. Re-enabling the pipeline without establishing a trusted baseline is prohibited.

### Vulnerability and Urgent Remediation Delivery

Security remediation shall use the ordinary controlled path wherever time permits. The pipeline should support expedited targeted builds, tests, signing, release, and customer notification without discarding critical controls.

The process shall identify affected versions, exploitability, exposure, fix, regression risk, artifact set, compatibility, rollback or forward recovery, disclosure, and distribution urgency.

Embargoed vulnerabilities require restricted source, runner, artifact, evidence, and communication access while retaining review and traceability. Broad secrecy shall not exclude necessary competent reviewers.

After release, affected old artifacts shall be marked, revoked, blocked, or otherwise treated according to risk and support policy. A fixed release does not remove vulnerable copies from customers automatically.

### Emergency Delivery

Emergency delivery is permitted only under the Emergency Quality Gate Profile defined in Section 4.6. It applies to active or imminent material incident, vulnerability, outage, corruption, or binding legal requirement, not ordinary schedule or commercial pressure.

The emergency path shall preserve verified source, minimum targeted testing, secret and tenant controls, artifact identity, provenance, approval, bounded deployment authority, observability, rollback or forward recovery, and evidence.

Omitted controls shall be recorded with reason, risk, compensating control, owner, and deadline. Emergency artifacts and configuration require retrospective reconciliation into the canonical source and standard pipeline.

The emergency path shall be exercised and secured before use where feasible. A manual process unknown until the incident is not a reliable continuity control.

### Third-Party CI/CD Services

Use of an external pipeline, runner, registry, signing, scanning, testing, or deployment service requires assessment of security, privacy, data destination, region, identity, access, tenancy, availability, incident, evidence, support, subcontractors, change control, and exit.

Provider certifications and contractual claims are inputs, not proof that ILAIOS's configuration or integration is secure. Shared responsibilities shall be explicit and tested.

Provider outages, compromise, acquisition, deprecation, pricing, retention, and platform behavior changes shall have monitoring and contingency. A proprietary feature shall not become an unexamined architecture dependency.

Provider abstraction shall not conceal the actual trust boundary. The pipeline record shall identify the service and version or configuration material to the result.

### External Contributors and Untrusted Changes

External and fork-originated changes shall run in an unprivileged validation context without production secrets, signing identity, trusted cache write, internal network access, or deployment capability.

Authoritative builds and tests shall be repeated from the accepted canonical source under a trusted workflow after required review. Results supplied by the contributor may inform review but do not acquire ILAIOS authority.

Workflow files, dependency definitions, build scripts, test code, and generated artifacts in the change shall be considered potentially hostile. The pipeline shall protect against command injection, exfiltration, cache poisoning, artifact overwrite, log forgery, and approval manipulation.

Contributor identity and license requirements shall follow repository and legal policy without exposing unnecessary personal data.

### Customer-Supplied Source and Integrations

Customer-controlled repositories, extensions, tools, schemas, and configuration shall remain tenant-, contract-, purpose-, and capability-bound. They shall not be admitted into canonical ILAIOS product source without separate repository and architecture governance.

Customer builds shall execute in isolated contexts and shall not access other customers, internal source, signing keys, or production control planes beyond the approved service.

The delivery process shall clarify which artifacts are ILAIOS-supported, customer-produced, jointly integrated, or unverified. Artifact provenance and evidence shall preserve that distinction.

Customer-supplied code cannot bypass Runtime System Policy Engine, approval, Tool Gateway, validation, audit, or evidence requirements through a delivery integration.

### Compliance and Evidence Mapping

CI/CD controls may be mapped to applicable secure-development, supply-chain, change-management, access, logging, evidence, privacy, and customer-assurance requirements. The exact framework edition, applicability, scope, and control interpretation shall be recorded.

Draft, final, superseded, and withdrawn standards shall be distinguished. A mapping to a control does not establish operating effectiveness, certification, or legal compliance.

Pipeline evidence shall support audit without granting auditors or customers unrestricted access to source, secrets, customer data, or exploitable configuration. Controlled summaries and independent attestations may be used where appropriate.

Changes to obligations or certifications shall trigger pipeline profile review and evidence-gap analysis.

### CI/CD Metrics and Governance Health

CI/CD metrics shall evaluate reliability, security, quality, recovery, and delivery flow. Relevant indicators include:

- integration lead time and feedback time by stage;
- change failure, rollback, forward-recovery, and incident rates;
- failed, blocked, inconclusive, waived, expired, and skipped gate trends;
- pipeline and runner availability, queue time, retry, and flakiness;
- artifacts without verified provenance, composition inventory, signature, or immutable identity;
- source-to-artifact reproducibility and unexplained build variance;
- deployment frequency by maturity and environment, without treating frequency as success alone;
- mean time to detect, contain, recover, and reconcile delivery failures;
- unauthorized workflow, permission, secret, registry, signing, or environment changes;
- drift, manual change, stale credentials, and unused privilege;
- emergency-path use and overdue retrospective closure;
- customer-controlled deployment verification and update lag;
- pipeline debt age and control-exception concentration; and
- escaped defects or incidents attributable to delivery-control gaps.

Pipeline count, job count, green percentage, deployment frequency, or short duration are not maturity measures by themselves. Metrics shall not reward bypass, unsafe batching, hidden failure, or excessive release fragmentation.

### CI/CD Debt

CI/CD debt includes manual undocumented steps, shared credentials, mutable dependencies, unpinned workflow components, persistent runners without proven cleanup, unreproducible builds, missing provenance, broad network access, unstable tests, stale templates, drift, untested rollback, and unsupported delivery paths.

Debt shall be registered with affected risks, products, environments, owner, treatment, target, and release consequence. Critical signing, production access, tenant isolation, evidence, and recovery debt requires priority treatment.

Temporary manual controls shall have evidence and expiry. Repeated manual intervention indicates a missing automation or architecture capability and shall not become invisible normal operation.

Remediation shall preserve current releases and customers while improving the canonical delivery path. A platform migration requires its own controlled transition and continuity plan.

### Exceptions

An exception to this standard shall identify the exact requirement, pipeline, repository, artifact, environment, release, duration, reason, alternatives, risk, compensating controls, owner, approver, expiry, and remediation.

An exception cannot authorize fabricated gate success; production-secret exposure; untrusted access to signing or deployment authority; cross-tenant data access; reasoning-based release authority; bypass of required runtime Policy Engine, approval, Tool Gateway, Validation Pipeline, Audit Engine, or Evidence Chain; unlawful processing; or silent modification of an approved artifact.

Provider limitation, legacy technology, customer request, or deadline shall be documented but does not itself justify deviation. The decision authority shall compare risk of the exception with delay or alternate scope.

Expired exceptions require remediation, renewal through new assessment, scope restriction, feature disablement, release deferral, or retirement. Continuation through inaction is non-conformant.

### CI/CD Invariants

The following invariants are canonical:

- authoritative artifacts originate only from registered canonical source and an approved controlled build process;
- CI integrates and verifies change, Continuous Delivery creates deployable approved candidates, and production deployment remains a separate authorized transition;
- Continuous Deployment is not the default and requires explicit ADR, risk, Quality Profile, and recovery approval;
- pipelines, reusable workflows, gate rules, runner images, and deployment logic are governed production assets;
- untrusted source and external contributions never obtain production secrets, signing keys, privileged cache writes, internal control-plane access, or deployment authority;
- pipeline workload identity is distinct from human identity, short-lived where practical, purpose-bound, and least-privileged;
- source authors, pipeline administrators, signers, release authorities, and production promoters remain separated where risk requires;
- builds use declared, verified inputs and produce immutable digest-identified artifacts;
- the same artifact is promoted unchanged across environments and is never rebuilt after release approval;
- provenance identifies source, builder, build definition, inputs, and output according to the approved profile, without claiming correctness beyond that scope;
- signatures bind exact bytes and signer assertions but do not independently prove quality, security, or release authorization;
- software bills of materials support composition analysis but do not independently prove vulnerability, license, or provenance status;
- missing, failed, blocked, inconclusive, cancelled, expired, or contradictory mandatory evidence stops progression;
- retries preserve original failures, and cached results require exact input equivalence and freshness;
- environment, policy, schema, configuration, and infrastructure drift remain detectable and governed;
- deployment strategies limit exposure but do not waive policy, validation, tenant, evidence, recovery, or security requirements;
- rollback is claimed only where safe and tested; otherwise forward recovery is explicit;
- post-deployment verification confirms actual artifact, configuration, controls, migrations, telemetry, and evidence before rollout closure;
- the AI Reasoning and Recommendation Engine may propose or analyze delivery work but never approves merge, gate, signing, release, deployment, or risk;
- the deterministic Policy Engine remains Runtime Control Plane authority, and delivery automation creates no alternate runtime action path;
- Tool Gateway, independent Validation Pipeline, Audit Engine, and Evidence Chain remain mandatory for governed runtime actions after deployment;
- Development System and Runtime System credentials, networks, data, authority, and evidence remain separated;
- CI/CD events are attributable from trigger through release, promotion, post-deployment validation, rollback or recovery, and closure;
- evidence retention follows approved record-class-specific schedules and is not indefinite by default;
- customer-controlled, offline, mobile, desktop, hosted, hybrid, and isolated delivery profiles preserve the same canonical trust invariants; and
- platform speed, deployment frequency, green status, provider convenience, or commercial urgency never substitutes for evidence-based release authority.

An integration, delivery, or deployment process is non-conformant if it builds an official artifact from an unregistered repository, personal fork, ambiguous revision, or dirty workspace; allows untrusted change content to modify its authoritative evaluator, access secrets, sign artifacts, poison privileged caches, or deploy; uses a developer's personal credential as pipeline identity; grants a build job broad production administration; downloads mutable unauthenticated dependencies during a release build; publishes an artifact without immutable identity or required provenance; treats an attestation, signature, composition inventory, scan, or green workflow as proof beyond its scope; rebuilds after approval and promotes different bytes; attaches tests from an intermediate artifact to a final artifact without equivalence; maps skipped, timed-out, unavailable, or cancelled work to success; erases a failure through retry; updates a baseline or expected result to obtain green status without separate approval; lets a model approve a merge, release, or deployment; uses CI/CD to bypass Runtime Policy Engine, human approval, Tool Gateway, independent validation, audit, or evidence; modifies production manually without attribution and reconciliation; promises rollback where only forward recovery is safe; copies customer or production data into lower environments without authority; publishes Draft documentation or unreleased capability as current; uses an emergency path for ordinary schedule pressure; or treats deployment frequency and pipeline speed as the primary definition of engineering quality.

## 4.8 Branching, Commit, Review, and Merge Strategy

### Purpose and Change-Control Intent

Branching, commit, review, and merge controls preserve the integrity of ILAIOS source while enabling small, attributable, independently reviewable change. They establish how work is isolated, how intent is recorded, how evidence is attached, how competent review occurs, and how an exact source revision becomes part of a protected canonical baseline.

The purpose of this strategy is not to enforce a preferred visual history or a provider-specific workflow. Its purpose is to prevent unauthorized, ambiguous, unreviewed, inseparable, untraceable, or architecture-changing work from entering authoritative source. Source history shall enable an authorized reviewer to determine what changed, why it changed, who authored and approved it, what evidence supported it, and how it can be reverted or remediated.

Branching is an isolation mechanism, not an authority mechanism. A commit is an immutable source record, not proof of correctness. A review is a competent assessment, not ceremonial approval. A merge is source integration, not release authorization. These meanings shall remain distinct.

### Scope

This strategy applies to all governed ILAIOS repositories and source-managed assets, including product code, tests, policies, schemas, migrations, infrastructure definitions, build and CI/CD logic, documentation, generated-source inputs, security rules, model-provider configuration, mobile and desktop clients, and customer-controlled integration assets.

It governs:

- primary, change, release, support, hotfix, security, experiment, automation, and archival branches;
- commit identity, content, message, signature, ordering, amendment, and history;
- Change Requests, reviewer selection, code ownership, specialist review, comments, approvals, and evidence;
- merge eligibility, freshness, queueing, integration method, conflict resolution, and post-merge verification;
- external contributions, forks, automated changes, dependency updates, generated content, and customer source;
- emergency source changes, backports, reverts, security embargoes, and incident remediation; and
- audit, evidence, metrics, exceptions, and repository recovery related to change integration.

Repository registration, naming, access, transfer, archival, and storage rules remain governed by Section 4.2. CI/CD execution remains governed by Section 4.7. Version and release semantics remain governed by Sections 4.9 and 4.10.

### Canonical Terminology

The following terms are canonical:

- **Primary Branch:** the protected branch that represents the current authoritative integrated source for a repository profile;
- **Change Branch:** a short-lived branch containing one coherent proposed change;
- **Change Request:** the governed request to integrate an exact change into a protected target branch; providers may call it a pull request or merge request;
- **Release Branch:** a controlled branch used only when stabilization or supported release maintenance cannot be managed safely from the Primary Branch;
- **Support Branch:** a branch maintained for an explicitly supported prior line, including Long-Term Support where applicable;
- **Hotfix Branch:** a short-lived branch for urgent correction of a released line;
- **Protected Branch:** a branch whose updates are governed by mandatory access, review, Quality Gate, history, and audit controls;
- **Commit:** an immutable source-tree record with parent relationship, author, committer, message, and integrity identity;
- **Approval:** an accountable reviewer decision on an exact Change Request revision;
- **Merge:** the controlled integration of approved source into a target branch; and
- **Backport:** the deliberate application of an already governed correction to another supported source line.

Branch display name, remote alias, local branch, URL, or default-provider label does not establish canonical authority. The Repository Register and protection configuration determine the authoritative Primary Branch.

### Core Principles

ILAIOS source-change governance follows these principles:

1. **One coherent change.** A Change Request addresses one bounded outcome and minimizes unrelated modification.
2. **Protected canonical source.** Authoritative branches cannot be changed through ordinary direct push.
3. **Short-lived divergence.** Change branches remain small and current to reduce conflict and stale assumptions.
4. **Atomic intent.** Commits and Change Requests preserve understandable purpose, evidence, and reversal boundaries.
5. **Review the exact revision.** Approval is invalidated by material change after review.
6. **Risk-based independence.** Review depth and separation of duties increase with consequence.
7. **All source classes are governed.** Tests, policies, workflows, migrations, documentation, and generated inputs do not receive weaker treatment merely because they are not executable application code.
8. **Quality Gates precede integration.** Failed, blocked, inconclusive, expired, cancelled, or missing mandatory evidence prevents merge.
9. **History is evidence.** Shared protected history is not rewritten to conceal error or simplify appearance.
10. **No self-created authority.** Authors, automation, models, bots, and repository providers do not approve their own authority.
11. **Architecture remains canonical.** Source integration cannot silently redesign accepted architecture.
12. **Merge is not release.** Integration, build, artifact admission, release, deployment, validation, and acceptance remain separate decisions.

### Primary Branch Policy

Every active governed repository shall identify one Primary Branch in the Repository Register. The existing name may be `master`, `main`, or another approved value. This standard does not require branch renaming solely for convention. A rename is a governed repository migration and shall preserve references, automation, protection, evidence, and customer dependencies.

The Primary Branch shall be protected and kept in a releasable or explicitly known controlled state appropriate to the repository profile. It shall not contain unresolved conflict markers, unreviewed temporary code, known live secrets, incomplete migrations without feature protection, or hidden customer-specific behavior.

Ordinary updates shall occur only through an approved Change Request and the permitted merge mechanism. Direct push, force push, history deletion, protection bypass, and branch deletion are prohibited except through controlled bootstrap, emergency, continuity, or administrative recovery procedures.

The Primary Branch is source authority within repository scope. It is not automatically the latest Stable release, production state, or customer deployment. Release and deployment evidence shall identify the exact commit and artifact.

### Branch Naming Standard

Change branch names shall use a controlled, concise, machine-safe form:

`<category>/<work-id>-<short-kebab-description>`

The work identifier may be omitted only for an approved repository profile that has no external work-tracking requirement. Canonical categories include:

- `feature` for approved new capability;
- `fix` for defect correction;
- `security` for non-embargoed security work;
- `refactor` for behavior-preserving structural improvement;
- `performance` for measured performance improvement;
- `test` for test-only change;
- `docs` for documentation-only change;
- `build` for build or dependency mechanics;
- `ci` for delivery-pipeline change;
- `chore` for bounded maintenance not represented by another type;
- `release` for an authorized release branch;
- `hotfix` for urgent supported-line correction; and
- `experiment` for isolated non-authoritative investigation.

Branch names shall not contain personal names, credentials, customer identities, incident-sensitive details, vulnerability disclosure, former brands, environment secrets, unsupported compliance claims, or temporary maturity claims. Restricted security work may use a non-descriptive identifier to protect embargo.

### Branch Creation and Baseline

A Change Branch shall be created from the intended current protected baseline. The branch record shall identify target branch, baseline commit, owner, purpose, work item, and applicable Quality Profile where not derivable from the Change Request.

A branch created from an obsolete or wrong baseline shall be updated before review. A branch targeting a support line shall not be based accidentally on the Primary Branch if doing so introduces unsupported behavior.

Branch creation shall not copy uncommitted local state, ignored secrets, generated caches, or files outside the registered repository. Repository identity, remote, branch, and baseline shall be verified before governed work begins.

The branch shall not become an alternative canonical source. Long-lived work that requires persistent divergence shall have an explicit architecture, product, release, or support decision.

### Short-Lived Change Branches

The default development model is short-lived change branches integrated frequently into the protected Primary Branch. Small branches reduce review burden, merge conflict, hidden dependency, and delayed security feedback.

A change shall be divided by coherent outcome rather than by file count. The branch shall include the implementation, tests, documentation, migration, policy, and operational updates necessary for that outcome. Artificially splitting required tests or security controls into a later branch is prohibited when it creates an unsafe intermediate state.

Large changes shall use decomposition, compatible intermediate states, feature controls, or staged architecture rather than an indefinitely open branch. If safe decomposition is impossible, the Change Request shall document review strategy, integration risk, and rollback or forward recovery.

Branch duration is a signal, not a universal limit. Stale branches shall be reviewed, updated, restricted, archived, or deleted according to evidence and retention needs.

### Release and Support Branches

Release and Support Branches are exceptions to the single-primary-line model and shall exist only when product release policy, customer support, certification, regulatory constraint, or compatibility requires separate maintenance.

Each such branch shall identify supported version range, owner, creation baseline, permitted change classes, merge direction, test profile, release authority, end-of-support date, and retirement plan. It shall be protected to the same or stronger level as the Primary Branch for the affected release.

New features shall not be developed primarily on a Support Branch. Changes shall normally be corrected on the earliest authoritative line where the defect exists and then propagated deliberately to other affected lines, subject to compatibility and test.

Release branch creation does not create a release. Section 4.10 defines maturity and release authorization. Unsupported branches shall be locked or archived and shall not accept ordinary changes.

### Hotfix Branches

A Hotfix Branch is created from the exact supported release or support baseline affected by an urgent defect. It shall contain the minimum safe correction, targeted regression evidence, version and release updates, and necessary documentation.

The fix shall be merged or otherwise reconciled into every still-affected authoritative line so that the defect does not reappear in a later release. Reconciliation order and compatibility shall be explicit.

Hotfix does not mean unreviewed. It follows the standard Change Request and Quality Gate process or the approved Emergency Profile when the incident warrants expedited handling.

A hotfix branch shall be deleted or archived after integration and evidence closure. It shall not become a permanent parallel development line.

### Security and Embargoed Branches

Embargoed vulnerability work shall use restricted repositories, branches, access groups, communications, runners, artifacts, and evidence appropriate to disclosure risk. The branch name and metadata shall not reveal exploitable detail.

Access shall be limited to competent personnel with a need to know. Required review and separation of duties remain; restriction shall not become unilateral unreviewed change. Test data and exploit material shall be handled under incident and vulnerability policy.

The branch shall not use ordinary public CI if logs, caches, artifacts, notifications, or external integrations could disclose the issue. Trusted release production, signing, distribution, and customer notification shall be coordinated.

After disclosure and release, the change shall be reconciled into the normal source history with appropriate public and restricted records. Sensitive details may remain in controlled evidence while the authoritative code history remains accurate.

### Experimental and Research Branches

Experimental branches support bounded research and shall be visibly non-authoritative. They shall not publish Stable artifacts, receive production credentials, modify protected environments, or be represented as supported product behavior.

The experiment shall identify hypothesis, owner, duration, data, security constraints, success criteria, and disposition. Customer, personal, regulated, or confidential data requires specific authority regardless of branch classification.

Promotion of experimental work into product source requires a new or updated Change Request against the current protected baseline, production-quality tests, documentation, security review, and applicable ADR. Experimental history alone is not acceptance evidence.

Abandoned experiments shall be deleted or archived according to classification and learning value. Temporary dependencies, secrets, artifacts, and environments shall be removed.

### Automation and Bot Branches

Automation may create branches for dependency updates, generated content, formatting, documentation synchronization, or routine maintenance. Each automation identity shall have a registered owner, least privilege, scoped triggers, versioned logic, and revocation path.

Automated Change Requests shall meet the same applicable test, review, security, license, and merge requirements as human-authored work. A bot shall not approve or merge its own change unless a narrowly defined low-risk automation profile explicitly provides independent deterministic authorization.

Automated updates shall identify source, version, provenance, affected dependencies, release notes, risk, and generated modifications. Bundling unrelated upgrades into one opaque change shall be avoided.

Compromise or anomalous behavior of automation shall trigger identity revocation, open-change quarantine, source and artifact assessment, and incident response.

### External Contributor Branches and Forks

External contributions shall originate from a fork or untrusted branch path without access to production secrets, signing keys, privileged caches, internal networks, or deployment authority. The source shall be treated as hostile until accepted.

The Change Request shall establish contribution rights, provenance, license, intended behavior, and communication contact as required. Contributor-provided test results and signatures may inform review but do not create ILAIOS approval.

Trusted CI shall re-execute the accepted source under controlled conditions after review. Workflow changes, dependency scripts, test code, generated files, and archives receive particular scrutiny because they may execute during review.

Merging an external contribution does not make the contributor an ongoing repository administrator or code owner. Access changes follow Section 4.2.

### Customer-Controlled Source and Private Extensions

Customer repositories, branches, forks, and extensions shall remain tenant-, contract-, purpose-, and lifecycle-bound. They shall not be merged into canonical product source merely to simplify a deployment.

Where a customer-specific change is accepted into the product, customer identifiers and confidential details shall be removed or generalized, rights shall be confirmed, and the change shall pass normal product review and architecture governance.

Private extensions require explicit ownership, support, version compatibility, security review, build provenance, deployment boundary, update process, and retirement. An indefinite customer fork is a product and maintenance risk, not a neutral branch choice.

Cross-customer reuse requires product and privacy review and shall not expose one customer's data, topology, policy, or contract to another.

### Branch Synchronization and Freshness

Before final review and merge, a Change Branch shall be current enough with the target branch to establish compatibility and Quality Gate validity. The required freshness may be enforced by merge queue, rebase, target-branch merge, or provider-equivalent mechanism.

Updating the branch after approval may invalidate the approval and affected tests. The platform shall require review of the exact final revision and rerun mandatory checks when the source tree changes materially.

Teams shall not perform habitual target-branch merges that create noisy history without resolving actual integration risk. The repository profile shall define the permitted synchronization method.

A stale branch with unresolved dependency or architecture assumptions shall be reassessed rather than mechanically rebased and merged.

### Branch Deletion, Archival, and Recovery

Merged short-lived branches should be deleted after the authoritative merge and evidence are durable. Branch deletion does not delete commit history reachable from the protected branch or Change Request record.

Unmerged branches shall be archived or deleted based on classification, open obligations, security, evidence, intellectual property, and expected reuse. Sensitive abandoned branches shall not remain indefinitely accessible.

Deletion shall verify exact branch, remote, owner, merge state, open Change Requests, release references, and legal hold. Protected, release, support, and security branches require elevated authority.

Recovery from accidental branch deletion shall use known commit identity and audit evidence. A recovered branch does not regain protected or canonical status automatically.

### Commit Atomicity

Each commit shall represent one coherent logical change that can be reviewed and understood independently. It shall not combine unrelated feature, refactor, formatting, dependency, generated, and documentation changes merely for convenience.

Atomicity is semantic rather than numerical. A correct feature commit may change multiple files and include tests and documentation. Artificially separating implementation from required tests or migration can make individual commits unsafe and is prohibited when intermediate states are expected to build or be reviewed.

Commits on a change branch may capture reviewable steps, but the final integrated history shall satisfy the repository's merge method and atomicity profile. Temporary `fixup`, `wip`, or experiment commits shall not enter a protected branch unless the profile deliberately preserves them for evidentiary reason.

A commit shall not include editor state, local caches, credentials, unrelated generated output, accidental file deletion, or formatting of untouched subsystems.

### Commit Content Requirements

A commit shall include all source artifacts necessary to understand and verify its intended outcome. Applicable content includes implementation, tests, schema, migration, configuration, policy, documentation, release notes, and generated-source inputs.

Before commit, the author shall inspect the staged tree rather than rely on working-directory appearance. Binary, large, generated, vendored, permission, line-ending, encoding, rename, and deletion changes shall be intentional.

The commit shall preserve repository formatting, type, lint, security, test, and documentation requirements. A local pass does not replace authoritative CI, but it reduces avoidable failures.

Secrets, customer data, personal data, production identifiers, unlicensed assets, and internal authoring notes prohibited by classification shall not be committed. Later deletion does not remove exposure from history.

### Commit Message Standard

The canonical subject format is:

`<type>(<scope>): <imperative summary>`

`<scope>` may be omitted when the repository or change is already unambiguous. Approved types are:

- `feat` for new product capability;
- `fix` for defect correction;
- `security` for security remediation or control improvement;
- `refactor` for behavior-preserving structural change;
- `perf` for measured performance improvement;
- `test` for test-only work;
- `docs` for documentation-only work;
- `build` for build system or dependency mechanics;
- `ci` for CI/CD configuration;
- `chore` for bounded maintenance; and
- `revert` for explicit reversal of a prior commit.

The summary shall be concise, imperative, specific, and free of trailing punctuation. The body shall explain reason, behavior, constraints, alternatives, migration, risk, and testing when the subject is insufficient. Footers shall carry work-item, ADR, issue, breaking-change, co-author, sign-off, or other structured references defined by the repository profile.

### Commit Message Semantics

The message shall explain the change that the commit actually contains. Generic subjects such as `update`, `changes`, `fix stuff`, `final`, `cleanup`, or a tool-generated description without human verification are prohibited on protected history.

Breaking change shall be declared through the repository's structured convention, including affected contract, migration, compatibility, and release implications.
