A `feat` label does not automatically create a minor version, and a `fix` label does not automatically authorize a patch release; Section 4.9 governs version decisions.

Messages shall not include secrets, customer-confidential information, vulnerability exploit detail under embargo, personal data, unsupported claims, or unapproved internal authoring metadata.

The message is durable documentation but shall reference, not duplicate, extensive ADRs, designs, test reports, or incident records.

### Author, Committer, and Attribution

Every commit shall identify the actual author and committer through verified organizational identity appropriate to the repository profile. Shared, fabricated, misleading, or generic identities are prohibited.

Author identifies the person or governed automation responsible for the change content. Committer identifies the person or system that created the commit object. These may differ for imported patches, rebases, automated updates, or maintained external contributions, and the distinction shall remain accurate.

Model-assisted or generated content remains attributed to the accountable human or registered automation that reviewed and submitted it. Assistance does not become a legal author, reviewer, approver, or risk owner.

Employment change, account rename, or key rotation shall not rewrite historical identity. The identity directory and signing trust records preserve interpretation over time.

### Commit Signing and Signature Verification

Commit signing requirements shall be defined by Repository and Quality Profile. Protected Trust Core, security, release, pipeline, policy, and high-assurance repositories should require verifiable signatures or equivalent source attestations.

Verification shall evaluate signature integrity, signer identity, trust, key or certificate validity at signing time, revocation information, allowed purpose, and commit subject. A `verified` display badge without trust-policy evaluation is insufficient.

Signing keys shall be personal or workload-bound, protected, rotated, revoked, and not shared. Automated commits shall use a distinct automation identity. Loss or compromise triggers impact analysis of affected commits and releases.

A valid signature establishes that the signer made an assertion over the commit bytes under defined trust. It does not prove code correctness, review, testing, merge authorization, or release status.

### Commit Sign-Off and Contribution Certification

Where a repository requires legal contribution certification or sign-off, the exact statement, authority, and recording format shall be documented. Sign-off shall represent the contributor's required rights and assertions; it shall not be added by another party without authority.

Sign-off and cryptographic signature are distinct. One may assert contribution terms, while the other provides integrity and signer evidence. Neither replaces code review or Quality Gates.

Repositories accepting external contributions shall make the contribution terms visible before submission. Retrospective rights uncertainty shall block integration or require legal resolution.

Internal repositories may use different contribution records, but intellectual-property ownership and third-party content obligations remain governed.

### Commit Ordering and Intermediate States

When multiple commits are preserved, their order shall form a logical progression and avoid intentionally broken protected states. Each commit should build and pass applicable fast checks where practical, especially when commits may be individually backported, bisected, or released.

Preparatory refactors should be separated from behavior change when doing so makes review safer, but the Change Request shall preserve their relationship. Generated output shall follow its controlled input change in an order that prevents ambiguity.

Migration sequences shall maintain compatibility through the accepted rollout model. A commit that removes old behavior before compatible deployment is possible shall not enter the Primary Branch without an approved staged plan.

The merge strategy may combine branch commits into an atomic integrated commit where intermediate states are not suitable for protected history.

### Amend, Rebase, and Local History Editing

Authors may amend, reorder, squash, split, or rebase commits on a private or explicitly author-controlled Change Branch before final approval, provided review and evidence bind the new commit identities.

History editing after another contributor has based work on the branch shall be coordinated. Force push to a Change Branch shall use the safest supported lease or equivalent protection and shall not overwrite unknown remote work.

Protected Primary, Release, Support, and security branches shall not be rebased or force-pushed during ordinary operation. Correction uses revert, forward fix, or controlled repository recovery that preserves evidence.

After rebase or amendment, signatures, approvals, test results, provenance, and Change Request comparisons may be invalid and shall be refreshed as required.

### Change Request Creation

A Change Request shall be opened early enough to expose intent and integration risk, but it shall not be represented as review-ready until the change is coherent and its required evidence is available.

The Change Request shall identify:

- title and stable Change Request ID;
- purpose, scope, non-goals, and user or system impact;
- target branch and source branch with exact revision;
- related requirement, work item, defect, incident, risk, and ADR;
- architecture, security, privacy, tenant, data, accessibility, operational, and release implications;
- tests and Quality Gate evidence;
- migration, compatibility, rollout, rollback or forward recovery;
- documentation and customer communication impact;
- known limitations, debt, waivers, and unresolved questions; and
- reviewer and approval requirements.

Templates may enforce completeness but shall not encourage meaningless checkbox completion. `Not applicable` decisions shall be justifiable for material categories.

### Draft and Review-Ready States

A Draft Change Request communicates work in progress and receives no merge authority. It may run unprivileged checks and receive early feedback but shall not obtain production secrets, signing authority, release approval, or final code-owner approval unless the platform preserves revision binding.

Review-Ready status means the author asserts that the scope, tests, documentation, and evidence are sufficient for formal review. The Change Request shall not contain unresolved temporary code, intentionally failing mandatory checks, hidden `TODO` for approved scope, or an unknown final migration.

Converting to Review-Ready shall trigger the required reviewers and Quality Gates. Material change after review may return the request to Draft or invalidate approvals.

A Draft that is merged through administrative override is an emergency or governance violation, not an ordinary merge.

### Change Size and Reviewability

Change Requests shall be small enough for reviewers to understand behavior, risk, and evidence without relying on author assertion. No universal line count defines reviewability; generated content, migrations, renames, language, and risk affect cognitive load.

Large changes shall explain why decomposition is unsafe or impractical and shall provide review aids such as commit structure, diagrams, generated-versus-authored separation, interface-first review, or staged compatibility plan.

Pure formatting, generated output, dependency lock changes, and semantic code should be separated when their combination obscures review. A mass rename shall not conceal behavior change.

Review urgency shall not justify an unreviewable diff. A Change Request that cannot be reviewed competently shall be split, supported with additional evidence, or escalated.

### Reviewer Selection and Code Ownership

Reviewer selection shall be based on affected ownership, competence, independence, and risk. Code-owner mapping may automate assignment but does not guarantee competence or current authority.

Required reviewers may include product, architecture, component, security, privacy, data, infrastructure, operations, accessibility, documentation, legal, compliance, release, and customer representatives. One reviewer may cover multiple roles only where qualified and permitted.

Ownership rules shall use stable teams or roles rather than a single individual's availability wherever possible. Sensitive paths such as identity, policy, capability, approval, Tool Gateway, Validation Pipeline, Audit Engine, Evidence Chain, cryptography, CI/CD, release, infrastructure, and migrations require specialized ownership.

An owner shall not approve beyond delegated scope. Repository administration shall not be mistaken for technical ownership.

### Review Independence and Two-Person Control

The Enterprise Profile requires at least one competent reviewer other than the author for changes to protected branches. Higher-risk profiles may require two or more independent approvals, specialist approval, or two-person control for every production source change.

The reviewer shall not be a nominal alternate account, automation controlled by the author, or a person unable to assess the change. Organizational reporting relationship does not automatically invalidate independence, but coercion and conflict of interest shall be managed.

Approvals shall apply to the latest exact revision. Material source change, target change, conflict resolution, altered workflow, or changed generated output invalidates affected approval.

Two-person control reduces unilateral-change risk but does not prove correctness. Quality Gates, testing, architecture, security, and release decisions remain required.

### Single-Maintainer Bootstrap Profile

ILAIOS may operate temporarily under a registered Single-Maintainer Bootstrap Profile while only one authorized maintainer is available. This profile acknowledges organizational reality without claiming independent review that did not occur.

Under this profile, every protected-source change shall still use a Change Request or equivalent durable change record, exact revision binding, self-review checklist, required automated Quality Gates, clean repository evidence, atomic scope, test and documentation evidence, and controlled merge. Direct unrecorded push remains prohibited except during approved repository bootstrap or emergency recovery.

The maintainer shall explicitly record `Independent Review: Not Available — Bootstrap Profile` and the residual risk. Critical changes affecting identity, tenant isolation, Policy Engine authority, capability, approval, Tool Gateway, Validation Pipeline, Audit Engine, Evidence Chain, cryptography, release signing, production deployment, or destructive migration should obtain an external qualified review before Stable release or receive formal risk acceptance with constrained release maturity.

The profile shall have an owner, start date, review date, exit criteria, and prohibition against marketing two-person review or equivalent assurance. It shall be retired when competent reviewer capacity becomes available.

### Review Responsibilities

Reviewers shall evaluate more than syntax and style. Review includes:

- correctness against requirements and intended behavior;
- consistency with the Product Constitution, canonical architecture, and ADRs;
- security, privacy, tenant, identity, policy, capability, approval, validation, audit, and evidence impact;
- error, denial, cancellation, concurrency, partial failure, recovery, and cleanup behavior;
- interface, schema, compatibility, versioning, migration, and deprecation;
- test adequacy, negative coverage, reliability, flakiness, and evidence;
- dependency, provenance, license, generated content, and supply-chain risk;
- performance, capacity, observability, operations, support, and cost;
- documentation, accessibility, localization, customer, and public claims; and
- scope discipline, maintainability, and rollback or forward-recovery readiness.

Review depth shall be proportional to consequence. Reviewers shall identify what they did not assess when scope exceeds their competence.

### Security and Privacy Review

Security review is required when a change affects trust boundary, authentication, authorization, tenant, secret, key, cryptography, external input, parser, network, tool execution, pipeline, dependency, evidence, logging, or vulnerability remediation.

Privacy review is required for new or changed collection, inference, storage, logging, indexing, provider transfer, retention, deletion, rights support, residency, or processing role. Role and applicability are assessed per processing purpose.

The Change Request shall not expose secrets, customer data, exploit detail, personal data, or restricted topology to unauthorized reviewers or public forks. Sensitive material may be provided through controlled evidence references.

Security or privacy approval does not replace product or architecture approval, and absence of a specialist comment is not approval.

### Architecture Review

Architecture review determines whether the change preserves component responsibility, dependency direction, trust boundaries, data ownership, operational flow, and accepted ADRs. It also determines whether a new ADR is required.

The review shall protect the deterministic Policy Engine in the Control Plane; the advisory role of the AI Reasoning and Recommendation Engine; provider abstraction without policy authority; constrained execution through Tool Gateway; independent Validation Pipeline; and continuous Audit Engine and Evidence Chain operation.

Development System and Runtime System separation and the Code Intelligence sequence—Code Entity Model, Source File Analyzer, Symbol Extraction, Dependency Extraction, and Repository Code Index—shall remain intact.

Source review cannot silently accept a de facto architectural redesign. Work shall stop or be constrained until the architecture decision is governed.

### Test Review

Reviewers shall assess whether tests demonstrate the intended behavior and material risks rather than merely increase count or coverage. Test changes shall be reviewed with the same attention as production changes.

Expected results shall derive from the Test Basis. A snapshot or golden file shall not be updated automatically because implementation changed. Removed or quarantined tests require reason, risk, owner, and replacement or exception.

Review shall verify negative, boundary, failure, authorization, tenant, evidence, migration, recovery, and regression coverage appropriate to scope. Mocks and simulators shall not overstate integration assurance.

A passing CI result does not make weak tests adequate. Reviewers may require exploratory, independent, security, performance, resilience, or acceptance evidence.

### Documentation Review

Documentation review shall verify source-of-truth, metadata, terminology, numbering, accuracy, examples, diagrams, accessibility, classification, redaction, version, release alignment, and customer claims under Section 4.4.

Changes to public or customer documentation shall identify the corresponding released capability. Roadmap or Draft content shall not be presented as current product behavior.

The reviewer shall distinguish editorial improvement from semantic architecture change. Accepted content shall not be shortened, expanded, or reworded in a way that changes architectural intent without authority.

Generated Word, PDF, HTML, or portal output shall be traceable to the controlled source and shall not contain internal authoring controls or hidden restricted content.

### Review Comments and Severity

Review comments shall identify the observed issue, consequence, applicable requirement or rationale, and requested outcome. Comments may be classified as:

- **Blocking:** merge cannot proceed until resolved or explicitly waived by competent authority;
- **Required:** correction is mandatory but may be handled through an agreed change within the current request;
- **Recommendation:** improvement is advised but is not required for this merge;
- **Question:** clarification is required to understand or assess the change; and
- **Observation:** non-blocking information or future consideration.

Style preference shall not be disguised as a security or architecture requirement. Conversely, a material risk shall not be softened to avoid conflict. The repository profile may use provider-specific labels while preserving these meanings.

### Comment Resolution

The author shall respond to material comments with a change, evidence, explanation, alternative, or request for decision. Marking a thread resolved without addressing its substance is prohibited.

The reviewer who raised a blocking concern should confirm resolution unless unavailable or no longer authorized; another competent reviewer may assume the role with an attributable explanation.

Disagreement shall be escalated to the relevant product, architecture, security, or engineering authority with options, evidence, risk, and delivery consequence. Merge shall not proceed by choosing the most convenient interpretation.

Resolved comments remain part of review evidence. They shall not be deleted to make the Change Request appear uncontested.

### Approval Semantics

Approval means that the reviewer evaluated the exact revision within declared scope and finds it eligible for merge subject to remaining Quality Gates and authorities. Approval is not authorship, release authorization, legal certification, or guarantee.

Conditional approval shall state the exact condition and shall not be recorded as unconditional success. Informal messages, reactions, meeting attendance, or absence of objection do not constitute approval.

Approvals shall identify reviewer identity, role, time, revision, and any scope limitation. Automated policy may validate the presence and freshness of approvals but does not invent human judgment.

Approval shall be dismissed automatically or manually when material change invalidates the basis. The Change Request shall not retain a stale green appearance.

### Required Quality Gates Before Merge

Before merge, the Change Request shall satisfy the applicable gates from Section 4.6, including source integrity, coding and static analysis, review, test, coverage, security, secrets, dependency, license, architecture, documentation, and specialized domain gates.

Mandatory results shall bind the latest revision and target baseline or merge-queue result as required. Failed, Blocked, Inconclusive, Expired, Cancelled, or missing mandatory checks prohibit merge.

Waivers remain visible and shall carry exact scope, risk, owner, approver, expiry, and remediation. A platform setting that allows failure does not create an authorized waiver.

The author shall not modify checks, thresholds, baselines, exclusions, or expected results in the same change to manufacture eligibility without independent rule review.

### Merge Readiness

A Change Request is merge-ready only when:

- scope and target remain correct;
- all required reviewers approved the latest revision;
- all blocking comments are resolved;
- mandatory Quality Gates passed or have valid permitted waivers;
- branch freshness and conflict rules are satisfied;
- source, tests, documentation, migrations, and generated output are complete;
- no prohibited secret, data, license, or security finding remains;
- release, deployment, and customer implications are recorded; and
- the selected merge method preserves required history, signature, and provenance.

Merge-ready is a temporary state. A target-branch change, gate expiry, new vulnerability, revoked approval, or modified source may remove eligibility.

### Merge Queue and Integration Freshness

Repositories with concurrent change shall use a merge queue or equivalent controlled serialization when independent approvals against an older target cannot prove the combined result. The queue shall evaluate the actual prospective integrated tree.

Queue order shall be transparent and may consider readiness, risk, dependency, incident priority, and fairness. Authors shall not bypass the queue through direct push or administrative merge.

If an earlier merge changes behavior or invalidates a queued change, the affected change shall be retested and, where material, re-reviewed. A synthetic merge result shall bind the same source and target content that is ultimately integrated.

Queue failure shall preserve diagnostics and shall not silently fall back to merging the original branch state.

### Permitted Merge Methods

The Repository Profile shall designate permitted merge methods based on history, signature, backport, provenance, and review needs. The supported methods are:

- **Squash Merge:** creates one integrated atomic commit from a Change Request; preferred when branch commits are iterative or not suitable for protected history;
- **Rebase and Merge:** preserves a linear sequence of individually reviewable commits with new parentage and commit identities;
- **Fast-Forward Merge:** advances the target directly when the exact reviewed commit sequence is already based on the current target; and
- **Merge Commit:** preserves branch topology where integration history, coordinated multi-commit work, or release lineage materially benefits from it.

The default for ordinary short-lived Change Requests should produce one or a small number of atomic reviewed commits. Merge method shall not invalidate required signatures or source-attestation guarantees without replacement evidence.

### Squash Merge Standard

Squash merge shall use an approved integrated commit message that describes the complete Change Request and references its ID. Iterative branch messages do not need to become protected history, but the Change Request record preserves review discussion and evidence.

The squashed tree shall be the exact tree that passed required final gates or shall be revalidated after the commit object is created when the profile requires exact commit binding.

Authorship and contribution attribution shall remain accurate. Co-authors or contributors shall be recorded according to policy and rights.

Squash shall not be used to hide independently significant changes that require separate ownership, rollback, release note, or security evidence.

### Rebase and Fast-Forward Standard

Rebase and fast-forward methods are appropriate when commits are individually atomic, ordered, reviewed, and suitable for direct protected history. The exact final commit identities shall receive required gate and signature validation.

Rebase changes commit identity and may invalidate approval, signatures, and evidence. The final rebased sequence shall be reviewed or proven semantically equivalent according to profile.

Fast-forward shall not bypass a Change Request merely because no merge commit is created. The same review and gate requirements apply.

These methods shall not be used on shared protected history in a way that removes previously integrated commits.

### Merge Commit Standard

Merge commits may be used for release lines, coordinated integration, or repositories where branch topology has durable operational value. They shall not be created routinely merely to avoid updating a branch or resolving commit quality.

The merge commit shall have an informative message and, where required, a signature. The integrated tree and conflict resolutions shall pass final Quality Gates.

Review approval of parent branches does not automatically approve conflict resolution performed in the merge commit. Material resolution requires review.

Merge bubbles that obscure simple history without adding information should be avoided according to the Repository Profile.

### Conflict Resolution

Conflicts shall be resolved by a person or controlled process that understands both changes and the target behavior. Choosing one side mechanically is prohibited where semantics may differ.

Conflict resolution shall consider requirements, architecture, tests, policies, schemas, migrations, generated output, documentation, and release behavior. New combined behavior may require additional tests or ADR review.

Resolved source shall be treated as a material new revision when behavior could change. Required reviewers and gates shall be refreshed.

Conflict markers, accidental file deletion, duplicate logic, reverted security control, and lost generated updates shall be specifically checked before merge.

### Direct Push Policy

Direct push to Protected Branches is prohibited in the Enterprise Profile. Provider administrators, repository owners, and service identities are subject to the same rule.

Permitted exceptional paths are limited to initial repository bootstrap, controlled recovery from repository corruption or provider failure, and an approved emergency change when no Change Request mechanism is available. Each shall have exact authority, reason, source, tests, evidence, and retrospective reconciliation.

The Single-Maintainer Bootstrap Profile still uses a Change Request or equivalent durable change record. Being the only maintainer does not make unrecorded direct push an ordinary process.

Detected direct push shall trigger investigation, branch protection review, impact assessment, and possible revert or revalidation. Later test success does not erase the governance violation.

### Force Push and History Rewrite

Force push, branch deletion, reference replacement, and protected-history rewrite are prohibited on Primary, Release, Support, and other protected branches during ordinary operation.

If sensitive data, secret, unlawful content, or severe repository corruption requires history remediation, the operation shall follow incident, legal, security, repository, and release governance. Exact affected commits, forks, clones, caches, artifacts, and customers shall be assessed.

History rewrite does not revoke an exposed secret, remove copied data, or change already released artifacts. Containment and notification remain necessary.

After authorized rewrite, all dependent branches, tags, builds, signatures, provenance, documentation, and evidence shall be reconciled. Old commit identities shall be denylisted or otherwise tracked where appropriate.

### Revert Strategy

Revert is the default mechanism for reversing an integrated source change while preserving history. A revert commit shall identify the original commit or Change Request, reason, affected behavior, risk, and follow-up.

Reverting source does not automatically revert schema, data, external side effects, artifacts, releases, or deployments. The change owner shall determine whether rollback, forward recovery, compensation, or a new release is required.

Reverts shall pass applicable review and Quality Gates. An urgent revert may use the Emergency Profile, but source and operational evidence shall remain attributable.

Revert of a security fix or migration requires particular caution because the prior state may no longer be safe or compatible.

### Cherry-Pick and Backport Strategy

Cherry-pick and backport create new commit identities and shall be treated as new changes to a different baseline. Original review and tests are supporting evidence but do not automatically prove compatibility.

The backport Change Request shall identify source commit, original issue, target support line, divergence, conflict resolution, targeted tests, release version, and customer impact.

Backports should contain the minimum compatible correction and shall not import unrelated features. If the original fix depends on later architecture, a separate supported-line design may be required.

Every affected maintained line shall be tracked so that partial remediation is visible. A security advisory shall identify fixed and unaffected versions accurately.

### Dependency Update Changes

Dependency updates shall identify package or service, old and new versions, source and provenance, release information, vulnerability or feature reason, license, transitive change, compatibility, and rollback.

Automated dependency Change Requests shall not be merged solely because generated tests passed. Maintainers shall review behavior, security, lifecycle, and usage. Major or materially breaking updates may require an ADR.

Multiple unrelated updates shall be separated where doing so improves diagnosis and rollback. Security updates may be grouped only when coordinated remediation requires it.

Lockfiles and resolved dependency changes are part of the review. A small manifest edit with a large unresolved tree change is not a small change.

### Generated, Vendored, and Binary Changes

Generated changes shall include or reference the controlled input, generator, version, configuration, and regeneration procedure. Review shall distinguish authored input from generated output and verify consistency.

Vendored content shall identify origin, exact version, integrity, license, local modifications, update process, and security review. Copying source into the repository does not make it first-party code.

Binary changes require source or generation provenance, digest, license, review method, expected behavior, and repository-profile permission. Opaque executable replacement without independently verifiable origin shall not merge.

Large mechanical diffs shall use specialized review evidence rather than asking reviewers to approve unreadable output blindly.

### Policy, Schema, and Migration Changes

Policy changes shall be reviewed as executable authority. They require deterministic tests for permit, deny, conflict, default, capability, risk, approval, failure, and version behavior.

Schema changes shall address compatibility, defaults, nullability, semantics, data classification, consumers, migration, and support. Syntactic compatibility alone is insufficient.

Migration changes shall include dry-run or equivalent evidence, source and target authority, reconciliation, interruption, resume, rollback or forward recovery, tenant, performance, and retention.

These changes may require specialist approval even when they contain no application code. File extension or directory location shall not reduce scrutiny.

### CI/CD and Repository-Control Changes

Changes to workflows, gate definitions, branch protection, code ownership, runner images, permissions, secrets, signing, registries, or release automation can alter the trust of every later change and require elevated review.

Untrusted proposed workflow content shall not execute with privileged credentials. The authoritative evaluator shall use reviewed configuration from a trusted baseline.

A Change Request shall not both weaken its mandatory gate and rely on the weakened gate for approval without independent governance. Protection changes shall be tested against bypass and failure scenarios.

Repository settings not represented as source shall have a corresponding controlled change record and drift evidence.

### Automated and Model-Assisted Contributions

Automation and model-assisted development may propose source, tests, documentation, or review observations. The accountable human or registered automation owner remains responsible for correctness, rights, security, privacy, and scope.

Generated content shall not receive automatic approval because it was produced by an approved service. Its source, inputs, data handling, license risk, and limitations shall be evaluated.

An automated system shall not be both author and sole reviewer of a protected change. Reasoning output shall not decide merge, risk acceptance, architecture, security, or release authority.

Transient authoring metadata or unapproved tool output shall not appear in publishable source history unless it is a required controlled product artifact.

### Merge Commit and Change Request Traceability

Every integrated commit shall be traceable to its Change Request, requirements, approvals, Quality Gate results, tests, ADRs, defects, incidents, and release impact as applicable.

Traceability may use structured commit footers, provider metadata, evidence records, or a controlled change registry. Links shall be durable enough for audit and future maintenance.

If the provider deletes or changes Change Request presentation, the authoritative evidence shall remain available through retention and export controls. Provider UI is not the sole record.

A source hash or Change Request number alone does not prove semantic approval. The associated identities, revisions, evidence, and outcomes are required.

### Post-Merge Verification

After merge, authoritative CI shall evaluate the exact integrated Primary Branch state. Pre-merge results may be reused only when the merge mechanism proves tree equivalence and the applicable Quality Profile permits it.

Post-merge failure shall trigger containment, notification, and correction. The repository shall not remain silently red while subsequent changes accumulate.

Possible outcomes include revert, forward fix, branch restriction, release hold, incident declaration, or gate correction. The decision shall reflect risk and whether any artifact or environment consumed the failing commit.

Successful post-merge verification does not create release authority. It establishes integrated-source evidence for later build and release processes.

### Release and Tag Relationship

Protected source branches and commits support release creation, but tags, versions, artifacts, and release records remain governed by Sections 4.9 and 4.10.

A release tag shall identify an exact approved commit and shall not be moved or recreated after publication. Signing requirements follow the release profile.

Branch name shall not be embedded as the sole version or maturity indicator. A Primary Branch commit may be unreleased, and a Support Branch commit may correspond to a maintained patch line.

Release preparation shall not modify source outside the governed Change Request process. Generated version files and release notes are source changes when stored in the repository.

### Repository Recovery and Continuity

The change-control system shall be recoverable from provider outage, repository corruption, accidental deletion, credential compromise, and protection misconfiguration. Recovery shall preserve objects, references, Change Requests, approvals, settings, identities, and evidence needed to re-establish trust.

A mirror or backup may support recovery but shall not become canonical until formal promotion validates completeness, integrity, protection, remote dependencies, and current authority.

Continuity procedures shall identify who may freeze changes, restore references, rotate credentials, reapply protections, and reopen integration. Recovered source shall be reconciled with artifact and release registries.

Emergency recovery updates to protected history shall receive retrospective independent review and evidence as soon as the trusted system is restored.

### Source-Control Incident Response

Unauthorized push, force push, deleted branch, compromised account, malicious Change Request, forged approval, secret commit, workflow attack, tag movement, or evidence tampering shall trigger source-control incident response.

Containment may include freezing merges, revoking credentials, invalidating sessions, restricting repositories, disabling automation, preserving provider audit logs, and blocking affected artifacts or deployments.

Investigation shall establish affected repositories, branches, commits, forks, clones, tags, workflows, artifacts, releases, customers, and time window. Restoring the visible branch pointer alone is insufficient.

Recovery shall establish a trusted baseline, revalidate affected changes, rotate secrets, repair protections, communicate impact, and preserve lessons in tests, controls, and documentation.

### Review and Merge Metrics

Metrics shall improve change quality and flow rather than reward approval speed or commit volume. Relevant indicators include:

- protected-branch changes without a valid Change Request;
- direct and force pushes, protection overrides, and administrative bypass;
- Change Request lead time separated into authoring, review, gate, and queue time;
- review age, unresolved blocking comments, and stale approvals;
- Change Request size, rework, conflict, and post-merge failure trends;
- critical paths lacking competent ownership or independent review;
- Single-Maintainer Bootstrap Profile use and progress toward exit criteria;
- merge queue failure and integrated-tree regression;
- reverted, backported, and cherry-picked changes with escaped defects;
- unsigned or unverifiable commits where signatures are required;
- history rewrites, secret commits, and source-control incidents;
- automated-change acceptance and failure rates;
- review findings by risk category and repeated root cause; and
- releases or incidents traceable to inadequate review or merge control.

Commit count, approval count, merge volume, short review time, or low comment count are not maturity measures alone. Metrics shall not incentivize superficial review, artificial change splitting, hidden bypass, or reduced documentation.

### Branch and Review Debt

Debt includes stale branches, long-lived divergence, orphaned ownership, unreviewable changes, missing tests, unsigned required commits, duplicated forks, unresolved review comments, broad bypass rights, obsolete release branches, and unreconciled customer patches.

Debt shall be registered with repository, affected risk, owner, treatment, target date, and release consequence. Critical security, tenant, policy, evidence, CI/CD, and release-control debt requires priority treatment.

A branch left open for historical convenience is not an archive. A Change Request kept indefinitely in Draft is not a decision record. Inactive material shall be closed, archived, restricted, or removed according to policy.

Remediation shall preserve needed history and customer support while reducing parallel authority and bypass.

### Emergency Changes

Emergency source change applies only to active or imminent material incident, vulnerability, outage, corruption, or binding obligation. It does not apply to ordinary deadlines or commercial urgency.

The emergency path shall preserve verified repository, exact baseline, minimal coherent diff, competent authority, targeted tests, secrets checks, artifact identity, deployment recovery, and evidence. Independent review shall occur before merge where available and immediately after when not.

Any bypass of ordinary Change Request, approval, or Quality Gate rules shall be explicit, scoped, time-bound, and reconciled. The Primary Branch and release history shall remain accurate.

Repeated emergency changes indicate architecture, capacity, testing, or process failure and require corrective action.

### Exceptions and Waivers

An exception shall identify the exact requirement, repository, branch, commits, Change Request, product, risk, reason, alternatives, compensating controls, owner, approver, start date, expiry, and remediation.

An exception cannot authorize secret or unlawful data in source; fabricated author or reviewer identity; false claim of independent review; permanent unprotected Primary Branch; reasoning-based merge authority; hidden architecture change; removal of required Runtime Policy Engine, approval, Tool Gateway, validation, audit, or evidence; or rewriting history to conceal misconduct.

Provider limitation, single-maintainer status, customer demand, legacy repository, or deadline may shape controls but does not create automatic permission. The Bootstrap Profile is a declared risk treatment, not a representation of Enterprise two-person review.

Expired exceptions require remediation, renewed assessment, scope restriction, release limitation, repository quarantine, or retirement. Continuation through inaction is non-conformant.

### Branching, Commit, Review, and Merge Invariants

The following invariants are canonical:

- every governed repository has one registered protected Primary Branch, whose name alone does not establish authority;
- existing Primary Branch names are not changed merely for convention; rename is a governed migration;
- ordinary changes enter protected branches only through an exact revision-bound Change Request and applicable Quality Gates;
- direct push, force push, and protected-history rewrite are prohibited except through explicitly controlled bootstrap, emergency, incident, or recovery paths;
- change branches are short-lived, purpose-bounded, based on a verified target, and never become alternate canonical sources through age;
- Release and Support Branches exist only for explicit release and support needs and have owners, permitted changes, and retirement;
- commits are coherent, attributable, accurately messaged, free of prohibited secrets and customer data, and suitable for review;
- signing, sign-off, review, merge, build, release, and deployment are distinct assurances and authorities;
- approval applies only to the exact latest reviewed revision and is invalidated by material post-review change;
- Enterprise protected-source changes receive competent non-author review, with stronger two-person control where the Quality Profile requires it;
- the Single-Maintainer Bootstrap Profile records the absence of independence, preserves all other controls, limits assurance claims, and has exit criteria;
- automated and model-assisted content remains human- or registered-owner accountable and cannot approve its own merge or risk;
- Quality Gate failure, block, inconclusive result, expiry, cancellation, or missing evidence prevents merge;
- merge queues or equivalent mechanisms validate the actual prospective integrated tree where concurrent change creates risk;
- merge method is selected by Repository Profile and preserves required atomicity, review, signatures, provenance, and history;
- conflict resolution is a new semantic change when behavior may differ and receives renewed review and testing;
- revert preserves source history but does not claim automatic reversal of data, external effects, artifacts, releases, or deployments;
- cherry-picks and backports are new target-baseline changes with their own compatibility, tests, and release evidence;
- protected history is never rewritten for cosmetic convenience or to conceal error, dissent, incident, or unauthorized change;
- the deterministic Policy Engine, advisory reasoning role, Model Orchestration without policy authority, Tool Gateway, independent Validation Pipeline, continuous Audit Engine and Evidence Chain, Development/Runtime separation, and Code Intelligence order cannot be silently changed through source review;
- integration into the Primary Branch does not create an artifact, version, release, deployment, acceptance, or customer commitment;
- source-control, review, and merge events remain attributable and retained according to approved record-class-specific schedules; and
- architecture decisions remain canonical until an authorized ADR explicitly supersedes them and affected source and documentation are reconciled.

An engineering or repository process is non-conformant if it treats branch name, administrator role, provider badge, commit hash, signature, approval count, green CI status, or merge as authority beyond its scope; renames the existing Primary Branch without migration governance; permits ordinary direct push or force push to protected history; creates an official release from an unregistered fork or long-lived private branch; allows a Change Request author, bot, or model to be its sole claimed independent reviewer; retains approval after material source or conflict-resolution change; merges with mandatory checks Failed, Blocked, Inconclusive, Expired, Cancelled, or missing; resolves a blocking comment without addressing its substance; uses a blanket documentation or file-extension exception to bypass review of executable content; commits secrets, customer data, unlicensed assets, generated caches, or hidden workflow changes; rewrites history to remove a failure, dissent, security incident, or unauthorized commit; backports without target-line testing; updates snapshots or tests merely to make changed behavior pass; uses a hotfix or emergency label for ordinary schedule pressure; represents the Single-Maintainer Bootstrap Profile as two-person review; changes Policy Engine placement, reasoning authority, Tool Gateway, validation, audit, evidence, Development/Runtime separation, or Code Intelligence order without an ADR; or treats integration into source as release or production authorization.

## 4.9 Versioning

### Purpose and Versioning Intent

Versioning provides the controlled language through which ILAIOS identifies change, communicates compatibility, binds released content to immutable evidence, and governs coexistence between product generations. A version is an engineering and customer contract. It shall convey defined semantics, be assigned by an accountable authority, and remain traceable to the exact source, artifacts, interfaces, schemas, policies, documentation, and support state to which it applies.

The purpose of versioning is not to generate labels for every build or to imply maturity through a larger number. Its purpose is to make change comprehensible and governable across hosted, customer-controlled, hybrid, isolated, regional, and long-lived enterprise deployments. Correct versioning allows customers and engineering teams to determine what changed, whether an upgrade is compatible, which controls and evidence apply, what is supported, and how a deployed state can be reproduced or investigated.

ILAIOS adopts Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 as the canonical semantic model for released product contracts unless a formally approved Architecture Decision Record establishes a different model for a precisely defined version domain. This standard supplements that model with enterprise requirements for prerelease maturity, artifact identity, interface compatibility, data evolution, policy and evidence formats, support lines, distributed deployments, and auditability.

### Scope

This standard applies to every governed ILAIOS asset whose identity, compatibility, persistence, distribution, independent consumption, verification, or support depends on an explicit version. It covers the integrated product, platform services, deployable components, packages, libraries, command-line and client applications, APIs, protocols, events, schemas, database migrations, policies, capabilities, evidence formats, audit records, plugins, tools, integrations, infrastructure bundles, documentation, models and model-routing configurations, evaluation sets, knowledge structures, and Code Intelligence indexes.

It applies to internal, public, customer-specific, partner, hosted, on-premises, hybrid, isolated, offline, regulated, development, test, staging, recovery, and production contexts. An asset is not exempt merely because it is internal when another controlled asset persists, consumes, verifies, deploys, or depends upon it.

This section defines version semantics and relationships. Section 4.2 governs repository and naming controls; Section 4.3 governs architecture-significant changes; Section 4.7 governs construction, provenance, and promotion automation; Section 4.8 governs source integration and tags; and Section 4.10 governs release maturity, channels, approval, publication, support, and retirement. A version assignment does not replace any of those controls.

### Versioning Principles

ILAIOS versioning follows these principles:

1. **Contract before label.** A version expresses a defined compatibility and support contract; it is not an arbitrary marketing identifier.
2. **One meaning per namespace.** Every version belongs to a registered domain with a known owner, syntax, increment rules, and compatibility boundary.
3. **Immutable publication.** Published version content is never silently replaced. Changed content receives a new identity and, where contract semantics changed, a new semantic version.
4. **Exact traceability.** A released version resolves to exact source revisions, build identities, artifact digests, dependency sets, schemas, policies, documentation, approvals, and evidence.
5. **Compatibility is explicit.** Compatibility is determined by documented contracts and tested matrices, not by version-number resemblance or optimistic inference.
6. **Maturity is distinct from precedence.** Alpha, Beta, Release Candidate, Stable, and Long-Term Support states do not become interchangeable merely because they share a numeric core.
7. **Build identity is distinct from semantic identity.** Rebuilds, packaging variations, and deployment instances are identifiable without misrepresenting contract change.
8. **No hidden breaking change.** Security urgency, provider behavior, customer pressure, or implementation convenience does not permit an incompatible change to be mislabeled as a patch.
9. **Persisted and externally consumed formats evolve deliberately.** APIs, events, schemas, policies, and evidence formats receive stricter treatment than transient implementation details.
10. **Automation verifies; authority remains governed.** Tools may calculate, validate, and propose versions, but accountable release authority approves the public contract.
11. **Evidence accompanies every material version transition.** Allocation, build, approval, publication, withdrawal, support, and retirement remain auditable.
12. **Architecture remains canonical.** A version increment cannot silently supersede an accepted architectural decision; an authorized ADR is still required.

### Canonical Semantic Version Model

The canonical public semantic version has the form:

`MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`

`MAJOR`, `MINOR`, and `PATCH` are non-negative decimal integers without leading zeroes. A stable example is `2.4.7`. Numeric magnitude has no independent meaning outside the registered version domain and its history.

The version shall be incremented as follows:

- `MAJOR` for an incompatible change to a supported public or persisted contract;
- `MINOR` for backward-compatible capability, behavior, or contract expansion; and
- `PATCH` for a backward-compatible correction, security remediation, or operational improvement.

When one component is incremented, lower-order components reset to zero. For example, the successor to `2.4.7` is `2.4.8` for a patch, `2.5.0` for a minor release, or `3.0.0` for a major release. Version gaps are permitted; reuse is not.

The optional lowercase prefix `v` may be used in source-control tags and human-readable references, such as `v2.4.7`, when required by the applicable naming standard. It is not part of the semantic version value and shall not be persisted where a strictly conforming semantic version is expected.

### Initial Development and Version Zero

Versions in the `0.y.z` range represent initial development or a contract explicitly declared not yet stable. Version zero does not eliminate governance, security, traceability, or customer obligations. It indicates that the public compatibility contract may evolve more rapidly and that the precise stability promise shall be stated with the release.

During version zero, a backward-incompatible change shall still be identified, documented, tested, migrated, and communicated. It shall normally increment `MINOR`; backward-compatible corrections increment `PATCH`. A team shall not use `0.y.z` indefinitely to avoid declaring support expectations or to introduce silent incompatibilities.

The transition to `1.0.0` declares the first stable public contract for that version domain. It requires documented scope, compatibility boundaries, supported interfaces, migration posture, release evidence, and approval under Section 4.10. The `Version: 1.0` metadata of this Architecture and Engineering Handbook is a document version and does not by itself declare ILAIOS product release `1.0.0`.

### Prerelease Identifiers

A prerelease version appends a hyphen and ordered identifier to the numeric core. ILAIOS uses the controlled forms:

- `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH-alpha.N` for early integration and incomplete capability validation;
- `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH-beta.N` for feature-complete or substantially complete validation with known limitations; and
- `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH-rc.N` for a release candidate intended to become Stable if no disqualifying issue is found.

`N` is a positive integer that increases within the same prerelease series. Examples are `2.5.0-alpha.1`, `2.5.0-beta.3`, and `2.5.0-rc.2`. Ad hoc synonyms such as `preview`, `candidate`, `final`, `production`, or `gold` shall not replace the registered maturity terms in an authoritative version.

Prerelease versions have lower precedence than the associated stable version. A prerelease shall not be represented as Stable, even if deployed in a production-like environment or used by a customer under an explicit evaluation agreement. Its allowed use, support, data handling, and upgrade expectations are governed by Section 4.10.

Each prerelease increment identifies a distinct released contract and immutable artifact set. Correcting or rebuilding a published candidate does not permit replacement of `rc.1`; the next candidate becomes `rc.2` or receives another valid new version as determined by the change.

### Build Metadata

Build metadata may be appended after a plus sign, for example `2.5.0-rc.2+build.184` or `2.4.7+region.eu`. Metadata identifiers shall contain only characters permitted by the canonical syntax and shall not disclose secrets, personal data, customer identifiers, internal vulnerabilities, or uncontrolled environment information.

Build metadata does not affect semantic precedence, compatibility, maturity, or support. `2.4.7+build.184` and `2.4.7+build.185` have equal semantic precedence even though they identify different build contexts. Consumers shall not use metadata ordering to decide which contract is newer.

Build metadata shall not be the sole means of artifact integrity or uniqueness. Some package and distribution systems ignore, normalize, or reject it. Exact artifacts shall therefore also be identified through an immutable artifact digest, build record, provenance statement, and Release Manifest. Where a distribution ecosystem cannot preserve build metadata, the semantic version remains unchanged and the controlled manifest carries the additional identity.

### Version Precedence and Comparison

Automated comparison shall follow the canonical semantic precedence rules. Numeric core components compare numerically. A stable version has higher precedence than a prerelease with the same numeric core. Prerelease identifiers compare according to their numeric or lexical type as defined by the canonical specification; build metadata is ignored.

Version comparison shall use a validated parser rather than lexical string sorting. Lexical sorting can incorrectly place `2.10.0` before `2.9.0`, accept leading zeroes, or treat metadata as precedence. Invalid or ambiguous values shall be rejected rather than normalized silently at a trust boundary.

Ranges shall be used only where their compatibility meaning is explicit. A dependency declaration such as “latest,” an unbounded wildcard, an unqualified branch, or a mutable channel does not establish a reproducible version. Production and release inputs shall resolve to an exact approved version and artifact identity in the Release Manifest.

### Version Syntax and Normalization

Authoritative systems shall store the canonical version without whitespace, locale-specific digits, hidden prefixes, date decorations, or duplicated maturity labels. Leading zeroes are prohibited in numeric identifiers. Case-sensitive prerelease identifiers shall use the registered lowercase form.

Human interfaces may display a product name, version prefix, channel, edition, support designation, or publication date around the canonical value, but those fields shall remain separately parseable. `ILAIOS 2.4.7 Stable LTS` therefore contains a semantic version, release maturity, and support designation; it is not a single compound version value.

Calendar dates, sprint identifiers, ticket numbers, branch names, build counters, customer names, and commercial editions shall not replace the semantic version. They may be recorded as independent metadata. Adoption of calendar versioning or another scheme for a defined domain requires an ADR that establishes migration, comparison, compatibility, and customer communication rules.

### Version, Maturity, Channel, and Support State

A semantic version answers which contract is represented. Release maturity answers how far the release has progressed through Alpha, Beta, Release Candidate, or Stable acceptance. A release channel identifies how recipients discover or receive a release. A support state identifies whether and under what terms the release receives maintenance.

These concepts shall not be conflated. `2.4.7` may be Stable, distributed through an enterprise channel, and designated Long-Term Support; `2.5.0-beta.2` may be available through an evaluation channel without Stable support. Long-Term Support is a release and maintenance designation recorded in release metadata, not a fourth semantic-version component and not a prerelease suffix.

Promotion from Release Candidate to Stable changes the semantic version from, for example, `2.5.0-rc.2` to `2.5.0`. Stable publication shall use artifacts built from the approved source and verified under the Stable release process. Whether byte-identical candidate artifacts may be promoted without rebuilding is governed by the approved pipeline and release policy; the Release Manifest shall make the relationship explicit.

### Version, Source, Artifact, and Deployment Identity

A version is not a branch, commit, tag, build, artifact, digest, image, package, environment, deployment, or runtime instance. Those identities are related but distinct:

- the source revision identifies the exact canonical source state;
- the tag associates an immutable repository reference with an approved version;
- the build identity identifies one controlled construction event;
- the artifact digest identifies exact bytes;
- the semantic version identifies the compatibility contract;
- the Release Manifest binds all released components and evidence;
- the deployment identity identifies a promotion or installation event; and
- the runtime identity identifies an executing instance and its effective configuration.

Two artifacts may share a semantic version only when they implement the same contract and their platform, packaging, or edition distinction is explicitly represented in the registered artifact namespace and Release Manifest. They shall never be treated as interchangeable solely because the numeric version matches.

A deployment shall report both semantic and exact operational identity sufficient for support and incident response: product version, component versions where relevant, artifact digests, configuration or profile version, schema and migration state, policy bundle version, deployment identifier, and effective support designation. Secrets and protected topology data shall not be exposed through public version endpoints.

### Version Authority and Accountability

Each version domain shall have a Version Owner and an accountable Release Authority. The Version Owner maintains the domain definition, compatibility contract, change classification, version registry, and tooling. The Release Authority approves publication and maturity under Section 4.10. Neither role may override architecture, security, privacy, legal, Quality Gate, or evidence requirements.

Engineering teams may propose an increment based on the actual change set. Automated tooling may detect contract changes and recommend a version. Final classification shall be reviewed by competent owners for the affected interfaces and persisted formats. A model-generated recommendation is advisory and grants no authority.

Where a change affects multiple domains, the integrated release owner coordinates the version matrix but does not force every component to use the same number. Disagreement over a breaking-change classification shall be resolved before publication and escalated through architecture, product, security, or customer-governance channels according to impact.

### Version Domain Registry

ILAIOS shall maintain a controlled Version Domain Registry for independently versioned assets. Each entry shall define:

- stable Domain ID, name, owner, repository, and authoritative registry;
- asset type and consumer population;
- public, partner, customer, or internal visibility;
- version syntax and current version line;
- compatibility boundary and breaking-change criteria;
- prerelease and support rules;
- tag, package, artifact, and documentation naming;
- dependency and negotiation behavior;
- migration, deprecation, and retirement requirements;
- retention and evidence classification; and
- any approved exception or superseding ADR.

Independent versioning is justified when an asset is independently released, consumed, persisted, negotiated, verified, or supported. Private functions and transient implementation details should not receive public versions merely for completeness. Avoiding unnecessary version domains reduces coordination burden and false compatibility promises.

An unregistered suffix, package fork, customer build, private tag, or undocumented schema identifier shall not become an authoritative version through repeated use.

### Integrated Product Version

The integrated ILAIOS product version represents the customer-visible contract of the Enterprise AI Operating System as a coherent release. It covers the supported combination of control-plane behavior, runtime behavior, interfaces, deployment packaging, documentation, operational controls, and declared compatibility.

The product version shall not conceal independently versioned components. Its Release Manifest shall map the product version to exact service, package, schema, policy, evidence, infrastructure, and documentation versions and artifact digests. A customer shall be able to identify whether an observed component state belongs to a supported integrated combination.

An integrated product `MAJOR` increment is required when the supported customer contract becomes incompatible, even if the implementation change occurs in only one component. A component may require its own major increment without forcing a product major increment when the integrated product absorbs the change behind a stable boundary and remains backward-compatible to customers.

### Service and Deployable Component Versions

Independently deployable services and components may use independent semantic versions when they have separately managed lifecycle, interface, rollback, or support needs. Each shall be registered and represented in the Release Manifest.

An internal service version shall reflect its actual contract to other governed components, including APIs, messages, state, operational behavior, and required configuration. A deployment counter or container tag shall not substitute for the service version. Mutable image tags such as `latest` may be convenience aliases but shall not be authoritative deployment inputs.

Service version skew shall be governed through a tested compatibility matrix. Rolling upgrades, canary deployments, and regional transitions can temporarily place multiple versions in one environment; the allowed combinations, duration, routing behavior, state implications, and recovery path shall be explicit.

### Package, Library, SDK, and Client Versions

Libraries, packages, Software Development Kits, command-line tools, desktop applications, mobile clients, and other independently distributed clients shall be versioned according to the contracts visible to their consumers. Public functions, command syntax, exit codes, configuration formats, serialization behavior, authentication assumptions, and supported platform ranges form part of that contract where documented or reasonably relied upon.

Dependency constraints shall state supported ranges deliberately. Libraries shall not broaden a range beyond tested compatibility or pin an unnecessary exact version that prevents secure maintenance without reason. Lockfiles and release manifests shall still resolve exact build inputs even when consumer compatibility uses a range.

Client auto-update, package-manager resolution, and enterprise software-distribution behavior shall respect channel and customer control. An available higher version does not authorize installation. Unsupported client versions shall fail safely or provide a controlled degraded experience rather than silently bypassing security or policy behavior.

### API Versioning

An API version identifies a defined request, response, error, authentication, authorization, pagination, idempotency, rate, and behavioral contract. The versioning mechanism may use a path, media type, header, protocol field, schema reference, or another implementation-appropriate method. The logical contract and negotiation rules are canonical; a particular transport mechanism is not mandated by this handbook.

Adding optional response fields, operations, or request parameters can be backward-compatible only when consumers are required and tested to tolerate them. Changing field meaning, type, requiredness, default behavior, error semantics, authorization effect, ordering guarantee, pagination model, identifier interpretation, or side effect may be breaking even if the wire shape appears similar.

Unsupported API majors shall fail explicitly with a documented error and supported-version information where safe. The server shall not silently reinterpret an unsupported request as another version. Authentication and authorization occur independently of version selection; an older API version cannot bypass current security or policy requirements.

API descriptions shall declare the API contract version separately from the version of the description language or tool used to express it. Documentation, examples, conformance tests, client generation, and deprecation status shall resolve to the same API version.

### Event and Message Versioning

Events and messages are persisted or delayed contracts and require explicit versioning when producers and consumers can evolve independently. An event version shall describe envelope, payload, semantics, ordering, delivery, idempotency, tenancy, privacy classification, and retention-relevant behavior.

Consumers shall not infer compatibility from topic name or field presence alone. Additive fields are safe only where consumers ignore unknown content as required. Removing fields, changing identifiers, modifying meaning, altering units, changing nullability, or changing delivery guarantees is breaking unless mediated by a compatible transformation.

During migration, producers may dual-publish or consumers may support multiple versions only under a bounded plan that prevents duplicate side effects and preserves evidence. The plan shall define authoritative event identity, replay behavior, cutover, reconciliation, and retirement.

The event version and producer software version shall both be observable. A new producer build does not automatically imply a new event contract, and an unchanged producer product version cannot excuse an undocumented contract change.

### Schema and Data Model Versioning

Persisted schemas and data models shall have stable identity and explicit evolution rules. This includes relational structures, document formats, configuration schemas, policy inputs, evidence records, exports, imports, cache persistence where durability matters, and customer-managed data contracts.

Schema compatibility shall be assessed for readers, writers, validators, migrations, backups, restores, replicas, analytics, retention, privacy operations, and older supported software. Additive structure is not automatically non-breaking when storage limits, validation, canonicalization, signatures, encryption, indexing, or downstream assumptions change.

Schema version shall be stored or derivable at the record, collection, dataset, or manifest level appropriate to reliable interpretation. A parser shall reject or quarantine unknown incompatible versions rather than guessing. Conversion shall preserve provenance and record the source version, target version, transformation identity, outcome, and exceptions.

Canonical schemas shall be immutable once released. Correcting a released schema requires a new version even when the previous file contained an error.

### Database and Migration Versions

Database schema version, migration sequence, and product version are related but distinct. A migration identifier establishes ordering and identity of a controlled state transition; it is not necessarily a semantic version. The Release Manifest shall identify required starting states, ordered migrations, expected target state, checksums, reversibility, and compatible software range.

A migration that has executed in a shared or customer environment shall not be edited in place. Correction requires a new migration. Migration tooling shall detect checksum mismatch, partial execution, unexpected state, and out-of-order application and shall fail safely.

Backward-compatible expansion and contraction patterns should be used where rolling operation requires old and new software to coexist. Destructive changes require verified backups or recovery points, legal and privacy assessment, migration rehearsal, reconciliation, and an explicit forward-recovery or rollback decision.

Downgrading application software does not imply that the database can be downgraded. Supported downgrade paths shall be declared and tested; otherwise forward recovery is the canonical response.

### Policy, Rule, and Capability Versions

Every policy, rule bundle, capability definition, approval template, risk classification table, and deterministic decision configuration that can affect authorization or execution shall have immutable version identity. Policy version is a material input to the Policy Engine and shall be included in the Immutable Context, audit events, Evidence Chain, and decision record.

A policy update is not merely configuration when it changes permitted actions, required approval, tenant boundary, tool access, data handling, risk classification, or validation. It shall follow controlled change, test, review, approval, and deployment. Its semantic increment is determined within the policy domain according to compatibility for policy consumers and decision reproduction.

An older product version may operate with more than one approved policy version only where the compatibility matrix and customer governance permit it. The effective combination shall be visible. The AI Reasoning and Recommendation Engine may explain or propose policy content but cannot select, approve, or override the authoritative version.

Policy aliases such as `current` or `default` may assist administration but shall resolve to an immutable version before evaluation. Historical decisions shall remain reproducible against the exact policy version used at the time.

### Evidence, Audit, and Verification Format Versions

Evidence packages, audit event schemas, signature envelopes, hash-link structures, provenance statements, validation reports, and verifier protocols shall be versioned as durable trust contracts. The version shall allow an independent verifier to select the correct canonicalization, algorithms, field semantics, trust anchors, and validation rules.

An evidence-format change is breaking when an accepted verifier can no longer parse, authenticate, interpret, or validate the record, or when assurance meaning changes. Adding fields may also be breaking if canonicalization, hashing, signatures, retention, redaction, or disclosure behavior changes.

The Evidence Chain shall record format version, producer version, validation profile, cryptographic algorithm identifiers, trust material references, and migration or transformation history. A hash value alone does not establish completeness, authenticity, lawful collection, or correct semantic interpretation.

Historical evidence shall not be rewritten to the latest format in place. If normalization or migration is necessary, preserve the original record and create a linked derived record with transformation evidence. Verifier support and retirement plans shall reflect legal, contractual, incident, defense, and record-class-specific retention obligations without making retention indefinite by default.

### Protocol and Integration Versions

Protocols and external integrations shall version the contract between ILAIOS and the external system, including authentication, authorization, transport, message structure, retry, error, rate, transaction, idempotency, webhook, and lifecycle behavior.

Third-party marketing labels or endpoint names shall not be treated as stable versions unless the provider contract defines them as such. The integration registry shall record the provider version, effective dates, compatibility assumptions, observed behavior, test profile, and fallback or exit strategy.

When a provider changes behavior without changing its advertised version, ILAIOS shall treat the event as a dependency or compatibility incident. Evidence shall record the observed provider identity and relevant response metadata. Compatibility shall be revalidated before broader use.

An integration adapter may isolate provider changes from the integrated product contract. That isolation does not eliminate the need to version the adapter, update its tests, or classify customer-visible effects accurately.

### Plugin, Tool, and Extension Versions

Plugins, Tool Gateway adapters, extensions, connectors, and executable integrations shall have independent version identity where they are installed, enabled, or supported separately. Their contract includes declared capabilities, input and output schemas, execution boundaries, side effects, permission needs, policy hooks, validation behavior, and evidence output.

A tool version shall not expand its own capability or authority. The deterministic Policy Engine evaluates the requested operation against the registered capability definition, policy version, risk, and approval. Tool version and artifact digest are evidence inputs, not authorization sources.

Compatibility shall be checked among product, Tool Gateway, adapter, external API, policy bundle, and schema versions. Installation shall fail closed when a required major is unsupported or when integrity cannot be verified.

Customer-developed extensions shall use a registered namespace and compatibility profile. They shall not appropriate the ILAIOS product namespace or imply first-party support without an explicit commercial and engineering decision.

### Model, Provider, and Reasoning Configuration Versions

Model and provider identities shall be recorded separately from ILAIOS product versions. Where a provider exposes a precise immutable revision, ILAIOS shall record it. Where the provider exposes only a mutable label, ILAIOS shall record the label, provider, observation time, routing decision, configuration, and other available identifiers and shall not represent the label as immutable.

Reasoning configuration, instruction sets, routing rules, safety settings, tool descriptions, evaluation datasets, and output schemas shall be versioned when they can materially change recommendations or plans. The exact effective combination shall be available for evaluation, incident analysis, and evidence subject to privacy and intellectual-property controls.

A model or configuration version never grants permission, approves risk, or initiates execution. The AI Reasoning and Recommendation Engine remains advisory; the deterministic Policy Engine remains the authority for permitted action. Model Orchestration and Provider Abstraction may select an approved provider and configuration but has no policy authority.

Because model behavior can vary without a conventional deterministic binary change, release acceptance shall rely on controlled evaluations, policy enforcement, bounded output contracts, independent validation, and observed performance rather than version number alone.

### Knowledge, Code Intelligence, and Index Versions

Knowledge graphs, retrieval corpora, embeddings, symbol indexes, dependency graphs, Code Intelligence indexes, and derived analysis structures shall expose the versions needed to determine source freshness, schema compatibility, and reproducibility.

The Code Intelligence order remains canonical: Code Entity Model, Source File Analyzer, Symbol Extraction, Dependency Extraction, and Repository Code Index. A version change cannot reorder or replace these architectural responsibilities without an ADR.

An index identity shall bind to source snapshot, entity-model version, analyzer version, extraction configuration, dependency rules, repository scope, and build time. An index may be regenerated under the same semantic contract but shall receive a distinct build identity and digest. Material interpretation change requires an increment in the applicable semantic domain.

Stale or incompatible indexes shall be detected and shall not silently inform architecture, security, impact, or release decisions. Regeneration and migration shall preserve traceability to the source on which the result was based.

### Infrastructure and Deployment Bundle Versions

Infrastructure definitions, deployment charts, manifests, machine images, runner images, policy bundles, and installation packages shall be versioned when independently distributed or operated. Their compatibility includes infrastructure APIs, cluster or operating environment, storage, network controls, secrets interfaces, security baseline, and product component versions.

An infrastructure bundle version does not replace the product version. The Release Manifest maps a supported bundle to the exact product and component set. Environment-specific values are controlled configuration and shall not be embedded into a new product version merely because a customer or region differs.

Mutable aliases may identify a recommended channel but shall resolve to an immutable bundle version and artifact digest before deployment. Customer-controlled environments shall be able to verify the bundle offline where required and compare the installed state with the approved manifest.

Manual infrastructure drift shall not receive retrospective legitimacy through a version label. It shall be detected, assessed, remediated, and recorded as a controlled change or incident.

### Documentation Versions

Canonical architecture, engineering standards, product documentation, operating procedures, API references, security guidance, and customer manuals shall have versions appropriate to their authority and audience. Documentation version is distinct from product version but shall state the product, API, deployment, policy, or release range to which it applies.

This handbook uses its own controlled document metadata and change history. Accepted architectural decisions remain canonical until an ADR explicitly supersedes them; incrementing the handbook version alone does not authorize architectural redesign.

Published documentation for a release shall be immutable or recoverably archived.
