Corrections that do not change the described product may increment the document patch version or revision according to its registered domain. A correction that reveals a product incompatibility or security issue shall trigger the relevant product and incident process rather than being hidden as an editorial update.

URLs labeled `latest` may aid navigation but shall not be the only references in evidence, contracts, support cases, or regulated records. Those references shall resolve to an immutable documentation version.

### Control Framework and Profile Versions

Quality Profiles, deployment profiles, security baselines, compliance mappings, control catalogs, threat-model templates, and assurance profiles shall be versioned when their requirements can change. The effective profile version shall be recorded with the change, build, release, deployment, audit, and evidence context to which it applies.

Changing a profile from requiring a control to omitting it may be breaking for assurance even if product behavior is unchanged. Such a change requires risk assessment, accountable approval, communication, and an accurate update to claims. A profile version never establishes certification or legal conformity by itself.

The Enterprise Profile and Single-Maintainer Bootstrap Profile remain distinct assurance states. A profile version shall not be manipulated to represent bootstrap evidence as independent two-person review.

Control mappings to external standards shall include the exact standard edition, amendment, jurisdictional status, and applicability assumptions. Use of a version number does not establish readiness, certification, authorization, or conformity.

### Release Manifest and Version Bill of Materials

Every governed integrated release shall have an immutable Release Manifest that functions as its authoritative version bill of materials. The manifest shall bind, as applicable:

- integrated product version and release maturity;
- source repositories, exact revisions, and signed or otherwise protected tags;
- component, service, package, client, plugin, schema, migration, API, event, policy, evidence-format, infrastructure, documentation, model-configuration, and evaluation versions;
- artifact names, platforms, editions, digests, signatures, provenance, and software bills of materials;
- dependency and external-service constraints;
- Quality Profile, test and Quality Gate results, approvals, exceptions, and ADR references;
- compatibility matrix and supported upgrade or recovery paths;
- publication time, channel, support designation, and release authority; and
- withdrawal, supersession, or retirement state when subsequently applicable.

The manifest shall be machine-readable and human-reviewable. It shall have its own schema version and integrity protection. A display page or release note may summarize the manifest but shall not replace it.

If two artifacts claim the same semantic version but have different bytes, the manifest shall distinguish them by platform, package identity, build identity, and digest and demonstrate that they implement the same contract. Unexplained divergence blocks release.

### Change Classification

Version classification is based on the strongest affected supported contract, not the volume of code, perceived implementation effort, ticket category, or team preference. A small field-semantics change can require a major increment; a large internal refactor can remain a patch when all supported contracts and observable behavior remain compatible.

Classification shall consider:

- public and partner APIs;
- events, protocols, file and export formats;
- persisted schemas and migration expectations;
- command-line, SDK, client, and configuration contracts;
- policy, capability, approval, validation, audit, and evidence semantics;
- security, privacy, identity, tenant-isolation, and availability assumptions;
- deployment, operations, monitoring, backup, and recovery contracts;
- performance or capacity guarantees where contractual;
- accessibility, localization, and supported platform commitments;
- documented behavior and behavior reasonably relied upon by supported consumers; and
- removal, deprecation, or change of an existing capability.

The classification and rationale shall be recorded in the Change Request and release evidence. Multiple changes in one release take the highest required increment.

### Major Version Changes

A `MAJOR` increment is required when a supported consumer must change to preserve correct operation, security, interpretation, or support, unless a previously declared and expired deprecation policy explicitly establishes a compatible transition within the current major.

Examples include removing or renaming a supported operation; changing field meaning or type; making an optional input required; changing default authorization or side effects; invalidating supported clients; changing event or evidence interpretation; requiring an incompatible data migration; removing a deployment model; weakening or materially changing an assurance claim; or altering a customer-visible recovery contract.

A major increment does not authorize every breaking change. The change still requires business justification, ADR where architecture-significant, migration tooling, customer communication, coexistence or cutover strategy, security and privacy assessment, evidence, and approval.

Security improvement is not a blanket exception. If a vulnerable behavior must be removed incompatibly, the release shall be classified honestly and managed through emergency and customer-risk procedures. An exceptional out-of-band compatibility break within a support line requires explicit executive, product, architecture, and security approval, precise scope, evidence, and communication; it shall not be mislabeled as an ordinary patch.

### Minor Version Changes

A `MINOR` increment introduces backward-compatible capability or materially expands a supported contract without requiring an existing conforming consumer to change. Examples can include a new optional API operation, a new capability disabled by default, an additive schema that all supported consumers tolerate, a new adapter, or a newly supported deployment profile.

Introducing a deprecation normally requires at least a minor increment because it changes the future support contract and demands consumer awareness. The existing capability shall continue to operate according to the declared compatibility and support window.

An addition is not automatically compatible. New response fields may break closed parsers; new events may trigger unsafe wildcard consumers; new permissions may alter risk; new defaults may change behavior; and new resource use may violate capacity assumptions. The classification shall be supported by tests and consumer analysis.

Minor versions may include compatible corrections that would independently qualify as patches. They shall not include hidden breaking behavior.

### Patch Version Changes

A `PATCH` increment introduces a backward-compatible correction that preserves supported contracts. Examples include a defect correction, compatible security remediation, performance correction within existing behavior, documentation-aligned operational improvement, or dependency update that does not alter the supported contract.

A patch shall not require supported consumers to migrate an API, reinterpret evidence, change stored data incompatibly, adopt new mandatory configuration, accept weaker security, or change ordinary use. If it does, it is not a patch regardless of urgency.

Patch releases shall be built, tested, evidenced, and approved with the same integrity controls as other releases. “Small change” does not mean low risk. Security patches can require elevated threat assessment, confidential coordination, embargoed handling, and accelerated publication while retaining version accuracy.

Backported patches for different supported lines receive the next patch value in each target line and their own build, tests, manifest, release notes, and evidence.

### Breaking-Change Determination

A breaking change exists when a supported and conforming consumer, operator, verifier, integration, deployment, or persisted record can no longer function correctly or maintain its documented assurance without modification. Breaking impact can be syntactic, semantic, behavioral, operational, security-related, privacy-related, performance-related, or support-related.

The assessment shall examine more than compilation and schema validation. It shall include default behavior, error codes, retry patterns, ordering, latency and capacity commitments, authorization, approval, logging, evidence, retention, observability, accessibility, failure behavior, backup, recovery, and administrative workflows.

Undocumented implementation behavior is not automatically a supported contract, but widespread reasonable reliance shall be assessed before removal. The absence of documentation does not justify surprising customers where ILAIOS knowingly allowed or promoted the behavior.

When evidence is insufficient to establish compatibility, the change is not presumed non-breaking. It shall be blocked, tested further, constrained to experimental scope, or classified conservatively.

### Experimental and Feature-Flagged Behavior

Experimental capability shall be visibly identified, disabled or access-controlled as appropriate, and excluded from Stable compatibility commitments unless the release terms explicitly include it. Its interface, data handling, security boundaries, allowed environments, support, retention, and removal conditions shall be documented.

A feature flag does not make a breaking change non-breaking when supported customers already rely on the enabled behavior. Changing a default flag state can itself change the contract. Flag identity, configuration version, audience, owner, expiry, and effective state shall be captured in release and deployment evidence.

Experimental does not mean ungoverned. Identity, policy, tenant isolation, privacy, Tool Gateway, Validation Pipeline, Audit Engine, Evidence Chain, and incident controls remain applicable. An experiment cannot be used to create an alternate execution path.

Graduation into the Stable contract requires explicit classification, tests, documentation, migration analysis, support readiness, and release approval. Abandoned experiments shall be removed through a controlled change and their data handled according to approved retention rules.

### Version Allocation and Reservation

A version may be reserved to coordinate planning, documentation, packaging, or external communication. Reservation does not constitute build, approval, publication, support, or release. Reserved values shall have owner, intended domain, target scope, and lifecycle state.

Allocation shall occur through the authoritative version registry or controlled automation. Parallel release lines shall prevent collision. A failed, cancelled, yanked, revoked, or unpublished build may leave a version unused, but a version already published to any governed recipient shall never be reused for different content.

Version numbers shall not be assigned merely to match a date, competitor, customer expectation, commercial campaign, or another component. Coordinated version alignment is permitted when it improves integrated-product clarity and does not misstate component compatibility.

Automation shall reject duplicate publication, invalid syntax, unauthorized increments, missing manifest relationships, and attempts to overwrite an immutable version.

### Source Tags and Version References

The canonical source tag form is `vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH[-prerelease]`, for example `v2.4.7` or `v2.5.0-rc.2`, unless a registered repository namespace requires a documented prefix to prevent collision. Build metadata should not normally appear in the source tag because a tag identifies the approved source state rather than every packaging variant.

The tag shall point to the exact reviewed revision used for the release and shall be created through the authorized release process. Stable and externally distributed prerelease tags shall be annotated and signed or otherwise integrity-protected according to the Quality Profile. A signature authenticates the signing identity and content under the applicable trust model; it does not by itself prove review, security, quality, release approval, or deployment authorization.

Published tags are immutable. Moving, deleting, or recreating a published tag to point to different source is prohibited. If a tag is incorrect, it shall be withdrawn or superseded transparently and a new version issued. Repository administrators shall not use elevated access to conceal the error.

Branch names and mutable aliases such as `main`, `master`, `stable`, `release`, or `latest` are not version references in a Release Manifest. The existing registered Primary Branch is not renamed merely for convention; any rename remains a governed migration under Section 4.8.

### Immutable Artifacts and Rebuilds

Every released artifact shall be immutable within its repository or registry namespace. Publication shall prevent replacement where the platform supports it, and monitoring shall detect mutation, deletion, or digest drift. A copied artifact remains the same exact artifact only when its digest and provenance validate.

Rebuilding the same source can produce different bytes because of toolchain, dependency, timestamp, signing, packaging, or environment differences. The rebuild receives a distinct build identity and digest. It may retain the same semantic version only when it is a formally governed packaging or reproducibility case that preserves the identical contract, remains unambiguous in its artifact namespace, and is represented in the Release Manifest.

If previously distributed bytes are corrected, the correction normally receives a new patch or prerelease version. Overwriting an existing package or image under the same authoritative reference is prohibited even when the original artifact was unusable.

Reproducible-build comparison shall distinguish allowed nondeterminism from unexplained divergence. Unexplained divergence blocks promotion and triggers investigation.

### Compatibility Contract

Every supported version domain shall define what compatibility means. The contract shall state supported consumers, inputs, outputs, persisted state, side effects, security and privacy guarantees, performance assumptions, deployment environments, support period, negotiation behavior, and permitted evolution.

Backward compatibility means a newer provider or implementation continues to support existing conforming consumers within the declared contract. Forward compatibility means an older consumer can tolerate defined newer content or behavior. These are different properties and shall not be asserted without evidence.

Wire compatibility, source compatibility, binary compatibility, data compatibility, operational compatibility, and assurance compatibility shall be assessed separately where relevant. Passing one form does not imply the others.

Compatibility claims shall be bounded by supported version ranges and configurations. Unsupported custom modifications, expired releases, uncontrolled extensions, or provider behavior outside the declared contract are not silently included.

### Compatibility Matrix

ILAIOS shall maintain a controlled compatibility matrix for integrated releases and independently evolving domains. It shall identify supported combinations of product, service, API, client, SDK, schema, database, event, policy, plugin, infrastructure, operating environment, model configuration, evidence verifier, and documentation versions as applicable.

Each matrix entry shall have state such as Supported, Transitional, Evaluation, Deprecated, Blocked, or Unsupported, with rationale, test evidence, effective dates, and owner. Blank cells shall not be interpreted as compatible.

The matrix shall include permitted version skew during rolling upgrade, regional promotion, disaster recovery, offline synchronization, and customer-controlled maintenance. It shall identify which component must upgrade first, how long mixed versions may operate, and what happens when the window expires.

Automated deployment and startup checks should enforce the matrix where feasible. Where enforcement is not possible, preflight validation and operational procedure shall provide equivalent assurance.

### Version Negotiation

When independently deployed parties communicate, they shall negotiate or validate compatible protocol, API, schema, and capability versions before performing consequential work. Negotiation shall be deterministic, authenticated where necessary, and resistant to downgrade manipulation.

The parties shall exchange only the minimum version and capability information required. A common supported version shall be selected according to a documented rule. Unsupported or ambiguous combinations shall fail explicitly before side effects rather than be guessed from payload shape.

Negotiation shall not authorize the requested business action. Identity, tenant, request integrity, Immutable Context, policy, capability, risk, approval, Tool Gateway, validation, acceptance, audit, and evidence remain required according to the canonical operational flow.

Security minimums shall override compatibility convenience. A client shall not force use of a retired cryptographic, authentication, evidence, or policy protocol merely because it advertises an old version.

### Deprecation

Deprecation declares that a supported capability remains available temporarily but is scheduled for change or removal. It shall identify the affected domain and versions, reason, replacement, migration instructions, announcement date, earliest removal version or date, support implications, telemetry basis where lawful, and accountable owner.

Deprecation shall be introduced through at least the appropriate minor release and communicated through release notes, versioned documentation, machine-readable interface metadata where applicable, and direct enterprise notice when contractual or operational impact requires it.

The notice period shall reflect customer deployment cycles, regulated validation, offline environments, integration complexity, contractual commitments, and security risk. A generic statement that behavior “may change” is not adequate deprecation.

Removal requires confirmation that the declared conditions were met. Security or legal necessity may shorten the period only through documented risk decision, alternative controls, migration assistance, and precise communication.

### Support Lines and Long-Term Support

A support line is a maintained version family, normally identified by a major or selected minor baseline. Section 4.10 defines eligibility, duration, service level, and release maturity. Versioning shall make the line and each patch unambiguous.

Long-Term Support is a support designation applied to an approved Stable release or line. It shall not be encoded as a numeric component, used as a substitute for contractual terms, or inferred from a branch name. The Release Manifest and support registry state its start, end, maintenance scope, platform matrix, and successor path.

Multiple supported lines increase security, testing, documentation, migration, and incident burden. A new line shall not be created without owner, capacity, release process, dependency strategy, and retirement plan.

End of Standard Support, Extended Support, security-only maintenance, and End of Life shall be separate states with clear dates and obligations. A version remains historically identifiable after support ends; it does not remain safe or supported merely because artifacts are still downloadable.

### Backports and Parallel Maintenance

A backport applies a correction to an older supported line without importing unrelated change. It is a new target-baseline change and receives its own Change Request, review, tests, version, artifacts, manifest, release notes, and evidence.

The source change may be cherry-picked or reimplemented according to Section 4.8, but source similarity is not proof of behavioral equivalence. Tests shall cover the older line's dependencies, schemas, deployment environments, policy behavior, and security assumptions.

Backport eligibility shall be based on support commitment, severity, exposure, customer impact, compatibility, and recovery risk. It shall not be driven solely by customer prominence or ease of implementation.

Parallel lines shall use clearly separated branches, artifact namespaces, dependency constraints, and publication channels. A fix intended for one line shall not be accidentally published under another line's version.

### Security Releases

Security releases use the same semantic classification as other releases. A backward-compatible remediation increments `PATCH`; a backward-compatible security capability can increment `MINOR`; an incompatible correction requires `MAJOR` or a formally governed exceptional response that does not misrepresent compatibility.

Embargo, coordinated disclosure, restricted testing, and accelerated approval may limit who can view a change before publication. They shall not eliminate traceability, separation of duties, artifact integrity, Quality Gates, or post-release evidence. Confidential metadata shall be protected while authoritative classification remains accurate.

The security release record shall identify affected version ranges, fixed versions, exploitability assumptions, mitigations, upgrade priority, support-line coverage, and advisory publication state. It shall not claim absence of impact merely because a vulnerable component is present; reachability and effective controls require evidence.

If an external dependency is compromised or withdrawn, ILAIOS shall identify all affected manifests and version lines, contain distribution where necessary, and issue new immutable artifacts. Existing versions shall not be silently rebuilt under their old identities.

### Withdrawal, Revocation, and Yanking

A released version may be yanked, withdrawn, or revoked when it is defective, vulnerable, unlawful to distribute, incorrectly built, improperly authorized, or otherwise unsafe. The action shall preserve the historical record and distinguish availability restriction from deletion of evidence.

The registry shall record reason, authority, time, affected artifacts, customer impact, replacement, mitigation, incident or legal reference, and whether installation, upgrade, execution, or support is blocked. Customers and dependent teams shall receive notice proportionate to risk.

A withdrawn version number shall never be reused. Mutable channels shall move away from it only after the withdrawal event is recorded; direct immutable references shall continue to resolve to a warning or controlled tombstone where legally and technically possible rather than different bytes.

Cryptographic revocation or deny-list controls may prevent trust in an artifact. They shall be scoped carefully to avoid disabling evidence needed for incident analysis, legal hold, or recovery.

### Upgrade and Migration

Every supported upgrade path shall define eligible source versions, target version, prerequisites, compatibility, data and schema transitions, policy changes, expected downtime, capacity, backup or recovery point, validation, cutover, rollback or forward recovery, and post-upgrade acceptance.

Skipping versions is supported only when explicitly tested or when the installer executes and verifies every required intermediate transition. The presence of a higher semantic version does not prove that a direct upgrade is safe.

Upgrade automation shall preflight identity, environment, current versions, integrity, capacity, dependencies, schema, backups, permissions, and incompatible extensions. It shall fail before destructive action when prerequisites are unmet.

Customer-controlled and regulated deployments may require evidence packages, maintenance-window approval, validation scripts, and documented residual risk. ILAIOS shall provide accurate compatibility information without assuming authority over the customer's final deployment decision.

### Downgrade, Rollback, and Forward Recovery

Downgrade changes installed software to a lower version. Rollback reverses a deployment transition or routes traffic to a prior artifact. Neither necessarily reverses data migration, external side effects, policy decisions, messages, cryptographic changes, or customer actions.

A release shall declare whether software rollback, configuration rollback, schema rollback, data restoration, traffic reversal, and evidence compatibility are supported. Unsupported downgrade attempts shall be blocked or require an exceptional recovery procedure.

Forward recovery applies a new correction to restore safe operation when reversal would be destructive, incompatible, or misleading. It is often preferred after irreversible migration or externally visible side effects. The new artifact receives a new version and full evidence.

Recovery shall preserve the Audit Engine and Evidence Chain across the failed and corrective transitions. A rollback label shall not close the incident until state, data, policy, security, external effects, and customer acceptance are reconciled.

### Minimum Supported Versions and Version Skew

Every communicating component or supported environment may declare a minimum and maximum compatible version range. The declaration shall be governed, tested, and included in the compatibility matrix. It shall not be widened automatically because a syntactic handshake succeeds.

Version skew during rolling deployment shall have a maximum width and duration. Mixed-version operation shall preserve tenant isolation, policy semantics, evidence verifiability, message interpretation, and recovery. The system shall detect and alert on skew outside the approved range.

Minimum security versions may be raised when older versions cannot meet current threat, legal, or support requirements. The decision shall include impact assessment, notice, mitigation, and customer transition support.

An expired or unsupported version shall not automatically receive privileged compatibility treatment. It may be isolated, read-only, blocked, or permitted temporarily through an approved exception with compensating controls.

### Distributed, Offline, and Customer-Controlled Deployments

ILAIOS shall support version governance where customer environments cannot continuously access a central registry. Release packages shall carry signed or otherwise integrity-protected manifests, artifacts, dependencies, schemas, policies, documentation, compatibility data, and verification instructions sufficient for offline validation.

Installation shall not depend on a mutable remote alias. The customer shall be able to identify exact installed versions and digests, compare them with an approved release, and export a protected status report without exposing secrets.

Delayed update cycles shall be addressed through published support windows, security advisories, offline patch packages, dependency mirrors, and controlled migration paths. Offline status does not extend support indefinitely or make a retired version secure.

When multiple sites synchronize after operating independently, protocol and data-version negotiation shall prevent silent loss, replay, duplicate action, or tenant crossing. Conflict resolution shall be deterministic where possible and evidence-producing throughout.

### Customer-Specific Configuration and Builds

Customer-specific configuration shall not create an ad hoc private product version. A supported installation shall reference the official base product version plus a controlled deployment profile, configuration version, policy version, extension set, and exact artifact digests.

Customer name, contract number, region, or environment shall not be embedded into a public semantic version. Such values belong in protected deployment metadata. This prevents namespace fragmentation and disclosure.

If executable behavior diverges from the official artifact, the result is a distinct governed build or product variant. It requires an owner, registered namespace, source provenance, version, tests, security maintenance, compatibility statement, documentation, and support decision. A patched binary cannot retain the unqualified official identity.

Commercial edition or entitlement differences shall be represented through product catalog, license, capability, and policy metadata rather than misleading version numbers. Entitlement never overrides runtime policy.

### Third-Party Dependency Versions

Third-party libraries, services, operating platforms, cryptographic modules, model providers, and tools shall be referenced by the most precise available immutable identity. Version range, source, digest, license, support, known vulnerability state, and transitive relationship shall be captured in the applicable bill of materials and Release Manifest.

Mutable dependency selectors are prohibited for authoritative builds unless resolved and locked before construction with evidence. A package name and version from an untrusted source do not establish authenticity; source registry, signatures or attestations where applicable, digest, and provenance shall also be verified.

Upgrading a dependency does not determine the ILAIOS version mechanically. The resulting public behavior, security, compatibility, licensing, build, and operational change shall be assessed. A major dependency update may be an ILAIOS patch if fully isolated and compatible; a minor dependency change may require an ILAIOS major if it breaks the supported contract.

Provider end-of-life and forced version transitions shall be tracked early. Emergency provider change still requires policy, validation, evidence, and accurate release classification.

### Version Representation in Runtime, Telemetry, and Evidence

Every material lifecycle event shall carry the version identities required for interpretation and accountability. This includes request intake, Immutable Context creation, reasoning proposal, policy decision, risk classification, approval, capability issuance, Tool Gateway execution, validation, acceptance or rejection, delivery, closure, and review.

As applicable, events shall include product, service, API, schema, policy, tool, adapter, evidence-format, model/configuration, and deployment versions plus exact artifact or configuration identities. The Audit Engine and Evidence Chain operate continuously across all material stages rather than being appended only at completion.

Version telemetry shall support inventory, vulnerability response, compatibility analysis, incident scope, upgrade planning, and customer support. It shall not expose secrets, personal data, internal topology, tenant identifiers, or sensitive vulnerability detail through unauthenticated endpoints.

Observed runtime identity shall be compared with desired and released state. Unknown, malformed, drifted, revoked, or unsupported versions shall trigger deterministic policy or operational response appropriate to risk.

### Documentation and Customer Communication

Every release shall provide versioned release notes that identify scope, change classification, compatibility, affected interfaces and schemas, new capability, corrections, security information appropriate for disclosure, deprecations, known limitations, upgrade and recovery requirements, support status, and documentation version.

Release notes shall distinguish product change from packaging, build, configuration, or channel change. They shall not use “no breaking changes” without an evidenced compatibility assessment, call a prerelease Stable, or call a release LTS before approval.

Customer communication shall be proportionate to impact and timed to allow enterprise planning. Major changes, security-critical patches, support retirement, forced provider transitions, irreversible migrations, and shortened deprecations require direct, controlled notification where contracts or risk require it.

Marketing names may accompany a version but shall not replace it. Claims concerning security, compliance, certification, performance, maturity, or compatibility shall remain within approved evidence and applicability.

### Tooling and Automation

Version tooling shall validate syntax, compare precedence, detect contract change where feasible, allocate values, create manifests, protect tags, prevent duplicate publication, verify digests, generate compatibility reports, and reconcile deployed state. Tooling shall be versioned and tested itself.

Automated suggestions shall be treated as inputs. A source diff may miss behavioral, data, operational, security, or customer-contract impact. The accountable owner remains responsible for classification.

Pipelines shall derive the declared version from one authoritative controlled source and compare it with tags, package metadata, manifests, documentation, and artifacts. Contradiction shall fail the release rather than be resolved through implicit precedence.

Access to allocate, sign, publish, yank, or revoke versions shall use least privilege and separation of duties. Events shall be attributable and retained according to approved record-class-specific schedules.

### Versioning Metrics and Review

Versioning effectiveness shall be measured to improve compatibility and release governance, not to reward high or low increment counts. Useful measures may include escaped breaking changes, version collisions, mutable-artifact incidents, unsupported deployment prevalence, upgrade success, rollback or forward-recovery success, deprecation completion, compatibility-matrix coverage, manifest completeness, patch latency, and mean time to identify affected versions.

Metrics shall be segmented by product, component, support line, deployment profile, and severity where useful. A low major-version count is not evidence of stability if incompatible changes are hidden in minor or patch releases.

Periodic review shall examine version-domain sprawl, stale support lines, dependency freshness, customer upgrade concentration, prerelease duration, unretired aliases, undocumented skew, withdrawn artifacts, and exceptions. Findings shall feed product roadmap, Section 4.10 release policy, security operations, and architecture governance.

Metric definitions, sources, limitations, and owners shall be documented. Personal performance assessment shall not incentivize misclassification or premature release.

### Exceptions

An exception to this standard requires documented scope, affected version domains and releases, business reason, compatibility and customer impact, security and privacy assessment, alternatives, compensating controls, owner, approver, start date, expiry, and remediation or migration plan.

An exception cannot authorize silent replacement of published bytes; reuse of a released version; fabricated compatibility or maturity; hidden breaking change; unsupported architectural redesign; unversioned policy or evidence format where historical interpretation depends on it; mutable production dependency without resolution; false claim of Stable or LTS status; or removal of identity, policy, approval, Tool Gateway, validation, audit, or evidence controls.

Provider limitation, legacy constraints, customer urgency, security incident, or offline deployment may justify a narrowly scoped treatment but does not create automatic permission. The exception and its effective configuration shall be represented in the Release Manifest and relevant customer communication.

Expired exceptions shall result in remediation, renewed assessment, restricted distribution, support limitation, isolation, or retirement. Continuation through inaction is non-conformant.

### Versioning Invariants

The following invariants are canonical:

- public product contracts use `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` semantics unless a domain-specific ADR explicitly supersedes the model;
- `alpha.N`, `beta.N`, and `rc.N` identify controlled prerelease maturity; Stable has no prerelease suffix;
- Long-Term Support is a governed support designation, not a semantic-version component;
- build metadata does not change semantic precedence, compatibility, maturity, or support;
- the optional `v` source-tag prefix is not part of the semantic version value;
- version, source revision, tag, build, artifact digest, manifest, release channel, support state, deployment, and runtime instance remain distinct identities;
- every independently released, persisted, negotiated, verified, or supported domain has a registered owner and compatibility contract;
- integrated releases bind exact component, schema, policy, evidence, infrastructure, documentation, configuration, dependency, source, and artifact identities in an immutable Release Manifest;
- published versions, tags, schemas, policies, evidence formats, migrations, and artifacts are not silently replaced or rewritten;
- a published version value is never reused, including after withdrawal, revocation, or failed publication;
- the highest-impact supported contract change determines `MAJOR`, `MINOR`, or `PATCH` classification;
- security urgency does not permit a breaking change to be mislabeled as a patch;
- version zero permits faster evolution but not silent incompatibility or absence of governance;
- compatibility is established through declared contracts, matrices, negotiation, and evidence rather than number similarity;
- unsupported or ambiguous major versions fail explicitly before consequential side effects;
- policy and capability versions are immutable material inputs to deterministic Policy Engine decisions;
- evidence and audit formats preserve independent verification and historical interpretation across versions;
- model, provider, reasoning configuration, and routing versions are observable but grant no permission and assume no policy authority;
- customer configuration references an official base version and controlled profile rather than creating an ad hoc private product identity;
- rollback, downgrade, data restoration, and forward recovery remain distinct operations with declared support;
- tags and signatures support traceability and integrity but do not by themselves prove approval, quality, security, release, or deployment authority;
- the Audit Engine and Evidence Chain record material version events continuously across the canonical lifecycle;
- Development System version authority remains separated from Runtime System business-action authority;
- the Code Intelligence order remains Code Entity Model, Source File Analyzer, Symbol Extraction, Dependency Extraction, and Repository Code Index; and
- architecture decisions remain canonical until an authorized ADR explicitly supersedes them.

A versioning practice is non-conformant if it overwrites a published artifact, moves a published tag, reuses a released version, treats `latest`, a branch, a commit, a build number, a date, or a deployment as the semantic version, relies on build metadata for precedence, represents Alpha, Beta, or Release Candidate content as Stable, represents a release as Long-Term Support without approval, hides an incompatible change in a minor or patch increment, assumes additive structure is always compatible, permits an unsupported major to be reinterpreted silently, edits an executed migration or released schema in place, omits the effective policy or evidence-format version from material decisions, treats a model label as immutable authority, allows a customer-patched binary to retain an unqualified official identity, treats a signature as release approval, uses version zero to avoid governance, claims compatibility without a defined contract and evidence, changes the canonical architecture through a version increment without an ADR, or treats version allocation as authorization to build, publish, deploy, or operate.

## 4.10 Release Policy and Release Standards

### Purpose and Release Intent

Release management is the governed process through which an exact ILAIOS product state becomes approved for a defined audience, distribution channel, deployment profile, and support commitment. It converts verified engineering output into an accountable enterprise commitment while preserving security, compatibility, privacy, availability, customer control, artifact integrity, and architectural consistency.

The purpose of a release is not merely to publish software or increase delivery frequency. A release communicates that an identified set of immutable artifacts, documentation, policies, schemas, dependencies, operational procedures, and evidence has satisfied a declared maturity standard and may be used under stated conditions. The maturity claim shall be no broader than the evidence supports.

A source merge is not a release. A successful build is not a release. A tag, version number, signed artifact, green pipeline, registry publication, deployment, or marketing announcement is not independently sufficient to create release authority. A release exists only when the designated Release Authority has approved the exact Release Manifest for the specified maturity, scope, channel, and support state and the approval has been recorded.

### Scope

This standard applies to releases of the integrated ILAIOS Enterprise AI Operating System and every independently distributed or supported service, package, library, client, command-line tool, Software Development Kit, plugin, Tool Gateway adapter, deployment bundle, infrastructure package, policy bundle, schema, evidence verifier, documentation set, model configuration, and other governed asset.

It applies to hosted, customer-controlled, on-premises, hybrid, isolated, offline, regional, regulated, development, evaluation, recovery, and production contexts. It covers planned releases, prereleases, feature releases, patches, security releases, emergency releases, hotfixes, major migrations, Long-Term Support maintenance, withdrawals, supersession, and retirement.

Section 4.5 defines testing strategy; Section 4.6 defines Quality Gates; Section 4.7 defines CI/CD controls; Section 4.8 defines branching, review, and merge; and Section 4.9 defines version semantics. This section governs the release decision, maturity claim, publication, distribution, adoption, support, and closure. It shall not be used to alter the responsibilities assigned to those sections.

### Release Terminology

For this standard:

- a **Release** is an approved immutable deliverable set with defined maturity, audience, compatibility, and support terms;
- a **Release Candidate** is an immutable candidate intended to become Stable if no disqualifying issue is found;
- a **Release Manifest** is the authoritative version bill of materials and evidence index defined in Section 4.9;
- a **Release Record** is the governance record containing the decision, authority, scope, conditions, and lifecycle events;
- a **Release Channel** is a controlled distribution path through which eligible recipients discover or receive a release;
- a **Deployment** is the installation or promotion of an approved artifact into an environment;
- a **Rollout** is the controlled sequence through which deployment exposure expands;
- **General Availability** means that an approved Stable release is available to its defined market or customer population, subject to commercial, geographic, contractual, and deployment constraints;
- **Long-Term Support** is an explicit maintenance designation applied to a qualifying Stable release or line; and
- **End of Life** is the governed state after which ordinary maintenance and support commitments have ended.

These terms shall remain distinct. Publication does not prove deployment; deployment does not prove acceptance; acceptance by one environment does not expand the release audience; and availability does not create an indefinite support obligation.

### Release Principles

ILAIOS release governance follows these principles:

1. **Evidence before release.** Approval is based on complete, exact, reviewable evidence bound to the candidate.
2. **Maturity must be earned.** Alpha, Beta, Release Candidate, Stable, and Long-Term Support claims require their own criteria and cannot be assigned for convenience.
3. **Build once and promote unchanged.** The approved artifact progresses through environments without rebuilding or silent replacement.
4. **Exact scope.** Approval identifies product, version, artifacts, audience, channel, deployment profiles, regions, tenants, and support state.
5. **Fail closed.** Missing, expired, inconclusive, contradictory, or failed mandatory evidence blocks release.
6. **Separation of duties.** Authoring, gate administration, artifact signing, release approval, production promotion, and exception approval remain separated where risk requires.
7. **Customer control.** Availability does not authorize installation in a customer-controlled environment or override a customer change process.
8. **Progressive exposure.** Risk is constrained through controlled channels, cohorts, and observation periods where the deployment model permits.
9. **Recoverability before exposure.** Rollback, forward recovery, containment, and communication are prepared before material rollout.
10. **No architectural bypass.** Release urgency cannot change the deterministic Policy Engine, advisory reasoning role, Tool Gateway, independent validation, continuous audit and evidence, or Development/Runtime separation.
11. **Transparent lifecycle.** Publication, promotion, pause, withdrawal, supersession, and retirement are attributable and communicated appropriately.
12. **Support is explicit.** Stable and Long-Term Support commitments are stated, resourced, and bounded rather than inferred.

### Release Maturity Model

ILAIOS uses four canonical release maturity stages—Alpha, Beta, Release Candidate, and Stable—and one canonical extended-support designation, Long-Term Support. Collectively, these form the five release classifications used by this standard. A release shall use exactly one current maturity stage; Long-Term Support may be applied only to a qualifying Stable release or line and does not replace its Stable maturity.

| Maturity | Intended Purpose | Permitted Audience | Core Exit Standard | Support Posture |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Alpha | Validate architecture integration, core behavior, and high-risk assumptions | Authorized internal or tightly controlled design partners | Defined capability works in representative conditions; blocking unknowns are bounded; no uncontrolled exposure | Best-effort evaluation support; no Stable commitment |
| Beta | Validate substantially complete capability, integration, operability, and customer fit | Controlled external cohort and approved non-critical use | Feature scope substantially complete; known risks documented; upgrade and telemetry paths proven | Time-bounded prerelease support |
| Release Candidate | Validate an exact candidate for Stable approval | Approved validation environments and selected production-like cohorts | No known release blocker; all Stable gates complete or awaiting final observation only | Candidate-specific support and rapid remediation |
| Stable | Provide an approved production release for the declared deployment profiles | Defined general or enterprise customer population | All mandatory gates, evidence, operations, documentation, and release approval complete | Standard support under published terms |
| Long-Term Support | Provide a Stable baseline with extended, planned maintenance | Customers requiring longer validation and upgrade cycles | Stable qualification plus LTS selection, resourcing, dependency, backport, and lifecycle approval | Extended maintenance under explicit terms |

Maturity is not inferred from version magnitude, branch name, environment name, customer use, elapsed time, number of downloads, or absence of reported incidents. A release remains at its approved maturity until a separate decision promotes, withdraws, or retires it.

### Alpha Release Standard

Alpha releases validate incomplete or rapidly evolving capability within a bounded risk envelope. They may contain unfinished interfaces, limited deployment profiles, incomplete performance tuning, restricted documentation, or known defects, provided those limitations are explicit and do not compromise mandatory trust boundaries.

An Alpha release shall define its purpose, hypotheses, included and excluded capability, audience, data classifications, permitted environments, expiration, telemetry, evaluation plan, known limitations, and termination criteria. Production customer data is prohibited by default unless a specific assessment, contract, privacy basis, security review, and approval authorize the exact use.

Alpha does not authorize weak security. Identity verification, tenant isolation, least privilege, policy enforcement, human approval where required, Tool Gateway execution, Validation Pipeline, Audit Engine, Evidence Chain, secret protection, and incident response remain mandatory for the capabilities exercised. Experimental reasoning may propose plans but cannot grant permission or initiate execution.

Alpha artifacts shall be immutable, versioned with `alpha.N`, traceable to source, and distributed only through an Alpha channel. Each new published Alpha receives a new prerelease version. An Alpha shall not be marketed as production-ready, certified, generally available, or representative of the final performance and support commitment.

Exit from Alpha requires evidence that the material architecture integrations operate as intended, critical unknowns have been reduced, severe defects are controlled, the Beta evaluation scope is defined, and owners accept the remaining risk. Promotion creates a new Beta release; it does not relabel the Alpha artifact.

### Beta Release Standard

Beta releases validate a substantially complete product contract, enterprise usability, integration behavior, performance envelope, upgrade process, operational readiness, and customer adoption assumptions. Scope should be feature-complete or sufficiently stable that remaining change is correction, hardening, or explicitly bounded refinement.

The Beta audience shall be controlled through eligibility, agreement, tenant or environment registration, and channel access. Each participant shall receive accurate limitations, support route, data-handling terms, upgrade expectations, feedback mechanism, and notice that compatibility may change before Stable.

Beta use in a production business process requires explicit customer and ILAIOS approval, a defined criticality limit, recovery plan, enhanced monitoring, and contractual treatment. It shall not be the only control for a safety-critical, legally determinative, or otherwise prohibited use. Customer reliance shall remain within the documented Beta contract.

Beta readiness requires completion of core functional, integration, security, privacy, tenant-isolation, migration, backup, recovery, observability, and support testing appropriate to the scope. Known defects and residual risk shall be classified and visible. High or critical release-blocking defects are not waived merely to obtain external feedback.

Exit from Beta requires stable scope, demonstrated upgrade and recovery, acceptable performance and reliability, resolved release blockers, complete Stable acceptance plan, customer-facing documentation readiness, and a candidate baseline suitable for release-candidate hardening.

### Release Candidate Standard

A Release Candidate is an exact immutable set of artifacts believed to satisfy the Stable release standard. It shall use the `rc.N` prerelease form defined in Section 4.9 and shall be built through the same trusted process, dependency controls, signing path, packaging, installation path, and verification procedures intended for Stable.

The candidate shall have no known unresolved defect classified as a Stable blocker. All mandatory tests and Quality Gates shall be Passed, except a gate explicitly designed to conclude only after the candidate observation period. Such pending observation shall have a defined duration, metric, threshold, and owner; it is not a general waiver.

Candidate scope is frozen. Any change to source, dependency resolution, build environment, configuration baseline, schema, policy, model-routing configuration, documentation required for safe operation, or artifact bytes invalidates the exact candidate and requires a new `rc.N`. Re-running unchanged validation does not create a new candidate, but its evidence shall remain bound to the original digest.

Release Candidate validation shall exercise production-representative installation, upgrade, rollback or forward recovery, mixed-version operation where applicable, backup and restore, security monitoring, customer documentation, support triage, and post-deployment checks. Candidate deployment shall remain in authorized cohorts and shall not be represented as General Availability.

Stable approval may use byte-identical candidate artifacts when the pipeline and Release Manifest prove that no artifact or effective configuration changed and the release process supports promotion without rebuilding. If Stable packaging changes any released byte, a new build identity and candidate validation are required.

### Stable Release Standard

A Stable release is approved for production use within its declared deployment profiles, compatibility matrix, geographic scope, customer eligibility, and support terms. Stable is an engineering, operational, security, product, documentation, and support commitment; it is not only a test result.

Stable readiness requires all mandatory Quality Gates to be Passed, all Release Manifest relationships resolved, no unapproved blocker, complete installation and migration paths, proven recovery, production monitoring, incident readiness, customer documentation, support training, licensing and entitlement readiness, and accountable Release Authority approval.

Residual defects may remain only when they are below the blocking threshold, understood, documented, mitigated, assigned, and acceptable to the relevant owners. A known limitation that undermines the advertised core capability, a mandatory security control, tenant isolation, evidence integrity, data protection, recoverability, or a contractual commitment blocks Stable.

Stable publication shall identify supported deployment profiles, environments, clients, interfaces, schemas, integrations, policy and evidence versions, minimum and maximum compatible versions, known limitations, support period, and upgrade path. Claims shall remain within the evidence and shall not imply certification, conformity, or legal suitability where none has been established.

Stable availability does not authorize automatic production deployment. Hosted and customer-controlled rollouts remain subject to Sections 4.7 and this section's deployment controls.

### Long-Term Support Standard

Long-Term Support is a deliberate maintenance commitment applied to a qualifying Stable release or support line. It exists for enterprise customers that require extended validation cycles, predictable change, regulated operation, long-lived offline installations, or controlled migration windows.

LTS shall not be assigned automatically to every Stable release, appended as an informal label, or promised before the required capacity and dependencies are secured. Selection requires Product, Engineering, Security, Operations, Support, and commercial approval, with legal or compliance review where applicable.

An LTS decision shall define support start and end, maintenance phases, eligible deployment profiles, supported dependencies and platforms, security-patch obligations, defect thresholds, backport policy, documentation, migration successor, customer notification, and End-of-Life process. The binding duration is stated in the applicable release schedule and customer terms rather than embedded in the semantic version.

LTS prioritizes stability, not stagnation. Security, privacy, legal, and critical reliability corrections continue through controlled patches. New capability is excluded by default unless it is necessary for continued support, remains backward-compatible, and is approved for the line. Major functional expansion belongs in a later feature release.

The LTS owner shall demonstrate staffing, build reproducibility, dependency availability, test environments, signing continuity, vulnerability monitoring, backport capacity, and recovery of release infrastructure for the full commitment. An unsupported third-party dependency can constrain or terminate an LTS promise and shall be managed before designation.

### Release Types

Release type and maturity are separate. ILAIOS recognizes:

- **Feature Release:** introduces backward-compatible capability or a planned major contract change;
- **Patch Release:** corrects backward-compatible defects or operational behavior;
- **Security Release:** remediates a vulnerability or materially changes security posture;
- **Emergency Release:** follows an accelerated path in response to immediate material risk;
- **Major Migration Release:** changes incompatible contracts or requires significant customer transition;
- **Prerelease:** an Alpha, Beta, or Release Candidate distributed for bounded validation;
- **LTS Maintenance Release:** backports an approved correction to an LTS line; and
- **Documentation or Metadata Release:** corrects independently versioned documentation or controlled release metadata without silently changing product artifacts.

A release can belong to more than one operational type, such as an emergency security patch, but it shall have one semantic version, one maturity state, one authoritative Release Manifest, and an unambiguous approval path. Labels shall not be used to bypass the strongest applicable control.

### Release Lifecycle States

Section 5.3 defines the canonical end-to-end Release Lifecycle and its complete state model. This section defines release policy, maturity, eligibility, assurance, support, and claim requirements and shall not create a competing release state machine. Any platform, registry, deployment system, or support tool may use different display labels only when an approved mapping preserves the semantics and transition controls of Section 5.3. The terms Candidate, Active, and Retired, where retained in operational interfaces, shall map explicitly to Candidate Created, Accepted or Supported as applicable, and End of Support plus Closed as applicable; they shall not operate as additional canonical states.

### Release Governance and Roles

Every release shall have a Release Owner who coordinates scope, evidence, schedule, readiness, and closure. The Release Owner does not unilaterally approve risks owned by Product, Engineering, Security, Privacy, Operations, Support, Legal, Compliance, or the customer.

The governance model shall assign at least:

- **Product Authority** for intended capability, customer value, scope, market readiness, and communicated limitations;
- **Engineering Authority** for implementation integrity, compatibility, tests, defects, technical debt, and maintainability;
- **Architecture Authority** for consistency with canonical decisions and required ADRs;
- **Security Authority** for threat, vulnerability, supply-chain, identity, secret, tenant, and incident readiness;
- **Privacy and Compliance Authority** for applicable processing, records, claims, and obligations;
- **Operations Authority** for deployment, observability, capacity, resilience, backup, recovery, and on-call readiness;
- **Documentation and Support Authority** for customer instructions, known issues, triage, and escalation readiness; and
- **Release Authority** for the final bounded release decision.

One person may hold multiple roles in an approved bootstrap organization, but the record shall not claim independence that did not occur. The Single-Maintainer Bootstrap Profile preserves automated gates, exact evidence, risk disclosure, and exit criteria; it does not simulate two-person review or Enterprise separation of duties.

### Release Authority

Release Authority shall be granted through a registered role with least privilege, defined scope, competency, term, delegation rules, and revocation. Repository administration, pipeline administration, signing access, artifact publication access, commercial authority, or executive title does not automatically confer Release Authority.

The approval shall bind to the exact Release Manifest digest, maturity, audience, channels, deployment profiles, conditions, and validity period. Any change to an approval-bound input invalidates the decision and requires renewed review.

Conditional approval may authorize release only after explicitly named deterministic conditions have Passed. It shall not use vague language such as “when ready” or delegate uncontrolled judgment to automation. Conditions shall have owners, evidence sources, expiry, and failure behavior.

Release Authority may deny, pause, limit, withdraw, or revoke a release. Commercial schedule pressure, customer demand, sunk cost, or prior public announcement does not require approval when mandatory criteria are unmet.

### Separation of Duties

High-impact releases shall separate source authorship, independent review, Quality Gate administration, build and signing authority, release approval, production promotion, and exception approval. The applicable Quality Profile determines the minimum combination.

An individual or service that changes the release candidate shall not be the sole claimed independent approver of that change. A pipeline may enforce approved policy but cannot approve its own altered policy, credentials, or trusted execution environment.

Emergency operation may compress the number of participants only through the approved emergency model, with explicit record of reduced independence, compensating controls, restricted scope, and post-event review. It shall not fabricate normal-path evidence.

Customer deployment approval remains with the competent customer authority where the customer controls the environment. ILAIOS release approval does not impersonate that authority.

### Release Record

Each release shall have one authoritative Release Record with a stable Release ID. It shall include the proposed and approved version, maturity, type, scope, owner, authorities, target audience, channels, deployment profiles, regions, customers or cohorts where bounded, release dates, support status, Release Manifest digest, gate decisions, exceptions, known risks, approvals, publications, rollout events, incidents, withdrawal, supersession, and closure.

The record shall link rather than duplicate controlled evidence. It shall preserve the exact state visible to decision-makers at approval time and later amendments. Corrections shall be append-only or versioned; the original decision shall not be overwritten.

Sensitive security, customer, commercial, personal, or legal information shall be access-controlled and separated from public release notes. Redaction shall not destroy the ability of authorized reviewers to understand the decision.

Release records shall follow an approved record-class-specific retention schedule that reconciles legal, contractual, certification, product-support, incident, defense, privacy, and data-minimization requirements. Retention is not indefinite by default.

### Release Planning

Release planning shall define intended outcome, scope, target maturity, version, supported deployment profiles, target audience, schedule, dependencies, architecture changes, migration, capacity, documentation, support, security and privacy work, rollout model, and success or abort criteria.

The plan shall identify critical path, freeze points, candidate windows, customer notice, external-review lead time, app or package-store review where applicable, regional constraints, and recovery windows. Schedule shall reflect evidence needs rather than assume that uncompleted gates will pass.

Release trains may provide predictable cadence, but the train does not lower acceptance criteria. A change that misses scope or readiness moves to a later release without creating an exception solely to protect the date.

The plan shall remain linked to the Product Development Workflow and roadmap without turning roadmap aspiration into release commitment. A planned version is not approved, published, supported, or contractually available until the corresponding decisions occur.

### Scope Control and Freeze

Release scope shall be traceable to approved requirements, Change Requests, defects, ADRs, documentation, migrations, and risk treatments. Unrelated opportunistic changes shall not be added after candidate formation.

Freeze is a risk-control state, not a prohibition on all work. During freeze, only changes within the declared admissible categories may enter, such as release blockers, critical security corrections, required documentation corrections, or approved operational fixes.

Every post-freeze change shall identify why it is necessary, affected evidence, retest scope, compatibility, new candidate version, and approval. A “small” or “documentation-only” label does not exempt executable examples, policy text, schemas, defaults, or safety instructions from impact analysis.

Removing scope after validation also requires assessment because it can change dependencies, navigation, packaging, tests, documentation, migrations, and customer expectations.

### Candidate Construction

Release candidates shall be constructed only from registered canonical repositories and exact reviewed revisions through the trusted CI/CD system. Uncommitted files, developer workspaces, unofficial forks, mutable branches, or locally modified dependencies shall not be authoritative release inputs.

The build shall resolve exact dependencies, use approved runner and toolchain identities, isolate untrusted content, apply least privilege, protect secrets, generate provenance, produce bills of materials, and record deterministic inputs. Candidate creation shall fail on unresolved or mutable inputs.

Build once and promote unchanged is the default. Environment configuration is injected through controlled, versioned mechanisms and does not modify artifact bytes. If an environment requires distinct binaries, those binaries are separate artifacts with their own digests and manifest entries.

The candidate shall be reproducible or otherwise independently verifiable to the assurance level established by the Quality Profile. Unexplained difference between expected and produced artifacts blocks release.

### Release Manifest

The Release Manifest defined in Section 4.9 is the authoritative technical identity of the release. It shall enumerate exact product, component, service, package, client, API, event, schema, migration, policy, evidence-format, infrastructure, documentation, model-configuration, evaluation, dependency, source, and artifact identities as applicable.

The release decision shall bind to the manifest digest, not to a filename, mutable web page, branch, channel, or general product description. The manifest shall include maturity, support designation, compatibility matrix, Quality Profile, gate evidence, provenance, bills of materials, approvals, exceptions, publication scope, and recovery relationships.

The manifest itself shall have a versioned schema, integrity protection, accountable issuer, and verification procedure. It shall be machine-readable and human-reviewable. A release-note summary shall not replace it.

If the candidate and manifest disagree, the release fails closed. Manual correction after approval invalidates the decision and requires a new manifest and review.

### Artifact Integrity and Provenance

Every released artifact shall have an immutable digest and traceable provenance describing where, when, and under which trusted process it was built. Provenance shall bind source revisions, build definition, builder identity, resolved dependencies, parameters, outputs, and available verification material.

Artifact signing or attestation shall use approved keys, identities, algorithms, protection, rotation, revocation, and verification. A valid signature demonstrates only what the applicable trust model establishes; it does not independently prove code quality, absence of vulnerability, policy approval, license compliance, or release authority.

Registries shall prevent replacement of published artifacts and detect deletion, mutation, unauthorized replication, namespace takeover, and digest mismatch. Convenience aliases such as `latest`, `stable`, or channel pointers may move only after the immutable release is recorded and shall never be used as the sole deployment evidence.

Promotion shall copy or reference the same verified artifact. Rebuild after approval produces a different build identity and requires renewed evidence even when source is unchanged.

### Software Bill of Materials and Dependency Evidence

Releases shall include a machine-readable Software Bill of Materials appropriate to the asset, including direct and transitive components, versions, suppliers, licenses, and identifiers sufficient for vulnerability and license analysis. Where an ordinary software bill does not cover models, datasets, policies, infrastructure, or services, equivalent governed inventories shall supplement it.

The bill of materials shall correspond to the actual released artifact, not only the declared source dependencies. Generated, bundled, vendored, dynamically loaded, native, container-base, build-time, and runtime dependencies shall be included according to risk and applicable requirements.

Known-vulnerability evaluation shall use current authoritative sources, reachability and effective-control analysis, exploitability, exposure, and support state. Presence alone does not prove exploitability; absence from a scanner does not prove safety. Decisions and suppressions require rationale, owner, expiry, and evidence.

License, export, provenance, and distribution restrictions shall be resolved before publication. An unresolved component identity or prohibited license blocks the affected release channel.

### Quality Gate Acceptance

All mandatory Quality Gates from Section 4.6 shall reach Passed for the exact candidate and target maturity. Failed, Blocked, Inconclusive, Expired, Cancelled, Not Run, stale, or missing status blocks release.

Gate evidence shall identify input revision, artifact digest, configuration, environment, tool and rule version, time, outcome, defects, exceptions, and owner. A green provider badge without these bindings is insufficient.

Risk-based profiles may add gates for regulated deployments, offline packages, high-risk tools, cryptographic modules, major migrations, mobile distribution, or customer-specific extensions. They may not remove canonical trust controls.

Flaky tests, unavailable environments, false-positive scanners, or deadline pressure shall be remediated or governed through a precise exception. Re-running until a favorable result without addressing instability is not evidence of quality.

### Release Readiness Review

The Release Readiness Review is the structured decision meeting or equivalent recorded workflow through which owners examine the candidate as a complete enterprise deliverable. It shall occur after evidence is substantially complete and before final approval.

The review shall cover scope, version classification, unresolved defects, architecture decisions, security and privacy risk, compliance applicability, supply chain, compatibility, migration, backup and recovery, capacity, observability, incident readiness, documentation, support, customer communication, rollout, abort thresholds, and exceptions.

Participants shall have access to the exact evidence sufficiently in advance. Silence, attendance, or absence of objection is not approval. Each required authority shall record Approved, Approved with explicit conditions, or Denied.

New information discovered during the review may return the release to preparation or candidate validation. The meeting date shall not become a deadline that overrides evidence.

### Defect and Risk Acceptance

Release defects shall be classified by severity, likelihood, exposure, detectability, affected customers, security and privacy impact, data integrity, tenant isolation, recoverability, and contractual effect. Severity names shall map to deterministic criteria.

Critical and High defects are release-blocking by default. A lower-severity defect may also block when cumulative impact, core workflow, migration, evidence, support, or customer trust is materially affected. Defect count alone is not a readiness measure.

Risk acceptance shall identify the exact defect, affected version and profiles, evidence, reason, customer impact, compensating controls, detection, owner, accountable accepter, expiry, remediation target, and communication. Acceptance transfers no legal obligation and does not make the defect safe.

No role may accept risk outside its authority. Security cannot alone accept a product commitment; Product cannot alone accept a security or privacy breach; Engineering cannot alone accept customer legal exposure.

### Security Release Readiness

Security review shall confirm threat-model coverage, attack-surface change, identity and authorization behavior, tenant isolation, secret handling, cryptography, dependency and provenance state, Tool Gateway boundaries, policy enforcement, abuse cases, monitoring, response, and residual risk.

The candidate shall have no unresolved critical vulnerability or release-blocking high vulnerability unless an exceptional legal or operational necessity is approved at the highest applicable authority with containment, customer communication, and a time-bounded remediation path. Such approval shall not be represented as ordinary Stable security acceptance.

Security evidence may be restricted, but its existence, owner, decision, and applicability shall remain auditable. Embargoed vulnerability information shall not leak through public manifests, filenames, build metadata, or premature release notes.

Security readiness also includes the ability to identify affected versions, revoke trust, withdraw artifacts, issue advisories, rotate credentials, and distribute a corrective release.

### Privacy, Legal, and Compliance Readiness

Release review shall determine applicable privacy, legal, regulatory, contractual, localization, accessibility, licensing, export, records, and customer commitments for the exact deployment and processing purposes. Inclusion of a framework or control mapping does not establish applicability, certification, authorization, or conformity.

Processing roles shall be determined per purpose and activity. Where the customer acts as controller and ILAIOS as processor, responsibilities are defined contractually and operationally. Where ILAIOS acts in another legally recognized role, the documented role and applicability assessment governs.

The release shall support applicable rights and safeguards, including where relevant protections relating to qualifying automated decision-making, meaningful human intervention, contest, explanation, or review. The advisory reasoning layer shall not make a legal applicability decision.

Evidence and release records shall follow approved record-class-specific schedules. Personal data and other protected information shall not be retained longer than necessary or lawfully required for the defined purpose. Legal holds and extensions shall be narrow, authorized, documented, and reviewed.

### Architecture Conformance

Release readiness shall verify that the candidate remains consistent with accepted architecture and all applicable Architecture Decision Records (ADRs). Architecture-significant change without an accepted ADR blocks release even when tests pass.

The deterministic Policy Engine remains a Control Plane component. The AI Reasoning and Recommendation Engine may prepare plans or recommendations but grants no permission and initiates no execution. Model Orchestration and Provider Abstraction manages approved model access without policy authority.

Execution remains constrained through identity, tenant and request-integrity verification; Immutable Context and authority scope; policy and capability evaluation; risk classification; explicit human approval where required; time-bound execution authority; Tool Gateway; independent Validation Pipeline; acceptance or rejection; and controlled closure.

The Audit Engine and Evidence Chain operate continuously across all material stages. A release cannot create an alternate unlogged path, postpone evidence until completion, or treat model output as policy, validation, or acceptance evidence.

### Model and Intelligence-Layer Release Readiness

A model, provider, routing, instruction, evaluation, or reasoning-configuration change is release-significant when it can materially change recommendations, plans, latency, cost, privacy, safety, output contract, language coverage, or operational behavior. It shall be versioned, evaluated, and represented in the Release Manifest.

Readiness shall use representative evaluation datasets, adversarial and boundary cases, regression baselines, provider-failure scenarios, output-schema validation, privacy controls, and human review appropriate to the use. Model quality averages shall not conceal material failures for protected, high-risk, or core workflows.

Provider labels may be mutable. Evidence shall capture the observed provider identity, available model revision, routing configuration, time, and evaluation state. A provider's assertion does not replace ILAIOS validation.

No model release receives action authority. Policy, approval, capability issuance, Tool Gateway constraints, Validation Pipeline, Audit Engine, and Evidence Chain remain deterministic or independently governed controls around model behavior.

### Policy and Capability Release Readiness

Policy bundles, capability definitions, approval templates, risk tables, and validation rules are security-sensitive release inputs. Their exact versions shall be immutable and included in the candidate, compatibility matrix, deployment plan, audit, and evidence.

Readiness shall prove allow, deny, conflict, missing-data, stale-context, revoked-capability, expiry, tenant boundary, approval, and fail-closed behavior. Policy changes shall be tested against representative existing decisions and expected customer configurations.

A policy update that changes permitted action, approval, tool access, data handling, or risk may require its own release and customer communication even when software bytes do not change. A mutable `default` alias shall resolve to an approved immutable version before deployment and evaluation.

Reasoning output may explain or propose policy content but cannot approve, activate, or override the policy release.

### Data, Schema, and Migration Readiness

A release containing data or schema change shall identify compatible starting states, ordered migrations, checksums, duration, capacity, lock behavior, validation, reconciliation, privacy effect, backup or recovery point, mixed-version operation, and forward-recovery or rollback support.
