Retrospectives provide structured reflection on a bounded period, release, feature, project, incident, change, or workflow. They shall produce evidence-backed learning rather than generic sentiment or blame.

A retrospective should examine:

- intended outcome and actual outcome;
- what supported value, trust, quality, and flow;
- what created delay, rework, defect, risk, confusion, or customer impact;
- decisions, assumptions, dependencies, handoffs, tools, and environmental conditions;
- missing or misleading metrics;
- near misses and unreported work;
- practices to preserve, change, stop, or test; and
- owned improvement records with priority and evidence.

Participation shall support psychological safety while maintaining accountability. Sensitive information shall use protected handling. A retrospective is not complete because a meeting occurred; material actions require stable identities and lifecycle follow-through.

### Post-Incident and Post-Change Learning

Incidents, failed changes, rollbacks, emergency releases, and recovery events require learning proportionate to impact. The review shall examine prevention, detection, response, containment, communication, recovery, and recurrence.

It shall identify:

- triggering and contributing conditions;
- why controls did or did not operate;
- customer, tenant, data, security, privacy, compliance, and evidence impact;
- decision and authority quality;
- observability and Evidence Chain gaps;
- recovery and continuity effectiveness;
- documentation, training, provider, staffing, and coordination issues; and
- corrective and preventive improvements.

Corrective action is not complete when a ticket, policy, or training assignment exists. The resulting outcome must be independently verified. Lessons shall not expose confidential incident, exploit, customer, or personal data beyond need.

### Defect Prevention and Quality Improvement

Defect data shall be analyzed for recurrence, escape stage, affected boundary, detection gap, root cause, component, release, provider, and customer impact.

Quality improvement may include:

- clearer requirements and acceptance criteria;
- architecture simplification and stronger interfaces;
- coding-profile and static-analysis rules;
- targeted unit, integration, contract, security, migration, resilience, and regression tests;
- better test data, environment equivalence, nondeterminism control, and evidence;
- improved review competence, code ownership, or change size;
- stronger Quality Gates and release or change validation;
- observability, reconciliation, and incident detection; and
- deprecation of unsafe or unsupportable behavior.

Defect-count reduction shall not be achieved through severity downgrading, duplicate suppression, reduced reporting, premature closure, or narrowing scope after impact.

### Engineering Flow Improvement

Flow improvement shall reduce safe time to value without weakening assurance. Analysis shall distinguish active work from wait, rework, blocked authority, dependency delay, environment delay, review queue, gate instability, and release or customer-window delay.

Potential interventions include:

- smaller coherent work units;
- clearer intake and acceptance;
- earlier architecture, security, privacy, data, and operational assessment;
- reusable components, test harnesses, and controlled templates;
- deterministic automation of repetitive checks;
- improved reviewer allocation and knowledge distribution;
- stable environments and reproducible builds;
- reduced provider and dependency uncertainty;
- better release and change coordination; and
- removal of unnecessary approval that provides no assurance while preserving required authority.

Faster flow is invalid if defect escape, security exposure, evidence gaps, support burden, customer disruption, or long-term maintenance increases unacceptably.

### Quality Gate and Test-System Improvement

Quality Gates and tests shall be improved based on defects, incidents, false positives, false negatives, flakiness, bypasses, runtime evidence, and changing threats.

Improvement shall assess:

- whether the gate tests the intended property;
- coverage of trust boundaries and failure modes;
- rule, tool, baseline, suppression, and threshold quality;
- execution time, determinism, environment, and feedback usefulness;
- evidence binding to exact revisions and candidates;
- developer and reviewer understanding;
- maintenance and ownership; and
- risk of incentivizing bypass or gaming.

Removing or weakening a gate requires evidence that assurance is maintained through a better control. Slow or inconvenient gates are not automatically unnecessary.

### Code Review Improvement

Review improvement shall use evidence from escaped defects, blocked time, review quality, ownership concentration, stale approvals, specialist coverage, bootstrap exposure, and post-merge failures.

Interventions may include:

- smaller changes and improved descriptions;
- risk-based reviewer assignment;
- code-owner and specialist mapping;
- review checklists tied to architecture and threat models;
- protected evidence routes;
- reviewer training and rotation;
- automated diff, dependency, schema, and policy analysis;
- clearer blocking-finding semantics; and
- post-merge verification and feedback.

Review speed shall not be improved through rubber-stamping, comment suppression, reduced independence, or author-controlled approval.

### Release and Change Improvement

Release and Change Management shall be improved using candidate rejection, gate failure, emergency use, rollback, migration, change collision, support, customer adoption, and recovery evidence.

Improvement may address:

- candidate immutability and manifest completeness;
- build reproducibility, provenance, Software Bill of Materials, and signing;
- scope control and smaller releases;
- deployment automation and environment consistency;
- progressive rollout and observation;
- migration rehearsal and data reconciliation;
- Standard Change Template quality;
- change calendar, freeze, and collision management;
- rollback and forward-recovery readiness;
- customer-controlled delivery and evidence; and
- support handover and withdrawal.

Higher release frequency or automation is not an improvement when release identity, validation, customer authority, or recovery is weakened.

### Security, Privacy, and Compliance Improvement

Security, privacy, and compliance improvement shall be driven by threat intelligence, incidents, vulnerabilities, assessments, customer assurance, obligation changes, and control evidence.

Improvement shall preserve the distinction between:

- legal applicability and technical recommendation;
- control implementation and operating effectiveness;
- alignment and certification;
- current obligation and proposed regulation;
- customer and ILAIOS processing roles; and
- evidence integrity and evidence completeness.

Potential improvements include threat-model coverage, phishing-resistant authentication, authorization checks, key custody, secret rotation, dependency security, data minimization, rights support, retention schedules, evidence reconciliation, incident response, and customer assurance.

Compliance labels or audit completion shall not become the improvement objective by themselves. The objective is sustainable fulfillment of applicable obligations and accurate claims.

### Model and Intelligence Improvement Boundaries

Improvement of reasoning, recommendations, confidence, context, knowledge, planning, model routing, or provider quality shall remain within the canonical intelligence boundary.

The process may improve:

- task population and evaluation coverage;
- context provenance, freshness, relevance, and minimization;
- model selection and provider abstraction;
- prompt or instruction quality;
- confidence calibration and uncertainty presentation;
- human review and contestability;
- latency, cost, fallback, and provider exit;
- adversarial robustness and output validation; and
- documentation of limitations.

It shall not transfer identity, policy, approval, capability, execution, validation, release, legal, compliance, or evidence authority to probabilistic systems. A model shall not modify its own policy, tools, permissions, code, tests, evaluation criteria, or production configuration without the normal governed change path.

Learning signals may propose an update. They shall not authorize or apply it. Section 6.8 defines the detailed Learning Boundaries.

### Provider and Supply-Chain Improvement

Provider and dependency improvement shall reduce concentration, vulnerability, licensing, data-processing, continuity, cost, and exit risk while preserving supported behavior.

The process shall assess:

- provider or dependency performance against current requirements;
- security and incident history;
- maintenance, end-of-life, compatibility, and patching;
- data role, region, transfer, retention, training use, and subprocessor state;
- service, interface, version, model, rate, latency, and availability changes;
- licensing, redistribution, provenance, and Software Bill of Materials;
- portability, substitution, migration, and customer impact; and
- contract and shared responsibility.

Replacement shall follow normal architecture, development, release, migration, and change controls. Provider marketing or benchmark leadership is not sufficient evidence.

### Technical Debt Management

Technical debt is a governed future cost or risk created by complexity, duplication, obsolete dependency, unsupported variation, inadequate tests, missing documentation, temporary control, architecture drift, or deferred maintenance. It shall not be used as a vague label for disliked code.

Technical-debt records shall identify:

- affected product, component, control, interface, dependency, or workflow;
- specific future cost, risk, failure, or constraint;
- origin and whether it was deliberate;
- current containment and evidence;
- customer, security, privacy, operational, support, and roadmap impact;
- remediation options, dependencies, and expected outcome;
- owner, priority, review trigger, and expiry for temporary debt; and
- relationship to canonical architecture and ADRs.

Debt priority shall consider compound risk and cost, not only immediate feature value. Repeated emergency work, exceptions, brittle migration, unsupported provider, unowned code, and persistent bootstrap dependence are debt signals.

Refactoring shall follow product and architecture authority and shall not become an opportunity for speculative redesign.

### Process Debt and Control Debt

Process debt exists when a workflow depends on undocumented knowledge, manual heroics, stale templates, ambiguous authority, repeated exception, weak evidence, or unowned handoff. Control debt exists when an intended security, privacy, quality, operational, or governance control is incomplete, temporary, difficult to validate, or routinely bypassed.

Such debt shall be recorded with:

- exact process or control;
- affected outcomes and risks;
- evidence of recurrence or fragility;
- temporary safeguards;
- responsible owner and authority;
- remediation and validation plan; and
- deadline or review trigger.

Control debt involving non-waivable protections cannot be normalized as permanent operation. Stable or Enterprise claims shall reflect the actual assurance state.

### Knowledge and Capability Improvement

Improvement shall reduce dependence on undocumented individual knowledge and strengthen competent decision-making. Activities may include controlled documentation, training, exercises, mentoring, rotation, runbook rehearsal, architecture walkthroughs, incident simulations, recovery tests, and specialist development.

Capability improvement shall be tied to observable needs and outcomes. Training completion alone is not evidence of competence. Validation may include review quality, exercise performance, reduced error, successful recovery, or independent demonstration.

Knowledge artifacts shall identify authority, version, owner, audience, confidentiality, and review date. Training shall not teach shortcuts that conflict with canonical architecture or protected controls.

### Automation Improvement

Automation improvements shall target repeatable, deterministic, measurable work. Appropriate areas may include formatting, testing, scanning, build, manifest generation, evidence collection, change prechecks, deployment, reconciliation, monitoring, and reporting.

Automation shall be assessed for:

- scope and authority;
- false positive and false negative behavior;
- determinism, idempotency, retries, timeouts, and failure handling;
- privilege, secrets, keys, data, tenant, provider, and network access;
- versioning, review, tests, deployment, rollback, and observability;
- audit and evidence completeness;
- human override and accountability; and
- new operational or maintenance burden.

Automation shall not improve a process by hiding failure, suppressing evidence, removing meaningful approval, or granting probabilistic systems authority.

### Documentation and Standard Improvement

Documentation shall evolve to improve clarity, accuracy, discoverability, accessibility, and consistency without changing accepted architectural intent silently.

Documentation improvement shall:

- preserve one authoritative source for each controlled fact;
- remove genuine duplication and conflict;
- update cross-references, terminology, metadata, and status;
- distinguish current, planned, deprecated, and retired behavior;
- preserve accepted decisions unless an authorized ADR supersedes them;
- verify public claims against product and release evidence;
- protect confidential information;
- validate generated Word, PDF, portal, or other publication outputs at the final production stage; and
- retain historical versions and supersession relationships.

Editorial improvement shall not become redesign. Final document publication remains deferred until Sections 1–9 and the Final Canonical Audit are complete.

### Customer Feedback and Co-Improvement

Customer feedback shall be collected and interpreted under approved confidentiality, purpose, data, and contractual conditions. Customers may identify problems, outcomes, integration needs, support gaps, and operational constraints, but they do not unilaterally define ILAIOS architecture or waive protected controls.

The process shall distinguish:

- individual configuration preference from repeatable product need;
- support request from defect;
- feature request from obligation;
- purchasing interest from product outcome;
- customer-controlled responsibility from ILAIOS-controlled behavior; and
- anecdote from representative evidence.

Co-improvement pilots shall have bounded scope, maturity, responsibilities, data treatment, support, evidence, and exit. Customer participation does not convert experimental capability into Stable support.

### Improvement Governance and Decision Rights

Every improvement shall have an accountable owner and competent decision rights. Roles may include:

- product authority for problem, customer outcome, Product Scope, priority, and adoption;
- architecture authority for conformance and ADR decisions;
- engineering authority for feasibility, implementation, quality, and maintainability;
- security, privacy, data, compliance, licensing, and legal authorities for their domains;
- quality authority for measurement, validation, and evidence;
- operational authority for service, recovery, and sustained monitoring;
- release and change authorities for implementation and rollout;
- support and customer authorities for customer impact and shared responsibility; and
- leadership or governance authority for cross-product standards and resource allocation.

No role may approve beyond competence. An improvement owner cannot validate the intervention independently by assertion. Model output, provider recommendation, sales commitment, customer preference, or metric movement has no unilateral decision authority.

### Single-Maintainer Bootstrap Profile

During a registered Single-Maintainer Bootstrap Profile, one authorized maintainer may identify, analyze, implement, and self-review improvement work within the documented bootstrap scope. The absence of independent prioritization, review, validation, or governance shall be recorded honestly.

Bootstrap improvement shall maintain:

- stable Improvement Record and evidence;
- explicit hypotheses, baselines, guardrails, and stop criteria;
- canonical architecture and ADR conformance;
- atomic branch, protected primary branch, Pull Request or Change Request, self-review, mandatory automated Quality Gates, controlled merge, and post-merge verification;
- limited maturity and customer or production exposure;
- independent external review or validation for high-impact improvements before adoption into a Stable release, production standard, or Enterprise operating profile;
- protected key, signing, tenant, data, security, privacy, audit, and Evidence Chain controls; and
- dated exit criteria and periodic review.

Self-review and self-validation shall not be represented as Enterprise independence. Multiple accounts do not create independent governance. A second competent reviewer or authority shall be added when the Enterprise Profile becomes applicable. Bootstrap operation shall not become permanent through inaction.

### Improvement Automation and Reasoning Assistance

Automation may detect trends, correlate records, calculate metrics, identify candidate causes, generate experiment proposals, recommend tests, and track actions. Reasoning assistance may synthesize evidence or propose alternatives.

Such systems shall not:

- redefine the Product Constitution, Product Scope, architecture, standard, metric, or success criterion;
- approve their own hypothesis or intervention;
- change production code, policy, configuration, model, provider, tool, or permission without the normal change path;
- select or exclude customer or personal data outside approved purpose;
- accept risk, dismiss findings, close corrective actions, or certify success;
- suppress contrary evidence; or
- authorize runtime action.

Outputs remain untrusted recommendations subject to provenance, validation, accountable ownership, deterministic policy, required approval, constrained capability, Tool Gateway execution, independent Validation Pipeline assessment, audit, and Evidence Chain.

### Audit and Evidence Across Continuous Improvement

The Audit Engine and Evidence Chain operate continuously across signal intake, triage, baseline, analysis, hypothesis, approval, experiment, implementation, measurement, validation, adoption, standardization, monitoring, reversal, and closure.

Material evidence shall bind, as applicable, to:

- Improvement ID and linked feature, defect, incident, review, release, change, ADR, risk, customer, provider, audit, and corrective-action records;
- actor, role, authority, tenant or product scope, time, and independence state;
- baseline, metric definition, dataset, query, instrumentation, release, environment, provider, cohort, and limitation;
- hypothesis, intervention, input, output, result, guardrail, deviation, decision, and preceding event;
- source, revision, candidate, artifact, deployment, configuration, policy, and standard version; and
- confidentiality, access, retention, legal hold, supersession, and closure.

Cryptographic integrity does not establish causal validity, measurement correctness, or evidence completeness. Improvement evidence requires expected-event models, data-quality controls, independent validation, and reconciliation.

Personal, customer, employee, security, and operational data shall be minimized and retained under approved record-class-specific schedules. Continuous Improvement is not a justification for indefinite analytics retention.

### Continuous Improvement Metrics

Continuous Improvement shall measure both improvement flow and improvement effectiveness. Metric families include:

- signal-to-triage, triage-to-analysis, analysis-to-decision, approval-to-experiment, validation, standardization, and closure time;
- opportunity backlog, blocked time, deferral, rejection, adaptation, stopped, reversed, and reopened rates;
- hypothesis confirmation, inconclusive result, guardrail breach, and sustained-outcome rate;
- defect recurrence, incident recurrence, change failure, rollback, release rejection, review escape, and Quality Gate detection;
- deployment time, evidence coverage, policy compliance, task success, recovery time, security incidents, and customer adoption;
- technical-debt age, control-debt age, expired exception, temporary-flag age, unsupported dependency, provider concentration, and bootstrap exposure;
- documentation accuracy, training effectiveness, ownership concentration, reviewer capacity, and continuity; and
- customer outcome, support effort, accessibility, operational burden, cost, and sustainability.

Metric definitions, data sources, privacy basis, owners, segmentation, limitations, thresholds, and review cadence shall be controlled. Improvement metrics shall not reward action-item volume, meeting frequency, tool adoption, or process growth without verified outcome.

### Anti-Gaming and Unintended Incentives

Every material improvement metric shall be reviewed for incentives and gaming. The process shall detect behavior such as:

- splitting work to improve cycle time;
- suppressing or downgrading defects;
- closing records before outcome verification;
- avoiding high-risk customers or complex work;
- weakening tests to improve pass rate;
- reducing review depth to improve turnaround;
- relabeling emergency or failed changes;
- excluding adverse cohorts;
- delaying incident declaration;
- moving residual work outside measured systems; or
- collecting unnecessary personal data to improve observability.

Guardrails, independent evidence, qualitative review, and metric rotation or retirement shall be used where measures distort behavior. No single metric shall determine individual performance, product quality, or change authority.

### Improvement Review Cadence

Continuous Improvement shall operate at multiple cadences appropriate to risk and decision horizon. Cadences may include:

- immediate learning after Critical or High incidents and failed changes;
- release and deployment reviews;
- periodic product, security, privacy, quality, reliability, support, and provider reviews;
- quarterly or strategic portfolio review;
- annual standards, maturity, continuity, and enterprise-readiness review; and
- event-driven review after regulatory, contractual, architecture, customer, threat, or provider change.

Cadence shall not become ceremonial. Each review shall use current evidence, identify decisions, assign owners, and track outcomes. Stable performance does not eliminate event-driven reassessment.

### Closure and Knowledge Preservation

An Improvement Record may close only when its decision and resulting obligations are reconciled. Closure shall confirm:

- final outcome: adopted, adapted, rejected, stopped, reversed, or deferred;
- evidence, limitations, guardrails, and sustained-monitoring state;
- implementation, release, change, customer, and operational relationships;
- standards, ADRs, Quality Gates, documentation, training, ownership, and support updates;
- cleanup of experiments, data, access, providers, environments, flags, credentials, and temporary instrumentation;
- residual actions with stable identity, owner, and review trigger;
- communication to affected stakeholders; and
- retention, confidentiality, legal hold, access, and disposal authority.

Knowledge shall be preserved in authoritative artifacts rather than private memory. Negative and inconclusive results shall remain discoverable within their confidentiality class. Closure does not prevent reopening when new evidence invalidates the result.

### Improvement Exceptions

An improvement-process exception shall identify the exact Improvement ID, requirement, scope, reason, risk, authority, affected customers and claims, alternatives, compensating controls, evidence, owner, start, expiry, review, remediation, and effect on adoption or standardization.

An exception cannot authorize:

- violation of law or unauthorized data use;
- silent change to Product Constitution, Product Scope, canonical architecture, or non-waivable control;
- architecture redesign without an ADR;
- tenant-isolation failure, probabilistic policy authority, missing required approval, unconstrained capability, Tool Gateway bypass, self-validation, Audit Engine bypass, Evidence Chain fabrication, privacy violation, or loss of human accountability;
- ungoverned self-modification by a model, provider, tool, or automation system;
- metric manipulation, suppression of negative evidence, or false causal claim;
- failed mandatory Quality Gate represented as pass;
- ordinary direct push to a protected primary branch;
- false independent review, validation, Enterprise maturity, certification, or compliance representation;
- indefinite experiment, pilot, temporary control, risk acceptance, emergency state, or bootstrap operation; or
- closure without verified outcome and ownership.

Expired exceptions block adoption or standardization or require competent renewal. Repeated exceptions indicate systemic governance, architecture, capacity, measurement, or process weakness.

### Continuous Improvement Invariants

The following invariants are canonical:

- every material improvement has a stable Improvement ID, accountable owner, evidence-backed problem, baseline, hypothesis, scope, guardrails, authority, validation, and Improvement Record;
- continuous improvement is a governed learning loop and does not authorize uncontrolled self-modification, perpetual redesign, or speculative feature expansion;
- Product Constitution, Product Scope, canonical architecture, accepted ADRs, and non-waivable controls remain binding;
- architecture-changing improvement requires an authorized ADR before implementation or standardization;
- observation, analysis, recommendation, approval, experiment, implementation, validation, adoption, standardization, monitoring, and closure remain distinct events;
- implementation completion or positive short-term metric movement does not establish improvement;
- negative and inconclusive results remain attributable and cannot be suppressed to justify adoption;
- metrics have controlled definitions, privacy basis, limitations, segmentation, guardrails, and no independent authority;
- a primary metric cannot establish success when a non-waivable guardrail fails;
- customer, employee, personal, security, and operational data is collected and retained only under approved purpose and minimization;
- deterministic Policy Engine authority, required human approval, constrained capabilities, Tool Gateway execution, independent Validation Pipeline assessment, tenant isolation, Audit Engine, Evidence Chain, privacy, security, safety, and human accountability remain protected;
- reasoning, models, providers, analytics, and automation may propose improvements but grant no permission, apply no production change, validate no result independently, accept no risk, and close no record;
- successful local practice becomes an Enterprise standard only after transfer assessment, authorization, evidence, ownership, documentation, and sustained monitoring;
- defect, incident, audit, release, review, change, and customer histories are not rewritten to manufacture an improvement narrative;
- ordinary direct push to protected primary branches remains prohibited under the canonical workflow;
- emergency and bootstrap profiles remain constrained, honest, temporary, and subject to dated exit or retrospective obligations;
- bootstrap self-review and self-validation are not represented as independent Enterprise assurance;
- the Audit Engine and Evidence Chain operate continuously across all material improvement events;
- closure requires outcome, standardization, monitoring, communication, cleanup, evidence, and residual ownership to be reconciled;
- final Word and PDF publication of this handbook occurs only after Sections 1–9 and the Final Canonical Audit are complete; and
- Improvement Records follow approved record-class-specific retention schedules and are not retained indefinitely by default.

A Continuous Improvement implementation is non-conformant if it starts with a preferred tool or solution without a defined problem and baseline; treats faster, cheaper, more automated, more frequently released, or more widely used as inherently better; silently changes Product Scope or architecture; implements improvement outside the Development, Review, Release, and Change lifecycles; lets reasoning, models, providers, analytics, or automation approve and apply their own change; bypasses deterministic policy, required human approval, capability restrictions, Tool Gateway, independent validation, tenant isolation, Audit Engine, Evidence Chain, privacy, security, or human accountability; uses customer or employee data without approved purpose; selects a favorable cohort or period while hiding adverse outcomes; suppresses failed or inconclusive experiments; changes metrics after results to manufacture success; improves a primary measure while violating a non-waivable guardrail; treats publication of a standard, creation of a ticket, completion of training, code merge, deployment, or short-term metric movement as verified improvement; permits ordinary direct push to a protected primary branch; represents bootstrap self-validation as independent Enterprise assurance; standardizes a local result without transfer evidence; retains analytics data indefinitely without purpose; closes with unowned corrective action; or rewrites history to conceal failure, incident, defect, rollback, or prior nonconformance.

# 6. AI & Intelligence Layer

Qualified external review shall be completed before an affected capability, profile, model route, graph use, repository analysis, context profile, plan, or learning-derived artifact influences a Stable release, production environment, customer-controlled production deployment, or Enterprise operating profile; otherwise it shall remain blocked, prerelease, non-production, advisory-only, or constrained. This section-wide terminology distinguishes Stable release maturity from production deployment and Enterprise operating assurance and applies consistently to Sections 6.1–6.8.

## 6.1 AI Reasoning and Recommendation Engine

### Purpose and Canonical Role

The AI Reasoning and Recommendation Engine is the intelligence-layer capability that transforms an authorized, bounded request and its approved context into structured analysis, candidate plans, options, explanations, and recommendations. Its purpose is to amplify human and organizational capability while preserving the deterministic control boundaries of the ILAIOS Enterprise AI Operating System.

The engine is advisory by design. It may interpret information, identify relevant relationships, compare alternatives, detect ambiguity, decompose objectives, formulate candidate actions, estimate uncertainty, and recommend a preferred course. It shall not authenticate an identity, determine legal authority, grant a capability, approve risk, waive a control, authorize execution, invoke a controlled tool directly, declare its own output valid, accept a result, or close an accountable business record.

The term reasoning describes the production of analysis and recommendations from controlled inputs. It does not establish consciousness, independent authority, factual infallibility, or organizational accountability. The term recommendation identifies a proposed course that remains subject to deterministic policy evaluation, risk classification, required human approval, constrained capability issuance, controlled execution, independent validation, and recorded acceptance or rejection.

The engine therefore occupies a deliberately bounded position in the canonical operational flow. It acts after request intake, identity and tenant verification, request-integrity verification, and Immutable Context creation. It acts before deterministic policy and capability evaluation. Its output is an input to later control decisions; it is never the decision itself.

### Architectural Status

The AI Reasoning and Recommendation Engine is an Intelligence Plane component. It is not part of the deterministic Control Plane and shall not be represented as a replacement for the Policy Engine, Approval Engine, authorization services, risk authority, Tool Gateway, Validation Pipeline, Audit Engine, or Evidence Chain.

The Policy Engine remains the deterministic authority for evaluating applicable policy, capability constraints, prohibitions, obligations, and conditions against controlled inputs. The Approval Engine remains the authority for creating, binding, expiring, revoking, and evidencing approvals. The Tool Gateway remains the only authorized boundary for controlled execution. The Validation Pipeline remains independent from the reasoning process and from the component that performed execution. The Audit Engine and Evidence Chain operate continuously across every material reasoning event.

The engine may use probabilistic methods, learned representations, search, retrieval, rules, symbolic processing, statistical analysis, or combinations of these methods. The use of a probabilistic technique does not make the surrounding control system probabilistic. ILAIOS shall contain probabilistic reasoning within deterministic contracts, schemas, policies, authority boundaries, failure behavior, audit requirements, and validation obligations.

No model, provider, prompt, inference configuration, ranking method, retrieval source, recommendation, or confidence estimate becomes a source of authority merely because it is accurate, widely adopted, commercially supported, or technically advanced. Models are replaceable components. Canonical authority remains with applicable law, the Product Constitution, accepted architecture, deterministic controls, competent organizational roles, and approved records.

### Objectives

The engine shall support the following objectives:

- produce useful analysis without acquiring execution authority;
- convert complex requests into bounded and reviewable problem statements;
- develop one or more candidate approaches rather than concealing material alternatives;
- distinguish facts, supplied assertions, retrieved information, assumptions, inferences, estimates, and recommendations;
- identify missing information, uncertainty, conflicts, dependencies, constraints, and potential failure modes;
- produce machine-readable and human-reviewable Recommendation Envelopes;
- preserve tenant, identity, purpose, data, regional, confidentiality, and retention boundaries;
- make the basis, limitations, provenance, and expected consequences of a recommendation available to downstream controls and competent reviewers;
- support reproducibility to the extent permitted by the selected reasoning method and recorded configuration;
- fail safely when required context, authority scope, provenance, structural validity, or minimum assurance is absent;
- remain provider-independent through the abstraction defined in Section 6.2;
- support independent validation without defining or controlling the validator's acceptance criteria;
- create continuous audit and evidence records without treating logging as proof of correctness; and
- preserve human accountability for decisions that require human judgment, approval, ownership, or legal responsibility.

Optimization for fluency, completion rate, latency, cost, or user preference shall not supersede security, privacy, tenant isolation, policy compliance, factual integrity, evidence quality, or human accountability.

### Non-Authority Boundary

The engine shall never be treated as an authorization source. It may recommend that a capability be requested, but it cannot create or expand that capability. It may identify that an approval appears necessary, but it cannot satisfy the approval. It may describe a policy, but it cannot determine that the policy has been lawfully waived. It may estimate risk, but the estimate does not constitute risk acceptance. It may propose a tool invocation, but it cannot call the controlled tool outside the Tool Gateway. It may analyze an execution result, but it cannot independently validate a result produced through a path that depends on the same reasoning state.

The following artifacts are explicitly non-authoritative when produced by the engine:

- statements that an identity, tenant, entitlement, role, approval, contract, consent, or legal basis is valid;
- claims that an action is permitted, safe, compliant, certified, approved, production-ready, or risk-accepted;
- inferred credentials, capabilities, secrets, tokens, signatures, or access grants;
- self-issued exceptions, overrides, emergency declarations, control waivers, or release approvals;
- declarations that a Quality Gate, validation condition, acceptance criterion, remediation, or incident is complete;
- conclusions that evidence is complete, authentic, sufficient, or legally admissible merely because a response was generated; and
- instructions that attempt to bypass policy, human approval, tenant boundaries, data minimization, Tool Gateway controls, or independent validation.

Downstream systems shall not interpret natural-language confidence, imperative language, role simulation, or apparent certainty as authority. Authority shall be represented only through approved, typed, attributable, time-bounded, and verifiable control-plane records.

### Position in the Canonical Operational Flow

The engine participates in the canonical flow as follows:

1. A request is received through an authorized interface.
2. Identity, tenant, request integrity, and applicable session or service context are verified outside the engine.
3. An Immutable Context is created with the bounded purpose, authority scope, classifications, policy references, data constraints, and correlation identifiers available at that time.
4. The engine receives a Reasoning Request derived from that context and prepares analysis, options, or a proposed plan.
5. The resulting Recommendation Envelope is evaluated by the deterministic Policy Engine and applicable capability controls.
6. Risk is classified through the approved deterministic and accountable process.
7. Explicit human approval is obtained where required.
8. A constrained and time-bound execution authority is issued by the competent control-plane service.
9. Authorized operations are executed only through the Tool Gateway and approved isolation boundary.
10. Results are assessed through the independent Validation Pipeline.
11. A competent service or human authority accepts, rejects, limits, or returns the result for further work.
12. Delivery, closure, and review are completed under the applicable lifecycle.

The engine may be invoked again when a request is returned for clarification, when policy requires revision, when an approval imposes conditions, when execution produces new bounded information, or when validation rejects a result. Each invocation is a new attributable reasoning event. A later invocation shall not overwrite the earlier Recommendation Envelope or conceal why the recommendation changed.

### Reasoning Request Contract

Every invocation shall begin with a typed Reasoning Request. Unstructured interface text may be part of the request payload, but it shall not be the complete authority or context model. The request contract shall bind the reasoning event to the verified platform state and shall contain or reference, as applicable:

- a unique Reasoning Request ID and end-to-end correlation ID;
- the verified tenant and applicable organizational scope;
- the authenticated requesting subject or service identity reference;
- the request origin, channel, time, integrity status, and classification;
- the bounded business purpose and requested outcome;
- the authority scope made available for analysis, without implying execution permission;
- applicable data classifications, residency restrictions, confidentiality constraints, and handling rules;
- the Immutable Context version or digest;
- permitted context sources and prohibited source classes;
- the requested reasoning mode and output contract;
- required language, locale, jurisdictional, accessibility, and audience constraints where relevant;
- applicable policy, approval, risk, retention, and evidence references known before reasoning;
- token, cost, latency, depth, and resource limits where governed;
- the minimum provenance, citation, explanation, and confidence requirements;
- expected downstream consumers and their schema versions;
- a deadline or expiry where the analysis is time-sensitive; and
- an explicit statement that the request grants no execution authority.

The engine shall reject or return for clarification a request that lacks a tenant boundary, cannot be associated with a valid Immutable Context, has an invalid schema, exceeds an approved purpose, requests prohibited data use, attempts to grant authority through narrative text, or requires a decision reserved to a competent human or deterministic control.

Request normalization shall preserve material meaning. Ambiguous terms, conflicting constraints, missing units, unstated time frames, inconsistent identities, and undefined success criteria shall be surfaced rather than silently resolved when the resolution could affect risk, scope, cost, rights, security, or outcome.

### Immutable Context Consumption

The engine consumes a projection of Immutable Context appropriate to the request. It shall not mutate the authoritative context, expand its own visibility, or infer that inaccessible information is authorized merely because it may improve an answer. Context enrichment shall occur through a controlled service that preserves source, purpose, tenant, classification, time, and access metadata.

The engine shall distinguish between:

- authoritative context supplied by verified platform records;
- customer-provided information whose accuracy is asserted but not independently verified;
- retrieved information with recorded source and retrieval time;
- derived context produced by deterministic processing;
- prior reasoning output that remains non-authoritative;
- assumptions introduced to explore an alternative; and
- unknown or unavailable information.

A recommendation shall not elevate an assumption, prior model output, user assertion, or retrieved fragment into an authoritative fact. Material dependencies on non-authoritative information shall be visible in the Recommendation Envelope.

Context shall be minimized to what is relevant and permitted for the defined purpose. Broad historical data, unrelated tenant information, personal data, secrets, privileged legal material, security-sensitive configuration, or unrestricted repository content shall not be included merely because it is technically accessible. Context selection shall follow least privilege, privacy by design, need to know, and record-class-specific handling requirements.

### Reasoning Modes

An approved implementation may support multiple reasoning modes, each with a defined contract, limitations, and downstream use. Modes may include:

- **Interpretation:** clarifies a request, document, requirement, event, or result without granting authority;
- **Decomposition:** separates an objective into bounded problems, dependencies, constraints, and candidate work items;
- **Option Generation:** produces materially distinct alternatives and identifies their expected benefits, costs, constraints, and risks;
- **Recommendation:** identifies a preferred option and explains the evidence, assumptions, trade-offs, and residual uncertainty;
- **Planning Proposal:** creates an ordered, bounded, reversible where possible, and policy-evaluable candidate plan for the Planning Engine;
- **Diagnostic Analysis:** proposes possible causes, discriminating observations, and safe investigative steps without declaring an unverified cause as fact;
- **Impact Analysis:** identifies potentially affected components, customers, data, controls, contracts, operations, documentation, or lifecycle records;
- **Summarization for Decision Support:** condenses approved information for a defined audience while preserving material qualifications and traceability;
- **Classification Recommendation:** suggests a category or risk indicator for deterministic or human determination; and
- **Explanation:** describes the basis and limitations of an existing recommendation, policy result, validation result, or system event without rewriting the authoritative record.

Modes shall not be used to obscure authority. A classification recommendation is not an authoritative classification. A planning proposal is not an approved plan. A diagnostic hypothesis is not a resolved defect. An impact analysis is not an accepted risk assessment. A summary is not a replacement for the controlled source when the source remains necessary to make a decision.

### Recommendation Envelope

Every material output shall be represented as a Recommendation Envelope rather than as unrestricted prose alone. Human-readable explanation may be included, but the machine-readable envelope is the controlled interface to downstream systems.

The Recommendation Envelope shall contain or reference, as applicable:

- a unique Recommendation ID and the originating Reasoning Request ID;
- the tenant, subject, purpose, correlation, and Immutable Context references;
- the reasoning mode and output-schema version;
- a concise problem statement and requested outcome;
- the facts relied upon, with authority and provenance classifications;
- customer assertions and other unverified inputs relied upon;
- assumptions introduced by the reasoning process;
- missing, conflicting, stale, or inaccessible information;
- the options considered and the basis for excluding material alternatives;
- the recommended option or proposed plan;
- expected outcomes, preconditions, dependencies, side effects, and failure modes;
- affected resources, tenants, data classes, environments, contracts, policies, and lifecycle records where known;
- requested capabilities expressed as proposals, not grants;
- predicted risk indicators and escalation triggers without constituting risk acceptance;
- proposed validation and rollback considerations without controlling the independent validator;
- confidence and uncertainty representations with their interpretation and limitations;
- source, retrieval, configuration, model-family, provider-abstraction, and reasoning-policy references needed for traceability;
- warnings, limitations, prohibited interpretations, and required human review;
- validity period or conditions under which the recommendation becomes stale;
- the engine outcome status; and
- integrity metadata sufficient to associate the envelope with the Evidence Chain.

The envelope shall not contain active credentials, reusable secrets, unrestricted capabilities, or narrative fields that downstream systems interpret as direct execution commands. Proposed actions shall use a typed, inert representation. The Tool Gateway shall accept only separately authorized operations that bind to approved capability and policy decisions; it shall not treat a Recommendation Envelope as an execution token.

### Output Status Model

Every invocation shall produce one registered outcome status. The minimum status model is:

- **Completed:** the requested analysis was produced within the contract, subject to stated limitations;
- **Completed with Limitations:** useful output was produced, but material constraints, uncertainty, source gaps, or reduced assurance remain;
- **Clarification Required:** the request cannot be responsibly completed without additional bounded information or an accountable choice;
- **Insufficient Context:** required authorized context is absent or unavailable;
- **Policy Referral:** the request appears to require deterministic policy evaluation before further reasoning can proceed safely;
- **Human Determination Required:** the requested conclusion is reserved to a competent human authority;
- **Unsupported:** the approved reasoning capability cannot perform the requested mode or satisfy the required contract;
- **Refused:** the request is prohibited, outside purpose, attempts to bypass controls, or creates unacceptable safety, security, privacy, or rights risk;
- **Expired:** the request or supporting context became stale before completion;
- **Cancelled:** the invocation was stopped through an authorized cancellation path; and
- **Failed:** an internal or dependent-service failure prevented a conformant output.

Status shall be distinct from downstream approval, execution, validation, acceptance, and closure. Completed means that a Recommendation Envelope was produced; it does not mean that the recommendation is correct, permitted, approved, executed, validated, or accepted.

### Facts, Assumptions, Inferences, and Recommendations

The engine shall maintain explicit epistemic separation. A controlled output shall distinguish at least:

- **Verified Fact:** supported by an authoritative source whose identity and applicable validity were verified for the purpose;
- **Supplied Assertion:** provided by a customer, user, provider, document, or system but not independently verified as authoritative;
- **Retrieved Statement:** obtained from an approved source with recorded provenance and retrieval time;
- **Derived Fact:** produced by a deterministic transformation whose inputs and method are recorded;
- **Inference:** a reasoned conclusion that is plausible but not directly established by authoritative evidence;
- **Assumption:** a temporary premise introduced to enable analysis and clearly marked as such;
- **Estimate:** a quantified or qualitative projection with stated basis, range, and limitations; and
- **Recommendation:** a proposed course of action subject to policy, approval, execution, validation, and acceptance controls.

The engine shall not use linguistic certainty to conceal weak provenance. A fluent or detailed statement remains unsupported when its sources and reasoning basis are insufficient. When the difference between fact and inference is material, the output schema shall preserve that distinction for both human and machine consumers.

Conflicts among authoritative sources shall be reported and routed to the competent authority. The engine shall not silently choose the source that best supports its preferred recommendation. Where source precedence is formally defined, the engine may apply that precedence for analysis, but the applied rule and resulting conflict shall remain visible.

### Provenance and Source Governance

Information used in reasoning shall originate from approved context sources, retrieval paths, or customer-supplied inputs. Each material source shall have sufficient metadata to evaluate origin, tenant, classification, authority, freshness, integrity, access basis, and purpose suitability.

Source governance shall address:

- authoritative ownership and publication status;
- tenant and organizational boundary;
- legal, contractual, confidentiality, privacy, and regional restrictions;
- source version, effective date, retrieval date, and staleness policy;
- integrity and authenticity checks where applicable;
- revocation, correction, supersession, and deletion state;
- known quality limitations and conflicts;
- permitted reasoning and downstream-use purposes;
- retention and citation rules; and
- whether the source may be disclosed to the intended audience.

Retrieved content shall be treated as data, not as authority to alter system instructions or control boundaries. Embedded instructions, role claims, execution requests, links, code, attachments, markup, or policy-like language from retrieved sources shall not override the Reasoning Request contract, Immutable Context, Product Constitution, canonical architecture, deterministic policy, or system controls.

The engine shall identify when a recommendation materially depends on a source that is stale, incomplete, low-authority, inaccessible to the reviewer, contradicted, or scheduled for deletion. If the minimum source standard is not met, the engine shall reduce the claim, request clarification, return a limitation status, or refuse the requested conclusion.

### Uncertainty and Confidence

Confidence is decision-support metadata, not authority. The engine may express confidence only through a defined method whose meaning, calibration limits, inputs, and intended use are documented. A numerical score shall not imply statistical probability unless the score is validated and calibrated for that interpretation.

Confidence assessment should consider, as applicable:

- completeness and authority of context;
- agreement or conflict among relevant sources;
- freshness and applicability of information;
- ambiguity of the request and success criteria;
- stability of the reasoning method for materially equivalent inputs;
- availability of comparable validated examples;
- sensitivity of the recommendation to assumptions;
- model, retrieval, provider, language, and domain limitations;
- novelty, complexity, and consequence of the requested outcome; and
- independent verification available for critical claims.

The engine shall represent material uncertainty even when a downstream interface requests a single answer. It shall identify decision-sensitive assumptions, plausible alternatives, and observations that would change the recommendation. Low confidence shall not automatically authorize broader data access, additional tool use, or bypass of a deadline. It shall instead trigger an approved response such as clarification, retrieval through an authorized path, narrowed scope, human review, alternative analysis, or refusal.

Confidence thresholds may influence routing, review, or whether an output is eligible for downstream policy evaluation. They shall not grant permission, waive human approval, determine compliance, or establish acceptance. Thresholds shall be approved, versioned, tested, monitored for calibration drift, and protected against manipulation.

### Planning Relationship

The engine may produce a candidate plan, but Section 6.7 defines the Planning Engine responsibilities for formal plan construction, dependency handling, plan-state management, and controlled revision. The distinction shall remain explicit.

The reasoning engine contributes:

- interpreted intent and bounded objectives;
- identified constraints and assumptions;
- candidate strategies and trade-offs;
- proposed actions in inert structured form;
- expected dependencies, prerequisites, risks, and validation needs; and
- questions requiring policy, approval, technical, customer, or human determination.

The Planning Engine converts eligible recommendations into a formal proposed plan. Neither component authorizes execution. The proposed plan remains subject to policy, risk classification, approval, capability issuance, Tool Gateway enforcement, independent validation, and acceptance.

If a recommendation changes after policy feedback, approval conditions, execution evidence, or validation findings, the revision shall create a new version linked to the prior Recommendation ID and changed inputs. The system shall preserve whether the change was caused by new facts, corrected context, policy constraints, human direction, execution failure, or validation rejection.

### Model Orchestration and Provider Abstraction Relationship

Section 6.2 defines model orchestration, routing, compatibility, provider independence, configuration, availability, and lifecycle concerns. The reasoning engine consumes those capabilities through an approved abstraction. It shall not hard-code a provider as architectural authority or assume that all providers share equivalent behavior, data handling, assurance, context capacity, output schema support, or regional availability.

The reasoning contract shall remain stable across provider or model changes to the extent possible. A provider change, model change, configuration change, retrieval change, or reasoning-policy change that may alter material behavior shall be assessed, tested, versioned, approved, and evidenced under the applicable change and release processes.

Provider routing may consider approved factors such as capability, assurance, data classification, tenant contract, region, latency, cost, availability, performance, and observed quality. The engine cannot select a provider outside those constraints. A lower-cost or faster option shall not override a security, privacy, contractual, residency, quality, or customer-isolation requirement.

Fallback shall be explicit. A failure shall not silently route protected information to an unapproved provider, weaker deployment boundary, unsupported region, different retention model, or incompatible output contract. When no conformant route exists, the engine shall return an approved failure or limitation status.

### Deterministic Policy and Capability Evaluation

The Recommendation Envelope is evaluated after reasoning. The deterministic Policy Engine shall assess the proposed actions, data use, tools, environments, destinations, capabilities, conditions, prohibitions, and obligations against the controlled context.

The reasoning engine may include policy-relevant attributes to support evaluation, but it cannot authoritatively decide whether the attributes satisfy policy. It shall not omit a material attribute because inclusion might cause denial or additional approval. It shall not rewrite a denied proposal into semantically equivalent fragments to evade a prohibition.

Capability requirements shall be explicit, minimal, purpose-bound, tenant-bound, resource-bound, action-bound, and time-bounded. A recommendation may request read access, write access, network access, execution, data transformation, publication, signing, deployment, or another capability, but the request remains inert until the competent service issues a constrained authority.

If policy denies the recommendation, the engine may produce a revised alternative only when the revision genuinely respects the denial. It shall not interpret denial as an invitation to find a bypass. The policy decision, reason code, affected proposal version, and any allowed revision path shall remain recorded.

### Human Review and Accountability

Human review is a substantive control, not a user-interface confirmation. When approval or determination is required, the reviewer shall receive information sufficient to understand the request, recommendation, relevant facts, assumptions, uncertainty, consequences, alternatives, policy result, requested capability, validation plan, and residual risk.

The engine shall support human review by:

- presenting the recommendation in language appropriate to the accountable audience;
- distinguishing material facts from assumptions and inferences;
- identifying the decision requested from the reviewer;
- disclosing known limitations, conflicts, and unavailable information;
- presenting material alternatives rather than manufacturing false inevitability;
- identifying reversible and irreversible consequences;
- explaining why escalation or additional expertise may be required;
- avoiding manipulative urgency, unsupported certainty, or concealment of adverse evidence; and
- preserving the reviewer's decision, conditions, rationale, identity, authority, and time separately from model output.

The engine shall not impersonate an approver, infer approval from silence, reuse an approval for a materially changed recommendation, or generate an approval record on behalf of a human. Human acceptance of a recommendation does not transfer legal or organizational responsibility to the engine.

For qualifying automated decision-making or other legally protected contexts, the applicable role and law may require meaningful human intervention, the opportunity to express a viewpoint, contestation, explanation, or review. The engine may support those processes but shall not determine their legal applicability or substitute for the competent controller, authority, or reviewer.

### Structured Explanation

An explanation shall be proportionate to consequence, audience, and decision need. It should identify what was recommended, why, on which sources and assumptions, with which uncertainty, what alternatives were considered, what would change the conclusion, and which controls remain outstanding.

Explanation quality shall not be measured by length alone. A long narrative may obscure decisive limitations, while a concise structured explanation may be more accountable. The approved explanation profile shall define required fields, audience, language, accessibility, confidentiality, and source-disclosure constraints.

The engine shall not fabricate a retrospective rationale that was not part of the actual reasoning event. Where the internal method cannot provide a faithful causal account, the system shall present a bounded explanation based on recorded inputs, outputs, tests, and known behavior, and disclose that limitation. Explanation shall not expose secrets, protected system instructions, security-sensitive controls, personal data, privileged material, or another tenant's information.

### Tool and Execution Separation

The reasoning engine shall not execute controlled operations directly. Any ability to query a context source during reasoning shall be mediated by an approved retrieval boundary and shall not be confused with operational execution authority.

Proposed tool operations shall be inert, typed, and separately reviewable. They shall identify the intended tool class, action, target, data classes, preconditions, expected effect, requested capability, validation criteria, rollback considerations, and unresolved questions. They shall not include unrestricted shell text, hidden side effects, reusable credentials, or dynamically generated authority.

The Tool Gateway shall independently verify the issued capability, tenant, subject, resource, action, time, conditions, request integrity, and policy references before dispatch. It shall not trust the reasoning engine's assertion that an action was approved. The execution handler shall receive only the minimum approved inputs and shall return an attributable result through the controlled path.

When an operation fails, the reasoning engine may analyze the failure and recommend a revision. It cannot silently retry with broader authority, a different tool, a different destination, disabled validation, weaker isolation, or changed data scope. Retry policy remains deterministic and subject to the applicable authorization and risk controls.

### Independent Validation Boundary

The engine shall not validate its own recommendation or execution result as the sole assurance source. The Validation Pipeline shall evaluate the relevant artifact, action, or result against independently defined criteria and controlled evidence.

The engine may propose validation considerations, but it shall not define success after seeing the result in order to manufacture a pass. Acceptance criteria shall be established before execution where practicable, bound to the approved scope, and changed only through an attributable controlled process.

Validation may assess schema conformance, policy conditions, security properties, data integrity, functional outcome, evidence completeness, side effects, tenant isolation, privacy constraints, reversibility, performance, compatibility, or other applicable criteria. The engine may explain a validation result, but the authoritative result remains the signed or otherwise protected Validation Record.

A validation failure shall not be rewritten as partial success without competent authority and an explicit bounded status. The failed result, affected recommendation, execution record, evidence, and next action shall remain linked.

### Audit Architecture and Evidence Chain Integration

Audit and evidence are continuous cross-cutting controls. They do not begin after a recommendation is produced. The Audit Engine shall record material events throughout request creation, context assembly, retrieval, routing, reasoning, output production, policy evaluation, revision, approval, execution, validation, acceptance, and closure.

Material reasoning events include:

- request creation, normalization, rejection, cancellation, and expiry;
- context-source selection, access, denial, redaction, and staleness findings;
- reasoning-policy, model-class, provider-route, retrieval-profile, and schema selection;
- invocation start, completion, limitation, refusal, failure, timeout, and fallback;
- creation and versioning of Recommendation Envelopes;
- material assumptions, source conflicts, uncertainty, and human-review flags;
- policy referrals, denials, revision requests, and recommendation supersession;
- security, privacy, safety, tenant, data, and integrity anomalies;
- human review, approval, rejection, condition, and escalation events; and
- linkage to execution, validation, acceptance, incident, defect, change, and improvement records.

Audit records shall identify the actor or service, tenant, event type, time, correlation identifiers, input and output references, configuration references, outcome, reason code, and integrity metadata appropriate to the record class. Sensitive reasoning material shall not be copied indiscriminately into logs. Auditability requires sufficient traceability, not uncontrolled duplication of protected content.

The Evidence Chain shall bind material records through the canonical integrity mechanism. Hash linkage demonstrates ordered integrity for the records included in the chain; it does not by itself prove factual correctness, completeness, lawful processing, source authenticity, or legal admissibility. Evidence coverage, source assurance, validation, custody, time assurance, access controls, and review remain necessary.

Reasoning records shall follow an approved record-class-specific retention schedule. Personal data, customer information, retrieved content, intermediate analysis, prompts, Recommendation Envelopes, and telemetry shall not be retained indefinitely by default. Legal holds and justified extensions shall be documented, narrowly scoped, authorized, and periodically reviewed.

### Security Architecture

The engine is exposed to untrusted requests, retrieved content, malformed context, adversarial instructions, data poisoning, model behavior variance, provider failure, and attempted authority escalation. It shall therefore operate under Zero Trust and assume that no input is trustworthy solely because it originated inside a customer environment, repository, document store, provider response, prior output, or authenticated session.

Security controls shall address at least:

- instruction injection and attempts to override system or policy boundaries;
- cross-tenant context contamination and source confusion;
- unauthorized context expansion or retrieval;
- disclosure of secrets, credentials, protected prompts, policy details, customer data, or personal information;
- malicious or malformed structured output;
- recommendation smuggling through comments, encoding, attachments, markup, or tool parameters;
- insecure fallback or provider routing;
- resource exhaustion, excessive context, denial of service, and cost abuse;
- model or configuration substitution;
- supply-chain compromise in model, retrieval, evaluation, or orchestration components;
- adversarial examples, data poisoning, retrieval poisoning, and misleading evidence;
- unauthorized persistence or learning from protected information;
- output manipulation intended to evade Policy Engine evaluation;
- replay of stale Recommendation Envelopes or approvals; and
- fabricated provenance, confidence, validation, approval, or audit claims.

Controls shall combine input validation, schema enforcement, context isolation, source labeling, instruction hierarchy, output encoding, secret scanning, data-loss prevention where applicable, resource quotas, rate controls, integrity checks, least privilege, monitoring, and independent validation. No single filter or model behavior shall be treated as sufficient protection.

Security-sensitive failures shall default to a safe state. The engine shall not expose hidden configuration, broaden scope, return raw protected context, or disable safeguards merely to produce an answer. Suspected compromise shall trigger the applicable incident, evidence-preservation, key, secret, access, provider, and change-management procedures.

### Privacy and Data Protection

Reasoning shall follow purpose limitation, data minimization, accuracy, storage limitation, confidentiality, and accountability requirements applicable to the defined processing role and deployment. The engine shall process only the information necessary and authorized for the bounded purpose.

The reasoning profile shall identify, where applicable:

- categories of personal and protected data;
- processing purpose and applicable legal or contractual basis as determined by competent authority;
- controller, joint-controller, processor, or other role determined for the specific processing activity;
- tenant instructions and restrictions;
- data residency and transfer conditions;
- permitted providers and subprocessors;
- retention, deletion, correction, access, objection, and review obligations;
- prohibited secondary use, training, profiling, or enrichment;
- requirements for human intervention or contestation; and
- disclosure, redaction, and audience constraints.

The engine shall not infer sensitive attributes merely because an inference may improve personalization or prediction. Sensitive or protected inferences require an approved purpose, applicable legal basis, strict necessity assessment, appropriate controls, and competent authorization. If those conditions are absent, the inference shall not be produced or retained.

Customer content shall not be reused for unrelated training, evaluation, provider improvement, or cross-customer optimization without explicit approved governance, role assessment, contractual authority, and legally valid basis. A provider's default behavior shall not override ILAIOS or customer restrictions.

Data-subject or customer requests affecting reasoning records shall be handled through the applicable governed process. The engine may locate or classify relevant records but cannot determine legal entitlement or final disposition independently.

### Tenant Isolation

Every Reasoning Request, context item, retrieval operation, Recommendation Envelope, cache entry, telemetry record, and evidence reference shall be tenant-bound. Tenant identity shall originate from verified platform context, not from narrative input or model inference.

The engine shall not:

- retrieve or compare another tenant's content without an explicitly approved cross-tenant purpose and authority;
- use one tenant's output as evidence for another tenant merely because the requests are similar;
- place protected cross-tenant material in shared prompts, caches, evaluation sets, logs, or provider state;
- infer tenant membership from names, domains, document content, or prior conversations; or
- permit provider, retrieval, analytics, or observability systems to weaken tenant boundaries.

Shared model infrastructure may be used only when the approved deployment profile preserves logical or physical isolation, data-handling commitments, routing controls, access control, monitoring, and deletion obligations. Higher-assurance profiles may require dedicated resources or independently verified boundaries.

A tenant-isolation anomaly is a security event. The affected output shall be quarantined, downstream use blocked, evidence preserved, exposure assessed, credentials or routes restricted as necessary, and incident-response procedures initiated.

### Safety and Rights Protection

The engine shall identify and control uses that may materially affect health, safety, employment, finance, access to essential services, legal rights, regulated decisions, vulnerable individuals, or other high-impact interests. It shall not present a recommendation as a substitute for competent professional judgment or legally required decision authority.

Applicable profiles shall define prohibited uses, mandatory escalation, human-review requirements, explanation obligations, testing, monitoring, appeal or contestation support, and outcome-quality controls. The engine shall surface when a request falls outside validated capability or when the available evidence is insufficient for the consequence.

Optimization shall not systematically disadvantage a protected or vulnerable population. Quality assessment shall consider relevant cohorts, languages, accessibility needs, regional contexts, and foreseeable misuse. Aggregate performance shall not conceal unacceptable harm in a material subgroup.

The engine shall not manipulate a reviewer through false urgency, emotional pressure, asymmetric disclosure, deceptive personalization, or concealed alternatives. Recommendations shall preserve the reviewer's ability to make an informed and attributable decision.

### Quality Attributes

The engine shall be designed and evaluated for the following quality attributes:

- **Relevance:** addresses the bounded request and approved purpose;
- **Groundedness:** material claims are supported by permitted sources or clearly identified as inference or assumption;
- **Completeness:** covers mandatory output fields and decision-relevant constraints without claiming exhaustive knowledge;
- **Consistency:** does not contain unresolved internal contradictions or materially conflicting structured and narrative outputs;
- **Traceability:** links output to request, context, sources, configuration, policy, audit, and evidence records;
- **Structural Validity:** conforms to the approved schema and type constraints;
- **Safety:** avoids prohibited content, authority escalation, concealed high-impact risk, or unsafe operational instruction;
- **Security:** preserves tenant, identity, secret, data, capability, and control boundaries;
- **Privacy:** minimizes and protects personal and customer information;
- **Explainability:** provides an audience-appropriate basis, limitations, and alternatives;
- **Calibration:** expresses uncertainty in a manner supported by observed performance;
- **Robustness:** remains within contract under malformed, adversarial, ambiguous, or incomplete input;
- **Reproducibility:** permits material behavior to be investigated through recorded inputs and configuration, recognizing probabilistic variation;
- **Provider Portability:** preserves the controlled interface across approved model or provider changes;
- **Availability:** meets the approved service profile without unsafe fallback;
- **Efficiency:** uses bounded resources without compromising mandatory controls; and
- **Maintainability:** supports controlled versioning, testing, monitoring, rollback, and retirement.

Quality targets shall be defined per use case and consequence. A generic global accuracy percentage is insufficient. The approved profile shall identify datasets or scenarios, cohort coverage, acceptance thresholds, error taxonomy, safety constraints, review process, and known limitations.

### Evaluation and Testing

The engine shall be tested under the Engineering Standards and applicable Secure Software Development Lifecycle. Testing shall include deterministic contract tests and empirical behavior evaluation.

The minimum evaluation portfolio shall address, as applicable:

- Reasoning Request and Recommendation Envelope schema conformance;
- required-field, invalid-field, tenant, identity, classification, and expiry behavior;
- fact, assertion, assumption, inference, estimate, and recommendation separation;
- provenance and citation integrity;
- ambiguity detection and clarification behavior;
- handling of missing, stale, conflicting, and revoked sources;
- instruction-injection and authority-escalation attempts;
- data exfiltration, secret disclosure, and cross-tenant contamination;
- policy-evasion and capability-smuggling attempts;
- refusal, limitation, failure, cancellation, and timeout behavior;
- model, provider, retrieval, configuration, language, and regional variation;
- confidence interpretation and calibration;
- high-impact scenario escalation and human-review support;
- resilience to adversarial, malformed, excessive, encoded, and multilingual input;
- fallback and degraded-operation behavior;
- linkage to audit and Evidence Chain records;
- downstream Policy Engine compatibility;
- separation from Tool Gateway execution and Validation Pipeline acceptance;
- privacy, retention, deletion, and correction controls; and
- regression against previously accepted scenarios and known defects.

Evaluation data shall have documented provenance, purpose, representativeness, quality, rights, privacy treatment, version, limitations, and retention. Production customer data shall not be copied into evaluation merely because it is available. Synthetic data may reduce exposure but shall not be assumed representative without validation.

Qualified external review shall be completed before an affected high-impact reasoning capability or profile influences a Stable release, production environment, customer-controlled production deployment, or Enterprise operating profile; otherwise it shall remain blocked, prerelease, non-production, advisory-only, or constrained. Where true independence is unavailable during a registered bootstrap phase, the absence shall be recorded and shall not be represented as independent evaluation.

### Quality Gates

A reasoning-engine change shall not progress to a higher maturity, broader audience, production use, or Enterprise profile unless the applicable Quality Gates pass. Gates shall cover code and configuration integrity, schema compatibility, security, privacy, tenant isolation, provenance, grounding, evaluation, calibration, provider behavior, observability, rollback, documentation, and operational readiness.

A gate decision shall bind to the exact versions of relevant code, reasoning policy, model route, retrieval profile, prompt or instruction package, context schema, output schema, evaluation set, threshold configuration, and deployment profile. A material change invalidates prior eligibility to the extent defined by policy.

Gate failure shall block progression unless a formally permitted exception exists. Exceptions shall be specific, time-bound, owned, evidenced, monitored, and incapable of waiving non-waivable security, privacy, tenant-isolation, authorization, audit, evidence, safety, or human-accountability controls.

### Observability and Operational Monitoring

Operational monitoring shall provide sufficient visibility to identify degradation, misuse, cost anomaly, provider drift, quality regression, latency, failure, security events, privacy events, tenant anomalies, and control bypass attempts without indiscriminately collecting protected content.

Metrics may include:

- request volume and outcome status by approved dimensions;
- latency and resource consumption by reasoning profile;
- context-source availability and staleness;
- schema-valid output rate;
