Where semantic mapping is ambiguous, the result shall remain unresolved or be represented through a broader non-authoritative type. False precision is prohibited.

### Deterministic Derivation and Inference

The graph may contain deterministic derivations and probabilistic inferences. Their semantics shall remain distinct.

A deterministic derivation shall identify its exact inputs, transformation version, and output. Examples may include repository containment, parsed symbol definitions, exact manifest membership, or mechanically calculated temporal status.

An inference may propose hidden dependencies, entity matches, impact, ownership, topic, intent, similarity, or causal hypotheses. Every inference shall carry:

- the inference method and version;
- model route or heuristic configuration;
- input assertion identities;
- Confidence Assessment;
- Applicability Profile;
- known limitations;
- expiry or reassessment conditions; and
- a resolution state of Inferred unless independently verified.

Inference shall not create identity, authority, approval, policy, ownership, legal obligation, or execution permission. A high-confidence inferred edge remains inferred.

The graph shall prevent inferred relationships from recursively reinforcing themselves without independent source evidence. Depth, cycle, and confidence propagation rules shall be governed.

### Confidence Integration

Section 6.3 governs Confidence Scoring. The graph may link a Confidence Assessment to an assertion, resolution candidate, derived path, or query result.

Confidence shall not be copied as an unversioned property. The graph shall preserve the assessment identity, subject digest, profile, calibration status, validity, and limitations.

Graph-level confidence aggregation shall account for source correlation, path length, transformation loss, counterevidence, temporal mismatch, and weakest critical dependency. The number of paths or edges shall not determine confidence by itself.

When a source, model route, ontology, entity resolution, or Confidence Assessment changes, dependent assertions and query results shall be identified for reevaluation. Historical graph snapshots retain their original confidence context.

### Query Architecture

Every Graph Query shall be typed, tenant-bound, purpose-bound, authenticated through the platform, and evaluated against applicable access policy before graph traversal.

A query shall contain or reference:

- Query ID and correlation ID;
- verified tenant and subject or service identity;
- purpose and intended consumer;
- Graph Space and ontology version;
- requested entity, relationship, path, aggregate, or time scope;
- allowed resolution states and source classes;
- data classification and disclosure constraints;
- maximum depth, breadth, result count, cost, and time;
- required provenance, confidence, and evidence fields;
- temporal perspective;
- freshness and completeness requirements;
- export or downstream-use restrictions; and
- expiry and cache behavior.

Graph traversal is not authority traversal. An authorized user who may view one Entity does not automatically gain access to connected Entities or edge properties. Authorization shall be evaluated across the result set and, where necessary, at node, relationship, property, path, or source-reference level.

Queries that exceed bounds, cross unauthorized tenants, request prohibited inference, or cannot preserve required provenance shall fail safely or return an explicitly partial result.

### Query Result Contract

A Graph Query Result shall include:

- Query ID, Graph Snapshot or knowledge-time reference, and ontology version;
- tenant and purpose scope;
- returned Entities and Assertions;
- source, provenance, resolution, temporal, confidence, and evidence metadata required by the profile;
- filtering, redaction, truncation, and pagination state;
- partial, stale, incomplete, conflicted, or degraded status;
- query cost and limit information where governed;
- validity and expiry;
- downstream-use restrictions; and
- Audit Engine and Evidence Chain references.

Empty result, no authorized result, no matching assertion, filtered result, unavailable source, and query failure shall remain distinguishable. Absence of a returned edge does not prove that the relationship does not exist.

A query result is a governed projection. Consumers shall not persist it as a new authoritative source without an approved purpose, retention class, and provenance link.

### Graph Views and Purpose Limitation

Graph Views present purpose-specific projections. A view may restrict entity types, edge types, properties, sources, resolution states, time, confidence, region, and audience.

Views shall support least privilege and minimize unintended inference. An operational support view may expose service relationships without revealing personal, contractual, security-sensitive, or cross-tenant data. A repository view may expose code dependencies without exposing customer context.

View configuration shall be versioned, tested, access-controlled, and audited. A view shall not be used to conceal material uncertainty from an accountable reviewer. Security redaction and decision transparency shall be balanced through role-appropriate access.

No view shall weaken the underlying tenant, source, policy, retention, or deletion requirements.

### Relationship to Context Engine

The Context Engine may use Graph Queries to assemble relevant context for reasoning and planning. The graph shall return only authorized, purpose-relevant, and bounded information.

Graph proximity alone shall not determine context relevance. Context selection shall consider source authority, temporal validity, resolution state, Confidence Assessment, data classification, token or resource budget, and task purpose.

The Context Engine shall preserve graph provenance when transforming results. Summarization or compression shall not convert inferred or disputed assertions into facts.

The graph shall not expand context recursively without governed depth and breadth. Sensitive relationship inference, such as organizational, security, behavioral, or personal linkage, may require additional policy or be prohibited.

### Relationship to AI Reasoning and Recommendation Engine

The AI Reasoning and Recommendation Engine may consume graph assertions as controlled context and may propose new inferred relationships. It cannot write verified graph facts by its own authority.

Reasoning-produced graph proposals shall enter through a controlled assertion or candidate-resolution workflow. They shall be marked Inferred or Asserted as appropriate, linked to the originating Recommendation Envelope and model route, and subject to validation or qualified review.

The reasoning engine shall not cite the graph as a single undifferentiated source. Material claims shall preserve the underlying source and resolution state.

If reasoning identifies a graph conflict or likely correction, it may create a proposal. The original assertion remains until the competent source or governance process resolves it.

### Relationship to Repository Intelligence

Repository Intelligence supplies version-bound entities and relationships such as repositories, files, modules, symbols, imports, calls, dependencies, tests, ownership declarations, changes, and artifacts.

The graph shall preserve the exact repository revision, analyzer version, language coverage, ignored paths, generated-code treatment, parser errors, and unsupported constructs.

Deterministic repository facts may be represented as Derived or Verified according to source and method. Intended architecture, business ownership, runtime behavior, security impact, or change consequence may remain Asserted or Inferred until independently supported.

Repository history shall not be collapsed into the current state. A dependency at one commit is not assumed to exist at another. Renames, moves, splits, merges, generated artifacts, vendored dependencies, and deleted code require explicit identity and temporal treatment.

### Relationship to Planning Engine

The Planning Engine may use graph dependencies, ownership, lifecycle, evidence, policy, and impact relationships to construct proposed plans. Graph information remains subject to its source, resolution, temporal, and confidence semantics.

A graph path may identify a possible dependency chain; it does not prove that the plan order is complete or approved. Planning shall consider missing nodes, unindexed systems, dynamic relationships, human responsibilities, customer constraints, and validation requirements.

The Planning Engine may propose new tasks to resolve graph ambiguity, stale information, or missing ownership. It shall not silently treat an unresolved graph edge as a prerequisite or authority.

Execution and validation results may update graph assertions through governed ingestion after the authoritative records exist.

### Relationship to Policy Engine

The deterministic Policy Engine may consume approved graph assertions, such as exact resource classification, tenant ownership, component dependency, data location, control applicability, or current lifecycle state.

Policy use shall require:

- an approved ontology and interface;
- eligible resolution states;
- authoritative source class;
- tenant and purpose binding;
- temporal validity and freshness;
- integrity and provenance;
- deterministic handling of missing, conflicted, stale, or unavailable graph data; and
- protected versioning and change control.

Policy shall not infer permission from general graph connectedness, organizational proximity, repository contribution, model-produced ownership, or confidence alone. If a mandatory graph fact is unavailable, policy shall use the approved fail-safe behavior.

Graph changes that affect policy inputs require impact analysis, testing, controlled rollout, and evidence. Ontology migration shall not silently alter authorization semantics.

### Relationship to Audit Engine and Evidence Chain

The graph may make audit and evidence relationships discoverable, including which request, context, recommendation, policy decision, approval, capability, execution, validation, acceptance, incident, defect, release, and change records relate to one another.

The graph is not a substitute for append-only audit or cryptographic evidence integrity. A graph database update, snapshot, or traversal does not prove that the underlying event occurred.

Evidence references shall link to authoritative records and preserve access restrictions. The graph shall not duplicate protected evidence content merely for convenience.

If a graph assertion about evidence is corrected, the underlying Evidence Chain remains unchanged. Corrections are represented through new graph assertions and Audit Engine events.

### Security Architecture

The Knowledge Graph is a high-value target because relationships can reveal structure, ownership, dependencies, security boundaries, customers, incidents, and sensitive inferences even when individual data items appear harmless.

Threats include:

- cross-tenant traversal;
- unauthorized relationship inference;
- graph poisoning and malicious assertions;
- entity-resolution collision or forced merge;
- source or provenance forgery;
- ontology manipulation;
- inference escalation;
- query amplification and resource exhaustion;
- path-based authorization bypass;
- sensitive aggregate disclosure;
- stale or revoked assertion replay;
- graph export exfiltration;
- cache contamination;
- unauthorized schema migration;
- deletion or correction suppression;
- monitoring evasion; and
- compromise of connectors, analyzers, adapters, or graph administration.

Controls shall include strong service identity, tenant-aware authorization, source allowlisting, typed schemas, assertion signing or integrity controls where required, provenance validation, ingestion quarantine, resolution review, query limits, depth and breadth controls, egress restrictions, sensitive-path protection, anomaly detection, rate control, resource quotas, secure administration, backup and recovery, and independent validation.

The graph shall not expose protected relationships through counts, timing, error differences, autocomplete, recommendation, or aggregate endpoints. Authorization testing shall consider inference channels, not only direct record access.

Models and reasoning components shall not receive graph-administrator credentials or authority to change access policy, ontology, source precedence, resolution state, retention, or audit controls.

### Privacy and Data Protection

Graph relationships can create new personal or confidential information through linkage. Data minimization shall apply to entities, properties, relationships, provenance, indexes, caches, snapshots, and query telemetry.

The graph shall not infer sensitive attributes, associations, behavior, health, finances, beliefs, location, employment, or risk merely because connected data could support such inference. Sensitive inference requires an approved purpose, applicable legal basis and role assessment by competent authority, strict necessity, proportionality, transparency where required, and appropriate safeguards.

Privacy governance shall address:

- lawful and defined purpose;
- data categories and relationship sensitivity;
- controller, processor, joint-controller, or other applicable roles;
- tenant and customer instructions;
- data minimization and field-level access;
- regional processing and transfer;
- correction, erasure, restriction, objection, access, and portability where applicable;
- automated-decision and human-review safeguards;
- retention and deletion propagation;
- cross-source linkage and secondary use;
- re-identification risk; and
- explanation and contestation of material inferred relationships.

Deletion shall propagate to graph indexes, cached views, derived assertions, exports, and downstream context according to approved retention and legal-hold rules. A minimal tombstone may remain only when necessary and lawful for integrity, security, or obligation management.

Historical accuracy does not justify indefinite retention of personal data. Record-class-specific schedules shall reconcile history, audit, legal, contract, incident, privacy, and minimization requirements.

### Tenant Isolation

Every Entity, Assertion, Source Reference, Resolution Record, Graph View, Query, Snapshot, cache entry, export, telemetry record, and evidence link shall have an explicit tenant or approved global scope.

Global entities may exist only where governance defines their authority, data classification, permitted relationships, and tenant visibility. A global software component or public standard does not authorize attachment of one tenant's usage, configuration, incidents, or contractual information to another tenant's view.

Cross-tenant relationships are prohibited unless a specific shared-service, consortium, regulatory, parent-subsidiary, or other approved purpose and authority exists. Such relationships shall use restricted Graph Spaces or federated views with explicit disclosure and isolation controls.

Tenant identity shall originate from verified platform context. It shall not be inferred from names, domains, repository content, document text, email patterns, or model output.

A cross-tenant graph anomaly is a security and privacy event. Affected assertions and query results shall be quarantined, access blocked, evidence preserved, impact assessed, and incident procedures initiated.

### Cross-Tenant Analytics and Federated Views

Cross-tenant analytics may provide benchmarking, shared threat intelligence, product quality, or ecosystem insight only through approved governance. It shall not create unrestricted cross-customer knowledge.

The approved profile shall define:

- purpose and legal or contractual authority;
- included tenants and data classes;
- minimum aggregation or de-identification;
- re-identification and inference controls;
- opt-in, opt-out, and customer instructions where applicable;
- permitted entity and relationship types;
- access and disclosure;
- retention and deletion;
- model and provider use;
- output review; and
- monitoring and incident response.

De-identification shall be assessed against graph re-identification risk. Removing direct identifiers may be insufficient when relationship structure is unique.

Federated views shall preserve source ownership and shall not copy data into a central Graph Space unless authorized. Query planning shall not expose one participant's data to another through intermediate results.

### Data Classification and Relationship Sensitivity

Classification shall apply to relationships as well as nodes and properties. The existence of a relationship may be more sensitive than either endpoint.

Examples include relationships involving customer identity, security vulnerabilities, incident impact, legal matters, employee roles, privileged administration, key custody, data transfers, regulated processing, unreleased products, or critical infrastructure dependencies.

Classification may be inherited, combined, or elevated according to controlled rules. It shall not be lowered automatically because a query returns only identifiers or aggregates.

Graph exports shall preserve classification and downstream-use restrictions. A consumer that cannot enforce required restrictions shall not receive the result.

### Graph Integrity and Consistency

The graph shall enforce structural and semantic integrity appropriate to the ontology. Controls may include:

- type and cardinality validation;
- required provenance and temporal fields;
- tenant-scope consistency;
- entity identity uniqueness;
- relationship endpoint validity;
- source and resolution-state compatibility;
- cycle and containment rules;
- version and migration compatibility;
- deletion and tombstone constraints;
- confidence-reference validity;
- policy-use eligibility; and
- referential integrity to authoritative records where feasible.

Distributed or asynchronous ingestion may create temporary inconsistency. The graph shall expose convergence state, lag, partial status, and failed updates. It shall not present an incomplete view as complete.

Strong consistency, eventual consistency, and snapshot isolation are implementation choices governed by use-case requirements. Policy and high-impact decisions shall use an approved consistency profile and fail safely when the required state is unavailable.

### Scalability and Resource Governance

Graph scale shall be controlled through purpose, partitioning, Graph Spaces, indexing, retention, query limits, archival, and lifecycle governance. Technology selection remains implementation-independent.

Resource controls shall address:

- maximum traversal depth and breadth;
- query time and memory;
- result and export size;
- ingestion throughput and backpressure;
- tenant quotas and fairness;
- expensive path, pattern, similarity, and aggregate queries;
- cache scope and expiry;
- snapshot frequency and storage;
- inference budgets;
- bulk correction and deletion; and
- capacity monitoring and recovery.

Resource exhaustion shall not cause authorization bypass, cross-tenant fallback, uncontrolled truncation, or silent omission of material limitations. A bounded partial result shall be labeled clearly.

### Search, Similarity, and Ranking

Graph search and similarity may assist discovery, entity resolution, context selection, and human review. Ranking is advisory and shall not determine authority.

Search results shall preserve tenant, source, resolution, time, confidence, and classification. Ranking shall not elevate an inferred or low-authority assertion above an authoritative current record without disclosure.

Similarity between entities does not establish identity, ownership, dependency, or causation. Similarity thresholds and models shall be versioned, evaluated, monitored for drift, and restricted by Applicability Profile.

Search indexes shall follow correction, revocation, deletion, and tenant-isolation requirements. A deleted or restricted assertion shall not remain discoverable through stale indexes or autocomplete.

### Correction, Dispute, and Appeal

The graph shall support correction and dispute without rewriting history. A correction request shall identify the affected assertion, requester, authority, reason, supporting source, desired treatment, and urgency.

The lifecycle may include Submitted, Triaged, Under Review, Restricted Pending Review, Corrected, Rejected, Superseded, Revoked, and Closed. This lifecycle is a graph-governance workflow and does not replace the Defect or Change lifecycles where those also apply.

During dispute, high-impact assertions may be restricted from policy, reasoning, planning, or customer use. The graph shall preserve the disputed state and affected downstream records.

Corrections shall create new assertions, resolution transitions, and audit events. Prior query results remain historically attributable. Downstream caches, contexts, plans, Confidence Assessments, and decisions shall be identified for reassessment where material.

### Deletion, Retention, and Legal Hold

Graph retention shall follow approved record-class-specific schedules. Different elements may have different requirements, including current operational assertions, historical versions, provenance, query telemetry, personal data, security evidence, and derived indexes.

Deletion shall address:

- authoritative source deletion or restriction;
- graph assertions and properties;
- derived and inferred relationships;
- search and similarity indexes;
- caches and materialized views;
- snapshots and backups;
- exports;
- calibration and evaluation datasets;
- Audit Engine and Evidence Chain references; and
- downstream context or plan artifacts.

Deletion from the graph does not delete an authoritative source unless the competent source process does so. Conversely, source deletion shall propagate according to approved rules and shall not leave unauthorized derived content.

Legal holds and justified retention extensions shall be documented, narrowly scoped, authorized, and periodically reviewed. Retention is not indefinite by default.

### Audit Architecture and Evidence Chain Integration

The Audit Engine shall record material graph events, including:

- source registration and connector changes;
- ingestion, rejection, quarantine, retry, and failure;
- entity creation and candidate resolution;
- merge, split, and rejected match;
- assertion creation, derivation, inference, correction, dispute, supersession, revocation, expiry, and deletion;
- ontology and mapping changes;
- query, high-risk traversal, export, and denied access;
- policy-consumed graph facts;
- Confidence Assessment linkage;
- cross-tenant or sensitive-inference attempts;
- administrative access and configuration change;
- snapshot, backup, restore, and recovery;
- retention, legal hold, and deletion events;
- security, privacy, data, and integrity incidents; and
- lifecycle, release, migration, and retirement.

Audit records shall identify actor or service, tenant, event type, time, prior and new state, source, ontology, graph identity, reason, authority, outcome, and integrity metadata appropriate to the event.

The Evidence Chain binds material graph events and source references through the canonical mechanism. Graph provenance and Evidence Chain integrity complement each other but are not interchangeable.

### Observability and Monitoring

Monitoring shall assess graph availability, integrity, freshness, isolation, quality, and operational health. Metrics may include:

- ingestion volume, latency, lag, rejection, and quarantine;
- assertion counts by source and resolution state;
- provenance completeness;
- entity-resolution match, ambiguity, merge, split, and error rates;
- ontology validation failures;
- stale, expired, revoked, disputed, and orphaned assertions;
- query latency, depth, breadth, truncation, and failure;
- policy-query freshness and consistency;
- tenant and authorization denials;
- cross-tenant anomalies;
- sensitive-inference and export events;
- correction and deletion propagation time;
- snapshot, backup, and restore status;
- confidence and inference drift;
- storage and resource consumption; and
- incident, defect, change, and improvement trends.

Metrics shall preserve denominator, scope, tenant, source, ontology, and time. A low observed error rate does not prove completeness if unindexed sources or failed connectors are excluded.

Alerts shall trigger investigation, source suspension, assertion quarantine, view restriction, policy fail-safe behavior, correction, rollback, incident response, or customer communication as applicable.

### Quality Attributes

The Knowledge Graph shall be evaluated for:

- semantic correctness;
- source fidelity;
- provenance completeness;
- temporal correctness;
- entity-resolution accuracy;
- assertion and ontology integrity;
- tenant isolation;
- access-control correctness;
- current-view freshness;
- historical reproducibility;
- query determinism where required;
- inference calibration;
- correction and deletion propagation;
- availability and recoverability;
- portability and schema evolvability;
- explainability; and
- operational maintainability.

Completeness claims shall define included sources, entity types, relationship types, time, tenant, and known exclusions. No graph is assumed complete merely because ingestion succeeded.

### Evaluation and Testing

Testing shall include:

- ontology and schema validation;
- entity identity, collision, merge, split, and ambiguity behavior;
- assertion-state transitions;
- provenance and lineage reconstruction;
- source conflict and precedence;
- bitemporal query behavior;
- tenant and field-level authorization;
- path-based inference and disclosure attacks;
- ingestion idempotency, ordering, retry, quarantine, and backpressure;
- normalization loss and missing-value semantics;
- deterministic derivation and probabilistic inference separation;
- Confidence Assessment linkage;
- policy-consumption fail-safe behavior;
- cross-tenant isolation and federated views;
- correction, dispute, revocation, expiry, and deletion;
- search-index invalidation;
- snapshot, backup, restore, and disaster recovery;
- schema migration and rollback;
- performance and resource limits;
- Audit Engine and Evidence Chain coverage; and
- adversarial graph poisoning, identity collision, provenance forgery, and query amplification.

Evaluation datasets shall have controlled provenance, rights, privacy treatment, tenant scope, representativeness, version, and retention. Synthetic graph data may support testing but shall not be assumed representative of production complexity.

Qualified external review shall be completed before an affected high-impact graph use, especially policy, security, rights, customer, regulated, or production-impact analysis, influences a Stable release, production environment, customer-controlled production deployment, or Enterprise operating profile; otherwise the graph use shall remain blocked, prerelease, non-production, advisory-only, or constrained.

### Quality Gates

A Knowledge Graph change shall not progress to broader maturity or policy use unless applicable Quality Gates pass. Gates shall cover ontology, source authority, identity, provenance, temporal semantics, tenant isolation, authorization, privacy, security, quality, migration, correction, deletion, backup, recovery, observability, and evidence.

Gate decisions shall bind to exact ontology, mapping, connector, analyzer, inference method, Confidence Profile, access policy, query interface, graph schema, migration, and deployment versions.

A failed mandatory gate blocks progression. An exception cannot waive identity, tenant, authorization, privacy, security, evidence, audit, deletion, or human-accountability requirements.

### Schema Versioning and Migration

Ontology, graph schema, mappings, query contracts, and resolution methods shall be versioned. A schema change shall identify compatibility, affected Graph Spaces, sources, assertions, queries, policies, views, exports, and consumers.

Migration shall preserve:

- stable Entity and Assertion identities;
- source-native references;
- provenance and temporal history;
- tenant and classification boundaries;
- resolution and dispute state;
- Confidence Assessment linkage;
- audit and evidence references;
- deletion and retention state; and
- historical query reproducibility where required.

Semantic migration shall not be performed as a blind mechanical rename when meaning changes. Incompatible changes require explicit versioning, transformation rules, validation, staged rollout, and rollback.

Policies depending on graph semantics shall be pinned to compatible schema versions until migration is validated.

### Change, Release, and Rollback

Graph changes follow Sections 4 and 5. The change record shall identify affected tenants, sources, ontology elements, mappings, identities, assertions, policies, contexts, plans, data, privacy, security, performance, migration, rollback, and evidence.

Changes requiring an ADR include those that alter graph authority, source-of-record relationships, tenant model, identity semantics, temporal model, policy integration, Evidence Chain boundaries, or canonical component placement.

Rollout shall support bounded Graph Spaces, tenants, source classes, and query consumers. Observation shall assess semantic correctness, migration integrity, policy behavior, performance, incidents, and deletion propagation.

Rollback shall restore an approved schema and operational state without reviving revoked, deleted, unauthorized, or superseded assertions. A rollback shall preserve audit and history of the failed change.

### Backup, Recovery, and Continuity

Graph backup and recovery shall follow Sections 3.10 and 3.11. Backups shall preserve schema, ontology, Entity and Assertion identities, tenant boundaries, provenance, temporal state, resolution state, access controls, and integrity metadata.

Restore shall not revive data deleted after the backup without applying current deletion, revocation, access, key, and retention state. Restored graph data shall be validated against authoritative sources and current control records before policy or high-impact use resumes.

Recovery procedures shall address ingestion replay, duplicate prevention, ordering, search-index rebuild, cache invalidation, schema compatibility, and Evidence Chain reconciliation.

Availability through replication is not backup. A consistent graph service with corrupted semantics is not a successful recovery. Recovery acceptance requires semantic and control validation.

### Governance and Roles

Governance shall assign accountable ownership for:

- graph purpose, scope, and claims;
- ontology and semantic definitions;
- source authority and connector approval;
- entity identity and resolution;
- provenance and temporal model;
- tenant, authorization, privacy, and data classification;
- deterministic derivation and inference;
- Confidence Assessment integration;
- policy and context consumption;
- correction, dispute, deletion, and retention;
- security, operations, backup, recovery, and incident response;
- quality, evaluation, migration, release, and rollback; and
- audit, evidence, records, and customer transparency.

No model, provider, framework, connector, source owner, customer comment, sales commitment, or engineering preference may define graph authority unilaterally or override canonical controls.

Separation of duties shall be proportionate to impact. The person who designs a high-impact ontology or resolution rule shall not be the sole claimed independent approver, production migrator, policy integrator, and incident closer under the Enterprise Profile.

### Single-Maintainer Bootstrap Profile

A registered Single-Maintainer Bootstrap Profile may temporarily combine ontology, connector, resolution, implementation, migration, and operational roles. The absence of independent review shall be recorded and shall not be represented as Enterprise assurance.

The bootstrap profile shall maintain:

- organizational ownership of graph infrastructure and source accounts;
- exact change attribution and explicit self-review;
- mandatory automated schema, tenant, security, privacy, provenance, migration, and Quality Gates;
- protected Audit Engine and Evidence Chain records;
- restricted tenants, data classes, Graph Spaces, sources, inference, policy use, and release maturity;
- backups, restore tests, and controlled deletion;
- least-privilege administrative access and separately protected recovery factors;
- qualified external review completed before an affected graph use involving high-impact identity, tenant, privacy, security, policy, evidence, migration, or production concerns influences a Stable release, production environment, customer-controlled production deployment, or Enterprise operating profile; otherwise the graph use remains blocked, prerelease, non-production, advisory-only, or constrained;
- dated exit criteria for independent ontology review, data governance, administration, incident response, and continuity; and
- periodic review to prevent temporary controls from becoming permanent through inaction.

Where lack of independent source verification, entity resolution, privacy review, security review, or policy validation creates unacceptable risk, affected graph capabilities shall remain disabled, prerelease, non-production, advisory-only, or limited to synthetic and non-sensitive data.

### Prohibited Behaviors

The following behaviors are prohibited:

- treating the graph as authoritative merely because data is indexed;
- treating a node as fact or an edge as verified relationship without resolution semantics;
- granting authorization from graph proximity, inferred ownership, or organizational relationship;
- merging entities from weak identity signals without controlled resolution;
- erasing conflicting, historical, disputed, superseded, or revoked assertions;
- converting inference into Verified state through repetition or confidence alone;
- omitting provenance from material assertions;
- counting circular or correlated graph paths as independent evidence;
- using current graph state to rewrite historical knowledge;
- traversing across tenant boundaries without explicit authority;
- exposing sensitive relationships through search, ranking, counts, errors, timing, or exports;
- allowing retrieved or ingested instructions to alter ontology, access, or policy;
- allowing models to write verified facts or administer the graph;
- using graph completeness as a claim without bounded scope and exclusions;
- suppressing source conflict, ingestion failure, staleness, truncation, or deletion state;
- retaining personal or customer graph data indefinitely by default;
- using deletion-resistant derived edges to circumvent source deletion;
- migrating schemas without provenance, temporal, tenant, and policy validation;
- using graph snapshots as a substitute for backup or Evidence Chain integrity;
- representing bootstrap self-review as independent Enterprise assurance; or
- allowing temporary experimental graph structures to become canonical through inaction.

### Non-Goals

The Knowledge Graph is not intended to:

- replace authoritative systems of record;
- create a universal unrestricted enterprise data lake;
- guarantee complete organizational knowledge;
- infer permission, legal obligation, identity, ownership, or intent without approved authority;
- replace the Policy Engine, Risk Classification Engine, Approval Engine, Tool Gateway, Validation Pipeline, Audit Engine, or Evidence Chain;
- convert correlation into causation;
- make every source semantically equivalent;
- retain every historical or personal relationship indefinitely;
- expose unrestricted cross-tenant analytics;
- let models self-author verified knowledge;
- guarantee truth from graph connectivity;
- eliminate human correction, dispute, or governance; or
- redesign the canonical architecture.

### Conformance Requirements

An implementation conforms to this section only when it demonstrates that:

- every material Entity and Assertion has a stable identity and governed scope;
- nodes, properties, and edges preserve source, provenance, resolution, temporal, tenant, confidence, and evidence semantics;
- authoritative facts, supplied assertions, deterministic derivations, probabilistic inferences, disputes, and unresolved candidates remain distinguishable;
- entity resolution preserves ambiguity and requires controlled merge or split;
- ontology and mapping changes are versioned and governed;
- effective time and knowledge time are preserved;
- current views do not rewrite historical knowledge;
- source conflicts and counterevidence remain visible;
- circular and correlated evidence paths are not counted as independent;
- every query is tenant-bound, purpose-bound, access-controlled, resource-bounded, and auditable;
- graph traversal cannot create access to connected protected information;
- Context Engine, reasoning, planning, Repository Intelligence, and policy consumption preserve graph semantics;
- inferred relationships cannot grant permission or become verified without approved evidence;
- tenant isolation covers graph data, indexes, caches, views, queries, telemetry, snapshots, exports, and deletion;
- privacy controls address relationship sensitivity and re-identification;
- correction, dispute, revocation, expiry, supersession, and deletion propagate to dependent views and indexes;
- policy use fails safely on missing, stale, conflicted, or invalid graph facts;
- backup and recovery preserve semantic and control integrity;
- Audit Engine and Evidence Chain records operate continuously across material graph events;
- bootstrap limitations remain explicit, constrained, temporary, and subject to external review; and
- retention follows approved record-class-specific schedules and is not indefinite by default.

### Canonical Invariants

The following invariants are binding:

- the Knowledge Graph is a governed semantic relationship layer and not the universal source of truth;
- authoritative sources remain authoritative after indexing;
- a graph node is not automatically a fact and an edge is not automatically verified;
- every material assertion is tenant-bound, source-bound, provenance-bound, temporally bounded, versioned, attributable, and governed by a resolution state;
- Verified, Asserted, Derived, Inferred, Disputed, Superseded, Revoked, Expired, Rejected, and Unresolved semantics are not silently conflated;
- inference, confidence, popularity, repetition, and connectivity cannot create authority;
- effective time and knowledge time remain distinguishable;
- entity merges and splits preserve history, provenance, tenant boundaries, and downstream impact;
- graph queries and traversals do not grant access beyond deterministic authorization;
- cross-tenant linkage requires explicit approved authority and isolation;
- relationship sensitivity may exceed the classification of individual nodes;
- Context Engine and reasoning preserve source and resolution semantics;
- Policy Engine consumes only approved, typed, current, authoritative graph facts and remains deterministic;
- Tool Gateway remains the controlled execution boundary;
- Validation Pipeline remains independent;
- Audit Engine and Evidence Chain controls operate continuously across ingestion, resolution, assertion, inference, query, correction, migration, deletion, recovery, and retirement;
- graph history does not override privacy, deletion, retention, and legal-hold governance;
- bootstrap operation remains honest, constrained, temporary, and subject to dated exit criteria; and
- architecture-changing graph proposals require an authorized ADR and cannot modify canonical controls by their own force.

A Knowledge Graph implementation is non-conformant if it treats indexed data as universal truth; presents nodes or edges without source, tenant, time, provenance, and resolution semantics; merges identities from weak signals; converts inference into fact through repetition or confidence; erases conflict or history; counts circular paths as independent evidence; infers authorization from relationships; permits cross-tenant traversal; exposes sensitive relationships through indirect channels; lets models write verified facts or administer the graph; bypasses source authority, deterministic policy, privacy, Tool Gateway, validation, audit, evidence, or human accountability; ignores correction and deletion propagation; uses stale or conflicted graph data for policy without fail-safe treatment; represents a snapshot as Evidence Chain proof; migrates schemas without semantic validation; retains protected graph data indefinitely; represents bootstrap self-review as independent assurance; or gives any model, provider, framework, graph store, customer preference, sales commitment, or engineering convenience architectural authority.

## 6.5 Repository Intelligence

### Purpose and Canonical Role

Repository Intelligence transforms verified repository facts, history, lifecycle records, and governed organizational metadata into contextual analysis about change, impact, ownership, architecture, quality, security, validation, release readiness, and planning. It enables ILAIOS to reason about software systems at repository and multi-repository scale without granting the intelligence layer authority to modify source, merge changes, publish artifacts, deploy software, or alter Runtime state.

Repository Intelligence builds upon the Code Intelligence capability defined in Section 2.11. Code Intelligence establishes the canonical dependency sequence of Code Entity Model, Source File Analyzer, Symbol Extraction, Dependency Extraction, and Repository Code Index. It produces baseline-bound, attributable, queryable facts and bounded analytical signals. Repository Intelligence consumes those accepted outputs together with approved repository history, engineering records, ADRs, tests, releases, incidents, and ownership metadata to create higher-level insights and recommendations.

The distinction is binding. Repository Intelligence shall not reimplement, bypass, reorder, or fabricate the accepted Code Intelligence sequence. It shall not analyze an ambiguous repository, silently select a different baseline, or convert a probabilistic interpretation into a verified code fact.

### Architectural Status and Authority Boundary

Repository Intelligence is an Intelligence Plane capability. It is advisory and analytical. It may identify likely impact, candidate owners, architecture drift, test scope, security exposure, change coupling, release risk, documentation gaps, and planning constraints. It shall preserve whether each result is a verified repository fact, deterministic derivation, imported assertion, inferred relationship, recommendation, or unresolved condition.

Repository Intelligence shall not:

- select or change the authoritative repository, origin, branch, commit, tree, workspace, or artifact baseline;
- execute repository content during ordinary analysis;
- modify files, create commits, push branches, open or merge changes, publish releases, deploy artifacts, or change Runtime state;
- grant repository access, approval, capability, merge authority, release authority, or deployment authority;
- waive mandatory review, testing, security, validation, or evidence controls;
- declare a repository, change, release, or deployment safe or accepted solely from analysis;
- treat repository ownership inference as authorization;
- replace authoritative source control, build, release, issue, incident, or policy systems; or
- redesign canonical architecture through generated recommendations.

Operational actions resulting from repository analysis remain subject to the deterministic Policy Engine, applicable risk classification, required approval, time-bound capability issuance, Tool Gateway execution, independent Validation Pipeline assessment, Audit Engine, Evidence Chain, and human accountability.

### Relationship to Code Intelligence

Section 2.11 remains the authority for foundational repository representation and analysis order. Repository Intelligence consumes the Repository Code Index and associated coverage, provenance, diagnostic, and limitation records.

The responsibilities are separated as follows:

- **Code Intelligence** establishes exact repository baseline identity, source-file metadata, code entities, symbols, supported dependency relationships, index coverage, and change-bound facts.
- **Repository Intelligence** combines those facts with approved contextual records to develop higher-level insights about architecture, ownership, impact, change, quality, security, validation, planning, and release.

Repository Intelligence shall not repair an invalid Code Entity, missing file identity, parse failure, unresolved symbol, unsupported dependency, or stale Repository Code Index through model inference. It may describe the limitation, estimate likely impact with an Inferred state, request renewed Code Intelligence analysis, or restrict the conclusion.

The canonical Code Intelligence order remains unchanged:

1. Code Entity Model.
2. Source File Analyzer.
3. Symbol Extraction.
4. Dependency Extraction.
5. Repository Code Index.

Any change to this order requires an authorized ADR. Repository Intelligence is a downstream consumer and shall not be inserted as an alternative stage within that sequence.

### Objectives

Repository Intelligence shall:

- bind every analysis to exact verified repository and index baselines;
- preserve facts, derivations, inferences, recommendations, gaps, and unsupported conditions as distinct result types;
- combine source structure with approved engineering and lifecycle context without erasing source authority;
- support repository and multi-repository impact analysis;
- identify candidate change scope, validation scope, ownership, dependencies, risks, and release considerations;
- detect architecture drift and inconsistency against accepted decisions without rewriting those decisions;
- support Context Engine and Planning Engine with bounded repository context;
- provide Confidence Assessments for uncertain insights;
- protect source code, secrets, customer data, security findings, and tenant metadata;
- expose analysis coverage, freshness, and limitations;
- support incremental refresh without treating incremental processing as weaker correctness;
- produce attributable Repository Insight Records;
- remain language-, framework-, repository-host-, and provider-independent; and
- fail safely when repository identity, baseline, index compatibility, authority, or coverage is insufficient.

The objective is not to maximize the number of findings. Useful repository intelligence prioritizes material, actionable, traceable insights and preserves uncertainty instead of manufacturing completeness.

### Canonical Domain Model

The Repository Intelligence domain shall distinguish:

- **Repository Identity:** the stable tenant-bound identity of an authoritative repository;
- **Repository Baseline:** an immutable or equivalently protected source state identified by repository, origin, branch or reference, commit or tree, content identity, and verification status;
- **Code Intelligence Snapshot:** the Repository Code Index and associated entity, symbol, dependency, coverage, provenance, diagnostic, and analyzer versions for one baseline;
- **Repository Context Set:** the approved engineering, architecture, ownership, test, release, incident, issue, change, policy, and operational metadata eligible for analysis;
- **Repository Intelligence Request:** the typed, bounded request for repository analysis;
- **Repository Analysis Profile:** the versioned definition of sources, methods, coverage, output types, limits, and assurance requirements;
- **Repository Fact:** a source-bound or deterministic fact accepted from Code Intelligence or another authoritative system;
- **Repository Inference:** a probabilistic or heuristic conclusion that remains non-authoritative;
- **Repository Insight:** an explained analytical result combining facts, context, inference, and limitations;
- **Impact Hypothesis:** a bounded proposal about components, systems, tests, owners, customers, data, controls, or operations potentially affected by a change;
- **Ownership Candidate:** an inferred or asserted responsibility relationship that does not grant access or approval authority;
- **Architecture Conformance Finding:** a verified or inferred relationship between repository state and accepted architectural decisions;
- **Validation Recommendation:** proposed validation additions or priorities that cannot remove the mandatory policy baseline;
- **Repository Intelligence View:** a tenant-, purpose-, classification-, baseline-, and audience-bounded projection;
- **Repository Insight Record:** the versioned output containing subject, facts, inferences, provenance, confidence, limitations, and recommended treatment;
- **Repository Comparison:** a controlled analysis between exact baselines without combining their entities as one current state; and
- **Repository Intelligence Run:** the attributable execution of an Analysis Profile against defined baselines and context.

These objects shall not be collapsed. A Repository Baseline is not a working directory. A Code Intelligence Snapshot is not the authoritative repository. A Repository Fact is not an inference. An Ownership Candidate is not an access grant. An Impact Hypothesis is not validated impact. A Validation Recommendation is not a Quality Gate decision. A Repository Insight is not authorization to change code.

### Repository Identity and Baseline Binding

Every analysis shall bind to an exact verified Repository Baseline. The baseline shall include or reference:

- tenant and repository identity;
- authoritative origin or equivalent repository source;
- branch, tag, reference, or detached baseline as applicable;
- immutable commit, tree, archive, or artifact identity;
- verification time and verifying component;
- working-tree state where relevant;
- submodule, nested repository, generated source, vendored source, and large-object treatment;
- sparse, shallow, partial, or filtered state;
- repository policy and classification;
- Code Intelligence Snapshot identity;
- applicable analyzer and configuration versions; and
- integrity and Evidence Chain references.

The requested baseline shall be established by the Bootstrap Validator and Immutable Context. Repository Intelligence shall not choose another local directory, cached copy, fork, branch, origin, commit, generated archive, or provider snapshot because it is available or easier to analyze.

If the repository state changes during analysis, the run shall remain bound to the original baseline or be cancelled and restarted under a new baseline. Results from different baselines shall not be silently merged.

An uncommitted or mutable workspace may be analyzed only through an explicitly approved Development profile that captures exact content identities and limitations. It shall not be represented as the accepted repository baseline or release candidate.

### Repository Intelligence Request

Every material analysis shall begin with a typed request containing or referencing:

- a unique request and correlation identity;
- verified tenant, subject or service, and purpose;
- Repository Identity and exact Baseline;
- Code Intelligence Snapshot and coverage status;
- requested analysis mode and subject scope;
- included and excluded repositories, paths, entities, languages, artifacts, and metadata sources;
- applicable architecture, policy, security, privacy, data, and release references;
- required context sources and prohibited sources;
- expected output contract and audience;
- minimum source authority, provenance, freshness, confidence, and validation requirements;
- resource, time, depth, breadth, and cost limits;
- data classification, regional, retention, and disclosure rules;
- whether multi-repository analysis is permitted;
- validity and expiry; and
- an explicit statement that analysis grants no mutation or execution authority.

Narrative text shall not expand repository scope, baseline, access, tool use, provider route, or output audience. Invalid, ambiguous, stale, unauthorized, or incompatible requests shall fail safely.

### Repository Context Set

Repository Intelligence may consume approved contextual records in addition to Code Intelligence. Potential sources include:

- architecture documents and accepted ADRs;
- repository governance and ownership declarations;
- review, merge, build, test, and Quality Gate records;
- version, release, deployment, and support records;
- defects, incidents, vulnerabilities, risk treatments, and corrective actions;
- change and feature records;
- documentation and API contracts;
- dependency and supply-chain metadata;
- service catalogs and deployment inventories;
- data classification and processing records;
- customer or tenant configuration where authorized;
- observability and Validation Pipeline results;
- Audit Engine and Evidence Chain references; and
- qualified human assertions.

Each context item shall preserve source authority, tenant, baseline or time, version, classification, purpose, and limitations. Repository Intelligence shall not elevate an issue description, review comment, model output, stale ownership file, or informal note into an authoritative fact.

Context shall be minimized. Broad repository history, customer records, employee data, credentials, secrets, security-sensitive configuration, or privileged material shall not be included merely because it could improve analysis.

### Analysis Modes

Approved Analysis Profiles may support:

- **Repository Overview:** summarizes structure, languages, components, coverage, supported analysis, and known limitations;
- **Change Impact:** identifies potentially affected entities, dependencies, tests, interfaces, owners, data, controls, and downstream systems;
- **Architecture Conformance:** compares repository facts against accepted architecture and ADR constraints;
- **Dependency and Coupling Analysis:** identifies direct, transitive, cyclic, optional, dynamic, unresolved, and cross-repository relationships;
- **Ownership and Stewardship Analysis:** identifies declared and candidate owners, maintainers, reviewers, and responsibility gaps;
- **Validation Scope Recommendation:** proposes additional checks or priority based on impact without reducing mandatory validation;
- **Security and Privacy Context:** identifies relevant attack surfaces, sensitive paths, data handling, secrets indicators, controls, and review needs without replacing security validation;
- **Release and Migration Context:** identifies compatibility, upgrade, schema, deprecation, rollback, documentation, and support considerations;
- **Test Intelligence:** maps changed entities and dependencies to relevant test assets and coverage evidence;
- **Historical Change Analysis:** examines evolution, co-change, defect, review, incident, and release history under controlled time semantics;
- **Documentation Alignment:** identifies possible divergence among code, schemas, public contracts, ADRs, and documentation;
- **Technical Debt and Maintainability:** identifies evidence-backed complexity, instability, duplication, ownership, support, or lifecycle concerns;
- **Planning Support:** develops bounded work, dependency, sequencing, evidence, and uncertainty inputs for the Planning Engine; and
- **Repository Comparison:** compares exact baselines, repositories, variants, or release lines without treating them as one state.

Each mode shall define its authoritative inputs, deterministic facts, permissible inferences, required confidence, known blind spots, and prohibited interpretations.

### Repository Fact and Inference Separation

Repository Intelligence shall label material outputs using controlled epistemic categories:

- **Verified Repository Fact:** directly supported by the authoritative baseline or another authoritative source with required integrity;
- **Deterministic Derivation:** mechanically produced from identified facts and a versioned method;
- **Imported Assertion:** supplied by an approved system or human but not independently verified as repository fact;
- **Inferred Relationship:** probabilistic or heuristic interpretation;
- **Recommendation:** a proposed course requiring policy and human treatment;
- **Unknown:** material information cannot be determined;
- **Unsupported:** the current analyzers or profiles cannot establish the result;
- **Conflicted:** sources or analyses disagree; and
- **Excluded:** content was intentionally outside approved scope.

The interface shall not present all output as findings of equal authority. A static import relationship can be a deterministic fact for a supported language and baseline. Runtime call behavior, business ownership, customer impact, exploitability, architectural intent, and necessary remediation may remain inferred or unresolved.

A model-generated explanation shall not change the authority class of the underlying result.

### Repository Insight Record

Every material insight shall be represented through a Repository Insight Record containing or referencing:

- unique Insight ID and analysis-run identity;
- tenant, repository, baseline, and Code Intelligence Snapshot;
- Analysis Profile and method versions;
- subject entities and exact source locations where applicable;
- statement and insight type;
- supporting Repository Facts and deterministic derivations;
- imported assertions and contextual records;
- inferences, assumptions, counterevidence, and unresolved conditions;
- provenance and source authority;
- Confidence Assessment;
- affected components, paths, interfaces, tests, data, controls, owners, customers, and environments where supported;
- proposed action, validation, or review treatment;
- severity or priority recommendation without constituting authoritative risk classification;
- limitations, exclusions, unsupported languages, parser errors, and coverage gaps;
- temporal validity, expiry, and invalidation triggers;
- disclosure and downstream-use restrictions; and
- Audit Engine and Evidence Chain references.

The record shall not contain reusable credentials, unrestricted source dumps, hidden customer data, or direct execution commands. Proposed repository changes shall be inert and separately governed through the Product Development Workflow.

### Multi-Repository Intelligence

Enterprise systems commonly span multiple repositories. Multi-repository analysis may identify shared contracts, services, packages, deployment definitions, policies, data schemas, clients, libraries, and release dependencies.

Every repository shall retain its own verified identity, baseline, tenant, classification, coverage, and Code Intelligence Snapshot. The system shall not create one synthetic baseline that hides repository differences.

Cross-repository relationships shall identify:

- source and target repository identities and baselines;
- relationship type and direction;
- source of the relationship;
- version or compatibility constraint;
- temporal validity;
- confidence and resolution state;
- tenant and organizational authority; and
- known gaps or dynamic behavior.

The analysis shall distinguish direct source dependency, published artifact dependency, shared schema, deployment coupling, operational dependency, organizational coordination, and inferred co-change. These relationships have different authority and impact semantics.

Access to one repository does not grant access to another. Cross-repository traversal follows deterministic authorization at each boundary.

### Change-Impact Analysis

Change-impact analysis begins with an exact baseline comparison or bounded change set. It shall identify what changed before estimating what may be affected.

The analysis may consider:

- changed files, entities, symbols, schemas, contracts, policies, configuration, and documentation;
- direct and transitive dependencies;
- dynamic, unresolved, optional, generated, and external relationships;
- public and internal interfaces;
- test and validation coverage;
- build, package, deployment, and migration paths;
- data classification, storage, transfer, and retention;
- security boundaries, privileges, secrets, and keys;
- tenant and customer-specific behavior;
- release and support lines;
- incidents, defects, and prior regressions;
- ownership and review requirements;
- observability and rollback; and
- affected canonical controls and ADRs.

Impact shall be represented as verified, derived, inferred, possible, excluded, or unknown. An incomplete index, unsupported language, reflection, dynamic loading, generated code, remote configuration, infrastructure behavior, or unavailable external dependency shall widen uncertainty.

Repository Intelligence may expand review and validation scope. It cannot remove policy-required checks. Absence of a discovered dependency is not proof of no impact when coverage is incomplete.

### Architecture Conformance Analysis

Architecture Conformance compares repository evidence with the Product Constitution, Canonical Architecture and Engineering Standards, accepted ADRs, approved component boundaries, dependency direction, security controls, and repository rules.

The analysis may identify:

- component placement inconsistent with accepted architecture;
- duplicate authority or bypass paths;
- forbidden dependency direction;
- direct tool execution outside Tool Gateway boundaries;
- policy logic moved into probabilistic components;
- validation coupled to execution;
- missing continuous audit or evidence events;
- Development and Runtime boundary violations;
- tenant or data-isolation inconsistencies;
- unmanaged provider or model integration;
- Code Intelligence dependency-order violations;
- unapproved repository or release workflows; and
- implementation-specific decisions requiring an ADR.

Repository evidence may establish structural facts, but interpretation against architecture may require qualified review. A conformance finding shall identify the exact canonical rule, repository evidence, confidence, severity recommendation, and resolution path.

Repository Intelligence cannot amend architecture to make implementation appear conformant. If implementation and architecture conflict, the conflict follows change, ADR, and governance processes.

### Dependency and Coupling Intelligence

Dependency analysis shall preserve direct, transitive, static, dynamic, optional, conditional, generated, external, unresolved, and cyclic relationships. Co-change and similarity shall not be labeled dependency without appropriate evidence.

Coupling analysis may use:

- source-level dependency facts;
- package and artifact manifests;
- schema and API relationships;
- build and deployment configuration;
- version and release history;
- co-change patterns;
- incident and defect propagation;
- shared data and infrastructure; and
- approved operational topology.

Historical correlation is advisory. Files that often change together may share hidden coupling, team convention, release timing, or incidental history. The result shall retain the method and Confidence Assessment.

Cyclic dependency findings shall distinguish syntactic cycles, build cycles, runtime cycles, data cycles, organizational cycles, and inferred coordination loops. Remediation shall not be recommended without understanding the relationship type and accepted architecture.

### Ownership and Stewardship Intelligence

Repository Intelligence may combine declared ownership, review history, contribution history, organizational roles, support records, incident response, architecture authority, and customer commitments to identify candidate owners and responsibility gaps.

Ownership semantics shall remain distinct:

- source maintainer;
- code reviewer;
- component owner;
- product owner;
- architecture authority;
- security owner;
- privacy or data owner;
- release owner;
- service operator;
- incident owner;
- customer-account authority; and
- accountable business authority.

Contribution frequency, authorship, commit count, file proximity, or prior review does not grant approval authority. An Ownership Candidate is advisory until verified against an authoritative organizational or repository governance source.

Personal contribution and review data shall be processed under an approved purpose and shall not become an unrestricted employee-performance score. Stale or absent ownership data shall be surfaced, not filled through assumption.

### Test and Validation Intelligence

Repository Intelligence may map code entities, dependencies, historical defects, incidents, test assets, Quality Gates, environments, and release profiles to recommend validation scope.

Recommendations may include:

- directly associated unit and component tests;
- dependency and integration tests;
- contract and schema tests;
- security, privacy, tenant, and authorization tests;
- migration, backup, restore, and rollback tests;
- performance, capacity, and resilience tests;
- cross-platform, language, and compatibility tests;
- regression tests linked to prior defects or incidents;
- documentation and operational readiness checks; and
- qualified human review.

The Validation Pipeline and policy-defined baseline remain authoritative. Repository Intelligence may add, prioritize, or explain checks; it cannot remove, waive, mark passed, or reorder a mandatory control contrary to policy.

Test existence is not test coverage. Test execution is not pass. Pass is not acceptance. Historical pass does not establish current-baseline validity.

### Security and Privacy Intelligence

Repository Intelligence may identify security- and privacy-relevant context, including trust boundaries, privileged operations, secrets indicators, authentication and authorization paths, cryptographic use, data flows, tenant handling, logging, external calls, provider integrations, dependencies, and unsafe patterns.

Findings shall distinguish:

- deterministic pattern or configuration fact;
- vulnerability or advisory match;
- exploitability hypothesis;
- architectural concern;
- missing control evidence;
- privacy or data-handling indicator;
- false-positive candidate; and
- confirmed issue established through the competent security or privacy process.

Repository Intelligence does not determine final vulnerability severity, legal applicability, breach status, data-protection role, or risk acceptance. It may trigger escalation and additional validation.

Sensitive findings shall be access-controlled and excluded from general context, search, model prompts, and customer-visible output unless authorized. The system shall avoid reproducing secrets or exploit instructions unnecessarily.

### Supply-Chain Intelligence

Repository Intelligence may combine manifests, lock data, vendored content, generated artifacts, build definitions, provenance records, release metadata, advisories, licenses, and provider dependencies to support supply-chain analysis.

It shall distinguish:

- declared dependency;
- resolved dependency;
- built artifact content;
- transitive dependency;
- optional or development-only dependency;
- runtime-loaded dependency;
- vendored or copied code;
- generated code;
- provider service dependency;
- unknown or unresolved dependency; and
- inferred dependency.

A declared version range is not proof of the deployed version. A lock record is not proof of runtime presence. A repository scan is not a complete software inventory without build and artifact evidence.

Licensing, export, sanction, legal, security, and contractual conclusions remain with competent processes. Repository Intelligence supplies attributable context and alerts.

### Historical Intelligence

History analysis may identify evolution, change concentration, coupling, recurring defects, ownership drift, review latency, release patterns, rollback frequency, incident linkage, and architecture change.

Historical analysis shall bind every event to its repository baseline, branch or release line, author or service identity where lawful, time, and record source. Rewritten or imported history shall be identified.

Metrics such as churn, commit count, review time, defect count, or ownership concentration require controlled definitions and context. They shall not be used as employee-performance measures by default.

Historical correlation shall not be represented as causation. A file with frequent changes may be actively maintained, unstable, generated, central, or undergoing planned migration. Interpretation shall include relevant context and uncertainty.

History shall not be rewritten to conceal failed builds, rejected changes, incidents, reverts, or prior nonconformance. Current corrections coexist with the historical record.

### Technical Debt and Maintainability Intelligence

Technical debt and maintainability are multi-dimensional. Repository Intelligence may identify evidence-backed indicators such as:

- unresolved architecture deviation;
- excessive or cyclic dependency;
- unsupported language or framework version;
- repeated defect or incident concentration;
- missing ownership;
- weak test or validation evidence;
- stale documentation;
- duplication and inconsistent contracts;
- excessive change coupling;
- fragile migration or rollback;
- abandoned feature flags or temporary controls;
- dependency end-of-support exposure; and
- unowned security, privacy, or operational risk.

No single complexity, size, churn, coverage, or age metric determines technical debt. The insight shall identify business consequence, evidence, uncertainty, owner, proposed treatment, and whether an ADR or risk decision exists.

Repository Intelligence may recommend prioritization. It cannot accept debt, defer mandatory remediation, or alter product scope.

### Documentation and Contract Alignment

Repository Intelligence may compare repository facts with documentation, API definitions, schemas, configuration references, release notes, migration guides, architecture diagrams, and customer-facing claims.

Potential divergence shall be reported with exact versions and evidence. The system shall not assume code is always correct and documentation is always stale. Either may be wrong or apply to a different version.

Public contract, internal interface, generated specification, implementation, test, and documentation are separate artifacts. Alignment analysis shall preserve their authority and release context.

A generated documentation update remains a proposal subject to review. Repository Intelligence shall not publish customer-facing documentation directly.

### Query and Retrieval Architecture

Every Repository Intelligence query shall be typed, tenant-bound, purpose-bound, baseline-bound, authenticated through the platform, and evaluated by deterministic authorization.

A query shall contain or reference:

- Query ID and correlation ID;
- verified tenant and requesting identity;
- repository and exact baseline;
- Code Intelligence Snapshot;
- Analysis Profile and requested view;
- path, entity, symbol, dependency, change, time, or record scope;
- allowed fact, inference, confidence, and source classes;
- data classification and disclosure limits;
- maximum result, traversal, resource, and time bounds;
- required provenance and evidence;
- freshness and completeness requirements;
- export and downstream-use restrictions; and
- expiry and cache behavior.

Authorization may apply at repository, path, file, symbol, finding, insight, source, customer, security, or evidence level. Access to an insight does not automatically grant access to the underlying source if classification differs.

Empty, filtered, unavailable, incomplete, unsupported, stale, and failed results shall remain distinguishable. Absence of a finding is not proof of absence when coverage is incomplete.

### Natural-Language Repository Analysis

Natural-language interfaces may improve access to Repository Intelligence but shall not bypass typed queries, baseline binding, tenant authorization, resource limits, or output contracts.

The AI Reasoning and Recommendation Engine may translate a user request into a proposed Repository Intelligence query. The deterministic control path shall validate the query before execution.

Natural-language terms such as current, production, main, latest, owned by, safe, impacted, complete, or approved are ambiguous unless resolved to controlled identities and semantics. The system shall request clarification or present bounded interpretations.

Generated explanations shall cite the Repository Insight Records and underlying sources. They shall not invent files, symbols, dependencies, owners, tests, commits, incidents, or validation outcomes.

### Relationship to Knowledge Graph

Repository Intelligence may publish governed repository entities and relationships to the Knowledge Graph. Section 6.4 governs ontology, provenance, temporal semantics, tenant isolation, resolution state, and query behavior.

Published graph assertions shall preserve repository identity, exact baseline, source location, analyzer and Analysis Profile versions, and epistemic category. A relationship inferred by Repository Intelligence remains Inferred in the graph until independently verified.

The Knowledge Graph may supply organizational, service, policy, incident, data, customer, and lifecycle context. Graph information shall not override the authoritative repository or Code Intelligence facts.

Graph merges, schema changes, or entity resolution shall not silently alter repository identities or combine entities from different baselines.

### Relationship to Context Engine

The Context Engine may retrieve Repository Insight Records and underlying facts for reasoning and planning. It shall enforce purpose, tenant, repository, baseline, classification, source, confidence, and resource boundaries.

Repository context shall be minimized. Full source files, secrets, customer configuration, security findings, and history shall not be included when a smaller structured fact set is sufficient.

Context summaries shall preserve unsupported, conflicted, excluded, and incomplete conditions. A summarized impact view shall not be presented as complete when analyzer coverage is partial.

### Relationship to Confidence Scoring

Section 6.3 governs Confidence Scoring. Repository inferences, impact hypotheses, ownership candidates, architecture interpretations, and historical correlations shall link to Confidence Assessments when material.

Deterministic Code Intelligence facts may not require probabilistic confidence, but they still require provenance, integrity, scope, and coverage. A score shall not replace those properties.

Confidence shall account for baseline integrity, index coverage, language support, unresolved dependencies, source authority, historical representativeness, model fitness, counterevidence, and assumption sensitivity.

A high-confidence repository insight cannot authorize a change, waive review, reduce mandatory validation, or establish release readiness.

### Relationship to Planning Engine

Repository Intelligence supplies the Planning Engine with candidate scope, dependencies, owners, validation needs, sequencing constraints, architecture considerations, risks, evidence gaps, and rollback context.

The Planning Engine shall distinguish verified repository facts from inferred impact. A proposed plan shall include discovery or validation tasks where repository intelligence is incomplete.

Repository Intelligence cannot approve a plan or assign work to a person by inferred ownership. It may recommend a responsible role or team for verification.

Plan execution follows Policy Engine, Approval Engine, capability, Tool Gateway, Validation Pipeline, and lifecycle controls. Repository Intelligence shall not monitor a plan by mutating repository state.

### Relationship to Policy Engine

The deterministic Policy Engine may consume typed Repository Facts and bounded signals only where policy defines their exact semantics and fail-safe behavior.

Eligible policy inputs may include verified repository identity, baseline, file classification, exact changed entities, declared dependency, approved ownership record, coverage state, release line, or validation evidence reference.

Inferred impact, ownership candidates, similarity, historical correlation, model explanation, and confidence cannot create permission. They may increase review, restrict capability, add validation, or cause denial when policy explicitly defines this treatment.

Policy shall reject stale, ambiguous, cross-baseline, incomplete, or integrity-failed repository inputs for mandatory decisions.

### Relationship to Validation Pipeline

The Validation Pipeline may use Repository Intelligence to select additional checks, prioritize execution, explain coverage, or identify affected components. It cannot allow Repository Intelligence to remove or waive mandatory checks.

Validation results may become context for later repository insights and calibration. The analysis shall preserve exact baseline, artifact, environment, rule, and outcome.

Repository Intelligence shall not mark a change as validated because recommended tests exist, were invoked, or historically passed. The authoritative Validation Record remains separate.

A failed validation is counterevidence and shall not be hidden from impact, readiness, or confidence analysis.

### No-Mutation and Tool Separation

Ordinary Repository Intelligence is read-only. It shall not execute build scripts, package lifecycle hooks, macros, tests, binaries, generated commands, repository hooks, or untrusted content.

Any operational action, including checkout, file modification, patch application, dependency installation, build, test, commit, branch creation, push, merge, tag, release, or deployment, requires a separately authorized Tool Gateway operation in an approved isolated environment.

A Repository Insight Record is not a tool request. A generated patch is not an approved change. A recommended command is not an execution capability.

The Tool Gateway shall verify exact repository, baseline, target, operation, parameters, tenant, purpose, capability, approval, and expiry. Results return through controlled records and independent validation.

Retry after tool failure shall not broaden repository scope, disable hooks, lower validation, use a different branch, or force an operation without renewed authority.

### Security Architecture

Repository Intelligence processes adversarial source and high-value intellectual property. Threats include:

- repository substitution;
- branch, commit, path, or baseline confusion;
- malicious source designed to exploit parsers or models;
- archive, symlink, or path escape;
- oversized or resource-exhausting repositories;
- injected instructions in source, comments, documents, issues, or metadata;
- secrets and credential disclosure;
- cross-tenant index or cache contamination;
- sensitive-code exposure;
- dependency and advisory poisoning;
- fabricated ownership or review history;
- index tampering;
- stale analysis replay;
- model hallucination presented as repository fact;
- unauthorized graph or context publication;
- malicious generated patch or command;
