- no unrestricted cross-task, cross-user, or cross-tenant memory;
- protected administrative, provider, source, key, and recovery credentials;
- qualified external review completed before an affected context profile involving high-impact source, instruction, privacy, tenant, policy, memory, production, or release concerns influences a Stable release, production environment, customer-controlled production deployment, or Enterprise operating profile; otherwise the profile remains blocked, prerelease, non-production, advisory-only, or constrained;
- dated exit criteria for independent source review, privacy governance, administration, incident response, and continuity; and
- periodic review to prevent temporary controls from becoming permanent through inaction.

Where lack of independent review, source assurance, deletion validation, or injection testing creates unacceptable risk, the affected Context profile shall remain disabled, prerelease, non-production, advisory-only, or limited to synthetic and non-sensitive data.

### Prohibited Behaviors

The following behaviors are prohibited:

- mutating or replacing Immutable Context through context assembly;
- treating relevance, ranking, similarity, graph proximity, repository ownership, model confidence, or source availability as authorization;
- maximizing context without purpose limitation and minimization;
- retrieving from unregistered or unauthorized sources;
- accepting tenant, scope, provider, tool, policy, or instruction changes from source content;
- concatenating untrusted data into privileged instruction channels without structural separation;
- allowing retrieved instructions to override canonical or tenant controls;
- silently omitting mandatory instructions, counterevidence, denials, failed validation, conflicts, or limitations;
- converting assertions, recommendations, summaries, or inferences into authoritative facts;
- resolving source conflict through model preference;
- using stale, revoked, deleted, or cross-tenant cache entries;
- broadening retrieval because a model requests more information;
- hiding truncation, redaction, summarization loss, or incomplete coverage;
- following links, attachments, scripts, macros, or embedded tools without approved capability;
- retaining hidden long-term memory across tenants, users, tasks, or purposes;
- using customer content for unrelated provider training, evaluation, personalization, or cross-tenant ranking;
- retaining personal, customer, source, cache, or context data indefinitely by default;
- representing bootstrap self-review as independent Enterprise assurance; or
- allowing temporary sources, caches, or memory profiles to become canonical through inaction.

### Non-Goals

The Context Engine is not intended to:

- replace the Immutable Context Manager;
- determine policy, authorization, approval, risk acceptance, or legal basis;
- provide unrestricted search over all enterprise data;
- maximize data disclosure to models;
- create a universal permanent memory;
- treat every accessible source as eligible;
- resolve authoritative source conflict autonomously;
- guarantee complete knowledge;
- replace source systems of record;
- execute external business actions;
- validate recommendations or results independently;
- infer hidden protected information;
- eliminate human correction and governance;
- use summaries as substitutes for required authoritative sources; or
- redesign canonical architecture.

### Conformance Requirements

An implementation conforms to this section only when it demonstrates that:

- every Context Request and Package binds to a verified tenant, purpose, consumer, Immutable Context, and validity period;
- context assembly never mutates or expands the Immutable Context silently;
- source eligibility is deterministic and request-specific;
- authoritative facts, assertions, derivations, inferences, instructions, untrusted content, recommendations, validation results, conflicts, unknowns, and exclusions remain distinguishable;
- instruction authority is structurally separated from source data;
- source content cannot select tools, providers, credentials, policies, tenants, or authority;
- retrieval is bounded by source, tenant, purpose, time, depth, breadth, cost, token, and resource limits;
- mandatory context and counterevidence are protected from ranking and truncation;
- provenance, version, time, confidence, classification, and transformation lineage remain available;
- summarization, redaction, deduplication, and compression disclose material loss;
- cache use revalidates current authorization, source state, tenant, purpose, and deletion;
- no unrestricted cross-task, cross-user, or cross-tenant memory exists;
- source correction, revocation, deletion, and policy changes invalidate affected packages and caches;
- model and provider routing preserves data, tenant, region, retention, and assurance controls;
- Context Engine does not grant tool or execution authority;
- Validation Pipeline remains independent;
- tenant isolation covers retrieval, indexes, packages, summaries, caches, prompts, telemetry, exports, evaluation, and evidence;
- changes follow Engineering and Product Development controls;
- Audit Engine and Evidence Chain records operate continuously across the context lifecycle;
- bootstrap limitations remain explicit, constrained, temporary, and subject to external review; and
- retention follows approved record-class-specific schedules and is not indefinite by default.

### Canonical Invariants

The following invariants are binding:

- Immutable Context is the authoritative task basis; the Context Engine only produces governed projections;
- context relevance never creates authorization;
- more context never creates more authority;
- every Context Package is tenant-bound, purpose-bound, consumer-bound, source-bound, versioned, attributable, time-bound, and integrity-protected;
- approved instructions remain structurally separate from untrusted source data;
- retrieved or embedded instructions cannot override Product Constitution, canonical architecture, policy, approval, Tool Gateway, Validation Pipeline, Audit Engine, Evidence Chain, or human accountability;
- authoritative facts, assertions, derivations, inferences, recommendations, validation results, conflicts, and unknowns are not silently conflated;
- context assembly follows least privilege, minimization, provenance, freshness, and counterevidence requirements;
- mandatory context cannot be displaced by advisory relevance ranking;
- summaries and transformations do not replace authoritative sources and disclose material loss;
- source, policy, tenant, repository, graph, model, or context changes may invalidate prior packages;
- caches do not bypass current authorization, deletion, revocation, or tenant isolation;
- no unrestricted permanent memory exists across tenants, users, tasks, or purposes;
- models and providers remain replaceable and non-authoritative;
- Policy Engine remains deterministic;
- Tool Gateway remains the controlled path for external side effects;
- Validation Pipeline remains independent;
- Audit Engine and Evidence Chain controls operate continuously across request, eligibility, retrieval, transformation, packaging, delivery, use, correction, deletion, change, recovery, and retirement;
- bootstrap operation remains honest, constrained, temporary, and subject to dated exit criteria; and
- architecture-changing context proposals require an authorized ADR and cannot modify canonical controls by their own force.

A Context Engine implementation is non-conformant if it mutates or replaces Immutable Context; treats relevance, similarity, source availability, model confidence, graph connectivity, repository ownership, user preference, or cached state as authorization; retrieves unregistered or cross-tenant data; maximizes context without minimization; lets source content override instructions or controls; concatenates untrusted content into privileged instruction channels; hides counterevidence, denials, conflicts, truncation, redaction, or transformation loss; converts assertions or inferences into facts; resolves source conflicts through model preference; broadens scope when a model asks; follows links or executes embedded content without capability; reuses stale or revoked caches; retains hidden permanent memory; uses customer data for unrelated training or ranking; bypasses Policy Engine, Tool Gateway, Validation Pipeline, Audit Engine, Evidence Chain, privacy, security, deletion, or human accountability; represents bootstrap self-review as independent assurance; or gives any model, provider, retrieval framework, source owner, customer preference, sales commitment, or engineering convenience architectural authority.

## 6.7 Planning Engine

### Purpose and Canonical Role

The Planning Engine converts an eligible recommendation, authorized Context Package, and verified task basis into a structured Proposed Plan suitable for deterministic policy evaluation, risk classification, human review, capability determination, controlled execution, independent validation, and accountable disposition. It formalizes what is proposed, in which order, under which preconditions, against which exact targets, with which requested capabilities, expected effects, validation criteria, failure handling, and rollback or compensation considerations.

The Planning Engine does not approve or execute the plan. A Proposed Plan is an inert, versioned control artifact. It is not a capability, tool command, approval, release decision, deployment authorization, risk acceptance, validation result, or Task Orchestrator state transition.

The Task Orchestrator remains the Control Plane owner of the canonical task lifecycle. It invokes the governed planning path, submits the plan for policy and risk evaluation, coordinates required approval and capability issuance, dispatches authorized operations through the Tool Gateway, initiates independent validation, and records acceptance or rejection. The Planning Engine owns plan construction and revision semantics only; it does not advance authoritative task state.

### Architectural Status and Authority Boundary

The Planning Engine is an Intelligence Plane capability. It may use deterministic planning rules, graph algorithms, repository facts, constraints, model-generated recommendations, scheduling methods, optimization, and human-supplied requirements. These methods remain subordinate to the Product Constitution, canonical architecture, Immutable Context, deterministic policy, accountable authority, and non-waivable controls.

The Planning Engine shall not:

- change Immutable Context or authority scope;
- select a different tenant, repository, baseline, resource, environment, or destination without renewed context;
- grant or expand a capability;
- approve its own plan;
- classify or accept risk authoritatively;
- waive a policy, Quality Gate, validation requirement, or human review;
- execute a step directly;
- create standing credentials or reusable secrets;
- declare execution complete, validated, accepted, delivered, or closed;
- change Task Orchestrator lifecycle state; or
- redesign canonical architecture by recommendation alone.

The deterministic Policy Engine determines whether the Proposed Plan and requested capabilities are permitted. The Risk Classification Engine determines required treatment. The Approval Engine records accountable approval where required. The Identity and Capability Manager issues constrained execution authority. The Tool Gateway enforces each operation. The Validation Pipeline independently assesses results. Audit Engine and Evidence Chain controls operate continuously across planning and every downstream stage.

### Objectives

The Planning Engine shall:

- transform analysis into an explicit, reviewable, policy-evaluable plan;
- bind the plan to exact tenant, task, Immutable Context, target, repository, artifact, and environment identities;
- decompose work into bounded Plan Steps with clear dependencies and expected effects;
- distinguish goals, facts, assumptions, constraints, decisions, proposals, actions, results, and unknowns;
- identify required capabilities without granting them;
- expose irreversible, destructive, privileged, external, customer-visible, or high-impact steps;
- define preconditions, postconditions, validation, observation, timeout, cancellation, retry, rollback, and compensation expectations;
- preserve uncertainty, alternatives, conflicts, and Context Gaps;
- prevent implicit scope expansion and hidden side effects;
- support safe parallelism only where dependencies and isolation permit;
- support deterministic policy and human review through typed plan contracts;
- create a stable Plan Digest that binds downstream decisions;
- support controlled revision without rewriting prior versions;
- use repository, graph, context, confidence, and provider capabilities without granting them authority;
- support continuous audit and evidence; and
- remain technology-, provider-, tool-, workflow-product-, and deployment-independent.

The objective is not to maximize automation or minimize step count. A longer plan that exposes controls, validation, and rollback may be more appropriate than a shorter plan that hides risk or combines incompatible authority.

### Canonical Domain Model

The planning domain shall distinguish:

- **Planning Request:** the typed, tenant-bound request to produce or revise a Proposed Plan;
- **Planning Basis:** the exact Immutable Context, Recommendation Envelope, Context Package, repository and graph baselines, policies, constraints, and source references available for planning;
- **Plan Objective:** the bounded outcome the plan proposes to achieve;
- **Plan Constraint:** a mandatory scope, time, data, security, privacy, quality, resource, contract, or operational limit;
- **Plan Assumption:** a non-authoritative premise required for planning and explicitly marked for verification or treatment;
- **Plan Decision Point:** a future bounded choice reserved to deterministic policy, validation, or accountable human authority;
- **Plan Step:** one inert unit of proposed work with typed input, action class, target, requested capability, expected effect, and controls;
- **Plan Dependency:** a required ordering, data, artifact, authority, validation, resource, or external condition between steps;
- **Plan Condition:** a precondition, guard, branch criterion, stop condition, or postcondition;
- **Capability Request:** the minimum proposed authority needed for one or more exact steps;
- **Validation Requirement:** the pre-established criteria and independent checks proposed for an artifact, operation, or result;
- **Observation Requirement:** the operational signals and period needed before progression or acceptance;
- **Rollback Action:** a proposed action that restores a prior known state where feasible;
- **Compensation Action:** a proposed action that mitigates or reconciles an irreversible or externally visible effect when rollback is not possible;
- **Plan Branch:** a bounded alternative path selected only through an approved condition and authority;
- **Plan Graph:** the complete dependency and control structure of the Proposed Plan;
- **Plan Version:** one immutable or equivalently protected plan representation;
- **Plan Digest:** the integrity identity of all material plan fields and references that bind downstream decisions;
- **Plan Assessment:** the feasibility, completeness, uncertainty, risk-indicator, capability, validation, and readiness metadata for a plan;
- **Proposed Plan:** the complete versioned artifact submitted to the Control Plane; and
- **Plan Revision Record:** the attributable relationship between prior and new plan versions, changed inputs, rationale, and invalidated decisions.

These objects shall not be collapsed. An Objective is not a Step. A Step is not a tool invocation. A Capability Request is not a capability. A Validation Requirement is not a validation result. A branch condition is not permission. A rollback proposal is not proof of reversibility. A Plan Digest is not approval. A Proposed Plan is not authoritative task state.

### Planning Request Contract

Every material planning operation shall begin with a typed Planning Request containing or referencing:

- Planning Request ID and task correlation ID;
- verified tenant, requester, and planning consumer;
- exact Immutable Context version or digest;
- Recommendation Envelope and Context Package versions;
- Plan Objective and requested outcome;
- exact targets, repository or artifact baselines, environment, and destination scope;
- required and prohibited action classes;
- policy, risk, security, privacy, data, contract, release, and operational constraints;
- required planning depth and output schema;
- available tools as descriptive capability classes, not granted authority;
- required validation, rollback, evidence, and human-review profiles;
- deadlines, resource limits, cost limits, and service objectives;
- source authority, confidence, freshness, and completeness requirements;
- allowed alternatives, branching, parallelism, retry, and compensation patterns;
- expiry and cancellation behavior; and
- an explicit statement that planning grants no permission or execution authority.

Natural-language requests may be normalized into a proposed Planning Request, but deterministic validation shall establish the final typed scope. Ambiguous targets, environments, terms, units, deadlines, ownership, success criteria, or destructive effects shall trigger clarification or an incomplete plan state.

An unauthorized, expired, inconsistent, unverified, or out-of-scope Planning Request shall fail safely.

### Planning Basis

The Planning Basis shall contain only authorized and relevant information. It may include:

- Immutable Context;
- Recommendation Envelope and alternatives;
- Context Package and Context Gaps;
- applicable Product Constitution, architecture, ADR, policy, and standards references;
- Knowledge Graph entities and relationships;
- Repository Intelligence facts and insights;
- exact repository, artifact, release, and environment identities;
- risk indicators and required treatment inputs;
- available capability classes and Tool Gateway contracts;
- Validation Pipeline rule classes and Quality Gates;
- incidents, defects, changes, releases, migrations, and support obligations;
- data, privacy, security, tenancy, and regional constraints;
- qualified human requirements and customer instructions; and
- prior plan, execution, validation, and outcome records where authorized.

Every basis item shall preserve authority, source, tenant, time, confidence, and limitation semantics. The Planning Engine shall not elevate model output, graph inference, repository ownership candidate, historical correlation, or customer preference into authoritative scope.

If the Planning Basis is insufficient, the engine shall identify the exact Context Gap. It shall not invent missing tools, owners, approvals, capabilities, repository facts, policies, deadlines, budgets, or validation criteria.

### Plan Objective and Success Definition

Every Proposed Plan shall define one or more bounded objectives. An objective shall identify:

- intended business or technical outcome;
- subject and target scope;
- observable success conditions;
- required constraints and quality attributes;
- excluded outcomes and non-goals;
- acceptable partial or alternative outcomes where authorized;
- deadline or validity period;
- accountable owner or required owner role;
- validation and acceptance authority; and
- known assumptions and dependencies.

Success shall not be defined solely as completion of steps. An execution may complete while the objective fails. Validation may pass technical rules while business acceptance remains required. Delivery may fail after acceptance. These outcomes remain distinct.

The Planning Engine may propose success criteria but cannot approve them unilaterally when competent product, customer, security, privacy, legal, operational, or human authority is required.

### Plan Step Contract

Every Plan Step shall contain or reference:

- stable Step ID within the Plan Version;
- objective contribution;
- action class and inert action specification;
- exact target, resource, repository, artifact, environment, and destination identities where known;
- tenant and purpose;
- required inputs and authoritative sources;
- preconditions and dependency state;
- requested capability and least-privilege scope;
- required approval class;
- expected effect, side effects, and prohibited effects;
- data read, write, creation, deletion, transfer, and disclosure expectations;
- security, privacy, tenant, key, secret, and isolation requirements;
- timeout, cancellation, retry, idempotency, and concurrency behavior;
- observation and telemetry requirements;
- validation criteria and evidence requirements;
- rollback or compensation action;
- failure and escalation behavior;
- human decision points;
- confidence, assumptions, limitations, and unresolved conditions;
- output and artifact contract; and
- Plan Digest contribution.

The action specification shall be typed and inert. It shall not contain hidden executable authority, reusable credentials, unrestricted scripts, dynamically generated destinations, or semantics that permit a worker to broaden the operation.

If a required field cannot be established, the step shall be incomplete, conditional, blocked, or routed for clarification. The engine shall not use a generic best effort instruction to conceal missing controls.

### Plan Graph and Dependency Semantics

The Plan Graph represents ordering and control relationships among steps. Dependency types may include:

- completion dependency;
- successful-validation dependency;
- artifact or data dependency;
- policy-decision dependency;
- approval dependency;
- capability dependency;
- human-decision dependency;
- resource or capacity dependency;
- temporal or schedule dependency;
- security or privacy precondition;
- observation-period dependency;
- external-system dependency;
- rollback or compensation dependency; and
- mutually exclusive or conditional branch relationship.

Dependencies shall be explicit and typed. A simple sequence shall not be used when progression actually depends on validation, approval, observation, or external confirmation.

The Plan Graph shall detect cycles, unresolved prerequisites, unreachable steps, missing terminal paths, inconsistent branches, and compensation gaps. A cycle may be permitted only when it represents a bounded iteration with termination, resource, authority, and evidence rules.

The graph shall not infer that a step may execute merely because its predecessor completed. All applicable policy, approval, capability, current-state, and validation conditions remain required at enforcement time.

### Decomposition

Planning shall decompose work to the level necessary for independent authorization, execution, validation, rollback, and evidence. A step shall not combine materially different targets, capabilities, risk classes, tenants, environments, or irreversible effects merely for convenience.

Decomposition shall consider:

- least-privilege capability scope;
- separation of read, write, delete, publish, sign, deploy, and external communication;
- reversible and irreversible effects;
- distinct approval authorities;
- validation isolation;
- tenant and data boundaries;
- repository and environment boundaries;
- failure containment;
- parallelism and resource use;
- audit and Evidence Chain granularity; and
- human comprehensibility.

Over-decomposition may also create risk through excessive complexity, repeated data transfer, fragmented evidence, or unmanageable approval. The approved Planning Profile shall balance atomic control and operational coherence.

### Capability Requests

The Planning Engine may identify the minimum capability required for a Plan Step. The request shall specify:

- action and target;
- tenant, purpose, environment, and destination;
- permitted parameters and data classes;
- time, invocation count, resource, and rate limits;
- preconditions and dependent approvals;
- plan, step, Immutable Context, and artifact digests;
- permitted worker and Tool Gateway adapter class;
- required evidence and validation; and
- revocation, consumption, and expiry behavior.

A Capability Request grants no authority. The Identity and Capability Manager may issue a narrower capability, deny the request, require additional approval, or return it for revision.

The Planning Engine shall not request broad administrative, wildcard, standing, cross-tenant, or transferable authority when a narrower capability can satisfy the objective.

Plan revision affecting a capability-bound field invalidates the capability or requires deterministic reassessment. The plan cannot preserve authority by changing only narrative text while altering operational meaning.

### Preconditions, Guards, and Postconditions

Preconditions define what must be true before a step is eligible for execution. They may include:

- current task and plan state;
- exact resource, repository, artifact, and environment identity;
- policy and risk result;
- approval and capability state;
- required prior validation;
- dependency completion;
- source freshness and integrity;
- key, secret, credential, and revocation state;
- backup, rollback, or recovery readiness;
- capacity and maintenance window;
- human confirmation; and
- evidence-ingestion readiness.

Guards shall be machine-evaluable where appropriate. Natural-language conditions such as if safe, when ready, as needed, or if acceptable are insufficient for controlled execution unless a competent human decision point is explicitly defined.

Postconditions define expected immediate state and artifacts. They do not establish acceptance. Independent validation determines whether required properties hold.

### Branching and Decision Points

A Proposed Plan may include branches only when branch criteria, authority, scope, and consequences are explicit. Branch types may include:

- deterministic data or status condition;
- Policy Engine outcome;
- Risk Classification treatment;
- Approval Engine outcome;
- Validation Pipeline result;
- bounded operational health signal;
- human determination; and
- external authoritative event.

The Planning Engine shall not choose a branch reserved to another authority. It may model the alternatives and their required controls.

Every branch shall have allowed successors, termination behavior, resource and capability implications, rollback or compensation, and evidence requirements. An undefined else path shall fail safely.

Branching shall not create a route around denial. A denied action cannot be decomposed, renamed, retried, or routed through another tool to evade policy.

### Parallelism and Concurrency

Plan Steps may execute in parallel only when their dependencies, targets, data, locks, resource limits, side effects, failure containment, and validation permit it.

The plan shall identify:

- independent and shared resources;
- ordering and serialization requirements;
- transaction or consistency boundaries;
- race, duplicate, and lost-update risks;
- tenant and rate limits;
- combined capability exposure;
- cancellation and partial-failure behavior;
- observation and reconciliation; and
- rollback or compensation order.

Parallelism shall not be used to bypass cumulative policy, approval, cost, or rate controls. Two individually permitted steps may be prohibited in combination.

The Task Orchestrator and Tool Gateway enforce runtime concurrency according to current state. The Planning Engine's parallelism proposal is not execution permission.

### Scheduling, Time, and Resource Planning

Planning may represent deadlines, durations, dependencies, maintenance windows, service objectives, quotas, budgets, capacity, and external availability. Estimates shall remain distinguishable from commitments.

Every estimate shall identify basis, range, confidence, assumptions, exclusions, and sensitivity. Historical performance may inform estimates but shall not be treated as deterministic for a new tenant, environment, provider, repository, or workload.

The Planning Engine shall not create a commercial, contractual, regulatory, release, or customer commitment. Competent authorities approve commitments.

Schedule pressure shall not remove mandatory security, privacy, policy, approval, validation, evidence, rollback, or human-review steps.

If the objective cannot be achieved within approved time or resources, the engine shall propose scope reduction, sequencing, alternative plan, escalation, or refusal. It shall not silently lower assurance.

### Validation Planning

Every material Plan Step and final objective shall have pre-established validation requirements appropriate to consequence. Validation planning shall identify:

- artifact or result subject;
- exact baseline and environment;
- mandatory and advisory rule classes;
- security, privacy, tenant, data, functional, quality, compatibility, performance, resilience, and operational checks;
- expected evidence sources;
- independent execution boundary;
- pass, fail, blocked, error, waived, and inconclusive treatment;
- observation period;
- acceptance handoff; and
- remediation or renewed-plan behavior.

The Planning Engine may propose validation scope using Repository Intelligence, Knowledge Graph, policy, prior incidents, and Context Packages. It cannot define criteria after seeing the result to manufacture success.

Policy and the Validation Pipeline determine the authoritative rule set and result. Planning may add or prioritize checks but cannot remove mandatory ones.

### Rollback, Compensation, and Reversibility

Plans shall distinguish rollback from compensation. Rollback restores a prior known state. Compensation mitigates or reconciles an effect that cannot be undone exactly.

For each material step, the plan shall identify:

- whether the effect is reversible, partially reversible, compensable, or irreversible;
- the prior-state identity and recovery evidence;
- rollback or compensation action;
- required capability and approval;
- latest safe initiation point;
- dependencies and ordering;
- data, customer, legal, financial, and operational consequences;
- validation of recovery; and
- residual obligations.

The Planning Engine shall not label a step reversible merely because an opposite command exists. External communication, deletion, data disclosure, payment, signing, customer action, physical effect, and third-party state may not be fully reversible.

Rollback and compensation remain controlled operations through Tool Gateway and require current authority. Failure handling shall not invoke them automatically beyond the approved plan and capability.

### Retry, Replanning, and Failure Handling

Retry shall be planned, bounded, and idempotency-aware. The plan shall define retryable outcomes, maximum attempts, backoff, cumulative cost and time, duplicate-effect prevention, and escalation.

A retry shall not change target, tool, provider, region, data scope, capability, validation, or approval silently. A materially changed approach is a new Plan Version.

Replanning may occur after policy denial, risk treatment, approval condition, execution failure, validation failure, source change, incident, timeout, cancellation, or new Context Gap. Replanning shall preserve the prior Plan Version and cause.

The Planning Engine shall not interpret denial or failure as permission to find a bypass. Revised plans shall satisfy the substance of the applicable decision.

Repeated replanning shall be bounded. The system shall prevent indefinite loops that consume resources, hide inability, or repeatedly seek a favorable policy or model outcome.

### Plan Lifecycle

The Planning Engine shall use a plan-artifact lifecycle distinct from the Task Orchestrator's authoritative task lifecycle. Minimum plan states are:

- **Requested:** a valid Planning Request exists;
- **In Construction:** the engine is creating a plan;
- **Clarification Required:** material input or accountable choice is missing;
- **Incomplete:** a plan exists but mandatory fields, dependencies, or controls are unresolved;
- **Proposed:** a complete candidate Plan Version has been produced for review and control evaluation;
- **Returned for Revision:** policy, risk, human review, capability, or validation feedback requires a new version;
- **Superseded:** a newer Plan Version replaces the plan for current use;
- **Withdrawn:** the proposer or competent authority removes the plan from consideration;
- **Expired:** the plan or Planning Basis is no longer valid; and
- **Archived:** the plan is retained as historical record after applicable disposition.

These states do not include Approved, Executing, Validated, Accepted, Delivered, or Closed because those belong to separate authoritative records and the task lifecycle. A user interface may display combined status only when it preserves ownership and semantics.

Plan-state transitions shall be attributable, versioned, and audited. A mutable dashboard is not the authoritative Plan Record.

### Proposed Plan Contract

The Proposed Plan shall contain or reference:

- stable Plan ID and Plan Version;
- Plan Digest;
- tenant, task, purpose, and Immutable Context;
- Recommendation Envelope and Context Package;
- objectives, non-goals, success, validation, and acceptance conditions;
- Planning Basis and source manifest;
- exact target, repository, artifact, environment, and destination identities;
- Plan Graph, Steps, dependencies, branches, and decision points;
- requested capabilities and approval classes;
- policy-relevant attributes and risk indicators;
- data, security, privacy, tenant, regional, contract, and operational constraints;
- validation and observation requirements;
- rollback, compensation, retry, cancellation, and timeout;
- resource, schedule, and cost estimates;
- assumptions, Context Gaps, conflicts, alternatives, and rejected approaches;
- Confidence Assessments and limitations;
- required human decisions and owners;
- expiry and invalidation triggers;
- disclosure, retention, and downstream-use rules;
- schema and Planning Profile versions; and
- Audit Engine and Evidence Chain references.

The Proposed Plan shall be immutable or version-addressable. Downstream components shall verify schema, tenant, Plan Digest, Immutable Context, validity, and current state before use.

### Plan Digest and Material Change

The Plan Digest shall bind all fields that can affect policy, risk, approval, capability, execution, validation, evidence, customer understanding, or outcome. It shall include stable references to large external artifacts where direct inclusion is impractical.

Material changes include, as applicable:

- objective or success criteria;
- target, tenant, repository, baseline, artifact, environment, or destination;
- action, parameter, data, side effect, or tool class;
- capability scope;
- step order, dependency, branch, concurrency, retry, or timeout;
- validation, observation, rollback, or compensation;
- risk indicator or irreversible effect;
- provider, region, data classification, or disclosure;
- assumption, Context Gap, or source basis; and
- human approval or accountability requirement.

A material change creates a new Plan Version and digest. Bound policy decisions, risk classifications, approvals, capabilities, execution leases, and validation contracts become invalid or require deterministic reassessment according to their own rules.

The Planning Engine cannot declare its own material change non-material to preserve authority. Materiality rules are deterministic and governed.

### Policy and Risk Integration

The Task Orchestrator submits the Proposed Plan and Immutable Context to the Policy Engine and Risk Classification Engine. The Planning Engine does not evaluate itself into permission.

The plan shall expose policy-relevant attributes explicitly. It shall not hide destructive effects, external destinations, data transfer, privilege, tenant impact, provider use, uncertainty, or validation gaps in narrative fields.

Policy may permit, deny, restrict, require revision, require approval, reduce capability, add validation, or impose conditions. Risk Classification may impose treatment based on consequence and uncertainty.

Feedback shall identify the Plan Version and affected fields. A revised plan shall preserve the prior decision and demonstrate how the controlling issue was addressed.

A high Confidence Assessment or favorable historical outcome cannot waive policy or risk treatment.

### Human Review and Approval

Human review shall receive a comprehensible representation of the exact Proposed Plan. The review package shall show:

- objective and requested decision;
- tenant, requester, target, environment, and destination;
- material steps and capabilities;
- destructive, irreversible, external, privileged, security, privacy, customer, and data effects;
- alternatives and rejected approaches;
- assumptions, uncertainty, Context Gaps, and counterevidence;
- policy and risk outcomes;
- validation, observation, rollback, and compensation;
- resource and schedule impact;
- residual obligations; and
- exact Plan Digest and validity period.

Approval is created and governed by the Approval Engine, not by the Planning Engine. Silence, prior similar approval, reviewer familiarity, user-interface placement, or model recommendation is not approval.

Approval binds to the exact Plan Digest and Immutable Context. A material plan change invalidates approval unless the applicable deterministic approval policy explicitly preserves a bounded condition.

The Planning Engine shall not impersonate an approver, infer consent, split a plan to avoid a high-risk approval threshold, or present the preferred option as inevitable.

### Execution Handoff

After required policy, risk, approval, and capability controls complete, the Task Orchestrator may dispatch eligible Plan Steps to the Tool Gateway.

The execution handoff shall include:

- task, plan, step, and Immutable Context identities;
- current state and dependency evidence;
- exact capability;
- target, operation, parameters, environment, and destination;
- required worker and adapter class;
- timeout, retry, cancellation, resource, and rate limits;
- data and isolation constraints;
- expected output and artifact contract;
- validation and evidence references; and
- current integrity and revocation state.

The Tool Gateway independently revalidates authority and shall reject a step not represented by the approved Plan Digest or capability. The Planning Engine shall not call tools directly.

Execution output does not update the plan as if the expected effect occurred. Actual Execution Records remain separate and feed validation, reconciliation, and possible replanning.

### Validation and Acceptance Handoff

The Task Orchestrator submits immutable result and context references to the Validation Pipeline according to the approved validation contract.

The Validation Pipeline determines structured rule outcomes independently. The Planning Engine may explain the planned validation but cannot recalculate, omit, or override an unfavorable result.

Acceptance or rejection remains a separate deterministic and accountable decision. Completion of all Plan Steps is not acceptance. Validation pass may still require customer, product, security, privacy, release, or other accountable disposition.

A failed result may trigger a new Planning Request for remediation. The original Plan, execution, validation, and evidence remain unchanged.

### Relationship to AI Reasoning and Recommendation Engine

The AI Reasoning and Recommendation Engine supplies analysis, alternatives, and a Planning Proposal. The Planning Engine converts eligible recommendations into a formal Proposed Plan.

Reasoning may suggest actions, but the Planning Engine shall require typed targets, dependencies, capabilities, conditions, validation, and failure behavior. It shall not copy unrestricted prose directly into executable fields.

If the reasoning output lacks necessary detail, the Planning Engine records a Context Gap or requests clarification. It does not invent authority or operational parameters.

Model-generated plan content remains non-authoritative and is governed by the Plan schema, policies, Quality Gates, and review.

### Relationship to Context Engine

The Context Engine supplies an authorized Context Package containing goals, constraints, sources, graph and repository relationships, policy references, confidence, and gaps.

The Planning Engine shall preserve source authority, tenant, time, confidence, and limitation semantics. A summarized or inferred item shall not become a verified precondition without support.

The Planning Engine cannot expand context to make the plan feasible. Supplemental context follows a new governed Context Request and, where material, a renewed Immutable Context.

### Relationship to Knowledge Graph

The Planning Engine may use Knowledge Graph relationships for dependencies, ownership, policy, lifecycle, incidents, evidence, data, services, and organizational context.

Graph paths remain subject to source, provenance, temporal, tenant, resolution, and confidence semantics. Inferred or disputed edges shall not be treated as authoritative dependencies or owners.

The Proposed Plan may include discovery steps to resolve graph ambiguity. It shall not write Verified graph assertions by its own authority.

### Relationship to Repository Intelligence

Repository Intelligence supplies baseline-bound change scope, dependencies, impact hypotheses, architecture findings, ownership candidates, validation recommendations, and rollback context.

The Planning Engine shall distinguish deterministic repository facts from inferred impact and unsupported conditions. Incomplete Code Intelligence coverage widens plan uncertainty and may require additional validation or discovery.

Repository Intelligence cannot authorize a code change, select a branch, assign an approver, or reduce mandatory validation. Generated patches remain proposed artifacts governed through the Development, Review, Change, and Release lifecycles.

### Relationship to Confidence Scoring

Confidence Scoring may assess objectives, assumptions, dependencies, estimates, impact, feasibility, validation premises, and rollback claims. Confidence does not approve the plan.

A high aggregate confidence shall not conceal one low-confidence critical dependency, irreversible effect, owner, policy input, or validation assumption. Material Plan Steps shall retain dimension-level assessments.

Low confidence may trigger clarification, discovery, stronger review, narrower scope, additional validation, or denial through policy. It shall not create broader data or tool access.

### Relationship to Model Orchestration and Provider Abstraction

Model-based planning passes through Section 6.2. The model route shall be eligible for the tenant, purpose, data, region, context, planning profile, and consequence.

Provider fallback shall not alter plan semantics, authority, data handling, or output contract. A model or provider change may require plan-quality reassessment.

No provider feature, tool-calling interface, or model-specific plan format shall become the canonical planning contract. Adapters normalize output into inert Plan structures.

### Security Architecture

Planning is security-sensitive because a plan can organize privileged operations and reveal how to reach protected outcomes. Threats include:

- plan injection through untrusted context;
- hidden or encoded executable commands;
- scope expansion;
- target or destination substitution;
- capability inflation;
- step splitting to evade approval;
- branch or retry paths around denial;
- validation removal;
- rollback fabrication;
- cross-tenant target confusion;
- secret inclusion;
- malicious generated patches or scripts;
- dependency manipulation;
- Plan Digest substitution or replay;
- stale approval reuse;
- infinite planning loops and resource exhaustion;
- model or provider manipulation; and
- suppression of destructive effects, counterevidence, or failure paths.

Controls shall include typed schemas, Immutable Context binding, exact target identity, source-as-data treatment, instruction separation, capability minimization, static validation, plan-graph analysis, dangerous-action classification, explicit side-effect fields, digest protection, versioning, resource limits, policy evaluation, human review, Tool Gateway enforcement, independent validation, and continuous audit and evidence.

Plan content shall not carry active credentials, private keys, reusable tokens, unrestricted commands, or hidden binary payloads. References to protected secrets shall use approved identifiers and be resolved only at the execution boundary.

A suspected plan-manipulation event shall quarantine the plan, block downstream use, preserve evidence, and initiate incident response.

### Privacy and Data Protection

Planning shall minimize personal, customer, employee, security, and operational information. The plan shall describe required data categories and operations without embedding unnecessary records.

The plan shall identify, where applicable:

- processing purpose and data categories;
- source and destination;
- read, creation, modification, deletion, transfer, and disclosure;
- applicable role and legal or contractual basis as determined by competent authority;
- tenant and customer instruction;
- region and transfer restrictions;
- retention and deletion;
- provider and subprocessor use;
- human review and protected automated-decision safeguards; and
- residual data after rollback or compensation.

The Planning Engine shall not infer legal basis or controller-processor roles. It may require competent determination as a Plan Decision Point.

Plans and planning telemetry shall follow record-class-specific retention. Personal data is not retained indefinitely by default.

### Tenant Isolation

Every Planning Request, Basis item, Objective, Step, Capability Request, Plan Version, Digest, cache entry, model context, telemetry record, and evidence reference shall be tenant-bound.

The engine shall not:

- combine steps or targets across tenants without explicit approved authority;
- reuse one tenant's Plan as executable content for another;
- disclose tenant-specific tools, repositories, resources, policies, incidents, costs, or constraints;
- infer tenant identity from plan text;
- place protected plans in shared prompts, caches, logs, or evaluation data; or
- allow global templates to override tenant-specific controls.

Reusable plan templates may contain abstract structures only. Instantiation requires current tenant, purpose, target, policy, risk, approval, capability, and validation evaluation.

A cross-tenant plan event is a security and privacy incident.

### Plan Templates and Reuse

Templates may improve consistency for recurring operations. A template shall define abstract objectives, step classes, controls, required inputs, decision points, validation, rollback, and evidence without embedding active authority.

Every template shall have owner, version, applicability, prohibited uses, required tenant parameters, policy dependencies, evaluation, release state, expiry, and change history.

Template instantiation creates a new Proposed Plan bound to current Immutable Context. Prior approval, capability, validation, or acceptance does not transfer.

The engine shall not select a template solely because a request is textually similar. Eligibility shall consider target, data, environment, risk, tenant, provider, and consequence.

### Emergency Planning

Emergency planning may shorten time available for analysis but shall not create a permanent bypass. An Emergency Plan shall define:

- triggering incident or condition;
- competent emergency authority;
- constrained objective, scope, duration, and target;
- reduced independence or evidence explicitly recorded;
- non-waivable security, tenant, capability, Tool Gateway, audit, and evidence controls;
- minimum validation and monitoring;
- rollback or compensation;
- communication and customer impact;
- expiry and authority revocation; and
- mandatory retrospective review, remediation, and documentation.

Schedule pressure, customer preference, or ordinary defect does not establish emergency. The Planning Engine cannot declare the emergency authoritatively.

Emergency completion does not satisfy the ordinary release-readiness requirements for a Stable release, production deployment, customer-controlled production deployment, or Enterprise operating profile without the required follow-up.

### Failure and Degraded Operation

Planning shall use controlled outcomes:

- **Proposed:** a conformant Proposed Plan is available for control evaluation;
- **Proposed with Limitations:** a plan is usable for bounded review but material advisory limitations remain;
- **Clarification Required:** an accountable choice or request detail is missing;
- **Incomplete:** mandatory plan fields, dependencies, validation, rollback, or ownership remain unresolved;
- **Infeasible:** no plan satisfies the current objective and mandatory constraints;
- **Conflicted:** authoritative requirements cannot be reconciled within planning authority;
- **Out of Scope:** the objective or action lies outside approved capability or product scope;
- **Stale:** the Planning Basis or plan is no longer valid;
- **Quarantined:** suspected malicious, cross-tenant, corrupt, or manipulated content is isolated;
- **Refused:** the request is prohibited or attempts control bypass;
- **Cancelled:** an authorized cancellation occurred; and
- **Failed:** an internal or dependent-service error prevented conformant planning.

Failure shall not produce an empty plan marked ready, generic unrestricted steps, fabricated tools, or fallback to weaker controls. Infeasibility shall be reported honestly.

### Observability and Monitoring

Monitoring shall assess plan quality, control integrity, operational usefulness, security, isolation, and drift. Metrics may include:

- Planning Requests and outcomes;
- time to Proposed, clarification, revision, and expiry;
- steps, dependencies, branches, decision points, and critical paths;
- missing target, owner, capability, validation, rollback, or evidence fields;
- policy denial and revision reasons;
- risk-treatment and approval requirements;
- Plan Digest invalidation and stale-plan rejection;
- execution divergence from approved steps;
- validation pass, fail, blocked, error, and inconclusive outcomes;
- rollback, compensation, retry, cancellation, and replanning outcomes;
- human review, correction, rejection, and override;
- repository and graph uncertainty;
- model and provider route behavior;
- cross-tenant and plan-manipulation alerts;
- resource, latency, and cost; and
- incident, defect, change, release, and improvement trends.

Metrics shall include denominator, plan type, tenant, model route, risk, consequence, time, and known exclusions. Fewer steps, faster planning, fewer denials, higher execution rate, or lower review time are not inherently better.

Planning telemetry shall not expose secrets, protected source, customer data, or personal information unnecessarily.

### Quality Attributes

The Planning Engine shall be evaluated for:

- objective and scope correctness;
- Immutable Context and target binding;
- plan completeness and structural validity;
- dependency and branch correctness;
- capability minimization;
- policy and risk transparency;
- validation and acceptance separation;
- rollback and compensation realism;
- uncertainty and Context Gap representation;
- security, privacy, and tenant isolation;
- resistance to injection and control bypass;
- execution interpretability without embedded authority;
- Plan Digest and revision integrity;
- human review quality;
- model and provider portability;
- reproducibility;
- scalability and resource control; and
- operational maintainability.

Quality claims shall identify plan types, tools, environments, tenants, languages, domains, consequences, model routes, and known exclusions.

### Evaluation and Testing

Testing shall include:

- Planning Request, Basis, Plan, Step, Capability Request, Digest, and Revision schemas;
- Immutable Context and exact-target binding;
- objective, success, non-goal, assumption, unknown, and conflict semantics;
- dependency, cycle, branch, termination, and unreachable-step behavior;
- decomposition and least-privilege capability requests;
- policy, risk, approval, capability, Task Orchestrator, Tool Gateway, validation, acceptance, and delivery separation;
- material-change and Plan Digest invalidation;
- destructive, irreversible, privileged, external, customer, data, and cross-tenant actions;
- validation, observation, rollback, compensation, retry, cancellation, and timeout;
- concurrent steps and combined-policy effects;
- repository, graph, context, confidence, and provider integration;
- template instantiation and non-transfer of authority;
- emergency-plan constraints;
- malicious source, hidden commands, scope expansion, step splitting, and denial bypass;
- stale plans, replay, tampering, and approval mismatch;
- partial, incomplete, infeasible, conflicted, quarantined, refused, and failed outcomes;
- Audit Engine and Evidence Chain coverage;
- performance, budgets, and planning-loop limits;
- retention and deletion; and
- change, migration, rollback, backup, recovery, and retirement.

Evaluation scenarios shall have controlled provenance, purpose, rights, privacy treatment, tenant scope, representativeness, version, and retention.

Qualified external review shall be completed before an affected high-impact plan or Planning Profile influences a Stable release, production environment, customer-controlled production deployment, or Enterprise operating profile; otherwise it shall remain blocked, prerelease, non-production, advisory-only, or constrained.

### Quality Gates

A Planning Engine change shall not progress to broader maturity or production use unless applicable Quality Gates pass. Gates shall cover:

- Immutable Context and target binding;
- plan and step schema;
- dependency and branch correctness;
- capability minimization;
- policy, risk, approval, and Task Orchestrator separation;
- no direct execution and Tool Gateway enforcement;
- validation and acceptance independence;
- rollback, compensation, and failure handling;
- Plan Digest and revision invalidation;
- security, privacy, tenant isolation, and injection resistance;
- model and provider compatibility;
- observability, rollback, backup, and recovery;
- documentation and support; and
- audit and evidence coverage.

Gate decisions shall bind to exact Planning Profiles, templates, schemas, model routes, context sources, policy mappings, validation contracts, evaluation sets, and deployment versions.

A failed mandatory gate blocks progression. Exceptions cannot waive tenant, authority, capability, Tool Gateway, validation, audit, evidence, privacy, security, or human-accountability controls.

### Versioning and Change Governance

The Planning Engine shall version:

- Planning Request, Basis, Plan, Step, Graph, Capability Request, Digest, and Revision schemas;
- Planning Profiles and templates;
- decomposition, dependency, scheduling, branching, and optimization methods;
- validation, rollback, compensation, retry, and failure patterns;
- policy and risk mappings;
- model and provider routes;
- evaluation baselines; and
- monitoring and alerting.

A change record shall identify affected plan types, tenants, actions, tools, policies, risks, approvals, capabilities, validations, environments, customers, and claims. It shall define evaluation, rollout, observation, rollback, support, and treatment of existing plans.

Changes requiring an ADR include those that alter plan authority, Task Orchestrator ownership, Policy Engine placement, capability semantics, Tool Gateway boundary, Validation Pipeline independence, Plan Digest materiality, tenant model, or canonical operational flow.

Historical Proposed Plans retain their original versions. Migration shall not rewrite the plan reviewed or executed in a prior task.

### Backup, Recovery, and Reconciliation

Planning state required for accountability shall be durable or reconstructible from authoritative records. Recovery shall distinguish plan artifacts from Task Orchestrator state, approvals, capabilities, execution, validation, and acceptance.

Recovery shall verify:

- current task and Immutable Context;
- exact Plan Version and Digest;
- source and Context Package availability;
- policy, risk, approval, and capability current state;
- expiry, revocation, consumption, cancellation, and external side effects;
- execution and validation records;
- retention and deletion state;
- Audit Engine and Evidence Chain reconciliation; and
- whether replanning is required.

Historical approvals or capabilities shall not become active merely because a plan was restored. Uncertain state defaults to non-executable.

Reconciliation shall identify whether an external side effect occurred before a timeout or failure. A replacement step or capability is not issued until the state is resolved or safely compensated.

### Governance and Roles

Governance shall assign accountable ownership for:

- Planning Engine purpose, scope, and claims;
- Planning Request, Basis, Plan, Step, Graph, and Digest contracts;
- templates and Planning Profiles;
- Context Engine, Knowledge Graph, Repository Intelligence, and Confidence integration;
- policy, risk, approval, capability, Tool Gateway, validation, and Task Orchestrator boundaries;
- security, privacy, tenant, data, and regional controls;
- validation, rollback, compensation, retry, emergency, and recovery patterns;
- model and provider use;
- evaluation, Quality Gates, human review, and explainability;
- operations, monitoring, incident, backup, and reconciliation;
- change, release, rollback, deprecation, and retirement; and
- audit, evidence, records, documentation, customer transparency, and support.

No model, provider, template, framework, tool description, generated plan, customer preference, sales commitment, or engineering convenience may approve itself or override canonical controls.

Separation of duties shall be proportionate to impact. Under the Enterprise Profile, the person who designs a high-impact Planning Profile shall not be the sole claimed independent evaluator, policy integrator, production deployer, exception approver, and incident closer.

### Single-Maintainer Bootstrap Profile

A registered Single-Maintainer Bootstrap Profile may temporarily combine planning design, implementation, evaluation, and operational roles. The absence of independent review shall be recorded and shall not be represented as Enterprise separation of duties.

The bootstrap profile shall maintain:

- exact tenant, task, Immutable Context, Plan Version, Digest, target, and baseline binding;
- explicit self-review and exact change attribution;
- mandatory automated plan-schema, dependency, capability, security, privacy, tenant, digest, no-execution, and Quality Gates;
- protected Audit Engine and Evidence Chain records;
- restricted actions, tools, data classes, tenants, environments, model routes, production influence, and release maturity;
- no ordinary direct execution outside Tool Gateway;
- protected administrative, repository, provider, key, secret, and recovery credentials;
- qualified external review completed before an affected plan or Planning Profile involving high-impact security, privacy, tenant, destructive, irreversible, production, release, or architecture concerns influences a Stable release, production environment, customer-controlled production deployment, or Enterprise operating profile; otherwise it remains blocked, prerelease, non-production, advisory-only, or constrained;
- dated exit criteria for independent plan review, approval separation, release authority, incident response, and continuity; and
- periodic review to prevent temporary controls from becoming permanent through inaction.

Where lack of independent review, validation, approval separation, or recovery evidence creates unacceptable risk, affected planning profiles shall remain disabled, prerelease, non-production, advisory-only, or limited to synthetic and non-sensitive operations.

### Prohibited Behaviors

The following behaviors are prohibited:

- treating a Proposed Plan as approval, capability, execution instruction, validation result, acceptance, or Task Orchestrator state;
- mutating Immutable Context or expanding scope through planning;
- allowing the plan to approve or execute itself;
- embedding active credentials, unrestricted commands, hidden payloads, or wildcard authority in Plan Steps;
- concealing destructive, irreversible, external, privileged, data, tenant, customer, or security effects;
- splitting or renaming actions to evade policy, risk, approval, or validation;
- using branches, retries, fallbacks, compensation, or emergency labels to bypass denial;
- allowing model confidence or provider features to grant authority;
- treating inferred graph, repository, ownership, or schedule information as authoritative without support;
- declaring material changes non-material to preserve approval or capability;
- changing the plan after approval without a new digest and required reassessment;
- executing tools directly from the Planning Engine;
- allowing impact analysis to remove mandatory validation;
- defining success after observing results;
- representing completion as validation or acceptance;
- reusing templates with prior tenant authority, approval, capability, or evidence;
- creating indefinite retry or replanning loops;
- retaining personal, customer, plan, or model data indefinitely by default;
- representing bootstrap self-review as independent Enterprise assurance; or
- allowing temporary plans or templates to become canonical through inaction.

### Non-Goals

The Planning Engine is not intended to:

- own the authoritative task lifecycle;
- replace the Task Orchestrator;
- replace AI Reasoning and Recommendation;
- determine policy permission, risk acceptance, legal basis, approval, or capability issuance;
- execute tools, change repositories, publish releases, deploy systems, or communicate externally;
- validate results or accept outcomes;
- guarantee feasibility, reversibility, schedule, cost, or success;
- eliminate human review;
- create unrestricted self-directed operation;
- infer authority from context, graph, repository, ownership, model, or provider signals;
- turn templates into standing authorization;
- remove unknown, conflicted, or infeasible state; or
- redesign canonical architecture.

### Conformance Requirements

An implementation conforms to this section only when it demonstrates that:

- every plan binds to a verified tenant, task, Immutable Context, Planning Basis, exact target, Plan Version, and Digest;
- the Planning Engine owns plan construction but not Task Orchestrator lifecycle state;
- Proposed Plans, Capability Requests, validation requirements, approvals, capabilities, execution, validation results, and acceptance remain separate artifacts;
- every Plan Step is typed, inert, least-privilege-oriented, dependency-aware, and evidence-bearing;
- objectives, success, non-goals, assumptions, unknowns, conflicts, and limitations remain explicit;
- destructive, irreversible, external, privileged, data, security, privacy, tenant, and customer effects are visible;
- dependencies, branches, concurrency, retry, cancellation, timeout, rollback, and compensation have bounded semantics;
- material plan changes create a new digest and trigger required reassessment;
- the plan cannot declare its own changes non-material;
- policy, risk, approval, and capability decisions remain external and authoritative in their scope;
- Tool Gateway is the only controlled execution path;
- Validation Pipeline remains independent and planning cannot remove mandatory checks;
- completion, validation, acceptance, delivery, and closure remain distinct;
- Context, Knowledge Graph, Repository Intelligence, Confidence, model, and provider inputs preserve their authority and limitations;
- tenant isolation covers requests, basis, plans, templates, caches, prompts, telemetry, execution references, and evidence;
- changes follow Engineering and Product Development controls;
- Audit Engine and Evidence Chain records operate continuously across planning and downstream lifecycle events;
- bootstrap limitations remain explicit, constrained, temporary, and subject to external review; and
- retention follows approved record-class-specific schedules and is not indefinite by default.

### Canonical Invariants

The following invariants are binding:

- the Planning Engine produces Proposed Plans and grants no permission;
- the Task Orchestrator owns authoritative task state and lifecycle progression;
- a Plan Step is not a tool invocation;
- a Capability Request is not a capability;
- a Validation Requirement is not a validation result;
- a Plan Digest is not approval;
- completion of plan steps is not validation, acceptance, delivery, or closure;
- every Proposed Plan is tenant-bound, task-bound, purpose-bound, Immutable-Context-bound, target-bound, versioned, attributable, time-bound, and integrity-protected;
- material plan changes invalidate or require reassessment of bound policy, risk, approval, capability, execution, and validation records;
- the Planning Engine cannot classify its own material change as non-material to preserve authority;
- plan content remains inert and contains no active credential or hidden execution authority;
- dependencies, branches, concurrency, retry, rollback, compensation, and emergency paths cannot bypass denial;
- context relevance, graph connectivity, repository inference, ownership candidate, confidence, model output, provider feature, template, customer preference, or schedule pressure cannot create authority;
- Policy Engine remains deterministic;
- Risk Classification Engine remains authoritative for required risk treatment;
- Approval Engine remains authoritative for accountable approval;
- Identity and Capability Manager remains authoritative for capability issuance;
- Tool Gateway remains the controlled execution boundary;
- Validation Pipeline remains independent;
- Audit Engine and Evidence Chain controls operate continuously across request, basis, construction, revision, policy, risk, approval, capability, execution, validation, acceptance, delivery, closure, and review;
- bootstrap operation remains honest, constrained, temporary, and subject to dated exit criteria; and
- architecture-changing plan proposals require an authorized ADR and cannot modify canonical controls by their own force.

A Planning Engine implementation is non-conformant if it owns or advances authoritative task state; treats a plan as approval, capability, tool command, validation, acceptance, or release authority; mutates Immutable Context; expands tenant, target, repository, environment, destination, data, or capability scope; hides destructive or irreversible effects; embeds credentials or unrestricted commands; splits steps or uses branches, retries, fallbacks, compensation, or emergency labels to evade controls; changes approved material plan content without a new digest and reassessment; declares its own changes non-material; executes tools directly; removes mandatory validation; defines success after results; equates completion with acceptance; reuses template authority; creates indefinite replanning loops; bypasses Policy Engine, Risk Classification, Approval Engine, Identity and Capability Manager, Tool Gateway, Validation Pipeline, Audit Engine, Evidence Chain, privacy, security, tenant isolation, or human accountability; represents bootstrap self-review as independent assurance; retains protected data indefinitely; or gives any model, provider, framework, template, customer preference, sales commitment, or engineering convenience architectural authority.

## 6.8 Learning Boundaries

### Purpose and Canonical Role

Learning Boundaries define the conditions under which observations, feedback, outcomes, corrections, evaluations, incidents, and other operational information may influence future ILAIOS behavior. The purpose of this section is to permit controlled improvement without allowing runtime experience, model output, provider behavior, user preference, or operational pressure to become an ungoverned source of authority.

ILAIOS distinguishes learning from ordinary inference, context use, retrieval, memory, analytics, configuration, policy administration, software change, and release management. These mechanisms can affect future behavior in different ways, carry different risks, and require different controls. Describing all adaptation as learning would hide material changes in authority, data use, reversibility, validation, and accountability. Every learning mechanism shall therefore have an explicit type, purpose, scope, owner, data basis, assurance profile, release path, and rollback method.

The default production posture is no autonomous learning. A production request, response, approval, rejection, execution outcome, validation result, correction, customer comment, operator action, incident, or metric shall not automatically modify model weights, prompts, routing logic, confidence thresholds, retrieval sources, graph assertions, persistent memory, policies, capabilities, approval rules, validation requirements, or executable behavior. Any such modification is a governed change and must enter the applicable data, privacy, security, engineering, validation, change, and release processes.

Learning Boundaries do not create a new execution authority. They do not displace the Product Constitution, canonical architecture, deterministic Policy Engine, Approval Engine, Risk Classification Engine, Identity and Capability Manager, Tool Gateway, Validation Pipeline, Audit Engine, Evidence Chain, or accountable human decision-maker. Learning may propose improvement; it cannot authorize itself, deploy itself, validate itself, or declare itself safe.

### Architectural Status and Authority Boundary

Learning capability belongs to the AI and Intelligence Layer only to the extent that it prepares or evaluates bounded improvement candidates. Authoritative policy, identity, capability, approval, release, acceptance, and compliance decisions remain outside that layer. A learning process may identify an apparent pattern, produce an evaluation report, create a candidate artifact, recommend a threshold, or propose a change. Those outputs remain non-authoritative until accepted by the competent process.

The deterministic Policy Engine shall not learn policy from observed behavior. Policy is an approved, versioned, attributable, testable, reviewable, and auditable control artifact. A recurring approval, common operator choice, historical exception, model recommendation, customer preference, or successful execution does not become policy through repetition. Policy changes shall follow the applicable governance and change process, and an authorized Architecture Decision Record is required where the accepted change modifies architecture.

The Approval Engine shall not infer standing approval from prior approvals. The Identity and Capability Manager shall not expand authority because a capability was frequently requested or previously issued. The Tool Gateway shall not make a tool, action, destination, or parameter eligible because prior invocations succeeded. The Validation Pipeline shall not reduce mandatory checks because earlier outcomes passed. Audit and evidence controls shall not be sampled away merely because a pattern appears low risk.

No model, provider, dataset, training process, evaluation framework, optimization objective, learning metric, tool, customer instruction, sales commitment, or engineering preference has authority to supersede non-waivable controls. Applicable law and competent-authority requirements remain binding. Contracts are binding only within their lawful and formally approved scope and do not silently weaken the Product Constitution, canonical architecture, tenant isolation, security, privacy, safety, authorization, validation, audit, evidence, or human-accountability controls.

Learning Signals are advisory inputs. They shall not authorize or directly apply any change to a model, prompt, template, routing policy, context source, ranking method, Knowledge Graph, Repository Intelligence rule, Confidence Scoring method, Planning Profile, policy, capability, tool, validation rule, or production configuration. Every proposed learning change shall enter the applicable Development Lifecycle, Code Review Process, Quality Gates, Release Lifecycle, and Change Management process and shall receive deterministic policy evaluation, required human approval, independent validation, Audit Engine coverage, and Evidence Chain evidence before controlled promotion.

### Objectives

The Learning Boundaries shall:

- permit measurable improvement through controlled, attributable, reversible, and evidence-bearing processes;
- prevent production activity from causing silent or self-authorized behavioral change;
- preserve deterministic control over policy, approval, capability, execution, validation, and acceptance;
- distinguish feedback from verified truth and correlation from causation;
- preserve tenant, purpose, data, jurisdiction, and contractual boundaries;
- prevent one tenant's data or behavior from influencing another tenant without explicit and lawful governance;
- ensure that training, adaptation, indexing, memory, calibration, and configuration have distinct control profiles;
- protect against poisoning, manipulation, bias amplification, privacy leakage, model extraction, and metric gaming;
- require evaluation against an approved baseline before any material change is promoted;
- preserve reproducibility, lineage, rollback, retirement, and correction capabilities;
- make limitations, uncertainty, residual risk, and absent independence explicit;
- support deletion, restriction, correction, and lawful retention obligations without making unsupported claims of complete unlearning;
- ensure that qualified external review is completed before an affected high-impact learning-derived artifact influences a Stable release, production environment, customer-controlled production deployment, or Enterprise operating profile, with the artifact otherwise remaining blocked, prerelease, non-production, advisory-only, or constrained; and
- maintain continuous audit and evidence coverage from signal capture through final retirement.

### Canonical Learning Domain Model

The following concepts are distinct canonical objects. An implementation may use different storage or interface labels only when the mapping preserves these semantics.

**Learning Signal.** A Learning Signal is an observed event that may be relevant to improvement. It can include a correction, rating, approval, rejection, validation outcome, incident, performance measurement, drift indicator, user report, repository change, retrieval failure, or operational observation. A signal is not verified truth, policy, consent, permission, or an instruction to change behavior.

**Feedback Event.** A Feedback Event is an attributable Learning Signal submitted or generated through an approved feedback channel. It records source, tenant, purpose, time, subject, affected artifact, declared meaning, collection method, data classification, integrity state, and known limitations. Feedback can be honest, mistaken, incomplete, coerced, adversarial, duplicated, biased, or unrelated to the actual cause.

**Learning Proposal.** A Learning Proposal describes a candidate improvement and the evidence supporting investigation. It defines the problem, hypothesis, intended benefit, affected behavior, excluded behavior, eligible data, risk, evaluation design, success criteria, regression limits, rollback method, owner, reviewers, and release implications. It grants no permission to access data, train a model, alter policy, deploy a change, or use customer information for a new purpose.

**Learning Dataset.** A Learning Dataset is a governed collection of records approved for a stated learning purpose. It has defined provenance, ownership, lawful basis or other applicable authorization, tenant scope, permitted uses, exclusions, classification, retention, quality criteria, and access controls. A convenient collection of logs, prompts, responses, tickets, repository content, or telemetry is not a Learning Dataset until it has passed the required assessment.

**Dataset Snapshot.** A Dataset Snapshot is an immutable or integrity-protected, versioned reference to the exact data used for an evaluation, calibration, training, or adaptation run. It records inclusion and exclusion logic, transformations, labels, redactions, splits, deduplication, provenance, and unresolved limitations. A mutable query without reproducible selection semantics is insufficient for high-impact learning.

**Learning Run.** A Learning Run is a bounded evaluation, calibration, training, fine-tuning, indexing, or adaptation activity performed against an approved proposal and snapshot. It records environment, code, configuration, model, provider, randomization where applicable, parameters, data references, operators, start and end times, outputs, failures, and evidence.

**Candidate Artifact.** A Candidate Artifact is the output proposed for controlled adoption. It may be a model version, adapter, embedding configuration, prompt package, routing rule, confidence calibration, retrieval index, ontology mapping, graph update set, planning heuristic, evaluation rule, or another versioned artifact. A Candidate Artifact has no production authority merely because a Learning Run completed successfully.

**Evaluation Baseline.** An Evaluation Baseline is the approved reference against which a Candidate Artifact is assessed. It includes functional, safety, security, privacy, fairness, tenant-isolation, performance, reliability, explainability, evidence, and operational criteria appropriate to the use case. The baseline is versioned and cannot be changed after seeing candidate results merely to make the candidate pass.

**Learning Decision Record.** A Learning Decision Record documents the competent decision to reject, revise, approve for limited testing, promote, constrain, suspend, roll back, or retire a Candidate Artifact. It cites evidence, scope, conditions, dissent, exceptions, residual risk, release status, and accountable authority. It is not replaced by a metric dashboard or model-generated summary.

**Correction and Unlearning Record.** A Correction and Unlearning Record tracks data correction, restriction, deletion, exclusion, re-indexing, re-training, artifact retirement, or another required remediation. It distinguishes deletion from source systems, exclusion from future datasets, removal from retrieval, invalidation of derived artifacts, and any technically substantiated model-unlearning action.

### Learning Mechanism Classification
