- Audit Engine and Evidence Chain controls operate continuously and are not replaced by Kubernetes logs or events;
- tenant isolation is a full-stack property and namespaces alone are insufficient;
- privileged workloads are denied by default and exceptions remain bounded and evidenced;
- admission, workload security, network, identity, secret, and artifact controls are enforced rather than merely declared;
- retries, restarts, rescheduling, and failover cannot duplicate unauthorized or irreversible external action;
- desired-state reconciliation cannot approve its own source or overwrite canonical authority;
- cluster upgrades preserve compatibility, security, availability, validation, rollback, and evidence;
- managed services do not eliminate ILAIOS or customer responsibilities;
- unsupported clusters, versions, extensions, and modifications are represented honestly;
- bootstrap operation does not imply independent administration or Enterprise assurance; and
- architecture-significant Kubernetes decisions require an authorized ADR.

A Container Orchestration implementation is non-conformant if it makes Kubernetes mandatory without an authorized architecture decision; conflates the Kubernetes control plane with the ILAIOS Control Plane; treats cluster access, Kubernetes authorization, namespace membership, service account, label, or network location as business permission; bypasses deterministic ILAIOS policy or the Tool Gateway; lets a scheduler, Pod, Job, controller, operator, deployment system, or cluster administrator create ILAIOS authority or accept its own result; relies on namespaces as complete tenant isolation; admits privileged or unsafe workloads without bounded policy; uses ineffective network rules, unrestricted egress, uncontrolled cloud metadata, shared credentials, or exposed orchestration APIs; stores or exposes secrets without approved protection; schedules untrusted workloads onto higher-trust nodes without justified isolation; deploys mutable or unverified artifacts; retries irreversible action without reconciliation; treats rollout, health, Kubernetes audit, or provider status as independent validation, canonical audit, or Evidence Chain proof; permits ungoverned drift, manual production change, extension privilege, unsupported version skew, or unrecoverable upgrade; misrepresents customer-controlled or bootstrap operation as independent Enterprise assurance; or gives any distribution, provider, cluster, operator, controller, webhook, tool, customer preference, sales commitment, or engineering convenience architectural authority.

## 7.4 Container Strategy

### Purpose and Canonical Role

Container Strategy defines how ILAIOS software is packaged, built, identified, verified, distributed, promoted, executed, maintained, and retired as container artifacts. It establishes a controlled software-supply-chain boundary between accepted source and an eligible runtime package without making a container format, build tool, registry, runtime, operating system, or provider an architectural authority.

A container image is a deployable software artifact. It is not business permission, policy approval, deployment acceptance, validation evidence, tenant identity, or a complete security boundary. A valid image digest identifies exact content under the applicable digest rules; it does not prove that the content is safe, approved, correctly built, lawfully usable, or suitable for an ILAIOS workload. A signature can bind an artifact to an accepted signer and verification policy; it does not independently establish functional correctness or release eligibility.

The deterministic Policy Engine remains within the ILAIOS Control Plane. Container build, registry, admission, and runtime mechanisms enforce infrastructure and supply-chain controls within their approved scope. They shall not issue ILAIOS business capabilities, satisfy human approval requirements, bypass the Tool Gateway, accept runtime results, or modify canonical architecture.

### Scope

This section applies to container artifacts used across ILAIOS-managed, customer-controlled, hybrid, isolated, development, test, evaluation, staging, recovery, and production Deployment Profiles. It covers image format, build inputs, build isolation, base images, dependencies, build secrets, provenance, Software Bills of Materials, vulnerability and malware assessment, artifact identity, tagging, signing, registry governance, promotion, retention, image composition, runtime user and privilege, filesystem behavior, process structure, configuration interfaces, network surface, health integration, platform architecture, specialized hardware, restricted execution, third-party images, customer images, patching, drift, incident response, evidence, and conformance.

Section 7.3 defines container orchestration, cluster, admission, scheduling, network-policy, node, and workload-controller requirements. Section 7.5 defines durable storage architecture. Sections 7.6 through 7.10 define networking, scalability, observability, monitoring, and logging in greater depth. Section 4.7 governs Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery; Section 4.10 governs release policy; Section 5.3 governs the canonical Release Lifecycle. This section defines the container-specific controls those sections shall preserve.

### Technology Independence and Open Format

ILAIOS shall prefer open, interoperable container-image and distribution semantics. An approved Container Profile may use an Open Container Initiative-compatible image, manifest, index, layout, runtime bundle, distribution service, or equivalent format. The approved profile shall record the exact compatibility and any extensions relied upon.

No particular commercial container engine, build service, registry, operating-system distribution, packaging method, signing service, scanner, or runtime implementation is canonical by default. A technology may be required by an exact product or Deployment Profile only through an approved decision supported by portability, security, support, licensing, operational, recovery, and exit analysis.

Containerization shall not be imposed on a workload when it adds material risk or operational complexity without an accepted benefit. Device-bound execution, certain cryptographic appliances, platform-native services, or constrained customer environments may require a non-container package. Such exceptions shall preserve equivalent identity, provenance, integrity, vulnerability, release, deployment, validation, audit, and evidence controls.

### Strategic Objectives

The Container Strategy shall:

- produce immutable, uniquely identified, traceable deployable artifacts;
- separate source acceptance, build execution, artifact verification, release approval, promotion, deployment, and runtime acceptance;
- reduce unnecessary software, privilege, credentials, writable state, and network surface;
- bind every production artifact to accepted source, build instructions, dependencies, builder identity, provenance, SBOM, verification results, and release eligibility;
- prevent development convenience from becoming an unreviewed production dependency;
- support controlled patching and rapid revocation without mutable in-place modification;
- support supported target architectures without hidden behavioral divergence;
- preserve tenant, environment, trust-domain, and workload boundaries;
- allow technology and provider replacement without changing ILAIOS authority semantics;
- provide offline or isolated delivery where an approved Deployment Profile requires it;
- distinguish artifact integrity from software correctness, security, authorization, and acceptance;
- support continuous Audit Engine and Evidence Chain operation for material lifecycle events; and
- remain operable under the approved organizational and Single-Maintainer Bootstrap Profiles.

### Canonical Container Domain Model

The following terms are distinct:

**Container Source.** The accepted source revision, build definition, dependency declarations, configuration templates, and policy inputs from which a container artifact is produced.

**Build Definition.** The version-controlled instructions and parameters defining how source and approved inputs become a container image or related artifact.

**Build Context.** The exact files and metadata made visible to the build. It shall be minimal, classified, and free from unintended credentials or workstation state.

**Builder.** The identified and governed system that executes the Build Definition within an approved Build Profile.

**Build Profile.** The accepted builder platform, isolation, identity, network, secret, cache, dependency, provenance, and output controls for a class of artifacts.

**Base Image.** An image or root-filesystem input inherited by another image. It is a governed transitive dependency, not a trusted constant.

**Image Manifest.** The content-addressed description that binds a configuration object and filesystem layers for an exact platform.

**Image Index.** A content-addressed object referring to platform-specific manifests or related variants. Inclusion in an index does not establish that every variant has equivalent assurance.

**Container Artifact.** An image, manifest, index, signature, provenance statement, SBOM, scan result, policy result, or related immutable object managed by the container supply chain.

**Artifact Digest.** The algorithm-qualified content identity of an exact artifact. A digest is not a human release name and does not establish approval by itself.

**Release Reference.** A governed human-usable release, channel, or support reference mapped to one or more immutable artifact digests.

**Container Runtime Profile.** The approved image-level and process-level assumptions for user identity, privilege, capabilities, filesystem, process, device, resource, configuration, network, health, shutdown, and telemetry behavior.

**Promotion.** The controlled act of making an already built and verified digest eligible in a higher environment or release scope. Promotion shall not silently rebuild or alter the artifact.

**Revocation.** The authoritative removal of artifact eligibility because of compromise, defect, policy change, support state, or another approved cause.

### Container Eligibility

Every container workload shall reference an approved Container Profile appropriate to its service, risk, environment, tenant model, data classification, Deployment Profile, release maturity, and support line. The profile shall define:

- source repository and accepted source authority;
- build definition, builder, isolation, and network rules;
- allowed base images, package ecosystems, and dependency sources;
- required provenance, SBOM, signature, scan, and policy evidence;
- target operating systems, CPU architectures, accelerators, and runtime compatibility;
- image composition, user, privilege, filesystem, process, health, configuration, and network requirements;
- registry namespaces, replication, promotion, retention, revocation, and recovery;
- vulnerability and end-of-support thresholds;
- release, deployment, rollback, and emergency rules; and
- owner, review period, exceptions, and dated exit criteria.

An artifact shall not become production-eligible solely because it builds successfully, has a valid format, is available in a registry, has no known findings from one scanner, has a signature, or starts in a runtime. Eligibility is a recorded outcome of the complete required Quality Gates.

### Accepted Source and Build Inputs

Production images shall be built only from accepted, version-controlled source and build definitions. The exact source revision shall be immutable or equivalently protected and linked to the change, review, Quality Gates, release scope, and builder invocation.

Build inputs shall be explicitly enumerated or resolvable through controlled dependency declarations. Remote downloads, generated code, package indexes, base images, toolchains, plugins, scripts, certificates, and external metadata used during a build are supply-chain inputs and shall be governed accordingly.

Unpinned or floating inputs shall be prohibited for a release build unless the Build Profile explicitly captures and verifies the exact resolved content before output acceptance. A human-readable version constraint may coexist with an immutable resolved identity, but it shall not replace it.

The build context shall exclude repository history, test data, local configuration, credentials, private keys, personal files, unrelated binaries, environment files, and other material not required for the build. Exclusion rules shall be version-controlled and tested where accidental inclusion would create material risk.

### Build Isolation and Builder Trust

Release builds shall execute in an approved, attributable, isolated builder. The builder shall use least privilege, controlled inputs, bounded network access, protected identity, protected signing interaction, monitored execution, and disposable or verified-clean build state appropriate to risk.

A developer workstation shall not be the ordinary authoritative builder for a Stable release. Local builds may support development and diagnosis, but they shall not be promoted as release artifacts unless an explicitly approved constrained profile establishes equivalent evidence and the limitation is represented honestly.

Build workloads shall not receive unrestricted production credentials, cluster-administrator access, container-runtime sockets, host filesystem access, or signing keys. Where privileged build behavior is technically unavoidable, the Build Profile shall isolate it from production trust domains, constrain duration and inputs, monitor use, and document a migration or containment plan.

The build service shall not approve its own source change or release. Builder success is a supply-chain event, not a release decision. Compromise or ambiguity in builder identity, configuration, provenance, or output custody shall block promotion until resolved.

### Hermeticity, Determinism, and Reproducibility

Builds should minimize undeclared environmental influence and should be hermetic where justified by assurance and feasibility. Time, locale, file ordering, generated identifiers, external repositories, package metadata, randomness, network responses, and host-specific state shall be controlled or recorded when they can affect output.

Reproducibility claims require evidence that independent or equivalently isolated builds from the declared inputs produce the defined equivalent output. A deterministic build script does not by itself prove a reproducible supply chain. Differences in signatures, timestamps, compression, metadata, or platform-specific layers shall be understood before equivalence is claimed.

Where byte-for-byte reproducibility is not feasible, the Build Profile shall define the accepted equivalence boundary, residual nondeterminism, verification method, and risk treatment. Undocumented nondeterminism is a defect in release evidence.

Rebuilds shall produce new provenance and assessment records even when the resulting digest matches an earlier artifact. A matching digest supports content identity but shall not erase the distinct build event.

### Base Image Governance

Base images shall come from approved sources and shall be referenced by immutable digest for release builds. Tags may support human discovery, but a tag alone shall not determine production content. The selected base shall have a known publisher or internal owner, license posture, update channel, support state, platform scope, provenance posture, and vulnerability-management path.

The smallest practical base compatible with operational, diagnostic, cryptographic, accessibility, localization, and support requirements shall be used. Minimality shall not remove libraries, trust stores, time-zone data, certificates, diagnostic hooks, or operating controls that are required for correct and recoverable service operation.

General-purpose build toolchains, package managers, shells, compilers, source, caches, and debugging utilities should remain outside the runtime image unless justified. Multi-stage or equivalent separated builds should transfer only required runtime outputs into the final artifact.

Base-image inheritance shall be tracked transitively. A base-image update does not automatically authorize application promotion, and an unchanged application source does not eliminate the need to rebuild, verify, test, and release when the base changes.

End-of-support, publisher compromise, license change, critical vulnerability, trust-root change, or unavailable update path shall trigger reassessment, replacement, constraint, or retirement. An exception shall be time-bound and shall not convert an unsupported base into a supported ILAIOS artifact.

### Dependency and Package Governance

Application, system, language, native, cryptographic, model-runtime, and tooling dependencies included in an image shall follow Section 3.7 and the engineering dependency standards. Dependency declarations and resolved versions shall be attributable to the artifact.

Release builds shall use approved repositories, mirrors, or verified packages. Dependency confusion, namespace substitution, typosquatting, malicious maintainer changes, compromised mirrors, and unexpected post-install execution shall be considered in the threat model.

Lockfiles and checksums shall be used where the ecosystem supports them, but they do not replace publisher, provenance, license, maintenance, and vulnerability assessment. Vendored dependencies shall remain identifiable and updateable.

Installation shall avoid recommended, optional, development, test, and documentation packages unless required. Package cleanup shall not conceal which packages were used. The SBOM and provenance shall represent the resulting runtime content and relevant build inputs according to the approved profile.

### Build Secrets and Sensitive Inputs

Secrets shall not be embedded in image layers, build arguments, source archives, labels, annotations, environment defaults, package-manager configuration, command history, logs, caches, provenance, or SBOM content. Removing a secret in a later layer does not remove it from earlier layer content.

Build secrets shall use an approved ephemeral secret-delivery mechanism that avoids persistence in the image and minimizes exposure to the builder. Access shall be purpose-bound, least-privilege, time-bounded where possible, attributable, monitored, and revocable under Section 3.4.

Signing keys and high-impact cryptographic material shall remain within approved cryptographic boundaries under Sections 3.5 and 3.6. A build process should request a constrained signing operation or attestation rather than receive exportable private key material.

Any suspected secret exposure shall trigger artifact quarantine, credential revocation or rotation, impact analysis, registry and cache investigation, downstream notification where required, and incident evidence. Deleting a registry tag is insufficient remediation when the layer may remain addressable or cached.

### Build Provenance

Every production-eligible container image shall have verifiable provenance appropriate to its risk and release maturity. Provenance shall bind the output digest to the builder identity, build definition, source revision, relevant parameters, declared materials, execution context, and build event.

Provenance shall be generated by or protected from the build subject according to the approved assurance target. A self-authored statement from an untrusted build has limited evidentiary value and shall be represented accordingly. Higher-impact releases should use a hardened build service that produces tamper-resistant, independently verifiable provenance.

Provenance completeness, authenticity, accuracy, availability, and verification status are separate properties. Presence of a provenance document is not proof that all inputs were declared or that the build environment was uncompromised.

Provenance verification shall occur before promotion into a scope that requires it. Verification shall check accepted identity, artifact digest, source, builder, build definition, parameters, materials, trust roots, policy, time, revocation, and profile constraints. Verification failure shall default to ineligibility.

### Software Bill of Materials

Each production image shall have an SBOM in an approved machine-readable format. The SBOM shall identify the artifact digest and represent the runtime software components with sufficient names, versions, suppliers or origins where available, package identifiers, relationships, and license data for the defined use.

Build-time and runtime SBOM scope shall be distinguished. A runtime SBOM shall not be assumed to describe toolchains or ephemeral build dependencies; a build-input inventory shall not be represented as the exact runtime filesystem.

SBOM generation should combine build metadata, package databases, dependency declarations, and artifact inspection as appropriate. A tool-generated SBOM is subject to completeness and accuracy limitations and shall be validated against the profile.

An SBOM is an inventory aid, not proof of security, license compliance, absence of undeclared software, or absence of vulnerabilities. It shall support vulnerability response, license review, customer disclosure, incident investigation, support, and retirement without becoming the sole decision source.

Protected information shall not be added to public or customer-delivered SBOMs without an approved disclosure basis. Internal and distributable SBOM variants may differ only through a governed transformation that preserves required truth and records exclusions.

### Artifact Signing and Attestations

Required images, indexes, provenance, SBOMs, scan results, policy decisions, and other release attestations shall be signed or otherwise integrity-protected according to the Container Profile. Trust shall be based on approved signer identity, key custody, certificate or identity validity, scope, policy, time, and revocation state—not on the existence of a signature field.

Signing authority shall be separated by purpose. Build provenance, release approval, registry replication, customer delivery, emergency release, and evidence sealing shall not silently share one unrestricted identity.

The signed subject shall be an immutable digest or equivalent exact content identity. Signing a mutable tag without binding the resolved digest is insufficient. Multi-platform indexes and their referenced manifests shall be assessed so that approval of an index does not conceal an unapproved platform variant.

Signature verification shall be deterministic and fail safely for non-waivable profiles. Missing, invalid, expired, revoked, untrusted, wrongly scoped, or policy-incompatible signatures shall block eligibility. Temporary verification outages shall not become an unrecorded fail-open path.

### Artifact Identity, Names, Tags, and Digests

Repository and artifact names shall follow Section 4.2. Names shall identify ownership and purpose without embedding secrets, personal data, mutable environment state, or unsupported claims.

Tags are mutable references unless a registry demonstrably enforces immutability. Tags such as `latest`, `stable`, `production`, branch names, and channel names shall not be the sole production identity. Runtime and release records shall preserve the resolved digest.

Human-readable semantic version, release, channel, and support references may map to immutable digests under Section 4.9 and Section 4.10. Reassignment of an existing published version reference to different content is prohibited except through a formal withdrawal and corrected-release process that preserves historical truth.

Digest algorithms and accepted media types shall be governed and crypto-agile. A digest collision concern, algorithm deprecation, parser ambiguity, canonicalization defect, or media-type confusion shall trigger impact assessment and migration controls.

### Multi-Architecture Images

Images may target multiple operating systems, processor architectures, instruction variants, or accelerator environments only through an approved compatibility matrix. Each platform manifest is a distinct artifact with its own build inputs, dependencies, vulnerabilities, testing, provenance, and runtime behavior.

An image index shall not imply equivalent assurance across all referenced manifests. Every production-eligible variant shall satisfy the applicable gates. An unsupported or experimental variant shall not be included under a general production reference in a way that permits unintended selection.

Cross-compilation, emulation, native builds, and accelerator-specific compilation shall be represented in provenance. Platform-specific test gaps, numerical behavior, library availability, and performance limits shall be documented.

Deployment systems shall resolve the expected platform and digest deterministically. A platform mismatch shall fail safely instead of substituting an unapproved variant.

### Image Composition and Minimal Runtime Surface

The final runtime image shall contain only software, data, configuration defaults, trust material, and diagnostic interfaces required for its approved purpose. Unused services, interpreters, package managers, compilers, source, test fixtures, sample credentials, interactive tools, and administrative utilities shall be removed or excluded.

Minimality shall be evidence-based. Removing every shell or diagnostic utility can reduce attack surface but may impair safe diagnosis and recovery. The Container Profile shall define whether diagnostics occur through a separate, governed support artifact or approved ephemeral mechanism.

Files shall have explicit ownership and least-required permissions. Set-user-ID, set-group-ID, world-writable paths, unnecessary device nodes, unsafe symbolic links, unexpected archive content, and executable temporary directories shall be prohibited unless justified and controlled.

The image shall not contain customer data, production secrets, tenant-specific mutable state, environment-specific credentials, or records that belong in governed storage. Test fixtures shall use synthetic or approved non-sensitive content.

### Runtime User, Privilege, and Kernel Surface

Workloads shall run as a dedicated non-root identity by default. The image shall declare or support an explicit runtime user and shall not depend on arbitrary numeric identity assumptions that conflict with the Deployment Profile.

Root, privileged mode, host namespace access, device access, additional kernel capabilities, relaxed security profiles, runtime socket access, or host filesystem mounts require an approved exception based on demonstrated need. The image itself shall not request or assume elevated privilege as a convenience.

Linux capabilities or equivalent operating-system privileges shall be dropped by default and added individually only when required. Privilege requirements shall be testable and documented. A workload that fails under the approved least-privilege profile shall not silently receive broader privilege.

Rootless container execution should be used where it provides meaningful risk reduction and is supported. Rootless operation does not eliminate kernel, runtime, filesystem, network, or tenant risks and shall not be represented as complete isolation.

### Filesystem and Mutable State

Runtime root filesystems shall be read-only by default where the workload supports it. Required writable paths shall be explicit, minimal, capacity-bounded, permission-controlled, and classified as ephemeral or durable.

Application state shall not depend on undocumented mutation of image content. A running container shall not install packages, patch binaries, rewrite canonical configuration, or become the source for a new production image.

Ephemeral files, caches, temporary outputs, sockets, and process state shall use approved locations and shall tolerate restart, rescheduling, replacement, and scale-out. Sensitive temporary content shall have constrained access and disposal behavior.

Durable data shall use the storage architecture defined in Section 7.5. An image is not a backup, and committing a running container does not constitute backup, recovery, or evidence preservation.

### Process and Entrypoint Design

Each container should have a clear primary responsibility and a deterministic startup contract. The entrypoint and command shall be explicit, version-controlled, and suitable for signal handling, graceful termination, status reporting, and bounded shutdown.

Wrapper scripts shall fail safely, preserve exit status, avoid unsafe evaluation, and not download unverified code or configuration at startup. Runtime package installation or code generation shall be prohibited unless an approved profile requires it and captures equivalent integrity and evidence.

Process supervision inside a container shall be used only where multiple related processes are intentionally part of one support and failure boundary. Unrelated services shall not be bundled merely to avoid orchestration or deployment governance.

Crash loops, repeated startup migration, or automatic repair shall not create duplicate external actions, authority changes, data corruption, or hidden state transitions. Task execution remains subject to idempotency, capability, Tool Gateway, and reconciliation requirements.

### Configuration Interface

Images shall be environment-neutral where practicable. Environment, tenant, region, endpoint, feature, policy, model-provider, and operational configuration shall be supplied through approved external configuration mechanisms at deployment or runtime.

Configuration defaults shall be safe, explicit, documented, and versioned. Missing mandatory configuration shall fail closed with a diagnosable error. Development defaults shall not silently enable production operation.

Configuration schemas shall define types, allowed values, sensitivity, mutability, restart behavior, compatibility, and ownership. Unknown, deprecated, conflicting, or invalid values shall not be ignored when doing so could weaken a control.

Policy, approval, capability, tenant, and business authority shall not be encoded as mutable environment variables or image labels. Such values may carry references or bounded configuration only when the authoritative decision remains in the canonical ILAIOS components.

### Runtime Secrets and Identity Material

Runtime secrets shall be injected through approved mechanisms and shall not be baked into the image. Secret access shall bind to verified workload identity, tenant, environment, purpose, audience, version, and lifecycle.

Secrets should be delivered as short-lived references, mounted material, or runtime retrieval according to the threat model. Environment variables may expose secrets through process inspection, diagnostics, crash reporting, or child processes and shall be used only when the profile accepts those risks.

Secret files shall have least-required permissions and shall not be copied into writable application directories, logs, support bundles, or persistent layers. Rotation and revocation shall define whether a workload reloads, restarts, or obtains new credentials without uncontrolled downtime.

The image shall not contain a universal tenant secret, provider credential, signing key, recovery factor, or reusable privileged token. Workload identity material shall not be confused with ILAIOS task capability.

### Network Surface and External Dependencies

The image shall expose only required ports and protocols. Declared exposed ports are documentation and packaging metadata; they do not authorize network reachability. Actual ingress and egress remain governed under Sections 7.3 and 7.6.

Outbound destinations, protocols, certificate expectations, proxies, DNS dependencies, model-provider access, artifact retrieval, time sources, and external services required by the workload shall be documented and policy-controllable.

Containers shall not assume unrestricted internet access, cloud metadata access, cluster API access, local network trust, or direct access to customer systems. Where external action is governed by ILAIOS, it shall remain mediated through the Tool Gateway under constrained capability.

Certificate validation, trust-store management, proxy behavior, redirect handling, and name resolution shall fail safely. Disabling certificate verification or embedding unmanaged trust anchors is prohibited.

### Health, Lifecycle, and Shutdown Contract

The image shall provide health interfaces appropriate to the workload without conflating process liveness, readiness, functional validity, release acceptance, or business acceptance.

Startup checks shall account for initialization, schema compatibility, configuration, secret availability, dependencies, and recovery. Liveness checks shall not terminate a healthy but temporarily slow workload. Readiness shall not be asserted before the workload can safely receive its intended traffic or task.

Termination shall stop new work, preserve or reconcile in-flight state, respect capability expiry and cancellation, flush required telemetry and evidence, release resources, and exit within a bounded period. Forced termination behavior shall be known and tested.

A passing health endpoint does not validate model output, Tool Gateway effects, tenant isolation, evidence completeness, or business result. The independent Validation Pipeline remains authoritative within its defined scope.

### Resource and Runtime Assumptions

The Container Profile shall state CPU, memory, storage, file-descriptor, process, thread, accelerator, temporary-space, startup, and shutdown assumptions. These values inform orchestration but do not replace the resource governance in Sections 7.3 and 7.7.

Out-of-memory behavior, CPU throttling, disk exhaustion, dependency latency, accelerator loss, and partial network failure shall be tested for high-impact workloads. Resource pressure shall not cause authorization bypass, truncated evidence represented as complete, or silent result acceptance.

Images shall not require unlimited resources or hidden host tuning. Kernel parameters, huge pages, devices, drivers, runtime classes, or host modules shall be declared as compatibility constraints and included in the Deployment Profile.

Resource optimization shall not remove required security, cryptographic, validation, audit, evidence, or recovery behavior.

### Restricted Execution Images

Images used for restricted task execution shall be purpose-bounded and shall contain only the tools and libraries approved for the execution class. General administrative suites, cloud command-line tools, cluster clients, registry credentials, or broad network utilities shall be excluded unless explicitly required.

Restricted workers shall run with a constrained workload identity and task capability. The image, container runtime, orchestration identity, namespace, or node shall not create ILAIOS authority.

Every governed external action shall remain mediated through the Tool Gateway. Direct provider, repository, infrastructure, customer-system, or operating-system action outside the approved gateway path is prohibited.

The worker shall not modify Policy Engine state, issue approvals, expand capability, alter immutable context, validate its own output, or write authoritative audit and evidence state. Scratch state shall be disposable and tenant-bounded.

### Model and Accelerator Images

Images containing model runtimes, inference libraries, tokenizers, native extensions, accelerator libraries, or model assets shall identify those materials separately from application code. Model identity, weight identity, license, origin, integrity, compatibility, and approval shall remain governed under Section 6.

Large model assets should not be embedded into a general service image when doing so prevents efficient lifecycle, independent verification, licensing control, or secure distribution. Packaging choice shall preserve immutable identity and exact binding between runtime, model, configuration, and release.

Drivers and host accelerator components shall not be hidden as ordinary image dependencies. Their compatibility, privilege, device access, scheduling, patching, and isolation requirements shall be declared.

Numerical or behavioral differences across CPU, GPU, accelerator, library, or instruction variants shall be evaluated when they can affect confidence, validation, safety, or reproducibility.

### Third-Party and Customer-Provided Images

Third-party images are untrusted until qualified. Public availability, publisher reputation, official labeling, popularity, signature, or registry hosting does not establish ILAIOS eligibility.

Qualification shall verify immutable identity, publisher or supplier, license, provenance where available, SBOM, composition, vulnerabilities, malware, embedded secrets, privilege assumptions, network behavior, support state, update path, platform compatibility, and operational fit.

Customer-provided images shall be evaluated under an explicit shared-responsibility profile. Customer ownership does not permit bypass of non-waivable ILAIOS tenant, security, privacy, authorization, Tool Gateway, validation, audit, evidence, or human-accountability controls.

When a supplied image cannot meet the required controls, it shall be rebuilt from accepted source, wrapped within an effective isolation boundary, limited to a constrained environment, or rejected. Unknown composition or unsupported provenance shall be represented honestly.

### Registry Governance

Container registries shall use approved organizational ownership, namespaces, identities, authentication, authorization, encryption, immutability, audit, retention, replication, recovery, and incident controls. Public and private visibility shall be explicit.

Push, delete, retag, mutate, replicate, sign, promote, and administer permissions shall be separated according to risk. Ordinary runtime identities shall receive pull access only to required repositories. Build identities shall not automatically receive production promotion or deletion authority.

Production repositories shall enforce or verify immutable digest identity. Tag immutability should be enforced for published release references. Registry garbage collection, retention, replication, migration, and restoration shall not break active release references or required evidence.

Registry availability is not artifact approval. Mirroring or replication shall preserve digest and required signatures, attestations, metadata, and policy relationships. A mirror shall not substitute different content under the same approved reference.

Administrative and recovery access shall be protected, monitored, periodically reviewed, and tested. Provider-managed registries remain subject to shared-responsibility, exit, export, and evidence requirements.

### Artifact Promotion

Promotion shall move or authorize an existing immutable digest across environment, registry, release, or customer-delivery boundaries without rebuilding it. Development, test, staging, and production should use the same accepted artifact where the target platform and profile are compatible.

Promotion shall verify artifact digest, provenance, source, builder, SBOM, signatures, vulnerability disposition, malware assessment, license disposition, test evidence, release state, target compatibility, policy, approval, and revocation state.

Copying an artifact between registries shall preserve exact content identity. If platform conversion, recompression, metadata mutation, signing, encryption, or repackaging changes the digest, the output is a new artifact that requires explicit provenance and eligibility assessment.

Promotion authority shall be distinct from ordinary build and runtime authority. Emergency promotion remains time-bounded, attributable, constrained, and subject to retrospective review and permanent remediation.

### Vulnerability, Malware, and Secret Assessment

Container artifacts shall be assessed at controlled points including build, release candidacy, promotion, deployment eligibility, periodic rescanning, and material threat-intelligence change. Assessment shall include operating-system packages, language dependencies, native libraries, application binaries, model-runtime components, configuration, embedded secrets, and malware indicators as applicable.

Scanner findings are inputs, not deterministic truth. False positives, false negatives, incomplete package identification, stale vulnerability data, disputed severity, exploitability, reachability, compensating controls, and environment context shall be governed through documented disposition.

Severity alone shall not determine acceptance. The policy shall consider exposure, reachability, execution path, privilege, tenant impact, data classification, known exploitation, fix availability, support state, deployment model, and time-to-remediate.

Suppression requires an owner, rationale, exact artifact or component scope, evidence, expiry, monitoring, and review. A global or indefinite ignore rule is prohibited. Absence of known findings does not establish that an artifact is secure.

Discovery of a material issue after release shall trigger impact analysis across all digests, tags, registries, environments, tenants, backups, caches, and derivatives. The response may include blocking, revocation, rebuild, replacement, isolation, notification, and evidence preservation.

### Patching, Rebuild, and Immutable Update

Production containers shall be patched by rebuilding and promoting a new immutable artifact, not by modifying running containers in place. Emergency runtime containment may restrict network, scale, quarantine, or disable a workload, but it shall not become the undocumented permanent fix.

Rebuild triggers include application change, base-image update, dependency update, vulnerability, trust-root change, signing-policy change, builder change, support transition, material threat intelligence, or reproducibility correction.

An unchanged source revision rebuilt against changed inputs is a distinct release candidate with new provenance, SBOM, assessment, and evidence. Automated rebuild does not imply automated production promotion.

Rollback shall use an eligible prior digest whose revocation, compatibility, data, migration, and security state remains acceptable. A known-vulnerable or incompatible artifact shall not be restored solely because it previously ran successfully.

### Runtime Drift and Image Verification

Deployment shall verify that the resolved runtime artifact matches the eligible digest and platform. Mutable tag resolution shall not create unrecorded content changes.

Runtime drift includes modification of image-derived files, installed packages, changed binaries, injected tools, unauthorized writable overlays, unexpected processes, altered entrypoints, or divergence from the approved Runtime Profile.

Detection shall distinguish expected ephemeral state from unauthorized mutation. Material drift shall trigger containment, replacement, investigation, and evidence rather than normalization into a new image.

Recreating a workload from an approved immutable image is preferred to repairing a drifted instance. Runtime inspection tools shall be governed so that diagnostic access does not introduce persistent unauthorized content or expose tenant data.

### Air-Gapped and Isolated Delivery

Isolated Deployment Profiles shall define how images, indexes, signatures, provenance, SBOMs, vulnerability intelligence, trust roots, revocation state, and release metadata are exported, transferred, verified, imported, updated, and retired without relying on uncontrolled external access.

Offline bundles shall use immutable manifests and authenticated integrity protection. Transfer media, staging systems, import identities, quarantine, malware assessment, chain of custody, and failed-import handling shall be governed.

An isolated registry may lag external vulnerability intelligence or revocation data. The profile shall define bounded update intervals, emergency update paths, local verification, accepted residual risk, and support limitations.

Offline delivery does not waive license, privacy, security, tenant, evidence, or support requirements. The exact customer and ILAIOS responsibilities shall be documented.

### Development and Debug Profiles

Development images may include additional tools, source mappings, diagnostics, reload mechanisms, or relaxed optimization only under a distinct non-production profile. They shall not receive production credentials, customer data, signing authority, or production network reachability by default.

Debug artifacts and ephemeral diagnostic containers shall be separately identified, access-controlled, short-lived, logged, and prevented from silent production promotion. Their presence shall not weaken the approved workload profile.

Development and production behavior should remain sufficiently aligned to support meaningful testing, but parity shall not be claimed where privilege, dependencies, architecture, configuration, network, or image composition differ materially.

Diagnostic output shall follow data-minimization and secret-handling rules. Support convenience shall not justify embedding a permanent administrative backdoor.

### Retention, Deletion, and Retirement

Artifact retention shall follow an approved record-class-specific schedule that reconciles release support, rollback, incident, vulnerability, customer, legal, privacy, evidence, and storage requirements. Retention is not indefinite by default.

Active releases, supported rollback candidates, customer-delivered artifacts, investigation subjects, legal holds, signatures, provenance, SBOMs, and required evidence shall remain retrievable for their approved period.

Deleting a tag does not necessarily delete manifests or layers. Garbage collection shall verify that content is no longer referenced by active indexes, releases, deployments, customers, evidence, investigations, or recovery plans.

Retirement shall revoke eligibility, stop new deployment, update release and support records, preserve required evidence, notify affected parties where required, and dispose of unneeded artifacts and sensitive metadata securely.

### Audit Engine and Evidence Chain Integration

The Audit Engine shall record material container-lifecycle events including source acceptance, build request, builder identity, input resolution, build outcome, provenance generation, SBOM generation, scan and policy results, signing, registry publication, promotion, deployment resolution, revocation, rollback, exception, incident action, and retirement.

The Evidence Chain shall bind the material records needed to reconstruct why an exact digest was considered eligible, who or what acted, under which policy and approval, with which inputs and results, and how it progressed through release and deployment.

Registry logs, build logs, scanner reports, signature records, and runtime metadata are evidence sources. They do not individually replace the canonical Audit Engine or prove evidence completeness. Hashing an incomplete record set does not make it complete.

Audit Engine and Evidence Chain controls operate continuously across all material stages. Evidence shall be produced during the lifecycle rather than assembled only after deployment. Protected information in evidence shall follow classification, access, retention, and privacy controls.

### Independent Validation

The Validation Pipeline shall independently assess the container-specific assertions required by the applicable gate. Validation may verify digest, media type, platform, provenance, signer, SBOM, composition, vulnerability disposition, secrets, malware, privilege, filesystem, process, configuration, health contract, and runtime compatibility.

The builder, scanner, registry, signer, deployment system, or running workload shall not be the sole validator of its own success. Tool results may be consumed as evidence, but acceptance requires deterministic interpretation under the approved validation profile.

Validation shall distinguish artifact integrity, supply-chain provenance, policy eligibility, functional correctness, runtime security, deployment readiness, and business result. Success in one category shall not be generalized to the others.

Validation failure, unavailable required evidence, identity ambiguity, digest mismatch, or revoked trust shall block promotion or trigger the exact approved constrained response.

### Container Supply-Chain Incident Response

The threat model shall include malicious or compromised source, dependency, base image, package repository, builder, cache, registry, signing identity, scanner, plugin, runtime, maintainer account, mirror, and customer-supplied artifact.

Response shall be able to identify every affected source revision, build, digest, index, tag, signature, registry, environment, cluster, tenant, customer delivery, cache, backup, and derivative artifact.

Containment may suspend builds, quarantine repositories, revoke signatures, block digests, disable promotion, rotate credentials, isolate workloads, restrict egress, or withdraw releases. The chosen action shall preserve evidence and avoid uncontrolled duplicate effects.

Recovery requires restoration of trustworthy source, builder, credentials, trust roots, registries, policies, and artifact eligibility. Re-signing compromised content or rebuilding through an untrusted path is not recovery.

### Change, Release, and ADR Governance

Changes to image format, Build Profile, builder trust model, base-image family, dependency source, registry, signing system, provenance schema, SBOM format, admission expectation, Runtime Profile, platform matrix, or customer-delivery model shall follow Section 5.7.

Architecture-significant changes require an authorized ADR. Routine version updates within an approved compatibility and risk envelope may follow the standard lifecycle without a new ADR, but they still require evidence and applicable Quality Gates.

Section 5.3 remains the canonical Release Lifecycle. Container build and promotion states shall map to it and shall not create a competing release state machine. A signed or published image is not automatically an Approved, Published, Accepted, or Supported ILAIOS release.

Exceptions shall be exact, time-bound, owned, monitored, and reviewed. A customer request, sales commitment, provider default, tool limitation, or engineering preference shall not silently waive non-waivable controls.

### Governance and Responsibilities

Product authority defines product scope, release claims, and accepted maturity. Architecture authority defines canonical boundaries and approves architecture-significant exceptions. Security defines supply-chain, runtime, vulnerability, signing, and incident requirements. Platform engineering operates builders, registries, runtime profiles, and promotion controls. Service owners define workload requirements and remediate findings. Release authority approves eligible artifacts within the Release Lifecycle.

Compliance and privacy functions determine applicable record, license, disclosure, data, and contractual requirements within their authority. Operations monitors deployed artifact identity, health, drift, and support state. Incident command coordinates containment and recovery. Customers retain the responsibilities assigned by the Deployment Profile and contract.

One actor or system may perform multiple functions only where the approved operating profile permits it. Role combination shall not erase the distinction between source authoring, build, verification, promotion, deployment, validation, and release acceptance.

No model output, build tool, scanner, registry, runtime, provider, customer, sales function, or individual engineer may unilaterally redefine canonical container authority.

### Single-Maintainer Bootstrap Profile

During a registered Single-Maintainer Bootstrap Profile, one authorized maintainer may temporarily perform multiple container-lifecycle roles when independent personnel are unavailable. This state shall be recorded and shall not be represented as independent review, dual control, or Enterprise separation of duties.

The bootstrap profile shall require exact source and artifact attribution, protected organizational ownership, mandatory automated Quality Gates, immutable or equivalently protected provenance and evidence, explicit self-review, least privilege, separately protected recovery factors, administrative-event logging, periodic access review, constrained release maturity, and a dated exit plan.

High-impact builder, signing, registry, base-image, privilege, restricted-execution, tenant, production, or release changes shall receive qualified external review before they affect a Stable release, production environment, or Enterprise operating profile; otherwise the affected capability shall remain blocked or constrained through formal risk treatment.

The bootstrap profile shall not waive controls where one-person compromise would create unacceptable platform, tenant, signing, evidence, release, recovery, or customer risk. External managed custody, protected build services, independent verification mechanisms, or reduced scope shall be used where required. Continued single-maintainer operation shall not become permanent through inaction.

### Quality Gates

Before a container artifact becomes eligible for its target scope, the applicable gates shall verify:

- accepted source, review, and change identity;
- version-controlled Build Definition and minimal Build Context;
- approved builder identity, isolation, and configuration;
- immutable and verified base images and dependencies;
- absence of embedded secrets and prohibited material;
- artifact format, manifest, index, platform, and digest integrity;
- provenance completeness and authenticity for the required assurance target;
- SBOM generation, identity binding, and adequacy;
- vulnerability, malware, license, secret, and composition disposition;
- required signatures, attestations, trust roots, scope, and revocation status;
- runtime user, privilege, capabilities, filesystem, process, configuration, network, health, and resource conformance;
- functional, integration, security, tenant-isolation, shutdown, recovery, and compatibility testing appropriate to risk;
- registry namespace, immutability, promotion, retention, and recovery controls;
- release state, approval, target Deployment Profile, and support eligibility;
- independent Validation Pipeline outcome;
- Audit Engine and Evidence Chain completeness for the defined gate; and
- exception ownership, expiry, monitoring, and residual-risk acceptance.

No single tool result shall satisfy the complete gate. A gate shall fail safely when mandatory identity, evidence, verification, or policy state is missing or ambiguous.

### Prohibited Practices

The following practices are prohibited unless an explicitly defined canonical exception applies:

- using a mutable tag as the sole production artifact identity;
- using `latest` as a controlled release reference;
- building production images from unaccepted source or a developer workstation without an approved constrained profile;
- allowing unpinned remote content to enter a release build without exact capture and verification;
- embedding secrets, private keys, credentials, customer data, or tenant state in images or layers;
- passing secrets through persistent build arguments, logs, labels, annotations, history, provenance, SBOMs, or caches;
- giving build workloads unrestricted network, host, runtime-socket, cluster-administrator, signing-key, or production access;
- treating a valid digest, signature, SBOM, scan result, registry location, or successful startup as complete approval;
- admitting an unverified platform variant through a trusted multi-architecture index;
- using unsupported, unowned, unlicensed, or unpatchable base images without bounded risk treatment;
- installing packages or changing application binaries inside running production containers;
- committing a running container as a production artifact;
- running as root or privileged by default;
- adding broad kernel capabilities, host namespaces, device access, host mounts, or runtime sockets for convenience;
- storing durable business state in undocumented writable container layers;
- downloading and executing unverified code at startup;
- allowing direct governed external action outside the Tool Gateway;
- allowing restricted workers to change policy, approval, capability, validation, audit, or evidence authority;
- rebuilding during promotion without treating the result as a new artifact;
- reassigning an immutable published release reference to different content;
- suppressing findings globally or indefinitely;
- deleting evidence or active artifacts through uncontrolled garbage collection;
- treating registry replication, runtime pull, rollout, or health as independent validation;
- representing bootstrap self-review as independent Enterprise assurance; or
- giving any container engine, build system, registry, scanner, signer, format, provider, customer commitment, or engineering convenience architectural authority.

### Non-Goals

This section does not require every ILAIOS component, device workload, customer workload, or first-MVP capability to use containers. It does not mandate a container engine, operating-system distribution, base-image family, registry, builder, scanner, signing service, SBOM format, provenance service, or packaging tool.

It does not define Kubernetes cluster architecture or scheduling assigned to Section 7.3, durable storage assigned to Section 7.5, network architecture assigned to Section 7.6, scalability assigned to Section 7.7, observability assigned to Section 7.8, monitoring assigned to Section 7.9, or logging assigned to Section 7.10.

It does not claim that minimal images, rootless execution, signatures, provenance, SBOMs, vulnerability scanning, reproducible builds, immutable tags, or a managed registry independently make a workload secure, compliant, correct, authorized, validated, or accepted.

It does not make container packaging an ILAIOS business authority, tenant boundary, human approval, release decision, compliance certification, or substitute for defense in depth.

### Conformance Requirements

An implementation conforms to this section only when it demonstrates that:

- containers are used through an approved Container Profile and not treated as mandatory universal architecture;
- container format, builder, registry, runtime, and provider remain replaceable within the approved portability boundary;
- accepted source, build definitions, inputs, builders, outputs, and release records are attributable;
- production artifacts are immutable and referenced by exact digest;
- base images and dependencies are approved, traceable, supported, and updateable;
- build secrets and signing material are protected and absent from image content and persistent metadata;
- provenance and SBOMs bind to the exact artifact and meet the profile's assurance target;
- signatures and attestations are verified against identity, scope, policy, time, and revocation state;
- multi-platform variants receive platform-specific assurance;
- images use minimal runtime content, least privilege, bounded writable state, and explicit process and configuration contracts;
- runtime secrets, network dependencies, health, shutdown, resources, and specialized hardware assumptions are governed;
- restricted execution preserves Policy Engine, Approval Engine, capability, Tool Gateway, Validation Pipeline, Audit Engine, Evidence Chain, tenant, and human-accountability boundaries;
- third-party and customer-provided images do not bypass non-waivable controls;
- registries preserve ownership, access, immutability, integrity, promotion, recovery, and evidence;
- promotion uses an already verified immutable artifact and does not conceal a rebuild;
- vulnerability, malware, secret, license, and support findings receive documented disposition;
- patching produces a new verified artifact rather than mutable production repair;
- deployed artifact identity and material runtime drift are detectable;
- isolated delivery preserves integrity, provenance, trust, revocation, and support constraints;
- Audit Engine and Evidence Chain controls operate continuously across material events;
- the Validation Pipeline remains independent;
- bootstrap limitations remain explicit, temporary, constrained, and subject to dated exit criteria; and
- architecture-significant container decisions require an authorized ADR.

### Canonical Invariants

The following invariants are binding:

- a container image is a deployable artifact, not business authority;
- a digest establishes exact content identity under the accepted algorithm, not safety or approval;
- a signature authenticates according to its trust policy, not functional correctness or release acceptance;
- an SBOM is an inventory, not proof of completeness, security, or license compliance;
- a scanner result is a decision input, not deterministic truth;
- source acceptance, build, verification, signing, promotion, deployment, validation, and business acceptance remain distinct;
- production artifacts are immutable and promotion does not silently rebuild them;
- production runtime modification is replaced by rebuild and controlled rollout;
- container isolation is one defense layer and not a complete tenant or security boundary;
- least privilege, non-root execution, minimal content, read-only filesystems, bounded writable state, and constrained network are defaults subject to exact justified profiles;
- secrets, private keys, customer data, and tenant state are not embedded in images;
- artifact provenance, SBOM, signature, scan, release, and deployment records bind to exact digests;
- the deterministic Policy Engine remains within the ILAIOS Control Plane;
- the Approval Engine and human accountability remain independent of container tooling;
- every governed external action remains mediated by the Tool Gateway under constrained capability;
- restricted execution cannot mutate its authority or accept its own output;
- the Validation Pipeline remains independent;
- Audit Engine and Evidence Chain controls operate continuously and are not replaced by build, registry, scanner, or runtime logs;
- third-party, customer, managed-service, and offline artifacts remain subject to the applicable non-waivable controls;
- bootstrap operation does not imply independent Enterprise assurance; and
- architecture-significant container decisions require an authorized ADR.

A Container Strategy implementation is non-conformant if it treats containers as mandatory without an authorized architecture decision; uses mutable references as sole production identity; permits untrusted or untraceable build inputs; exposes secrets or signing material; relies on developer workstations as ordinary release builders; accepts unsupported base images or dependencies without bounded treatment; promotes artifacts without exact digest, provenance, SBOM, required signatures, assessment, release state, and independent validation; conflates a digest, signature, scan, registry, startup, rollout, or health result with approval; hides unapproved platform variants in an image index; runs unnecessarily privileged or mutable workloads; embeds customer or tenant state; permits governed external action outside the Tool Gateway; lets restricted workers change or validate their own authority; mutates production containers instead of rebuilding; loses active artifacts or evidence through registry operations; misrepresents offline, customer-provided, third-party, or bootstrap limitations; or gives any image format, container engine, builder, registry, scanner, signer, provider, tool, customer preference, sales commitment, or engineering convenience architectural authority.

## 7.5 Storage Architecture

### Purpose and Canonical Role

Storage Architecture defines how ILAIOS information is classified, owned, persisted, isolated, protected, retrieved, replicated, backed up, restored, retained, archived, deleted, and evidenced across supported Deployment Profiles. It establishes durable information boundaries without making a database, object store, file system, block device, cache, search index, graph store, vector store, volume provider, or cloud service a source of business authority.

Storage persists state; it does not decide whether an action is permitted, whether human approval is sufficient, whether model output is correct, whether a task result is accepted, or whether evidence is legally adequate. The deterministic Policy Engine remains the business-policy authority. The Approval Engine governs accountable approval. The Tool Gateway remains the governed path for external action. The Validation Pipeline independently assesses results. The Audit Engine and Evidence Chain continuously record and bind material lifecycle events.

Possession of a storage credential, database role, volume attachment, object URL, encryption key reference, network path, replica, snapshot, or backup does not create ILAIOS business permission. Storage-layer controls are mandatory defense-in-depth controls, but they shall not replace tenant policy, task capability, purpose limitation, approval, validation, or human accountability.

### Scope

This section applies to authoritative transactional state, tenant data, configuration state, operational metadata, audit records, evidence objects, artifacts, documents, repository intelligence, knowledge representations, model and provider metadata, indexes, caches, queues with persistence, temporary data, backups, snapshots, archives, recovery copies, and deletion records used by ILAIOS.

It covers storage domain classification, authoritative and derived state, data ownership, schemas, identity, access, tenant isolation, encryption, keys, integrity, consistency, concurrency, transactions, idempotency, replication, availability, durability, backup, restore, disaster recovery, retention, legal hold, privacy, residency, lifecycle, sanitization, capacity, performance, caching, migration, observability, incident response, customer-controlled storage, Kubernetes integration, evidence, and conformance.

Section 3.4 governs secrets, Section 3.5 governs cryptographic keys, Section 3.6 governs encryption, Section 3.10 governs Backup and Recovery, Section 3.11 governs Disaster Recovery, and Section 3.12 governs compliance applicability, privacy roles, retention, and legal requirements. Section 7.3 governs orchestration storage integration; Section 7.4 prohibits durable reliance on container-writable layers. This section defines the storage architecture those controls shall preserve.

### Technology Independence

ILAIOS shall select storage technologies through approved Storage Profiles based on data semantics, assurance, availability, performance, scale, recovery, residency, portability, operational capability, and cost. No database engine, query language, persistence framework, cloud service, replication product, file system, object protocol, search technology, graph implementation, or volume interface is canonical by default.

Technology independence does not require lowest-common-denominator design. An implementation may use transactions, conditional writes, append-only objects, immutable retention, change streams, distributed consensus, full-text search, graph traversal, vector retrieval, or provider-specific resilience where justified. The canonical requirement is that the resulting semantics, boundaries, risks, evidence, and exit path are explicit.

A customer or product profile may require a specific technology only through an authorized decision within lawful and formally approved scope. Provider marketing, sales commitment, developer preference, benchmark result, or model-generated recommendation shall not silently redefine canonical storage semantics.

### Strategic Objectives

Storage Architecture shall:

- preserve exact ownership, tenant, purpose, classification, region, lifecycle, and authority boundaries;
- distinguish authoritative, evidentiary, derived, cached, temporary, replicated, backed-up, and archived information;
- protect confidentiality, integrity, availability, authenticity, durability, and recoverability according to risk;
- minimize retained data and avoid collection or duplication without a defined purpose;
- prevent storage access from becoming implicit business authorization;
- support deterministic state transitions and independent validation;
- preserve append-only Audit Engine and Evidence Chain semantics;
- provide explicit consistency, concurrency, idempotency, and failure behavior;
- support controlled schema evolution and reversible migration where required;
- separate availability replication from backup and disaster recovery;
- satisfy applicable residency, sovereignty, retention, erasure, legal-hold, and customer-control requirements;
- detect corruption, unauthorized change, drift, loss, and capacity risk;
- support verifiable restoration to a trusted state;
- remain portable across approved Deployment Models; and
- operate honestly under Enterprise and Single-Maintainer Bootstrap Profiles.

### Canonical Storage Domain Model

The following terms are distinct:

**Storage Profile.** The approved combination of data classes, technologies, regions, identities, encryption, consistency, availability, backup, recovery, retention, monitoring, responsibilities, and limitations for an exact Deployment Profile and release scope.

**Data Asset.** A governed collection of information with a defined owner, purpose, classification, tenant scope, authoritative source, schema, lifecycle, and access model.

**Authoritative State.** State designated as the canonical source for a defined business or system fact. Authority is assigned by architecture and governance, not inferred from where a copy exists.

**Derived State.** Reconstructable or recomputable information produced from one or more authoritative sources, such as indexes, embeddings, caches, summaries, projections, or search structures.

**Ephemeral State.** Information whose loss is acceptable within a defined task or process boundary and whose lifetime is intentionally short.

**Replica.** A synchronized or asynchronously copied representation used primarily for availability, locality, or read scale. A replica is not automatically an independent backup.

**Snapshot.** A point-in-time storage representation created by a storage system. Snapshot consistency, independence, retention, and restorability shall be established rather than assumed.

**Backup.** A separately governed recovery copy created to restore defined data and service state after loss, corruption, deletion, compromise, or operational failure.

**Archive.** Information moved to a long-duration, lower-change storage state under a defined retention and retrieval policy. An archive is not necessarily a backup.

**Legal Hold.** A formally authorized suspension or modification of ordinary deletion for exact information and scope. It is not indefinite retention by default.

**Storage Identity.** The verified human, workload, service, customer, recovery, or administrative identity acting on a storage resource. It is distinct from tenant identity and ILAIOS business capability.

**Recovery Point.** The identified, time-bounded, integrity-assessed state selected for restoration. The newest available copy is not necessarily the last known good copy.

### Storage Domains

ILAIOS storage shall be organized into explicit domains. A domain may share physical infrastructure only where logical and cryptographic controls preserve its accepted boundary.

**Control Plane State** includes task lifecycle, Immutable Context references, deterministic policy results, risk classifications, approval state, capability issuance and revocation, and authoritative disposition. It requires strong integrity, concurrency control, availability, and attributable mutation.

**Trust Core State** includes Audit Engine records, Evidence Chain links, validation evidence, signatures, timestamps, and chain-verification metadata. It requires append-only or equivalently protected semantics, ordering, tamper detection, controlled retention, and independent verification.

**Tenant Business Data** includes customer inputs, documents, task material, outputs, approved results, and customer-specific configuration. It requires explicit tenant, purpose, classification, residency, access, retention, and deletion controls.

**Platform Configuration State** includes versioned service configuration, feature configuration, deployment references, schema state, and operational policy references. It shall not become an undocumented substitute for source-controlled configuration or canonical policy.

**Artifact State** includes releases, container artifacts, SBOMs, provenance, packages, deployment bundles, and integrity metadata. It follows Section 7.4 and release governance.

**Intelligence-Derived State** includes repository indexes, knowledge graphs, embeddings, retrieval indexes, confidence inputs, and contextual projections. It remains derived unless a specific record is formally designated authoritative.

**Operational State** includes queues, leases, locks, checkpoints, idempotency records, schedules, and workflow coordination. Its failure semantics shall be explicit because seemingly temporary data may protect against duplicate or unauthorized effects.

**Telemetry State** includes metrics, traces, logs, events, and diagnostic data. It remains distinct from authoritative audit and evidence records and is governed further in Sections 7.8 through 7.10.

### Data Classification and Metadata

Every persistent data asset shall have an owner, purpose, classification, tenant scope, data-subject relevance where applicable, residency constraints, authoritative source, retention class, encryption profile, access profile, backup profile, recovery objective, and disposal method.

Classification shall account for confidentiality, integrity, availability, legal, contractual, privacy, safety, security, intellectual-property, evidence, and operational impact. A data asset may require high integrity even when it is not confidential.

Classification metadata shall be protected against unauthorized downgrading. Absence of a classification shall default to the most restrictive applicable handling profile until resolved; it shall not default to unrestricted use.

Labels, database names, bucket names, schemas, paths, and tags may assist governance but shall not be the sole control. Effective enforcement shall occur through identity, authorization, encryption, network, query, lifecycle, and validation controls.

### Authoritative and Derived State

Each material fact shall have one declared authoritative source or an explicitly governed multi-authority reconciliation model. Duplicate writable sources without conflict semantics are prohibited.

Indexes, search stores, knowledge graphs, embeddings, analytical stores, caches, reports, and materialized views shall be treated as derived unless architecture explicitly assigns authority. Derived state shall preserve lineage to the authoritative source, transformation version, tenant, time, and rebuild conditions.

Loss or corruption of derived state should be recoverable by controlled rebuild. A rebuild shall not overwrite authoritative source, cross tenant boundaries, expand purpose, or silently accept stale or unverified inputs.

A storage technology's internal primary, leader, source, or master terminology does not determine ILAIOS business authority. Authority remains a canonical architecture decision.

### Data Ownership and Stewardship

Every data asset shall have an accountable business owner and an operational steward. Ownership shall define permitted purposes, quality expectations, access approval, retention, disclosure, recovery priority, migration, and retirement.

Custody by ILAIOS, a provider, a customer, or a subcontractor does not by itself determine legal role or ownership. Controller, joint-controller, processor, and other legally recognized roles shall be established per processing purpose through Section 3.12.

Service owners shall not create new persistent copies, exports, indexes, or caches without assigning purpose, classification, lineage, access, retention, and deletion behavior. Convenience copies are governed data assets when they contain governed information.

Stewardship shall include periodic review of access, schema, quality, residency, retention, backup, recovery, support state, and unused data.

### Data Modeling and Schema Governance

Authoritative data structures shall use versioned schemas or equivalently controlled contracts. Schemas shall define identity, tenant, ownership, field meaning, type, nullability, constraints, classification, relationships, lifecycle, and compatibility.

Semantic meaning shall not depend solely on undocumented application behavior. Enumerations, units, time zones, precision, ordering, state transitions, and deletion markers shall be explicit where material.

Schema validation shall occur at trusted boundaries. Storage acceptance does not prove semantic validity, authority, or business acceptance. Invalid, unknown, ambiguous, out-of-range, or cross-tenant references shall fail safely according to the data contract.

Schema ownership and approval shall be defined. A persistence framework's generated migration or inferred model is an implementation artifact, not an architectural decision.

### Storage Identity and Authentication

Human, workload, service, node, provider, customer, backup, recovery, replication, migration, and emergency identities shall remain distinct. Shared database or storage credentials are prohibited for ordinary operation.

Workload access shall use a verified workload identity bound to environment, service, tenant scope where applicable, purpose, audience, and lifecycle. Credentials should be short-lived and automatically rotated where supported.

Storage systems shall strongly authenticate administrative access. Privileged human access should use phishing-resistant authentication where the approved Deployment Profile supports it and shall follow Section 3.2.

Recovery and break-glass identities shall be separately governed, protected, monitored, time-bounded, and reviewed. They shall not become routine application credentials.

### Authorization and Least Privilege

Storage authorization shall enforce least privilege across control-plane administration, data-plane read, write, append, delete, schema, backup, restore, replication, export, key use, retention override, and audit access.

Application identities shall receive only the operations, data domains, tenants, schemas, tables, collections, objects, prefixes, or paths required for their purpose. Administrative ownership shall not be granted for convenience.

The deterministic Policy Engine decides ILAIOS business authorization. Storage authorization enforces technical access to storage resources. Neither shall be represented as the other. A permitted database query does not authorize the business purpose, and a business capability does not automatically grant direct database access.
