Clients shall validate service identity after discovery. A discovered endpoint shall not be trusted solely because it was returned by a registry or cluster service.

Failover and load balancing through discovery shall preserve region, tenant, release, data, policy, and support constraints.

### IP Address Management

Address spaces, subnets, prefixes, service ranges, Pod ranges, node ranges, customer ranges, public addresses, virtual addresses, and reserved ranges shall be inventoried and assigned through an approved process.

Overlapping ranges shall be avoided or explicitly handled because they can cause routing ambiguity, unintended translation, policy bypass, and hybrid integration failure.

Public IP allocation shall have an owner, purpose, endpoint, environment, protection profile, and lifecycle. Unused public addresses and stale DNS records shall be removed.

IPv4 and IPv6 shall be governed together. Security controls that cover only one protocol family are incomplete where the other is enabled or reachable.

Dynamic addresses shall not be used as durable workload identity. Address changes shall not invalidate audit attribution or policy semantics.

### Routing and Path Governance

Routes shall be least-privilege, attributable, version-controlled or equivalently governed, and reviewed for destination, next hop, propagation, priority, translation, and failure behavior.

Default routes shall be intentional. Route propagation, peering, transitive connectivity, gateway sharing, and provider-managed routing can create paths beyond the apparent diagram and shall be verified.

Production routing changes shall use controlled rollout, pre-change validation, impact analysis, rollback, monitoring, and post-change verification. Emergency routes shall be time-bounded and removed after review.

Asymmetric routing, black holes, loops, path maximum transmission unit, fragmentation, and stateful-firewall behavior shall be considered for supported protocols.

Route reachability does not grant application authorization.

### Load Balancing and Proxying

Load balancers and proxies shall have explicit frontend, backend, health, protocol, timeout, connection, retry, certificate, identity, and observability configuration.

Source identity, client address, request identifiers, tenant context, and authenticated claims shall be forwarded only through integrity-protected and trusted mechanisms. Direct backend paths shall not permit spoofing of proxy-added metadata.

Retries shall be limited to operations whose semantics permit them. A proxy shall not repeat non-idempotent Tool Gateway or customer-system actions without end-to-end reconciliation.

Health-based removal and failover shall not route traffic to an incompatible release, tenant, region, or data authority. Load distribution success is not result validation.

### Network Address Translation and Identity Preservation

Network address translation may obscure original endpoints and cause many subjects to share one address. IP-based controls shall account for this loss of identity.

Translated source addresses shall not be used as the sole tenant, user, customer, or device identity. Authenticated application and workload identity shall remain authoritative.

Port exhaustion, connection reuse, asymmetric translation, overlapping address spaces, and logging correlation shall be considered in capacity and incident design.

Translation logs may support investigation but shall follow privacy, retention, access, and evidence requirements.

### Metadata Service and Link-Local Protection

Cloud and platform metadata endpoints, node-local services, link-local addresses, control-plane proxies, and credential endpoints shall be denied to ordinary workloads unless explicitly required.

Access shall use the strongest supported identity, token, hop, audience, and path restrictions. Legacy unauthenticated metadata access is prohibited for protected workloads.

Server-side request forgery defenses shall block requests to local, private, metadata, administrative, and prohibited address ranges unless the exact connector authorizes them.

DNS resolution and redirects shall be re-evaluated throughout request processing so that an initially allowed name cannot redirect or rebind to a protected endpoint.

### Firewall and Network-Policy Governance

Every rule shall have an owner, purpose, source, destination, protocol, port, direction, environment, tenant behavior, creation record, review date, and expiry where temporary.

Rules shall be as narrow as operationally feasible. Broad address ranges, all-port access, wildcard destinations, any-to-any rules, and perpetual temporary exceptions require explicit risk treatment.

Rule changes shall be version-controlled or equivalently recorded, tested, peer-reviewed or bootstrap-reviewed, approved, deployed through controlled automation, and verified after enforcement.

Unused, shadowed, duplicate, conflicting, ineffective, and stale rules shall be detected and removed through governed change. Cleanup shall not remove required recovery or evidence paths without impact analysis.

Policy existence is not enforcement evidence. Tests shall demonstrate permitted flows succeed and prohibited flows fail.

### Rate Limiting and Abuse Controls

Rate controls shall protect availability, cost, provider quotas, tenant fairness, and abuse boundaries without becoming the sole authorization mechanism.

Limits may apply by authenticated identity, tenant, endpoint, operation, model, connector, destination, device, address, region, or risk class. IP-only limits are insufficient where addresses are shared or easily changed.

Burst, sustained rate, concurrency, payload size, timeout, retry, queue, and backoff shall be coordinated end to end. A downstream provider limit shall not cause uncontrolled retry amplification.

Rate-limit responses shall avoid exposing sensitive thresholds or cross-tenant activity. Emergency limit changes shall be attributable, time-bounded, monitored, and reviewed.

### Denial-of-Service Resilience

The Network Profile shall identify volumetric, protocol, application, authentication, expensive-query, model, connector, and state-exhaustion denial-of-service risks.

Defenses may include provider filtering, content delivery, connection controls, protocol validation, rate limits, quotas, caching, prioritization, circuit breakers, autoscaling, load shedding, and isolation.

Security, approval, validation, audit, and evidence controls shall not be disabled merely to preserve throughput. Load shedding shall prioritize safe rejection over unaudited or unauthorized processing.

Tenant-level abuse shall not exhaust shared resources without detection and containment. Critical control and evidence paths should have protected capacity.

DDoS failover shall preserve domain, certificate, identity, data, region, privacy, and support constraints.

### Network Capacity and Performance

Capacity planning shall cover bandwidth, packets, connections, flows, DNS queries, certificate operations, proxy resources, gateway limits, tunnel limits, NAT ports, load balancer rules, and provider quotas.

Objectives shall include latency, throughput, jitter, loss, connection setup, tail behavior, and availability for exact flows. Average response time alone is insufficient.

Capacity shall account for encryption, inspection, service proxies, replication, backup, model payloads, artifact transfer, telemetry, failover, and incident conditions.

Optimization shall not bypass segmentation, encryption, identity, validation, audit, evidence, or tenant isolation. Direct paths created for performance require the same authority and security controls.

### Multi-Region Networking

Multi-region designs shall define active and standby regions, data authority, routing, health, failover, failback, DNS, anycast or equivalent mechanisms, certificates, identity, keys, provider dependencies, and customer connectivity.

Traffic shall not fail over into a region that violates residency, customer, model-provider, storage, release, or support constraints.

Health checks shall distinguish network reachability from application, data, policy, validation, and evidence readiness. A reachable region is not necessarily eligible to accept authoritative work.

Split-brain routing shall be prevented or reconciled with Section 7.5. Failback shall be controlled and evidence-backed.

### Network Availability and Dependency Management

Network availability depends on more than link redundancy. DNS, certificates, identity, keys, gateways, proxies, routes, firewalls, load balancers, service discovery, providers, control planes, and monitoring can each be critical dependencies.

Single points of failure shall be identified by flow and recovery objective. Redundant components that share one account, region, control plane, route, certificate, or administrative identity may not provide independent resilience.

Failover behavior shall be deterministic and tested. Automatic failover shall not select an unapproved provider, public path, region, endpoint, or tenant scope.

Maintenance and provider outages shall have customer communication, degraded-mode, queue, timeout, recovery, and validation plans appropriate to the service.

### Time Synchronization

Reliable time is required for certificate validation, token expiry, capability expiry, approval validity, evidence ordering, incident reconstruction, rate windows, leases, and distributed coordination.

Approved time sources, hierarchy, authentication where supported, redundancy, drift limits, monitoring, and failure behavior shall be defined. Workloads shall not use arbitrary public time servers.

Clock uncertainty shall not silently extend approval, capability, certificate, token, retention, or lease validity. Authority-sensitive operations shall fail safely or enter a documented constrained mode.

Time synchronization traffic shall be protected from spoofing, redirection, and unauthorized configuration. Time correction events shall be observable and evidenced when material.

### Network Telemetry and Flow Records

Network telemetry shall provide sufficient source, destination, identity where available, direction, protocol, port, bytes, outcome, time, enforcement point, environment, tenant-safe correlation, and rule context for operations and investigation.

Payload capture shall be exceptional, purpose-bound, authorized, minimized, encrypted, access-controlled, time-limited, and reviewed. Packet captures can contain credentials, personal data, customer content, model inputs, and secrets.

Flow logs, firewall logs, proxy logs, DNS logs, service-mesh telemetry, and provider events are operational evidence sources. They do not replace the Audit Engine or Evidence Chain.

Telemetry gaps, sampling, aggregation, NAT, encryption, proxying, and provider limitations shall be documented. Absence of a log entry is not proof that traffic did not occur.

Detailed observability, monitoring, and logging requirements are defined in Sections 7.8 through 7.10.

### Audit Engine and Evidence Chain Integration

The Audit Engine shall record material network events including endpoint publication, certificate issuance and revocation, rule change, route change, gateway change, connectivity grant, privileged session, Tool Gateway connection, provider path selection, failover, isolation, emergency bypass, incident containment, and retirement.

The Evidence Chain shall bind the records required to reconstruct which flow was intended, which identity and tenant acted, which policy and capability applied, which enforcement points participated, which external endpoint was reached, and how the outcome was validated.

Network devices and providers may produce their own audit logs. These remain evidence sources with known completeness and trust limitations. They do not become canonical ILAIOS audit truth merely because they are immutable or provider-signed.

Audit Engine and Evidence Chain controls operate continuously across material network events. Network outage, telemetry delay, or provider unavailability shall have explicit buffering, backpressure, loss, and recovery behavior.

### Independent Validation

The Validation Pipeline shall independently assess network controls required by the applicable gate. Validation may test public exposure, route scope, certificate identity, encryption, ingress, east–west, egress, tenant isolation, DNS, metadata protection, firewall rules, Kubernetes NetworkPolicy, failover, and prohibited paths.

Validation shall include positive and negative tests. Demonstrating that an allowed connection succeeds does not prove that unapproved connections are blocked.

The system that configures a rule, route, gateway, certificate, or policy shall not be the sole validator of its enforcement. Provider configuration status is an input, not independent acceptance.

Network validation does not replace application, policy, tenant, Tool Gateway, storage, release, or business validation. The applicable outcomes shall remain distinct.

### Network Change Management

Network changes shall follow Section 5.7 and include intent, owner, affected flows, dependency analysis, security impact, tenant impact, customer impact, rollout, validation, rollback, monitoring, and evidence.

Infrastructure as code or equivalent declarative control should define routes, rules, endpoints, gateways, and policies. Direct console changes are prohibited for ordinary production operations.

High-impact changes shall use staged rollout and independent or bootstrap-appropriate review. The change that opens a path shall not be considered complete until effective behavior is verified.

Temporary diagnostic or incident rules shall have automatic or dated expiry. Emergency change does not waive retrospective review and permanent remediation.

Architecture-significant changes to trust boundaries, public exposure, tenant isolation, Tool Gateway routing, provider connectivity, administrative access, multi-region topology, or encryption termination require an authorized ADR.

### Network Incident Response

The threat model shall include exposed services, credential compromise, route manipulation, DNS hijack, certificate compromise, DDoS, lateral movement, data exfiltration, server-side request forgery, metadata theft, tunnel abuse, proxy bypass, tenant crossover, malicious provider, and insider misuse.

Detection and investigation shall identify affected identities, tenants, endpoints, routes, domains, certificates, rules, sessions, providers, regions, services, data, Tool Gateway actions, and evidence gaps.

Containment may revoke identities and certificates, block flows, isolate workloads or tenants, remove public endpoints, disable connectors, restrict egress, withdraw routes, change DNS, or move services into constrained operation.

Containment shall preserve required evidence and avoid creating uncontrolled alternate paths. A broad network shutdown may be unsafe if it prevents audit, evidence, key, identity, or recovery services; dependencies shall be understood.

Recovery shall restore trusted identities, certificates, configuration, routing, enforcement, monitoring, and eligible service state, followed by independent validation and heightened observation.

### Governance and Responsibilities

Architecture authority defines network trust boundaries, canonical flow responsibilities, and architecture-significant decisions. Security defines Zero Trust, segmentation, encryption, exposure, administrative access, exfiltration, DDoS, and incident controls.

Platform and network engineering implement and operate Network Profiles, routes, gateways, firewalls, certificates, DNS, connectivity, monitoring, recovery, and lifecycle. Service owners declare required flows and application identities. Tool Gateway owners govern external action paths. Model platform owners govern provider paths.

Privacy and compliance functions determine applicable transfer, residency, monitoring, inspection, retention, and contractual requirements within their authority. Customers and providers retain the responsibilities assigned by the Deployment Profile and contract.

No network administrator, provider, customer, sales function, tool, gateway, service mesh, or model output may unilaterally redefine business authorization, tenant scope, non-waivable controls, legal obligations, or canonical architecture.

### Single-Maintainer Bootstrap Profile

During a registered Single-Maintainer Bootstrap Profile, one authorized maintainer may temporarily perform multiple network roles when independent personnel are unavailable. The absence of independent administration shall be recorded and shall not be represented as dual control or Enterprise separation of duties.

The bootstrap profile shall maintain organizational ownership of domains and network accounts, strong authentication, separately protected recovery factors, least privilege, declarative configuration, mandatory automated Quality Gates, exact change attribution, protected audit and evidence, periodic access review, tested rollback, and a dated exit plan.

Public exposure, administrative paths, Tool Gateway egress, tenant boundaries, certificate authorities, DNS ownership, hybrid connectivity, and production routing changes shall receive qualified external review before affecting a Stable release, production environment, or Enterprise operating profile; otherwise the affected capability shall remain blocked or constrained.

Controls shall not be waived where single-person compromise would create unacceptable tenant, credential, signing, evidence, production, customer, or recovery risk. Managed external protection, independent validation, constrained scope, or prerelease operation shall be used where required. Single-maintainer operation shall not become permanent through inaction.

### Quality Gates

Before a Network Profile or material network change becomes eligible for its target scope, the applicable gates shall verify:

- approved topology, zones, trust boundaries, owners, regions, environments, and tenant model;
- complete flow inventory for ingress, east–west, egress, administration, Tool Gateway, model, storage, backup, build, registry, telemetry, and recovery;
- verified human, workload, device, customer, provider, and recovery identities;
- least-privilege authorization distinct from ILAIOS business permission;
- effective segmentation and tenant isolation across IPv4, IPv6, overlays, proxies, host paths, and alternate routes;
- approved transport encryption, certificates, trust stores, rotation, and revocation;
- limited public exposure and protected edge enforcement;
- constrained egress, metadata protection, server-side request-forgery defense, and data-disclosure controls;
- Kubernetes NetworkPolicy or equivalent actual enforcement where applicable;
- DNS, service discovery, IP address, routing, load-balancing, proxy, and time controls;
- customer, hybrid, isolated, and provider connectivity responsibilities;
- rate, DDoS, capacity, availability, failover, and recovery behavior;
- telemetry, monitoring, privacy, incident, and evidence readiness;
- controlled change, rollback, drift detection, and expiry of temporary access;
- independent Validation Pipeline positive and negative tests;
- required Audit Engine and Evidence Chain records; and
- exception ownership, scope, expiry, monitoring, and residual-risk acceptance.

No single successful connection, scan, route table, firewall status, certificate check, NetworkPolicy object, provider health status, or penetration test shall satisfy the complete gate.

### Prohibited Practices

The following practices are prohibited unless an explicitly defined canonical exception applies:

- granting trust or business authority based solely on IP address, subnet, zone, namespace, cluster, tunnel, VPN, private link, device location, or network ownership;
- treating firewall, gateway, mesh, proxy, or Kubernetes policy as the deterministic ILAIOS Policy Engine;
- exposing storage, orchestration, key, secret, build, validation, audit, evidence, or administrative endpoints publicly without an exact approved profile;
- permitting unrestricted east–west or internet egress for protected workloads;
- allowing restricted execution to reach governed external systems outside the Tool Gateway;
- allowing workload, node, or namespace identity to create tenant or task capability;
- trusting client-supplied internal identity, tenant, approval, or capability headers;
- disabling certificate validation, transport encryption, DNS controls, or network policy for convenience;
- using wildcard certificates, broad trust anchors, any-to-any rules, or perpetual temporary access without bounded treatment;
- treating private connectivity as sufficient encryption or authentication;
- relying on a declared NetworkPolicy when the network implementation does not enforce it;
- leaving IPv6, host networking, metadata endpoints, alternate protocols, redirects, or DNS rebinding outside the policy model;
- using direct public administrative access or shared bastion credentials for ordinary operations;
- using IP allowlists as the sole customer or tenant authentication control;
- permitting proxy retry of non-idempotent governed action without reconciliation;
- allowing failover into an ineligible region, provider, release, or data authority;
- treating DNS resolution, route reachability, gateway acceptance, TLS success, or health checks as result validation;
- capturing protected payloads without purpose, authorization, minimization, access, retention, and evidence controls;
- treating provider or network-device logs as the canonical Audit Engine or Evidence Chain;
- making unreviewed direct production network changes;
- allowing emergency routes or rules to become permanent through inaction;
- representing bootstrap self-review as independent Enterprise assurance; or
- giving any firewall, network, service mesh, proxy, gateway, provider, customer preference, contract, sales commitment, or engineering convenience architectural authority.

### Non-Goals

This section does not mandate a cloud network, service mesh, API gateway, web application firewall, content-delivery network, dedicated circuit, private endpoint, virtual private network, software-defined network, container network, or specific protocol implementation.

It does not define detailed scalability assigned to Section 7.7, observability assigned to Section 7.8, monitoring assigned to Section 7.9, or logging assigned to Section 7.10.

It does not claim that private addressing, segmentation, encryption, mutual authentication, a service mesh, DDoS protection, Kubernetes NetworkPolicy, or Zero Trust branding independently establishes security, business authorization, tenant isolation, compliance, validation, or evidence completeness.

It does not make the network a substitute for application identity, deterministic policy, human approval, constrained capability, Tool Gateway mediation, independent validation, audit, evidence, or human accountability.

### Conformance Requirements

An implementation conforms to this section only when it demonstrates that:

- every production environment is governed by an approved Network Profile;
- network reachability and ILAIOS business authorization remain distinct;
- topology, trust boundaries, identities, flows, enforcement points, ownership, and lifecycle are explicit;
- Zero Trust principles protect resources rather than relying on network location;
- public, east–west, egress, administrative, provider, customer, hybrid, isolated, storage, build, recovery, and telemetry paths are governed;
- service identities and transport protection meet the exact risk profile;
- certificates, trust stores, DNS, service discovery, addresses, routes, gateways, proxies, and time are lifecycle-managed;
- public exposure is intentional, minimal, protected, and inventoried;
- tenant isolation covers every relevant protocol family and alternate path;
- Kubernetes NetworkPolicy or equivalent controls are actually enforced;
- restricted execution reaches governed external systems only through the Tool Gateway;
- model-provider access traverses the approved Model Gateway boundary;
- metadata endpoints, server-side request forgery, DNS rebinding, redirects, and exfiltration paths are controlled;
- rate, DDoS, capacity, availability, failover, and recovery preserve authority and security;
- network telemetry is sufficient, privacy-aware, and not misrepresented as canonical audit truth;
- the Validation Pipeline independently verifies required allowed and denied behavior;
- Audit Engine and Evidence Chain controls operate continuously across material network events;
- network change and incident response are attributable, reversible where required, monitored, and evidenced;
- bootstrap limitations remain explicit, temporary, constrained, and subject to dated exit criteria; and
- architecture-significant networking decisions require an authorized ADR.

### Canonical Invariants

The following invariants are binding:

- network reachability is not trust and does not create ILAIOS business authority;
- IP address, subnet, zone, namespace, cluster, tunnel, VPN, private link, DNS name, or location is not complete identity;
- private connectivity does not replace authentication, authorization, encryption, or tenant checks;
- segmentation is defense in depth and not a substitute for application-layer policy;
- the deterministic Policy Engine remains within the ILAIOS Control Plane;
- the Approval Engine remains the accountable approval authority;
- every governed external action remains mediated by the Tool Gateway under constrained capability;
- restricted execution cannot obtain authority through a network path;
- model-provider connectivity remains governed through the Model Gateway boundary;
- the Validation Pipeline remains independent;
- Audit Engine and Evidence Chain controls operate continuously and are not replaced by firewall, proxy, DNS, mesh, provider, or flow logs;
- public exposure is explicit and minimal;
- protected ingress, east–west, egress, administrative, storage, build, provider, and recovery traffic is governed;
- transport encryption and endpoint identity are verified across applicable trust boundaries;
- tenant isolation covers application, workload, network, protocol, identity, routing, proxy, telemetry, and alternate paths;
- declared policy without demonstrated enforcement is insufficient;
- DNS resolution and TLS success do not establish business permission or result correctness;
- failover cannot select an ineligible region, provider, release, tenant, or data authority;
- emergency access remains bounded and cannot become ordinary operation;
- bootstrap operation does not imply independent Enterprise assurance; and
- architecture-significant networking decisions require an authorized ADR.

A Networking implementation is non-conformant if it grants trust or permission from location or reachability; conflates network enforcement with the deterministic Policy Engine; exposes protected internal or administrative services without exact authorization; permits unrestricted lateral movement or egress; bypasses the Tool Gateway or Model Gateway; trusts spoofable identity metadata; weakens encryption, certificate, DNS, tenant, or metadata controls; declares but does not enforce segmentation; leaves IPv6, host, proxy, redirect, rebinding, tunnel, or alternate paths ungoverned; uses private connectivity or IP allowlists as sufficient authentication; retries irreversible traffic without reconciliation; fails over into an ineligible scope; represents connectivity, TLS, routing, health, provider status, or network logs as independent validation or canonical evidence; permits ungoverned direct production change; misrepresents customer-controlled, isolated, or bootstrap limitations; or gives any address, route, firewall, network policy, gateway, proxy, mesh, provider, tool, customer preference, sales commitment, or engineering convenience architectural authority.

## 7.7 Scalability

### Purpose and Canonical Role

Scalability defines how ILAIOS increases, decreases, partitions, prioritizes, and governs capacity as demand, tenant population, data volume, model workload, connector activity, regions, and deployment responsibilities change. It establishes measurable operating envelopes and safe elasticity without promising unlimited growth or allowing scaling mechanisms to redefine canonical authority.

Scaling creates or reallocates capacity; it does not create policy permission, human approval, tenant authority, task capability, release acceptance, validation, evidence completeness, or architectural authority. A new replica, worker, node, partition, queue consumer, model endpoint, database shard, or region shall inherit only the exact identity and bounded permissions assigned by its approved profile.

The deterministic Policy Engine remains within the ILAIOS Control Plane. The Approval Engine remains the accountable approval authority. Every governed external action remains mediated by the Tool Gateway. The Validation Pipeline remains independent. Audit Engine and Evidence Chain controls operate continuously during both normal and scaled operation.

### Scope

This section applies to request intake, identity verification, policy evaluation, approvals, AI Reasoning and Recommendation, model-provider access, Tool Gateway execution, Validation Pipeline processing, Audit Engine ingestion, Evidence Chain persistence, storage, networking, queues, caches, registries, orchestration, customer connectivity, and recovery capacity.

It covers load envelopes, capacity units, headroom, horizontal and vertical scaling, partitioning, cellular architecture, scheduling, autoscaling signals, admission, backpressure, queues, concurrency, tenant fairness, quotas, provider limits, stateful scaling, data growth, caching, multi-region expansion, load testing, performance budgets, degraded modes, cost, security, observability, incident response, validation, evidence, and conformance.

Section 7.3 governs orchestration, Section 7.5 governs storage, and Section 7.6 governs networking. Sections 7.8 through 7.10 define observability, monitoring, and logging in greater depth. This section defines the scaling semantics those components shall preserve.

### Technology Independence

ILAIOS scalability shall remain independent of a specific cloud elasticity service, Kubernetes autoscaler, queue, database, cache, load balancer, model provider, serverless platform, scheduler, accelerator, or capacity-purchasing model.

An implementation may use replicas, processes, threads, asynchronous workers, containers, virtual machines, functions, nodes, partitions, shards, read replicas, regional cells, provider endpoints, or dedicated customer capacity when the resulting behavior is explicit and verified.

Technology independence does not mean identical scaling mechanisms for every workload. Stateless APIs, stateful stores, evidence appenders, batch analysis, model inference, external connectors, and customer-controlled deployments have different constraints. Each requires an approved Scalability Profile.

No provider's theoretical maximum, automatic mode, unlimited label, or benchmark shall be represented as ILAIOS-supported scale without end-to-end evidence.

### Strategic Objectives

Scalability shall:

- define supported demand and data envelopes for exact Deployment Profiles;
- preserve security, privacy, tenant isolation, policy, approval, validation, audit, and evidence under load;
- allocate capacity according to measured need and risk rather than uncontrolled growth;
- protect critical Control Plane and Trust Core paths from ordinary workload saturation;
- enforce tenant fairness, quotas, priorities, and bounded resource use;
- use admission and backpressure before overload becomes silent corruption or unauthorized behavior;
- support safe horizontal, vertical, partitioned, and regional expansion;
- prevent retry, fan-out, queue, cache, or autoscaling amplification;
- preserve deterministic task and external-side-effect semantics;
- scale down without losing accepted state, in-flight authority, or required evidence;
- provide capacity and cost transparency;
- remain supportable in managed, hybrid, isolated, and customer-controlled profiles;
- validate scaling behavior through representative testing; and
- avoid architectural complexity before demonstrated need.

### Canonical Scalability Domain Model

The following terms are distinct:

**Scalability Profile.** The approved workload, demand, capacity, scaling methods, limits, signals, dependencies, failure behavior, cost, evidence, and responsibilities for an exact service, Deployment Profile, environment, region, tenant model, release, and support scope.

**Load Envelope.** The supported range and shape of requests, tasks, concurrency, data, payload size, tenant count, model use, external actions, and time distribution for which the system has evidence-backed behavior.

**Capacity Unit.** A defined unit of usable service capacity, such as a worker, replica, partition, node, database allocation, model endpoint, connector allowance, or regional cell. Units shall not be assumed equivalent across environments.

**Headroom.** Reserved capacity above expected demand required for bursts, failover, maintenance, recovery, dependency slowdown, or uncertainty.

**Scaling Signal.** An observed or forecast value used to recommend or initiate capacity change. It is not a business-policy decision.

**Scaling Decision.** The deterministic infrastructure decision to change capacity within an approved range and policy. It does not grant task authority.

**Scaling Action.** The attributable creation, resizing, activation, deactivation, partitioning, relocation, or removal of a Capacity Unit.

**Saturation.** A condition in which one or more constrained resources approach or exceed the point where objectives, safety, or correctness can no longer be maintained.

**Backpressure.** A controlled mechanism that slows, queues, limits, or rejects upstream work when downstream capacity cannot safely accept it.

**Cell.** A bounded deployment unit containing defined compute, storage, network, tenant, failure, and operating capacity. A cell reduces blast radius but is not automatically a complete tenant boundary.

**Noisy Neighbor.** A tenant, workload, operation, or dependency whose resource use degrades another scope beyond the approved fairness objective.

### Scalability Profiles and Supported Envelopes

Every production service shall have a Scalability Profile that defines:

- workload class, business criticality, tenant model, data classification, and dependencies;
- normal, peak, burst, recovery, and exceptional Load Envelopes;
- capacity metrics, Capacity Units, minimums, maximums, and headroom;
- latency, throughput, concurrency, queue, freshness, availability, and error objectives;
- horizontal, vertical, partition, cache, provider, and regional scaling methods;
- admission, quotas, prioritization, backpressure, shedding, timeout, retry, and recovery;
- scale-up and scale-down signals, thresholds, stabilization, cooldown, and safety gates;
- state, identity, secret, network, storage, evidence, and release requirements for new capacity;
- test evidence, observability, cost boundaries, owners, review, and limitations; and
- customer, provider, and ILAIOS responsibilities.

The supported envelope shall state what has been validated, not what a component vendor claims could be possible. Demand outside the envelope shall enter an explicit constrained, queued, rejected, or separately approved mode.

### Demand Modeling

Demand models shall account for request rate, concurrent sessions, task duration, payload and response size, tenant distribution, model tokens or compute, connector calls, storage operations, evidence volume, network transfer, retries, and scheduled work.

Averages shall not substitute for distributions. Peak, tail, correlated bursts, tenant concentration, regional events, provider outages, release migrations, recovery, and abuse can dominate capacity needs.

Forecasts shall distinguish organic growth, customer onboarding, feature adoption, seasonal demand, planned events, incident traffic, replay, migration, model changes, and load-test activity.

Forecast uncertainty shall be explicit. Capacity shall not be committed solely from model-generated forecasts without accountable review and observed evidence.

### Capacity Planning

Capacity planning shall translate supported demand into compute, memory, accelerator, storage, I/O, connection, queue, network, provider, key-service, validation, audit, and evidence requirements.

Plans shall include baseline capacity, headroom, failure-domain loss, maintenance, deployment overlap, regional failover, backup and restore, incident investigation, and growth lead time.

Provider quotas, procurement lead times, accelerator scarcity, customer hardware, licensing, IP ranges, database limits, certificate issuance, and support staffing may be harder constraints than raw compute.

Capacity reviews shall occur before material launches, large customer activation, model change, migration, region addition, Stable release, or support commitment. Underprovisioned critical control paths shall block the affected scope rather than rely on emergency scale.

### Scaling Methods

Horizontal scaling adds or removes parallel Capacity Units. It requires workload partitionability, deterministic routing, distributed state, identity issuance, coordination, and safe removal.

Vertical scaling changes resources assigned to an existing unit. It may reduce distribution complexity but can require restart, rescheduling, downtime, or host support. Maximum unit size and failure impact shall be understood.

Partition scaling divides data, tenants, keys, tasks, regions, or functions across bounded authorities. It adds routing, migration, balancing, consistency, and recovery complexity.

Cellular scaling adds a repeatable bounded deployment cell. Cells can limit blast radius and support residency, but they require explicit tenant placement, cross-cell services, fleet governance, capacity balance, and failover semantics.

Scaling method selection shall follow measured bottlenecks and accepted risk. Adding replicas shall not be presented as a solution to a serial, externally limited, lock-bound, or stateful bottleneck.

### Stateless Workload Scaling

Stateless services should avoid local authoritative state and support safe replacement, parallelism, and routing. Required state shall reside in governed external stores or explicit ephemeral coordination.

Each replica shall be independently authenticated and receive least-privilege identity, configuration, secrets, and network access. A shared replica credential shall not expand with scale without bounded risk treatment.

Session affinity shall be avoided unless required. When used, it shall have failover, expiry, tenant, load, and security semantics and shall not create hidden authoritative state.

Replica startup shall verify release eligibility, configuration, dependencies, identity, and readiness before receiving traffic. Process liveness is insufficient.

Scale-down shall drain requests, cancel or transfer work safely, preserve evidence, revoke identity where appropriate, and avoid truncating in-flight tasks.

### Stateful Workload Scaling

Stateful scaling shall preserve a declared authority, consistency, concurrency, partition, replication, backup, and recovery model under Section 7.5.

Adding replicas may increase read availability without increasing write throughput. Write scaling may require partitioning, batching, index change, contention reduction, or redesign within the accepted architecture.

Leaders, primaries, partitions, replicas, and quorum members shall have fencing and failover semantics. Infrastructure role names do not create ILAIOS business authority.

State movement and rebalancing shall protect encryption, tenant boundaries, ordering, integrity, capacity, and performance. Migration shall be observable, rate-bounded, recoverable, and validated.

Scale-down shall not remove the last valid copy, reduce quorum below safety, abandon a partition, invalidate backups, or create an unsupported recovery topology.

### Partitioning and Sharding

Partition keys shall align with access, tenant, locality, growth, distribution, privacy, and recovery requirements. Poor keys can create hotspots, cross-tenant coupling, and unbounded fan-out.

Partition ownership, routing, split, merge, migration, rebalance, failure, and repair shall be deterministic and attributable. A request shall not silently reach multiple authoritative partitions.

Cross-partition transactions and queries shall use explicit consistency and compensation. Global scans and fan-out shall be bounded and prohibited from overwhelming critical paths.

Tenant-based partitioning may improve isolation but can produce highly uneven load. Large tenants may require dedicated or sub-partitioned capacity under an approved profile.

Partition identifiers shall not substitute for verified tenant identity or policy authorization.

### Cellular Architecture

Cells may contain bounded application, execution, storage, network, validation, audit-forwarding, and operational capacity. Shared global services shall be minimized and explicitly governed because they can reintroduce common failure and scaling bottlenecks.

Tenant placement shall use an authoritative registry and deterministic routing. Placement changes shall preserve data, keys, policy, identities, connectors, evidence, residency, and customer obligations.

Cell capacity, failure, evacuation, expansion, and retirement shall be managed independently where possible. A cell shall not fail over into another cell without capacity and eligibility verification.

Cross-cell requests shall be limited and observable. A global fan-out request shall have explicit cost, timeout, partial-result, privacy, and validation behavior.

### Request Admission

Admission control shall decide whether the platform can safely accept new work within the applicable policy, capacity, tenant, and dependency boundaries.

Admission may consider authenticated tenant, task class, priority, concurrency, queue depth, provider availability, evidence capacity, regional health, cost limit, and estimated resource demand.

Capacity admission is distinct from business authorization. A permitted task may be delayed or rejected for capacity; available capacity shall not authorize a prohibited task.

Rejected or deferred work shall receive an explicit, stable outcome with safe retry guidance. The system shall not acknowledge acceptance and then silently discard work.

Admission shall reserve capacity for critical control, cancellation, incident, audit, evidence, recovery, and customer-safety operations.

### Backpressure

Backpressure shall propagate before downstream saturation becomes data loss, duplicate action, timeout amplification, or unaudited processing. It may use bounded queues, concurrency limits, producer slowdown, credits, circuit breakers, or safe rejection.

Backpressure boundaries shall define ownership, thresholds, timeouts, overflow behavior, tenant fairness, and recovery. Unbounded buffering is prohibited.

The Control Plane shall not continue issuing execution authority faster than Tool Gateway, validation, audit, or evidence capacity can safely process it.

Backpressure shall not be bypassed by alternate endpoints, priority abuse, retries, or direct internal calls. Emergency overrides shall be narrowly scoped and evidenced.

### Queue Architecture

Queues shall have defined producers, consumers, message identity, tenant, ordering, visibility, delivery semantics, retention, capacity, encryption, retry, dead-letter, replay, and recovery.

At-least-once delivery requires idempotency or reconciliation. At-most-once delivery implies possible loss and shall not be claimed as reliable completion. Exactly-once claims shall describe the exact boundary and external-effect limitations.

Queue depth alone is an incomplete scaling signal. Arrival rate, age, processing time, retry rate, tenant distribution, priority, downstream limits, and oldest work are material.

Dead-letter handling shall not become indefinite hidden storage. Reprocessing shall re-evaluate current identity, policy, approval, capability, expiry, tenant, and release state.

Queue consumers shall not accept their own results; output remains subject to validation and disposition.

### Concurrency Governance

Concurrency limits shall be defined by service, tenant, operation, connector, model, provider, database, partition, region, and risk class as applicable.

Concurrency shall not exceed the safe downstream capacity merely because compute replicas are available. Database connections, provider quotas, Tool Gateway destinations, signing services, and validation may be limiting resources.

Locks, leases, rate windows, semaphores, and worker reservations shall use fencing, expiry, recovery, and observability. Orphaned coordination state shall not block work indefinitely or allow duplicate authority.

High concurrency shall not weaken ordering, tenant isolation, evidence, approval, idempotency, or state-transition validation.

### Tenant Fairness and Quotas

Shared capacity shall enforce tenant fairness through quotas, weights, priorities, reservations, concurrency, rate, queue, storage, model, connector, and cost limits appropriate to the product profile.

One tenant shall not exhaust shared Control Plane, Tool Gateway, Validation Pipeline, Audit Engine, Evidence Chain, model-provider, storage, network, or support capacity.

Enterprise contracts may reserve capacity within lawful and formally approved scope, but they shall not silently weaken another tenant's security, evidence, or non-waivable controls.

Quota changes shall be attributable, reviewed, monitored, and consistent across ingress, queues, workers, providers, and storage. A frontend quota without downstream enforcement is incomplete.

Tenant metrics shall not expose another tenant's activity or capacity commitment.

### Priority and Load Shedding

Priority classes shall be few, explicit, and tied to business and safety needs. User-supplied priority shall not be trusted without authorization.

Critical priorities may include cancellation, revocation, incident containment, audit and evidence continuity, health, recovery, and customer-protection operations. Ordinary high-cost work shall not preempt these paths.

Load shedding shall reject or degrade the least critical eligible work before unsafe saturation. Degraded behavior shall be documented and shall not bypass policy, approval, validation, tenant, privacy, audit, or evidence controls.

Partial results shall be labeled as partial and shall not be represented as accepted complete outcomes. Shed work shall preserve an attributable disposition.

### Retry and Amplification Control

Retries shall have bounded attempts, exponential or equivalent backoff, jitter, time budget, idempotency, and classification of retryable failures.

Every layer shall avoid independently retrying the same operation without a shared end-to-end budget. Client, gateway, service, queue, connector, model provider, and storage retries can multiply load dramatically.

Non-idempotent Tool Gateway actions shall not be retried without reconciliation of the prior attempt. Ambiguous timeouts shall be investigated as unknown outcomes rather than assumed failures.

Retry storms, thundering herds, cache stampedes, synchronized refresh, and failover surges shall be addressed through coordination, stagger, request coalescing, circuit breaking, and admission.

### Autoscaling Signals

Scaling signals shall correspond to the constrained resource and service objective. CPU utilization alone may be insufficient for I/O-bound, queue-driven, model, connector, memory, storage, or latency-sensitive workloads.

Signals may include request rate, concurrency, queue age, queue depth, processing duration, saturation, memory, CPU, accelerator use, storage I/O, connection pools, provider capacity, validation lag, evidence backlog, or forecast demand.

Signal source, freshness, completeness, sampling, tenant aggregation, spoof resistance, and failure behavior shall be defined. Missing or stale signals shall not trigger unsafe scale-down.

Business metrics and model recommendations may inform planning but shall not directly create unbounded infrastructure authority. Autoscaling decisions shall remain deterministic within approved limits.

### Autoscaling Policy

Autoscaling policy shall define minimum and maximum capacity, scale-up and scale-down thresholds, step sizes, stabilization windows, cooldown, rate limits, headroom, failure behavior, and manual override.

Scale-up should respond quickly enough to protect objectives while avoiding uncontrolled cost and dependency overload. Scale-down should be deliberately conservative where it can terminate work, reduce redundancy, or cause oscillation.

Hysteresis and stabilization shall prevent flapping. The policy shall account for startup time, readiness, warm-up, load-balancer propagation, cache population, model loading, connection establishment, and metric delay.

Autoscaling shall not exceed provider quota, storage capacity, network capacity, downstream rate, license, customer hardware, security, or budget bounds. Maximum capacity is a safety boundary, not a guarantee of successful service.

### Planned and Scheduled Scaling

Known launches, migrations, customer events, seasonal peaks, batch windows, model changes, and disaster-recovery exercises should use planned scaling when forecasts are more reliable than reactive signals.

Scheduled capacity shall still verify release, identity, configuration, health, network, storage, secrets, and evidence before receiving work.

Unused planned capacity shall be removed through controlled scale-down after the event and review. Temporary increases shall not become permanent baseline through inaction.

Planning shall include provider reservation and procurement lead time where capacity cannot be obtained instantly.

### Scale-Up Safety

Every new Capacity Unit shall use an eligible release, verified configuration, approved identity, least-privilege secrets, network policy, storage mapping, tenant boundary, health contract, and observability profile.

Units shall not receive traffic until readiness establishes that they can safely process the intended workload. Startup success or scheduler placement is insufficient.

Mass scale-up shall not overwhelm identity issuance, secret stores, DNS, registries, storage, databases, model providers, audit, evidence, or load balancers.

Provisioning failure shall leave no orphaned privileged identity, public endpoint, volume, secret, route, or customer-visible partial service.

### Scale-Down Safety

Scale-down shall identify in-flight requests, tasks, approvals, capabilities, Tool Gateway actions, validation work, audit buffers, evidence buffers, leases, queues, storage writes, and customer sessions.

Units shall drain, checkpoint, transfer, cancel, reconcile, or complete work according to the workload profile before termination. Forced termination behavior shall be tested.

Scale-down shall revoke or expire workload identities and credentials where appropriate, remove routes and registrations, preserve required telemetry and evidence, and avoid orphaned state.

Stateful scale-down shall preserve quorum, replica safety, partition ownership, backup, recovery, and regional objectives. Cost reduction shall not violate minimum resilience.

### Kubernetes Horizontal Workload Scaling

Kubernetes Horizontal Pod Autoscaler or equivalent mechanisms may adjust replica count from approved resource, custom, object, or external metrics. Configuration shall define target, minimum, maximum, metrics, behavior, stabilization, rate, and failure semantics.

Resource requests shall be accurate enough for utilization-based decisions. Missing requests or misleading metrics can disable or distort scaling.

Multiple metrics shall be evaluated for interaction. Scaling on queue depth while ignoring downstream provider limits may increase congestion rather than capacity.

Horizontal scaling shall not be used for workloads that cannot safely parallelize, share state, handle duplicate delivery, or drain. A controller's desired replica count is infrastructure state, not business authority.

### Kubernetes Vertical Workload Scaling

Vertical Pod Autoscaler, in-place resource resize, or equivalent mechanisms may recommend or apply CPU and memory changes when the exact platform profile supports them.

Vertical changes can restart, evict, resize, or temporarily disrupt workloads depending on platform and mode. Stateful services, long tasks, restricted execution, and evidence appenders require explicit impact analysis.

Horizontal and vertical autoscalers shall not compete over the same resource signals without a coordinated policy. Requests, limits, scheduler placement, node capacity, and runtime behavior shall remain consistent.

Recommendations shall be observed before automatic production application for high-impact workloads. Provider or autoscaler recommendation is not acceptance evidence.

### Kubernetes Node Scaling

Node autoscaling may add or remove worker capacity in response to unschedulable demand, utilization, consolidation, or policy. Workload requests, topology, taints, affinity, storage, devices, and disruption controls shall be accurate.

Node provisioning time and provider quota may be longer than workload scale-up time. Headroom or overprovisioning may be required for latency-sensitive services.

Consolidation and node removal shall respect disruption budgets, local state, restricted workloads, evidence buffers, storage attachment, node trust, and termination grace.

New nodes shall pass identity, operating system, runtime, policy, network, observability, and eligibility checks before hosting protected work. More nodes do not create more business permission.

### Autoscaler Interaction

Workload, vertical, node, queue, database, provider, and regional autoscalers form a control system. Their feedback loops, delays, thresholds, and shared signals shall be analyzed together.

One autoscaler shall not cause another to oscillate, chase stale metrics, or repeatedly provision and remove capacity. Ownership of desired resource fields shall be explicit.

Autoscaler failure, metrics outage, quota exhaustion, and contradictory recommendations shall have a safe operating mode and alerting.

Manual override shall be attributable, bounded, monitored, and returned to controlled automation after review.

### Model and Accelerator Scalability

Model workload capacity shall account for tokens, context size, batch size, latency, concurrency, model size, accelerator memory, warm-up, provider quota, regional availability, and cost.

Model-provider fallback or additional capacity shall remain within approved model, privacy, residency, data-use, customer, release, and support boundaries. Availability does not authorize a different provider or model.

Batching, caching, speculative execution, parallel model calls, and ensemble methods may multiply cost, disclosure, latency, and evidence. Their use shall be explicit and policy-governed.

Accelerator scaling shall account for device scarcity, drivers, runtime compatibility, partitioning, topology, scheduling, model loading, numerical behavior, and failover.

AI Reasoning and Recommendation capacity shall not starve deterministic Policy Engine, Approval Engine, Tool Gateway, Validation Pipeline, Audit Engine, or Evidence Chain capacity.

### Tool Gateway and Connector Scalability

Each connector shall have a Scalability Profile covering destination limits, credentials, tenant fairness, concurrency, rate, timeout, retry, idempotency, queue, circuit breaker, and external side effects.

Adding Tool Gateway workers shall not exceed customer-system or provider capacity. Connector scaling shall be constrained by policy and destination-specific limits.

Credentials and connections shall remain tenant- and purpose-bound. Pooling shall not mix tenant identity or authorization.

External rate limiting, partial availability, or ambiguous outcomes shall trigger backpressure and reconciliation rather than blind scale or retry.

### Validation Pipeline Scalability

Validation capacity shall scale with task volume, result complexity, evidence volume, and risk class. Validation shall not become a bypassed bottleneck under pressure.

High-risk validation may require independent systems, external services, human review, or serialized checks that cannot scale linearly. Admission and delivery objectives shall account for these constraints.

Validation queues shall preserve tenant, task, result, artifact, policy, release, and evidence identity. Stale validation shall re-evaluate relevant current state before acceptance.

If required validation capacity is unavailable, affected results shall remain pending, rejected, or constrained; they shall not be accepted by timeout.

### Audit Engine and Evidence Chain Scalability

Audit and evidence capacity shall be planned from request, decision, approval, capability, action, validation, delivery, change, and incident event rates—not only business request volume.

The accepted buffered append design shall use bounded queues, durable buffering, ordering, backpressure, retry, deduplication, and loss detection. It shall not report durable evidence before the required persistence boundary.

Audit and Evidence Chain capacity shall be protected from ordinary tenant saturation. If non-waivable evidence cannot be persisted safely, the affected workflow shall fail closed, pause, or enter the exact approved constrained mode.

Partitioning shall preserve chain semantics, tenant boundaries, verification, retention, export, and reconstruction. Parallel append shall not produce ambiguous ordering where order is material.

Operational logs and autoscaler metrics do not replace canonical audit or evidence.

### Storage Scalability

Storage scale shall follow Section 7.5 and account for data growth, index growth, evidence, retention, tenant distribution, write amplification, backup, restore, replication, migration, and deletion.

Read replicas, caches, indexes, and search stores may increase read capacity but remain derived unless explicitly authoritative. Stale data shall not drive authority-sensitive decisions.

Sharding and partitioning shall preserve tenant, consistency, key, residency, backup, recovery, and deletion behavior.

Capacity expansion shall not be delayed until exhaustion. Storage autoscaling, where supported, shall have maximums, cost controls, monitoring, and rollback or migration plans.

### Network Scalability

Network scaling shall account for bandwidth, connections, packets, DNS, TLS, NAT ports, gateways, load balancers, service proxies, tunnels, provider quotas, and DDoS conditions under Section 7.6.

Adding compute without sufficient network capacity can increase timeouts and retry amplification. Scaling tests shall include network bottlenecks and cross-region behavior.

New endpoints, addresses, routes, certificates, and policy rules created through scale shall remain governed and inventoried.

Scale shall not create alternate unencrypted, public, cross-tenant, or unmonitored paths.

### Cache Scalability

Caches may reduce latency and authoritative-store load but can create stampede, staleness, poisoning, privacy, tenant, and invalidation risk.

Cache capacity, partitioning, eviction, replication, warm-up, failure, and rebuild shall be defined. A cache shall not become the only durable copy.

Hot keys and uneven tenant use shall be detected. Key design shall prevent cross-tenant collisions and sensitive-data exposure.

Cache scale-up shall not exceed source capacity during warm-up. Cache loss shall trigger controlled recovery rather than synchronized unbounded requests.

### External Dependency Scaling

Every external dependency shall have known quotas, concurrency, latency, availability, payload, regional, support, and commercial limits. ILAIOS capacity shall not be represented independently of those constraints.

The dependency budget shall define how much service capacity can be consumed by each upstream and downstream relationship. Circuit breakers, concurrency limits, admission, and fallbacks shall preserve that budget.

Fallback shall be policy-eligible and semantically compatible. An available but unapproved provider, model, region, connector, storage service, or network path is not valid capacity.

Provider quota increase is an operational change requiring ownership, cost, security, and evidence. It does not by itself increase supported ILAIOS scale.

### Multi-Region and Geographic Scaling

Regional expansion shall have an approved Deployment Profile, data residency, tenant placement, identity, keys, storage, network, model providers, Tool Gateway connectors, validation, evidence, release, support, and recovery.

Traffic distribution shall not route work to a region that lacks the required data authority, provider approval, customer contract, release, or evidence capability.

Global services shall be evaluated for common bottleneck and failure. Region-local capacity does not eliminate reliance on centralized identity, policy, DNS, registry, key, or provider services.

Regional failover demand shall be included in headroom. Two regions each operating near full capacity do not provide credible failover capacity.

### Customer-Controlled and Isolated Capacity

Customer-controlled, on-premises, edge, and isolated Deployment Profiles may have fixed hardware, delayed procurement, limited provider access, or no automatic scaling.

The supported Load Envelope shall be measured against the customer's actual configuration and responsibilities. ILAIOS shall not claim elastic capacity it cannot control or observe.

Capacity alerts, expansion procedures, hardware compatibility, maintenance, license, network, storage, backup, and support responsibilities shall be contractually and operationally defined.

Offline or fixed-capacity systems shall prioritize admission, quotas, queues, load shedding, and safe degraded modes. Local resource exhaustion shall not weaken non-waivable controls.

### Performance Budgets

Each critical flow shall allocate an end-to-end budget across ingress, identity, policy, approval, reasoning, model provider, Tool Gateway, validation, storage, audit, evidence, and delivery.

Local optimization shall not consume the entire end-to-end budget or shift unacceptable latency to validation, evidence, recovery, or customer systems.

Budgets shall cover normal and tail latency, timeout, retry, queue, and dependency behavior. The slowest percentile and oldest queued work are often more material than averages.

Performance targets shall not force removal of required security, privacy, approval, validation, audit, evidence, or tenant controls.

### Load and Stress Testing

Scalability claims shall be supported by representative load, burst, soak, stress, spike, failover, recovery, and degradation tests appropriate to the profile.

Tests shall represent tenant distribution, payloads, model behavior, connector limits, data size, cache state, encryption, evidence rate, queue backlog, regional latency, and failure conditions.

Test environments and generators shall be isolated from production authority and shall use synthetic or approved data. Load testing customer or provider systems requires explicit authorization.

Results shall record configuration, release, dataset, topology, limits, duration, error, latency distributions, saturation, cost, and observed bottlenecks. A single best-case benchmark is insufficient.

### Soak and Endurance Testing

Long-duration testing shall identify memory leaks, connection leaks, queue drift, cache growth, evidence backlog, compaction, fragmentation, certificate renewal, token rotation, clock drift, and cumulative provider limits.

Short tests may conceal resource exhaustion and recovery defects. Stable support claims shall include duration appropriate to expected continuous operation.

Soak tests shall include controlled scaling events, deployment changes, backup activity, maintenance, and dependency variation.

Findings shall enter the Defect Lifecycle and block affected claims until treated.

### Failure and Degraded Modes

Scalability Profiles shall define behavior when capacity, metrics, autoscalers, providers, queues, storage, network, identity, keys, validation, audit, or evidence are unavailable or saturated.

Degraded mode shall be explicit, observable, time-bounded, and limited to operations that preserve required security and authority. It shall not become a silent permanent profile.

The platform may reject new work, queue bounded work, reduce optional intelligence, use an approved provider, limit tenants, pause execution, or preserve read-only access according to policy.

It shall not skip approval, expand capability, bypass Tool Gateway, accept unvalidated results, or discard required evidence to maintain apparent availability.

### Security Under Scale

Scaling shall not dilute least privilege, identity, secrets, encryption, tenant isolation, network policy, artifact verification, patch level, monitoring, or incident controls.

Rapid provisioning shall use approved images, configurations, identities, and trust roots. New capacity shall not default to broader access because specific policy is unavailable.

Attackers may trigger autoscaling to increase cost, expand attack surface, exhaust quotas, or hide activity. Signals and requests shall be authenticated, bounded, anomaly-monitored, and tenant-attributed where possible.

Security systems themselves shall have protected capacity. Authentication, Policy Engine, Approval Engine, Tool Gateway, Validation Pipeline, Audit Engine, Evidence Chain, key, and secret services shall not be starved by optional workload growth.

### Privacy and Data Minimization Under Scale

Scaling shall not create uncontrolled copies of customer data, prompts, outputs, embeddings, caches, logs, snapshots, or support data.

Replicas, partitions, regions, caches, queues, and temporary workers shall inherit purpose, classification, tenant, residency, retention, deletion, and encryption requirements.

Autoscaling metrics shall avoid personal data and protected customer identifiers unless necessary and authorized. Aggregation shall not leak tenant capacity or activity.

Scale-down and retirement shall remove ephemeral data, revoke identities, and apply retention and deletion without leaving orphaned copies.

### Cost and Economic Boundaries

Every Scalability Profile shall define cost drivers, budgets, alerts, allocation, customer commitments, provider pricing risks, and maximum automated exposure.

Cost optimization shall consider total end-to-end cost including model use, accelerators, storage, network transfer, observability, backup, validation, evidence, and support—not compute alone.

Automatic scaling shall have bounded maximums and anomaly controls. A pricing change, retry storm, abuse event, or erroneous metric shall not create unlimited spend.

Cost pressure shall not justify weakening non-waivable security, privacy, tenant, approval, validation, audit, or evidence controls. Unsupported capacity shall be represented honestly.

### Scalability Observability

Scalability telemetry shall include demand, admitted and rejected work, concurrency, queue depth and age, throughput, latency distribution, errors, retries, saturation, capacity, headroom, autoscaler decisions, provisioning time, scale events, tenant fairness, provider limits, and cost.

Metrics shall be segmented by service, environment, region, release, workload class, and privacy-safe tenant scope where appropriate.

Scaling signals and service objectives shall be versioned and attributable. A changed metric definition can alter capacity behavior and therefore requires governance.

Detailed observability, monitoring, and logging standards remain in Sections 7.8 through 7.10. Autoscaler metrics and provider dashboards do not replace the Audit Engine or Evidence Chain.

### Audit Engine and Evidence Chain Integration

The Audit Engine shall record material capacity-plan approvals, Scalability Profile changes, limit changes, autoscaling-policy changes, manual overrides, large scale actions, quota changes, cell and region additions, load-shedding activation, emergency capacity, and retirement.

The Evidence Chain shall bind the records necessary to reconstruct why a material scaling action occurred, which signal and policy applied, who or what acted, what capacity changed, which release and profile were used, and how safety was validated.

Routine high-frequency autoscaler samples may be retained as operational telemetry according to policy, while material decisions and summarized evidence remain canonical. This distinction shall not conceal required events.

Audit Engine and Evidence Chain controls operate continuously during bursts, overload, failover, and recovery. Capacity pressure shall not create an unaudited operating mode.

### Independent Validation

The Validation Pipeline shall independently assess the scaling properties required by the applicable gate. Validation may test load handling, tenant fairness, quotas, admission, backpressure, retries, queue recovery, autoscaling, scale-down, state integrity, failover, security, evidence, and cost bounds.

The autoscaler, provider, scheduler, load generator, or workload shall not be the sole validator of its own success. Desired replica count, resource allocation, provider status, or benchmark completion is not acceptance.

Validation shall confirm both performance and preservation of canonical controls under load. A faster system that bypasses policy, approval, Tool Gateway, validation, audit, evidence, or tenant isolation is non-conformant.

Capacity claims shall bind to exact release, configuration, topology, data, providers, and test conditions.

### Change and ADR Governance

Scalability changes shall follow Section 5.7 and include demand evidence, bottleneck analysis, capacity model, security, privacy, tenant, failure, cost, rollout, validation, rollback, and support impact.

Routine threshold changes within an approved range may use controlled operational change. Architecture-significant introduction of sharding, cells, multi-region active operation, new autoscaling authority, global queues, new provider capacity, or changed Trust Core partitioning requires an authorized ADR.

Scaling mechanisms shall not create a competing Release Lifecycle. New capacity shall run an eligible release, and a performance test does not approve a release.

Temporary emergency capacity shall have purpose, owner, expiry, monitoring, and retrospective review. It shall not become permanent architecture through inaction.

### Scalability Incident Response

The threat model shall include overload, autoscaler failure, metric corruption, cost attack, quota exhaustion, provider throttling, noisy neighbor, hot partition, retry storm, queue explosion, evidence backlog, scale-down data loss, and regional capacity failure.

Detection shall identify affected services, tenants, regions, providers, queues, partitions, models, connectors, storage, network, validation, audit, evidence, and cost exposure.

Containment may reduce admission, activate quotas, shed optional work, disable abusive tenants, restrict retries, isolate connectors, pause execution, reserve Trust Core capacity, or add bounded emergency capacity.

Recovery shall reconcile queued and ambiguous work, restore safe autoscaling policy, validate authoritative state and external effects, remove temporary capacity, and preserve incident evidence.

### Governance and Responsibilities

Product authority defines supported customer scale and commercial claims. Architecture authority defines scale boundaries, partition models, cells, and architecture-significant decisions. Security defines non-waivable behavior under load and abuse.

Platform engineering owns capacity models, infrastructure scaling, orchestration, quotas, and cost controls. Service owners define workload behavior and bottlenecks. Storage, network, model, Tool Gateway, validation, audit, and evidence owners define their capacity constraints.

Operations monitors demand, saturation, scale events, and incidents. Finance and product functions govern cost and commercial commitments within approved authority. Customers and providers retain responsibilities assigned by the Deployment Profile and contract.

No autoscaler, provider, scheduler, model output, customer request, sales commitment, or engineering preference may unilaterally alter canonical authority or non-waivable controls.

### Single-Maintainer Bootstrap Profile

During a registered Single-Maintainer Bootstrap Profile, one authorized maintainer may temporarily perform multiple scalability roles where independent personnel are unavailable. The absence of independent capacity review shall be recorded and shall not be represented as Enterprise separation of duties.

The profile shall maintain organizational ownership, least privilege, bounded automated scale, mandatory Quality Gates, exact configuration and override attribution, cost alerts, protected audit and evidence, periodic review, tested rollback, and a dated exit plan.

High-impact changes to tenant quotas, public capacity, provider commitments, Tool Gateway concurrency, Trust Core capacity, database partitioning, multi-region operation, or Stable release claims shall receive qualified external review before production or Enterprise adoption; otherwise the affected scope shall remain constrained.

Automatic scaling maximums shall remain conservative until measured evidence supports expansion. Continued single-maintainer operation shall not become permanent through inaction.

### Quality Gates

Before a Scalability Profile or material scaling change becomes eligible, the applicable gates shall verify:

- declared workload, tenant, data, provider, release, and support scope;
- evidence-backed normal, peak, burst, failure, and recovery Load Envelopes;
- Capacity Units, minimums, maximums, headroom, lead time, and cost bounds;
- horizontal, vertical, partition, cell, regional, and provider scaling semantics;
- request admission, quotas, tenant fairness, priorities, backpressure, and load shedding;
- bounded queues, concurrency, retries, idempotency, and amplification controls;
- safe scale-up readiness and scale-down draining, identity revocation, and state preservation;
- Kubernetes workload and node autoscaler interaction where applicable;
- stateful consistency, partition, quorum, storage, backup, and recovery safety;
- model, Tool Gateway, Validation Pipeline, Audit Engine, Evidence Chain, storage, and network capacity;
- external dependency quotas and policy-eligible fallback;
- load, stress, burst, soak, failover, and recovery evidence;
- security, privacy, tenant, release, and cost behavior under load;
- observability, alerting, incident, manual override, and rollback readiness;
- independent Validation Pipeline outcome;
- required Audit Engine and Evidence Chain records; and
- exception ownership, scope, expiry, monitoring, and residual-risk acceptance.

No single benchmark, provider quota, autoscaler status, replica count, low average latency, or successful stress test shall satisfy the complete gate.

### Prohibited Practices

The following practices are prohibited unless an explicitly defined canonical exception applies:

- representing scalability as unlimited or independent of exact test conditions and dependencies;
- treating a new replica, worker, node, partition, model endpoint, or region as business authority;
- allowing autoscalers, schedulers, providers, or model recommendations to expand non-waivable authority;
- scaling compute while ignoring storage, network, provider, validation, audit, evidence, or customer-system limits;
- accepting work without a bounded queue, rejection, or backpressure path;
- using unbounded queues, retries, concurrency, fan-out, or automatic spend;
- retrying non-idempotent Tool Gateway actions without reconciliation;
- allowing one tenant to exhaust shared critical capacity without controls;
- disabling policy, approval, validation, audit, evidence, security, or tenant isolation to improve throughput;
- using stale, missing, unauthenticated, or manipulable metrics for unsafe scale-down;
- allowing horizontal and vertical autoscalers to fight over resource ownership;
- scaling down without draining work, preserving evidence, revoking identity, and protecting state;
- adding nodes or replicas that bypass release, identity, secret, network, storage, or artifact eligibility;
- treating read replicas, caches, indexes, or queues as authoritative without explicit designation;
- failing over to an unapproved provider, model, region, release, or data authority;
- representing provider maximums, scheduler placement, autoscaler desired state, or benchmark success as validation;
- allowing capacity pressure to create unaudited or unvalidated operation;
- making unreviewed direct production scaling-policy changes;
- allowing emergency capacity or limits to become permanent through inaction;
- representing bootstrap self-review as independent Enterprise assurance; or
- giving any autoscaler, cloud service, scheduler, queue, database, provider, customer preference, sales commitment, model output, or engineering convenience architectural authority.

### Non-Goals

This section does not require Kubernetes, automatic scaling, serverless infrastructure, sharding, cellular architecture, multi-region active operation, accelerators, or elastic cloud capacity for every ILAIOS deployment.

It does not define detailed observability assigned to Section 7.8, monitoring assigned to Section 7.9, or logging assigned to Section 7.10.

It does not promise unlimited tenants, tasks, requests, tokens, storage, connectors, regions, or concurrent actions. Supported scale is profile-specific and evidence-backed.

It does not make autoscaling a substitute for efficient design, capacity planning, admission, backpressure, security, validation, audit, evidence, recovery, or accountable commercial commitments.

### Conformance Requirements

An implementation conforms to this section only when it demonstrates that:

- every production service is governed by an approved Scalability Profile;
- supported Load Envelopes, capacity, headroom, limits, dependencies, and cost are explicit;
- scaling mechanisms remain technology-independent and do not create business authority;
- horizontal, vertical, stateful, partitioned, cellular, regional, and provider scaling preserve canonical semantics;
- admission, bounded queues, backpressure, quotas, fairness, priority, and load shedding protect the platform;
- concurrency, retries, idempotency, failover, and external effects remain controlled;
- scale-up admits only eligible identity, release, configuration, network, storage, secret, and evidence profiles;
- scale-down drains, reconciles, revokes, and preserves required state and evidence;
- autoscaling signals, policies, interactions, failures, and manual overrides are governed;
