Inhibition may suppress dependent alerts when a higher-level condition makes them redundant, such as suppressing individual service dependency alerts during a confirmed shared provider failure.

Inhibition rules shall define source, target, equal-scope labels, duration, and safety. Missing labels shall not accidentally inhibit broad unrelated alerts.

Security, Audit Engine, Evidence Chain, tenant-isolation, and data-loss alerts shall not be inhibited merely because a general outage is active unless the risk treatment explicitly permits it.

Inhibition reduces notifications, not signal collection, alert state, evidence, or investigation availability.

### Silences and Suppression

Silences shall be exact, attributable, time-bounded, purpose-bound, and approved according to severity. Open-ended or all-alert silences are prohibited.

Silence matchers shall be reviewed to prevent broader scope than intended. Silence of one tenant, region, release, or maintenance activity shall not hide another.

Silencing a notification does not resolve the condition, stop data collection, modify the service objective, or waive incident obligations.

Active and expired silences shall be periodically reviewed. Repeated silence of the same alert indicates a defect in the service, rule, objective, or operating model.

### Maintenance Windows

Planned maintenance shall define scope, owner, expected signals, allowed suppression, customer communication, start, end, rollback, validation, and evidence.

Maintenance windows shall not suppress unexpected security, tenant, data-integrity, Audit Engine, Evidence Chain, or broader dependency failures.

Monitoring should distinguish expected maintenance effects from unrelated degradation through change identifiers and exact scope.

Expired maintenance suppression shall end automatically. A maintenance window shall not be extended indefinitely to conceal unresolved failure.

### Alert Quality

An actionable alert shall indicate what is wrong, affected scope, severity, start time, relevant evidence, likely impact, owner, runbook, and immediate safe action.

Alert quality shall be measured through precision, recall where assessable, actionability, duplicate rate, acknowledgement time, escalation, stale rate, false-positive rate, false-negative discoveries, and operator feedback.

Alerts that cannot lead to a meaningful decision should be removed, converted to dashboards, aggregated, or redesigned. Deleting noise shall not remove required coverage.

Post-incident review shall identify which alerts were early, late, missing, misleading, redundant, or unactionable.

### Alert Fatigue Control

Alert volume shall remain within the human and organizational capacity to respond. Excessive alerts reduce detection quality and encourage unsafe silencing.

Priority shall favor user impact, security, data, policy, validation, audit, evidence, and imminent saturation over low-value infrastructure variation.

Grouping, inhibition, pending duration, hysteresis, better indicators, and automation may reduce noise. Broad suppression is not an acceptable substitute for rule quality.

Alert load shall be measured by owner, severity, service, time, and recurrence. Chronic alert burden shall enter Continuous Improvement and Defect Lifecycles.

### Runbooks

Every material alert shall reference a versioned runbook or equivalent response guidance appropriate to the operating profile.

Runbooks shall define intent, scope, prerequisites, identity, data protection, diagnostic steps, safe containment, escalation, rollback, validation, customer communication, evidence, and stop conditions.

Commands and links shall be reviewed and safe against wrong environment, tenant, region, or broad target. Destructive steps shall require explicit confirmation and authority.

Runbooks shall not grant permission merely by being accessible. Every action remains subject to current identity, role, policy, approval, Tool Gateway, and change requirements.

### Escalation

Escalation shall define who is notified, when, through which independent channels, and what happens if acknowledgement or progress targets are missed.

High-severity conditions shall have paths to incident command, security, privacy, legal, customer, provider, architecture, and executive authority as applicable.

Escalation shall preserve accurate scope and uncertainty. An alert shall not be represented as confirmed breach or root cause before qualified assessment.

Escalation paths and contacts shall be tested and kept current. One unavailable individual shall not be a permanent Enterprise dependency.

### Automated Response

Monitoring may trigger bounded infrastructure or protective actions such as scaling within approved limits, opening a circuit, pausing admission, isolating a workload, revoking an identity, disabling a connector, or initiating a rollback candidate.

Automated response shall be deterministic, least-privilege, idempotent or reconcilable, time-bounded, attributable, reversible where required, and constrained by an approved Response Profile.

Monitoring shall not directly approve business tasks, expand capabilities, bypass the Tool Gateway, accept results, alter Evidence Chain history, or make legal determinations.

Governed external action initiated by monitoring remains mediated through the Tool Gateway. High-impact actions require human approval where policy requires it.

The response shall validate preconditions, current state, target scope, release, tenant, and expected effect. Failure or ambiguous outcome shall escalate rather than repeat blindly.

### Response Profiles

Every automated or semi-automated response shall define trigger, authority, actor identity, scope, preconditions, action, maximum impact, timeout, retry, rollback, evidence, human oversight, and exit conditions.

Response profiles shall distinguish advisory, approval-required, automatic reversible, automatic protective, and prohibited actions.

Anomaly or model-generated recommendations may propose a response but shall not execute it without deterministic evaluation and required approval.

Response automation shall enter a safe mode when monitoring input is stale, contradictory, incomplete, or unavailable.

### Black-Box Monitoring

Black-box monitoring evaluates externally visible behavior from an approved user, customer, region, or network perspective without relying on internal implementation state.

Checks may verify DNS, certificate, network reachability, authentication, API response, representative read-only workflow, latency, and expected content according to the profile.

Synthetic identities, tenants, data, and credentials shall be clearly segregated and least-privilege. Synthetic checks shall not perform irreversible customer or Tool Gateway actions unless a dedicated safe target and reconciliation exist.

Black-box success demonstrates only the tested path, location, identity, and moment. It does not prove all tenants, functions, security controls, or regions are healthy.

### White-Box Monitoring

White-box monitoring evaluates internal signals such as queues, errors, saturation, state transitions, dependency latency, policy outcomes, validation backlog, audit buffers, and evidence persistence.

Internal indicators provide diagnostic depth but can remain green while the customer journey fails. They shall complement, not replace, outcome-oriented monitoring.

White-box access shall be least-privilege and protect topology, secrets, tenant data, and security controls.

Monitoring queries shall be efficient and shall not create load that causes the condition being monitored.

### Synthetic Transaction Monitoring

Synthetic transactions shall use controlled test accounts, data, destinations, schedules, rate, and cleanup. They shall be distinguishable from customer traffic and excluded or included in objectives according to explicit policy.

End-to-end synthetics may test canonical flow through identity, policy, approval simulation where safe, Tool Gateway test connectors, validation, and delivery. They shall not use production approval authority or irreversible external systems without exact control.

Synthetic failures shall be correlated with internal telemetry before severity is assigned. A test harness defect shall not be represented as customer outage.

Synthetic data and credentials shall follow secrets, retention, and tenant-isolation controls.

### User-Journey Monitoring

Critical product journeys shall have defined entry, successful outcome, failure categories, dependencies, latency, and validation requirements.

Journeys may include authenticated request intake, plan preparation, approval, constrained execution, result validation, evidence retrieval, administrative configuration, and recovery access.

Monitoring shall distinguish user waiting from processing, provider latency, approval delay, queueing, validation, and delivery.

Journey completion shall not be inferred solely from a final HTTP response if authoritative state or validation is pending.

### Canonical Flow Monitoring

Monitoring shall evaluate the twelve canonical operational stages and their waiting, failure, retry, rejection, and completion states without collapsing authority boundaries.

Material conditions include identity verification failure, tenant mismatch, Immutable Context creation failure, reasoning unavailability, policy error, risk-classification delay, approval backlog, capability issuance error, Tool Gateway ambiguity, Validation Pipeline backlog, rejected results, and delivery failure.

Audit Engine and Evidence Chain health apply continuously across all stages. Evidence backlog or append failure shall not be monitored only after execution.

Stage monitoring shall use canonical state rather than inferred trace order where the two differ.

### Identity and Access Monitoring

Monitoring shall detect authentication failure patterns, privileged access, unusual elevation, dormant-account use, recovery-factor use, impossible or anomalous access where reliable, credential expiry, certificate expiry, token-validation failure, and authorization-denial changes.

An anomaly is not proof of compromise. Response shall consider identity assurance, device, service, tenant, environment, time, and supporting evidence.

Monitoring shall not expose authentication secrets or personal behavior beyond the approved purpose. Security monitoring access shall be restricted.

Privileged access monitoring shall integrate with the Audit Engine and Incident Response while preserving legal and human-review requirements.

### Policy Engine Monitoring

Policy Engine monitoring shall include availability, latency, evaluation volume, outcome categories, rule and bundle version, error, timeout, cache freshness, dependency state, and deny/allow distribution within privacy-safe bounds.

A sudden change in outcomes may indicate release, policy, traffic, tenant, or attack behavior and requires contextual investigation.

Monitoring shall not expose sensitive policy logic or allow telemetry to modify policy. A monitoring rule cannot override a deterministic Policy Engine decision.

Policy Engine error or unavailable state shall trigger the defined fail-safe behavior rather than default allow.

### Approval Engine Monitoring

Approval monitoring shall cover queue size and age, expiry, assignment, escalation, duplicate requests, decision latency, unavailable approvers, high-risk backlog, and integrity failures.

Human productivity metrics shall be minimized and shall not become intrusive personnel surveillance. The purpose is process safety and service reliability.

Monitoring shall distinguish waiting for required approval from system latency. Approval timeout shall not become implicit approval.

Operational alerts shall reference canonical approval records without duplicating protected identity unnecessarily.

### Model and Provider Monitoring

Model monitoring shall cover approved provider and model availability, latency, token or compute use, cost, error categories, routing, fallback, rate limits, safety outcomes, response truncation, configuration, and supported-region state.

Model output quality, confidence, drift, and validation outcomes shall use Section 6 semantics. Provider success and low latency do not establish correctness.

Fallback alerts shall verify that selection remained within approved privacy, residency, customer, release, and model boundaries.

Raw prompts, responses, reasoning content, embeddings, or customer documents shall not be copied into alerts by default.

### Tool Gateway Monitoring

Tool Gateway monitoring shall cover connector availability, destination health, credential expiry, capability denial, rate limit, queue age, timeout, ambiguous outcome, retry, reconciliation, tenant fairness, and external side-effect failures.

Direct governed action outside the Tool Gateway shall generate a high-priority security condition where detectable.

An external success code is not proof of intended effect. Alerts shall distinguish confirmed failure, rejected action, ambiguous result, duplicate protection, and validation rejection.

Monitoring-triggered connector control shall remain within an approved Response Profile and current policy.

### Validation Pipeline Monitoring

Validation monitoring shall cover throughput, backlog, oldest age, outcome categories, rule version, dependency health, evidence availability, timeout, incomplete state, and independent-service availability.

Unavailable or saturated validation shall not cause results to be accepted by default. Pending or constrained outcomes shall remain visible.

A high rejection rate may indicate source defects, provider change, attack, policy change, or validator defect. Monitoring shall not assume the cause.

Monitoring the Validation Pipeline is not equivalent to performing validation.

### Audit Engine and Evidence Chain Monitoring

Monitoring shall cover Audit Engine ingestion, buffer depth, durable append latency, ordering, duplication, storage, export, access anomalies, and retention operations.

Evidence Chain monitoring shall cover chain construction, verification, missing links, signing or sealing, key availability, evidence backlog, export, retention, and independent verification.

Audit and Evidence conditions shall have protected capacity and high-priority routing. Ordinary service overload shall not silence them.

A healthy monitor does not prove audit or evidence completeness. Canonical verification remains separate.

### Infrastructure Monitoring

Compute, orchestration, containers, nodes, storage, networking, DNS, certificates, queues, registries, load balancers, autoscalers, backups, restores, and recovery infrastructure shall be monitored according to risk.

Kubernetes monitoring may use resource and full metrics pipelines, system-component metrics, events, and provider signals. Collection availability, permissions, metric stability, and version shall be governed.

Infrastructure monitoring shall distinguish resource pressure from service impact. High CPU is not inherently an incident; low CPU is not proof of health.

Provider-native alarms are inputs and shall be normalized, owned, tested, and correlated with ILAIOS outcomes.

### Capacity and Saturation Monitoring

Monitoring shall cover demand, admission, rejected work, queue age, concurrency, resource use, headroom, provider quotas, database connections, storage growth, network limits, model capacity, validation capacity, and evidence capacity.

Forecast and trend conditions shall provide sufficient lead time for non-emergency capacity action. Thresholds shall account for failover and maintenance headroom.

Autoscaler activity, desired capacity, actual capacity, provisioning delay, failures, oscillation, and maximum limits shall be monitored under Section 7.7.

Capacity alarms shall not trigger unbounded automatic spend or unsafe downscaling.

### Security Continuous Monitoring

Security monitoring shall maintain ongoing awareness of assets, identities, vulnerabilities, threats, control status, configuration, privilege, data movement, network exposure, and incident indicators.

Coverage shall include authentication, authorization, secrets, keys, encryption, tenant boundaries, public endpoints, egress, supply chain, workloads, storage, backups, logging, Audit Engine, and Evidence Chain.

Security detection rules shall have threat rationale, data sources, assumptions, severity, response, false-positive handling, coverage gaps, and validation.

Monitoring supports risk management but does not automatically establish compliance, breach, attacker identity, or legal consequence.

### Vulnerability and Support-State Monitoring

Monitoring shall track vulnerabilities, exploitability, known exploitation, fix availability, base images, dependencies, operating systems, clusters, databases, providers, certificates, algorithms, and end-of-support dates.

Inventory linkage shall identify affected releases, environments, tenants, images, nodes, artifacts, and support lines.

Scanner severity is an input. Risk disposition shall consider reachability, privilege, data, tenant impact, compensating controls, and current threat intelligence.

Exceptions shall expire and alert before expiry. Unsupported technology shall not remain unnoticed through missing inventory.

### Backup, Recovery, and Disaster-Recovery Monitoring

Monitoring shall cover backup completion, age, scope, immutability, replication, key availability, capacity, retention, restore-test status, RPO, RTO, and failed recovery dependencies.

Backup job success is not recovery acceptance. Restore tests and Validation Pipeline outcomes remain distinct.

Disaster-recovery readiness shall include standby environment eligibility, data lag, routes, certificates, identities, keys, Tool Gateway connectors, Audit Engine, Evidence Chain, and capacity.

Dormant recovery paths shall not be considered healthy solely because no failure has been reported.

### Change and Release Monitoring

Deployments, configuration, policy, model, provider, schema, network, storage, autoscaling, observability, monitoring, and logging changes shall produce attributable change markers.

Monitoring shall compare relevant indicators before, during, and after rollout. Canary, progressive, and full release stages shall remain distinguishable.

Automatic rollback conditions shall be bounded and validated. Rollback shall not restore revoked authority, vulnerable artifacts, incompatible schemas, or ineligible provider configuration.

Change correlation suggests association but does not prove root cause. Investigation remains required.

### Cost Monitoring

Monitoring shall cover compute, accelerator, model, storage, network transfer, observability, backup, validation, evidence, provider, and support costs within approved budgets.

Cost conditions shall identify service, environment, provider, region, release, operation, and privacy-safe tenant scope where feasible.

Anomalous spend may indicate legitimate growth, retry storm, abuse, misconfiguration, provider pricing, or instrumentation defect. Automated cost response shall preserve service and security obligations.

Cost pressure shall not justify suppressing mandatory validation, Audit Engine, Evidence Chain, security, privacy, or tenant controls.

### Customer-Impact Monitoring

Customer-impact conditions shall use actual product and service semantics rather than infrastructure symptoms alone. Impact shall identify affected tenants, regions, functions, releases, and time within privacy boundaries.

Shared-service failure does not imply every tenant is affected. Conversely, aggregate success can hide a single tenant outage.

Customer-specific monitoring and communication shall prevent cross-tenant disclosure. Support and status views shall show only authorized scope.

Impact estimates shall be labeled as preliminary until validated. Monitoring shall not create unverified contractual or regulatory statements.

### Customer-Facing Status

Public or customer status communication shall use an approved incident and communication process, not automatic publication of raw alerts.

Status components, regions, products, severity, start time, update cadence, and resolution shall be accurate, privacy-safe, and attributable.

A monitoring alert may propose a status change, but accountable authority shall approve publication where policy requires it.

Resolved status shall follow verified service recovery and communication review, not merely alert disappearance.

### Multi-Region Monitoring

Monitoring shall preserve region, authority, data, release, provider, and failover context. Global aggregates shall not hide regional failure.

Regional monitoring paths should remain available during central or inter-region failure. Centralized monitoring shall not become the sole unmonitored dependency.

Failover conditions shall verify target region eligibility, data readiness, identity, keys, network, storage, Tool Gateway, validation, audit, evidence, and capacity.

Split-brain and asymmetric monitoring shall be detected. Each region shall not independently declare global authority without the approved recovery model.

### Customer-Controlled, Hybrid, and Isolated Monitoring

Deployment Profiles shall define which signals ILAIOS receives, which remain customer-local, who owns alerts, how escalation occurs, and what support claims are possible.

Customer-managed monitors and routes shall be verified where the contract assigns responsibility. Missing customer configuration shall not be represented as an ILAIOS-completed control.

Hybrid link loss shall preserve local monitoring and a bounded way to report or retrieve critical conditions. Isolated environments require local time, routing, retention, and response capability.

Where ILAIOS cannot observe a control, the limitation, evidence requirement, and customer responsibility shall be explicit.

### Monitoring the Monitoring System

The monitoring system shall monitor its own rule evaluation, data source freshness, queue, scheduler, notification delivery, storage, configuration, replicas, permissions, certificates, routes, integrations, time, and capacity.

Independent heartbeat or synthetic paths shall detect failure of the primary monitoring path. One dashboard backed by the same failed system is insufficient.

Rule load failure, configuration rejection, evaluation delay, notification failure, silence expansion, inhibition error, and missing owner shall create actionable conditions.

Monitoring-system failure shall not be represented as healthy service. Critical services shall have a fallback awareness and escalation mechanism appropriate to the profile.

### Monitoring Coverage

Coverage shall map critical services, flows, dependencies, controls, risks, data sources, alerts, owners, runbooks, and response profiles.

Coverage shall be assessed for availability, performance, capacity, security, privacy, tenant, policy, approval, Tool Gateway, validation, audit, evidence, backup, recovery, and customer impact.

Coverage percentage shall not be reported without a defined denominator and criticality weighting. Many low-value rules do not compensate for one missing critical control.

Known gaps shall have an owner, risk, compensating control, target date, and customer or support limitation where relevant.

### Monitoring Data Quality

Monitoring shall inherit signal quality from Section 7.8 and add rule-evaluation, threshold, state, routing, and notification quality.

Every material alert shall expose signal freshness, evaluation time, rule version, pending duration, last successful evaluation, and missing-data behavior.

Rule and objective results shall be reproducible from retained inputs or sufficiently evidenced summaries according to the profile.

Data-quality failure shall not silently evaluate to healthy. Unknown, stale, partial, or sampled conditions shall remain explicit.

### Monitoring Privacy and Tenant Isolation

Alerts, notifications, tickets, status pages, runbooks, dashboards, and exports shall minimize personal, customer, model, repository, security, and infrastructure data.

Tenant isolation shall cover rule evaluation, labels, grouping, routing, notifications, silences, dashboards, incident tools, exports, storage, and support access.

One tenant shall not infer another tenant's load, outage, provider, region, connector, or contract from shared monitoring interfaces.

Notification systems may forward data outside the primary platform and therefore require approved recipients, encryption, retention, deletion, and contractual controls.

### Monitoring Security

Monitoring configuration, objectives, thresholds, silences, inhibition, routes, response profiles, and access are security-sensitive assets.

Administrative access shall use strong authentication, least privilege, attributable elevation, logging, review, and protected recovery.

Attackers may disable alerts, create noise, manipulate signals, poison baselines, change routes, or trigger automated response. Integrity, change control, separation, and anomaly monitoring shall address these risks.

Monitoring interfaces shall treat labels, annotations, queries, templates, links, and telemetry as untrusted content and prevent injection or credential disclosure.

### Retention and Historical Analysis

Alert state, objective results, acknowledgements, silences, routes, response actions, and monitoring changes shall follow an approved record-class-specific retention schedule. Retention is not indefinite by default.

Historical data shall support trend, objective calculation, incident review, capacity planning, alert quality, audit, evidence, and customer commitments within privacy and minimization constraints.

Changing a rule or objective shall preserve enough version history to interpret past results. Recalculated history shall be identified as recalculated rather than original evaluation.

Raw observability-signal retention remains governed by Section 7.8 and logs by Section 7.10.

### Incident Response Integration

Alerts shall enter Incident Response through a defined triage and handoff process. Alert identity, source, time, severity, scope, evidence, owner, and uncertainty shall be preserved.

Multiple alerts may map to one incident, and one alert may never become an incident. The mapping shall be explicit.

Incident command may change monitoring, sampling, severity, routing, or response within authorized emergency procedures. Changes shall be time-bounded and reviewed.

Incident resolution shall not automatically delete or rewrite alert history. Post-incident review shall improve coverage, rules, runbooks, and response.

### Independent Validation

The Validation Pipeline shall independently verify monitoring requirements appropriate to the gate. Validation may test indicators, objectives, conditions, pending periods, missing-data behavior, severity, routing, deduplication, inhibition, silences, runbooks, responses, tenant isolation, and monitoring-system failure.

Rule evaluation and alert delivery shall be tested with controlled signals. Both expected firing and expected non-firing behavior shall be verified.

The monitoring system shall not be the sole validator of its own correctness. Configuration loaded successfully is not proof that the intended alert will reach the right owner.

Monitoring validation does not validate the underlying business outcome. Canonical functional, security, and result validation remain separate.

### Audit Engine and Evidence Chain Integration

The Audit Engine shall record material Monitoring Profile approvals, objective changes, critical rule changes, severity changes, routing changes, silences, inhibition changes, automated responses, privileged access, customer-status decisions, monitoring outages, and incident handoff.

The Evidence Chain shall bind records required to demonstrate which signals, rule version, condition, severity, owner, response, validation, and monitoring limitations applied to a material event or claim.

Routine high-volume evaluations may be summarized under an approved evidence model, but material state transitions and control changes shall remain attributable.

Audit Engine and Evidence Chain controls operate continuously and are not replaced by alert history, monitoring databases, notification channels, status pages, or provider alarms.

### Change and ADR Governance

Monitoring changes shall follow Section 5.7 and include purpose, affected services, indicators, objectives, thresholds, data quality, severity, routing, tenant, privacy, response, customer commitments, validation, rollout, and rollback.

Rules and objectives shall be version-controlled or equivalently governed. Direct production edits are prohibited for ordinary operation.

Architecture-significant changes to global monitoring, automated high-impact response, cross-tenant aggregation, customer-status automation, security monitoring, or Audit/Evidence integration require an authorized ADR.

Temporary emergency rules and silences shall have expiry and retrospective review. They shall not become permanent through inaction.

### Governance and Responsibilities

Product authority defines customer-visible reliability and product claims. Architecture authority defines monitoring boundaries and architecture-significant decisions. Reliability and platform functions own service objectives, rule quality, routing, monitoring infrastructure, and operational improvement.

Security owns security-monitoring requirements and escalation. Privacy and compliance functions define monitoring data use, access, retention, transfer, and regulatory integration within their authority. Service owners own indicators, alerts, and runbooks for their services.

Incident command owns incident coordination after handoff. Customer and provider responsibilities follow the Deployment Profile and contract.

No monitoring backend, alert manager, anomaly system, provider, dashboard, customer preference, sales commitment, or model output may unilaterally redefine business authority, legal obligations, service agreements, or canonical architecture.

### Single-Maintainer Bootstrap Profile

During a registered Single-Maintainer Bootstrap Profile, one authorized maintainer may temporarily own multiple monitoring roles where independent personnel are unavailable. The absence of independent review and on-call redundancy shall be recorded and shall not be represented as Enterprise continuity.

The bootstrap profile shall maintain organizational ownership, strong authentication, protected recovery factors, version-controlled rules, mandatory rule tests, bounded automated response, exact change and silence attribution, independent notification where feasible, protected Audit and Evidence integration, periodic review, and a dated exit plan.

High-impact changes to security monitoring, tenant alerts, customer status, Tool Gateway response, Audit Engine or Evidence Chain monitoring, public service objectives, and automated production containment shall receive qualified external review before affecting a Stable release, production environment, or Enterprise operating profile; otherwise they shall remain constrained.

The bootstrap profile shall not claim continuous two-person coverage or independent administration. A second competent responder and appropriate separation shall be added when the Enterprise Profile becomes applicable. Single-maintainer operation shall not become permanent through inaction.

### Quality Gates

Before a Monitoring Profile or material change becomes eligible, the applicable gates shall verify:

- owner, service, criticality, Deployment Profile, environment, region, release, tenant, and support scope;
- critical journeys, canonical stages, dependencies, failure modes, and protected controls;
- service-level indicators with exact numerator, denominator, unit, scope, source, window, and quality;
- evidence-backed objectives, error-budget semantics, exclusions, and customer-commitment boundaries;
- conditions, thresholds, anomalies, evaluation, pending, recovery, and missing-data behavior;
- stable alert identity, bounded labels, severity, routing, ownership, escalation, and runbooks;
- safe deduplication, grouping, inhibition, silences, maintenance, and acknowledgement;
- deterministic bounded automated response with Tool Gateway and human-approval controls;
- black-box, white-box, synthetic, user-journey, security, capacity, backup, recovery, and monitoring-system coverage;
- privacy, tenant isolation, security, residency, retention, and access;
- controlled rule, objective, route, response, and customer-status change;
- positive and negative independent Validation Pipeline tests;
- required Audit Engine and Evidence Chain records; and
- exception ownership, scope, expiry, monitoring, and residual-risk acceptance.

No single green dashboard, active alert, successful notification, rule test, objective report, provider status, or monitoring-platform health state shall satisfy the complete gate.

### Prohibited Practices

The following practices are prohibited unless an explicitly defined canonical exception applies:

- treating alerts, anomalies, objectives, dashboards, or monitoring systems as business authority or independent validation;
- conflating Monitoring with Observability, Logging, Audit, Evidence, Validation, Incident Response, or the Defect Lifecycle;
- defining objectives without exact indicators, scope, windows, data quality, and ownership;
- using error budget as permission to violate security, privacy, policy, approval, validation, evidence, safety, or law;
- treating missing or stale monitoring data as healthy by default;
- using unbounded alert labels, customer data, prompts, model outputs, secrets, or personal data in alerts;
- routing protected alert content to unauthorized recipients or channels;
- creating alerts without owners, escalation, or actionable response;
- using broad, indefinite, or unaudited silences and inhibition;
- allowing maintenance suppression to hide unrelated security, tenant, data, audit, or evidence failures;
- allowing anomaly systems or model recommendations to execute high-impact actions without deterministic policy and required approval;
- permitting monitoring-triggered governed external action outside the Tool Gateway;
- accepting results, approvals, or capabilities based on alert state;
- treating provider alarms or Kubernetes metrics as complete service monitoring;
- allowing monitoring failure to be represented as normal service;
- publishing customer status directly from unverified raw alerts where accountable review is required;
- making unreviewed direct production rule, route, severity, or response changes;
- allowing emergency rules, silences, or elevated response to become permanent through inaction;
- representing bootstrap self-review and single-person coverage as independent Enterprise assurance; or
- giving any alert engine, anomaly service, provider, dashboard, notification system, customer preference, sales commitment, or engineering convenience architectural authority.

### Non-Goals

This section does not mandate a specific metrics engine, alert manager, query language, status page, notification service, synthetic platform, anomaly system, or incident-routing product.

It does not redefine Observability in Section 7.8, detailed Logging in Section 7.10, Incident Response in Section 3.9, Defect Lifecycle in Section 5.4, or Continuous Improvement in Section 5.8.

It does not promise that every failure, attack, customer impact, model-quality problem, or provider defect can be detected before consequence. Coverage and limitations shall be represented honestly.

It does not make monitoring a substitute for sound architecture, deterministic policy, accountable approval, Tool Gateway mediation, independent validation, canonical audit, Evidence Chain, testing, recovery, or human judgment.

### Conformance Requirements

An implementation conforms to this section only when it demonstrates that:

- every production service and critical control is governed by an approved Monitoring Profile;
- Monitoring remains distinct from Observability, Logging, Audit, Evidence, Validation, Incident Response, and Defect Lifecycle;
- indicators, objectives, error budgets, conditions, thresholds, anomalies, and missing-data behavior are exact and governed;
- alerts have stable identity, bounded labels, severity, ownership, routing, escalation, runbooks, and history;
- deduplication, grouping, inhibition, silences, maintenance, and acknowledgement preserve truth and scope;
- automated response is deterministic, least-privilege, bounded, attributable, and subject to Tool Gateway and approval controls;
- black-box, white-box, synthetic, user-journey, canonical-flow, security, capacity, infrastructure, backup, recovery, and cost monitoring are applied according to risk;
- Policy Engine, Approval Engine, Model Gateway, Tool Gateway, Validation Pipeline, Audit Engine, and Evidence Chain health are monitored without transferring authority;
- monitoring coverage, signal quality, alert quality, monitoring-system health, and known gaps are assessed continuously;
- privacy, tenant isolation, residency, access, retention, and notification-channel security are effective;
- change, release, customer impact, customer status, incident handoff, and recovery are governed;
- the Validation Pipeline independently verifies monitoring controls and does not accept business results through alert state;
- Audit Engine and Evidence Chain controls operate continuously and remain canonical;
- bootstrap limitations remain explicit, constrained, temporary, and subject to dated exit criteria; and
- architecture-significant monitoring decisions require an authorized ADR.

### Canonical Invariants

The following invariants are binding:

- monitoring evaluates signals but does not create ILAIOS business authority;
- an alert is an operational condition, not policy permission, approval, capability, validation, incident cause, or legal conclusion;
- Monitoring, Observability, Logging, Audit, Evidence, Validation, Incident Response, and Defect Lifecycle remain distinct;
- unknown, stale, sampled, partial, and missing monitoring data are not represented as healthy certainty;
- every actionable alert has bounded identity, owner, severity, routing, escalation, and response guidance;
- error budgets never waive non-waivable security, privacy, tenant, policy, approval, validation, audit, evidence, safety, or legal controls;
- silences and inhibition suppress notification, not truth, collection, evidence, or obligation;
- automated response remains deterministic, bounded, attributable, and separately authorized;
- the deterministic Policy Engine remains within the ILAIOS Control Plane;
- the Approval Engine remains the accountable approval authority;
- every governed external action remains mediated by the Tool Gateway under constrained capability;
- the Validation Pipeline remains independent and alert state does not become acceptance;
- Audit Engine and Evidence Chain controls operate continuously and are not replaced by alerts, objectives, dashboards, status pages, or provider alarms;
- monitoring systems monitor their own health, rules, data, routes, and notification paths;
- tenant isolation covers evaluation, labels, grouping, routing, notification, dashboards, status, and history;
- customer status and contractual claims use accountable approved processes;
- monitoring limitations and coverage gaps are represented honestly;
- bootstrap operation does not imply independent Enterprise continuity or assurance; and
- architecture-significant monitoring decisions require an authorized ADR.

A Monitoring implementation is non-conformant if it treats alerts, objectives, anomalies, dashboards, provider status, or monitoring tools as authority or validation; merges Monitoring with Observability, Logging, Audit, Evidence, Incident Response, or Defect Lifecycle; defines ambiguous indicators or unsupported objectives; treats missing data as healthy; uses unowned, unrouteable, unbounded, or privacy-unsafe alerts; hides conditions through broad silence, inhibition, maintenance, or rule deletion; permits automated response to bypass deterministic policy, required approval, or Tool Gateway; accepts results based on alert state; fails to monitor Validation, Audit, Evidence, monitoring infrastructure, or critical dependencies; misrepresents customer impact, status, coverage, or bootstrap continuity; or gives any rule engine, alert manager, anomaly detector, status page, notification provider, model output, customer preference, sales commitment, or engineering convenience architectural authority.

## 7.10 Logging

### Purpose and Canonical Role

Logging defines how ILAIOS creates, structures, protects, transports, stores, accesses, retains, and disposes of operational event records across the platform and its supported deployment models. It establishes a governed record of technical behavior for diagnosis, security detection, reliability engineering, capacity analysis, incident response, support, and controlled investigation without converting ordinary operational records into business authority, canonical audit records, or proof of successful execution.

A log record describes an observed event reported by a source. It may be accurate, incomplete, duplicated, delayed, malformed, sampled, reordered, or unavailable. Collection in a central platform improves accessibility but does not by itself prove origin, completeness, chronology, authenticity, or absence of tampering. Hashing a log record can protect a known representation but does not prove that every material event was emitted or collected.

The deterministic Policy Engine remains the authority for policy evaluation. The Approval Engine remains the accountable approval authority. Governed external action remains mediated by the Tool Gateway under constrained capability. The Validation Pipeline independently assesses results. The Audit Engine creates canonical attributable audit records, and the Evidence Chain binds material evidence. Logging supports those components but does not replace or silently redefine any of them.

Audit Engine and Evidence Chain controls operate continuously across material lifecycle events. A logging failure shall be visible and treated according to risk, but ordinary logging availability shall not be represented as proof that audit or evidence obligations were satisfied.

### Scope

This section applies to application, service, platform, runtime, operating-system, container, orchestration, network, storage, database, identity, security, policy, approval, model-access, Tool Gateway, validation, audit-support, evidence-support, deployment, release, backup, recovery, provider, administrative, and customer-support logging.

It covers Logging Profiles; event taxonomy; structured records; schemas; timestamps; severity; identity; correlation; exception handling; safe message construction; secret, personal-data, and customer-content controls; tenant isolation; collection; transport; buffering; backpressure; loss management; rotation; normalization; enrichment; routing; storage; indexing; querying; export; retention; legal hold; deletion; integrity; availability; recovery; access; investigation; cost; quality; governance; validation; and conformance.

Section 7.8 defines Observability across logs, metrics, traces, events, profiles, and topology. Section 7.9 defines Monitoring conditions, objectives, alerts, and responses. Section 2.10 defines the canonical Audit Architecture. Section 2.9 defines the Evidence Chain. Section 2.8 defines the Validation Pipeline. Section 3.9 defines Incident Response. This section governs operational logging while preserving those boundaries.

### Logging and Related Capability Boundaries

The following capabilities are distinct:

**Logging** emits and manages detailed records of technical and operational events.

**Observability** correlates governed signals so that system state and behavior can be inferred.

**Monitoring** evaluates selected signals against explicit expectations and creates conditions, alerts, escalations, or bounded responses.

**Audit** creates canonical attributable records of authority, security, governance, and lifecycle events under the Audit Architecture.

**Evidence** binds material artifacts and events required to prove, verify, or examine a governed outcome.

**Validation** independently determines whether a result, control, state, or artifact satisfies accepted criteria.

**Incident Response** governs investigation, containment, eradication, recovery, communication, and review when an event or condition becomes an incident.

An application log may help investigate an approval, policy evaluation, tool invocation, validation result, or evidence event. It is not the canonical approval, policy decision, execution authorization, validation record, or evidence object unless the governing architecture explicitly promotes and validates it through the relevant canonical component.

A log query result shall not grant permission, approve a change, accept a task, close a defect, declare compliance, establish legal fact, or modify architecture. Any action arising from log analysis must pass through the applicable policy, approval, capability, Tool Gateway, validation, audit, and evidence controls.

### Technology Independence and Portability

No logging library, framework, collector, transport, storage engine, search platform, analytics product, cloud service, provider-native facility, schema registry, or query language is canonical by default.

ILAIOS shall define portable event semantics independently of a specific vendor. Implementations may map canonical fields to an approved open telemetry model or another documented representation when meaning, type, scope, ordering limitations, security, and lifecycle controls remain intact.

New systems should prefer structured event emission and portable schemas. Existing text logs may be collected through controlled parsing, but parsing assumptions, ambiguity, loss, multiline behavior, timestamp behavior, and schema coverage shall be documented and validated.

Provider replacement shall preserve required event classes, correlation, access, retention, export, deletion, integrity, and investigation capability. Proprietary enrichment or detection may supplement canonical records but shall not become the only representation of a material event without an approved portability and continuity treatment.

Technology-specific logging decisions that materially affect tenant isolation, privacy, residency, availability, integrity, evidence, operational continuity, or provider independence require an authorized Architecture Decision Record.

### Strategic Objectives

Logging shall:

- provide timely, structured, attributable, and searchable records for approved operational and security purposes;
- preserve explicit boundaries between operational logs, canonical audit records, evidence, validation, monitoring, and authority;
- support end-to-end correlation across request, tenant, task, policy, approval, model, tool, validation, release, deployment, and incident contexts;
- minimize secrets, credentials, personal data, customer content, raw prompts, raw model outputs, and unnecessary payloads;
- protect tenant isolation and prevent cross-tenant inference through records, indexes, queries, exports, routes, and support workflows;
- detect and expose missing, malformed, delayed, duplicated, dropped, or unauthorized log records;
- support managed, customer-controlled, hybrid, isolated, multi-region, and constrained Deployment Profiles;
- remain usable during degradation, incident, failover, restoration, and forensic investigation;
- preserve lawful record-class-specific retention, legal hold, deletion, residency, and access requirements;
- provide bounded cost and cardinality without sampling away mandatory security, audit-support, or evidence-support events;
- support controlled debugging without creating permanent overcollection or bypassing privacy and security controls;
- validate event schemas, redaction, collection paths, access policies, retention, deletion, integrity, and recovery;
- maintain honest visibility into coverage gaps, clock uncertainty, source limitations, provider limitations, and bootstrap constraints; and
- remain implementation-independent except where an accepted product decision requires a specific deployment capability.

### Canonical Logging Domain Model

The following terms are distinct:

**Logging Profile.** The approved event classes, fields, schemas, levels, routes, retention classes, access rules, privacy controls, reliability requirements, tests, and responsibilities for an exact service, environment, Deployment Profile, tenant model, region, release, and support scope.

**Log Event.** An occurrence at a source that is eligible for recording under a Logging Profile.

**Log Record.** The structured or controlled textual representation emitted for a Log Event.

**Event Class.** A stable semantic category such as authentication, authorization, configuration, execution, validation, security, lifecycle, dependency, or diagnostic activity.

**Event Code.** A stable machine-readable identifier for a defined event meaning. Message text may change without changing the Event Code when semantics remain equivalent.

**Emitter.** The component, workload, runtime, device, provider, or controlled integration that creates a Log Record.

**Collector.** A component that receives, buffers, transforms, enriches, routes, or exports records without becoming their original emitter.

**Logging Pipeline.** The governed path from emission through collection, normalization, protection, transport, storage, access, retention, and disposal.

**Log Sink.** An approved destination for a defined record class and purpose. A sink may support search, archive, security analysis, customer-controlled export, or another bounded function.

**Severity.** The declared technical importance of an event according to an approved level model. Severity is not incident severity, defect priority, business impact, or legal classification.

**Correlation Reference.** A non-secret identifier that links related records or telemetry while preserving tenant, privacy, and authorization boundaries.

**Redaction Policy.** The approved rules and controls for excluding, masking, tokenizing, hashing, truncating, or otherwise protecting sensitive fields before or during log processing.

**Retention Class.** The record-class-specific schedule governing active retention, archival, legal hold, deletion, and review.

**Logging Coverage Gap.** A known or detected absence, degradation, ambiguity, delay, or loss in required event visibility.

These terms shall not be collapsed. A Log Record is not an Alert Instance, Audit Record, Evidence Object, Validation Result, Incident, or Defect merely because a system links them.

### Logging Profiles

Every production service, security-relevant component, and critical platform dependency shall have an approved Logging Profile proportionate to its risk and Deployment Profile.

The profile shall define:

- service, component, owner, criticality, environment, region, release, tenant model, and data classification;
- required Event Classes, Event Codes, levels, field schemas, versioning, and compatibility rules;
- operational, security, support, compliance, and forensic purposes;
- fields prohibited by default and any narrowly approved sensitive-field exceptions;
- correlation identifiers and their propagation, rotation, exposure, and tenant constraints;
- emission, collection, normalization, enrichment, routing, buffering, retry, and failure behavior;
- transport authentication, encryption, integrity, endpoint authorization, and certificate or key lifecycle;
- storage, index, query, export, residency, backup, recovery, retention, legal hold, and deletion behavior;
- access roles, approval requirements, support boundaries, break-glass conditions, and monitoring;
- volume, rate, record-size, cardinality, multiline, encoding, rotation, and capacity limits;
- sampling, suppression, deduplication, and rate-limiting rules, including protected event classes that shall not be discarded;
- tests for schema, redaction, injection resistance, loss detection, tenant isolation, access, retention, deletion, restoration, and failover;
- known limitations, provider dependencies, customer responsibilities, residual risk, and exit criteria; and
- Audit Engine and Evidence Chain integration for material logging-control events.

A service shall not enter an unrestricted production profile without an accepted Logging Profile or an approved, time-bounded exception that identifies the missing coverage and constrains the affected capability.

Profiles shall be versioned. A change to an Event Code meaning, sensitive-data treatment, tenant scope, retention class, mandatory field, routing rule, or protected event class is a governed change and shall not be introduced as an undocumented configuration adjustment.

### Event Taxonomy

The canonical event taxonomy shall support at least the following classes where applicable:

- service lifecycle, startup, shutdown, readiness, degradation, and recovery;
- request intake, parsing, routing, rejection, timeout, cancellation, and completion;
- identity authentication, session, token, credential, federation, recovery, and break-glass events;
- authorization requests, decisions, denials, capability issuance, capability use, expiry, and revocation;
- tenant-context creation, binding, validation, routing, isolation, and rejection;
- policy evaluation, policy-version selection, deterministic result, reason code, and failure;
- approval request, decision, expiry, withdrawal, delegation, escalation, and invalidation;
- model selection, provider routing, invocation state, timeout, fallback, refusal, and bounded usage metadata;
- plan, recommendation, and context-processing lifecycle without recording sensitive content by default;
- Tool Gateway request, capability check, dispatch, external-effect status, reconciliation, and failure;
- Validation Pipeline intake, check, result, rejection, uncertainty, and coverage limitation;
- Audit Engine and Evidence Chain service health, write status, verification, gap, and recovery;
- data access, mutation, deletion, export, retention, legal hold, and administrative override;
- secret and key administration without recording secret or key material;
- build, test, artifact, signing, release, deployment, rollback, configuration, and migration;
- container, orchestration, network, storage, database, queue, cache, and dependency behavior;
- security detection, integrity failure, privilege change, control bypass attempt, abuse, and rate-limit enforcement;
- backup, restore, failover, failback, disaster recovery, and continuity exercise;
- observability, monitoring, logging-pipeline, collection, transport, storage, and query-system health;
- customer-support access, diagnostic session, approved export, and support-action closure; and
- incident, defect, change, exception, risk-treatment, and conformance lifecycle references.

Event taxonomies shall describe stable semantic meaning, not product-specific screen labels. One event may belong to more than one approved class, but it shall retain one unambiguous primary Event Code and source identity.

Routine successful events and exceptional failures shall remain distinguishable. A generic message such as “operation failed” is insufficient for a material control path when a stable reason code and bounded state can be emitted safely.

### Structured Record Requirements

Machine-generated records shall be structured by default. Human-readable text may accompany structured fields but shall not be the sole source of material meaning.

Each applicable record shall include:

- event timestamp and timestamp precision;
- observation or collection timestamp where distinct;
- globally or source-locally unique event identifier according to the profile;
- Event Code, Event Class, schema name, and schema version;
- severity and outcome;
- emitter identity, service, component, runtime, instance, release, environment, region, and Deployment Profile as applicable;
- tenant-safe reference or explicit non-tenant scope;
- request, trace, span, task, action, approval, validation, audit, evidence, change, release, deployment, or incident correlation references as applicable;
- actor class and pseudonymous or approved subject reference where attribution is required;
- target class and approved target reference;
- operation, state transition, reason code, failure class, retry status, and external-effect state as applicable;
- data classification, retention class, redaction status, and source trust classification where required;
- collector, transformation, route, and ingestion metadata when added downstream; and
- indicators of sampling, truncation, partial capture, parse failure, enrichment failure, or clock uncertainty.

Field names, types, permitted values, null semantics, units, maximum lengths, normalization rules, and privacy classifications shall be defined in a versioned schema.

Raw request bodies, response bodies, prompts, model outputs, files, database rows, authorization tokens, secrets, cryptographic key material, cookies, session identifiers, and customer content shall not be included by default. A business identifier shall be logged only when necessary for an approved purpose and protected according to classification.

### Schema Governance and Compatibility

Logging schemas are governed interfaces. They shall have accountable ownership, machine-readable definitions where practical, compatibility tests, lifecycle status, and change history.

Additive optional fields may be introduced compatibly when consumers tolerate absence and unknown fields. Removal, rename, type change, semantic change, required-field introduction, enum narrowing, identifier format change, or retention-class change requires explicit compatibility treatment.

Event Codes shall not be silently reused for different semantics. Deprecated codes shall have a transition plan and an approved retention period sufficient for dependent detection, search, audit-support, and customer integration rules to migrate.

Collectors may normalize heterogeneous sources into a canonical envelope. The original source identity and transformation history shall remain attributable. Normalization shall not invent precision, identity, tenant, outcome, or completeness that the source did not provide.

Schema registries, semantic-convention catalogs, or code generation may support consistency but do not replace review. Vendor-defined fields shall be mapped explicitly and shall not override canonical meanings.

### Event Identity, Deduplication, and Idempotency

Event identifiers shall support detection of duplicates without creating a false claim of global uniqueness. The identity scope and generation method shall be documented.

Collectors and sinks may retry delivery. At-least-once transport may create duplicates; at-most-once transport may lose records. The Logging Profile shall declare delivery semantics and how consumers detect or tolerate duplication and loss.

Deduplication shall preserve a count, first-seen time, last-seen time, source set, and rule identity where removal of duplicates could affect investigation. It shall not erase evidence of repeated security attempts or independent occurrences that merely share message text.

An idempotency key used for business execution shall not automatically become a public log identifier. Correlation must preserve security and privacy boundaries.

### Severity and Level Semantics

ILAIOS may implement a standard level set such as Trace, Debug, Informational, Warning, Error, and Fatal, provided every level has stable semantics and mapping rules.

**Trace** records highly detailed execution diagnostics for narrowly controlled and time-bounded use.

**Debug** records diagnostic context useful for engineering investigation but unsuitable for permanent broad enablement in many production contexts.

**Informational** records expected material lifecycle or state events that support normal operations.

**Warning** records an abnormal or degraded condition that did not yet cause the defined operation to fail but requires awareness or treatment.

**Error** records failure of a defined operation or control path that requires investigation, retry, rejection, or recovery.

**Fatal** records an unrecoverable condition that causes the emitting process or critical service boundary to terminate or become unavailable. It shall not be used merely to increase alert urgency.

Severity shall describe the emitted event, not automatically determine alert severity, incident severity, defect priority, customer communication, or regulatory significance. Monitoring rules may derive operational conditions from records under Section 7.9.

Routine denials produced by correct policy enforcement are not necessarily errors. A denial may be informational, warning, or security-relevant depending on context, frequency, source, and risk. Conversely, a nominally successful operation that bypassed a required control is a critical security event.

Dynamic level changes require authorization, exact scope, start time, expiry, purpose, owner, rollback, and monitoring. Production Trace or Debug shall expire automatically where feasible. It shall not be used to capture prohibited data.

### Time, Ordering, and Clock Integrity

Emitters shall use synchronized time sources appropriate to the Deployment Profile. Timestamp precision and source shall be documented.

Records shall distinguish event time from collection or ingestion time. A late-arriving event shall retain its original event time and an observable arrival delay.

Distributed systems do not guarantee total order merely because timestamps exist. Clock skew, batching, buffering, retries, offline operation, region boundaries, provider queues, and restoration can reorder records. Investigations shall use correlation, sequence numbers, causal references, and source state where available.

Components on a material control path should emit bounded sequence or transition references when order matters. A sequence gap shall be detectable and shall not be silently closed by downstream sorting.

Clock synchronization failure, excessive skew, timestamp regression, unknown timezone, invalid timestamp, and timestamp precision loss shall be monitored and logged. Systems shall use a standard unambiguous time representation and preserve source offset only where needed.

Time corrections shall not rewrite historical records silently. Any normalization or correction applied downstream shall preserve the original value and transformation metadata.

### Correlation and Causality

Correlation identifiers shall connect the canonical operational flow from request intake through identity, tenant binding, context creation, recommendation, policy, risk, approval, capability issuance, Tool Gateway execution, validation, acceptance or rejection, delivery, closure, audit, and evidence.

Correlation shall be scoped to prevent cross-tenant discovery. Identifiers exposed to customers, providers, or untrusted clients shall not reveal internal topology, sequence, volume, account data, or reusable authority.

Trace, request, task, action, approval, capability, validation, audit, and evidence references remain semantically distinct even when included in the same record. A correlation reference is not the referenced canonical object.

Propagation shall be allowlisted across trust boundaries. Untrusted callers shall not be permitted to forge internal source identity, privileged actor identity, approval identity, policy result, audit identity, or evidence reference through arbitrary headers or payload fields.

Where an external provider supplies a request identifier, ILAIOS shall preserve it as provider-scoped metadata and bind it to an internally generated reference. It shall not replace internal identity.

### Error and Exception Logging

Errors shall be recorded with stable failure class, reason code, affected operation, bounded context, retryability, external-effect state, and correlation references. Human-readable messages should state the condition without exposing protected data.

Stack traces, query fragments, provider messages, serialized objects, environment variables, paths, and command output can contain secrets or customer information. They shall be filtered, truncated, classified, and access-controlled before leaving the trusted diagnostic boundary.

An exception handler shall not log the same failure repeatedly at every layer without added semantic value. The profile shall define the accountable recording boundary and preserve causal relationships without creating unbounded duplication.

Catch-and-ignore behavior shall not conceal a material error. If a failure is intentionally suppressed, the system shall record the governing reason, bounded impact, and responsible control where required.

Tool Gateway records shall distinguish not dispatched, dispatched, acknowledged, partially completed, completed, rejected, timed out, and outcome unknown. A transport timeout after dispatch shall not be logged as a definite execution failure when an external effect may have occurred.

Validation rejection shall remain distinct from technical execution failure. Model refusal, provider failure, policy denial, approval denial, capability expiry, tool failure, validation rejection, and delivery failure shall have different Event Codes.

### Safe Message Construction and Log-Injection Protection

Untrusted values shall be recorded as typed fields rather than concatenated into free-form messages where practical.

Emitters and collectors shall neutralize or encode newline characters, terminal control sequences, field delimiters, markup, escape sequences, bidirectional text controls, forged prefixes, and other content that can create false records or mislead operators.

Structured encoders shall escape values according to the selected format. String interpolation shall not change field boundaries. Raw values shall not be interpreted as a logging template or query fragment.

Record-size limits shall be enforced before transport and storage exhaustion. Oversized values shall be omitted, truncated, tokenized, or stored through an approved protected artifact mechanism. The record shall state that truncation occurred and shall not silently present partial content as complete.

Log viewers and export tools shall render untrusted content safely. They shall not execute scripts, resolve active links automatically, load remote content, interpret terminal sequences, or expose hidden fields without authorization.

Injection-resistance tests shall cover structured and legacy text sources, multiline messages, Unicode edge cases, control characters, malicious filenames, provider error payloads, customer-supplied identifiers, and model-generated text.

### Secrets, Credentials, and Cryptographic Material

Secrets shall never be logged by design. This prohibition includes passwords, access tokens, refresh tokens, session secrets, private keys, seed material, signing material, recovery codes, secret environment variables, database credentials, connection-string secrets, webhook secrets, authorization headers, cookies, and capability bearer values.

Key identifiers, secret-version identifiers, cryptographic operation classes, and custody boundaries may be logged only when required and shall not reveal material or enable unauthorized lookup.

Redaction shall occur as close to the emitter as practical. Collector-side filtering is defense in depth, not permission for applications to emit secrets.

Allowlisted field emission is preferred to pattern-only redaction. Pattern matching can miss novel formats and may over-redact benign values. Known secret formats shall also be detected in pipelines, tests, and protected scans.

Hashing a low-entropy secret or personal identifier may permit recovery through enumeration and is not automatically safe anonymization. Tokenization, keyed pseudonymization, truncation, or exclusion shall be selected through approved data-protection review.

If secret exposure is detected, the affected credential shall be treated as compromised according to Section 3.4, access shall be contained, copies and indexes shall be identified, rotation or revocation shall occur, and incident and evidence procedures shall be followed. Editing a displayed message alone is insufficient remediation.

### Personal Data, Customer Content, and Data Minimization

Logging shall collect only data necessary for an approved purpose. Diagnostic convenience does not justify indefinite or broad capture.

Personal data, confidential customer data, regulated data, proprietary source code, document contents, raw prompts, raw model outputs, repository content, tool payloads, and file bodies are excluded by default.

Where a narrowly defined purpose requires protected content, the Logging Profile shall document necessity, lawful basis or contractual authority where applicable, controller and processor roles, tenant scope, fields, redaction, access, location, retention, deletion, support procedure, and validation.

Production logging shall prefer opaque bounded identifiers, reason codes, counts, classifications, sizes, hashes where safe, and references to protected canonical objects over raw content.

Customer-configured verbosity shall not override ILAIOS's non-waivable privacy, security, tenant-isolation, secret, legal, safety, audit, or evidence controls. A contractual request to log additional content is binding only within lawful and formally approved scope.

Data-subject rights, customer deletion obligations, legal holds, and regulatory restrictions shall be applied according to the applicable role and record class. Log architecture shall support identification and controlled treatment of protected records without requiring unrestricted search by personal value.

### Tenant Isolation

Every tenant-scoped record shall carry a validated tenant reference derived from trusted context. Tenant identity shall not be accepted from an unverified user-controlled logging field.

Tenant isolation applies to emission, buffering, queues, collectors, transformations, indexes, caches, search, dashboards, alerts, exports, archives, backups, support tools, incident workspaces, and deletion.

Cross-tenant aggregations may be used only for approved platform operations and shall prevent exposure of tenant-specific values. Global operational views shall use minimized dimensions and controlled drill-down.

Authorization shall be enforced at the query and export boundary, not only in the user interface. A customer shall not infer another tenant's existence, volume, identifiers, failures, topology, provider selection, or security events through error messages, timing, cardinality, autocomplete, or aggregate results.

Shared collectors and sinks require verified logical isolation and resource controls. Higher-assurance profiles may require physically or cryptographically separated routes, accounts, keys, indexes, or storage.

Tenant reassignment, migration, merge, split, deletion, or restoration shall preserve correct record ownership and shall not create orphaned or cross-bound records.

### Identity, Authorization, and Administrative Events

Authentication logs shall record bounded attempt identity, method class, assurance context, outcome, reason code, source context, risk signal, session transition, and correlation without recording credentials.

Authorization logs shall distinguish policy evaluation, authorization decision, capability issuance, capability use, and resource enforcement. A downstream service shall not infer permission solely from the presence of an authorization log.

Privileged administration, role changes, organization ownership, recovery configuration, access-policy changes, break-glass activation, log access, search, export, retention change, legal hold, deletion, redaction override, routing change, and logging disablement shall be recorded canonically through the appropriate audit path and operationally where necessary.

Repeated authentication failures, token misuse, impossible travel, privilege escalation attempts, unauthorized query attempts, tenant-boundary violations, clock manipulation, logging disablement, schema bypass, and record deletion attempts shall be available to security monitoring according to risk.

Source network information and device context are protected data and shall be collected only as required. They are signals, not identity proof.

### Policy, Approval, and Capability Logging

Policy records shall identify the deterministic Policy Engine, policy bundle and version, evaluation correlation, decision class, reason code, input classification, and failure mode without exposing protected input values unnecessarily.

Model output, recommendation confidence, provider response, or free-form text shall not be recorded as a policy decision or allowed to overwrite a deterministic decision field.

Approval records shall identify the approval request, accountable approver reference, scope, decision, constraints, expiry, withdrawal, and correlation. Ordinary application logs may reference the approval but shall not substitute for the canonical Approval Engine record.

Capability logs shall record issuance, scope class, target, expiry, use, revocation, and rejection without recording reusable bearer material. Possession of a log reference shall confer no capability.

Policy denial, approval denial, capability absence, capability expiry, and global deny shall remain distinct. Global deny rules cannot be overridden through logging configuration, customer preference, provider behavior, or diagnostic mode.

### Intelligence and Model-Access Logging

The AI Reasoning and Recommendation Engine and Model Orchestration and Provider Abstraction components shall emit bounded lifecycle and operational records without becoming authority.

Records may include model profile, provider route, deployment or model-version reference, invocation state, latency, bounded token or resource usage, safety-control outcome, fallback, timeout, refusal, error class, and correlation where approved.

Raw prompts, raw outputs, hidden reasoning, retrieved documents, context bodies, embeddings, repository content, customer files, and provider payloads shall not be logged by default.

Approved diagnostic capture of model input or output requires exact purpose, environment, tenant, consent or legal basis where applicable, access, encryption, redaction, retention, deletion, and independent review. Capture shall be time-bounded and shall not be enabled platform-wide merely for convenience.

Model-generated text is untrusted content. It shall be protected against log injection, oversized-record attacks, sensitive-data propagation, and misleading control labels.

Provider usage records shall distinguish ILAIOS observation from provider-reported values. Provider billing or safety metadata may be reconciled but shall not automatically become authoritative evidence of task success, policy compliance, or customer charge.

### Tool Gateway and External-Effect Logging

Every governed external action shall remain mediated by the Tool Gateway under a time-bound and constrained capability.

Tool logging shall record request reference, capability reference, tenant, tool profile, target class, operation class, dispatch state, external request reference, response class, retry state, idempotency treatment, validation reference, and final known external-effect state.

Sensitive arguments and results shall be excluded or represented through protected references. Command text, credentials, file contents, message bodies, recipient data, and provider payloads shall not be copied into general logs by default.

The Tool Gateway shall distinguish pre-dispatch rejection from post-dispatch uncertainty. If a response is lost after an external system may have acted, the record shall state outcome unknown until reconciliation or independent validation resolves the state.

Retries shall preserve causality and idempotency information. A retry shall not be logged as a new independent business authorization.

Logging failures shall not create an alternative path around the Tool Gateway. Where a required operational record cannot be emitted, the gateway shall follow its approved fail-safe or constrained behavior according to risk, while canonical audit and evidence requirements retain their own independent failure semantics.

### Validation, Audit, and Evidence Integration

The Validation Pipeline shall verify logging controls independently of the emitting application where material. It may test schema conformance, field accuracy, event coverage, ordering limits, redaction, injection resistance, routing, loss detection, tenant isolation, retention, access, export, deletion, integrity, failover, and restoration.

An application assertion that a record was written is not sufficient validation. Tests shall observe the required sink or canonical receipt boundary and shall examine failure paths.

The Audit Engine shall record material governance and security events related to logging, including profile approval, privileged access, export, retention change, legal hold, deletion, route change, disablement, redaction exception, break-glass use, integrity failure, and coverage gap treatment.

The Evidence Chain may bind selected log artifacts, manifests, query results, exports, hashes, signatures, validation outcomes, or custody events when required. Evidence binding shall preserve source, time, scope, transformation, access, and limitations.

An ordinary log store shall not be described as the Evidence Chain. A hash chain over collected records may improve tamper evidence but does not prove that missing events were emitted, that timestamps are correct, or that the source was trustworthy.

Audit and evidence pipelines shall not depend solely on the same failure domain, mutable index, credentials, administrator, or retention policy as ordinary operational logging where the applicable assurance profile requires independence.

### Collection Architecture

Collection may occur through in-process appenders, sidecar collectors, host collectors, platform services, network receivers, provider exports, or controlled batch transfer. The selected pattern shall match isolation, reliability, performance, and operational constraints.

Emitters should write through non-blocking bounded interfaces for ordinary diagnostic records. Critical paths shall define whether logging failure causes local buffering, degraded operation, rejection, or continued execution.

Mandatory audit or evidence failure behavior is governed by the Audit and Evidence architectures and shall not be weakened by an ordinary asynchronous logging policy.

Collectors shall authenticate sources where feasible, authorize accepted tenants and event classes, enforce schema and size limits, apply safe normalization, detect malformed records, and expose their own health.

Collector enrichment shall use trusted platform metadata and shall not overwrite emitter fields silently. Original and enriched values shall remain distinguishable when both are material.
